Use the first-order language of [[def-language-of-set-theory]]: all quantified objects are sets, and a **definable class** $\{x:\varphi(x,p)\}$ abbreviates a formula with set parameters $p$. It is not a new set or a domain for unrestricted quantification. Work with the usual set axioms, in particular [[def-axiom-of-power-set]] and [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], and the ordered pairs, products and functions of [[def-ordered-pair]], [[def-cartesian-product]] and [[def-function]]. The power-set axiom supplies a collecting set; Separation trims it to exactly $\mathcal P(X)=\{Y:Y\subseteq X\}$.

A **small category** has a set $O$ of objects, a set $A$ of arrows, source and target functions $s,t:A\to O$, an identity function $e:O\to A$, and a composition function on the set $\{(a,b)\in A\times A:s(a)=t(b)\}$, where $ab$ denotes $a\circ b$ and the laws are $s(e(x))=t(e(x))=x$, $s(ab)=s(b)$, $t(ab)=t(a)$, $e(t(a))a=a=ae(s(a))$, and $(ab)c=a(bc)$ whenever the displayed compositions are defined. It is **locally small** when each specified hom-collection is a set. A definable large category is a schema of formulas for its objects, arrows and operations, with those laws asserted as formulas; it is not a set of all objects or a category of all large categories. No Grothendieck universe is assumed.

All indexed families in the local bundle construction have a supplied set index $I$. If $U_i\subseteq M$ and $G$ is a set, their tagged disjoint union is the subset $D=\{(i,x,z)\in I\times M\times G:x\in U_i\}$, formed by Separation. Given a set equivalence relation $E\subseteq D\times D$, each class $[u]_E=\{v\in D:(u,v)\in E\}$ is a subset of $D$, and the quotient is the set

$$
D/E=\{C\in\mathcal P(D):\exists u\in D\ \forall v\in D\ (v\in C\iff(u,v)\in E)\}.
$$

Thus the quotient is obtained by Separation in $\mathcal P(D)$, without choosing representatives. Transition-map graphs and connection data are subsets of specified finite products and power sets, not arbitrary proper-class objects.

For the Cauchy-development coding application, fix a set manifold $\Sigma$ and the tensor-bundle total spaces over $\Sigma\times\mathbb R$. A code consists of an open set $D\subseteq\Sigma\times\mathbb R$, graphs of a metric and a two-form on $D$ inside those fixed total spaces, a time orientation, and a fixed initial embedding. All of its coordinates belong to fixed products and power sets. Separation selects the tuples satisfying the specified smoothness, Lorentzian, field-equation and initial-data formulas. Hence these codes form a set. This size assertion does not prove field-equation existence, maximality or uniqueness, and makes no proper-class representative choice.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

By [[def-de-rham-cohomology]], $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^2(M)/B^2(M)$, where $Z^2(M)$ is the vector space of closed smooth two-forms and $B^2(M)$ is the vector space of exact smooth two-forms. Thus, for closed $F$, the statement $[F]=0$ means exactly that $F=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$. This equivalence is the quotient definition; it does not assert that every closed form is exact.

Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$ by $z=x+iy$ and set $U(1)=S^1:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. Its topology is the subspace topology. Specify its smooth structure by the four charts

$$V_{x,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon x>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto y,\quad y\mapsto(\epsilon\sqrt{1-y^2},y),$$

and

$$V_{y,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon y>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto x,\quad x\mapsto(x,\epsilon\sqrt{1-x^2}),$$

for $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, with each coordinate range $(-1,1)$. They cover $S^1$; their transition maps are restrictions of the positive square-root branch and coordinate projections, hence are smooth by [[lem-emg-positive-square-root-smoothness]] and [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]. In these coordinates multiplication is the restriction of $(x,y)(u,v)=(xu-yv,xv+yu)$ and inversion is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so both are smooth; they are also continuous for the stated topology. Thus this is a smooth Lie group and, in particular, a topological group as required by [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Let $E:\mathbb R\to U(1)$ be $E(t)=e^{it}=(\cos t,\sin t)$; the Cartesian formula is [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The trigonometric derivative identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], iterated, show that $E$ is smooth in the $C^\infty$ sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: every derivative of either coordinate is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, and these functions are continuous by [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]. Surjectivity is [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]. If $E(t)\in V_{x,\epsilon}$, the chart coordinate $\sin t$ has derivative $\cos t=x\ne0$; if $E(t)\in V_{y,\epsilon}$, the coordinate $\cos t$ has derivative $-\sin t=-y\ne0$. The smooth inverse-function theorem [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]] therefore makes $E$ a diffeomorphism from some open interval about $t$ onto an open circle arc. Every smooth map from an open subset of $M$ to $U(1)$ consequently has, near each point, a smooth real phase lift obtained by composing with such a local inverse.

A **normalized circle-connection datum** on $M$ consists of a supplied countable open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, smooth transition maps $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U(1)$, smooth real one-forms $a_i\in\Omega^1(U_i)$, and a fixed constant $\kappa_0>0$. Require $g_{ii}=1$ and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on every triple intersection. Around each point of $U_i\cap U_j$, take any smooth real phase lift $f_{ij}$ with $g_{ij}=e^{if_{ij}}$; require

$$
a_j=a_i+df_{ij}
$$

on every such phase-lift neighborhood. If $f$ and $\widetilde f$ are two lifts on a connected neighborhood, [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]] gives $f-\widetilde f\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ pointwise; continuity makes this difference constant, so $df=d\widetilde f$. Thus the compatibility condition is independent of the chosen lift. The globally defined form $\lambda(g):=-i\,g^{-1}dg$ is real, and [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] together with [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] gives $\lambda(g)=df$ on every phase-lift neighborhood. Hence the equivalent lift-free condition is $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$.

The right principal $U(1)$-bundle convention is as defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]: it has a continuous right action and locally trivial equivariant product charts, with free and transitive action on each fibre. The compatible transition functions are the gluing data for such a bundle, in the convention that a point with fibre coordinate $z_i$ in chart $i$ has coordinate $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$ in chart $j$. No global real-valued angle on $U(1)$ is assumed.

The constant $\kappa_0$ is a chosen normalization with units of webers; it is not Planck's constant and is not a unit of electric charge. On a chart whose coordinates have length units, the normalized connection components $a_i$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding local potential $A_i:=\kappa_0a_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and its curvature $F_i:=dA_i=\kappa_0\,da_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. This definition imposes no flux or charge quantization.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $n\geq1$, let $M^n$ be oriented, and let $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$. For $1\leq i\leq m$ let $D_i\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded open Jordan domains and $F_i:\overline D_i\to M$ continuous and smooth up to the boundary in target coordinates: near each parameter point, a target coordinate representative extends smoothly to a Euclidean neighborhood. Suppose $F_i|_{D_i}$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto an open $W_i\subset M$, the $W_i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $\operatorname{supp}\omega\subset\bigcup_i\overline W_i$. Then
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_{D_i}F_i^*\omega.$$
An empty family is allowed when the support is empty. No nonsingularity of $DF_i$ on $\partial D_i$, and no $M$-valued extension across a genuine target boundary, is assumed.

Work with the usual set axioms, in particular [[def-axiom-of-power-set]] and [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], and the ordered pairs, products and functions of [[def-ordered-pair]], [[def-cartesian-product]] and [[def-function]]. The power-set axiom supplies a collecting set; Separation trims it to exactly $\mathcal P(X)=\{Y:Y\subseteq X\}$.

A **small category** has a set $O$ of objects, a set $A$ of arrows, source and target functions $s,t:A\to O$, an identity function $e:O\to A$, and a composition function on the set $\{(a,b)\in A\times A:s(a)=t(b)\}$, where $ab$ denotes $a\circ b$ and the laws are $s(e(x))=t(e(x))=x$, $s(ab)=s(b)$, $t(ab)=t(a)$, $e(t(a))a=a=ae(s(a))$, and $(ab)c=a(bc)$ whenever the displayed compositions are defined. It is **locally small** when each specified hom-collection is a set. A definable large category is a schema of formulas for its objects, arrows and operations, with those laws asserted as formulas; it is not a set of all objects or a category of all large categories. No Grothendieck universe is assumed.

All indexed families in the local bundle construction have a supplied set index $I$. If $U_i\subseteq M$ and $G$ is a set, their tagged disjoint union is the subset $D=\{(i,x,z)\in I\times M\times G:x\in U_i\}$, formed by Separation. Given a set equivalence relation $E\subseteq D\times D$, each class $[u]_E=\{v\in D:(u,v)\in E\}$ is a subset of $D$, and the quotient is the set

$$
D/E=\{C\in\mathcal P(D):\exists u\in D\ \forall v\in D\ (v\in C\iff(u,v)\in E)\}.
$$

Thus the quotient is obtained by Separation in $\mathcal P(D)$, without choosing representatives. Transition-map graphs and connection data are subsets of specified finite products and power sets, not arbitrary proper-class objects.

For the Cauchy-development coding application, fix a set manifold $\Sigma$ and the tensor-bundle total spaces over $\Sigma\times\mathbb R$. A code consists of an open set $D\subseteq\Sigma\times\mathbb R$, graphs of a metric and a two-form on $D$ inside those fixed total spaces, a time orientation, and a fixed initial embedding. All of its coordinates belong to fixed products and power sets. Separation selects the tuples satisfying the specified smoothness, Lorentzian, field-equation and initial-data formulas. Hence these codes form a set. This size assertion does not prove field-equation existence, maximality or uniqueness, and makes no proper-class representative choice.

For $a>0$, integer $m$ and integer $n\ge1$, define the rational regime by

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. For the rational-exponent regime at base zero, retain the convention of [[def-rational-power]] and [[def-integer-power]]: $0^0=1$, $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$, and $0^r$ is undefined for rational $r<0$. This records the integer zero-exponent convention together with the positive-rational supplementary clause; it does not extend the real-exponent convention.

The separate real-exponent regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For real exponents at base zero, set $0^x=0$ only when $x>0$; $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are undefined, exactly as in [[def-real-power]]. The rational and real exponent operations are separate definitions; at zero base and exponent zero, state which regime is intended: the rational/integer convention gives $1$, while the real-power convention leaves the expression undefined. No arbitrary real power is assigned to a negative base. The real-power laws are supplied by that theorem, not inferred from the rational root formula. Use the real-number structure of [[def-real-numbers]].

In particular $s(q)=q^{1/2}$ for $q>0$ is the unique positive solution of $s(q)^2=q$. Its smoothness and derivative are a separate well-definedness result, not an assumption about fractional notation.

Let $M$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable oriented four-manifold, and let $(U_i,g_{ij},a_i;\kappa_0)$ be a normalized circle-connection datum as in [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]]. Use the set-sized-object and quotient convention of [[def-emg-set-size-and-class-schema]]. Then the chart data construct a smooth Hausdorff second-countable right principal $U(1)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and a global smooth real connection one-form $\omega$ on $P$. Its curvature is basic: there is a smooth closed two-form $f\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $d\omega=\pi^*f$ and $f|_{U_i}=da_i$. The local potentials $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ satisfy $dA_i=F$, where $F=\kappa_0 f$ is global. For two connections on the same fixed bundle with the same transition functions, their local-form differences are restrictions of one global base one-form; adding a global one-form to all local representatives stays in that bundle sector.

derivations.claim: Put $Q=x^2+y^2+z^2$. At every point with $Q>0$, [F5] gives a positive root $r_0$ of $s^2=Q$; the map $s\mapsto s^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ has derivative $2r_0\ne0$, so [F6] gives a smooth local inverse near $Q$, which agrees with the unique positive root by [F5]. Composing this local inverse with the smooth function $Q$ proves that $r=\sqrt Q$ is smooth near each point of the punctured space. Thus the Cartesian coefficients of $F_b$ are smooth. On the dense open set $x^2+y^2>0$, write $x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy=\iota_{x\partial_x+y\partial_y+z\partial_z}(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)$. The spherical-coordinate volume form is $r^2\sin\theta\,dr\wedge d\theta\wedge d\phi$, and the radial vector is $r\partial_r$, so contraction gives $r^3\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Hence $F_b=b\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$ and $dF_b=b\cos\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\theta\wedge d\phi=0$. Since $dF_b$ is continuous by [F4], it vanishes on the closure, which is the whole punctured space. Pulling back to the outward unit sphere and integrating gives $\int_{S^2}F_b=b\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi b$.

Let $\vartheta=-i z^{-1}dz$ be the invariant one-form on the fibre circle and let $
u=-i w^{-1}dw$ be the base angular form in the statement. In a local angle $z=e^{i	heta}$, $\vartheta=d	heta$, so it evaluates to $1$ on the vertical generator; it is right invariant, as is $\pi^*
u$. Thus $\omega=\vartheta+a\pi^*
u$ on the trivial bundle is a principal connection: for each base tangent vector $X$, the unique vertical component $-a
u(X)\partial_	heta$ makes $\omega$ vanish, so its kernel is a horizontal complement. Since the base circle has dimension one, $d
u$ is a two-form on a one-dimensional manifold and is zero by [F4]. Along $w=e^{i\phi}$, the explicit fibre curve $z(\phi)=z_0e^{-ia\phi}$ has $\dot	heta+a\dot\phi=0$, so it is horizontal and ends at $z_0e^{-2\pi ia}$. Hence the holonomy is $e^{-2\pi ia}$, and $F=dA=\kappa_0a\,d
u=0$.

Suppose $F_b=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$ on $M$. Choose a nondegenerate convex tetrahedron $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the origin in its interior and with positively oriented ordered vertices $v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3$. For each face $j$, let $\sigma_j$ be its affine parametrization by the standard $2$-simplex with increasing remaining-vertex order and boundary coefficient $(-1)^j$. No face contains the origin, so the radial map $R(x)=x/|x|$ is smooth on a neighborhood of every face and $R\circ\sigma_j$ is a smooth singular simplex. Shared edge restrictions are the same ordered affine edge maps with opposite boundary signs; hence $c=\sum_{j=0}^3(-1)^jR\circ\sigma_j$ is a finite smooth singular cycle.
For each outward face, write its plane as $n_j\cdot x=h_j$ with outward unit normal $n_j$ and $h_j>0$. Convexity and $0\in\operatorname{int}T$ imply every ray from the origin meets $\partial T$ exactly once. Thus $R:\partial T\to S^2$ is a homeomorphism; on each face interior it is a smooth diffeomorphism onto the corresponding open spherical patch, with inverse $u\mapsto h_j u/(n_j\cdot u)$. These four patches are disjoint and their closures cover $S^2$, with overlaps only along the finitely many projected edges. If $v,w$ are tangent vectors to a face and oriented by its outward boundary orientation, the outward unit-sphere area form $\omega_u(a,b):=\det(u,a,b)$ satisfies
$$
(R^*\omega)_{x}(v,w)=\frac{\det(x,v,w)}{|x|^3}=\frac{h_j\det(n_j,v,w)}{|x|^3}>0.
$$
The radial projection therefore preserves the face orientation. Every point away from the projected edges has exactly one preimage, with positive local orientation, so its signed preimage count (the degree in this piecewise-smooth setting) is $+1$. For each odd $j$, precompose $\sigma_j$ with the affine transposition $\rho(u_1,u_2)=(u_2,u_1)$ of the standard triangle, and for each even $j$ leave it unchanged; call the resulting parametrizations $\widetilde\sigma_j$. By the orientation convention in [[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]], $\int_{\widetilde\sigma_j}F_b=(-1)^j\int_{\sigma_j}F_b$, and each $R\circ\widetilde\sigma_j$ is orientation-preserving onto its face image. Their domains are bounded open Jordan triangles; they extend smoothly to their closures, and the whole sphere is covered by the closures of the four images. Applying [F15] to $F_b|_{S^2}$ gives the exact reparameterization identity $\int_cF_b=\sum_j\int_{\widetilde\sigma_j}F_b=\int_{S^2}F_b=4\pi b$; the projected edges have zero two-dimensional content and contribute no integral. By Stokes [F2], $\int_cF_b=\int_c dA=\int_{\partial c}A=0$, contradicting $4\pi b\ne0$. Thus no global potential exists when $b\ne0$.

Since $r\ge |z|$ and $(r+z)+(r-z)=2r>0$, at least one of $r+z,r-z$ is positive, so $U_N,U_S$ cover $M$. On the north patch, $(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/(r(r+z))$; the denominator is nonzero there, so $A_N$ extends smoothly across the north axis. On the south patch, $(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/(r(r-z))$; the denominator is nonzero there, so $A_S$ extends smoothly across the south axis. Differentiating on the dense overlap gives $dA_N=dA_S=b\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi=F_b$. Both sides are smooth, so the identities extend by continuity to the respective full patches. Subtraction gives $A_S-A_N=-2b\,d\phi$ on the overlap.

Let $u:M_0\to U(1)$ be any smooth gauge map and restrict it to $\gamma(\phi)=(x^0_*,e^{i\phi},y_*,z_*)$, with the other base coordinates fixed; write $v(\phi)=u(\gamma(\phi))$. The chain rule [F10] and smooth group inversion [F3] make $v$ and $v^{-1}$ smooth. Since $|v|=1$, differentiating $\bar v v=1$ gives $\overline{v^{-1}v'}+v^{-1}v'=0$, so $q(\phi):=-i v^{-1}v'$ is real and smooth. It is continuous on $[0,2\pi]$, hence integrable by [F7]. By [F12] and [F13], choose $\chi_0\in[0,2\pi)$ with $e^{i\chi_0}=v(0)$, and set $\chi(\phi)=\chi_0+\int_0^\phi q(s)\,ds$; [F8] gives $\chi'=q$. By [F10] and [F14], $h=e^{i\chi}$ satisfies $h'=iqh$, while the definition of $q$ gives $v'=iqv$. Thus $(vh^{-1})'=0$; applying [F9] to its real and imaginary parts, whose zero derivatives are integrable by [F7], yields $vh^{-1}=v(0)h(0)^{-1}=1$, so $v=e^{i\chi}$ on the full interval. Any other smooth phase lift $\widetilde\chi$ of $v$ has the same derivative as $\chi$ by [F10] and [F14]; applying [F9] to $\widetilde\chi-\chi$ shows the difference is constant. Since $v(2\pi)=v(0)$, $e^{i(\chi(2\pi)-\chi(0))}=1$, and [F11] gives $\chi(2\pi)-\chi(0)=2\pi n$ for some integer $n$, independently of the phase lift. Since this argument uses only a smooth circle-valued loop and its equal endpoint values, it proves the same phase-lift and winding claims for every smooth $g:S^1\to U(1)$. Hence $\int_\gamma(-iu^{-1}du)=2\pi n$.

Put $a_N=A_N/\kappa_0$ and $a_S=A_S/\kappa_0$. By [F3], the required transition convention is $a_S=a_N+df_{NS}$ with $g_{NS}=e^{if_{NS}}$. Here $f_{NS}=-2b\phi/\kappa_0$, so $g_{NS}=e^{-2ib\phi/\kappa_0}$. Replacing $\phi$ by $\phi+2\pi$ leaves this map unchanged exactly when $e^{-4\pi ib/\kappa_0}=1$, equivalently $n:=2b/\kappa_0\in\mathbb Z$. For this two-set cover set $g_{NN}=g_{SS}=1$ and $g_{SN}=g_{NS}^{-1}$; these maps obey the cocycle, and $a_N=a_S+\lambda(g_{SN})$ follows from $\lambda(g_{SN})=-\lambda(g_{NS})$, so both overlap directions satisfy [F3]. The degree of the smooth map $\phi\mapsto e^{-in\phi}$ is $-n$, while the flux quotient in step 1.1 is $n$. Under the set-size interface [A1], the conditional construction statement [L1] applies to these compatible countable-cover data and supplies the selected circle-bundle connection.

On any local angle arc $u=e^{i\psi}$, the gauge map sends $(x,e^{i\theta})$ to $(x,e^{i(\theta+\psi(x))})$, so [F10] and [F14] give $G_u^*\vartheta=\vartheta+d\psi=\vartheta-iu^{-1}du$. Its pullback adds $-iu^{-1}du$ to the base form of $\omega=\vartheta+a\pi^*\nu$, whose loop period is $2\pi(a+n)$ by step 2.3; consequently the holonomy remains $e^{-2\pi ia}$.

If $a
otin\mathbb Z$, [F11] makes $e^{-2\pi ia}
e1$, so no gauge can make the connection trivial. If $a\in\mathbb Z$, the global map $u(x)=w^{-a}$ is smooth by [F3] because it is an integer power in the smooth circle group; on a local parameter $w=e^{i\phi}$, [F10] and [F14] give $-iu^{-1}du=-a\,d\phi=-a
u$, cancelling the base form. Therefore gauge triviality is equivalent to $a\in\mathbb Z$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement fixes M=R times (R3 minus {0}) and the unit sphere, both nonempty explicit domains. Proof step 1.1 works only at Q=x^2+y^2+z^2>0; it never attempts to choose a point from an empty sphere.

Proof step 1.1 gives flux 4pi*b=0 at b=0, and step 3.1 then has constant transition 1. In the separate flat example step 1.2 gives holonomy1 at a=0, while step 4.1 supplies the identity trivializing gauge.
Proof step 3.1 gives transition exp(-i*phi) and winding -1 when 2b/kappa0=1. In the flat example step 4.1 gives the smooth single-valued gauge w^(-1) for a=1.

Proof step 2.2 writes the north and south potentials with denominators r(r+z) and r(r-z), nonzero on their named patches, so each extends over its own polar axis. Proof step 1.1 excludes the actual singular origin r=0.

Proof step 2.3 integrates the smooth real angular derivative on [0,2pi], matches the original loop from its chosen initial phase, and uses equality of endpoint images to obtain a phase difference in 2pi*Z. Step 2.2 separately checks the patch-axis coordinate degeneracy.

Proof step 2.3 fixes one initial phase for one loop, then defines all other phases by an explicit integral. The finite tetrahedron in step 2.1 is a single supplied construction; neither proof chooses a countable family of phases or representatives.
Proof step 3.1 uses single-valuedness after phi->phi+2pi to force 2b/kappa0 integral. Steps 3.2 and 4.1 show gauge invariance of the loop period and rule out gauge triviality for noninteger a.

Proof step 3.1 constructs the smooth transition exp(-i*n*phi) and cocycle for integer n=2b/kappa0. Proof step 4.1 constructs the global smooth gauge w^(-a) when a is integral, proving the reverse gauge-triviality direction.

Use the real ordered field of [[def-real-numbers]] and [[def-complete-ordered-field]]. For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ bounded above, $\sup S$ denotes the unique real upper bound $u$ such that $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$. Existence is the least-upper-bound property established for these reals by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]; if $u,u'$ both satisfy it, $u\le u'$ and $u'\le u$ imply equality. The notation is restricted to this domain.

For nonempty $S$ bounded below, use [[def-infimum]] and [[thm-infimum-property]]: $\inf S=-\sup(-S)$, where $-S=\{-s:s\in S\}$. Indeed a lower bound $l$ for $S$ gives the upper bound $-l$ for $-S$; negating its least upper bound gives a lower bound for $S$ greater than every other one.

Neither $\sup\varnothing$ nor $\inf\varnothing$ is defined in $\mathbb R$: every real is an upper and lower bound, with no least upper or greatest lower bound. If another construction stipulates the value zero for an empty path family, that stipulation is a separate total definition, not $\sup\varnothing=0$. Infinite values require an explicitly specified extended ordered set; no extended-real field operations are introduced here.

Let $X$ be a set and use the ordered real field of [[def-real-numbers]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and [[def-ordered-field]]. In the convention of [[def-metric-space]], a **real metric** is a function $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying, for all $x,y,z\in X$, separation $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$, symmetry $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ and the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. A **real pseudometric** replaces separation by $d(x,x)=0$ and retains the other two axioms. All values are finite real numbers. Neither definition assumes nonnegativity as an additional axiom.

For either structure, put $B_d(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$ for real $r>0$. The induced topology consists of the subsets $O\subseteq X$ for which every $x\in O$ admits $r>0$ with $B_d(x,r)\subseteq O$. After the nonnegativity deduction in the well-definedness lemma, these balls form a basis: $x\in B_d(x,r)$ by reflexivity, and if $z\in B_d(x,r)\cap B_d(y,s)$, the positive radius $t=\min\{r-d(x,z),s-d(y,z)\}$ has $B_d(z,t)$ contained in that intersection by the triangle inequality. This argument also works for pseudometrics and for empty $X$ (the empty topology). No infinite-distance, semimetric or quasimetric convention is consumed.

Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.

Given a set equivalence relation $E\subseteq D\times D$, each class $[u]_E=\{v\in D:(u,v)\in E\}$ is a subset of $D$, and the quotient is the set

$$
D/E=\{C\in\mathcal P(D):\exists u\in D\ \forall v\in D\ (v\in C\iff(u,v)\in E)\}.
$$

Thus the quotient is obtained by Separation in $\mathcal P(D)$, without choosing representatives. Transition-map graphs and connection data are subsets of specified finite products and power sets, not arbitrary proper-class objects.

For the Cauchy-development coding application, fix a set manifold $\Sigma$ and the tensor-bundle total spaces over $\Sigma\times\mathbb R$. A code consists of an open set $D\subseteq\Sigma\times\mathbb R$, graphs of a metric and a two-form on $D$ inside those fixed total spaces, a time orientation, and a fixed initial embedding. All of its coordinates belong to fixed products and power sets. Separation selects the tuples satisfying the specified smoothness, Lorentzian, field-equation and initial-data formulas. Hence these codes form a set. This size assertion does not prove field-equation existence, maximality or uniqueness, and makes no proper-class representative choice.

For $b\in\mathbb R$, let $M=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, $r=(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, and define the smooth real two-form

$$
F_b:=\frac{b}{r^3}\left(x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy\right).
$$

Give $M$ its canonical Minkowski metric

$$g:=-(dx^0)^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2,$$

of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, the time orientation selected by the smooth timelike vector field $N:=\partial_{x^0}$, and the product orientation $o:=dx^0\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. Thus $(M,g,N,o)$ is the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold required by [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its underlying product smooth structure and orientation are the standard ones on this open subset of $\mathbb R^4$.

Use the standard Euclidean inner product and norm on the spatial $\mathbb R^3$ factor in all spatial dot products and radii below.

On the locus $x^2+y^2>0$, define dimensionless polar coordinates by $x=r\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=r\sin\theta\sin\phi$, $z=r\cos\theta$, where $0<\theta<\pi$ and $\phi\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$. There $d\phi=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/(x^2+y^2)$; only this differential, not a global real-valued angle, is used on the north-south overlap. The displayed north and south potential formulas are interpreted on angular coordinate neighborhoods and extended across their respective axes as verified in step 2.2.

In a fixed $x^0$-slice, write $S^2:=\{u\in\mathbb R^3:|u|_2=1\}$, where $|u|_2=(u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2)^{1/2}$, and give it the outward orientation: its area form is $\omega_u(v,w):=\det(u,v,w)$ for tangent vectors $v,w\in T_uS^2$. This is a compact smooth sphere; compactness follows from closedness and boundedness by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]].

Let $U_N=\{(x^0,x,y,z)\in M:r+z>0\}$ and $U_S=\{(x^0,x,y,z)\in M:r-z>0\}$; these two open sets cover $M$. Then $dF_b=0$ and its flux through the unit sphere with outward orientation is $4\pi b$. If $b\ne0$, $F_b$ has no global one-form potential on $M$. On $U_N$ and $U_S$,

$$
A_N=b(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad A_S=-b(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi
$$

are smooth local potentials with $dA_N=dA_S=F_b$, and $A_S-A_N=-2b\,d\phi$ on the overlap. For a chosen normalization $\kappa_0>0$, these local forms define the normalized circle-connection data of [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]] precisely when the transition $g_{NS}=e^{-2ib\phi/\kappa_0}$ is single-valued, equivalently $2b/\kappa_0\in\mathbb Z$. For a smooth loop $g(e^{i\phi})=e^{i\chi(\phi)}$, its winding is $[\chi(2\pi)-\chi(0)]/(2\pi)$, with both circles oriented by increasing angle. Existence of a smooth phase lift, integrality of its endpoint change, and independence of the lift are proved in the phase-lift construction below. The transition winding has sign $-2b/\kappa_0$ in the stated north-to-south convention, while $\int_{S^2}F_b/(2\pi\kappa_0)=2b/\kappa_0$. This is an exact condition for this chosen circle normalization, not a claim that every classical real flux is quantized. When $2b/\kappa_0\in\mathbb Z$, the compatible two-set data also produce a smooth principal circle-bundle connection, using the actual set-size interface in [A1] and the gluing statement of [[lem-emg-circle-connection-gluing]].

There is also a flat example with nontrivial holonomy. On $M_0=\mathbb R\times S^1\times\mathbb R^2$ with product smooth structure, take $S^1=U(1)$ with the smooth structure defined above. Write $w\in S^1$ for the base-circle coordinate and let $\nu=-i w^{-1}dw$ be its global real angular one-form, normalized by $\int_{S^1}\nu=2\pi$. For dimensionless $a\in\mathbb R$, set $A=\kappa_0 a\,\nu$. On the product bundle $P_0=M_0\times U(1)$ with projection $\pi(x,z)=x$ and right action $(x,z)\cdot\zeta=(x,z\zeta)$, use $\omega=\vartheta+a\pi^*\nu$, where $z\in U(1)$ is the fibre coordinate and $\vartheta=-i z^{-1}dz$ is its real angular form. Holonomy means the fibre multiplier of the horizontal lift around the indicated base loop; gauge trivial means gauge-equivalent to $\vartheta$ under a smooth bundle map $G_u(x,z)=(x,z u(x))$ covering the identity. Then $F=dA=0$ but holonomy around the circle is $e^{-2\pi ia}$, so this connection is gauge trivial exactly when $a\in\mathbb Z$. If $b$ and $\kappa_0$ are assigned physical units, both are measured in webers; the ratio $2b/\kappa_0$ is dimensionless. No general classification of circle bundles is asserted.

derivations.claim: Under the exact planned conditional interfaces in [A1], substitute $b=\kappa_0/2$ into the flux $4\pi b$ from [L1] to obtain $\int_{S^2}F=2\pi\kappa_0$ and hence $\int_{S^2}F/(2\pi\kappa_0)=1$.
The same substitution gives $A_S-A_N=-\kappa_0\,d\phi$ and $g_{NS}=e^{-i\phi}$. As $\phi$ runs from $0$ to $2\pi$, this transition makes one negative turn, so its winding number is $-1$.

The transition is single-valued because $e^{-i(\phi+2\pi)}=e^{-i\phi}$; the local forms are smooth at their respective poles and both differentiate to $F$. By [[lem-emg-sphere-flux-holonomy]], the nonzero flux rules out a global potential. The calculation is conditional mathematical verification, not evidence about nature.

Use the real ordered field of [[def-real-numbers]] and [[def-complete-ordered-field]]. For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ bounded above, $\sup S$ denotes the unique real upper bound $u$ such that $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$. Existence is the least-upper-bound property established for these reals by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]; if $u,u'$ both satisfy it, $u\le u'$ and $u'\le u$ imply equality. The notation is restricted to this domain.

For nonempty $S$ bounded below, use [[def-infimum]] and [[thm-infimum-property]]: $\inf S=-\sup(-S)$, where $-S=\{-s:s\in S\}$. Indeed a lower bound $l$ for $S$ gives the upper bound $-l$ for $-S$; negating its least upper bound gives a lower bound for $S$ greater than every other one.

Neither $\sup\varnothing$ nor $\inf\varnothing$ is defined in $\mathbb R$: every real is an upper and lower bound, with no least upper or greatest lower bound. If another construction stipulates the value zero for an empty path family, that stipulation is a separate total definition, not $\sup\varnothing=0$. Infinite values require an explicitly specified extended ordered set; no extended-real field operations are introduced here.

Let $X$ be a set and use the ordered real field of [[def-real-numbers]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and [[def-ordered-field]]. In the convention of [[def-metric-space]], a **real metric** is a function $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying, for all $x,y,z\in X$, separation $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$, symmetry $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ and the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. A **real pseudometric** replaces separation by $d(x,x)=0$ and retains the other two axioms. All values are finite real numbers. Neither definition assumes nonnegativity as an additional axiom.

For either structure, put $B_d(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$ for real $r>0$. The induced topology consists of the subsets $O\subseteq X$ for which every $x\in O$ admits $r>0$ with $B_d(x,r)\subseteq O$. After the nonnegativity deduction in the well-definedness lemma, these balls form a basis: $x\in B_d(x,r)$ by reflexivity, and if $z\in B_d(x,r)\cap B_d(y,s)$, the positive radius $t=\min\{r-d(x,z),s-d(y,z)\}$ has $B_d(z,t)$ contained in that intersection by the triangle inequality. This argument also works for pseudometrics and for empty $X$ (the empty topology). No infinite-distance, semimetric or quasimetric convention is consumed.

For $a>0$, integer $m$ and integer $n\ge1$, define the rational regime by

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. The supplementary convention is $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$; $0^0$ and negative powers of zero remain undefined.

The separate real regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For $x>0$ set $0^x=0$; no arbitrary real power is assigned to a negative base. The real-power laws are supplied by that theorem, not inferred from the rational root formula. Use the real-number structure of [[def-real-numbers]].

In particular $s(q)=q^{1/2}$ for $q>0$ is the unique positive solution of $s(q)^2=q$. Its smoothness and derivative are a separate well-definedness result, not an assumption about fractional notation.

Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.
