citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$, curvature tensors
$R^{a}{}_{bcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, scalar curvature $S$ and Einstein
tensor $G_{ab}$ ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). Let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, let $K\subseteq U$ be compact, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an
open interval with $0\in I$, and let $s\mapsto g(s)$, $s\in I$, be a family of
smooth Lorentzian metrics of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $M$ such that

- $g(0)=g$ and $g(s)=g$ on $M\setminus K$ for every $s\in I$; and
- the components $g(s)_{ab}$ in the chart are smooth functions of $(s,x)$ on
  $I\times x(U)$ ([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]).

Write $h_{ab}:=\partial_sg(s)_{ab}|_{s=0}$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field with support in $K$, and
$q^{ab}:=\partial_sg(s)^{ab}|_{s=0}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]).

**(a) Variation of the inverse metric; realizability.** $q^{ab}
=-g^{ac}g^{bd}h_{cd}$; conversely, for every smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h_0$ with compact support in $U$ there is $\lambda_0>0$ such
that for every $|\lambda|<\lambda_0$ the family $s\mapsto g+s\lambda h_0$
satisfies the hypotheses above on the parameter interval $(-1,1)$ (with
$K=\operatorname{supp}h_0$). In particular any prescribed smooth compactly
supported inverse-metric direction $q$ is realized by $g+s h$ on a
sufficiently small interval, with $h_{ab}=-g_{ac}g_{bd}q^{cd}$.

**(b) Variation of the Christoffel symbols.** The field
$\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_s\Gamma(s)^{a}{}_{bc}|_{s=0}$ is a smooth
tensor field on $U$ and

$$\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12g^{ad}\bigl(\nabla_bh_{cd}+\nabla_ch_{bd}-\nabla_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(c) Variation of the Ricci tensor (Palatini identity).**
$\delta\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\partial_s\operatorname{Ric}(s)_{bd}|_{s=0}$
satisfies

$$\delta\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\nabla_a\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{db}-\nabla_d\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{ab}.$$

**(d) Variation of the curvature density.** With
$V^{a}:=g^{bd}\delta\Gamma^{a}{}_{db}-g^{ab}\delta\Gamma^{d}{}_{db}$ and
$w(s):=\sqrt{|\det(g(s)_{ab})|}$ the metric density of
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]],

$$\partial_s\bigl(w(s)S(s)\bigr)\big|_{s=0}=w\,G_{ab}q^{ab}+\partial_a\bigl(wV^{a}\bigr).$$

**(e) Variation of the chart action integral.** For every constant
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, the function
$F(s):=\int_U\bigl[(S(s)-2\Lambda)w(s)-(S(0)-2\Lambda)w(0)\bigr]\,d^4x$ is the compactly supported chart action difference, differentiable at $0$, and

$$F'(0)=\int_U\bigl(G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}\bigr)q^{ab}\,w\,d^4x,$$

where the integrand is compactly supported in $K$ and the integral is an
ordinary Riemann integral in the chart coordinates
([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]).

**(f) Variation of the timelike length and particle action.** Let
$\gamma:[a,b]\to U$ and $H$ be as in
[[lem-gr-first-variation-of-proper-time]], so that $\gamma$ is $C^2$, future
timelike, parametrized with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-c^2$, the variation is $C^2$
with fixed endpoints and future timelike fibres, and $L(s)$ is the length
functional of that lemma. Then the first-variation formulas (1)-(3) of that
lemma hold verbatim. Consequently for every $m>0$ the particle action
$S_p(\gamma):=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))}\,dt$ satisfies
$\partial_sS_p(H(s,\cdot))|_{s=0}=-mc\,L'(0)$, so within this class of curves
and variations $\gamma$ is stationary for $S_p$ if and only if
$D_t\gamma'=0$, i.e. if and only if $\gamma$ is a geodesic in its proper-time
parameter ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, and define the local **metric density** by
$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$ on $U$, using the matrix of metric components
in this chart. This definition requires no orientation or volume form. Write
$g^{ab}$ for the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]) and
$\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}$ for the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in the chart.

**(a) Derivative of the density.** At every point of $U$,

$$\partial_a w=\tfrac12\,w\,g^{bc}\,\partial_a g_{bc}.$$

**(b) Trace of the Christoffel symbols.** At every point of $U$,

$$\Gamma^{b}{}_{ba}=w^{-1}\partial_a w .$$

**(c) Divergence formula.** For every smooth vector field $J$ on $M$, at every
point of $U$,

$$\nabla_aJ^a=\partial_aJ^a+\Gamma^{a}{}_{ab}J^b=w^{-1}\partial_a\bigl(w\,J^a\bigr),$$

where $\nabla_aJ^a=g^{ab}\nabla_bJ_a$ is the divergence of $J$ contracted with
the metric and $J^a$ are the components of $J$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).

The identity of (c) is a chart formula for a chart-independent scalar: the
right-hand side is independent of the chart, as the left-hand side is.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with signature
$(-,+,+,+)$, metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and oriented metric volume
form $\mathrm{vol}_g$. Let $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ be a smooth real two-form and
$j\in\Gamma(TM)$ a smooth vector field. Fix constants $\mu_0>0$ and $c>0$;
$\mu_0$ is a real coefficient here, and $c$ is the positive coordinate
conversion in $x^0=ct$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Assume the mathematical
field equations

$$dF=0,\qquad \nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b.$$

The equations are conditional hypotheses, not physical postulates in this
mathematical item. Define $v\in\Gamma(TM)$ by $v^b:=\nabla_aF^{ab}$ and
define the current three-form by $\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$, the contraction
specified in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]. Then:

**(a) Sign identity.** On $M$,

$$d(\star_gF)=-\iota_v\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Consequently the sourced equation is equivalently

$$\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

**(b) Current conservation.** Either equivalent sourced equation implies
$\nabla_aj^a=0$. This conclusion requires the sourced equation and $\mu_0>0$;
it does not require $dF=0$.

**(c) Local component check.** At any $p\in M$, choose a positively oriented
point-normal chart supplied by
[[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]. In that chart,
write $E_i(x):=-cF_{0i}(x)$ and
$B_i(x):=\frac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}(x)$, where $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ and
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is alternating. These are local component abbreviations in
the chosen chart, not global observer fields. With
$\operatorname{div}E:=\partial_iE_i$,
$(\operatorname{curl}E)_k:=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iE_j$, and similarly
for $B$, the pointwise component identities are

$$v^0=-\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad v^k=\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k,$$

$$ (d\star_gF)_{123}=\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad (d\star_gF)_{0ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}\left(\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k\right),$$

$$ (dF)_{123}=\operatorname{div}B,\qquad (dF)_{0ij}=\frac{\epsilon_{ijk}}{c}\left(\partial_tB_k+(\operatorname{curl}E)_k\right),$$

where $\partial_t:=c\,\partial_0$. The equations are pointwise identities
in normal coordinates; they do not assert that these component abbreviations
form global three-vector fields on curved spacetime.

On an open flat Minkowski domain with a fixed inertial Cartesian chart
$x^0=ct$, define $\rho:=j^0/c$, $J^i:=j^i$, and
$\epsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. The same component formulas at every point give

$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE=\mu_0J,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \partial_tB+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$

These are a coordinate reduction of the stated tensor and form equations, not
claims that the smooth fields describe an experiment.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For an oriented smooth manifold $M^n$, possibly with boundary, and $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$, choose a smooth partition $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to connected interior or boundary charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$. For $n\geq1$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\rho_i\omega).$$
Each product has compact support in its chart and only finitely many are nonzero, by [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]]. For $n=0$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p).$$
$\Lambda^0T_p^*M\cong\mathbb R$ has two orientations; define $\varepsilon(p)=+1$ when $1$ is positive in the chosen orientation and $\varepsilon(p)=-1$ when $-1$ is positive.
A zero-manifold is discrete; the singleton open cover of a compact subset has a finite subcover. Thus this sum too is finite. Empty support or empty $M$ gives zero. Independence of the choices is discharged by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The compact-support integral on an oriented manifold is independent of the chart cover, coordinate maps, subordinate partition, and refinement. If $U\subset M$ is open and contains $\operatorname{supp}\omega$, with its restricted orientation, then $\int_U\omega|_U=\int_M\omega$.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

By [[def-de-rham-cohomology]], $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^2(M)/B^2(M)$, where $Z^2(M)$ is the vector space of closed smooth two-forms and $B^2(M)$ is the vector space of exact smooth two-forms. Thus, for closed $F$, the statement $[F]=0$ means exactly that $F=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$. This equivalence is the quotient definition; it does not assert that every closed form is exact.

Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$ by $z=x+iy$ and set $U(1)=S^1:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. Its topology is the subspace topology. Specify its smooth structure by the four charts

$$V_{x,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon x>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto y,\quad y\mapsto(\epsilon\sqrt{1-y^2},y),$$

and

$$V_{y,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon y>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto x,\quad x\mapsto(x,\epsilon\sqrt{1-x^2}),$$

for $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, with each coordinate range $(-1,1)$. They cover $S^1$; their transition maps are restrictions of the positive square-root branch and coordinate projections, hence are smooth by [[lem-emg-positive-square-root-smoothness]] and [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]. In these coordinates multiplication is the restriction of $(x,y)(u,v)=(xu-yv,xv+yu)$ and inversion is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so both are smooth; they are also continuous for the stated topology. Thus this is a smooth Lie group and, in particular, a topological group as required by [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Let $E:\mathbb R\to U(1)$ be $E(t)=e^{it}=(\cos t,\sin t)$; the Cartesian formula is [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The trigonometric derivative identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], iterated, show that $E$ is smooth in the $C^\infty$ sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: every derivative of either coordinate is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, and these functions are continuous by [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]. Surjectivity is [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]. If $E(t)\in V_{x,\epsilon}$, the chart coordinate $\sin t$ has derivative $\cos t=x\ne0$; if $E(t)\in V_{y,\epsilon}$, the coordinate $\cos t$ has derivative $-\sin t=-y\ne0$. The smooth inverse-function theorem [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]] therefore makes $E$ a diffeomorphism from some open interval about $t$ onto an open circle arc. Every smooth map from an open subset of $M$ to $U(1)$ consequently has, near each point, a smooth real phase lift obtained by composing with such a local inverse.

A **normalized circle-connection datum** on $M$ consists of a supplied countable open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, smooth transition maps $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U(1)$, smooth real one-forms $a_i\in\Omega^1(U_i)$, and a fixed constant $\kappa_0>0$. Require $g_{ii}=1$ and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on every triple intersection. Around each point of $U_i\cap U_j$, take any smooth real phase lift $f_{ij}$ with $g_{ij}=e^{if_{ij}}$; require

$$
a_j=a_i+df_{ij}
$$

on every such phase-lift neighborhood. If $f$ and $\widetilde f$ are two lifts on a connected neighborhood, [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]] gives $f-\widetilde f\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ pointwise; continuity makes this difference constant, so $df=d\widetilde f$. Thus the compatibility condition is independent of the chosen lift. The globally defined form $\lambda(g):=-i\,g^{-1}dg$ is real, and [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] together with [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] gives $\lambda(g)=df$ on every phase-lift neighborhood. Hence the equivalent lift-free condition is $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$.

The right principal $U(1)$-bundle convention is as defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]: it has a continuous right action and locally trivial equivariant product charts, with free and transitive action on each fibre. The compatible transition functions are the gluing data for such a bundle, in the convention that a point with fibre coordinate $z_i$ in chart $i$ has coordinate $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$ in chart $j$. No global real-valued angle on $U(1)$ is assumed.

The constant $\kappa_0$ is a chosen normalization with units of webers; it is not Planck's constant and is not a unit of electric charge. On a chart whose coordinates have length units, the normalized connection components $a_i$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding local potential $A_i:=\kappa_0a_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and its curvature $F_i:=dA_i=\kappa_0\,da_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. This definition imposes no flux or charge quantization.

Let $M$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable oriented four-manifold, and let $(U_i,g_{ij},a_i;\kappa_0)$ be a normalized circle-connection datum as in [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]]. Use the set-sized-object and quotient convention of [[def-emg-set-size-and-class-schema]]. Then the chart data construct a smooth Hausdorff second-countable right principal $U(1)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and a global smooth real connection one-form $\omega$ on $P$. Its curvature is basic: there is a smooth closed two-form $f\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $d\omega=\pi^*f$ and $f|_{U_i}=da_i$. The local potentials $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ satisfy $dA_i=F$, where $F=\kappa_0 f$ is global. For two connections on the same fixed bundle with the same transition functions, their local-form differences are restrictions of one global base one-form; adding a global one-form to all local representatives stays in that bundle sector.

derivations.claim: Interpret a compactly supported variation as a smooth family equal to its background off one fixed compact set $K$ for all sufficiently small parameters. Connection variations $A+s\alpha$ have $K=\operatorname{supp}\alpha$ and $F(s)=F+s\,d\alpha$ in the fixed sector. For a prescribed metric direction $q$, put $h_{ab}=-g_{ac}g_{bd}q^{cd}$ and $g(s)=g+sh$. Compactness of $K=\operatorname{supp}h$ and openness of the fixed-signature matrices give a uniform parameter interval on which this is Lorentzian: take a finite chart cover of $K$, use continuity and nondegeneracy on compact subneighborhoods, then take the minimum of the finitely many bounds. Off $K$ the metric is unchanged. Thus the action-density difference $\omega(s)-\omega(0)$ is a smooth top form supported in a common $K$, even when neither background action is finite. Its integral in [F12] is the relative action; additivity of integrals makes successive relative differences consistent. No subtraction of infinite action values is involved.

Fix the chart cover and partition $(\rho_i)$ of [F12] independently of $s$. Local finiteness gives a neighborhood of each point meeting only finitely many supports; a finite such neighborhood cover of $K$ shows that only finitely many $\rho_i$ meet $K$. Each $\rho_i(\omega(s)-\omega(0))$ has compact support inside its chart. Extend its coefficient by zero and enclose that support in a coordinate rectangle. On a closed parameter interval about zero the coefficient derivative is uniformly continuous on the product rectangle; the mean-value argument in [F3] makes its difference quotients converge uniformly. The estimate $|\int_Q u|\le\operatorname{vol}(Q)\sup_Q|u|$ from [F7] permits differentiation inside this chart integral. Summing finitely many terms proves $\delta\int_M(\omega(s)-\omega(0))=\int_M\delta\omega$. Choice independence is exactly [F12].

For any smooth compactly supported vector field $W$, the same partition has only finitely many terms meeting its support. Each $ho_iW$ is compactly supported inside one chart. In that chart its density divergence is $\partial_a(who_iW^a)$ by [F4]. Zero extension is smooth, and FTC/Fubini on a containing rectangle gives zero integral, because its coefficients vanish near every rectangle face. The global integral agrees with this chart integral by [F12]. On a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}W$, $\sum_iho_i=1$ and $\sum_i dho_i=0$, so $\sum_i
abla_a(ho_iW^a)=
abla_aW^a$; off the support both sides vanish. Finite additivity therefore gives $\int_M
abla_aW^a\,\mathrm{vol}_g=0$. This proves the compact divergence rule without requiring the support to fit one chart.

For a connection variation in [A1], $\delta F=d\alpha$; in components
$\delta F_{ab}=2\nabla_{[a}\alpha_{b]}$ because the Levi-Civita Christoffel
symbols are symmetric in their lower indices. Holding $g$ fixed gives
$\delta(F_{ab}F^{ab})=2F^{ab}\delta F_{ab}
=4F^{ab}\nabla_a\alpha_b$. Differentiating the coefficient in the action
therefore yields
$\delta_A S_{\mathrm{EM}}=-(\mu_0c)^{-1}\int_MF^{ab}\nabla_a\alpha_b\,\mathrm{vol}_g$.

Let $q^{ab}=\delta g^{ab}$ and hold $F_{ab}$ fixed. From
$F_{cd}F^{cd}=g^{ca}g^{db}F_{cd}F_{ab}$, symmetry of $q$ and antisymmetry
of $F$ give
$\delta(F_{cd}F^{cd})=2F_{ac}F_b{}^c q^{ab}$. The volume variation in [F3]
then gives
$$\delta_g(F_{cd}F^{cd}\mathrm{vol}_g)=\left(2F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac12g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right)q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g.$$
By [F2], this is the variation of the same action density as its wedge-form
representative.
Multiplying by $-1/(4\mu_0c)$ and comparing with the definition in part (b)
gives the displayed $T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}$. The variation is local and
compactly supported, so no boundary term is discarded.

Set $W^a:=F^{ab}\alpha_b$. The product rule gives
$
abla_aW^a=(
abla_aF^{ab})\alpha_b+F^{ab}
abla_a\alpha_b$.
By step 3.1, $\int_M
abla_aW^a\,\mathrm{vol}_g=0$, for arbitrary compact support of $\alpha$. Substitution into step 3.2 gives $\delta_A S_{\mathrm{EM}}=(\mu_0c)^{-1}\int_M(
abla_aF^{ab})\alpha_b\,\mathrm{vol}_g$, proving the connection-variation formula.

Adding [A2] to step 4.1 gives
$\delta_A(S_{\mathrm{EM}}+S_{\mathrm m})[\alpha]
=(\mu_0c)^{-1}\int_M(\nabla_aF^{ab}+\mu_0j^b)\alpha_b\,\mathrm{vol}_g$.
If $\nabla_aF^{ab}+\mu_0j^b=0$, this integral vanishes for every allowed
$\alpha$. Conversely, if it vanishes for every smooth compactly supported
one-form supported in one chart rectangle, fix a point and suppose a component
$K^{b_0}:=\nabla_aF^{ab_0}+\mu_0j^{b_0}$ is nonzero there. By continuity,
shrink to a coordinate ball with compact closure where $K^{b_0}$ has one
strict sign and $w>0$. In coordinates centered at that point define
$\phi(x)=\exp(-1/(r^2-|x|^2))$ for $|x|<r$ and $\phi(x)=0$ for $|x|\ge r$.
Every derivative approaching $|x|=r$ is a finite sum of a polynomial in
$1/(r^2-|x|^2)$ times the same exponential, and
$s^{-m}e^{-1/s}\to0$ as $s\downarrow0$ for every $m\ge0$; hence $\phi$ is a
smooth nonnegative compactly supported function, positive inside the ball.
Set $\alpha=\phi\,dx^{b_0}$ in the chart and extend it by zero outside the
compact support; this gives an admissible global one-form in [A1]. The bump
and rectangle are explicitly constructed, so the ambient convention [F5]
introduces no arbitrary choice. The product $K^{b_0}\phi w$ is continuous and
supported in a compact rectangle containing the bump support, so [F8] makes
its full integral well-defined. At the center,
$|K^{b_0}\phi w|>0$; continuity gives a smaller closed nondegenerate
rectangle $R$ on which this coefficient has one strict sign and absolute
value at least some $\eta>0$. By [F8] it is Riemann integrable there. Applying
[F11] to its sign-adjusted coefficient shows that the absolute value of the
integral over $R$ is at least $\eta\operatorname{vol}(R)>0$. On the entire
bump support the product has the same sign, since $K^{b_0}$ has one sign on
the ball and $\phi,w$ are nonnegative; therefore its full integral over the
support cannot vanish. This contradicts the assumed stationarity integral.
Thus every component $K^b$ vanishes at every point. Conversely its pointwise vanishing makes the variation zero for every compactly supported global one-form by step 4.1. This proves the stated global stationarity equivalence under [A2]–[A3].

When the Euler–Lagrange equation in step 5.1 holds, apply [F6] to obtain
$d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$. This uses the conditional current
interface of [A1] and the exact current-sign identity proved in the earlier
item; it adds no global potential or matter-action claim.

Use the real ordered field of [[def-real-numbers]] and [[def-complete-ordered-field]]. For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ bounded above, $\sup S$ denotes the unique real upper bound $u$ such that $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$. Existence is the least-upper-bound property established for these reals by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]; if $u,u'$ both satisfy it, $u\le u'$ and $u'\le u$ imply equality. The notation is restricted to this domain.

For nonempty $S$ bounded below, use [[def-infimum]] and [[thm-infimum-property]]: $\inf S=-\sup(-S)$, where $-S=\{-s:s\in S\}$. Indeed a lower bound $l$ for $S$ gives the upper bound $-l$ for $-S$; negating its least upper bound gives a lower bound for $S$ greater than every other one.

Neither $\sup\varnothing$ nor $\inf\varnothing$ is defined in $\mathbb R$: every real is an upper and lower bound, with no least upper or greatest lower bound. If another construction stipulates the value zero for an empty path family, that stipulation is a separate total definition, not $\sup\varnothing=0$. Infinite values require an explicitly specified extended ordered set; no extended-real field operations are introduced here.

Let $X$ be a set and use the ordered real field of [[def-real-numbers]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and [[def-ordered-field]]. In the convention of [[def-metric-space]], a **real metric** is a function $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying, for all $x,y,z\in X$, separation $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$, symmetry $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ and the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. A **real pseudometric** replaces separation by $d(x,x)=0$ and retains the other two axioms. All values are finite real numbers. Neither definition assumes nonnegativity as an additional axiom.

For either structure, put $B_d(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$ for real $r>0$. The induced topology consists of the subsets $O\subseteq X$ for which every $x\in O$ admits $r>0$ with $B_d(x,r)\subseteq O$. After the nonnegativity deduction in the well-definedness lemma, these balls form a basis: $x\in B_d(x,r)$ by reflexivity, and if $z\in B_d(x,r)\cap B_d(y,s)$, the positive radius $t=\min\{r-d(x,z),s-d(y,z)\}$ has $B_d(z,t)$ contained in that intersection by the triangle inequality. This argument also works for pseudometrics and for empty $X$ (the empty topology). No infinite-distance, semimetric or quasimetric convention is consumed.

For $a>0$, integer $m$ and integer $n\ge1$, define the rational regime by

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. The supplementary convention is $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$; $0^0$ and negative powers of zero remain undefined.

The separate real regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For $x>0$ set $0^x=0$; no arbitrary real power is assigned to a negative base. The real-power laws are supplied by that theorem, not inferred from the rational root formula. Use the real-number structure of [[def-real-numbers]].

In particular $s(q)=q^{1/2}$ for $q>0$ is the unique positive solution of $s(q)^2=q$. Its smoothness and derivative are a separate well-definedness result, not an assumption about fractional notation.

Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.

Use the first-order language of [[def-language-of-set-theory]]: all quantified objects are sets, and a **definable class** $\{x:\varphi(x,p)\}$ abbreviates a formula with set parameters $p$. It is not a new set or a domain for unrestricted quantification. Work with the usual set axioms, in particular [[def-axiom-of-power-set]] and [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], and the ordered pairs, products and functions of [[def-ordered-pair]], [[def-cartesian-product]] and [[def-function]]. The power-set axiom supplies a collecting set; Separation trims it to exactly $\mathcal P(X)=\{Y:Y\subseteq X\}$.

A **small category** has a set $O$ of objects, a set $A$ of arrows, source and target functions $s,t:A\to O$, an identity function $e:O\to A$, and a composition function on the set $\{(a,b)\in A\times A:s(a)=t(b)\}$, where $ab$ denotes $a\circ b$ and the laws are $s(e(x))=t(e(x))=x$, $s(ab)=s(b)$, $t(ab)=t(a)$, $e(t(a))a=a=ae(s(a))$, and $(ab)c=a(bc)$ whenever the displayed compositions are defined. It is **locally small** when each specified hom-collection is a set. A definable large category is a schema of formulas for its objects, arrows and operations, with those laws asserted as formulas; it is not a set of all objects or a category of all large categories. No Grothendieck universe is assumed.

All indexed families in the local bundle construction have a supplied set index $I$. If $U_i\subseteq M$ and $G$ is a set, their tagged disjoint union is the subset $D=\{(i,x,z)\in I\times M\times G:x\in U_i\}$, formed by Separation. Given a set equivalence relation $E\subseteq D\times D$, each class $[u]_E=\{v\in D:(u,v)\in E\}$ is a subset of $D$, and the quotient is the set

$$
D/E=\{C\in\mathcal P(D):\exists u\in D\ \forall v\in D\ (v\in C\iff(u,v)\in E)\}.
$$

Thus the quotient is obtained by Separation in $\mathcal P(D)$, without choosing representatives. Transition-map graphs and connection data are subsets of specified finite products and power sets, not arbitrary proper-class objects.

For the Cauchy-development coding application, fix a set manifold $\Sigma$ and the tensor-bundle total spaces over $\Sigma\times\mathbb R$. A code consists of an open set $D\subseteq\Sigma\times\mathbb R$, graphs of a metric and a two-form on $D$ inside those fixed total spaces, a time orientation, and a fixed initial embedding. All of its coordinates belong to fixed products and power sets. Separation selects the tuples satisfying the specified smoothness, Lorentzian, field-equation and initial-data formulas. Hence these codes form a set. This size assertion does not prove field-equation existence, maximality or uniqueness, and makes no proper-class representative choice.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with signature
$(-,+,+,+)$, metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and oriented metric volume
form $\mathrm{vol}_g$. Let $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ be a smooth real two-form and
$j\in\Gamma(TM)$ a smooth vector field. Fix constants $\mu_0>0$ and $c>0$;
$\mu_0$ is a real coefficient here, and $c$ is the positive coordinate
conversion in $x^0=ct$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Assume the mathematical
field equations

$$dF=0,\qquad \nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b.$$

The equations are conditional hypotheses, not physical postulates in this
mathematical item. Define $v\in\Gamma(TM)$ by $v^b:=\nabla_aF^{ab}$ and
define the current three-form by $\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$, the contraction
specified in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]. Then:

**(a) Sign identity.** On $M$,

$$d(\star_gF)=-\iota_v\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Consequently the sourced equation is equivalently

$$\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

**(b) Current conservation.** Either equivalent sourced equation implies
$\nabla_aj^a=0$. This conclusion requires the sourced equation and $\mu_0>0$;
it does not require $dF=0$.

**(c) Local component check.** At any $p\in M$, choose a positively oriented
point-normal chart supplied by
[[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]. In that chart,
write $E_i(x):=-cF_{0i}(x)$ and
$B_i(x):=\frac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}(x)$, where $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ and
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is alternating. These are local component abbreviations in
the chosen chart, not global observer fields. With
$\operatorname{div}E:=\partial_iE_i$,
$(\operatorname{curl}E)_k:=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iE_j$, and similarly
for $B$, the pointwise component identities are

$$v^0=-\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad v^k=\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k,$$

$$ (d\star_gF)_{123}=\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad (d\star_gF)_{0ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}\left(\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k\right),$$

$$ (dF)_{123}=\operatorname{div}B,\qquad (dF)_{0ij}=\frac{\epsilon_{ijk}}{c}\left(\partial_tB_k+(\operatorname{curl}E)_k\right),$$

where $\partial_t:=c\,\partial_0$. The equations are pointwise identities
in normal coordinates; they do not assert that these component abbreviations
form global three-vector fields on curved spacetime.

On an open flat Minkowski domain with a fixed inertial Cartesian chart
$x^0=ct$, define $\rho:=j^0/c$, $J^i:=j^i$, and
$\epsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. The same component formulas at every point give

$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE=\mu_0J,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \partial_tB+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$

These are a coordinate reduction of the stated tensor and form equations, not
claims that the smooth fields describe an experiment.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $M$ carry an orientation in the
sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] (so that its
charts that are oriented in that orientation have orientation-preserving
transition maps), and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection. This item
fixes the metric volume form, the flux of a current through oriented $3$-faces
and finite-chain charges. The orientation of $M$ is an independent datum: it is
not determined by the metric and not by the time orientation.

**(a) Metric volume density and volume form.** Let $(U,x)$ be an oriented
chart, with metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a)). Define the **metric volume
density**

$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a strictly positive smooth function because $g_{ab}$ is smooth and
$g_p$ is nondegenerate. In the chart define the local $4$-form

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}:=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3,$$

with the exterior product of [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]] and the
coordinate covector fields of
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. That these local
forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing
$4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together
with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively
oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has
$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

**(b) Current flux through oriented $3$-faces and chains.** Let $J$ be a
smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **current
$3$-form** of $J$ is the contraction

$$\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

the interior product of the $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ with $J$
([[def-interior-product-of-a-form-by-a-vector-field]]).

By a **smooth singular $k$-simplex** of $M$ — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-simplex` (differential-geometry track),
restated here so this page is self-contained — we mean a map
$\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ whose domain is the standard $k$-simplex
$$\Delta^k=\Bigl\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_it_i=1\Bigr\},$$
for which there exist an open set $O\subseteq A^k=\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\sum_it_i=1\}$
containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with
$\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$; the extension is not part of the simplex
data, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. With the integration of
forms over such simplices
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]), a **$3$-face** is
a smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$, and the **flux of $J$ through
$\sigma$** is the real number

$$\Phi_J(\sigma):=\int_\sigma\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

A **finite smooth singular $k$-chain** — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes`, restated here —
is a finite formal real linear combination $\Sigma=\sum_i c_i\sigma_i$ of
smooth singular $k$-simplices. For such a $3$-chain the **flux of $J$ through
$\Sigma$** is defined additively,

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma):=\sum_i c_i\,\Phi_J(\sigma_i),$$

a definition independent of the written expression for $\Sigma$, because a
finite formal sum is evaluated by adding the finitely many coefficients and
inserting a zero coefficient changes nothing. $\Phi_J(\Sigma)$ is the **charge**
of the current $J$ assigned to $\Sigma$ when the model reads $J$ as a conserved
current; that reading belongs to the physical postulates and is not part of
this definition.

**(c) Non-null faces and their unit normals.** A $3$-dimensional linear subspace
$H\subseteq T_pM$ is **nondegenerate** for $g_p$ when the restriction of $g_p$
to $H$ is nondegenerate, equivalently when $H\cap H^\perp=\{0\}$ in the
orthogonality of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. A
smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is **non-null at** a parameter point $t$
when the span of the three velocity vectors
$\sigma_*\partial_1|_t,\sigma_*\partial_2|_t,\sigma_*\partial_3|_t$ has
dimension $3$ and is nondegenerate at $\sigma(t)$, and **non-null** when this holds at every
parameter point. For a non-null face the **unit normal** $\nu$ at that point is
the unique vector of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$ with $\nu\in H^\perp$,
$g(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,+1\}$ and $(\nu,\sigma_*\partial_1,\sigma_*\partial_2,
\sigma_*\partial_3)$ a positively oriented basis of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$; its
existence, uniqueness and its sign $\varepsilon:=g(\nu,\nu)$ are proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c), together
with the density identity of clause (c) used to read $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ on
such a face. Rank-deficient faces and rank-three faces with degenerate induced
metric are not assigned a unit normal; their flux is defined
by the $3$-form $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ itself, as in clause (b).

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with an
orientation, metric-selected connection $\nabla$, metric volume form
$\mathrm{vol}_g$ and current flux $\Phi_J$ as in
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]], and let $J$ be a smooth vector
field on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). Write
$\nabla_aJ^a$ for the divergence of $J$.

**(a) Exterior derivative of the current form.** As smooth $4$-forms on $M$,

$$d\bigl(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g\bigr)=\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

**(b) Flux balance (Stokes).** For every finite smooth singular $4$-chain $C$
of $M$ — a finite formal real sum of smooth singular $4$-simplices, the
library convention `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes` restated
in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) — and the flux
$\Phi_J$ of the induced boundary $3$-chain
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]],
[[thm-stokes-theorem-for-smooth-singular-chains]]),

$$\Phi_J(\partial C)=\int_C\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

Consequently, if $\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$ for smooth singular $3$-chains
$\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2,B$, then

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)-\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)=-\Phi_J(B)+\int_C\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

In particular, if $\nabla_aJ^a=0$ on $C$ then
$\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)-\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)=-\Phi_J(B)$, and if moreover
$\Phi_J(B)=0$ then $\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)=\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)$: equal charges need a
vanishing side flux, not merely a divergence-free current.

a map $\sigma:\Delta^3\to M$ admitting a smooth extension to a neighbourhood
of the standard $3$-simplex inside its affine plane, the convention restated
in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) — that is
non-null at a parameter point $t$
([[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (c)), with
$v_i:=\sigma_*\partial_i|_t$ spanning the hyperplane $H$ and with the unit
normal $\nu^{*}$ adapted to the ordered basis $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ as in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c); write

$J=\varepsilon g(J,\nu^{*})\nu^{*}+w'$ with $w'\in H$, and only the normal
component contributes to the flux through the face.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
By [F1], $d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$. Integrate this
three-form over the finite smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$. By [F2],
$\int_\Sigma d(\star_gF)=\int_{\partial\Sigma}\star_gF$, so
$\mu_0\int_\Sigma\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g=\int_{\partial\Sigma}\star_gF$.
Divide by $\mu_0c>0$ and use the definition of $Q$ to obtain (a)'s formula.
The chain $\Sigma$ was fixed arbitrarily, and no family of chains is selected,
as [F4] records.

Let $V$ be a finite smooth singular three-chain. Apply [F2] to the
two-form $F$ on $V$ and use [A1]:
$\int_{\partial V}F=\int_VdF=0$. This proves (b) for bounding surfaces;
the argument supplies no primitive or flux statement for a nonbounding
cycle.

If $\partial\Sigma=0$, the right side of step 1.1 is the integral over
the zero two-chain, which is zero by finite additivity in [F2]. Hence
$Q(\Sigma)=0$. This conclusion uses a cycle, not merely a closed surface
whose homology class is unspecified.

For the four-chain $C$, [F1] gives $\nabla_aj^a=0$ throughout its domain.
By [F3],
$\Phi_j(\partial C)=\int_C(\nabla_aj^a)\mathrm{vol}_g=0$. Additivity of
the finite-chain integral and
$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$ give
$\Phi_j(\Sigma_2)-\Phi_j(\Sigma_1)+\Phi_j(B)=0$. Divide by $c>0$ and apply
the definition of $Q$ to obtain (c). The proof integrates only finite smooth
chains, so no boundary-at-infinity term is present.

Let $U\subseteq M$ be an open set with smooth observer congruence $n$, let $F$ be a smooth real two-form on $U$, and let $c>0$ be the coordinate conversion parameter of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Define covectors

$$E_a:=cF_{ab}n^b,\qquad B_a:=-({\star_gF})_{ab}n^b.$$

Here $c$ is the positive coordinate-conversion parameter of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with SI unit $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$ in its length-coordinate convention. The names electric and magnetic distinguish these two covectors; for arbitrary mathematical $F$ no physical field unit or measurement is assigned.

For each $p\in U$, define the **rest covector space** by

$$\mathcal R^*_{n,p}:=\{\alpha\in T_p^*M:\alpha(n_p)=0\}.$$

The musical isomorphism $\flat_p$ maps the vector rest space $n_p^\perp$ onto $\mathcal R^*_{n,p}$: $\alpha\in\mathcal R^*_{n,p}$ iff $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,n_p)=\alpha(n_p)=0$. Moreover, $g_p^{-1}(v^\flat,w^\flat)=g_p(v,w)$, so the restriction of $g_p^{-1}$ to $\mathcal R^*_{n,p}$ is positive definite by [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with the metric
volume form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ and metric-selected connection $\nabla$. Let
$F\in\Omega^2(M)$ be a smooth real two-form and let $c,\mu_0>0$ be fixed
real coefficients. The action density is

$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{EM}}\,\mathrm{vol}_g=-\frac{1}{4\mu_0c}F_{ab}F^{ab}\,\mathrm{vol}_g=-\frac{1}{2\mu_0c}F\wedge\star_gF.$$

When this density has a global integral, denote it by $S_{\mathrm{EM}}[g,F]$.
On a noncompact domain, every displayed variation below means the finite
action difference supported by the compactly supported variation.

Assume the fixed smooth bundle sector and connection-variation interface in
[A1] below. Then:

**(a) Connection variation.** For every smooth compactly supported global
one-form $\alpha$ allowed by that fixed-sector interface, holding $g$ fixed gives $\delta F=d\alpha$ and

$$\delta_A S_{\mathrm{EM}}[\alpha]=\frac{1}{\mu_0c}\int_M(\nabla_aF^{ab})\alpha_b\,\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

If a differentiable source-sector functional on the same variations satisfies
$\delta_A S_{\mathrm{m}}[\alpha]=c^{-1}\int_Mj^b\alpha_b\,\mathrm{vol}_g$ for a
smooth vector field $j$, then stationarity of
$S_{\mathrm{EM}}+S_{\mathrm m}$ under every such $\alpha$ is equivalent on $M$ to

$$\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b,$$

and hence to $d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$ by
[[lem-emg-maxwell-current-forms]]. This is a conditional variational
calculation; it asserts no matter-action existence or physical adoption.

**(b) Metric variation.** For a smooth compactly supported symmetric inverse
metric variation $q^{ab}:=\delta g^{ab}$, holding the lower components
$F_{ab}$ fixed and preserving Lorentz signature for sufficiently small
parameter, define $T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}$ by

$$\delta_gS_{\mathrm{EM}}[q]=-\frac{1}{2c}\int_M T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}q^{ab}\,\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Then

$$T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right).$$

This is the tensor obtained by varying the free electromagnetic action; it
contains no stress contribution from a source or matter functional.

derivations.claim:
Rewrite the first quadratic term as
$F_{ac}F_b{}^c=g^{cd}F_{ac}F_{bd}$. Since $g^{cd}=g^{dc}$ and scalar
component products commute, this expression is symmetric in $a,b$. The term
$g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}$ is also symmetric, so $T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}$ is symmetric.

The component calculation is finite and makes no additional choice,
consistent with the ambient convention [F2]. Fix a point and use the tetrad
components of [F1]. Raising the time index
with $\eta^{00}=-1$ gives $F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$, and spatial raising
leaves $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. The invariant in [F1] and the formula in
[A1] then give
$T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{00}=\mu_0^{-1}\bigl(\sum_i E_i^2/c^2+
\frac12\sum_i(B_i^2-E_i^2/c^2)\bigr)
=\frac12(\epsilon_0\sum_iE_i^2+\mu_0^{-1}\sum_iB_i^2)$.

Because $\eta^{0i}=0$, the trace term contributes nothing to
$T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{0i}$. The remaining contraction is
$\mu_0^{-1}\sum_jF^{0j}F^i{}_j
=\frac1{\mu_0c}\sum_j\epsilon_{ijk}E_jB_k$, which is the stated cross-product
component.

For spatial components, the time-index contraction is
$F^{i0}F^j{}_0=-E_iE_j/c^2$, and
$\sum_kF^{ik}F^j{}_k=\delta_{ij}\sum_\ell B_\ell^2-B_iB_j$ by the
three-dimensional alternating-symbol identity
$\sum_k\epsilon_{ik\ell}\epsilon_{jkm}
=\delta_{ij}\delta_{\ell m}-\delta_{im}\delta_{\ell j}$.
Subtracting $\frac14\delta_{ij}F_{cd}F^{cd}$ and using
$\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ yields exactly the formula for
$T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{ij}$ in (b). Lowering the first time index multiplies the
$0i$ component by $\eta_{00}=-1$, so
$T_{\mathrm{EM},0i}=-T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{0i}$.

Contract with $g^{ab}$. The first term gives
$g^{ab}F_{ac}F_b{}^c=F_{ac}F^{ac}$, while
$g^{ab}g_{ab}=4$ in four dimensions. Hence
$g^{ab}T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}=\mu_0^{-1}(F_{cd}F^{cd}-\frac44F_{cd}F^{cd})=0$.

In the tetrad, $u_n=T_{\mathrm{EM},00}=T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{00}$ because
$n^a=\delta^a_0$ and both lowered time indices contribute the same diagonal
metric factor. The projector in [F3] keeps exactly the spatial components,
and $n_c=(-1,0,0,0)$ gives
$S_n^i=-c\,T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{i0}n_0=cT_{\mathrm{EM}}^{i0}
=(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)_i/\mu_0$, while $S_n^0=0$. Positivity of
$\epsilon_0$ and $\mu_0$ makes the stated $u_n$ nonnegative.

Raising indices with the fixed inverse metric is linear, so $(\lambda H)_b{}^c=\lambda H_b{}^c$ and $(\lambda H)^{cd}=\lambda H^{cd}$. Each product in the definition of $Q_g$ therefore acquires exactly two factors of $\lambda$, proving $Q_g(\lambda H)=\lambda^2Q_g(H)$, including $\lambda=0$. Positivity of $G_N,\mu_0,c$ gives the unique positive $\alpha$ and $2\alpha^2=8\pi G_N/(\mu_0c^4)$. By [A1], $T_{\mathrm{EM}}=\mu_0^{-1}Q_g(F)$; hence $\kappa_ET_{\mathrm{EM}}=(8\pi G_N/(\mu_0c^4))Q_g(F)=2Q_g(\alpha F)$. The unit assignments give $[\alpha]^2=\mathrm{A^2\,s^4\,kg^{-2}\,m^{-2}}$, and $\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}\,A^{-1}}$, so $[\alpha F_{ab}]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$; the remaining displayed units follow by multiplication and by the two coordinate differentials of a two-form. This proves (d).

Use the real ordered field of [[def-real-numbers]] and [[def-complete-ordered-field]]. For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ bounded above, $\sup S$ denotes the unique real upper bound $u$ such that $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$. Existence is the least-upper-bound property established for these reals by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]; if $u,u'$ both satisfy it, $u\le u'$ and $u'\le u$ imply equality. The notation is restricted to this domain.

For nonempty $S$ bounded below, use [[def-infimum]] and [[thm-infimum-property]]: $\inf S=-\sup(-S)$, where $-S=\{-s:s\in S\}$. Indeed a lower bound $l$ for $S$ gives the upper bound $-l$ for $-S$; negating its least upper bound gives a lower bound for $S$ greater than every other one.

Neither $\sup\varnothing$ nor $\inf\varnothing$ is defined in $\mathbb R$: every real is an upper and lower bound, with no least upper or greatest lower bound. If another construction stipulates the value zero for an empty path family, that stipulation is a separate total definition, not $\sup\varnothing=0$. Infinite values require an explicitly specified extended ordered set; no extended-real field operations are introduced here.

Let $X$ be a set and use the ordered real field of [[def-real-numbers]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and [[def-ordered-field]]. In the convention of [[def-metric-space]], a **real metric** is a function $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying, for all $x,y,z\in X$, separation $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$, symmetry $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ and the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. A **real pseudometric** replaces separation by $d(x,x)=0$ and retains the other two axioms. All values are finite real numbers. Neither definition assumes nonnegativity as an additional axiom.

For either structure, put $B_d(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$ for real $r>0$. The induced topology consists of the subsets $O\subseteq X$ for which every $x\in O$ admits $r>0$ with $B_d(x,r)\subseteq O$. After the nonnegativity deduction in the well-definedness lemma, these balls form a basis: $x\in B_d(x,r)$ by reflexivity, and if $z\in B_d(x,r)\cap B_d(y,s)$, the positive radius $t=\min\{r-d(x,z),s-d(y,z)\}$ has $B_d(z,t)$ contained in that intersection by the triangle inequality. This argument also works for pseudometrics and for empty $X$ (the empty topology). No infinite-distance, semimetric or quasimetric convention is consumed.

Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.

Let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be real periods, let
$\Lambda:=L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R^3$,
and let $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/\Lambda$ be the quotient
map with the quotient topology. Then $q$ is a smooth local diffeomorphism and
$\mathbb T^3_L$ is a compact,
Hausdorff, second-countable smooth three-manifold without boundary.

The forms $dx^1,dx^2,dx^3$ and coordinate vector fields
$\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3$ on $\mathbb R^3$ descend to global smooth
forms and vector fields on $\mathbb T^3_L$. Every smooth $\Lambda$-periodic
function on $\mathbb R^3$ descends to a smooth function on $\mathbb T^3_L$.
Consequently, $M_L:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times\mathbb T^3_L$ has a smooth,
boundaryless four-manifold structure and carries the smooth Lorentzian metric,
orientation, and time orientation

$$g:=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2,\qquad N:=\partial_0,\qquad o:=dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3.$$

In the product charts from the quotient atlas the metric has constant matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and its metric-selected Christoffel symbols
vanish.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $M$ carry an orientation in the
sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] (so that its
charts that are oriented in that orientation have orientation-preserving
transition maps), and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection. This item
fixes the metric volume form, the flux of a current through oriented $3$-faces
and finite-chain charges. The orientation of $M$ is an independent datum: it is
not determined by the metric and not by the time orientation.

**(a) Metric volume density and volume form.** Let $(U,x)$ be an oriented
chart, with metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a)). Define the **metric volume
density**

$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a strictly positive smooth function because $g_{ab}$ is smooth and
$g_p$ is nondegenerate. In the chart define the local $4$-form

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}:=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3,$$

with the exterior product of [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]] and the
coordinate covector fields of
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. That these local
forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing
$4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together
with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively
oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has
$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

**(b) Current flux through oriented $3$-faces and chains.** Let $J$ be a
smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **current
$3$-form** of $J$ is the contraction

$$\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

the interior product of the $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ with $J$
([[def-interior-product-of-a-form-by-a-vector-field]]).

By a **smooth singular $k$-simplex** of $M$ — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-simplex` (differential-geometry track),
restated here so this page is self-contained — we mean a map
$\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ whose domain is the standard $k$-simplex
$$\Delta^k=\Bigl\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_it_i=1\Bigr\},$$
for which there exist an open set $O\subseteq A^k=\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\sum_it_i=1\}$
containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with
$\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$; the extension is not part of the simplex
data, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. With the integration of
forms over such simplices
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]), a **$3$-face** is
a smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$, and the **flux of $J$ through
$\sigma$** is the real number

$$\Phi_J(\sigma):=\int_\sigma\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

A **finite smooth singular $k$-chain** — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes`, restated here —
is a finite formal real linear combination $\Sigma=\sum_i c_i\sigma_i$ of
smooth singular $k$-simplices. For such a $3$-chain the **flux of $J$ through
$\Sigma$** is defined additively,

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma):=\sum_i c_i\,\Phi_J(\sigma_i),$$

a definition independent of the written expression for $\Sigma$, because a
finite formal sum is evaluated by adding the finitely many coefficients and
inserting a zero coefficient changes nothing. $\Phi_J(\Sigma)$ is the **charge**
of the current $J$ assigned to $\Sigma$ when the model reads $J$ as a conserved
current; that reading belongs to the physical postulates and is not part of
this definition.

**(c) Non-null faces and their unit normals.** A $3$-dimensional linear subspace
$H\subseteq T_pM$ is **nondegenerate** for $g_p$ when the restriction of $g_p$
to $H$ is nondegenerate, equivalently when $H\cap H^\perp=\{0\}$ in the
orthogonality of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. A
smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is **non-null at** a parameter point $t$
when the span of the three velocity vectors
$\sigma_*\partial_1|_t,\sigma_*\partial_2|_t,\sigma_*\partial_3|_t$ has
dimension $3$ and is nondegenerate at $\sigma(t)$, and **non-null** when this holds at every
parameter point. For a non-null face the **unit normal** $\nu$ at that point is
the unique vector of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$ with $\nu\in H^\perp$,
$g(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,+1\}$ and $(\nu,\sigma_*\partial_1,\sigma_*\partial_2,
\sigma_*\partial_3)$ a positively oriented basis of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$; its
existence, uniqueness and its sign $\varepsilon:=g(\nu,\nu)$ are proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c), together
with the density identity of clause (c) used to read $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ on
such a face. Rank-deficient faces and rank-three faces with degenerate induced
metric are not assigned a unit normal; their flux is defined
by the $3$-form $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ itself, as in clause (b).

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian
four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], let
$F\in\Omega^2(M)$ and $j\in\Gamma(TM)$ be smooth, and fix constants
$c,\mu_0>0$. Assume
$dF=0$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$, equivalently
$d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$ by
[[lem-emg-maxwell-current-forms]]. A finite smooth singular $k$-chain means
a finite formal real linear combination of smooth singular $k$-simplices,
with the boundary operation of
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] and
[[thm-stokes-theorem-for-smooth-singular-chains]].

For a finite smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define its charge by

$$Q(\Sigma):=\frac1c\int_\Sigma\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Then:

**(a) Gauss charge formula.** For every such $\Sigma$,

$$Q(\Sigma)=\frac{1}{\mu_0c}\int_{\partial\Sigma}\star_gF.$$

Consequently, if $\partial\Sigma=0$, then $Q(\Sigma)=0$. This is the
compact-cycle neutrality constraint for a smooth everywhere-defined sourced
field.

**(b) Bounding-surface restriction.** For every finite smooth singular
three-chain $V$, the magnetic flux through its boundary vanishes:

$$\int_{\partial V}F=0.$$

The equation $dF=0$ does not imply that the flux through every closed
two-cycle is zero; this item gives a zero-flux conclusion only when the cycle
is the boundary of a finite smooth chain in the field domain. Likewise, the
electric flux formula in (a) identifies charge with flux only for a bounding
surface.

**(c) Charge balance.** If a finite smooth singular four-chain $C$ satisfies
$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$ for three-chains
$\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2,B$, then

$$Q(\Sigma_2)-Q(\Sigma_1)=-Q(B).$$

Equal charge on the two slices therefore requires zero net side flux. No
asymptotic charge or flux at infinity is asserted; noncompact limits require
separate convergence and boundary-flux hypotheses.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.
