citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves and the relations $\le$, $\ll$, $I^{\pm}$, $J^{\pm}$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. All curves below are curves in
that sense.

**(a) Chronology and causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **chronological** when there is
no $p\in M$ with $p\ll p$, equivalently when there is no nonconstant future
timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$. It is **causal**
when there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with
$\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$; a nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
is called a **closed causal curve**, and a closed future timelike curve is
called a **closed timelike curve**.

**(b) Strong causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **strongly causal** when for every
$p\in M$ and every open set $U\subseteq M$ with $p\in U$ there is an open set
$V$ with $p\in V\subseteq U$ such that for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and all $a\le s<t\le b$ with $\gamma(s)\in V$ and
$\gamma(t)\in V$ one has $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V$. Thus no causal curve can
leave $V$ and later re-enter it; a set $V$ with this property for all causal
curves is called **causally convex for causal curves that meet it twice**.

**(c) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is **globally hyperbolic** when it is
strongly causal and for all $p,q\in M$ the **causal diamond**
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact in the subspace topology
([[def-compact-space]]).

**(d) Time functions.** A **time function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a function
$u:M\to\mathbb R$ which is continuous from the manifold topology to the usual topology of
$\mathbb R$: for every $p\in M$ and every open neighborhood $W$ of $u(p)$
there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ with $u(V)\subseteq W$
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). It also satisfies
$u(\gamma(a))<u(\gamma(b))$ for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ that is not constant on $[a,b]$.

**(e) Temporal functions.** A **temporal function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
function $u:M\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]])
whose gradient is past-directed timelike: writing $du$ for its differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]) and $\nabla u$ for the vector field
with $g(\nabla u,X)=du(X)$ for every smooth vector field $X$, constructed from
the inverse metric of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], one
has
$$g(\nabla u,\nabla u)<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad du(N)=g(\nabla u,N)>0 .$$
The first inequality says that the gradient is nowhere zero and timelike; the
second fixes it as past-directed for the chosen time orientation. No level set
of a temporal function is asserted here to be a hypersurface or to be
spacelike, and no relation between temporal functions and compactness is
asserted; those claims are proved separately where they are used.

**(f) Scope and conventions.** These are mathematical conditions on the
Lorentzian model. Different sources define global hyperbolicity by equivalent
but differently phrased conditions; this page fixes the formulation of (c)
and proves the implications it uses. In particular no equivalence between
global hyperbolicity and the existence of a Cauchy hypersurface is asserted
by this definition, and the physical reading of strong causality or global
hyperbolicity as predictability of a classical model is adopted only in the
framework postulates.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define
$$D^+(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve through }p \text{ meets }S\},$$
and dually $D^-(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve
through }p\text{ meets }S\}$, where "meets $S$" means that some parameter
value is mapped into $S$, and $D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$ is the **domain of
dependence** of $S$.

**(e) Cauchy horizon.** For a closed set $S\subseteq M$ the **future Cauchy
horizon** is
$$H^+(S):=D^+(S)\setminus I^-(D^+(S)),$$
the set of points of $D^+(S)$ that are not chronologically preceded by any
point of $D^+(S)$; dually $H^-(S):=D^-(S)\setminus I^+(D^-(S))$, and the
**Cauchy horizon** is $H(S):=H^+(S)\cup H^-(S)$.

**(f) Scope.** These are mathematical definitions. Neither existence of
Cauchy sets nor any relation between the objects defined here is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be an oriented time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

**(a) Characterization of Killing fields.** For every smooth vector field
$\xi$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), with
$\xi_b=g_{bc}\xi^c$ the lowered field,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0 .$$

**(b) Contraction along geodesics.** If $\xi$ is a Killing field and
$\gamma:I\to M$ is a geodesic with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its affine parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]), then $t\mapsto
g_{\gamma(t)}(\xi_{\gamma(t)},\gamma'(t))$ is constant on $I$.

**(c) Conserved current.** Let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let $T$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $U$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) with
$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$, and let $\xi$ be a Killing field on $U$. Then
$J^{a}:=T^{ab}\xi_b$ is a smooth vector field on $U$ with
$\nabla_aJ^a=0$; consequently the flux balance of
[[thm-gr-density-divergence-and-finite-chain-flux]] clause (b) applies to $J$
on every smooth singular $4$-chain contained in $U$.

**(d) On-shell conservation of the Hilbert tensor.** Let $c>0$, let
$S:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be a model action with Hilbert stress-energy tensor
$T$ at $(g,\varphi)$ with respect to $c$
([[def-gr-hilbert-stress-energy-tensor]]). For the flow diffeomorphisms $F$
below, suppose the configuration set $\mathcal X$ carries specified maps
$P_F:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ with $P_{\mathrm{id}}=\mathrm{id}$; write
$F^*\varphi:=P_F(\varphi)$. For geometric matter fields these are the
model's pullbacks; no pullback operation on an arbitrary set is implicit.
For **every** smooth compactly supported vector field $\xi$, its flow
$\Phi_v$ is global
([[def-complete-vector-field]], [[def-local-and-global-flow]]); this holds for
every compactly supported smooth field, using the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] through
[[thm-compactly-supported-vector-fields-are-complete]]. Write
$G(u,v):=S(\Phi_v^*g,\Phi_u^*\varphi)$ for the simultaneous pullback by the
flow (this presupposes that the pairs lie in $\mathcal D$, which is part of the
hypotheses below). Suppose (H1)–(H4) hold for **every** such $\xi$ (with
its own $G$ and parameter neighborhood):

- **(H1)** the map $G$ is defined on a neighborhood of $(0,0)$ in
  $\mathbb R^2$ and is differentiable at $(0,0)$;
- **(H2)** $\partial_uG(0,0)=0$ (the matter configuration $\varphi$ satisfies
  its model equations in this direction);
- **(H3)** $\partial_vG(0,0)=-\frac{1}{2c}\int_MT_{ab}q^{ab}\mathrm{vol}_g$,
  where $q^{ab}:=\partial_v(\Phi_v^*g)^{ab}|_{v=0}$ (the metric variation is
  represented by the Hilbert tensor);
- **(H4)** $G(s,s)=S(g,\varphi)$ whenever $(s,s)$ lies in that neighborhood
  (invariance of the action under simultaneous pullback by the flow).

Then $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $M$.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].
The local Riemannian volume densities glue to a positive smooth density independent of coordinates.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold and assume countable choice. For a smooth compactly supported function $f:M\to\mathbb R$, define $\int_M f\mu_g$ by the intrinsic smooth density integral. More generally every compactly supported signed smooth density $\sigma$ on $M$ has its existing intrinsic integral, independently of a Riemannian metric.

[[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]] makes $f\mu_g$ a smooth compactly supported density. Apply [[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]] and [[thm-density-integration-is-defined-without-an-orientation]]; [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited precisely at chart-partition selection. In a chart the summand is the integral of the partition-weighted coefficient $f\sqrt{\det G}$. On a zero-manifold it is the finite sum of scalar density values, and empty support gives zero. No orientation is required.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Compactly supported smooth density integration is independent of charts and partition, linear, local, nonnegative on nonnegative densities and strictly positive for a nonzero nonnegative density. It is invariant under every diffeomorphism, without choosing an orientation. The finite-parametrization formula holds under the hypotheses of [[prop-integration-of-top-forms-by-finite-parametrizations]], with orientation preservation omitted and absolute Jacobians used.

Let $A \subseteq \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be **any** subset of the extended real
line ([[def-extended-reals]]) and write $A_{\mathbb{R}} := A \cap \mathbb{R}$.
Then $A$ has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound in
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-upper-bound]]), each unique, which we write
$\sup A$ and $\inf A$ with the ambient set always $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$.
Explicitly:

- $\sup A = +\infty$ if $+\infty \in A$, or if $A_{\mathbb{R}}$ is not bounded above in $\mathbb{R}$;
- $\sup A = -\infty$ if $+\infty \notin A$ and $A_{\mathbb{R}} = \emptyset$;
- $\sup A$ is the real supremum $\sup A_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) if $+\infty \notin A$ and $A_{\mathbb{R}}$ is nonempty and bounded above in $\mathbb{R}$;

and dually, with $-\infty$ and $+\infty$ exchanged and "above" replaced by
"below", for $\inf A$ ([[def-infimum]], [[thm-infimum-property]]).

**Agreement.** If $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is nonempty and bounded above in
$\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-bounded-set]]) then $\sup A$ computed in
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is the real number $\sup A$ of
[[def-complete-ordered-field]]; if $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is nonempty and
bounded below then $\inf A$ computed in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is the real
number $\inf A$ of [[thm-infimum-property]]. In particular the notation is
unambiguous on the sets for which the real supremum and infimum are defined, and
$\sup \emptyset = -\infty$, $\inf \emptyset = +\infty$ in
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}$.

**No hypothesis is placed on $A$.** This is exactly what the real supremum cannot
do, and it is why every $\limsup$ statement on this page holds for every sequence
rather than for bounded ones only. It is also not a weakening of the discipline
this library keeps around suprema: the operation supplied here is a *different*
operation, taken in a *different* ordered set, and the agreement clause records
exactly where the two coincide.

derivations.claim: Clause (a) reuses the exact global definitions in [F1]. For the smaller class in (d), on each compact parameter segment a finite $C^1$ partition has bounded coordinate derivatives on its compact pieces. Thus the coordinates are absolutely continuous there. On chart overlaps the ordinary chain rule carries the tangent by the transition Jacobian, preserving its nonzero future causal property; refinements of finite partitions preserve the class. The finitely many joining parameters on each compact segment have measure zero. Consequently the selected paths satisfy the global almost-everywhere causal convention, while retaining the stronger piecewise regularity required by this particular observable. The quantifiers in (d) define a subset of the specified $U$, whose relative topological boundary is unique even when the escape set is empty or all of $U$.

At a hypersurface point put $w=g^{-1}(df,\cdot)$. Nondegeneracy gives $w\ne0$ and $T_pH=w^\perp$. The radical of $g|_{T_pH}$ is $T_pH\cap(T_pH)^\perp=w^\perp\cap\operatorname{span}(w)$, so it is nonzero exactly when $g(w,w)=g^{-1}(df,df)=0$. Replacing the defining function replaces $df$ on $H$ by a nonzero scalar multiple and leaves this criterion unchanged. The Killing equivalence is precisely [F2]; no field equation is used.

The spacelike condition makes $h$ positive definite. Under a section coordinate change with Jacobian $J$, $h'=J^ThJ$, so $\sqrt{\det h'}=|\det J|\sqrt{\det h}$. Thus [F3] makes every test integral in (c) intrinsic and finite. The test family contains the zero function, whose integral is zero, and every test density $\chi\mu_h$ is nonnegative, so every integral is nonnegative by [F5]. Its set of values is a subset of $\overline{\mathbb R}$ and therefore has an extended-real supremum by [F6]. On compact $S$, the constant test $1$ is allowed. For every other test, linearity and nonnegativity in [F5] give $\int_S\mu_h-\int_S\chi\mu_h=\int_S(1-\chi)\mu_h\ge0$; hence the supremum equals $\int_S\mu_h$. The same definition gives zero on the empty section without choosing an orientation. The norm of the specified stationary field is a smooth scalar, so the positive-norm set is open; continuity excludes positive and negative norm at its boundary, proving that boundary lies in its zero set. No converse is inferred.

In a chart at an approached point the $C^2$ coefficients of $\widetilde g$ and their derivatives through order two are continuous. Nondegeneracy makes the inverse coefficients continuous by the cofactor-over-determinant formula and continuously differentiable as needed for the Christoffel expression. The curvature formula therefore has continuous coefficients, as does every specified polynomial complete contraction with inverse metrics. Such a scalar has a finite value at the point and converges to it along $j(x_n)$. On the embedded open image these scalars equal those of $g$, since the isometric embedding identifies the metric, connection and curvature. Their absolute values cannot be unbounded along that convergent sequence. This proves precisely the stated obstruction; it makes no assertion about distributional equations or parametrized geodesics.

On $H_*$, $g(\xi,\xi)$ vanishes, so its differential annihilates $TH$. The nonzero covector $\xi^\flat$ also annihilates $TH$, which has codimension one; hence the differential is a unique scalar multiple of $\xi^\flat$. Locally choose a smooth transverse field $Z$ with $\xi^\flat(Z)\ne0$. Then $\kappa_H=-d(g(\xi,\xi))(Z)/(2\xi^\flat(Z))$ is smooth and independent of $Z$, proving existence, uniqueness and patching. Constant scaling multiplies the left side by $a^2$ and the covector by $a$, giving $a\kappa_H$. The required nonempty dense $H_*$ excludes the identically zero Killing field and any open portion with zero generator, while allowing bifurcation zeros in its closure. At zeros of $\xi$ this division is unavailable. If a smooth extension from an adjacent nonzero portion exists, its values at closure points are uniquely fixed by continuity; no existence or zeroth-law claim follows.

The positive rest metric and projection supplied by [F4] uniquely identify each spatial covector with a spatial vector. Integral curves are maps into the spacetime, a chart is a coordinate map, and a tetrad is a basis field; identifying spatial component lists with one of those objects is not licensed. All clauses therefore define intrinsic objects with their stated inputs and qualifications, without imposing a potential or changing a field equation.

boundaries.evidence: Proof 1.1 defines the relative boundary even for empty/full escape sets; Proof 1.3 gives empty-section area zero.

Definition (b) and Proof 2.1 require the nonzero-generator part to be nonempty and dense, excluding the identically zero Killing field; bifurcation values are used only through an existing smooth extension. Zero surface gravity is allowed.
Definition and Proof 1.1: A Cauchy intersection is exactly one parameter value by clause (a), not merely one image point.
Proof 1.2 proves both directions of the null degeneracy criterion; the spacelike area metric and extended spacetime metric must remain nondegenerate in their stated senses.
Proof 1.1 uses finite partitions on every compact parameter segment, with one-sided piece derivatives; Proof 1.4 treats an explicitly approached added point.
Definition and Proof 1.3: Clause (c) explicitly assumes AC_omega for chart-partition integration. The area test family contains zero, so its supremum needs no arbitrary selection.
Proof 1.2 derives null conormal square from degeneracy; Killing equivalence is the exact canonical supplier.
Proof 1.2 derives degeneracy from null conormal square. No converse from stationary-limit zero to ergosurface or root to horizon is asserted.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented and time-oriented four-manifold with smooth Lorentz metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, as in [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Use its metric-selected connection and curvature convention. Fix $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $\mu_0>0$, and $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, and put

$$\kappa:=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}>0.$$

Within this formulation, $c$, $G_N$, $\mu_0$, and $\Lambda$ are primitive model parameters: respectively, the time-to-length conversion parameter, the gravitational coupling parameter, the electromagnetic normalization parameter identified with vacuum permeability in the SI convention, and the coefficient of the cosmological term. Their values are not derived by this definition, and no numerical value or empirical exactness claim is made here. The coupling $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$ is derived from $G_N$ and $c$. For the SI interpretation, $c$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $G_N$ has units $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\mu_0$ has units $\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$, $\kappa$ has units $\mathrm{s^2\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$, and $\Lambda$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$. In a length-coordinate chart $x^0=ct$, metric components are dimensionless and curvature components have units $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$.

For a smooth real two-form $F\in\Omega^2(M)$, define

$$Q_{ab}(g,F):=F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd},\qquad T^{\rm EM}_{ab}:=\mu_0^{-1}Q_{ab}(g,F).$$

Indices are raised with $g^{-1}$; $\star_g$ is the Lorentzian Hodge star of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. The electromagnetic stress tensor $T^{\rm EM}$ is a symmetric covariant two-tensor; in an orthonormal frame its components have energy-density units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. If $n$ is a future unit normal and $(\mathfrak e_1,\mathfrak e_2,\mathfrak e_3)$ is a positively oriented orthonormal spatial triad, define $e_i:=F(\mathfrak e_i,n)$ and $b_i:=\tfrac12\epsilon_i{}^{jk}F(\mathfrak e_j,\mathfrak e_k)$. By [[lem-emg-observer-field-decomposition]], these are $E_i/c$ and $B_i$ in the SI observer convention; both have units tesla.

For sign clarity only, a sourced extension would write $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0J^b$ for a smooth current vector $J$; the source-free system below is the case $J=0$.

The **source-free electrovacuum tensor Cauchy system** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is the system for a smooth Lorentz metric $g$ and smooth real two-form $F$ on $U$ given by

$$G_{ab}[g]+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T^{\rm EM}_{ab}[g,F],\qquad dF=0,\qquad d(\star_gF)=0.$$

Here $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 Sg_{ab}$ is the Einstein tensor. A **spacelike initial hypersurface** is a smooth spacelike embedded three-manifold $i:\Sigma\hookrightarrow U$ with induced Riemannian metric $h=i^*g$ and future unit normal $n$, using [[def-gr-spacelike-initial-data-and-constraints]]. Its second fundamental form is $K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$ for tangent vectors $X,Y$. The notation $K=\tfrac12\mathcal L_nh$ requires an induced-metric family: locally near each $p\in\Sigma$, define $\Phi(t,q)=\gamma_{q,n_q}(t)$ by the ambient geodesic with initial position $q$ and initial tangent $n_q$. Smooth dependence of geodesics and the inverse function theorem give, after shrinking around $(0,p)$, a local diffeomorphism $\Phi:(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\times V\to U_p$; its slices remain spacelike after a further shrinking. Put $h_t:=\Phi_t^*g$ on $V$. In local slice coordinates $y^i$, differentiating $(h_t)_{ij}=g_{ab}(\Phi(t,y))\partial_i\Phi^a\partial_j\Phi^b$ at $t=0$ gives
$$\left.\partial_t(h_t)_{ij}\right|_{0}=n^c\partial_cg_{ab}\,\partial_i\Phi^a\partial_j\Phi^b+g_{cb}(\partial_i n^c)\partial_j\Phi^b+g_{ac}\partial_i\Phi^a(\partial_jn^c)=g(\nabla_{\partial_i}n,\partial_j\Phi)+g(\nabla_{\partial_j}n,\partial_i\Phi)=2K_{ij},$$
using metric compatibility, torsion-freeness and symmetry of $K$. Thus $\mathcal L_nh$ denotes only this initial derivative of the local induced-metric family; no global normal foliation or uniform time width is assumed. A hypersurface is a **Cauchy hypersurface in $U$** exactly when every inextendible causal curve $\gamma:I\to U$ meets it at exactly one parameter value, that is, $\gamma^{-1}[i(\Sigma)]$ has exactly one element, using the causal-curve convention of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]. The local initial-data constructions require a spacelike initial hypersurface; they do not assume this global intersection property. The initial data are the induced $(h,K,e,b)$, where $e,b$ are the spatial fields just defined. No global electromagnetic potential is part of this definition.

In the SI convention the electromagnetic two-form has orthonormal-frame components in tesla, $T^{\rm EM}_{ab}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and every term of the Einstein equation has units $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$. The equations define a mathematical model; they do not assert that the model describes nature or that arbitrary Cauchy data have a development.

derivations.claim:
In a chart the inverse matrix of $g$ is $C^1$. Its Christoffel formula
has continuous coefficients symmetric in its lower indices. Substitution
into $\nabla_ag_{bc}$ cancels the first metric derivatives and gives zero,
so raising indices commutes with the connection on $C^1$ tensors. The
antisymmetrized connection terms also cancel, giving
$\nabla_aF_{bc}+\nabla_bF_{ca}+\nabla_cF_{ab}=0$ from $dF=0$.
Multiplying by $F^{ac}$ and exchanging $a,c$ in the third term gives
$2F^{ac}\nabla_aF_{bc}=\tfrac12\partial_b(F_{cd}F^{cd})$. Every term is
continuous and uses only the stated first derivatives.

Raise the first stress index and differentiate by the product rule:
$\nabla_a(T^{\mathrm{EM}})^a{}_b=\mu_0^{-1}[(\nabla_aF^{ac})F_{bc}+F^{ac}\nabla_aF_{bc}-\tfrac14\partial_b(F_{cd}F^{cd})]$.
The last two terms cancel by step 1.1. Inserting the sourced equation then
gives $-F_{bc}J^c$; setting $J=0$ gives conservation. Metric compatibility
identifies this with $\nabla^aT^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}$. Thus the identity
holds at $C^1$ without applying a smooth-only stress theorem.

In the orthonormal basis, $F_{0i}=-e_i$ and
$F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$, so
$F_{ab}F^{ab}=2(|b|^2-|e|^2)$. The $00$ component of
$F_{ac}F_b{}^c$ is $|e|^2$, and its $0i$ component is
$-e_j\epsilon_{ijk}b_k=-(e\times b)_i$.
Substitution into the stress formula gives its two displayed observer
projections. All calculations are at a single point, require no derivatives
of the basis, and apply also when either field is zero.

boundaries.evidence: Statement is a pointwise identity on a supplied manifold. On an empty open restriction every tensor identity is vacuous; proof1.1–3.1 selects no initial datum or solution.
Proof step3.1 gives T=0 when F=0 and the identity in2.1 remains valid with continuous J=0. Vanishing e or b separately is included without division by field amplitude.

boundaries.reason: Statement fixes a four-dimensional two-form and three spatial observer components; there is no variable one-component theory or cardinality parameter.

boundaries.evidence: Statement requires a nondegenerate C1Lorentzmetric and mu0>0. Proof1.1 inverts only that metric;2.1 divides only by mu0. Singular metrics and mu0=0 are excluded.

boundaries.reason: Statement proves a local differential identity, not existence or extension at a PDE or affine-parameter endpoint.
Proof step1.1 is a coordinate calculation and3.1 uses one pointwise orthonormal basis; it constructs no global frame, potential or selected family.
Statement derives stress divergence from closedness and the sourced Maxwell equation; it does not characterize Maxwell fields by an iff involving stress conservation.
Proof step2.1 does not infer Maxwell equations from stress conservation. Contracting the Maxwell divergence with F loses information when F is degenerate or zero.

citations.quote: Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

derivations.claim: The constraints in the Statement are the normal projections and Maxwell Gauss constraints of the model [L1] under the stated $K,e,b$ conventions. Initialization [L3] gives $H=0$ and the compatible derivative variables $p=\bar\nabla_0g$, $q_i=\bar\nabla_i g$ on the initial slice. The initial state lies in $H^s$: $h\in H^{s+1}$ gives $q_i\in H^s$, $K,e,b\in H^s$, and the harmonic normal derivatives are in $H^s$ by the smooth composition estimates [F7] on the compact range of the uniformly positive $h$. Compactness of $\mathbb T^3$ and $h\ge c_0I$ place the initial state in a compact subset of the open admissible set.

(Endpoint product and composition estimates.) Put $\langle k\rangle=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For integer $m\in\{2,3\}$, the inequality $\langle k\rangle^m\le 2^{m-1}(\langle\ell\rangle^m+\langle k-\ell\rangle^m)$ and the convolution formula for Fourier coefficients give $$\|uv\|_{H^m}\le C_m\bigl(\|\langle k\rangle^m\widehat u\|_{\ell^2}\|\widehat v\|_{\ell^1}+\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^1}\|\langle k\rangle^m\widehat v\|_{\ell^2}\bigr).$$ Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^1}\le(\sum_k\langle k\rangle^{-2m})^{1/2}\|u\|_{H^m}$, and the weight sum is finite in dimension three for $m\ge2$; the analogous bound holds for $v$. Young's convolution inequality (or the triangle inequality in $\ell^2$ followed by summation in $\ell^1$) therefore proves the algebra estimate in both $H^2$ and $H^3$. For a smooth finite-dimensional map $G$ on a neighborhood of a compact value set, Fourier approximation and the chain rule through order three show that $G(Z)\in H^3$ when $Z\in H^3$: the terms are bounded-coefficient multiples of $D^\alpha Z$, products $DZ\,D^2Z$, or products of at most three first derivatives; $H^3\hookrightarrow C^1$ places first derivatives in $L^\infty$ and the highest derivatives in $L^2$. The same expansions show continuity under strong $H^3$ convergence, since $H^3\hookrightarrow C^1$ gives uniform convergence of the coefficients and first derivatives while higher derivatives converge in $L^2$. This also covers smooth dependence on $(t,x)$ on a compact coefficient-time slab. Together with the supplied estimates at orders $H^k$ for $k\ge4$ in [F7], these are the endpoint estimates needed below.

By [F1], the metric and Maxwell principal blocks are symmetric with positive time matrices and have no derivative coupling. At the initial orthogonal state $g^{00}<0$, $(g^{ij})>0$ and $\alpha>0$; these strict inequalities persist on a compact admissible state neighborhood, so the complete coefficient family meets the positivity and compact-state assumptions of [L5]. Applying that draft supplier conditionally gives the reduced solution and its $L^\infty H^s\cap C H^{s-1}$ and $\partial_tU\in L^\infty H^{s-1}$ bounds. The actual inspected generic existence theorem [F4] states the same periodic coefficient interface and is marked published with precheck pending; it is independent current support, not acceptance of the CP01 draft supplier.

The first-order metric equations impose $ ar
abla_0g=p$ and $ ar
abla_0q_i- ar
abla_ip=\mathcal C_i$, where $\mathcal C_i=[ ar
abla_0, ar
abla_i]g$ is the fixed background-curvature commutator. For $Z_i=q_i- ar
abla_i g$, subtract the commutator identity for $g$ from the equation for $q_i$. The derivative-slot connection terms cancel and give a homogeneous linear ODE along each coordinate time line for $Z_i$; its initial value is zero by [L3], so uniqueness for a linear ODE gives $Z_i=0$. Thus $q_i= ar
abla_i g$ throughout the interval.

(Third-order spacetime regularity.) The Fourier norm identity $\|g\|_{H^{s+1}}^2\asymp\|g\|_{H^s}^2+\sum_i\|\partial_i g\|_{H^s}^2$, together with step 3.1 and the smooth background coefficients, gives $g\in L^\infty H^{s+1}$. The same identity at one lower order and the $C H^{s-1}$ continuity of the first-order state give $g\in C H^s$. The tetrad reconstruction of $F$ is a smooth algebraic function of $(g,e,b)$ on the compact admissible state set; [F7] gives $F\in L^\infty H^s\cap C H^{s-1}$. Solve the reduced system as $U_t=\mathcal R(t,x,U,\partial_iU)$ with $\mathcal R$ smooth on the compact admissible range. For every $s\ge5$, $U\in C H^{s-1}$ and $\partial_iU\in C H^{s-2}$; the composition estimates of [F7] at orders at least four and step 1.2 at orders two and three give $U_t\in C H^{s-2}$. Differentiating this identity in time, justified by Fourier approximation and the same chain/product estimates, gives $$U_{tt}=D_U\mathcal R(t,x,U,\partial U)U_t+D_{\partial U}\mathcal R(t,x,U,\partial U)\partial U_t.$$ Its coefficient maps lie in $C H^{s-2}$, while $\partial U_t\in C H^{s-3}$; the algebra estimates of [F7] for orders at least four and of step 1.2 for orders two and three imply $U_{tt}\in C H^{s-3}$. At the base order $s=5$, these spaces are $H^3$ and $H^2$, and for $s=6$ the lower product order is $H^3$, also covered by step 1.2. The identities $p=\bar\nabla_0g$ and $q_i=\bar\nabla_i g$ then give all third spatial derivatives of $g$ from two spatial derivatives of $q$, the $t^2x$ derivatives from one spatial derivative of $p_t$, and $t^3$ derivatives from $p_{tt}$; the other derivatives of total order at most three follow directly from $p,q\in C H^4$ and $p_t\in C H^3$. Since $H^2(\mathbb T^3)\hookrightarrow C^0$, all these derivatives are continuous. The same smooth composition argument gives $F\in C^2$ from $(g,e,b)$, so the classical regularity required by [F2] and [F3] holds.

Maxwell propagation [F2] now gives $dF=d\star_gF=0$. The exact Hodge-to-divergence identity in [L4] converts the second equation to $\nabla_aF^{ab}=0$, so the stress supplier applies with $j=0$ and gives $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$. Thus [F3] applies with the initial Einstein constraints and $H=0$ from [L3]; hence the reduced metric equation is the full Einstein equation. Smooth persistence [F5] applies to smooth data on the same interval. Finally, [F6] applies to any two reduced solutions on a common interval with these uniform compact-state and $H^s$ bounds and yields both uniqueness and the claimed $C H^{s-1}$ continuous-dependence estimate.

(Local smooth data on an arbitrary slice.) Fix a point of a smooth initial three-manifold and choose an orthogonal spacetime chart over a relatively compact slice ball, with the prescribed smooth background connection. The initial harmonic state from [L3] and its admissibility inequalities take values, after shrinking the ball, in a convex finite-dimensional neighborhood whose closure lies in the open symmetric-hyperbolic state set. Extend the state by a smooth cutoff to a constant admissible state on a periodic three-torus; convexity keeps all values in that neighborhood. Extend the coefficient matrices by the same spatial cutoff, interpolating $A^0$ to the identity and each symmetric $A^i$ and the lower-order term to zero. The convex cone of positive matrices preserves a positive time matrix, and the spatial matrices remain symmetric. The conditional local solver in [F1] therefore gives a smooth reduced solution on a torus cylinder, which satisfies the original reduced equations wherever the cutoff is one. The derivative-definition relations remain valid along the time lines there, by the same homogeneous commutator ODE as step 3.1. The Maxwell divergence residuals vanish near the chosen point by the local flow argument of [F2]. The Einstein constraints and $H=0$ hold on the initial ball; the local cone-energy proof of [F3] therefore gives $H=0$ in a smaller domain of dependence. On that neighborhood the reduced solution solves the full source-free system. This proves the additional local existence clause without imposing constraints on the auxiliary extension outside the slice ball.

$$g\in L^\infty H^{s+1}\cap C^0H^s,\qquad \partial_tg\in L^\infty H^s\cap C^0H^{s-1},\qquad F\in L^\infty H^s\cap C^0H^{s-1}.$$
The initial two-form is reconstructed by $F(n,\mathsf e_i)=-e_i$ and $F(\mathsf e_i,\mathsf e_j)=\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$; no independent Maxwell normal derivative is prescribed.

Let $s\ge5$ be an integer, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $A^\mu,B$ ($\mu=0,1,2,3$) be a periodic symmetric-hyperbolic coefficient family on $I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O$ in the exact sense of [[def-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-system]]: the coefficient maps are smooth, each $A^\mu$ is a real symmetric matrix, and $A^0$ is positive definite.

**(b) Continuous dependence.** Let $K'\subseteq O$ be compact with
$K\subseteq\operatorname{int}K'$ and let $T>0$ be a time for which the existence
theorem [[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-existence]] produces solutions
from every datum with values in $K$ and norm at most $R$, with values in $K'$
and the bounds $C(1+R)$ of that theorem.

for every $u_0\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ taking values in $K$ with
$\|u_0\|_{H^s}\le R$ there is a Sobolev solution
$u:(-T,T)\to H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ of $(\star)$ with
$u(0)=u_0$ which is classical and satisfies
$$u\in L^\infty((-T,T);H^s)\cap C^0((-T,T);H^{s-1}),\quad \partial_tu\in L^\infty((-T,T);H^{s-1}),$$
$$\sup_{|t|<T}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}\le C(1+R),\qquad \sup_{|t|<T}\|\partial_tu(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le C(1+R),$$
and whose values lie in $K'$.

For the geometric data convention, orient $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ by the ordered dimensionless coordinates $(\theta^1,\theta^2,\theta^3)$; the corresponding length-coordinate frame $(\partial_{X^1},\partial_{X^2},\partial_{X^3})$ has the same orientation.

Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as required by [[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]] and [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]; no use of the full Axiom of Choice is made here. Let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, its normalized measure, the componentwise real Sobolev spaces $H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$, and their weak-derivative and Fourier-coefficient conventions be exactly those of [[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]]. In particular, $H^s$ is defined for integer $s\ge0$, the weak-derivative norm is equivalent to the Fourier-weight norm by [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]], and the trigonometric characters are a complete orthonormal system by [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]. A field is a function with the domain and codomain declaration of [[def-function]]; Sobolev fields are its $L^2$-equivalence classes, not pointwise representatives.

For finite $m\ge1$, open $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, compact $K\subseteq O$, $R\ge0$, and integer $s\ge5$, define the bounded admissible initial-state class

$$\mathcal S_s(K,R):=\{u_0\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m):u_0\text{ has its continuous representative valued in }K,\ \|u_0\|_{H^s}\le R\}.$$

The representative is unique because two continuous functions equal almost everywhere on the torus agree everywhere. For a smooth periodic first-order reduction of the electrovacuum equations, its specified finite list of real state components is identified with one such $\mathbb R^m$-valued function; the state-component convention is part of that reduction. In the geometric data convention below, the component arrays are specified separately. This is a definition of admissible function-space classes only; it asserts no existence result for a coupled Einstein-Maxwell reduction.

For the geometric data convention, write the dimensionless torus coordinate as $\theta^i\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ and introduce a fixed length scale $L_0>0$ in metres. The corresponding length coordinates are $X^i=L_0\theta^i$ on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi L_0}:=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi L_0\mathbb Z)^3$; the Sobolev variable remains $\theta$, and $X$ is not a second name for a coordinate on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$. The arrays $h_{ij}(\theta)$ and $K_{ij}(\theta)$ are the covariant metric and second-fundamental-form components in the length-coordinate frame $\partial_{X^i}$, with $h_{ij}=h_{ji}$ and $K_{ij}=K_{ji}$. Let $\mathsf e_A(h)$, $A=1,2,3$, be the positively oriented $h$-orthonormal frame obtained by Gram-Schmidt from the ordered global frame $(\partial_{X^1},\partial_{X^2},\partial_{X^3})$. For spatial vectors $e,b$, the electromagnetic component arrays in this convention are $e_A:=h(e,\mathsf e_A)$ and $b_A:=h(b,\mathsf e_A)$; these are the orthonormal observer components used in the Einstein-Maxwell first-order reduction. The frame coefficients are smooth functions of the positive matrix $(h_{ij})$. If $h\in H^{s+1}$ has range in a compact subset of the positive-definite matrices, the composition supplier gives these coefficients in $H^{s+1}$; since $s\ge5$, the Sobolev-algebra supplier gives their products with coordinate vector components in $H^s$. The inverse frame matrix has the same property, so the coordinate and orthonormal component arrays describe the same $H^s$ vector fields.

Thus the data component spaces mean $(h_{ij})\in H^{s+1}(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^9)$ with values in symmetric positive matrices, $(K_{ij})\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^9)$ with values in symmetric matrices, and $(e_A),(b_A)\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^3)$. A smooth periodic first-order state also includes the specified component functions of that reduction and the first spatial metric derivatives; in the above length-coordinate convention $v_{kij}:=\partial_{X^k}h_{ij}=L_0^{-1}\partial_{\theta^k}h_{ij}$ and $K_{ij}$ carry one inverse-length factor. For a fixed field scale $F_0>0$ in tesla, the dimensionless physical component arrays are $h_{ij}$, $L_0K_{ij}$, $L_0v_{kij}$, $e_A/F_0$, and $b_A/F_0$. Each fixed rescaling is invertible and preserves the finite-component Sobolev topology. These are component and unit conventions, not additional field equations.

derivations.claim: The reduced equation has the form $A^0(U)\partial_tU+A^i(U)\partial_iU+B(U)=0$ in the sense of [[def-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-system]]. On the compact state set, $A^0(U)^{-1}$ and the coefficients are bounded smooth functions. Since $\|U\|_{H^s}$ is uniformly bounded and $H^{s-1}$ is an algebra for $s\ge5$, the equation and the composition estimates [F4] give a uniform bound $\|\partial_tU\|_{H^{s-1}}\le C_R$; this agrees with the bound in [F3]. This supplies endpoint time-derivative control even if it was not separately included in the displayed regularity.

For each finite Fourier projection $P_N$, every coefficient of $P_NU$ is absolutely continuous and its derivative is the corresponding coefficient of $P_N\partial_tU$. Thus $\|P_NU(t)-P_NU(t')\|_{H^{s-1}}\le C_R|t-t'|$. Letting $N\to\infty$ and using Fourier convergence in $H^{s-1}$ gives the same estimate for $U(t)-U(t')$. Hence $U(t)$ has a strong $H^{s-1}$ limit $U_T$ as $t\uparrow T$.

For each finite frequency set $\{|k|\le N\}$, strong convergence of its coefficients gives
$$\sum_{|k|\le N}(1+|k|^2)^s|\widehat U_T(k)|^2=\lim_{t\uparrow T}\sum_{|k|\le N}(1+|k|^2)^s|\widehat U(t,k)|^2\le R^2,$$
where $R=\sup_{t<T}\|U(t)\|_{H^s}$. Taking the supremum over $N$ in the Fourier definition [F4] proves $U_T\in H^s$ and $\|U_T\|_{H^s}\le R$. By the embedding in [F4], $U(t)\to U_T$ uniformly in space. Since each $U(t,x)$ lies in the fixed compact state set, the closedness of that set gives $U_T(x)$ in the same set for every $x$.

The derivative identities from [F1] pass to $U_T$: $q_T=\bar\nabla_i g_T$ because these relations are continuous in the strong $H^{s-1}$ limit. Since $q_T\in H^s$, the Fourier norm identity gives $g_T\in H^{s+1}$; likewise $p_T,e_T,b_T\in H^s$. At the endpoint order $H^3$ needed when $s=5$, the Fourier convolution estimate $\langle k\rangle^3\le4(\langle\ell\rangle^3+\langle k-\ell\rangle^3)$ and $\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^1}\le(\sum_k\langle k\rangle^{-6})^{1/2}\|u\|_{H^3}$ prove $\|uv\|_{H^3}\le C\|u\|_{H^3}\|v\|_{H^3}$; the same argument with exponent $2$ proves the $H^2$ product estimate. The chain rule through order three, $H^3\hookrightarrow C^1$, and Fourier approximation give continuity of smooth composition in $H^3$ on compact value sets: first derivatives converge uniformly, higher derivatives converge in $L^2$, and every chain-rule product therefore converges in $L^2$. In particular, matrix inversion is continuous in $H^3$ on a compact set of positive-definite metrics. For $s\ge6$ the supplied algebra/composition estimates at $H^{s-2}\ge H^4$ apply directly, and for $s=5$ these local $H^3$ estimates cover the curvature and connection products. The constraints involve at most two spatial derivatives of $h_T$ and one derivative of $K_T,e_T,b_T$, which converge in $H^{s-2}$ from the first-order state and its derivative identities; each inverse-metric factor and each product in the constraint expressions is thus continuous at the endpoint. The harmonic vector is a smooth function of $(g_T,p_T,q_T)$, so $H_T=0$ as the limit of $H(t)=0$. Therefore $U_T$ determines constrained data of precisely the regularity required by [F1].

Restart the same harmonic-reduced coefficient system at time $T$ with the actual complete state $U_T$, keeping the fixed background and coordinates unchanged. The coefficients are smooth on the same time-state domain, $T$ is interior to its time interval, and step 3.1 supplies an $H^s$ datum with compact admissible range and bounded norm. Applying [L1] (equivalently [F3] after translating time) gives a reduced solution $V$ on $(T-\varepsilon,T+\varepsilon)$ with $V(T)=U_T$. This uses no reinitialization to lapse one, shift zero, or the special metric jet of the original initial slice. The reduction's equations propagate $q_i- ar
abla_i g=0$ by the homogeneous background-commutator ODE, so $V$ has the metric derivative identities and regularity of [F1]. Its zero initial Maxwell divergence residuals from step 4.1 propagate by the normal-form transport argument of [F1]; the coordinate time foliation is smooth and its normal is $C^1$ at this regularity. Thus both full Maxwell equations hold, and the explicit classical stress identity carried by [F1] gives conservation at the restarted $C^3$ metric/$C^2$ field regularity; no smooth-only stress theorem is applied. The harmonic residual identity from [F1] gives the homogeneous wave equation for $H$. Initially $H=0$ by step 4.1, so its tangential derivatives vanish. In any orthonormal frame with future unit time vector $n$, the Einstein residual is $E_{ab}=	frac12(
abla_aH_b+
abla_bH_a-g_{ab}
abla_cH^c)$, hence $E(n,n)=	frac12
abla_nH_n$ and $E(n,\mathsf e_i)=	frac12
abla_nH_i$ there. The endpoint Einstein constraints from step 4.1 give $
abla_nH=0$. The same local wave-energy uniqueness argument of [F1], valid for this positive symmetric wave block with bounded coefficient derivatives, yields $H=0$ near the endpoint slice. Therefore $V$ is a full solution.

On the overlap before $T$, compare $V$ and the old solution $U$ using the difference-energy estimate [F2] on $[t,t']$ with $t<t'<T$, in the reverse time direction. The compact state sets and $H^s$ norms of both solutions have common bounds, so its constant is uniform as $t'\uparrow T$. Their strong $H^{s-1}$ traces both tend to $U_T$, giving $\|U(t)-V(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le C e^{C(t'-t)}\|U(t')-V(t')\|_{H^{s-1}}\to0$. Thus the solutions agree on the overlap, and $V$ extends the original full development through $T$. The same estimate identifies any two continuations. Time reversal gives the left-endpoint case. On each common interval the same [F2] estimate gives the stated $H^{s-1}$ continuous dependence, with constants depending on the coefficient time slab, compact state set, norm bound and $s$.

In each relatively compact initial coordinate ball choose an orthogonal chart and the initial harmonic jet [L4]. The metric block has time matrix $\operatorname{diag}(I,-g^{00}I,g^{ij}I)$ by [F1]'s reduced Einstein principal-part supplier, and the Maxwell block has time matrix $\alpha^{-1}I_6$ by [F1]. On the open state neighborhood where $g^{00}<0$, $(g^{ij})>0$ and $\alpha>0$, their block sum is positive definite; every spatial matrix is symmetric. Since $T(g,F)$ is algebraic in the state, it contributes only to lower-order terms and creates no off-diagonal derivative blocks. The prescribed local high-Sobolev construction [F2] applies after the compact chart localization in its proof and yields a reduced solution. Its derivative relations propagate; [F3] restores both Maxwell equations and the full Einstein equation on a smaller local domain. Every smooth physical solution in the same harmonic chart extracts to this same coefficient system because the component equations are precisely the harmonic-reduced Einstein equation and field-strength Maxwell evolution. This verifies the local symmetric-hyperbolic, recovery and compatibility hypotheses of [F4].

The equations $dF=0$ and $d\star_gF=0$ are covariant: pullback commutes with exterior differentiation, and for an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $\phi$, $\phi^*(\star_gF)=\star_{\phi^*g}(\phi^*F)$. The algebraic stress $T(g,F)$ is likewise natural under pullback. Thus the matter field, equations, stress and initial reconstruction define one fixed covariant model of the kind required by [F4]; no coordinate-dependent potential gauge is introduced.

The reconstructed field satisfies $dF=d\star_gF=0$ by [L1]. The exact Hodge conversion in [L3] gives $\nabla_aF^{ab}=0$, so the stress identity applies with $j=0$ and yields $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$, independently of the unreduced Einstein equation. The constraints in the Statement are exactly [L2]'s four normal-projection constraints with the same sign, orientation, $\kappa,\mu_0,\Lambda$ and $K$ conventions. This verifies the conservation and Einstein-constraint hypotheses of [F4].

We have now checked every specific input of [F4]: a fixed covariant model by step 2.1, complete matter data and smooth initialization by step 1.1 and [L4], a smooth symmetric-hyperbolic reduction and reconstruction by step 1.2, on-shell stress conservation by step 2.2, and the model's Einstein constraints by [L2]. The choice assumptions are those in the Statement. Applying [F4] gives the smooth local development, variable-width collar, intrinsic globally hyperbolic Cauchy neighborhood and data-fixing isometry matching $F$. derivations.claim: The flat torus has $R(h)=0$ and zero Christoffel symbols. Constant $e,b$ therefore have $D_ie^i=D_ib^i=0$; their collinearity gives $e\times_h b=0$. Since $K=Hh$ with constant $H$, $D K=0$, $\operatorname{tr}_hK=3H$, and $|K|_h^2=3H^2$. Hence the Hamiltonian left side is $0+9H^2-3H^2=6H^2$, which by the definition of $H$ equals $\kappa\mu_0^{-1}(|e|^2+|b|^2)$, exactly the right side of [L1] for $\Lambda=0$. The momentum left side and right side both vanish. Thus all four constraints hold. The scalar under the square root is positive since both fields are nonzero, and $H$ is finite and real.

The data are smooth and $h$ is uniformly positive on the compact torus. For any integer $s\ge5$ they belong to the Sobolev classes in [F1]; their verified constraints meet its hypotheses. Applying [F1] yields a smooth local full source-free solution. The reconstructed initial two-form has nonzero electric and magnetic components because $e,b\ne0$, so the solution is nontrivial. The argument is a model deduction, not an empirical claim.

(A nonzero magnetic period.) Let $\omega_b:=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}b_k\,dx^i\wedge dx^j$ be the magnetic two-form on the initial flat torus, determined by the initial condition $F(\mathsf e_i,\mathsf e_j)=\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$. Write the development supplied by step 2.1 as $M=(-T,T)\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and let $\iota_\Sigma(x)=(0,x)$ be its initial-slice embedding. For any index $i$ choose the cyclic pair $(j,k)$ with $\epsilon_{ijk}=1$, and let $\mathbb T^2_{jk}$ be the coordinate two-torus $x^i=0$, oriented by $dx^j\wedge dx^k$. Then $\omega_b|_{\mathbb T^2_{jk}}=b_i\,dx^j\wedge dx^k$, so its magnetic period, defined as the integral of this pulled-back two-form over the oriented closed two-torus, is $$\int_{\mathbb T^2_{jk}}\omega_b=(2\pi)^2b_i.$$ Since $b\ne0$, some $b_i\ne0$ and the corresponding period is nonzero. The local development has $\iota_\Sigma^*F=\omega_b$; if $F=dA$ for a globally defined smooth one-form on a neighborhood of the full initial torus, its restriction $\iota_\Sigma^*A=\sum_\ell A_\ell dx^\ell$ has periodic coefficients and $\omega_b=d(\iota_\Sigma^*A)$. The integral of $d(\iota_\Sigma^*A)$ over $\mathbb T^2_{jk}$ is zero because each coordinate derivative integrates to zero over a full period, contradicting the computed nonzero value. Thus this datum admits no global potential on any neighborhood containing the entire initial torus.

$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

It is smooth and positive on $J$, and its integral over each compact interval between $\epsilon_*$ and $\epsilon$ is finite. For each $\epsilon\in J$, choose a compact interval contained in $J$ whose interior contains both $\epsilon_*$ and $\epsilon$; [F2] on that interval gives $r'=q>0$. Since $r'=q$ is smooth, $r$ is smooth. For $\epsilon_1<\epsilon_2$, $r(\epsilon_2)-r(\epsilon_1)=\int_{\epsilon_1}^{\epsilon_2}q(z)\,dz>0$, so $r$ is injective; [F3] gives a smooth local inverse and an open image near every point. Continuity and the intermediate value theorem make $r(J)$ an interval, so it is an open interval. The local inverses agree on overlaps by injectivity, giving a smooth global inverse $r(J)\to J$; thus $r:J\to r(J)$ is a smooth diffeomorphism. In particular $\nabla_a r=c_s\nabla_a\epsilon/(\epsilon+p)$ and this change of variables is reversible on its image.

At a point choose local coordinates with $g_{00}<0$ and positive spatial block $(g_{ij})$, with the time direction future. For $y^i=u^i$, the future solution of $g_{ab}u^au^b=-1$ is
$$u^0=\frac{-g_{0i}y^i-\sqrt{(g_{0i}y^i)^2-g_{00}(1+g_{ij}y^iy^j)}}{g_{00}}.$$
The discriminant is positive, so this is smooth on its local state domain. Its three coordinate derivatives $e_A=\partial u/\partial y^A$ are linearly independent and satisfy $g(u,e_A)=0$ by differentiating the normalization with the metric fixed; by [F4] they form a basis of $u^\perp$. In the principal part, $\nabla_a u^b=e_A^b\partial_a y^A$ up to terms involving first derivatives of the metric state, and $\nabla_a r=\partial_a r$. Thus the energy row has coefficients $u^a$ on $\partial_a r$ and $c_s e_A^a$ on $\partial_a y^A$. Projecting the Euler row onto $e_B$ gives coefficients $c_s e_B^a$ on $\partial_a r$ and $u^a g(e_B,e_A)$ on $\partial_a y^A$. Therefore the four principal matrices are symmetric and their covector contraction on $(a,v)$ and $(a',v')$, with $v,v'\in u^\perp$, is exactly $\zeta(u)(aa'+g(v,v'))+c_s(a\zeta(v')+a'\zeta(v))$. The independent equation $u^a\partial_aZ=0$ adds the positive scalar block $\zeta(u)$ and zero cross entries. Connection terms, derivatives of the metric-dependent coordinates, and the Lorentz force are lower order once the metric first derivatives are included as state variables.

abla_a$, $\vartheta=

Second covariant derivatives include their derivative-slot connection. These known background-curvature terms are zeroth order in the first-order state and vanish for the flat coordinate background. Then the reduced Einstein equation can be solved for the second time derivatives in the form
$$\bar\nabla_0p_{ab}=-(g^{00})^{-1}\Bigl[2g^{0i}\bar\nabla_ip_{ab}+g^{ij}\bar\nabla_iq_{abj}+R_{ab}(x,u,T;\kappa,\Lambda,\bar g)\Bigr],$$
where the source is smooth in the first-order metric state and the prescribed matter data, with no derivatives of $T$, and includes $2\kappa(T_{ab}-\tfrac12(g^{cd}T_{cd})g_{ab})+2\Lambda g_{ab}$. The resulting first-order system for $u$ is symmetric hyperbolic on every
region where $g^{00}<0$ and the spatial block $(g^{ij})$ is positive definite:
the coefficient of $\bar\nabla_0u$ is the block diagonal
$\operatorname{diag}(I,-g^{00}I,g^{ij}I)$ (on the three slots
$g,p,q$), which is positive definite there, and the coefficients of the spatial
derivatives are symmetric. More generally, in a coupled reduction one may substitute a specified smooth algebraic stress map $T_{ab}=\mathcal T_{ab}(x,u,z)$, symmetric in $a,b$, where $z$ is a specified additional first-order matter state ranging in an open Euclidean set. This keeps the same metric principal matrices; symmetric hyperbolicity of the combined metric-matter system requires a separate check of the matter equations.

Assume Countable Choice for the enthalpy integral. Let smooth fields satisfy [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]], with $\epsilon\in J$, $u$ future unit timelike, and $0<p'(\epsilon)<1$. Put $c_s=\sqrt{p'(\epsilon)}$ and use the enthalpy coordinate

$$r(\epsilon)=\int_{\epsilon_*}^{\epsilon}\frac{\sqrt{p'(z)}}{z+p(z)}\,dz.$$

On a local chart with a smooth frame $e_1,e_2,e_3$ for the positive-definite subbundle $u^\perp$, the energy and momentum equations are equivalent to

$$u^a\nabla_a r+c_s\nabla_a u^a=0,\qquad u^a\nabla_a u_b+c_s(\delta_b{}^a+u_bu^a)\nabla_a r=\frac{F_{bc}j^c}{\epsilon+p},\qquad u^a\nabla_aZ=0.$$

In smooth local coordinates on the unit-velocity hyperboloid, the principal bilinear form on fluid variations $(a,v,z)$ and $(a',v',z')$, with $v,v'\in u^\perp$, is

$$Q_\zeta((a,v,z),(a',v',z'))=\zeta(u)\bigl(aa'+g(v,v')+zz'\bigr)+c_s\bigl(a\zeta(v')+a'\zeta(v)\bigr).$$

It is symmetric and positive definite for every timelike covector $\zeta$ with $\zeta(u)>0$. The Lorentz-force term is algebraic in $(g,F,\epsilon,u,Z)$ and therefore changes only the lower-order term. The transport equation for $Z$ contributes the positive scalar block $\zeta(u)$ and has no principal cross terms.

Let smooth fields on an open Lorentzian four-manifold satisfy [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]], with $\epsilon$ taking values in $J$. Then

$$u^a\nabla_a\epsilon+(\epsilon+p)\nabla_a u^a=0,\qquad \nabla_a(Nu^a)=0,\qquad \nabla_a j^a=0.$$

If the planned CP01 tensor [[lem-emg-maxwell-stress-conservation]] holds with its stated source sign, then the total stress also obeys

$$\nabla^a(T_{m,ab}+T_{\mathrm{EM},ab})=0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge5$ be an integer, let $A^\mu,B$ be a periodic symmetric
hyperbolic coefficient family on the open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, let
$K\subseteq\operatorname{int}K'\subseteq O$ be compact, let $R\ge0$, and let
$T>0$ and $C$ be as in [[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-existence]] for
the class $\mathcal S(K,R)$; for every datum $u_0\in\mathcal S(K,R)$ let $u$ be
the solution produced there on $(-T,T)$ with values in $K'$. Then:

**(a) [local existence]** For every $u_0\in\mathcal S(K,R)$ and every
$x_0\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ the solution $u$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of
$(0,x_0)$ in $(-T,T)\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and solves $(\star)$ pointwise
there.

**(b) [finite speed / independence of the extension]** Use the flat torus distance
$$d(q(x),q(y)):=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}|x-y+2\pi k|.$$
In any time-independent spatial chart $y$ with a local Euclidean lift $x(y)$ of $q$, put $h_{ij}(y)=\sum_a(\partial_i x^a)(\partial_j x^a)$; this is independent of the lift, since lifts differ by constant lattice translations, and write $h^{ij}$ for its inverse. A unit spatial covector in this clause means $\xi_i\,dy^i$ with $h^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j=1$. Let $\lambda_0>0$ be
determined by the coefficient bounds on a compact set containing the values of
the solutions in the following sense: for a truncated cone
$$D:=\{(t,x):0\le t\le t_0,\ d(x,x_0)\le\lambda(t_0-t)\}$$
with $0<t_0<T$, $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$, lying in a single such spatial chart of $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$
in which the coordinate representation of $A^\mu$ satisfies
$\lambda\,A^0+\xi_iA^i\ge0$ for every flat-metric unit covector $\xi$ at that point (such a $\lambda_0$ exists on compact coefficient sets by the norm-domination argument of clause (a) of [[lem-gr-finite-speed-independence-of-extension]], using the flat dual norm),
let $u,v$ be solutions of two periodic symmetric hyperbolic systems whose
coefficient functions agree on a neighborhood of $D$ in the independent variables and on one common open state set containing both solution ranges, with
$u(0,\cdot)=v(0,\cdot)$ on the ball $\{d(x,x_0)\le\lambda t_0\}$. Then
$u=v$ on $D$.

**(c) [local uniqueness and stability]** If two classical solutions of the same
system on a common interval have values in $K$, $H^s$ norms at most $R$ and the
same initial value, they coincide; and the continuous-dependence estimate of
[[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-uniqueness-stability]] clause (b) holds
for the solutions of clause (a).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let integers $s\ge m\ge0$ satisfy $s-m>3/2$, and
let $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ with the objects and notation of
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]]. Then:

**(a)** There is a unique representative $u^*\in C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$
of the class $u$, and for every $|\alpha|\le m$ the series
$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\chi_k$ converges absolutely and
uniformly on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ to $D^\alpha u^*$; moreover there is
$C=C(s,m,N)$ with
$$\|u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\,\|u\|_{H^s}.$$

**(b)** Writing $d(x,y):=\min\{\,|x-y+2\pi l|:l\in\mathbb Z^3\,\}$ for the
induced metric on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and fixing
$0<\theta\le\min\{1,s-m-\tfrac32\}$, there is $C'=C'(s,m,N,\theta)$ with
$$\bigl|D^\alpha u^*(x)-D^\alpha u^*(y)\bigr|\le C'\,\|u\|_{H^s}\,d(x,y)^\theta\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi},\ |\alpha|\le m).$$

**(c)** The assignment $u\mapsto u^*$ is linear; and if $(u_j)$ is a sequence in
$H^s$ with $u_j\to u$ in $H^s$, then $u_j^*\to u^*$ uniformly together with all
derivatives of order at most $m$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$, let $\bar g$ be a smooth background
metric, let $H^a=g^{bc}(\Gamma^a{}_{bc}-\bar\Gamma^a{}_{bc})$ be the
harmonic-gauge vector and let $E_{ab}=G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}-\kappa T_{ab}$ be
the Einstein residual of a smooth symmetric tensor $T$
([[def-gr-harmonic-gauge-and-reduced-equations]]). Then:

**(a)** On every open set where $(g,T)$ solves the reduced Einstein equation, the identity
$$E_{ab}=\tfrac12\bigl(\nabla_aH_b+\nabla_bH_a-g_{ab}\nabla_cH^c\bigr)$$
holds on that set; and

**(b)** if $(g,T)$ solves the reduced Einstein equation on an open set $U$ and
$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$, then the gauge vector satisfies the homogeneous
linear wave equation
$$\Box_gH_b+\operatorname{Ric}_{ba}H^a=0\qquad\text{on }U,$$
where $\Box_gH_b=\nabla^a\nabla_aH_b$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, and let $\Sigma\subseteq M$ be a smooth spacelike embedded hypersurface with future unit normal $n$, induced Riemannian metric $h$ and second fundamental form $K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$ ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], [[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]]). Write $D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $h$, $R^h$ for its curvature operator in the same operator convention as the ambient curvature, and $S_h$ for its scalar curvature. Explicitly distinguish the lowered tensor from the operator pairing by setting
$$\mathcal R^g(A,B,C,D):=g(R^g(C,D)B,A),\qquad \mathcal R^h(A,B,C,D):=h(R^h(C,D)B,A).$$
Thus $\mathcal R^g_{abcd}=R_{abcd}$ in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]; in particular $g(R^g(X,Y)Z,W)=\mathcal R^g(W,Z,X,Y)$. Let $G$ be the Einstein tensor defined there. At every $p\in\Sigma$ and for all $X,Y,Z,W\in T_p\Sigma$:

**(a) Gauss equation.**
$$\mathcal R^g(X,Y,Z,W)=\mathcal R^h(X,Y,Z,W)+K(X,Z)K(Y,W)-K(X,W)K(Y,Z).$$
Equivalently, in operator order,
$$g(R^g(X,Y)Z,W)=h(R^h(X,Y)Z,W)+K(Y,Z)K(X,W)-K(X,Z)K(Y,W).$$

**(b) Codazzi equation.**
$$g(R^g(X,Y)Z,n)=(D_YK)(X,Z)-(D_XK)(Y,Z).$$

**(c) Normal projections.** Define $(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)=h^{ij}(D_{e_i}K)(e_j,Y)$, $\tau=\operatorname{tr}_hK=h^{ij}K_{ij}$ and $|K|_h^2=h^{ik}h^{jl}K_{ij}K_{kl}$. Then
$$G(n,n)=\tfrac12(S_h+\tau^2-|K|_h^2),\qquad G(n,Y)=(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau.$$

**(d) Constraint equations.** If the tensor equation $G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ holds at $p$, for a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor $T$ and real constants $\kappa,\Lambda$, then
$$S_h+\tau^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T(n,n),\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau=\kappa T(n,Y).$$
With $\rho=T(n,n)$ and $j(Y)=-T(n,Y)$, the second equation is $(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau=-\kappa j(Y)$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Fix $\kappa>0$, $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ and one covariant matter model: specified smooth fields $\Psi$, equations $\mathcal E(g,\Psi)=0$ and stress expression $\mathcal T(g,\Psi)$. Pullback by local diffeomorphisms commutes with these equations and stress expression. Let $\Sigma$ be a smooth three-manifold without boundary, with smooth Riemannian metric $h$, smooth symmetric tensor $K$ and complete smooth matter Cauchy data $d$. The sign convention is $K(V,W)=g(\nabla_Vn,W)$ for the future unit normal. Initial matter tensors involving normal directions are specified on the abstract bundle $\mathcal V=\mathbb RN\oplus T\Sigma$, with metric $g_0(aN+X,bN+Y)=-ab+h(X,Y)$, rather than on a pre-existing spacetime.

Require the following explicit reduction hypotheses on each sufficiently small relatively compact initial coordinate ball with labels $x^i$, flat comparison metric $\bar g=-(dx^0)^2+\sum_i(dx^i)^2$, and finite variables
$$z=(g_{ab},p_{ab}=\partial_0g_{ab},q_{abi}=\partial_ig_{ab},w).$$

1. There are fixed smooth extraction and reconstruction rules and fixed smooth coefficient functions $A^\mu(x,z),B(x,z)$ on an open state set $O$ giving a system
$$A^0(x,z)\partial_0z+\sum_i A^i(x,z)\partial_iz+B(x,z)=0,$$
with symmetric $A^\mu$ and positive definite $A^0$. Its metric equations are exactly the first-order reduction of the reduced Einstein equations of [[def-gr-harmonic-gauge-and-reduced-equations]], with stress $T=\mathcal T(g,\Psi)$. Every smooth physical solution of this fixed model in harmonic coordinates extracts to this same system. Any internal matter gauge is already fixed with its specified equations and complete data; otherwise state the corresponding internal gauge equivalence in the conclusion.
2. Complete data determine a smooth initial value $w=\mathcal I(h,K,d)$, including all auxiliary variables and their compatibility constraints. The initial metric jet displayed in step 1.1 and this value lie in $O$. The reduction propagates its auxiliary compatibility constraints, so the reconstructed fields solve $\mathcal E(g,\Psi)=0$ on the reduced solution, before imposing $H=0$ or the unreduced Einstein equations. The initial reconstruction induces exactly $d$ and the specified initial stress.
3. Whenever the reconstructed metric and fields satisfy those matter equations, their stress obeys $\nabla^a\mathcal T(g,\Psi)_{ab}=0$, independently of the unreduced Einstein equations. In particular this applies to the reduced solution furnished by clause 2. This is stronger than conservation asserted only after the full coupled equations have been proved.

These are concrete PDE, initialization and reconstruction hypotheses; they do not assume existence or geometric uniqueness. Require the constraints of [[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]] for the stress determined by $(h,K,d)$:
$$S_h+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T_0(N,N),\qquad \operatorname{div}_hK-d\operatorname{tr}_hK=\kappa T_0(N,\cdot).$$

Then the data have a smooth time-oriented local development $(g,\Psi)$ on an open variable-width neighborhood of $\{0\}\times\Sigma$ in the literal manifold $\mathbb R\times\Sigma$, with induced data $(h,K,d)$, solving
$$G(g)+\Lambda g=\kappa\mathcal T(g,\Psi),\qquad\mathcal E(g,\Psi)=0.$$
After restriction to a smaller collar, $\Sigma$ lies in the interior of its intrinsic domain of dependence. The interior of that domain is a globally hyperbolic neighborhood with $\Sigma$ Cauchy. Any two developments of this same model and these complete data are related near the entire initial surface by a data-fixing time-orientation-preserving isometry matching all matter fields. There is no uniform noncompact time width or global-in-time conclusion.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with an
orientation, metric-selected connection $\nabla$, metric volume form
$\mathrm{vol}_g$ and current flux $\Phi_J$ as in
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]], and let $J$ be a smooth vector
