Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Here $N$ is the supplied smooth timelike field selecting the future cone, and $o$ is an independent orientation. Let $\nabla$ be the unique torsion-free, $g$-compatible connection of [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Use the curvature sign and contractions of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]; in particular $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 Sg_{ab}$. The geometric and observer conventions are those of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. The tangent-bundle smooth structure inherits only the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ from [[def-countable-choice]].

Fix formal parameters $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $G_N>0$ and $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$. In length coordinates $x^0=ct$, all four coordinates have units metres and $g_{ab}$ is dimensionless. These are mathematical parameters with the displayed SI bookkeeping; they assert no measured value, exactness of $\mu_0$, or physical law.

A field strength $F$ is a real $C^2$ antisymmetric covariant two-tensor field. Its metric-raised components are $F^{ab}=g^{ac}g^{bd}F_{cd}$. For a future unit observer $n$ ($g(n,n)=-1$), the rest space is $n^\perp$ and the projection is $h_n(v)=v+g(n,v)n$. The observer electric and magnetic covectors are $E_{n,a}=cF_{ab}n^b$ and $B_{n,a}=-({\star_gF})_{ab}n^b$, with the oriented Lorentzian Hodge convention of [[lem-emg-observer-field-decomposition]]. They annihilate $n$ and use the positive metric induced on the rest covector space. In a positively oriented orthonormal tetrad with time vector $n$, $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$.

For such an $F$, define

$$T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{ab}:=\frac1{\mu_0}\left(F^{ac}F^b{}_c-\frac14g^{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right),\qquad T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}:=g_{ac}g_{bd}T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{cd}.$$

For any symmetric covariant tensor $S_{ab}$ and unit observer $n$, its observer energy density is $S_{ab}n^an^b$. Its observer energy-current vector is $-S^a{}_bn^b$; the spatial energy flux measured by $n$ is the projection $h_n(-S^a{}_bn^b)$ into $n^\perp$. A nonzero causal vector is future-directed when it has negative inner product with $N$; future timelike means $g(v,v)<0$, and future null means the vector is nonzero and $g(v,v)=0$.

In four dimensions, define the **weak energy condition** (WEC) for $S$ by $S_{ab}v^av^b\ge0$ for every future timelike $v$; the **null energy condition** (NEC) by $S_{ab}\ell^a\ell^b\ge0$ for every nonzero future null $\ell$; and the **dominant energy condition** (DEC) by requiring $-S^a{}_bv^b$ to be future causal or zero for every future timelike $v$. Define the **strong energy condition** (SEC) by the WEC for $S_{ab}-\tfrac12(g^{cd}S_{cd})g_{ab}$. These are definitions of tensor inequalities only; no general matter positivity premise is included.

A matter tensor $T_m^{ab}$ is a $C^1$ symmetric contravariant two-tensor field; a current $j^a$ is a $C^1$ vector field. The **formal sourced Maxwell equations** are $dF=0$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$. The **matter exchange equation** is $\nabla_aT_m^{ab}=F^b{}_cj^c$. The **formal Einstein equation** is

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa\bigl(T_{m,ab}+T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}\bigr).$$

Here $T_{m,ab}$ is obtained by lowering both indices with $g$. Each displayed equation is a pointwise mathematical condition on the supplied fields with the regularities stated above. A formal Einstein–Maxwell–matter solution is a tuple satisfying whichever of these equations are explicitly assumed on the stated open domain; no existence or uniqueness of such a tuple is asserted.

Two matter forms used below are defined as follows. A **charged-dust form** has $T_m^{ab}=\rho U^aU^b$ and $j^a=\sigma U^a$, where $\rho,\sigma\in C^1$, $\rho\ge0$, and $U\in C^2$ is future timelike with $g(U,U)=-c^2$. On $\{\rho>0\}$ its charge-to-mass ratio is $\alpha=\sigma/\rho$; it is not defined by division on $\{\rho=0\}$. A **perfect-fluid form** has

$$T_m^{ab}=\frac{\epsilon+p}{c^2}U^aU^b+pg^{ab},$$

where $\epsilon,p\in C^1$ and $U$ has the same timelike normalization. No equation of state, conductivity law, entropy law, or matter evolution theorem is part of this definition. A current may additionally be written $j^a=\sigma U^a+q^a$ with $q^aU_a=0$; an Ohmic relation $q^a=\chi E_U^a$, $\chi\ge0$, is a separately imposed constitutive hypothesis, where $E_U^a=F^a{}_bU^b$.

On an open set $V$, a **local potential** for $F$ is a supplied smooth one-form $A$ with $dA=F$. Such a potential need not exist globally. A local gauge change is $A\mapsto A+d\lambda$ for a supplied smooth scalar $\lambda$; this leaves $F$ unchanged. No global bundle, potential, or point-source construction is asserted.

In the stated length-coordinate SI interpretation, $[F_{ab}]=\mathrm T$, $[A_a]=\mathrm{T\,m}$, $[j^a]=\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $[T_m]=[T_{\mathrm{EM}}]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[\sigma]=\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$, $[\alpha]=\mathrm{C\,kg^{-1}}$, $[\epsilon]=[p]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $[\chi]=\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}$. The equalities $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$ make the displayed tensor equations dimensionally consistent. No distributional product or stress tensor for a singular point source is defined.

Use the mathematical Lorentzian and SI conventions of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. Fix a length scale $L>0$, a speed $c>0$, a nonzero constant charge-to-mass parameter $\alpha=q/m$, and choose $0<\epsilon\le\epsilon_*\le1$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\mathcal K\Subset\Omega$ be a compact convex set. Use length coordinates $x^0=ct$ and $x^i=LX^i$, with $X\in\Omega$ dimensionless. Assume a smooth stationary (independent of $x^0$) Lorentzian metric $g^{(\epsilon)}$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on a neighborhood of $\mathbb R_{x^0}\times L\mathcal K$, with $\partial_0$ chosen future timelike and $t$ increasing along the considered curves, whose components have the form

$$ g_{00}^{(\epsilon)}(X)=-(1+2\epsilon\phi(X))+r_{00}^{(\epsilon)}(X),\qquad g_{ij}^{(\epsilon)}(X)=(1-2\epsilon\phi(X))\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}^{(\epsilon)}(X),\qquad g_{0i}^{(\epsilon)}(X)=r_{0i}^{(\epsilon)}(X). $$

Here $\phi$ is dimensionless and smooth. A spatial multi-index is $\beta=(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, with $|\beta|=\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3$ and $\partial_X^\beta:=\partial_{X^1}^{\beta_1}\partial_{X^2}^{\beta_2}\partial_{X^3}^{\beta_3}$. For each such $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le2$, assume the uniform bounds

$$ |\partial_X^\beta r_{00}^{(\epsilon)}|+ \max_{i,j}|\partial_X^\beta r_{ij}^{(\epsilon)}| \le C_g\epsilon^2,\qquad \max_i|\partial_X^\beta r_{0i}^{(\epsilon)}|\le C_g\epsilon^{3/2} $$

on $\mathcal K$, with a fixed finite nonnegative $C_g$. Let $\mathbf e,\mathbf b:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth dimensionless fields whose values and first derivatives are bounded on $\mathcal K$. Since $\mathcal K$ is compact, the fixed smooth function $\phi$ and its derivatives used below are also bounded there. Prescribe a smooth stationary (independent of $x^0$) real two-form $F^{(\epsilon)}$ by its Cartesian components

$$ F_{0i}^{(\epsilon)}=-E_i^{(\epsilon)}/c,\qquad F_{ij}^{(\epsilon)}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k^{(\epsilon)},\qquad \alpha\mathbf E^{(\epsilon)}(X)=\frac{\epsilon c^2}{L}\mathbf e(X),\qquad \alpha\mathbf B^{(\epsilon)}(X)=\frac{\sqrt\epsilon\,c}{L}\mathbf b(X). $$

No Maxwell or Einstein equation for this prescribed background field or metric is assumed. Define the dimensionless potential $\phi$ comparison system on $S\in[0,S_*]$ by

$$ \frac{d\mathbf X_N}{dS}=\mathbf W_N,\qquad \frac{d\mathbf W_N}{dS}=-\nabla_X\phi(\mathbf X_N)+\mathbf e(\mathbf X_N)+\mathbf W_N\times\mathbf b(\mathbf X_N), $$

where $(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)_i:=\sum_{j,k}\epsilon_{ijk}u_jv_k$. Let $f(\mathbf X,\mathbf W)$ denote the six-component right-hand side of this system. Assume that on a compact convex state set $\mathcal Q\subseteq\mathcal K\times\mathbb R^3$, containing both trajectories, its derivative satisfies $\|Df\|_{1\to1}\le L_f$ for a finite nonnegative $L_f$. Here $\|(\mathbf X,\mathbf W)\|_1$ is the sum of the absolute values of its six real components, and $\|Df\|_{1\to1}$ is the operator norm induced by this $\ell^1$ norm.

For each $\epsilon$, let $z_\epsilon$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve, parameterized by proper time $\tau$ as in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]], that solves the prescribed external Lorentz equation

$$ \nabla_U U=\alpha F^{(\epsilon)\sharp}(U),\qquad g^{(\epsilon)}(U,U)=-c^2,\qquad U=\frac{dz_\epsilon}{d\tau}. $$

Write its coordinate velocity as $\mathbf w=d\mathbf x/dt$ and assume $|\mathbf w|\le C_v\sqrt\epsilon\,c$ on $[0,S_*]$ for a fixed finite $C_v$. Suppose the relativistic scaled trajectory $(\mathbf X_\epsilon,\mathbf W_\epsilon)$ and the comparison trajectory $(\mathbf X_N,\mathbf W_N)$ exist throughout $[0,S_*]$, remain in $\mathcal Q$, and have the same initial data, where

$$ \mathbf X:=\mathbf x/L,\qquad \mathbf W:=\mathbf w/(\sqrt\epsilon\,c),\qquad S:=\sqrt\epsilon\,ct/L. $$

Then, after choosing $\epsilon_*>0$ sufficiently small in terms of the stated uniform constants, the exact relativistic trajectory satisfies

$$ \frac{d\mathbf X_\epsilon}{dS}=\mathbf W_\epsilon,\qquad \frac{d\mathbf W_\epsilon}{dS} =-\nabla_X\phi(\mathbf X_\epsilon)+\mathbf e(\mathbf X_\epsilon) +\mathbf W_\epsilon\times\mathbf b(\mathbf X_\epsilon)+\mathbf r_\epsilon(S), \qquad \|\mathbf r_\epsilon(S)\|_1\le C_r\epsilon, $$

where $C_r$ depends only on the displayed uniform bounds and the fixed coefficient bounds on $\mathcal K$, and is independent of $\epsilon$. Consequently,

$$ \sup_{0\le S\le S_*}\left(\|\mathbf X_\epsilon(S)-\mathbf X_N(S)\|_1+ \|\mathbf W_\epsilon(S)-\mathbf W_N(S)\|_1\right) \le C_r\epsilon S_*e^{L_fS_*}. $$

The estimate is conditional on existence and common compact containment through the specified finite scaled interval. It does not construct such a long-time family, solve Maxwell's equations for the prescribed fields, or produce a coupled Einstein–Maxwell family. In particular the $\sqrt\epsilon$ magnetic scaling can fail a coupled Einstein stress hierarchy unless additional matter scales are supplied.

Use the field, stress, matter, unit and curvature conventions of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and define the Einstein residual for the source-free field model by

$$ \mathscr R_{ab}(g,F;\Lambda):=G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}-\kappa T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}(g,F). $$

Suppose $G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=0$ on $U$, and let $F_0$ be a smooth real two-form with $dF_0=0$ and $d(\star_gF_0)=0$. For every real dimensionless $\delta$, the field $F_\delta:=\delta F_0$ obeys the same source-free Maxwell equations and

$$ \mathscr R_{ab}(g,F_\delta;\Lambda)=-\kappa\delta^2 T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}(g,F_0). $$

This is an exact residual identity on the fixed metric. If $\delta\ne0$ and $F_0$ is nonzero at a point, its observer energy there is positive and the residual is nonzero there; this does not estimate the distance to a different coupled solution.

Separately, let $\rho,\sigma\in C^1(\Omega)$ and a $C^2$ future timelike field $U$ with $g(U,U)=-c^2$ define charged dust on an open $\Omega\subseteq U$, with $\rho>0$, $T_m^{ab}=\rho U^aU^b$, $j^a=\sigma U^a$, and the formal matter-exchange equation of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. For any dimensionless $\eta>0$, replacing $(\rho,\sigma)$ by $(\eta\rho,\eta\sigma)$ multiplies $T_m$ and $j$ by $\eta$, leaves $\alpha=\sigma/\rho$ unchanged, and leaves the dust acceleration equation $\rho U^a\nabla_aU^b=\sigma F^b{}_cU^c$ unchanged when the prescribed $F$ and $U$ are held fixed. The sourced Maxwell equation must still match the changed current. If both $F$ and $j$ are scaled by $\eta$, Maxwell's equations remain linear but the electromagnetic stress scales by $\eta^2$, whereas the dust stress scales by $\eta$; no general coupled-solution family follows.

For a flat background with $\Lambda=0$ and $T_m=0$, a nonzero source-free Maxwell field cannot solve the exact Einstein equation with the unchanged Minkowski metric, because its observer energy density is positive somewhere.

Finally, in Minkowski space consider only the prescribed Coulomb profile on the finite annulus $\mathcal A_\ell:=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:\ell<|\mathbf x|<2\ell\}$, where $\ell>0$ is a length, $Q\ne0$ is a charge, $r:=|\mathbf x|$, $\mathbf e_r:=\mathbf x/r$, $\mathbf E(\mathbf x)=Q(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2)^{-1}\mathbf e_r$, and $\mathbf B=0$. Its Maxwell energy on that annulus is

$$ \mathcal E_\ell=\int_{\mathcal A_\ell}\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|\mathbf E|^2\,d^3x =\frac{Q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0\ell}. $$

Thus this fixed-charge Coulomb cutoff family has diverging shell energy as $\ell\downarrow0$. This finite-annulus calculation asserts no point-source construction, self-field evaluation, or obstruction theorem for arbitrary regularizations.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

derivations.claim: In Minkowski coordinates $U=(\gamma c,\gamma\mathbf w)$, where $\gamma=(1-|\mathbf w|_2^2/c^2)^{-1/2}>0$. Since $U^0=dx^0/d\tau=c\,dt/d\tau=\gamma c$, we have $d/d\tau=\gamma\,d/dt$. With $\mathbf E=0$, the time component of $\nabla_UU=\alpha F^\sharp(U)$ gives $\gamma c\,d\gamma/dt=0$, hence $d\gamma/dt=0$. The spatial component gives $\gamma\,d(\gamma\mathbf w)/dt=\alpha\gamma\,\mathbf w\times\mathbf B$; canceling $\gamma>0$ and then using constancy of $\gamma$ yields $d\mathbf w/dt=(\alpha/\gamma)\mathbf w\times\mathbf B$. The dot product with $\mathbf w$ is zero, so $|\mathbf w|_2$ and $\gamma$ stay constant. Initially, $ \gamma=\gamma_0=(1-\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|_2^2)^{-1/2},\qquad \gamma_0^{-1}=\sqrt{1-\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|_2^2}. $ The radicand is at least $1/2$, so the positive root is defined.

Rescaling time and velocity in the exact equation gives $\mathbf W'=(b_0/\gamma_0)\mathbf W	imes\mathbf e_z$. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $H:D\to(0,\infty)$ be of class $C^3$, meaning that every partial derivative of total order at most three exists and is continuous. Set $\mathcal M:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times D$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, with global coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$; each coordinate is assigned length units, with $x^0=ct$ when a time coordinate is wanted. The function $H$ depends only on $(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and is dimensionless.

Give $\mathcal M$ the coordinate orientation determined by $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$. Put $N_H:=H\partial_0$ and choose the time orientation whose future cone contains $N_H$; the lemma below proves that $N_H$ is timelike for the tensor defined here.

Define the symmetric coordinate tensor $g_H$ by
$$g_H=-H^{-2}(dx^0)^2+H^2\sum_{i=1}^3(dx^i)^2,$$
where $H^{-1}:=1/H$ and $H^{-2}:=(1/H)^2$. This exact coordinate form is called the positive-scalar conformastatic chart tensor in this item; no field equation or physical solution property is part of the definition.

Because $H>0$, the functions $H^{-1}$ and $H^{-2}$ are compositions and products of $H$ with positive-base powers of exponents $-1$ and $-2$. The derivative formula for these powers, repeated through any finite order, and closure of $C^k$ functions under composition and finite products show that the displayed coefficients are $C^3$ when $H$ is $C^3$, and smooth when $H$ is smooth.

For later component formulas define $H_i:=\partial_iH$, $H_{ij}:=\partial_i\partial_jH$, $q:=\sum_{i=1}^3H_i^2$, and $\Delta H:=\sum_{i=1}^3H_{ii}$.

derivations.claim: The coordinate matrix is diagonal and symmetric. Since $H>0$, all entries are nonzero, its inverse is $\operatorname{diag}(-H^2,H^{-2},H^{-2},H^{-2})$, and multiplying the two diagonal matrices gives the identity. The determinant is $(-H^{-2})(H^2)^3=-H^4<0$, so the matrix has exactly one negative and three positive diagonal entries and no zero eigenvalue. Thus it is nondegenerate of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ at every point. Its coefficients and inverse are C3 because $H$ is C3 and the reciprocal map $u\mapsto1/u$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$.

With the frame fields defined in the Statement, direct contraction against the diagonal matrix gives $g(n,n)=H^2(-H^{-2})=-1$, $g(n,e_i)=0$, and $g(e_i,e_j)=H^{-2}H^2\delta_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$. Each frame vector is a nonzero multiple of a distinct coordinate vector, so the four vectors form a basis. Their coordinate change matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(H,H^{-1},H^{-1},H^{-1})$, with positive determinant $H^{-2}$; hence the frame is positively oriented. The time orientation is the one specified in [F1], so $n$ is future-directed. The already computed metric determinant gives $\sqrt{|\det g|}=H^2$.

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa\bigl(T_{m,ab}+T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}\bigr).$$

Here $T_{m,ab}$ is obtained by lowering both indices with $g$. Each displayed equation is a pointwise mathematical condition on the supplied fields with the regularities stated above. A formal Einstein–Maxwell–matter solution is a tuple satisfying whichever of these equations are explicitly assumed on the stated open domain; no existence or uniqueness of such a tuple is asserted.

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. For the rational-exponent regime at base zero, retain the convention of [[def-rational-power]] and [[def-integer-power]]: $0^0=1$, $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$, and $0^r$ is undefined for rational $r<0$. This records the integer zero-exponent convention together with the positive-rational supplementary clause; it does not extend the real-exponent convention.

The separate real-exponent regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For real exponents at base zero, set $0^x=0$ only when $x>0$; $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are undefined, exactly as in [[def-real-power]]. Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

$$

$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$.
For $q>0$, let $s(q)$ be the unique positive root specified in [[def-emg-explicit-power-regimes]]. Then $s:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is smooth and $s'(q)=1/(2s(q))$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in [[def-countable-choice]], as required by the currently inspected general geometric convention in [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $H\in C^\infty(D,(0,\infty))$ satisfy $\Delta H\le0$. Use $\mathcal M=\mathbb R\times D$, its coordinate orientation, and the time orientation for which $n:=H\partial_0$ is future, all as fixed in [[def-emg-conformastatic-chart-data]] and verified in [[lem-emg-conformastatic-chart-is-lorentzian]]. Let $a^b:=U^a\nabla_aU^b$ be the covariant four-acceleration of the timelike field $U$. Then $U=cn$ is future timelike with $g_H(U,U)=-c^2$, all displayed fields are smooth, and $\rho\ge0$. Its observer energy density and energy flux in a positively oriented orthonormal rest frame are

$$u=\frac{|E|^2/c^2+|B|^2}{2\mu_0},\qquad \frac{E\times B}{\mu_0c},$$

and the DEC flux is future causal or zero. A charged-dust tensor with $\rho\ge0$ satisfies all four conditions. For a perfect-fluid tensor with rest energy density $\epsilon$ and pressure $p$, the exact pointwise conditions are

$$\mathrm{WEC}\iff \epsilon\ge0\text{ and }\epsilon+p\ge0,\quad \mathrm{NEC}\iff\epsilon+p\ge0,$$

$$\mathrm{SEC}\iff\epsilon+p\ge0\text{ and }\epsilon+3p\ge0,\quad \mathrm{DEC}\iff\epsilon\ge|p|.$$

$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

1. For every $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $u \ne 0$ and every real $c$, the affine
   hyperplane
   $$H_{u,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \langle u,x\rangle = c \,\}$$
   ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(H_{u,c}) = 0$, and so is every subset of it.
2. Every proper linear subspace $W \subsetneq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]) is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(W) = 0$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Since $r^2+b^2\ge b^2>0$, [F1] gives the unique positive root $\Psi$, and [F2] makes it smooth with $\partial_i\Psi=x^i/\Psi$. The chain, product and quotient rules [F12] then give $H_i=-ax^i/\Psi^3$ and $\partial_iH_i=-a(\Psi^{-3}-3(x^i)^2\Psi^{-5})$, so $\Delta H=-a\sum_{i=1}^3(\Psi^{-3}-3(x^i)^2\Psi^{-5})=-a(3\Psi^{-3}-3r^2\Psi^{-5})=-3ab^2/\Psi^5<0$. The integrand $\rho H^3=3c^2ab^2/[4\pi G_N(r^2+b^2)^{5/2}]$ is nonnegative and continuous on $\mathbb R^3$, hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable by [F9]. The coupled-dust theorem [F3] applies and supplies the smooth fields and exact formal solution.

On $x^0=\text{constant}$ the metric pullback is $h_{ij}=H^2\delta_{ij}$, so $\det h=H^6$ and its positive volume density is $\sqrt{\det h}=H^3$. Substituting the density from step 1.1 gives $\rho H^3=3c^2ab^2/[4\pi G_N(r^2+b^2)^{5/2}]$, a nonnegative Borel integrand for [F6].

The curvature formula [F5] and strict negativity in step 1.1 give $S_g=6ab^2/(H^3\Psi^5)>0$. The energy-condition theorem [F4] applies because $\rho\ge0$. Since the density formula in step 1.1 is strictly positive for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$, the set of points where it is nonzero is all of $\mathbb R^3$; no compact subset of $\mathbb R^3$ contains all those points.

If $a=\delta b$, then $H=1+z$ with $z=\delta h_0$ and $0<h_0\le1$, since $\Psi\ge b$. For $f(u)=(1+u)^{-2}$, $f(0)=1$, $f'(0)=-2$, and $0<f''(u)=6(1+u)^{-4}\le6$ for $u\ge0$ by [F12]. Fix $z>0$ and define $G_z(u):=(z-u)f'(u)+f(u)$ on $[0,z]$. The product rule [F12] gives $G_z'(u)=(z-u)f''(u)$ on its interior. This derivative is continuous on $[0,z]$, hence Riemann integrable by [F13]; $G_z$ is continuous there. Newton--Leibniz [F13] therefore gives
$$\int_0^z(z-u)f''(u)\,du=G_z(z)-G_z(0)=f(z)-1+2z.$$
The integrand lies between $0$ and $6(z-u)$. These continuous comparison functions are integrable by [F13], so [F14] and Newton--Leibniz applied to $6zu-3u^2$ give
$$0\le f(z)-(1-2z)\le\int_0^z6(z-u)\,du=3z^2\le3\delta^2.$$
At $z=0$ the same remainder and bound are zero directly; no theorem requiring a nondegenerate interval is applied there. Since $g_{00}=-H^{-2}$, this proves the stated time-component bound.

Apply the polar formula [F7] to the integrand in step 2.1; it is constant on each sphere of radius $r$. The area factor [F8] then gives $M_{\mathrm{prop}}=(3c^2ab^2/G_N)\int_0^\infty r^2(r^2+b^2)^{-5/2}\,dr$. All uses of the polar formula are under exactly [A1]'s $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis.

The radial integrand has finite value at $r=0$, and that singleton has measure zero by [F10], so its integral over $[0,\infty)$ equals its integral over $(0,\infty)$. On $(0,\pi/2)$, $\cos\theta>0$, and quotient differentiation with the sine/cosine derivatives and Pythagorean identity in [F12] gives $(b\tan\theta)'=b\sec^2\theta>0$. Also $\sin$ increases and $\cos$ decreases while remaining positive on this interval [F12], so $\tan=\sin/\cos$ is strictly increasing. Their continuity and quarter-turn values give limits $0$ and $+\infty$ at the interval's endpoints. For each $y>0$, choose interior points $\theta_-<\theta_+$ with $T(\theta_-)<y<T(\theta_+)$; continuity on $[\theta_-,\theta_+]$ and the intermediate value theorem [F12] give a preimage, and strict monotonicity gives uniqueness. Hence $T(\theta)=b\tan\theta$ is a bijection $(0,\pi/2)\to(0,\infty)$. Since $T'$ never vanishes, the inverse function theorem [F12] gives C1 local inverses, which agree by bijectivity to form a global C1 inverse. Thus [F10] applies, and using $\cos\theta>0$ to simplify gives $\int_0^\infty r^2(r^2+b^2)^{-5/2}\,dr=b^{-2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$. The integrand is continuous on $[0,\pi/2]$, so it is Riemann integrable and its Lebesgue integral agrees by [F13]; the endpoints have measure zero by [F10]. The function $G(\theta)=\sin^3\theta/3$ has derivative $\sin^2\theta\cos\theta$ on the interior by [F12], and Newton--Leibniz [F13] with $\sin 0=0$, $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ yields $1/3$. Thus the radial integral is $1/(3b^2)$, and step 3.1 gives $M_{\mathrm{prop}}=c^2a/G_N<\infty$.

Put $f=\rho H^3$. By step 4.1, $f\ge0$ and $\int f=M_{\mathrm{prop}}<\infty$, so $f$ is real integrable under [F11]. Since $\sigma H^3=sQ_sf$ and $sQ_s$ is a finite real constant, [F11] gives integrability of the signed charge density and $Q_{\mathrm{prop}}=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sigma H^3\,d\lambda_3=sQ_s\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\,d\lambda_3=sQ_sM_{\mathrm{prop}}$.

The spatial metric is exactly $g_{ij}=H^2\delta_{ij}=(1+2\delta h_0+\delta^2h_0^2)\delta_{ij}$, so the component error is $\delta^2h_0^2|\delta_{ij}|\le\delta^2$. Also $\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{lin}}=H^{-3}=(1+z)^{-3}$. By [F12], the function $P(u):=1-(1+u)^{-3}$ is continuously differentiable for $u\ge0$ with $P'(u)=3(1+u)^{-4}$. For $z>0$, [F13] makes this derivative integrable on $[0,z]$ and gives
$$1-(1+z)^{-3}=P(z)-P(0)=\int_0^z3(1+u)^{-4}\,du.$$
Its integrand lies between $0$ and $3$, so [F14] yields $0\le1-\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{lin}}\le3z\le3\delta$. At $z=0$ both sides vanish by substitution. This proves the density bound.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and steps 1.1–2.2: the domain is all nonempty R^3 and density is strictly positive everywhere for a,b>0; the mass integral is over this full domain, not an empty support or zero-volume sphere.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as stated in [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $a,b>0$ have length units, let $s\in\{-1,+1\}$, and on all of $\mathbb R^3$ set
$$r^2=(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2+(x^3)^2,\qquad \Psi(x):=\sqrt{r^2+b^2}>0,\qquad H(x):=1+\frac a{\Psi(x)}.$$
Use the constants and exact formal coupled family of [[thm-emg-smooth-counterpoised-dust]]. The function $H$ is smooth, positive, and satisfies
$$\Delta H=-\frac{3ab^2}{(r^2+b^2)^{5/2}}<0,\qquad \rho(x)=\frac{3c^2ab^2}{4\pi G_NH(x)^3(r^2+b^2)^{5/2}}.$$
On the slice $x^0=\text{constant}$ the induced spatial metric is $h=H^2\delta_{ij}dx^i dx^j$. Define the candidate proper mass and signed charge by
$$M_{\mathrm{prop}}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho H^3\,d\lambda_3,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{prop}}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sigma H^3\,d\lambda_3.$$
The proof establishes that the first is a finite nonnegative Lebesgue integral and the second is a finite signed Lebesgue integral. They equal
$$M_{\mathrm{prop}}=\frac{c^2a}{G_N},\qquad Q_{\mathrm{prop}}=sQ_s\frac{c^2a}{G_N}.$$
The scalar curvature is $S_g=-2\Delta H/H^3>0$, the total stress satisfies WEC, NEC, SEC, and DEC, and the smooth matter density is positive at every point and has infinite spatial extent. For $a=\delta b$ with $0<\delta\le1$, put $h_0(x):=b/\sqrt{r^2+b^2}$ and
$$\rho_{\mathrm{lin}}(x):=\frac{3c^2\delta b^3}{4\pi G_N(r^2+b^2)^{5/2}}.$$
The same exact coupled solutions obey the pointwise Cartesian-coordinate bounds
$$\left|g_{00}+\bigl(1-2\delta h_0\bigr)\right|\le3\delta^2,\qquad \left|g_{ij}-\bigl(1+2\delta h_0\bigr)\delta_{ij}\right|\le\delta^2,\qquad 0\le1-\frac{\rho}{\rho_{\mathrm{lin}}}\le3\delta.$$
These are ideal mathematical estimates, not measurements or stability statements.
For $q>0$, let $s(q)$ be the unique positive root specified in [[def-emg-explicit-power-regimes]]. Then $s:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is smooth and $s'(q)=1/(2s(q))$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $\Psi=(r^2+b^2)^{1/2}$. Since $r^2+b^2\ge b^2>0$, [F4] and the chain rule give $\partial_i\Psi=x^i/\Psi$. Differentiating $H=1+b/\Psi$ with the quotient rule in [F4] gives $H_i=-b x^i/\Psi^3$, hence $H_i(0)=0$. At $r=0$, $\Psi=b$ and $H(0)=2$. The Laplacian in [F3] gives $\Delta H(0)=-3b^3/b^5=-3/b^2$.
Applying [F3] with $a=b$ and $s=+1$ yields $M_{\mathrm{prop}}=c^2b/G_N$ and $Q_{\mathrm{prop}}=Q_sc^2b/G_N$. The exact-solution conclusion is [F1].

Substituting these values into [F1] gives $\rho(0)=3c^2/(4\pi G_Nb^2\cdot2^3)=3c^2/(32\pi G_Nb^2)$, and [F2] gives $S_g(0)=-2(-3/b^2)/2^3=3/(4b^2)$. For the electric components, the metric in [F1] gives the future unit vector $n=H\partial_0$ and positively oriented orthonormal spatial vectors $e_i=H^{-1}\partial_i$ by direct contraction. Since $A_0=s(c/Q_s)H^{-1}$ and $A_i=0$, [F4]–[F5] give $F_{i0}=-s(c/Q_s)H_i/H^2$. Therefore $E_i:=cF(e_i,n)=cF_{i0}=-s c^2H_i/(Q_sH^2)$, which vanishes at the center by step 1.1.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as stated in [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $a,b>0$ have length units, let $s\in\{-1,+1\}$, and on all of $\mathbb R^3$ set
$$r^2=(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2+(x^3)^2,\qquad \Psi(x):=\sqrt{r^2+b^2}>0,\qquad H(x):=1+\frac a{\Psi(x)}.$$
Use the constants and exact formal coupled family of [[thm-emg-smooth-counterpoised-dust]]. The function $H$ is smooth, positive, and satisfies
$$\Delta H=-\frac{3ab^2}{(r^2+b^2)^{5/2}}<0,\qquad \rho(x)=\frac{3c^2ab^2}{4\pi G_NH(x)^3(r^2+b^2)^{5/2}}.$$
On the slice $x^0=\text{constant}$ the induced spatial metric is $h=H^2\delta_{ij}dx^i dx^j$. Define the candidate proper mass and signed charge by
$$M_{\mathrm{prop}}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho H^3\,d\lambda_3,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{prop}}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sigma H^3\,d\lambda_3.$$
The proof establishes that the first is a finite nonnegative Lebesgue integral and the second is a finite signed Lebesgue integral. They equal
$$M_{\mathrm{prop}}=\frac{c^2a}{G_N},\qquad Q_{\mathrm{prop}}=sQ_s\frac{c^2a}{G_N}.$$
The scalar curvature is $S_g=-2\Delta H/H^3>0$, the total stress satisfies WEC, NEC, SEC, and DEC, and the smooth matter density is positive at every point and has infinite spatial extent. For $a=\delta b$ with $0<\delta\le1$, put $h_0(x):=b/\sqrt{r^2+b^2}$ and
$$\rho_{\mathrm{lin}}(x):=\frac{3c^2\delta b^3}{4\pi G_N(r^2+b^2)^{5/2}}.$$
The same exact coupled solutions obey the pointwise Cartesian-coordinate bounds
$$\left|g_{00}+\bigl(1-2\delta h_0\bigr)\right|\le3\delta^2,\qquad \left|g_{ij}-\bigl(1+2\delta h_0\bigr)\delta_{ij}\right|\le\delta^2,\qquad 0\le1-\frac{\rho}{\rho_{\mathrm{lin}}}\le3\delta.$$
These are ideal mathematical estimates, not measurements or stability statements.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in [[def-countable-choice]], as required by the currently inspected general geometric convention in [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $H\in C^\infty(D,(0,\infty))$ satisfy $\Delta H\le0$. Use $\mathcal M=\mathbb R\times D$, its coordinate orientation, and the time orientation for which $n:=H\partial_0$ is future, all as fixed in [[def-emg-conformastatic-chart-data]] and verified in [[lem-emg-conformastatic-chart-is-lorentzian]]. Use the metric $g_H$ and coordinates $x^0=ct,x^i$ of [[def-emg-conformastatic-chart-data]]. Fix formal constants $c,\mu_0,G_N>0$, put $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$, and define the positive charge-to-mass parameter $Q_s:=\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0G_N}$ using the positive root of [[def-emg-explicit-power-regimes]]. For a sign $s\in\{-1,+1\}$ set
$$A:=s\frac{c}{Q_s}H^{-1}dx^0,\qquad F:=dA,\qquad U:=cH\partial_0,\qquad \rho:=-\frac{c^2\Delta H}{4\pi G_NH^3},\qquad \sigma:=sQ_s\rho,\qquad j:=\sigma U,\qquad T_m^{ab}:=\rho U^aU^b.$$
Let $a^b:=U^a\nabla_aU^b$ be the covariant four-acceleration of the timelike field $U$. Then $U=cn$ is future timelike with $g_H(U,U)=-c^2$, all displayed fields are smooth, and $\rho\ge0$. On $\{\rho>0\}$ the charge-to-mass ratio is $\sigma/\rho=sQ_s$; no ratio is defined by division at $\rho=0$. The tuple satisfies the formal sourced Maxwell equations $dF=0$, $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$, the dust matter exchange equation $\nabla_aT_m^{ab}=F^b{}_cj^c$, and the formal Einstein equation with $\Lambda=0$,
$$G_{ab}=\kappa\bigl(T_{m,ab}+T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}\bigr),$$
where $T^{\mathrm{EM}}$ is exactly the tensor of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. Its total stress satisfies WEC, NEC, SEC, and DEC. The coordinate four-acceleration of the static dust field is $a^0=0$, $a^i=-c^2H_i/H^3$, and its Lorentz force per unit mass balances it wherever $\rho>0$; the undivided exchange identity also holds where $\rho=0$.

This is a conditional mathematical solution family for the stated formal equations. It makes no claim of physical realization, equilibrium stability, or coupled-field existence for arbitrary initial data.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

derivations.claim: Put $z=\delta h_0$. Since $r^2+b^2\ge b^2$ and both square roots are positive, $0<h_0\le1$ and $0<z\le\delta$. By the metric formula in [F1], $g_{00}=-(1+z)^{-2}$, so the time-component discrepancy is $|(1+z)^{-2}-1+2z|$.

Define $f(u):=(1+u)^{-2}-1+2u$ for $u\ge0$. Twice applying the quotient/product rules [F3] gives $f(0)=f'(0)=0$ and $f''(u)=6(1+u)^{-4}$, between $0$ and $6$. For fixed $z>0$, set $G_z(u):=(z-u)f'(u)+f(u)$ on $[0,z]$. It is continuous with continuous derivative $G_z'(u)=(z-u)f''(u)$, which is integrable by [F4]. Newton--Leibniz [F4] gives
$$f(z)=G_z(z)-G_z(0)=\int_0^z(z-u)f''(u)\,du.$$
The integrand lies between $0$ and $6(z-u)$, both continuous comparison functions. Integral monotonicity [F4], and Newton--Leibniz for the polynomial primitive $6zu-3u^2$, give $0\le f(z)\le3z^2$. Thus the discrepancy in step 1.1 is at most $3z^2\le3\delta^2$; [A1] further gives $3\delta^2\le3/100$. At $z=0$ the same sharper comparison is zero by direct evaluation, without applying the nondegenerate-interval theorem.

The spatial bound in [F1] gives $|g_{ij}-(1+2z)\delta_{ij}|\le\delta^2$, since $\delta_{ij}$ is $0$ or $1$. The density identity in [F1] gives $0\le1-\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{lin}}\le3\delta$. Applying [A1] and combining with step 2.1 yields the three numerical bounds in the Example.

For the worldline $\gamma_{\mathbf{x},x^0_*}$ defined in the Statement, $\dot\gamma=U$, so its covariant acceleration is the supplier field $a^b$. Here $\rho>0$ by [F1] and $H_i=-\delta b x^i/(r^2+b^2)^{3/2}$; hence $a^i=-c^2H_i/H^3$ is nonzero when $r>0$, while $a^i=0$ at $r=0$. The supplier also gives $a^0=0$. Dividing its all-component identity $\rho a^b=\sigma F^b{}_cU^c$ by positive $\rho$ gives $a^b=f^b=(\sigma/\rho)F^b{}_cU^c$ everywhere. Thus both vectors are nonzero for $r>0$ and vanish at the center; only the noncentral static worldlines fail the geodesic definition of free fall.

At a point $p\in\Omega$, an **observer** is a future-directed unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ satisfying $g(n,n)=-1$. A smooth field of such vectors is an **observer congruence**. A tetrad is a basis of a tangent space; an observer, a congruence, a tetrad and a coordinate chart are different objects. A **four-velocity field** $U$ is a $C^2$ future-timelike vector field with $g(U,U)=-c^2$; $n=U/c$ is its unit observer at each point. A **proper-time worldline segment** is a $C^2$ future-directed timelike curve $z:I\to\Omega$ on an interval $I$ of proper time $\tau$ in seconds, with $dz/d\tau=U$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$ along the segment. These are local model fields and curves; no global flow or completeness is included.

The matter variables are constitutive inputs of a selected model: rest-mass density $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, rest-charge density $\sigma$ in $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$, rest-energy density $\epsilon$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and isotropic pressure $p$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. A smooth matter current $j^a$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, and a symmetric matter stress tensor $T_m^{ab}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ in the stated length-coordinate convention. Their physical meanings are fixed only after a constitutive branch is selected:

- For charged dust, $T_m^{ab}=\rho U^aU^b$ and $j^a=\sigma U^a$. Here $\rho\geq0$ is rest-mass density, not energy density.
- For a perfect fluid, $T_m^{ab}=(\epsilon+p)U^aU^b/c^2+pg^{ab}$. Its rest-frame entries are $(\epsilon,p,p,p)$. No equation of state is included by this tensor definition.
- An optional conducting-fluid current is $j^a=\sigma U^a+q^a$, where $q^aU_a=0$ and $q^a$ is a rest-space conduction-current density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. The separate constitutive choice $q^a=\chi E_U^a$ uses a scalar conductivity $\chi\geq0$ in $\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}$ and is not part of the general definition.

For a smooth real electromagnetic two-form $F$ and positive $\mu_0$, define the electromagnetic stress by

$$T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{ab}:=\frac1{\mu_0}\left(F^{ac}F^b{}_c-\frac14g^{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right),\qquad T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}:=g_{ac}g_{bd}T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{cd}.$$

The components of $F$ in an orthonormal tetrad have tesla units. For an observer $n$, the observer electric field is $E_n^a:=cF^a{}_bn^b$ in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$; with $U=cn$, write $E_U^a:=F^a{}_bU^b=E_n^a$. The observer magnetic field is the spatial covector $B_{n,a}:=-({\star_gF})_{ab}n^b$ in tesla, with the orientation and Hodge convention of [[def-emg-geometry-units]]. These observer fields depend on $n$; they are not global observer-independent three-vectors.

Define the matter-plus-field force density by $f^a:=F^a{}_bj^b$, in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$, and the matter exchange equation by $\nabla_aT_m^{ab}=f^b$. This equation is a condition of a selected coupled model, not a consequence of the tensor definitions alone. For any unit observer $n$, define the measured energy density of a symmetric stress tensor $T_{ab}$ by $\mathcal E_n:=T_{ab}n^an^b$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. Define its spatial energy-current vector by $\mathcal S_n^a:=-h_n{}^a{}_cT^c{}_bn^b$, where $h_n{}^a{}_b=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b$ projects to $n^\perp$; its orthonormal-frame physical energy flux is $c\mathcal S_n^i$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. These contractions are derived, observer-dependent quantities.

Within the selected Einstein–Maxwell formulation, the fields $g$ and $F$ may be dynamical unknowns in a coupled branch or prescribed data in a test branch. The matter variables $\rho,\sigma,\epsilon,p$ and any chosen conductivity or equation of state are independent constitutive input. The current, stress, force density, electromagnetic stress, observer fields and observer contractions are derived from those inputs by the displayed definitions. This definition makes no identification with Newtonian or thermodynamic quantities solely because units agree; it records no measurement and asserts no matter evolution, entropy law, or coupled Einstein–Maxwell solution.

Use the energy-condition definitions of [[def-emg-pointwise-energy-conditions]] and the matter and Maxwell tensor definitions of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. At every point of an oriented time-oriented Lorentzian domain, the Maxwell tensor $T_{\mathrm{EM}}$ of that definition is symmetric, trace-free, and satisfies WEC, NEC, SEC and DEC. Its observer energy density and energy flux in a positively oriented orthonormal rest frame are

$$u=\frac{|E|^2/c^2+|B|^2}{2\mu_0},\qquad \frac{E\times B}{\mu_0c},$$

and the DEC flux is future causal or zero. A charged-dust tensor with $\rho\ge0$ satisfies all four conditions. For a perfect-fluid tensor with rest energy density $\epsilon$ and pressure $p$, the exact pointwise conditions are

$$\mathrm{WEC}\iff \epsilon\ge0\text{ and }\epsilon+p\ge0,\quad \mathrm{NEC}\iff\epsilon+p\ge0,$$

$$\mathrm{SEC}\iff\epsilon+p\ge0\text{ and }\epsilon+3p\ge0,\quad \mathrm{DEC}\iff\epsilon\ge|p|.$$

At a point, finite sums of tensors satisfying any one of these conditions still satisfy that condition; in particular $T_{\mathrm{EM}}+T_m$ satisfies all four for nonnegative dust. No general matter positivity assumption is made, and adding $T_{\mathrm{EM}}$ to an arbitrary fluid need not repair a violated fluid inequality.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

derivations.claim: Put $B_z=\sqrt\epsilon c b_0/(\alpha L)$ and supply the real one-form $A=(B_z/2)(x^1\,dx^2-x^2\,dx^1)$ on all of Minkowski space. Its coefficients are smooth and have SI units tesla metres, and direct differentiation gives $dA=B_z\,dx^1\wedge dx^2=F$, with $(dA)_{0i}=0$ and $(dA)_{12}=B_z$. Thus the local-potential hypothesis of [F6] is met on every finite curve segment, and the action model gives its proper-time Lorentz law throughout the Example's displayed range, independently of the general small-cutoff comparison in [F1]. In flat coordinates this law has $U^0=\gamma c$, $U^i=\gamma w^i$, and $\nabla=\partial$. With $E=0$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, its spatial components reduce to $d(\gamma m\mathbf w)/dt=q\mathbf w\times\mathbf B$. Its dot product with $\mathbf w$ is zero, so $|\mathbf w|$ and $\gamma=(1-|\mathbf w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}=(1-\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|^2)^{-1/2}$ are constant. Since $\mathbf W_0$ is transverse to $\mathbf e_z$, the motion stays in that transverse plane. Define $J\mathbf v:=\mathbf v\times b_0\mathbf e_z$ there; $J$ is skew-symmetric and $J^2=-b_0^2I$. Identify the transverse plane with the real Euclidean normed space $\mathbb R^2$ using the ordered coordinate basis $(\mathbf e_x,\mathbf e_y)$; it is Banach by [F3], and $|Jv|=|b_0||v|$ proves that $J$ is bounded with $\|J\|_{2\to2}=|b_0|$. Define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^nJ^n/n!$ by [F3], and write $e^{tJ}:=E(t)$. Rescaling the exact force equation gives $\mathbf W'=J\mathbf W/\gamma$ and $\mathbf X'=\mathbf W$. The formula $\mathbf W(S)=E(S/\gamma)\mathbf W_0$ has the matched initial velocity and satisfies the velocity equation by the derivative law in [F3]; the Newton–Lorentz comparison is $\mathbf W_N(S)=E(S)\mathbf W_0$. For either constant generator $aJ$ with $a=\gamma^{-1}$ or $a=1$, any solution with this initial value is unique: differentiating $E(-aS)\mathbf W(S)$ gives zero, so [F4] makes it constant and multiplication by $E(aS)$ recovers the displayed formula.

By [F3], $Q(t):=E(t)^TE(t)$ is smooth and $Q'(t)=E(t)^T(J^T+J)E(t)=0$, with $Q(0)=I$. Clause 2 of [F4], applied to its four entries as a real vector on any compact interval, gives $Q(t)=I$, so every $E(t)$ preserves the Euclidean norm. For fixed $S>0$, put $r=\gamma^{-1}$ and $P(s):=E(rs)E(S-s)$ on $[0,S]$. The semigroup and derivative laws in [F3] imply that these factors commute with $J$ and $P'(s)=(r-1)JE(rs)E(S-s)$. Its derivative is continuous, so the componentwise integral identity in [F4] gives $E(rS)-E(S)=\int_0^S(r-1)JE(rs)E(S-s)\,ds$. Apply this identity to $\mathbf W_0$ and then [F5]. Both exponential factors preserve norm, so $|\mathbf W-\mathbf W_N|\le S|b_0||1-\gamma^{-1}||\mathbf W_0|$. At $S=0$ the difference and integral vanish directly. The exact identity $1-\gamma^{-1}=\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|^2/(1+\sqrt{1-\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|^2})\le\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|^2$ proves the velocity bound throughout the displayed parameter range, including $\mathbf W_0=0$.

Define $J^{-1}=-J/b_0^2$ and the positions explicitly by $\mathbf X(S)=\mathbf X(0)+\gamma J^{-1}(E(S/\gamma)-I)\mathbf W_0$ and $\mathbf X_N(S)=\mathbf X(0)+J^{-1}(E(S)-I)\mathbf W_0$. Their derivatives are the respective velocities by [F3], and their initial positions match. Clause 1 of [F4] and [F5] give $|\mathbf X(S)-\mathbf X_N(S)|\le\int_0^S|\mathbf W(s)-\mathbf W_N(s)|\,ds\le |b_0|\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|^3\int_0^S s\,ds=\tfrac12|b_0|\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|^3S^2$, with $S=0$ immediate. The smooth orthogonal flows exist for all real $S$ and give $|\mathbf W|=|\mathbf W_N|=|\mathbf W_0|$ and $|\mathbf X-\mathbf X(0)|,|\mathbf X_N-\mathbf X_N(0)|\le S_*|\mathbf W_0|$ on the stated finite interval, hence common compact containment. Their constant speed is strictly below $c$ because $\epsilon|\mathbf W_0|^2\le1/2$, and setting proper time $\tau=t/\gamma$ reconstructs the future-directed proper-time test worldline satisfying the force law used in step 1.1. These direct calculations establish the displayed example throughout its stated range; for sufficiently small $\epsilon$ they also lie within the general theorem's hypotheses [F1]. The metric and field remain prescribed inputs by [F2], with no coupled-background equation.

and charge-current conservation $\nabla_aj^a=0$. On each open region $\Omega_+:=\{p\in\Omega:\rho(p)>0\}$ define $\alpha:=\sigma/\rho$. **Inputs.** Fix the integral domain
$P=\mathbb Q[r,y,M,a,q]$ on the ordered variables $(r,y,M,a,q)$ and its field of fractions
$K=\operatorname{Frac}(P)$. A run receives a symmetric $4\times4$ matrix
$g=(g_{ij})$ and a covector $A=(A_i)$ with entries in $K$, represented by
finite sparse polynomial numerator-denominator pairs, together with a specified
polynomial $w\in P$. It also receives the chart hypothesis that $\det g$ is
nonzero in $K$ and that on the real open chart under consideration all input
denominators are nonzero and $w=\sqrt{|\det g|}>0$. The coordinate derivations
are $\delta_0=\delta_3=0$, $\delta_1=\partial_r$, and $\delta_2=\partial_y$.
The chart hypothesis is input; the procedure does not prove Lorentz signature
or check the volume identity. For geometric interpretation use the curvature
convention $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$,
with $R^a{}_{bcd}$ the coefficient of $R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b$ and
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=R^a{}_{bad}$. Expanding this definition yields the
coordinate Ricci schedule in Instruction 3.

**Outputs.** Return the finite tables of: the sixteen entries of
$gg^{-1}-I$; the six independent components of
$F_{ij}:=\delta_iA_j-\delta_jA_i$; all sixteen raised components
$F^{ij}$; the four Maxwell-density residuals
$\sum_i\delta_i(wF^{ij})$; all sixty-four Christoffel entries; the sixteen
Ricci entries
$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ij} =\sum_k\left(\delta_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}-\delta_j\Gamma^k{}_{ik}\right) +\sum_{k,l}\left(\Gamma^k{}_{kl}\Gamma^l{}_{ij} -\Gamma^k{}_{jl}\Gamma^l{}_{ik}\right);$$
the scalar $F_{ij}F^{ij}$; the sixteen entries of
$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ij} -2\left(F_{ik}F_j{}^k-\frac14g_{ij}F_{kl}F^{kl}\right);$$
the scalar curvature and the Ricci-square. For every output rational function,
return its numerator-denominator pair, its exact numerator-zero flag, and the
finite list of all divisor polynomials used.

**Instructions.**

1. Represent a polynomial by its finite set of exponent-vector/coefficient
   pairs. Addition merges equal exponent vectors, multiplication enumerates
   every pair of input monomials and collects equal exponent vectors, and
   $\partial_r,\partial_y$ differentiate each monomial by the integer-power
   rule of [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]]. Represent a rational function by $(p,d)$ with $p,d\in P$ and
   $d\ne0$. Addition and multiplication use cross-products, and division
   replaces $(p,d)/(u,v)$ by $(pv,du)$ only when $u\ne0$ in $P$.
   Differentiation uses $(p'd-pd',d^2)$.

2. Compute $\det g$ by its twenty-four signed permutation products and form
   $g^{-1}$ from cofactors divided by $\det g$. Record and check all sixteen
   entries of $gg^{-1}-I$.

3. Compute every $F_{ij}$ and $F^{ij}$, then all four
   $\sum_i\delta_i(wF^{ij})$. Compute every Christoffel entry by
   $\Gamma^i{}_{jk}=\frac12\sum_lg^{il}
   (\delta_jg_{lk}+\delta_kg_{jl}-\delta_lg_{jk})$, then all sixteen Ricci
   entries by the displayed formula, with no symmetry-based component omitted.

If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is an integral domain for every $n\in\mathbb N$, including $n=0$.

If $D$ is an integral domain, then $D\setminus\{0\}$ is multiplicative. Its localisation
$$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$
is the **field of fractions** of $D$. Thus its elements are fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, modulo the localisation equivalence relation.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

or check the volume identity. For geometric interpretation use the curvature
convention $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$,
with $R^a{}_{bcd}$ the coefficient of $R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b$ and
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=R^a{}_{bad}$. Expanding this definition yields the
coordinate Ricci schedule in Instruction 3.

**Outputs.** Return the finite tables of: the sixteen entries of
$gg^{-1}-I$; the six independent components of
$F_{ij}:=\delta_iA_j-\delta_jA_i$; all sixteen raised components
$F^{ij}$; the four Maxwell-density residuals
$\sum_i\delta_i(wF^{ij})$; all sixty-four Christoffel entries; the sixteen
Ricci entries
$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ij} =\sum_k\left(\delta_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}-\delta_j\Gamma^k{}_{ik}\right) +\sum_{k,l}\left(\Gamma^k{}_{kl}\Gamma^l{}_{ij} -\Gamma^k{}_{jl}\Gamma^l{}_{ik}\right);$$
the scalar $F_{ij}F^{ij}$; the sixteen entries of
$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ij} -2\left(F_{ik}F_j{}^k-\frac14g_{ij}F_{kl}F^{kl}\right);$$
the scalar curvature and the Ricci-square. For every output rational function,
return its numerator-denominator pair, its exact numerator-zero flag, and the
finite list of all divisor polynomials used.

   pairs. Addition merges equal exponent vectors, multiplication enumerates

   $\partial_r,\partial_y$ differentiate each monomial by the integer-power
   rule of [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]]. Represent a rational function by $(p,d)$ with $p,d\in P$ and
   $d\ne0$. Addition and multiplication use cross-products, and division
   replaces $(p,d)/(u,v)$ by $(pv,du)$ only when $u\ne0$ in $P$.

2. Compute $\det g$ by its twenty-four signed permutation products and form
