Let $M,a,q\in\mathbb R$ have units of metres. Set
$$\Sigma=r^2+a^2\cos^2\theta,\quad \Delta=r^2-2Mr+a^2+q^2,\quad R=r^2+a^2,$$
and let $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ have unit round
metric $\gamma$ and outward area form $\omega$. Define the global one-form
$\beta:=X\,dY-Y\,dX$ and the product
$$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}:=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2,$$
oriented by $dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega$. On this product define
$$\begin{aligned}g_{\mathrm{in}}={}&-\left(1-\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}\right)dv^2+2\,dv\,dr-2a\,dr\,\beta-2a\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}dv\odot\beta+\Sigma\gamma+a^2\left(1+\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}\right)\beta^2,\\\mathcal A_{\mathrm{in}}={}&-\frac{qr}{\Sigma}(dv-a\beta),\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}:=d\mathcal A_{\mathrm{in}},\end{aligned}$$
where $u\odot w=(u\otimes w+w\otimes u)/2$. The time-orientation field
is $$f_0:=1-\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma},\qquad N:=\partial_v-\frac{1+f_0^2}{2}\partial_r.$$
These formulas define smooth Lorentzian metric and field data on the whole
sphere for every $r>0$, including each positive root of $\Delta$; no
maximal extension, $r=0$ locus, or global uniqueness is asserted. On the
dense pole-free set where $\Delta\ne0$, they are related to the
Boyer-Lindquist data by the advanced coordinate change proved below.

The source-free geometric electrovac equations extend across $\Delta=0$
conditionally on the exact current interface of
[[thm-emg-xs-kn-verification]]: its geometric pole-free equations are used
on the dense complement of the roots and axes, and smoothness then extends
their residuals. That supplier is a current draft theorem and is not claimed
as independently accepted here.

Let $M>0$ and $M^2\ge a^2+q^2>0$ in the selected ingoing KN model.
For either $r_H=r_\pm=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-a^2-q^2}$ set
$R_H=r_H^2+a^2$, $\Sigma_H=r_H^2+a^2\cos^2\theta$, and
$$\chi_H=\partial_v+\Omega_H\Psi,\qquad \Omega_H=\frac{a}{R_H},$$
where $\Psi=X\partial_Y-Y\partial_X$ is the smooth rotation field on
$S^2$. The surface $r=r_H$ is a null hypersurface and $\chi_H$ is its
future null normal and Killing generator. Under the specified normalization
$d(g(\chi_H,\chi_H))=-2\kappa_H\chi_H^\flat$ in
[[def-emg-causal-solution-and-horizon-vocabulary]],
$$\kappa_H=\frac{\Delta'(r_H)}{2R_H} =\frac{r_H-r_{\mathrm{other}}}{2R_H},\qquad \operatorname{Area}(S_H)=4\pi R_H,\qquad -\mathcal A_{\mathrm{in}}(\chi_H)=\frac{q r_H}{R_H}.$$
At the double root $\kappa_H=0$. These are local geometric calculations on
the specified model; they assert no maximality or uniqueness.

Consider either (i) the selected ingoing RN model with $M>0$, $Q^2>0$,
$M^2\ge Q^2$, and
$r_H=M+\sqrt{M^2-Q^2}$, or (ii) the selected ingoing KN model with $M>0$,
$M^2\ge a^2+q^2>0$, and
$r_H=M+\sqrt{M^2-a^2-q^2}$. In each case $r_H>0$. There is
$\delta>0$ and a collar
$$\mathcal C=\mathbb R_v\times(r_H-\delta,r_H+\delta)\times S^2$$
on which $\tau:=v-r$ is a smooth temporal function in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]: its gradient is past
timelike and $d\tau(Z)>0$ for every nonzero future causal vector $Z$. There
is a finite $C\ge0$ such that
$$dr(Z)\le C|r-r_H|\,d\tau(Z)$$
for every future causal $Z$ over the collar. On $r=r_H$ one also has
$dr(Z)\le0$. This is a local cone estimate on the two specified metrics; it
is not an event-horizon theorem.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$N_p^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,N_p)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and let $T_p$ be the
timelike set, with components $C_p^+$ (the one containing $N_p$) and $C_p^-$,
and with future and past causality as fixed in
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] and
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Then:

1. $N_p^{\perp}$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $T_pM$, and $g_p$ is
   positive definite on it; equivalently, every nonzero $v\in T_pM$ with
   $g_p(v,N_p)=0$ is spacelike.
2. $g_p(v,N_p)\neq0$ for every nonzero causal $v\in T_pM$.
3. $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)<0\}$, and
   $C_p^-=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)>0\}$.
4. A nonzero $v\in T_pM$ is causal and future-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$, and causal and past-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)$. Consequently
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the set of
   future-directed causal vectors and $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)\setminus\{0\}$
   exactly the set of past-directed causal vectors,
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)=\{0\}$, and every
   nonzero causal vector is exactly one of future-directed and past-directed.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable boundaryless four-manifold with smooth Lorentz metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time orientation. All definitions below are mathematical. A solution of a specified covariant field system is a tuple of fields of the regularity stated by that system satisfying its equations on its stated domain; this terminology alone supplies neither existence nor a global electromagnetic potential.

**(a) Global causal and Cauchy conventions.** Use exactly [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]: a future causal curve is locally absolutely continuous in coordinate charts, has nonzero future causal derivative almost everywhere, and has no constant subinterval. Inextendibility and causal reachability $J^\pm$ have that item's endpoint-extension meanings. A Cauchy set meets every inextendible causal curve at exactly one parameter value: its inverse image under each such curve is a singleton, as in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]. A spacelike hypersurface is a smooth embedded codimension-one submanifold with positive-definite induced metric; this local condition does not assert the global Cauchy property. Strong causality has the small-neighborhood no-leaving-and-reentering meaning of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]. Global hyperbolicity means strong causality and compactness of every $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$, exactly as there; no equivalence theorem is added here.

**(b) Null and Killing horizons.** A smooth embedded hypersurface $H\subset M$ is **null** when $g|_{TH}$ is degenerate. Equivalently, for any local defining function $f$ with $H=\{f=0\}$ and $df\ne0$ on $H$, $g^{-1}(df,df)=0$ on $H$. A specified smooth vector field $\xi$ is **Killing** when $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$, equivalently $\nabla_{(a}\xi_{b)}=0$, using [[def-gr-killing-field]] and [[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]]. A **Killing horizon for $\xi$** is a null hypersurface whose nonzero-generator part $H_*:=\{p\in H:\xi_p\ne0\}$ is nonempty and dense in $H$, and on that part the specified field is tangent, null and normal: $\xi_p\in T_pH$ and $g(\xi_p,X)=0$ for every $X\in T_pH$. A generator parameter or asymptotic normalization, when required, must be specified separately.

On $H_*$ the **signed surface gravity** for this precise $\xi$ is the unique smooth scalar $\kappa_H$ such that

$$d\bigl(g(\xi,\xi)\bigr)_p=-2\kappa_H(p)\,\xi^\flat_p\quad(p\in H_*).$$

This is an equality of ambient covectors at points of $H$, not merely of their pullbacks to $TH$. No constancy or positivity is asserted. Under a nonzero constant rescaling $\xi'=a\xi$, $\kappa'_H=a\kappa_H$. A **bifurcation surface** is a specified smooth spacelike two-surface $B$ where the extended Killing field vanishes and the specified horizon branches meet (or have $B$ as their common boundary). Surface gravity at such a surface means a smooth extension of the scalar from the adjacent nonzero-generator portions, with each point in their closure, only if that extension exists; the defining equation at $\xi=0$ alone determines no value. Neither a bifurcation surface nor such an extension is asserted to exist.

**(c) Sections, area and ergoregions.** A **horizon section** is a specified smooth spacelike embedded two-surface $S$ in the horizon, with positive induced metric $h$. Its area density is $\mu_h=\sqrt{\det(h_{ij})}\,|dy^1dy^2|$ of [[def-riemannian-volume-density]]. Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for intrinsic density integration, as in [[def-riemannian-volume-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]]. Its possibly infinite area is the nonnegative extended value

$$\operatorname{Area}_g(S):=\sup\left\{\int_S\chi\mu_h:\chi\in C_c^\infty(S),\ 0\le\chi\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

with the extended order of [[def-extended-reals]]. On compact $S$ this is $\int_S\mu_h$; orientation is unnecessary. The density glues by [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]]. A stationary field here is a specified Killing field timelike on a specified nonempty open region; no normalization is inferred from this adjective. Its **ergoregion** in the chosen model is $\{g(\xi,\xi)>0\}$, its **stationary-limit set** is $\{g(\xi,\xi)=0\}$, and its **ergosurface** is the relative boundary of its ergoregion. Every ergosurface point lies in the stationary-limit set; the converse requires a separate sign-change argument. Nullness, Killing-horizon status and escape-boundary status are separate claims; a coordinate root alone proves none of them.

**(d) Selected-model escape.** Fix a specified open spacetime model $U\subseteq M$ and specified smooth radius observable $r:U\to\mathbb R$. An admissible escape path is a continuous $\gamma:[0,T)\to U$, $0<T\le+\infty$, with $\gamma(0)=p$, such that every compact parameter segment has a finite subdivision on whose pieces the coordinate curve is $C^1$, with nonzero future causal tangent (one-sided at piece endpoints). Define

$$\mathcal E_{U,r}:=\left\{p\in U:\exists\gamma\text{ admissible from }p\ \forall R>0\ \exists t\in[0,T):r(\gamma(t))>R\right\}.$$

The **selected escape boundary** is $\partial_U\mathcal E_{U,r}$. This explicitly selected piecewise-$C^1$ path class is contained in the global causal-curve class of (a); it does not replace that class in Cauchy definitions. No geodesic restriction, conformal completion, event-horizon identification or maximal extension is implicit in this definition.

**(e) Approached metric extensions and curvature obstructions.** A $C^2$ nondegenerate metric extension of an open model $(U,g)$ consists of a smooth Hausdorff second-countable four-manifold $\widetilde M$, a $C^2$ Lorentz metric $\widetilde g$ of the same signature, and a smooth open embedding $j:U\to\widetilde M$ with $j^*\widetilde g=g$. An **approached added point** is $p\in\widetilde M\setminus j(U)$ with $j(x_n)\to p$ for a specified sequence $x_n\in U$ (or the corresponding limit of a specified curve). An **extension obstruction at that approach** means no such extension and added point can realize the stated approach. In particular, unbounded absolute values of a polynomial complete contraction of the curvature tensor and metric inverse along $x_n$ obstruct such an approached $C^2$ nondegenerate extension. This criterion concerns curvature without its covariant derivatives. A smooth metric extension is the same definition with smooth $\widetilde g$. These notions alone assert neither a distributional matter source nor geodesic incompleteness.

**(f) Observers and spatial fields.** Observers, smooth observer congruences and their integral curves, adapted charts and tetrads retain the distinct meanings of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Relative to a future unit observer $n$, an electric or magnetic spatial covector is identified with a spatial vector only by raising with the positive rest metric $h=g+n^\flat\otimes n^\flat$ on $n^\perp$. Such spatial vectors $e,b$ are not tetrad basis vectors. No singular-source product or action is defined by this vocabulary.

For $a>0$, integer $m$ and integer $n\ge1$, define the rational regime by

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. For the rational-exponent regime at base zero, retain the convention of [[def-rational-power]] and [[def-integer-power]]: $0^0=1$, $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$, and $0^r$ is undefined for rational $r<0$. This records the integer zero-exponent convention together with the positive-rational supplementary clause; it does not extend the real-exponent convention.

The separate real-exponent regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For real exponents at base zero, set $0^x=0$ only when $x>0$; $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are undefined, exactly as in [[def-real-power]]. The rational and real exponent operations are separate definitions; at zero base and exponent zero, state which regime is intended: the rational/integer convention gives $1$, while the real-power convention leaves the expression undefined. No arbitrary real power is assigned to a negative base. The real-power laws are supplied by that theorem, not inferred from the rational root formula. Use the real-number structure of [[def-real-numbers]].

In particular $s(q)=q^{1/2}$ for $q>0$ is the unique positive solution of $s(q)^2=q$. Its smoothness and derivative are a separate well-definedness result, not an assumption about fractional notation.

derivations.claim:
On a polar chart put
$$\ell=-\partial_r,\qquad n=\frac{R}{\Sigma}\partial_v+\frac{\Delta}{2\Sigma}\partial_r+\frac{a}{\Sigma}\partial_\psi.$$ 
Substitution of [F1]'s six metric entries gives $g(\ell,\ell)=g(n,n)=0$,
$g(\ell,n)=-1$, and
$$g(n,N)=-\frac12\left(\frac{\Delta}{\Sigma}+1+f_0^2\right).$$
The same components give $g(n,\partial_r)=1$ because
$R-a^2\sin^2\theta=\Sigma$, and direct contraction gives
$g(n,\partial_v)=-\Delta/(2\Sigma)$. Since
$N=\partial_v-(1+f_0^2)\partial_r/2$, these yield the displayed
$g(n,N)$. For the null identity, after multiplying by $\Sigma^3$ the
numerator is
$$R^2(-\Delta+a^2s^2)+R\Delta\Sigma-2a^2R(R-\Delta)s^2-a^2\Delta s^2\Sigma+a^2(R^2-a^2\Delta s^2)s^2=0,$$
where $s^2=\sin^2\theta$ and $\Sigma=R-a^2s^2$; the pairing
$g(\ell,n)=-1$ follows from the $rv$ and $r\psi$ terms. The vector $n$
extends smoothly across the polar axes as
$(R/\Sigma)\partial_v+(\Delta/(2\Sigma))\partial_r+(a/\Sigma)\Psi$.
For $r>r_+$, [F2] gives $\Delta>0$, so $g(n,N)<0$; [F4] makes $n$
future null. Its integral curves satisfy $dv/ds=R/\Sigma>0$,
$dr/dv=\Delta/(2R)$ and $d\psi/dv=a/R$.

For a path starting below $r_+$, apply [F3] on its final collar segment
before a proposed first root contact. With $w=r_+-r\ge0$,
$w'\ge-Cw\tau'$, so [F5] and the chain rule make
$(e^{C\tau}w)'\ge0$ on each $C^1$ piece. The fundamental theorem of
calculus makes this product nondecreasing on each piece, and continuity
patches those inequalities across the finite partition. This contradicts
$w$ reaching zero from its positive value at the starting point of that collar segment: use the initial point if already in the collar, or the last crossing of a fixed smaller collar lower boundary otherwise.
If a path starts at the root and has a positive excursion, a component of
$\{r>r_+\}$ has a left endpoint with $r=r_+$. Restrict to an initial portion inside the collar, stopping at the first crossing of $r_++\delta/2$ if necessary, where $\delta$ is a collar width from [F3]. On that portion
$h=e^{-C\tau}(r-r_+)$ has derivative $h'\le0$ by [F3] and [F5], so the
fundamental theorem of calculus on the finitely many smooth pieces makes
$h$ nonincreasing. Continuity from its zero left-end value contradicts
positivity. Therefore no point with $r\le r_+$ can escape.

Fix any $r_0>r_+$ and initial $v_0,\omega_0$. For $r\ge r_0$, set
$$v(r)=v_0+\int_{r_0}^r\frac{2R(s)}{\Delta(s)}\,ds,\qquad \alpha(r)=\int_{r_0}^r\frac{2a}{\Delta(s)}\,ds.$$
The integrands are smooth on each finite interval $[r_0,r]$ and [F5]
gives their derivatives. Rotate $\omega_0$ about the axis by $\alpha(r)$
to obtain a smooth sphere path, including if it passes through a pole.
The resulting curve has tangent
$$\gamma'(r)=\frac{2R}{\Delta}\partial_v+\partial_r+\frac{2a}{\Delta}\Psi =\frac{2\Sigma}{\Delta}n.$$
Its coefficient is positive because $\Sigma,\Delta>0$, so step 1.1 shows
it is future null. Reparameterizing by $s=r-r_0\in[0,\infty)$ gives the path domain in [L1]. It exists for every finite $r\ge r_0$ and reaches
arbitrarily large radii. Thus every point with $r>r_+$ belongs to $\mathcal E$.

Step 2.1 includes every point with $r>r_+$ in $\mathcal E$, while the
earlier collar argument excludes every point with $r\le r_+$. The boundary of this open radial
half-space in $\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2$ is exactly
$r=r_+$. This proves the stated boundary under the conditional escape
interface [L1].

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.2–3.1: the selected product has nonempty exterior and interior radial regions because r_+>0; the collar exclusion and explicit outgoing path identify both parts rather than assuming nonempty escape.
step 1.2: Paths at or below the outer root cannot escape outward.
Statement and step 2.1 build one rotating outgoing path from the given exterior point on the whole [0,infinity) domain; no collection of radius-dependent finite paths is substituted.
step Statement: The claim includes the extremal double root.
step 3.1: The escape boundary is the outer-root level.

boundaries.reason: Step 2.1 constructs the entire outgoing path by two explicit radial integrals and the fixed sphere rotation; step 1.2 uses finite subdivisions on compact path segments rather than choosing arbitrary curve families.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.2 and 3.1: the collar integrating-factor argument excludes outward crossing from r<=r_+, including the zero initial excursion; thus an escaping point must satisfy r>r_+.
Step 2.1: the explicit v(r) and sphere rotation define one future null path for every r>=r0>r_+, including initial poles; reparameterization gives a path on [0,infinity) with unbounded r.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters. Set
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$ and
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}.$$
The selected ingoing RN manifold is
$$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}:=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2,$$
where $v,r$ have units of metres, $S^2$ has unit round metric $\gamma$ and
outward area form $\omega$, and the signature is $(-,+,+,+)$. Orient the
product by $dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega$. Define
$$g_{\mathrm{in}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\gamma,\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dv\wedge dr+q_m\omega.$$
These are smooth on every $r>0$, including every positive root of $f$; the
domain excludes $r=0$. This is an extension of the static RN metric and field,
not a maximal extension or a specification of a source at the excluded
centre.

For the time orientation, define the global smooth fields
$$\ell:=-\partial_r,\qquad n:=\partial_v+\frac{f(r)}2\partial_r,\qquad N:=\ell+n=\partial_v+\left(\frac{f(r)}2-1\right)\partial_r.$$
The chosen future timelike field is $N$; the future cone is the component of
the timelike cone containing it. The well-definedness proof shows that $N$ is
timelike and that $\ell,n$ are future null. On $f\ne0$, the substitution
$v=t+r_*(r)$ with $r_*'=1/f$ identifies the metric and two-form with the
static dyonic RN formulas of [[def-emg-xs-rn-data]]. This coordinate
identification does not assert agreement of time orientations on the
interior static components: on $f>0$ the selected orientation agrees with
$\partial_t$, while on $f<0$ it is the opposite of the separate choice
$\partial_r$ made by that static definition.

conversion in $x^0=ct$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Assume the mathematical

mathematical item. Define $v\in\Gamma(TM)$ by $v^b:=\nabla_aF^{ab}$ and

$$\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

$\nabla_aj^a=0$. This conclusion requires the sourced equation and $\mu_0>0$;
it does not require $dF=0$.

point-normal chart supplied by

$B_i(x):=\frac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}(x)$, where $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ and
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is alternating. These are local component abbreviations in
the chosen chart, not global observer fields. With
$\operatorname{div}E:=\partial_iE_i$,
$(\operatorname{curl}E)_k:=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iE_j$, and similarly

$$v^0=-\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad v^k=\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k,$$

where $\partial_t:=c\,\partial_0$. The equations are pointwise identities
in normal coordinates; they do not assert that these component abbreviations
form global three-vector fields on curved spacetime.

$x^0=ct$, define $\rho:=j^0/c$, $J^i:=j^i$, and
$\epsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. The same component formulas at every point give

$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE=\mu_0J,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \partial_tB+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

derivations.claim: Since $\mathcal F_\sigma=d\mathcal A_\sigma$, the identity $d^2=0$ in [F5] gives $d\mathcal F_\sigma=0$. Raising the two indices of $\mathcal F_{i0}=-\sigma H_i/H^2$ with [F2] gives $\mathcal F^{i0}=\sigma H_i/H^2$ and $\mathcal F^{0i}=-\sigma H_i/H^2$. Contracting the antisymmetric pair yields $\mathcal F_{ab}\mathcal F^{ab}=2\sum_i\mathcal F_{i0}\mathcal F^{i0}=-2q_H/H^4$.

The last Christoffel term in $\nabla_a\mathcal F^{ab}=\partial_a\mathcal F^{ab}+\Gamma^a{}_{ac}\mathcal F^{cb}+\Gamma^b{}_{ac}\mathcal F^{ac}$ vanishes because $\Gamma^b{}_{ac}$ is symmetric in $a,c$ and $\mathcal F^{ac}$ is antisymmetric. Summing over $i$ yields $\Delta_\delta|z|^{-1}=-3|z|^{-3}+3|z|^2|z|^{-5}=0$. Every term in $H$ is smooth on $D$, and every term is positive there, so $H>0$ and $\Delta_\delta H=0$ on $D$.

Inverting the diagonal metric in [F1] gives $g^{00}=-H^2$ and $g^{ij}=H^{-2}\delta^{ij}$, so raising $\mathcal F_{i0}=-\sigma H_i/H^2$ gives $\mathcal F^{i0}=\sigma H_i/H^2$. The metric determinant is $(-H^{-2})(H^2)^3=-H^4$, so the oriented volume form is $\mathrm{vol}_g=H^2dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$. The Hodge formula [F4] therefore gives $(\star_g\mathcal F_\sigma)_{ij}=-\sigma\epsilon_{ijk}H_k$. Evaluating this two-form on an outward-oriented Euclidean sphere gives $\int_S\star_g\mathcal F_\sigma=-\sigma\int_S\partial_\nu H\,dS_\delta$, because $\partial_\nu H=n^kH_k$ and the induced oriented area form has components $\epsilon_{ijk}n^k dS_\delta$. The pullback of $\mathcal F_\sigma$ to each spatial sphere is zero because every term in [F1] contains $dx^0$, which vanishes on its tangent vectors; hence $q_m(S)=0$.

Let $S_r(a)$ be a Euclidean sphere with center $a$ and radius $r$, and let $m/|x-b|$ be one term in $H$, where $d:=|b-a|\ne r$. At $x=a+rn$ with $n\in S^2$, its outward normal derivative is $-m(r-n\cdot(b-a))/|rn-(b-a)|^3$. The sphere area element is $r^2d\Omega$, where $d\Omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$ and $\int_{S^2}d\Omega=2\pi\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta=4\pi$. If $d=0$, direct integration gives flux $-4\pi m$. If $d>0$, choose the polar axis along $b-a$; this orthogonal change preserves the induced sphere area. With $u=\cos\theta$ and $n\cdot(b-a)=du$, the flux is $-2\pi mr^2J$, where $$J:=\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{r-du}{(r^2+d^2-2rdu)^{3/2}}\,du.$$ Set $w=r^2+d^2-2rdu$. Then $du=-dw/(2rd)$, the endpoint square roots for $w$ are $r+d$ and $|r-d|$, and $r-du=(r^2-d^2+w)/(2r)$. Therefore $$J=\frac1{4r^2d}\left((r^2-d^2)\int_{(r-d)^2}^{(r+d)^2}w^{-3/2}\,dw+\int_{(r-d)^2}^{(r+d)^2}w^{-1/2}\,dw\right).$$ Using antiderivatives $-2w^{-1/2}$ and $2w^{1/2}$ gives $$J=\frac{(r^2-d^2)\bigl(|r-d|^{-1}-(r+d)^{-1}\bigr)+(r+d-|r-d|)}{2r^2d}.$$ If $d<r$, the numerator is $4d$, so $J=2/r^2$; if $d>r$, the numerator is $0$, so $J=0$. For an isolated sphere $S_A(r)$, its own center has $d=0$, while each other center has distance $d_{AB}>r$ by [A1]. Applying step 1.3 term by term gives $\int_{S_A(r)}\partial_\nu H\,dS_\delta=-4\pi m_A$. Step 1.2 yields $q_e(S_A(r))=\sigma m_A$, and that step also gives $q_m(S_A(r))=0$.

$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

Every datum of [[def-emg-xs-harmonic-mp]] satisfies the source-free geometric Einstein-Maxwell equations of [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]]:

$$d\mathcal F_\sigma=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F_\sigma)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F_\sigma),\quad Q_{ab}(F):=F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\tfrac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}.$$

More explicitly, with $q_H:=\sum_iH_i^2$, the only nonzero independent raised field components are $\mathcal F^{i0}_\sigma=\sigma H_i/H^2$ and the quadratic-field components are

$$\mathcal F_{\sigma,ab}\mathcal F_\sigma^{ab}=-\frac{2q_H}{H^4},\qquad Q_{00}=\frac{q_H}{2H^6},\qquad Q_{0i}=0,\qquad Q_{ij}=\frac{\delta_{ij}q_H-2H_iH_j}{2H^2}.$$

For arbitrary $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$, put $Q^2=q_e^2+q_m^2$ and
$f(r)=1-2M/r+Q^2/r^2$. On every open $J\subset(0,\infty)$ with $f\ne0$, the
dyonic RN datum of [[def-emg-xs-rn-data]] is a geometric electrovac datum of
[[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]] on
$\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J\times S^2$. In particular, its global two-form is
smooth, $d\mathcal F=d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0$, and
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$ everywhere on that domain.

For arbitrary formal $c,\mu_0,G_N>0$, set $\alpha=\sqrt{4\pi G_N/(\mu_0c^4)}$, $F=\mathcal F/\alpha$, and $T_{ab}:=\mu_0^{-1}Q_g(F)_{ab}$. Then the same datum satisfies

$$dF=d(\star_gF)=0,\qquad S=0,\qquad G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}T_{ab},$$

where $S$ is scalar curvature and $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\frac12Sg_{ab}$. This is the formal SI-to-geometric tensor normalization of [[lem-emg-maxwell-observer-stress]](d). It asserts neither measured parameter values nor a bundle realization for arbitrary flux. When the separate fixed-sector action hypotheses hold, $T$ is also the electromagnetic Hilbert tensor of that supplier.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $o$ is the manifold orientation, $N$ is a smooth future timelike field, and the metric volume form is chosen to agree with $o$. Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection, let $\mathcal F$ be a smooth real two-form on $M$, and use the curvature convention
$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$.
Define
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd},$$
where both raised indices use $g^{-1}$. A **geometric electrovac datum with zero cosmological constant** is the tuple $(M,g,N,o,\mathcal F)$ satisfying
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$$
at every point of $M$. Here $\star_g$ is the Lorentzian Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$; on two-forms $\star_g^2=-1$. No material current, matter tensor, global potential, asymptotic flatness, positive mass, horizon, or extension condition is part of this definition.

For an oriented embedded sphere $S$ on which the integrals converge, define its geometric electric and magnetic flux parameters by
$$q_e(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\star_g\mathcal F,\qquad q_m(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\mathcal F.$$
When $M$ and the coordinates have length units, these parameters have units of length. A magnetic flux need not have a global potential; no flux quantization is included. The background Lorentzian geometry and Hodge conventions carry the countable-choice assumption $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of their named suppliers; the algebraic identities in this definition require no additional choice principle.

derivations.claim: On $\rho>0$, $H=1+m/\rho$ is smooth and positive. Direct differentiation gives $\partial_i(\rho^{-1})=-x^i\rho^{-3}$ and $\partial_i^2(\rho^{-1})=-\rho^{-3}+3(x^i)^2\rho^{-5}$, so $\Delta_\delta H=m(-3\rho^{-3}+3\rho^2\rho^{-5})=0$; hence $H$ satisfies the hypotheses of [F1]. The map $\rho\mapsto R=\rho+m$ has smooth inverse $\rho=R-m$ on the stated open intervals and derivative $1$, so it is a diffeomorphism. Since $H=R/(R-m)$, we have $H^{-1}=1-m/R$ and $d\rho=dR$. Substitution into [F1] gives $g=-(1-m/R)^2(dx^0)^2+(1-m/R)^{-2}dR^2+R^2\gamma_{S^2}$, because the sphere coefficient is $H^2\rho^2=R^2$ and the radial coefficient is $H^2=(1-m/R)^{-2}$.

The potential transforms as $\mathcal A_\sigma=\sigma((R-m)/R-1)dx^0=-\sigma mR^{-1}dx^0$. Differentiating gives $\mathcal F_\sigma=-\sigma mR^{-2}dx^0\wedge dR$, which is exactly [F2] with $q_e=\sigma m$ and $q_m=0$. The coordinate map preserves the displayed orientation, and both future fields point along the positive $x^0$ direction on $R>m$.

We have $M=m>0$, $|q_e|=m=M$, and $q_m=0$. Thus the RN parameter relation is extremal, and $f(R)>0$ on $R>m$. The equality of the metrics in step 1.1 and two-forms in step 2.1 transfers the MP electrovac equations of [F3] to the identical RN exterior, with electrovac meaning the equations in [F4]. The conclusion does not extend the coordinate map to $\rho=0$ or $R=m$.

boundaries.evidence: The domain rho>0 is nonempty and maps onto R>m. Step 1.1 proves a bijective radial change on these explicit intervals, not an identification on an unspecified possibly empty center family.
m=0 and rho=0 are excluded by A1. The magnetic parameter q_m=0 is allowed and step 2.1 obtains it from the purely electric potential without dividing by that parameter.
This is the single-center case H=1+m/rho. Step 1.1 checks its harmonicity directly and step 2.1 identifies q_e=sigma m; the argument does not require a multicenter limit.
R>m implies 1-m/R>0; step 1.1 therefore gives an invertible RN metric and a smooth radial inverse rho=R-m. The zero-lapse surface R=m is outside the identification.
Steps 1.1 and 3.1 restrict the radial map to (0,infinity) onto (m,infinity). Neither rho=0 nor R=m is in these intervals, and the final step explicitly withholds a horizon extension.
The transformation R=rho+m and inverse rho=R-m are explicit functions. The sign sigma is an input, so matching orientation and the two-form in step 2.1 requires no choice of an isometry.

boundaries.reason: Equality of these two supplied exterior presentations and the extremal relation are direct conclusions; no necessary-and-sufficient test for all extremal spacetimes is stated.
The proposition does not infer a global single-center MP presentation from a general extremal solution. Its reverse radial formula is only the explicit inverse of this particular map.

finite_checks.evidence: Steps 1.1-3.1 verify the diffeomorphism, metric and field substitution, and extremal parameter relation.

citations.quote:
Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$ carry its induced unit round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$ and outward area form $\omega_{S^2}$. Let $L>0$ have length units. Choose either (i) $f(z)=z^2$ on an open $J\subset(0,\infty)$, or (ii) $f(z)=1+z^2$ on an open $J\subset\mathbb R$. The coordinate $z$ and $\tau$ are dimensionless. On $\mathcal M_{L,f}=\mathbb R_\tau\times J_z\times S^2$, orient by $d\tau\wedge dz\wedge\omega_{S^2}$ and define

$$g_{L,f}=L^2\bigl(-f(z)d\tau^2+f(z)^{-1}dz^2+\gamma_{S^2}\bigr),\qquad \mathcal F_L=-L\,d\tau\wedge dz.$$

The smooth field $N=(L\sqrt{f})^{-1}\partial_\tau$ is unit timelike; it selects the future direction. This explicit metric-field tuple is the **Bertotti-Robinson product data** for this library. “Electrovac” refers to the equations in [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]] and is not asserted by this definition. The product has sphere radius $L$ at every base point.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $o$ is the manifold orientation, $N$ is a smooth future timelike field, and the metric volume form is chosen to agree with $o$. Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection, let $\mathcal F$ be a smooth real two-form on $M$, and use the curvature convention
$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$.
Define
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd},$$
where both raised indices use $g^{-1}$. A **geometric electrovac datum with zero cosmological constant** is the tuple $(M,g,N,o,\mathcal F)$ satisfying
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$$
at every point of $M$. Here $\star_g$ is the Lorentzian Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$; on two-forms $\star_g^2=-1$. No material current, matter tensor, global potential, asymptotic flatness, positive mass, horizon, or extension condition is part of this definition.

For an oriented embedded sphere $S$ on which the integrals converge, define its geometric electric and magnetic flux parameters by
$$q_e(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\star_g\mathcal F,\qquad q_m(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\mathcal F.$$
When $M$ and the coordinates have length units, these parameters have units of length. A magnetic flux need not have a global potential; no flux quantization is included. The background Lorentzian geometry and Hodge conventions carry the countable-choice assumption $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of their named suppliers; the algebraic identities in this definition require no additional choice principle.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with signature
$(-,+,+,+)$, metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and oriented metric volume
form $\mathrm{vol}_g$. Let $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ be a smooth real two-form and
$j\in\Gamma(TM)$ a smooth vector field. Fix constants $\mu_0>0$ and $c>0$;
$\mu_0$ is a real coefficient here, and $c$ is the positive coordinate
conversion in $x^0=ct$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Assume the mathematical
field equations

$$dF=0,\qquad \nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b.$$

The equations are conditional hypotheses, not physical postulates in this
mathematical item. Define $v\in\Gamma(TM)$ by $v^b:=\nabla_aF^{ab}$ and
define the current three-form by $\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$, the contraction
specified in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]. Then:

**(a) Sign identity.** On $M$,

$$d(\star_gF)=-\iota_v\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Consequently the sourced equation is equivalently

$$\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

**(b) Current conservation.** Either equivalent sourced equation implies
$\nabla_aj^a=0$. This conclusion requires the sourced equation and $\mu_0>0$;
it does not require $dF=0$.

**(c) Local component check.** At any $p\in M$, choose a positively oriented
point-normal chart supplied by
[[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]. In that chart,
write $E_i(x):=-cF_{0i}(x)$ and
$B_i(x):=\frac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}(x)$, where $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ and
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is alternating. These are local component abbreviations in
the chosen chart, not global observer fields. With
$\operatorname{div}E:=\partial_iE_i$,
$(\operatorname{curl}E)_k:=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iE_j$, and similarly
for $B$, the pointwise component identities are

$$v^0=-\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad v^k=\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k,$$

$$ (d\star_gF)_{123}=\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad (d\star_gF)_{0ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}\left(\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k\right),$$

$$ (dF)_{123}=\operatorname{div}B,\qquad (dF)_{0ij}=\frac{\epsilon_{ijk}}{c}\left(\partial_tB_k+(\operatorname{curl}E)_k\right),$$

where $\partial_t:=c\,\partial_0$. The equations are pointwise identities
in normal coordinates; they do not assert that these component abbreviations
form global three-vector fields on curved spacetime.

On an open flat Minkowski domain with a fixed inertial Cartesian chart
$x^0=ct$, define $\rho:=j^0/c$, $J^i:=j^i$, and
$\epsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. The same component formulas at every point give

$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE=\mu_0J,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \partial_tB+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$

These are a coordinate reduction of the stated tensor and form equations, not
claims that the smooth fields describe an experiment.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. Tensoriality of $R$ is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a).
Lowering its output slot with the smooth metric and contracting with the
smooth inverse metric are intrinsic tensor operations
([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] clauses (b)-(c),
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]]). Thus these formulas give smooth
fields of types $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively,
independent of the chart. Symmetry of $\operatorname{Ric}$ and $G$ is proved
separately in [[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clause (d).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

derivations.claim: On the two-dimensional base, the inverse metric components are $g^{\tau\tau}=-1/(L^2f)$ and $g^{zz}=f/L^2$. Applying the Christoffel formula [F4] gives, apart from lower-index symmetry, $\Gamma^\tau{}_{\tau z}=f'/(2f)$, $\Gamma^z{}_{\tau\tau}=ff'/2$, and $\Gamma^z{}_{zz}=-f'/(2f)$. Their traces $\Gamma^a{}_{\tau a}$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{za}$ are zero. Substitution in the coordinate curvature formula [F6] and the Ricci contraction [F5], with convention [F2], gives $\operatorname{Ric}_{\tau\tau}=\partial_z(ff'/2)-2(f'/2f)(ff'/2)=ff''/2$; similarly $\operatorname{Ric}_{zz}=\partial_z(-f'/2f)-\{(f'/2f)^2+(-f'/2f)^2\}=-f''/(2f)$, and $\operatorname{Ric}_{\tau z}=0$. Since $f''=2$, these are $f$ and $-1/f$, respectively, which equal $-L^{-2}$ times the corresponding components of the base metric.

On a regular polar chart from [A2], the unit sphere metric $d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2$ has, by [F4], the only nonzero symbols $\Gamma^\theta{}_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\Gamma^\phi{}_{\theta\phi}=\Gamma^\phi{}_{\phi\theta}=\cot\theta$. The coordinate curvature formula [F6] and contraction [F5] give $\operatorname{Ric}_{\theta\theta}=-\partial_\theta\cot\theta-\cot^2\theta=1$ and $\operatorname{Ric}_{\phi\phi}=\partial_\theta(-\sin\theta\cos\theta)-\cos^2\theta+2\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\theta$; the mixed component is zero. Scaling the sphere metric by the constant $L^2$ leaves its connection unchanged, so in the orthonormal coframe of the Statement its Ricci entries are $L^{-2},L^{-2}$. The product metric has no mixed Christoffel symbols because each factor coefficient depends only on its own factor coordinates; hence its mixed Ricci entries vanish.

The field is constant in $(\tau,z)$ and has only $\mathcal F_{\tau z}=-L$ and $\mathcal F_{z\tau}=L$. Thus $d\mathcal F=0$. The determinant satisfies $\sqrt{|\det g|}=L^4\sin\theta$, and raising indices gives $\mathcal F^{\tau z}=L^{-3}$ and $\mathcal F^{z\tau}=-L^{-3}$. In $\nabla_a\mathcal F^{ab}=\partial_a\mathcal F^{ab}+\Gamma^a{}_{ac}\mathcal F^{cb}+\Gamma^b{}_{ac}\mathcal F^{ac}$, the last term vanishes by symmetry of the connection and antisymmetry of the field. For $b=\tau,z$, the only derivative terms are $\partial_z\mathcal F^{z\tau}$ and $\partial_\tau\mathcal F^{\tau z}$, both zero; their trace terms vanish because $\Gamma^a{}_{a\tau}=\Gamma^a{}_{az}=0$ from the base Christoffels and the product has no mixed symbols. For $b=\theta,\phi$, all $\mathcal F^{ab}$ vanish. Hence $\nabla_a\mathcal F^{ab}=0$; [F3] gives $d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0$.

In the orthonormal coframe, $\mathcal F_L=-L^{-1}e^0\wedge e^1$, so $\mathcal F_{AB}\mathcal F^{AB}=-2/L^2$. Direct contraction in signature $(-,+,+,+)$ gives $Q_{AB}=\frac1{2L^2}\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,1)_{AB}$: the electric pair contributes $+1/(2L^2)$ to the time entry and $-1/(2L^2)$ to the radial entry, while the trace term contributes $+1/(2L^2)$ to each sphere entry. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 give $\operatorname{Ric}=2Q$ on the regular polar locus. The metric and two-form are smooth on the full product by [F1], so $\operatorname{Ric}(g)$ and $Q(\mathcal F_L)$ are smooth tensor fields there; by density in [A2], their equality extends by continuity to both sphere poles. The displayed coframe components are local to those polar charts. Together with the Maxwell equations in step 3.1 this proves the full definition of a geometric electrovac datum on the stated domain.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: A BR datum uses a nonempty open base interval and a sphere factor as given in F1; there is no empty product among those inputs. Local tensor restrictions to an empty subchart carry no additional equation values.

L=0 is forbidden. For f=z^2, z=0 is excluded by its positive-domain definition, while the other branch f=1+z^2 permits z=0 with f=1. Step 1.1 uses f nonzero rather than assuming z nonzero on both branches.
For the branch f=1+z^2 at z=0, f=1 and f double-prime=2, so step 1.1 still yields Ric_tau,tau=1 and Ric_z,z=-1. Unit lapse does not make this product flat.

L>0 and f>0 make the coframe invertible away from polar coordinate singularities. The sphere metric is global, and the product Ricci computation in step 2.1 is a tensor identity rather than a degenerate metric at its poles.

boundaries.reason: The two allowed base charts are open; the f=z^2 branch does not include z=0. The final equation comparison in step 4.1 makes no continuation through a chart boundary or to a maximal product extension.

boundaries.evidence: The coframe and field are displayed explicitly. Steps 1.1–2.1 compute the two factor connections and zero mixed entries directly; the proof does not choose a constant-curvature model from an unspecified class.

boundaries.reason: Every defined BR product is verified as electrovac; the statement is not an equivalence between electrovac and product geometry.
Step 4.1 compares the two computed tensors for this product only. It does not classify electrovac solutions with these Ricci eigenvalues.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]) and standard smooth
sphere structure with induced unit round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

For arbitrary $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$, put $Q^2=q_e^2+q_m^2$ and
$f(r)=1-2M/r+Q^2/r^2$. On every open $J\subset(0,\infty)$ with $f\ne0$, the
dyonic RN datum of [[def-emg-xs-rn-data]] is a geometric electrovac datum of
[[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]] on
$\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J\times S^2$. In particular, its global two-form is
smooth, $d\mathcal F=d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0$, and
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$ everywhere on that domain.

For arbitrary formal $c,\mu_0,G_N>0$, set $\alpha=\sqrt{4\pi G_N/(\mu_0c^4)}$, $F=\mathcal F/\alpha$, and $T_{ab}:=\mu_0^{-1}Q_g(F)_{ab}$. Then the same datum satisfies

$$dF=d(\star_gF)=0,\qquad S=0,\qquad G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}T_{ab},$$

where $S$ is scalar curvature and $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\frac12Sg_{ab}$. This is the formal SI-to-geometric tensor normalization of [[lem-emg-maxwell-observer-stress]](d). It asserts neither measured parameter values nor a bundle realization for arbitrary flux. When the separate fixed-sector action hypotheses hold, $T$ is also the electromagnetic Hilbert tensor of that supplier.

Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$ carry its induced unit round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$ and outward area form $\omega_{S^2}$. Let $L>0$ have length units. Choose either (i) $f(z)=z^2$ on an open $J\subset(0,\infty)$, or (ii) $f(z)=1+z^2$ on an open $J\subset\mathbb R$. The coordinate $z$ and $\tau$ are dimensionless. On $\mathcal M_{L,f}=\mathbb R_\tau\times J_z\times S^2$, orient by $d\tau\wedge dz\wedge\omega_{S^2}$ and define

$$g_{L,f}=L^2\bigl(-f(z)d\tau^2+f(z)^{-1}dz^2+\gamma_{S^2}\bigr),\qquad \mathcal F_L=-L\,d\tau\wedge dz.$$

The smooth field $N=(L\sqrt{f})^{-1}\partial_\tau$ is unit timelike; it selects the future direction. This explicit metric-field tuple is the **Bertotti-Robinson product data** for this library. “Electrovac” refers to the equations in [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]] and is not asserted by this definition. The product has sphere radius $L$ at every base point.

Every datum in [[def-emg-xs-br-products]] is a geometric electrovac datum of [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]]. With the oriented orthonormal coframe

$$e^0=L\sqrt f\,d\tau,\quad e^1=L f^{-1/2}dz,\quad e^2=L\,d\theta,\quad e^3=L\sin\theta\,d\phi,$$

the Ricci and quadratic Maxwell tensors are

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{AB}=L^{-2}\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,1)_{AB},\qquad Q_{AB}(\mathcal F_L)=\frac1{2L^2}\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,1)_{AB}.$$

All mixed base-sphere entries vanish. The statement is on the chosen open chart domains; it makes no maximal-extension or asymptotic-flatness claim.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $o$ is the manifold orientation, $N$ is a smooth future timelike field, and the metric volume form is chosen to agree with $o$. Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection, let $\mathcal F$ be a smooth real two-form on $M$, and use the curvature convention
$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$.
Define
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd},$$
where both raised indices use $g^{-1}$. A **geometric electrovac datum with zero cosmological constant** is the tuple $(M,g,N,o,\mathcal F)$ satisfying
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$$
at every point of $M$. Here $\star_g$ is the Lorentzian Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$; on two-forms $\star_g^2=-1$. No material current, matter tensor, global potential, asymptotic flatness, positive mass, horizon, or extension condition is part of this definition.

For an oriented embedded sphere $S$ on which the integrals converge, define its geometric electric and magnetic flux parameters by
$$q_e(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\star_g\mathcal F,\qquad q_m(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\mathcal F.$$
When $M$ and the coordinates have length units, these parameters have units of length. A magnetic flux need not have a global potential; no flux quantization is included. The background Lorentzian geometry and Hodge conventions carry the countable-choice assumption $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of their named suppliers; the algebraic identities in this definition require no additional choice principle.

derivations.claim: The map $\Phi_\lambda$ is a diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R_T\times(0,\infty)_R\times S^2$ onto the RN exterior $r>L$, since $x^0=T/\lambda$ and $r=L+\lambda R$ have smooth inverses. Its pullback satisfies $dx^0=dT/\lambda$ and $dr=\lambda dR$, while $f(r)=(1-L/r)^2=\lambda^2R^2/(L+\lambda R)^2$. Substitution into the RN metric in [F1] gives the displayed $g_\lambda$. The starting RN datum is a geometric electrovac by the first clause of [F2]; the claim here is the exact coordinate pullback and its limit.
The RN two-form in [F1] pulls back to $-\frac{L}{(L+\lambda R)^2}\frac{dT}{\lambda}\wedge(\lambda dR)=-\frac{L}{(L+\lambda R)^2}dT\wedge dR$, which is the displayed $\mathcal F_\lambda$.

At $\lambda=0$ the coefficient formulas in the Statement are smooth for $R>0$. Fix any compact subset $K$ of $\mathbb R_T\times(0,\infty)_R\times S^2$ and choose a finite smooth atlas on its sphere projection. In each chart, $R$ is bounded below by a positive number and $L+\lambda R\ge L$ for $0\le\lambda\le1$. Every coordinate derivative of every displayed coefficient is therefore a continuous function of $(\lambda,T,R,\theta,\phi)$ on a compact set containing $\{0\}\times K$; uniform continuity implies that each such derivative converges uniformly on $K$ to its value at $\lambda=0$. Since this holds for every derivative order and the atlas is finite, the convergence is $C^\infty_{\rm loc}$.

Substituting $T=L\tau$ and $R=Lz$ into $g_0,\mathcal F_0$ gives $L^2(-z^2d\tau^2+z^{-2}dz^2+\gamma_{S^2})$ and $-L\,d\tau\wedge dz$, exactly [F3] with $f=z^2$. By [F4] this limiting product satisfies the equations defined in [F5]. This identification is on $z>0$ only and does not add a horizon chart.

boundaries.evidence: The scaling domain R_T times (0,infinity)_R times S2 is fixed and nonempty. In step 3.1 an empty compact test set gives vacuous convergence; any nonempty compact test set has a positive lower bound for R.

Phi_lambda is defined only for lambda>0 because x0=T/lambda. Step 3.1 instead extends the pulled-back coefficient formulas to lambda=0 with L>0,R>0; the limit is not a value of the singular coordinate map.
The parameter value lambda=1 is admitted: step 1.1 gives x0=T and r=L+R. The uniform-continuity proof in step 3.1 uses 0<=lambda<=1 and does not require lambda strictly below one.

Step 3.1: For lambda>=0 the coefficient denominator L+lambda R is at least L>0, and R>0 makes the limiting time and radial coefficients nonzero. Thus the limit metric is nondegenerate on its stated domain.

The endpoint lambda down to zero is proved in step 3.1 for every derivative order on compact subsets of R>0. Step 4.1 identifies the limit with z>0 BR data and expressly does not extend it through R=0.

Each compact test set is arbitrary but fixed; compactness supplies finitely many sphere charts in step 3.1. The explicit Phi_lambda and finite atlas do not require a countable sequence of independently selected charts.

boundaries.reason: The statement is an exact pullback formula and a one-parameter smooth limit; it does not claim every BR product arises uniquely from this RN scaling.
Identifying the limiting product in step 4.1 does not recover a unique RN exterior from the limit or reverse the convergence.

Use length coordinates $(u,v,x,y)$ on $\mathbb R^4$. Let $a,b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be smooth profiles with inverse-length units, and let $h:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth dimensionless function satisfying $h_{xx}+h_{yy}=0$ at every $(u,x,y)$. Define the dimensionless function

$$P(u,x,y)=-(a(u)^2+b(u)^2)(x^2+y^2)+h(u,x,y).$$

With orientation $du\wedge dv\wedge dx\wedge dy$, define

$$g=-2\,du\,dv+dx^2+dy^2+P\,du^2,\qquad \mathcal A=-(a(u)x+b(u)y)\,du,\qquad \mathcal F=d\mathcal A=a(u)\,du\wedge dx+b(u)\,du\wedge dy.$$

The vector field $N=\partial_u+\frac{P+1}{2}\partial_v$ has $g(N,N)=-1$ and selects the future direction. The $u,v$ block of $g$ has determinant $-1$, so together with the two positive transverse directions this is a smooth Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and $\sqrt{|\det g|}=1$. The tuple $(\mathbb R^4,g,N,o,\mathcal F)$ is the **null-wave candidate data** for the equations of [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]]; no field-equation claim is part of this definition. The metric coefficients are dimensionless, and $\mathcal F_{ui}$ has inverse-length units.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $o$ is the manifold orientation, $N$ is a smooth future timelike field, and the metric volume form is chosen to agree with $o$. Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection, let $\mathcal F$ be a smooth real two-form on $M$, and use the curvature convention
$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$.
Define
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd},$$
where both raised indices use $g^{-1}$. A **geometric electrovac datum with zero cosmological constant** is the tuple $(M,g,N,o,\mathcal F)$ satisfying
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$$
at every point of $M$. Here $\star_g$ is the Lorentzian Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$; on two-forms $\star_g^2=-1$. No material current, matter tensor, global potential, asymptotic flatness, positive mass, horizon, or extension condition is part of this definition.

For an oriented embedded sphere $S$ on which the integrals converge, define its geometric electric and magnetic flux parameters by
$$q_e(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\star_g\mathcal F,\qquad q_m(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\mathcal F.$$
When $M$ and the coordinates have length units, these parameters have units of length. A magnetic flux need not have a global potential; no flux quantization is included. The background Lorentzian geometry and Hodge conventions carry the countable-choice assumption $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of their named suppliers; the algebraic identities in this definition require no additional choice principle.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with signature
$(-,+,+,+)$, metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and oriented metric volume
form $\mathrm{vol}_g$. Let $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ be a smooth real two-form and
$j\in\Gamma(TM)$ a smooth vector field. Fix constants $\mu_0>0$ and $c>0$;
$\mu_0$ is a real coefficient here, and $c$ is the positive coordinate
conversion in $x^0=ct$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Assume the mathematical
field equations

$$dF=0,\qquad \nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b.$$

The equations are conditional hypotheses, not physical postulates in this
mathematical item. Define $v\in\Gamma(TM)$ by $v^b:=\nabla_aF^{ab}$ and
define the current three-form by $\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$, the contraction
specified in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]. Then:

**(a) Sign identity.** On $M$,

$$d(\star_gF)=-\iota_v\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Consequently the sourced equation is equivalently

$$\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

**(b) Current conservation.** Either equivalent sourced equation implies
$\nabla_aj^a=0$. This conclusion requires the sourced equation and $\mu_0>0$;
it does not require $dF=0$.

**(c) Local component check.** At any $p\in M$, choose a positively oriented
point-normal chart supplied by
[[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]. In that chart,
write $E_i(x):=-cF_{0i}(x)$ and
$B_i(x):=\frac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}(x)$, where $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ and
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is alternating. These are local component abbreviations in
the chosen chart, not global observer fields. With
$\operatorname{div}E:=\partial_iE_i$,
$(\operatorname{curl}E)_k:=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iE_j$, and similarly
for $B$, the pointwise component identities are

$$v^0=-\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad v^k=\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k,$$

$$ (d\star_gF)_{123}=\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad (d\star_gF)_{0ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}\left(\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k\right),$$

$$ (dF)_{123}=\operatorname{div}B,\qquad (dF)_{0ij}=\frac{\epsilon_{ijk}}{c}\left(\partial_tB_k+(\operatorname{curl}E)_k\right),$$

where $\partial_t:=c\,\partial_0$. The equations are pointwise identities
in normal coordinates; they do not assert that these component abbreviations
form global three-vector fields on curved spacetime.

On an open flat Minkowski domain with a fixed inertial Cartesian chart
$x^0=ct$, define $\rho:=j^0/c$, $J^i:=j^i$, and
$\epsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. The same component formulas at every point give

$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE=\mu_0J,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \partial_tB+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$

These are a coordinate reduction of the stated tensor and form equations, not
claims that the smooth fields describe an experiment.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$

chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

Use length coordinates $(u,v,x,y)$ on $\mathbb R^4$. Let $a,b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be smooth profiles with inverse-length units, and let $h:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth dimensionless function satisfying $h_{xx}+h_{yy}=0$ at every $(u,x,y)$. Define the dimensionless function
