Let $(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N,m_N)$ be a sigma-finite phase-reference measure
space from [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]]; the cotangent construction uses
the stated Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]). A **statistical state** is a probability measure
$P$ on $(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N)$, meaning a countably additive measure with
$P(\Gamma_N)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). A **density** of $P$ relative to $m_N$ is a
measurable $\rho:\Gamma_N\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$P(A)=\int_A\rho\,dm_N\quad(A\in\mathcal F_N),\qquad \int_{\Gamma_N}\rho\,dm_N=1.$$
Equivalently, $P=\rho\,m_N$ in the definition of a measure with density
([[def-measure-with-density]]); integration against that density has the
meaning supplied by [[thm-integration-against-a-density]]. A state need not
have a density.

An **observable** is a real-valued measurable function
$A:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]).
Its expectation $\langle A\rangle_P:=\int A\,dP$ is used only when $A$ is
integrable, that is, $\int|A|\,dP<\infty$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). Its
variance is
$$\operatorname{Var}_P(A):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_P)^2\,dP$$
when $A^2$ is integrable. For square-integrable $A,B$, their covariance is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_P(A,B):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_P)(B-\langle B\rangle_P)\,dP.$$
These expressions are finite under the stated square-integrability
hypotheses. Indeed, $P(\Gamma_N)=1$ makes $1\in L^2(P)$ with norm $1$.
By [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]],
$\int|A|\,dP\le(\int A^2\,dP)^{1/2}$, so the mean of a square-integrable
observable exists. If $a=\langle A\rangle_P$, then
$|A-a|^2\le2A^2+2a^2$ makes $A-a$ square-integrable; the same argument
applies to $B-b$. A second application of that inequality gives
$\int|(A-a)(B-b)|\,dP\le\|A-a\|_2\|B-b\|_2<\infty$.
Thus both the variance and covariance integrals above are well-defined.

If $P=\rho m_N$ and the integrals are defined, these expectations equal
$\int A\rho\,dm_N$ by [[thm-integration-against-a-density]].

A **macrostate map** is a measurable map
$M:(\Gamma_N,\mathcal F_N)\to(Y,\mathcal G)$. Its induced state on $Y$ is
the pushforward $M_*P(B):=P(M^{-1}(B))$. The measure of a macrocell and an
entropy assigned to that macrostate are additional constructions; they are
not identical to the expectation or variance of a microscopic observable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a measure space and let $p,q$ be probability
densities relative to $m$, with $q>0$ almost everywhere on $\{p>0\}$. Define
the relative entropy
$$D(p\Vert q):=\int_{\{p>0\}}p\log(p/q)\,dm,$$
allowing $+\infty$. Then $D(p\Vert q)\ge0$, and equality holds exactly
when $p=q$ almost everywhere. In particular, let $H$ be finite $p$-almost
everywhere, let $\beta>0$, and suppose
$$0<Z=\int e^{-\beta H}dm<\infty,\quad q=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H},\quad \int p|H|dm<\infty,\quad \int|p\log p|dm<\infty.$$
For $S[p]:=-k\int p\log p\,dm$ and $F:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, with $k>0$
and $\beta kT=1$, one has
$$D(p\Vert q)=\beta\bigl(\langle H\rangle_p-F-TS[p]\bigr)\ge0.$$
Thus the Gibbs density minimizes this specified free-energy functional
among the stated densities; this mathematical inequality does not derive a
physical preparation.

derivations.claim: For a canonical density $\rho=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$, $\log\rho=-\beta H-\log Z$. Integrating against $\rho$ gives $S=k_B(\log Z+\beta U)$, so $-k_BT\log Z=U-TS$ because $k_BT\beta=1$. For any competitor $p$, [F3] gives $D(p\Vert\rho)=\beta(\langle H\rangle_p-TS[p]-F)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $p=\rho$ almost everywhere. At fixed model, $U=-\partial_\beta\log Z$ by [F2]. Differentiating $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ and using $d\beta/dT=-1/(k_BT^2)$ gives $\partial_TF=-S$, proving the canonical differential.

On the grand disjoint union, $\log\rho=-\beta(H-\mu N)-\log\Xi$. Integration gives $S=k_B(\log\Xi+\beta(U-\mu\bar N))$, hence $\Omega=-k_BT\log\Xi=U-TS-\mu\bar N$. Applying [F2] to the sufficient statistics $H$ and $N$ gives $\partial_\mu\log\Xi=\beta\bar N$ and $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi|_\mu=U-\mu\bar N$. Thus $\partial_\mu\Omega=-\bar N$ and $\partial_T\Omega=-S$, proving the grand differential at fixed model.

For the joint isothermal-isobaric density, $\log\rho=-\beta(H+P_{\rm ext}V)-\log\Delta$. Integration gives $S=k_B(\log\Delta+\beta\langle H+P_{\rm ext}V\rangle)$ and therefore the displayed $G_{\rm isoP}$. Applying [F2] to $B=H+P_{\rm ext}V$ gives $-\partial_\beta\log\Delta|_P=\langle B\rangle$, while $\partial_P\log\Delta=-\beta\langle V\rangle$; hence $\partial_TG_{\rm isoP}=-S$ and $\partial_PG_{\rm isoP}=\langle V\rangle$. This proves the stated differential and completes the conditional identities.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a sigma-finite measure space, let $w\ge0$ be
measurable with $m(\{w>0\})>0$, let $r\ge1$ and let
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_r):\Omega\to\mathbb R^r$ be measurable and finite, and let
$\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For
each compact $K\subset\Theta$, assume an integrable $G_K$ satisfies
$$w(x)e^{\theta\cdot X(x)}\left(1+\sum_a|X_a(x)|^2\right)\le G_K(x)\quad(\theta\in K).$$
Then $Z(\theta)=\int w e^{\theta\cdot X}\,dm$ is finite, strictly positive
and $C^2$, and the probability density $\rho_\theta=Z(\theta)^{-1}we^{\theta\cdot X}$
satisfies
$$\partial_a\log Z=\langle X_a\rangle_\theta,\qquad \partial_a\partial_b\log Z=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b).$$
In particular, the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite.

derivations.claim: Set $\theta=(-\beta,\eta)$ and $X=(H,N)$ in [F1]. Its first and second derivatives give $\partial_\eta\log\Xi=\langle N\rangle$, $\partial_\eta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(N)$, and $\partial_\beta\log\Xi|_\eta=-\langle H\rangle$. At fixed $\mu$, the coordinate relation $\eta=\beta\mu$ makes the derivative direction $(-1,\mu)$ in $(\theta_H,\theta_N)$ coordinates, so $\partial_\beta\log\Xi|_\mu=-\langle H-\mu N\rangle$.

At fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu=\beta\partial_\eta$, so $\partial_\mu\langle N\rangle=\beta\partial_\eta^2\log\Xi =\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$. At fixed $\mu$, differentiating the first mean along direction $(-1,\mu)$ gives $\partial_\beta\langle N\rangle|_\mu =-\operatorname{Cov}(N,H)+\mu\operatorname{Var}(N) =-\operatorname{Cov}(N,H-\mu N)$. All terms are finite by [A1], proving the responses.

Fix $N$, dimension $d$, $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ as in

$Q_1\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ that is Lebesgue measurable with $|Q_1|_d=1$, and

the joint reference
$$d\nu_N=\frac{dV}{V_0}\,\frac{V^N\,dy\,dp}{N!a_0^{dN}},$$
where $a_0>0$ is the action reference in J s. For the chosen Hamiltonian
$H_N(V,y,p)$, assume
$$0<\Delta_N:=\int_0^\infty\!\int e^{-\beta(H_N(V,y,p)+P_{\rm ext}V)}\,d\nu_N<\infty.$$
Adopt the probability density proportional to this integrand. The displayed
$N!$ is the single-species convention; for several indistinguishable species
with fixed counts $N_a$, replace it by $\prod_aN_a!$ as in
[[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. The factor $dV/V_0$ is an
explicit volume-reference convention; a different piston state measure gives
a different preparation. This postulate includes no piston kinetic energy
unless it is explicitly included in the Hamiltonian, and does not claim a
smooth wall dynamics.

For a fixed $N$, controls $\lambda$, measurable classical Hamiltonian
$H_{N,\lambda}:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ and the declared
physical reference measure $m_N^{\rm phys}$ of
[[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]], choose $T>0$ and
$\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in J$^{-1}$ using the SI temperature convention of
[[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
$$0<Z_N(\beta,\lambda):=\int_{\Gamma_N}e^{-\beta H_{N,\lambda}}\,dm_N^{\rm phys}<\infty,$$
adopt the canonical state with density
$$\rho_{\beta,\lambda}=Z_N(\beta,\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\beta H_{N,\lambda}}$$
relative to $m_N^{\rm phys}$. Set $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$. Normalizability
is a required condition on the chosen model; bounded-below energy alone does
not imply it. This probability law is an adopted preparation, not a
consequence of deterministic mechanics or evidence of laboratory
equilibration.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, the exact choice strength required by
[[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]] to construct the smooth
cotangent manifold. Let $d,N\ge1$, let $Q$ be a smooth $d$-manifold, and
choose a countable smooth-chart subcover of its atlas. Such a subcover is
obtained from a countable basis of the second-countable topology by choosing,
for each basis element contained in a chart domain, one such chart domain; this
countable selection is covered by the stated Axiom of Countable Choice. Give
$Q_N:=Q^N$ the product topology and the product smooth structure generated by
the charts
$$\left(U_1\times\cdots\times U_N,\ (q_1,\ldots,q_N)\mapsto(\phi_1(q_1),\ldots,\phi_N(q_N))\right),$$
where each $(U_i,\phi_i)$ belongs to the chosen countable subcover of charts of
$Q$. These images are open in $\mathbb R^{dN}$, and their transition maps are
componentwise smooth, so they form a smooth atlas of dimension $n=dN$; the
finite product of the countable chart family is countable. Its generated
maximal atlas is the product smooth structure in the convention of
[[def-smooth-manifold]]. The induced cotangent charts are indexed by these
base charts and form a countable atlas of $\Gamma_N$. Its
**configuration space** is $Q_N$. Its **phase space** is the cotangent bundle
$$\Gamma_N:=T^*Q_N,$$
whose points are pairs $(q,p)$ with $p\in T_q^*Q_N$. Let
$\pi_N:T^*Q_N\to Q_N$ be the cotangent-bundle projection. The **tautological
one-form** and **canonical symplectic form** are
$$\lambda_{(q,p)}(\xi):=p(d\pi_N\xi),\qquad \omega_N:=-d\lambda.$$
Thus in an induced cotangent chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$,
$$\lambda=\sum_{j=1}^n p_j\,dq^j,\qquad \omega_N=\sum_{j=1}^n dq^j\wedge dp_j.$$
The cotangent supplier proves $\omega_N$ closed and nondegenerate under the
same Countable Choice premise. On an open phase chart this is exactly the
standard form of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]];
[[lem-cm-standard-symplectic-form-is-closed-and-nondegenerate]] gives its
closedness, contraction and nondegeneracy coordinate calculations.

The **Liouville density** $d\Lambda_N:=|\omega_N^n|/n!$ is the positive
density associated with the symplectic volume form. In each cotangent chart it
has coordinate density $dq^1\cdots dq^n\,dp_1\cdots dp_n$. Given any finite
constant $c_N>0$, define the **labelled reference measure**
$$m_N:=c_N\Lambda_N$$
on the Borel sigma-algebra of $\Gamma_N$. It is sigma-finite: $Q_N$ is
countable-atlased as just constructed, so it is covered by countably many
cotangent chart images. Each chart image is open in $\mathbb R^{2n}$ and is
covered by the countable family of bounded open boxes with rational endpoints
whose closures lie in that chart image: every point of an open set lies in one
such box. Each box has finite Euclidean Lebesgue measure, and its chart
preimage therefore has finite $m_N$-measure because the Liouville coordinate
density is the constant $c_N$. The countably many chart-box preimages cover
$\Gamma_N$ and establish sigma-finiteness directly, without a sigma-compactness
supplier.
The constant $c_N$ is mathematical normalization data; this definition assigns
no physical unit to it.

For a partition of the particle labels into species classes of sizes
$N_1,\ldots,N_s$, let $G:=S_{N_1}\times\cdots\times S_{N_s}$ act on
$Q_N=Q^N$ by permuting factors within each class and on $T^*Q_N$ by the
cotangent lift. In canonical coordinates each lift permutes corresponding
$q$ and $p$ coordinates, so it preserves $\omega_N$, $\Lambda_N$ and $m_N$.
Let $\Pi_N:\Gamma_N\to\Gamma_N/G$ be
the orbit map, equip the orbit set with the quotient sigma-algebra
$$\mathcal F_{\mathrm{quot}}:=\{B\subseteq\Gamma_N/G:\Pi_N^{-1}(B) \text{ is Borel in }\Gamma_N\},$$
and define the **quotient reference measure** by
$$\bar m_N(B):=\frac{1}{\prod_{a=1}^s N_a!}\,m_N(\Pi_N^{-1}(B)).$$
This is a measure because inverse images preserve complements and countable
disjoint unions and $m_N$ is countably additive. The stated invariance makes
it the normalized quotient pushforward. It is a measurable quotient;
no smooth quotient structure at configurations with stabilizers is asserted.
For one species the factor is $1/N!$.

The quotient factor here is mathematical counting data. A physical postulate
determines when labels are operationally indistinguishable and how the
reference scale is interpreted; neither follows from the cotangent geometry.

For a declared classical model with $N_a$ operationally indistinguishable
particles of each species $a$, label those particles by
$\{(a,i):1\le i\le N_a\}$ on the auxiliary labelled cover, and let
$S_{N_a}$ denote the permutation group of that species' finite label set.
The product group $G=\prod_a S_{N_a}$ acts on the labelled phase space
$\Gamma_N=T^*Q_N$ by the cotangent lifts of within-species permutations. Let
$\Pi_N:\Gamma_N\to\Gamma_N/G$ be its measurable orbit map from
[[def-csm-phase-space-reference]]. Choose $a_0>0$ as a fixed primitive
reference parameter with action units J s; [[def-cm01-units]] supplies its
dimension, not its value or the choice of this parameter. Here $d$ is the
number of spatial dimensions and $N=\sum_aN_a$. No numerical value or
identification of $a_0$ with Planck's constant is imposed.

Use the weighted labelled lift
$$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}:=\frac{1}{\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN}}\,d\Lambda_N =\frac{1}{\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN}}\,dq\,dp$$
on $\Gamma_N$, where $d\Lambda_N$ is the Liouville density and the last
expression is its coordinate density in canonical charts, with coordinates
read in SI numerical units. The coordinate volume $dq\,dp$ has action
dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$, so the reference is dimensionless. The
physical quotient reference is
$$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(B):=m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(\Pi_N^{-1}(B))\qquad(B\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{quot}}).$$
Thus $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on the labelled cover $\Gamma_N$, and
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}=(\Pi_N)_*m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on
$\Gamma_N/G$; with $c_N=a_0^{-dN}$, the latter is exactly the normalized
quotient reference of [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]].

Physical observables for indistinguishable particles are measurable
$G$-invariant functions $A:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R$, equivalently measurable
functions $\bar A$ on the quotient with $A=\bar A\circ\Pi_N$. For every such
observable with an integrable expectation, its integral against
$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ equals the quotient integral against
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$. A labelled density represents a physical state on
the quotient only if it is invariant under $G$ almost everywhere with respect
to $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$; an invariant representative may then be used. In
particular, an indistinguishable-particle Hamiltonian must be invariant under
these permutations (or agree almost everywhere with its permuted versions
when only its Gibbs density is at issue). A label-specific coordinate
statistic on the lift is not itself a quotient observable. Under a
permutation-invariant state its marginal law
can instead be interpreted as the law of a uniformly selected particle within
the same species, or of a uniformly selected coordinate of the same type
within that species. Symmetric sums and averages within each species are
quotient observables.
Calculations of labelled momentum components in
[[pthm-csm-canonical-momentum-equipartition]] use this symmetric labelled
lift, and their permutation-invariant kinetic sums and averages are physical
observables.

If labels are operationally distinguishable, omit the corresponding
permutation factor and use the labelled phase space directly. The convention
is part of the preparation and reference model; it is not deduced from
Hamiltonian mechanics. Whether a quantity is represented by a gauge-dependent
canonical momentum or by a gauge-invariant mechanical momentum is fixed by the
stated model and gauge convention. No quantum exchange law, actual preparation
mechanism, or empirical indistinguishability test is asserted.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be nonempty, bounded and open with compact
closure, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. Let the
static scalar potential be $\varphi:U\to\mathbb R$ and the static vector
potential be $A:U\to\mathbb R^3$, both of class $C^2$. Let $m>0$ kg, charge
$e\in\mathbb R$ C, and velocity $v\in\mathbb R^3$ m s$^{-1}$. The adopted
single-particle Lagrangian is the function
$$L:\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R,\qquad L(x,v)=\tfrac12m|v|^2+eA(x)\cdot v-e\varphi(x),$$
with $A$ in T m and $\varphi$ in V, as in
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. Its Legendre momentum is
$$p:=\partial_vL=mv+eA(x),$$
so for every $(x,p)\in T^*\Omega\cong\Omega\times\mathbb R^3$ the inverse is
$v=(p-eA(x))/m$. The **mechanical momentum** is
$\pi:=p-eA(x)=mv$; the **canonical momentum** is the cotangent coordinate
$p$ of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]. The Legendre transform
$H=p\cdot v-L$, in the convention of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]], is therefore
$$H(x,p)=\frac{|p-eA(x)|^2}{2m}+e\varphi(x).$$
At fixed $x$, the velocity derivative has linear part $mI_3$, so the
displayed affine momentum map has the explicit inverse
$v=(p-eA(x))/m$. Substitution into $p\cdot v-L$ cancels the two
$eA\cdot v$ terms and gives $\tfrac12m|v|^2+e\varphi$; using the inverse
gives the displayed Hamiltonian. The supplier [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]
provides the $p\cdot v-L$ convention for its hyperregular $K-U$ mechanical
presentation; the inverse branch for this velocity-linear electromagnetic
coupling is the local calculation above, not a consequence of that supplier's
$K-U$ scope. The units are $[eA]=$ kg m s$^{-1}$, $[e\varphi]=$ J, and
$[H]=$ J.

For a time-independent gauge function $\chi:U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^3$
(units V s), adopt the
static convention of [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]:
$A_\chi=A+\nabla\chi$ and $\varphi_\chi=\varphi$. The corresponding
canonical-coordinate change is $T_\chi(x,p)=(x,p+e\nabla\chi(x))$; the
mechanical momentum is unchanged under this paired transformation. This
definition specifies an external-potential model only and asserts no
existence of a global potential representation on arbitrary regions.

Let $c>0$, let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with its restricted inertial chart, let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the scalar-vector potential vocabulary on that region be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: a **potential pair** $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ consists of $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for a non-open time interval $I$ the joint classes in this item are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); for $k\ge1$ the **field pair** is

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is $G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. The definitions in this item are stated on the laboratory region; the framework's fields are those of [[def-em-fields]]. No field equation is required to define the vocabulary; the existence theorem recalled in (a) has the additional hypotheses stated there.

(a) [Representations] Let $k\ge2$ be an integer and let $(E,B)$ be a field pair of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$, meaning $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly as in [[def-em-fields]]. A **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\times I$. More generally, a potential pair of class $C^1$ represents a specified field pair whenever these two identities hold, even if the fields have greater regularity than the defining derivatives alone guarantee. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. When $\Omega$ is open and star-shaped, $I$ is an interval with at least two elements, and the jointly $C^r$ field data, $r\ge2$, satisfy $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] supplies $\varphi\in C^{r-1}$ and $A\in C^r$ in the stated restriction convention, and smooth potentials for smooth data satisfying the same equations; it does not assert a $C^r$ scalar potential for merely $C^r$ data. Equality of field pairs does not by itself assert gauge relatedness on an arbitrary region; a converse needs its own domain and regularity hypotheses.

(b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$, $m\ge2$, on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** sends a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$ to

$$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two potential pairs are **gauge related** when one is the gauge transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}\bigl(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A)\bigr)=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$; hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs, the inverse of $T_\chi$ being $T_{-\chi}$. For a fixed finite class the transform drops one order, and relatedness is used only through the transform it records.

(c) [Conditions] A potential pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving either condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not asserted by this definition.

(d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the values of $\varphi$, of $A$ and of any gauge function are convention dependent and are auxiliary, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential $\varphi$ carries the volt, the vector potential $A$ carries the tesla metre, and a gauge function carries V s $=$ T m$^2$, so its time derivative and gradient have the units of $\varphi$ and $A$, respectively, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]. No value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

For a declared classical model with $N_a$ operationally indistinguishable
particles of each species $a$, label those particles by
$\{(a,i):1\le i\le N_a\}$ on the auxiliary labelled cover, and let
$S_{N_a}$ denote the permutation group of that species' finite label set.
The product group $G=\prod_a S_{N_a}$ acts on the labelled phase space
$\Gamma_N=T^*Q_N$ by the cotangent lifts of within-species permutations. Let
$\Pi_N:\Gamma_N\to\Gamma_N/G$ be its measurable orbit map from
[[def-csm-phase-space-reference]]. Choose $a_0>0$ as a fixed primitive
reference parameter with action units J s; [[def-cm01-units]] supplies its
dimension, not its value or the choice of this parameter. Here $d$ is the
number of spatial dimensions and $N=\sum_aN_a$. No numerical value or
identification of $a_0$ with Planck's constant is imposed.

Use the weighted labelled lift
$$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}:=\frac{1}{\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN}}\,d\Lambda_N =\frac{1}{\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN}}\,dq\,dp$$
on $\Gamma_N$, where $d\Lambda_N$ is the Liouville density and the last
expression is its coordinate density in canonical charts, with coordinates
read in SI numerical units. The coordinate volume $dq\,dp$ has action
dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$, so the reference is dimensionless. The
physical quotient reference is
$$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(B):=m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(\Pi_N^{-1}(B))\qquad(B\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{quot}}).$$
Thus $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on the labelled cover $\Gamma_N$, and
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}=(\Pi_N)_*m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on
$\Gamma_N/G$; with $c_N=a_0^{-dN}$, the latter is exactly the normalized
quotient reference of [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]].

Physical observables for indistinguishable particles are measurable
$G$-invariant functions $A:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R$, equivalently measurable
functions $\bar A$ on the quotient with $A=\bar A\circ\Pi_N$. For every such
observable with an integrable expectation, its integral against
$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ equals the quotient integral against
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$. A labelled density represents a physical state on
the quotient only if it is invariant under $G$ almost everywhere with respect
to $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$; an invariant representative may then be used. In
particular, an indistinguishable-particle Hamiltonian must be invariant under
these permutations (or agree almost everywhere with its permuted versions
when only its Gibbs density is at issue). A label-specific coordinate
statistic on the lift is not itself a quotient observable. Under a
permutation-invariant state its marginal law
can instead be interpreted as the law of a uniformly selected particle within
the same species, or of a uniformly selected coordinate of the same type
within that species. Symmetric sums and averages within each species are
quotient observables.
Calculations of labelled momentum components in
[[pthm-csm-canonical-momentum-equipartition]] use this symmetric labelled
lift, and their permutation-invariant kinetic sums and averages are physical
observables.

If labels are operationally distinguishable, omit the corresponding
permutation factor and use the labelled phase space directly. The convention
is part of the preparation and reference model; it is not deduced from
Hamiltonian mechanics. Whether a quantity is represented by a gauge-dependent
canonical momentum or by a gauge-invariant mechanical momentum is fixed by the
stated model and gauge convention. No quantum exchange law, actual preparation
mechanism, or empirical indistinguishability test is asserted.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a measure space and let $p,q$ be probability
densities relative to $m$, with $q>0$ almost everywhere on $\{p>0\}$. Define
the relative entropy
$$D(p\Vert q):=\int_{\{p>0\}}p\log(p/q)\,dm,$$
allowing $+\infty$. Then $D(p\Vert q)\ge0$, and equality holds exactly
when $p=q$ almost everywhere. In particular, let $H$ be finite $p$-almost
everywhere, let $\beta>0$, and suppose
$$0<Z=\int e^{-\beta H}dm<\infty,\quad q=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H},\quad \int p|H|dm<\infty,\quad \int|p\log p|dm<\infty.$$
For $S[p]:=-k\int p\log p\,dm$ and $F:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, with $k>0$
and $\beta kT=1$, one has
$$D(p\Vert q)=\beta\bigl(\langle H\rangle_p-F-TS[p]\bigr)\ge0.$$
Thus the Gibbs density minimizes this specified free-energy functional
among the stated densities; this mathematical inequality does not derive a
physical preparation.

derivations.claim: For $r$ particles in position volume $W$, separate the $r$ position integrals and use [F1] in all $dr$ momentum coordinates. For one coordinate put $a=\beta/(2m)$; integrating $\frac{d}{dp}(pe^{-ap^2})=e^{-ap^2}-2ap^2e^{-ap^2}$ over $\mathbb R$ gives $\langle p^2\rangle=m/\beta$, as the boundary term vanishes by Gaussian decay. Thus the mean kinetic energy is $dr/(2\beta)$. The position law factorizes into $r$ uniform position laws. With $\lambda_T=a_0\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$, the partition function is $$Z_r(W)=\frac{W^r}{r!a_0^{dr}}\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{dr/2} =\frac{(W/\lambda_T^d)^r}{r!}.$$ For equal total particle count $2N$ before and after, the $\beta U$ terms in [F2] cancel, so the entropy change is $k_B$ times the logarithm of the partition-function ratio.

Initially the ratio is $Z_{2N}(2V)/Z_N(V)^2$ $=4^N(N!)^2/(2N)!$; for two fixed distinguishable species it is $[Z_N(2V)/Z_N(V)]^2=4^N$. The first ratio exceeds one because $(2N)!/(N!)^2=\binom{2N}{N}<\sum_{j=0}^{2N}\binom{2N}{j}=4^N$. Under the final positional law, the $2N$ particles independently fall in either half with probability $1/2$, so the central binomial probability is $\binom{2N}{N}/4^N$, the reciprocal of the identical-particle ratio.

For each integer $n\ge1$, monotonicity of $\log x$ on unit intervals gives $$n\log n-n+1\le\log(n!)\le n\log n-n+1+\log n.$$ Indeed the lower bound integrates $\log x\le\log j$ on $[j-1,j]$ for $j=2,\ldots,n$, and the upper bound integrates $\log x\ge\log j$ on $[j,j+1]$ for $j=1,\ldots,n-1$, then adds $\log n$. Substitution for $n=N$ and $n=2N$ cancels the terms linear in $N$ in $N\log4+2\log(N!)-\log((2N)!)$, leaving a quantity bounded in absolute value by a constant multiple of $\log(N+1)$. Therefore $\Delta S_{\mathrm{identical}}/N\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.

Thus $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on the labelled cover $\Gamma_N$, and
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}=(\Pi_N)_*m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on
$\Gamma_N/G$; with $c_N=a_0^{-dN}$, the latter is exactly the normalized
quotient reference of [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]].

Physical observables for indistinguishable particles are measurable
$G$-invariant functions $A:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R$, equivalently measurable
functions $\bar A$ on the quotient with $A=\bar A\circ\Pi_N$. For every such
observable with an integrable expectation, its integral against
$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ equals the quotient integral against
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$. A labelled density represents a physical state on
the quotient only if it is invariant under $G$ almost everywhere with respect
to $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$; an invariant representative may then be used. In
particular, an indistinguishable-particle Hamiltonian must be invariant under
these permutations (or agree almost everywhere with its permuted versions
when only its Gibbs density is at issue). A label-specific coordinate
statistic on the lift is not itself a quotient observable. Under a
permutation-invariant state its marginal law
can instead be interpreted as the law of a uniformly selected particle within
the same species, or of a uniformly selected coordinate of the same type
within that species. Symmetric sums and averages within each species are
quotient observables.
Calculations of labelled momentum components in
[[pthm-csm-canonical-momentum-equipartition]] use this symmetric labelled
lift, and their permutation-invariant kinetic sums and averages are physical
observables.

If labels are operationally distinguishable, omit the corresponding
permutation factor and use the labelled phase space directly. The convention
is part of the preparation and reference model; it is not deduced from
Hamiltonian mechanics. Whether a quantity is represented by a gauge-dependent
canonical momentum or by a gauge-invariant mechanical momentum is fixed by the
stated model and gauge convention. No quantum exchange law, actual preparation
mechanism, or empirical indistinguishability test is asserted.

$\ell_j,p_{0j}>0$ in each cotangent chart, of the respective coordinate and

preparation, uniform relative to phase volume in the band. Restricting either

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

Let $Q_N=\mathbb T^n$ be a flat compact configuration torus of volume $V_N$,
$n=dN\ge3$, with canonical cotangent reference $m_N=c_Ndq\,dp$ from
[[def-csm-phase-space-reference]]. Let $m_j>0$ for $1\le j\le n$, let
$U:Q_N\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and bounded, and set
$$H(q,p)=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{p_j^2}{2m_j}+U(q),\qquad \alpha=n/2,\qquad C_m=\prod_{j=1}^n\sqrt{2m_j}.$$
Let $B_n$ be the Euclidean volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb R^n$. Fix
an energy $E$ that is a regular value of $H$ and whose shell
$\Sigma_E=H^{-1}(\{E\})$ is nonempty. For every continuous $g:Q_N\to\mathbb R$,
the coarea shell measure from [[thm-csm-regular-shell-coarea]] satisfies
$$\mu_E(g\circ\pi_N)=c_N C_m\alpha B_n\int_{Q_N}g(q)(E-U(q))_+^{\alpha-1}\,dq,$$
where $x_+=\max(x,0)$. Thus the position marginal of $P_E$ has density
proportional to $(E-U)_+^{\alpha-1}$. In the scaled momentum coordinates
$r_j=p_j/\sqrt{2m_j}$, the coarea shell measure over each $q$ with
$E>U(q)$ has fiber factor $dA_r/(2|r|)$ on the sphere
$|r|=\sqrt{E-U(q)}$. Define $\sigma_{E,q}$ as Euclidean surface area on
that sphere divided by its total area. It satisfies
$$\int \frac{p_j^2}{2m_j}\,d\sigma_{E,q}=\frac{E-U(q)}{n},\qquad \int \sum_j\frac{p_j^2}{2m_j}\,dP_E=\int(E-U(q))\,dP_E(q).$$
The result concerns the full kinetic-plus-potential shell; it does not replace
it by a shell of potential energy alone.

derivations.claim:
In the kinetic shell theorem set $U=0$, $C_m=(2m)^{n/2}$ and
$\alpha=n/2$. The configuration integral of $1$ is $V^N$, so its exact
density formula gives the displayed $D(E)$. For each $j$ the conditional
component mean is $E/n$, and on the shell
$\sum_jp_j^2/(2m)=E$ pointwise; therefore $K=E$ and its variance is zero.

Integrating $D(s)=Cs^{\alpha-1}$ from
$0$ to $E$ gives cumulative phase volume
$$W(E)=\int_0^E Cs^{\alpha-1}ds=\frac{C}{\alpha}E^\alpha,$$
where $C=V^N(2m)^{n/2}\alpha B_n/(N!a_0^n)$. Thus
$\log(E_0D(E))=\log(E_0C)+(\alpha-1)\log E$ and
$\log(W(E)/W_0)=\log(C/(\alpha W_0))+\alpha\log E$. Differentiation
gives the two displayed derivatives. Since their difference is $k_B/E>0$,
they are distinct at every finite $E>0$.

For a fixed-$N$ canonical model with $H$ and reference measure independent of
$T$, let $Z(\beta)=\int e^{-\beta H}dm$ be finite and positive on an open
interval of $\beta>0$. Assume the local envelope hypotheses of
[[thm-csm-exponential-normalization-covariance]] hold for $X=H$ and
$\theta=-\beta$. Under the canonical preparation
[[post-csm-canonical-preparation]], the mean energy $U=\langle H\rangle$ obeys
$$\partial_\beta\log Z=-U,\qquad \partial_\beta U=-\operatorname{Var}(H),\qquad C_V:=\partial_TU=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(H)}{k_BT^2}\ge0,$$
where $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ and $C_V$ is the model heat capacity at the fixed
controls. This is a finite-model response identity, not an empirical claim.

For the grand preparation [[post-csm-grand-preparation]], write
$$\Xi(\beta,\mu)=\sum_N\int e^{-\beta H_N+\beta\mu N}\,dm_N,$$
where $\beta>0$, $\mu$ has units J per particle, and the local envelopes of
[[thm-csm-exponential-normalization-covariance]] hold uniformly on the
disjoint-union reference space for the sufficient statistics $H$ and $N$.
Then
$$\partial_\eta\log\Xi=\langle N\rangle,\quad \partial_\eta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(N),\quad \eta=\beta\mu,$$
and, at fixed $\mu$,
$$-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\langle H-\mu N\rangle,\qquad \partial_\mu\langle N\rangle=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N),\qquad \partial_\beta\langle N\rangle|_\mu=-\operatorname{Cov}(N,H-\mu N).$$
The covariance is computed in the full number-exchanging state. No
fixed-$N$ derivative or thermodynamic-limit identification is implied.

derivations.claim: Separate the position and momentum integrals and apply [F1] in each of the $dN$ momentum coordinates. This gives $$Z_N=\frac{V^N}{N!a_0^{dN}} \left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{dN/2} =\frac{(V/\lambda_T^d)^N}{N!}.$$ The position density is uniform on the region and each momentum factor is a centered Gaussian of variance $m/\beta$.

For $\beta$ in a compact interval $[\beta_0,\beta_1]\subset(0,\infty)$, the factors $H_N^r e^{-\beta H_N}$ for $r\le2$ are bounded by a constant times $e^{-\beta_0H_N/2}$, since $x^re^{-\beta_0x/2}$ is bounded for $x\ge0$; the latter has a finite Gaussian integral by [F1]. Thus [A3] verifies the canonical response theorem's envelope, which gives $U=-\partial_\beta\log Z_N=dN/(2\beta)$, $\operatorname{Var}(H_N)=\partial_\beta^2\log Z_N=dN/(2\beta^2)$, and the chain rule gives $C_V=dNk_B/2$.

The grand sum has sector weight $e^{\beta\mu j}Z_j=a^j/j!$, so its exponential series gives $\Xi=e^a$ and $P(N=j)=e^{-a}a^j/j!$. Summing the shifted series gives $\mathbb E[N]=a$ and $\mathbb E[N(N-1)]=a^2$, hence $\operatorname{Var}(N)=a$.

On a compact $(\beta,\mu)$ set, $a$ is bounded by some $A<\infty$. For each fixed $r$, the ratio of successive terms in $\sum_{j\ge0}(1+j^r)A^j/j!$ tends to zero, uniformly once $j$ is large; therefore the series converges uniformly. Combined with the Gaussian bound in step 2.1, this verifies the grand theorem's energy-number envelope. Applying its response identity gives $\partial_\mu\langle N\rangle=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)=\beta a$. Within each number sector, dividing the sector Boltzmann density by its sector probability cancels the grand factor, leaving precisely the canonical conditional phase law.

Fix $N$, dimension $d$, $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ as in
[[def-td-si-quantities]], external pressure
$P_{\rm ext}>0$ in J m$^{-d}$, a fixed dimensionless shape
$Q_1\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ that is Lebesgue measurable with $|Q_1|_d=1$, and
a positive volume reference $V_0$ in m$^d$. Write

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.

Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

Direct integration gives $I_0=1/s$; integration by parts, with $V^je^{-sV}\to0$ at infinity and vanishing lower boundary for $j\ge1$, gives $I_j=jI_{j-1}/s$. The normalized volume density is $V^Ne^{-sV}/I_N(s)$. Applying the same integral formula to $I_{N+1}$ and $I_{N+2}$ gives $\langle V\rangle=(N+1)/s$ and $\langle V^2\rangle=(N+1)(N+2)/s^2$. For each fixed $V$, [F1] and Gaussian integration by parts give $\langle K\mid V\rangle=n/(2\beta)$. Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, $H:S\to\mathbb R$, and $\beta>0$. Define $Z=\sum_{s\in S}e^{-\beta H(s)}$ and $\gamma(s)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(s)}$. For every probability vector $p$ on $S$, with $0\log0=0$, its Shannon entropy $H_{\rm Sh}(p)=-\sum_s p(s)\log p(s)$ and relative entropy $D(p\Vert\gamma)=\sum_{p(s)>0}p(s)\log(p(s)/\gamma(s))$ satisfy
$$D(p\Vert\gamma)=-H_{\rm Sh}(p)+\beta\sum_s p(s)H(s)+\log Z\geq0.$$
Equality holds exactly when $p=\gamma$. Equivalently, $\gamma$ is the unique minimizer of $\sum_s p(s)H(s)-\beta^{-1}H_{\rm Sh}(p)$, and the minimum is $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $\mu_0$ is a premeasure on an algebra $\mathcal A_0$ of subsets of $X$ and $\mu^*$ is its induced outer set function, then $\mathcal A_0\subseteq\mathcal M_{\mu^*}$ and $\mu^*|_{\mathcal A_0}=\mu_0$. The restriction of $\mu^*$ to $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$ is therefore a measure extending $\mu_0$.

Equivalently: assuming countable choice, the induced outer measure restricts to a complete measure on its Carathéodory sigma-algebra and to a measure on $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$ extending $\mu_0$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

derivations.claim: Enumerate the sites and order the finite alphabet. From any sequence in $X$, retain an infinite subsequence constant at $i_1$, then a further infinite subsequence constant at $i_2$, and so on. At each stage use the first alphabet value in the fixed order occurring infinitely often in the current sequence, and enumerate its retained indices increasingly. This is a specified recursive rule, not a sequence of arbitrary dependent choices. Taking the diagonal subsequence makes each fixed coordinate eventually constant. For $\varepsilon>0$, choose $K$ with $2^{-K}<\varepsilon$. Two sufficiently late diagonal terms agree at the first $K$ sites, so their metric distance is at most $2^{-K}<\varepsilon$ and they converge to the coordinatewise limit.

A cylinder depends on finitely many coordinates. For any two cylinder presentations of the same set, pass to the union of their finite coordinate sets and use consistency of the finite-dimensional probabilities; this proves that the induced weight on the cylinder algebra is well-defined. The same finite-coordinate representation proves finite additivity and normalization.

Write the given probability sequence as $(\mu_k)_{k\ge1}$. Enumerate the countable cylinder algebra as $C_1,C_2,\ldots$ (allow repetitions if it is finite). Specify a convergent-subsequence selector for any sequence $(u_k)$ in $[0,1]$ as follows. Start with the closed interval $I_0=[0,1]$ and all indices. Bisect the current interval and retain its left closed half if infinitely many current indices have values there; otherwise retain its right closed half. The retained index set is infinite because the two halves cover the previous interval. After stage $r$, let $k_r$ be the least retained index larger than $k_{r-1}$, with $k_0=0$. The intervals are nested with diameter $2^{-r}$, so any two selected values from stages at least $r$ differ by at most $2^{-r}$. By [F3] the bounded selected sequence has a subsequential limit; the diameter bound then makes the whole selected sequence converge to that limit. No witness subsequence from [F3] is selected by the rule: each interval, retained set and index is uniquely specified. Starting with $a_0(k)=k$, apply this selector to $(\mu_{a_{j-1}(k)}(C_j))_{k\ge1}$ and let $a_j$ be the resulting increasing subsequence of $a_{j-1}$. Ordinary deterministic recursion defines all $a_j$ without dependent choice. The diagonal indices $n_j=a_j(j)$ are strictly increasing, since $a_{j+1}(j+1)\ge a_j(j+1)>a_j(j)$; for each fixed cylinder their probabilities converge along this diagonal. Limits of finite sums preserve normalization and finite additivity, hence all finite-coordinate consistency identities.

To prove compactness directly, suppose an open cover has no finite subcover. Starting with $X$, successively split the current cylinder by the next coordinate into finitely many subcylinders; at least one remains without a finite subcover, and choose the first such cylinder in the fixed alphabet order. The resulting nested cylinders determine one configuration $\sigma$. Some cover member contains $\sigma$ and, being open, contains a basic cylinder fixing finitely many coordinates of $\sigma$. A sufficiently late nested cylinder is contained in that member, contradicting its selection. Thus every open cover has a finite subcover. The cylinders form a countable clopen basis, so they generate exactly the Borel sigma-algebra.

If a cylinder $C$ is a disjoint union of countably many cylinders $C_n$, compactness of $C$ gives a finite subcover from the open cover $(C_n)$. Disjointness forces every other $C_n$ to be empty, so finite additivity gives countable additivity whenever the union is in $\mathcal C$; the cylinder weight is therefore a premeasure. Apply [F1] to extend it under the stated Countable Choice assumption. The cylinder family is a pi-system generating $\sigma(\mathcal C)$, so [F2] gives uniqueness.

The extension in step 3.1 gives a probability measure with those cylinder values. Local functions are finite linear combinations of cylinder indicators. Every continuous $f$ is uniformly approximated by local functions. If uniform continuity failed, [A1] would choose, for each $K$, one pair agreeing on the first $K$ coordinates whose $f$-values differ by at least a fixed $\varepsilon>0$. These are independent nonempty sets of pairs indexed by $K$, so countable choice suffices. Step 1.1 gives a convergent subsequence of the first components; along the same indices the second components converge to the same configuration, since their distances are at most $2^{-K}$. Continuity then contradicts the fixed separation of their $f$-values. Thus for large $K$, fixing the coordinates after the first $K$ to any fixed reference tail gives a local approximation with uniform error at most $\varepsilon$. Cylinder convergence therefore gives convergence of integrals first for local functions and then for every continuous $f$.

Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, $H:S\to\mathbb R$, and $\beta>0$. Define $Z=\sum_{s\in S}e^{-\beta H(s)}$ and $\gamma(s)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(s)}$. For every probability vector $p$ on $S$, with $0\log0=0$, its Shannon entropy $H_{\rm Sh}(p)=-\sum_s p(s)\log p(s)$ and relative entropy $D(p\Vert\gamma)=\sum_{p(s)>0}p(s)\log(p(s)/\gamma(s))$ satisfy
$$D(p\Vert\gamma)=-H_{\rm Sh}(p)+\beta\sum_s p(s)H(s)+\log Z\geq0.$$
Equality holds exactly when $p=\gamma$. Equivalently, $\gamma$ is the unique minimizer of $\sum_s p(s)H(s)-\beta^{-1}H_{\rm Sh}(p)$, and the minimum is $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$.

Assume Countable Choice for the product-measure extension framework of [[def-countable-choice]] and [[lem-csm-lattice-product-and-measure-compactness]]. Work in the finite-alphabet configuration space $X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with its cylinder-generated Borel sigma-algebra. Let the finite-range interaction and its conditional energy be as in [[def-csm-finite-range-lattice-interaction]], and fix $\beta>0$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ and exterior configuration $\eta\in A^{\Lambda^c}$, put
$$Z_\Lambda^\eta=\sum_{\tau\in A^\Lambda}e^{-\beta E_\Lambda(\tau\mid\eta)},\qquad \gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)=\frac{\sum_{\tau\in A^\Lambda}f(\tau\eta)e^{-\beta E_\Lambda(\tau\mid\eta)}}{Z_\Lambda^\eta}$$
for bounded measurable $f:X\to\mathbb R$. Here $\gamma_\Lambda f$ denotes the function $\eta\mapsto\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)$, composition is operator composition, and $\mu\gamma_\Lambda(f)=\int\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)\,d\mu(\eta)$. A proper kernel leaves every exterior-measurable event fixed. A specification is a family $(\gamma_\Lambda)_{\Lambda\text{ finite}}$ of proper probability kernels satisfying $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$ whenever $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$. A DLR state is a probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ satisfying $\mu\gamma_\Lambda=\mu$ for every finite $\Lambda$.

For the existence and uniqueness results below, a specification has **finite range** when for every finite $\Delta$ and every cylinder event $C$ the function $\eta\mapsto\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_C\mid\eta)$ depends on only finitely many coordinates of $\eta$. The displayed finite-range Gibbs formula has this property because only finitely many interaction terms meet $\Delta$, and a cylinder indicator depends on only finitely many additional coordinates.

The formula is the candidate Gibbs specification; [[lem-csm-lattice-specification-consistency]] establishes its positive finite normalization, measurability, properness and consistency under the stated hypotheses. The Countable Choice assumption is used for the product-measure construction, not for any finite conditional sum.
