Fix a classical model with physical energy measured in joules and a positive inverse-temperature parameter $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J}^{-1}$. Its global configuration space is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathscr F)$. For each finite region $\Lambda$, specify a local state measurable space $(\mathcal X_\Lambda,\mathscr F_\Lambda)$, an admissible exterior measurable space $(\mathcal E_\Lambda,\mathscr E_\Lambda)$, and a measurable concatenation map $c_\Lambda:\mathcal X_\Lambda\times\mathcal E_\Lambda\to\mathcal X$; write $x\eta:=c_\Lambda(x,\eta)$. Specify a jointly measurable conditional energy $H_\Lambda:\mathcal X_\Lambda\times\mathcal E_\Lambda\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $+\infty$ marks a forbidden local state, and a measurable kernel $\eta\mapsto m_\Lambda^\eta$ of positive $\sigma$-finite reference measures on $(\mathcal X_\Lambda,\mathscr F_\Lambda)$; $\sigma$-finite means that $\mathcal X_\Lambda$ is a countable union of measurable sets of finite $m_\Lambda^\eta$-measure. The reference normalization and any units carried by its coordinates are part of the model data. For a thermodynamic partition function, choose the reference normalization so $Z_\Lambda^\eta$ is dimensionless. The product $\beta H_\Lambda$ is dimensionless.

For $\eta\in\mathcal E_\Lambda$, define
$$Z_\Lambda^\eta:=\int_{\mathcal X_\Lambda}e^{-\beta H_\Lambda(x\mid\eta)}\,dm_\Lambda^\eta(x),\qquad \gamma_\Lambda(C\mid\eta):=(Z_\Lambda^\eta)^{-1}\int_{\mathcal X_\Lambda}\mathbf1_C(x\eta)e^{-\beta H_\Lambda(x\mid\eta)}\,dm_\Lambda^\eta(x),\quad C\in\mathscr F,$$
with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}:=0$. Adopt these conditional probability kernels only when $0<Z_\Lambda^\eta<\infty$ for every finite $\Lambda$ and admissible $\eta$, and when their dependence on $\eta$ is measurable. A probability measure $\mu$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathscr F)$ is a DLR state for this adopted model if, for every finite $\Lambda$, its exterior restriction lies in $\mathcal E_\Lambda$ almost surely and, for every $C\in\mathscr F$,
$$\mu(C)=\int_{\mathcal X}\gamma_\Lambda(C\mid\eta|_{\Lambda^c})\,d\mu(\eta),$$
where $\eta|_{\Lambda^c}$ is the exterior restriction. A specification is a family of these probability kernels that is **proper** when $\gamma_\Lambda(C\mid\eta)=\mathbf1_C(\eta)$ for each exterior-measurable event $C$ (equivalently, whenever $\mathbf1_C(x\eta)=\mathbf1_C(\eta)$ for every local state $x$), and **consistent** when $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta f=\gamma_\Lambda f$ for every bounded measurable $f$ and finite $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$; kernel composition means $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta f=\gamma_\Lambda(\gamma_\Delta f)$. These identities are required when a DLR specification is asserted; normalization alone does not imply them.

In the finite-alphabet lattice instance, let $A$ be finite and nonempty, $\mathcal X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with the cylinder-generated Borel $\sigma$-algebra, $\mathcal X_\Lambda=A^\Lambda$ with its power-set $\sigma$-algebra, and $\mathcal E_\Lambda=A^{\Lambda^c}$. Concatenation is the coordinatewise patching map. For the finite-range interaction of [[def-csm-finite-range-lattice-interaction]], use counting measure on $A^\Lambda$ and the energy $E_\Lambda(\cdot\mid\eta)$ in joules; the resulting kernels are exactly those in [[def-csm-lattice-gibbs-specification]]. The consistency result [[lem-csm-lattice-specification-consistency]] supplies their properness and consistency. The cylinder-measure extension in [[lem-csm-lattice-product-and-measure-compactness]] uses the Countable Choice axiom [[def-countable-choice]] to construct an infinite-volume probability; no finite conditional sum spends that choice assumption.

When particle-number sectors are present, use the exact interface of [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. For species counts $N_a$ with total $N=\sum_aN_a\ge1$ in $d$ spatial dimensions, the phase-space definition [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]] sets the labelled reference to $m_N=c_N\Lambda_N$ with arbitrary $c_N>0$. This postulate chooses $c_N=a_0^{-dN}$, where $a_0>0$ is a prescribed reference action in joule-seconds, and uses the species factor $1/\prod_aN_a!$ in the normalized quotient reference. Equivalently, the symmetric labelled integral uses $(\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN})^{-1}dq\,dp$; the factorial is included once, and the phase-volume dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$ makes this reference dimensionless. For the vacuum sector $N=0$, define the zero-fold phase space to be a singleton with unit Dirac reference measure (consistent with $0!=1$ and $a_0^0=1$); in a finite region with nonempty exterior, the local vacuum still has the energy $H_\Lambda(\varnothing\mid\eta)$ in its Gibbs weight. If the thermal-wavelength convention of [[def-csm-gibbs-physical-parameters]] is used, set $h_{\rm ref}=a_0$; omit the species factorial for operationally distinguishable labels. These are adopted reference and counting conventions, not consequences of Hamiltonian mechanics or evidence of equilibration. No empirical parameter, measured transition temperature, or uncertainty is asserted here.

This is a model postulate. Normalization, stationarity of a Hamiltonian flow, and finite-volume calculations do not prove equilibration or establish that the model describes nature.

For a declared classical model with $N_a$ operationally indistinguishable
particles of each species $a$, label those particles by
$\{(a,i):1\le i\le N_a\}$ on the auxiliary labelled cover, and let
$S_{N_a}$ denote the permutation group of that species' finite label set.
The product group $G=\prod_a S_{N_a}$ acts on the labelled phase space
$\Gamma_N=T^*Q_N$ by the cotangent lifts of within-species permutations. Let
$\Pi_N:\Gamma_N\to\Gamma_N/G$ be its measurable orbit map from
[[def-csm-phase-space-reference]]. Choose $a_0>0$ as a fixed primitive
reference parameter with action units J s; [[def-cm01-units]] supplies its
dimension, not its value or the choice of this parameter. Here $d$ is the
number of spatial dimensions and $N=\sum_aN_a$. No numerical value or
identification of $a_0$ with Planck's constant is imposed.

Use the weighted labelled lift
$$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}:=\frac{1}{\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN}}\,d\Lambda_N =\frac{1}{\prod_aN_a!\,a_0^{dN}}\,dq\,dp$$
on $\Gamma_N$, where $d\Lambda_N$ is the Liouville density and the last
expression is its coordinate density in canonical charts, with coordinates
read in SI numerical units. The coordinate volume $dq\,dp$ has action
dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$, so the reference is dimensionless. The
physical quotient reference is
$$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(B):=m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}(\Pi_N^{-1}(B))\qquad(B\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{quot}}).$$
Thus $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on the labelled cover $\Gamma_N$, and
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}=(\Pi_N)_*m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ is on
$\Gamma_N/G$; with $c_N=a_0^{-dN}$, the latter is exactly the normalized
quotient reference of [[def-csm-phase-space-reference]].

Physical observables for indistinguishable particles are measurable
$G$-invariant functions $A:\Gamma_N\to\mathbb R$, equivalently measurable
functions $\bar A$ on the quotient with $A=\bar A\circ\Pi_N$. For every such
observable with an integrable expectation, its integral against
$m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$ equals the quotient integral against
$\bar m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$. A labelled density represents a physical state on
the quotient only if it is invariant under $G$ almost everywhere with respect
to $m_N^{\mathrm{phys}}$; an invariant representative may then be used. In
particular, an indistinguishable-particle Hamiltonian must be invariant under
these permutations (or agree almost everywhere with its permuted versions
when only its Gibbs density is at issue). A label-specific coordinate
statistic on the lift is not itself a quotient observable. Under a
permutation-invariant state its marginal law
can instead be interpreted as the law of a uniformly selected particle within
the same species, or of a uniformly selected coordinate of the same type
within that species. Symmetric sums and averages within each species are
quotient observables.
Calculations of labelled momentum components in
[[pthm-csm-canonical-momentum-equipartition]] use this symmetric labelled
lift, and their permutation-invariant kinetic sums and averages are physical
observables.

If labels are operationally distinguishable, omit the corresponding
permutation factor and use the labelled phase space directly. The convention
is part of the preparation and reference model; it is not deduced from
Hamiltonian mechanics. Whether a quantity is represented by a gauge-dependent
canonical momentum or by a gauge-invariant mechanical momentum is fixed by the
stated model and gauge convention. No quantum exchange law, actual preparation
mechanism, or empirical indistinguishability test is asserted.

Use SI units. Let $k_B>0$ be Boltzmann's constant in joules per kelvin, let $T>0$ be absolute temperature in kelvin, and define $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$. For a finite-alphabet lattice model in dimension $d\geq1$, the lattice spacing $a>0$ is in metres; a spin is a dimensionless label. In the nearest-neighbor Ising convention
$$H_\Lambda=-J_{\rm I}\sum_{\{i,j\}\subset\Lambda,\ |i-j|_1=1}s_i s_j-h\sum_{i\in\Lambda}s_i,$$
the coupling $J_{\rm I}$ and field parameter $h$ are energies in joules, so $\beta J_{\rm I}$ and $\beta h$ are dimensionless. Here $h$ is an energy bias per spin, not by itself a magnetic-field strength.

For a finite region, use the energy convention of [[def-csm-finite-range-lattice-interaction]], with each physical interaction value $\Phi_r$ and total energy $H_\Lambda$ measured in joules. Let $Z_\Lambda=\sum_{\sigma\in A^\Lambda}e^{-\beta H_\Lambda(\sigma)}$ and define dimensionless pressure per site $p_\Lambda=|\Lambda|^{-1}\log Z_\Lambda$. When $p=\lim_{n\to\infty}|B_n|^{-1}\log Z_{B_n}$ exists for cubes $B_n=[-n,n]^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$, define physical pressure $\mathsf P=k_BT\,p/a^d$ in J m$^{-d}$ (pascals when $d=3$). For a stationary state $\mu$ on a finite alphabet, let $H_n=-\sum_{\sigma\in A^{B_n}}\mu_{B_n}(\sigma)\log\mu_{B_n}(\sigma)$ with $0\log0=0$; when the limit exists, its Shannon entropy density is $h_{\rm Sh}=\lim_{n\to\infty}H_n/|B_n|$ in nats per site. The mean energy per site is $u=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\mathbb E_\mu[\Phi_r]$ in joules per site. Define reference spin entropy density $s=k_Bh_{\rm Sh}/a^d$ and free-energy density $f=u/a^d-Ts$; both are per physical volume. Thus $f$ and $\mathsf P$ have units J m$^{-d}$, while $s$ has units J K$^{-1}$ m$^{-d}$; for $d=3$ these are the usual per-cubic-metre units.

For a continuum model in dimension $d$, let $x,p\in\mathbb R^d$ be position and momentum, let $m_{\rm p}>0$ be particle mass in kilograms, and use kinetic energy $|p|^2/(2m_{\rm p})$. Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue change-of-variables interface [[def-countable-choice]]. Tonelli's theorem [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and the one-dimensional Gaussian integral [[thm-gaussian-integral]] give $\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-|q|^2}\,d^dq=\pi^{d/2}$. Set $c=\sqrt{\beta/(2m_{\rm p})}>0$ and apply the nonnegative change-of-variables theorem [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]] to the $C^1$ diffeomorphism $q\mapsto cq$ of $\mathbb R^d$ and $f(q)=e^{-|q|^2}$. Since its Jacobian determinant is $c^d$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m_{\rm p})}\,d^dp=c^{-d}\pi^{d/2}=(2\pi m_{\rm p}k_BT)^{d/2}.$$
Under the phase-space reference measure $d^dx\,d^dp/h_{\rm ref}^d$, with reference action $h_{\rm ref}>0$ in joule-seconds, the integrated momentum factor is
$$h_{\rm ref}^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m_{\rm p})}\,d^dp=\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\pi m_{\rm p}k_BT}}{h_{\rm ref}}\right)^d=\lambda_T^{-d},\qquad \lambda_T=\frac{h_{\rm ref}}{\sqrt{2\pi m_{\rm p}k_BT}}.$$
For chemical potential $\mu$ in joules, define the classical activity $z_c=e^{\beta\mu}\lambda_T^{-d}$, with units $\mathrm m^{-d}$. Thus $\lambda_T$ is a length and $z_c$ is inverse volume. This momentum integration explains the one-particle thermal factor; it does not derive particle indistinguishability or a factorial convention. The choice of $h_{\rm ref}$ is a reference convention, not a consequence of the classical equations of motion. For continuum interactions, the potential hypotheses and energy meaning are as in [[def-csm-stable-superstable-continuum-interaction]].

The parameter status in these formulas is model-relative. $T$, $a$, $J_{\rm I}$, and $h$ are inputs for the chosen lattice model; $m_{\rm p}$ and $\mu$ are inputs for the chosen continuum model. Here $h$ is an energy bias per dimensionless spin, not a magnetic-field strength. The reference action $h_{\rm ref}>0$ is a primitive normalization convention, not a derived quantity or an assertion that it equals Planck's constant. In the current SI, $k_B$ has the exact defining value $1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$; it is a fixed SI conversion constant, not a measured fit parameter in this model. The inverse temperature $\beta$, thermal wavelength $\lambda_T$, activity $z_c$, pressure and entropy densities, energy density $u$, entropy density $s$, and free-energy density $f$ are defined or derived from those inputs and the state as specified above; their formulas do not calibrate the inputs to a material or assert empirical accuracy.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

7. **Uniform tempered exterior boundary.** Under full $\mathrm{AC}$, a superstable regular interaction, a genuine finite-valued positive core with divergent radial integral as in [[lem-tdmath-superquadratic-positive-core]], and fixed $z,\beta>0$, the free-wall grand pressure converges uniformly over the exact square-count exterior class $\Omega(t)$ defined in [[thm-tdmath-uniform-tempered-exterior-pressure]], for each finite $t$. Its limit is the free-cube pressure. This class excludes volume-filling external fields.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

Use $e^t:=\exp(t)$ for real $t$, with $\exp$ defined by [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]; for a real measurable function $f$, $e^f$ means the pointwise composition $\exp\circ f$. For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $\exp(-\lambda)\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to $\exp(-\lambda)\exp(\lambda)=\exp(0)=1$ by the exponential power series and [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. This item is a mathematical reference construction and makes no physical claim.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix $d\geq1$. For every bounded Borel set $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $n\in\mathbb N_0$, the unit-intensity Poisson law restricted to $N_D=n$, represented on ordered simple tuples in $D^n$ before forgetting labels, is the pushforward of $e^{-|D|}/n!$ times product Lebesgue measure. Now fix a nonempty bounded Borel region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$, a stable even Borel pair potential $\phi$ with finite range $R>0$ as in [[def-csm-continuum-dlr-kernels]], a locally finite exterior configuration $\eta\subset\Lambda^c$, and $z,\beta>0$. Let $m=N_{\Lambda^R}(\eta)$, with $\Lambda^R=\{y:\operatorname{dist}_2(y,\Lambda)\leq R\}$. Then the partition integral in [[def-csm-continuum-dlr-kernels]] obeys
$$e^{-|\Lambda|}\leq Z_\Lambda^\eta(z,\beta)\leq e^{-|\Lambda|}\exp\!\left(z|\Lambda|e^{\beta B(1+2m)}\right)<\infty.$$
Consequently $\gamma_\Lambda^\eta$ is a Borel probability kernel in $\eta$. For every nonempty bounded Borel region $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$, the extended kernels satisfy $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$, and their fixed measures are exactly the probability laws whose conditional distribution inside each $\Lambda$, given the exterior, is $\gamma_\Lambda^\eta$.

Assume AC, fix $d\geq1$ and $\lambda>0$, and let $Q_\lambda$ be the configuration law of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Define the intensity measure on Borel sets by $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A):=E_{Q_\lambda}N_A$, where $N_A=\omega(A)$ and the nonnegative expectation may be infinite. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A)=\lambda|A|$ for every Borel $A$. For every bounded Borel $A$ and real $a$, its count also has the exact exponential moment
$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\exp\!\left(\lambda|A|(e^a-1)\right).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Under [A3], an $N$-particle configuration has numerical positional energy $H_N^c=cN$. Its unit-Poisson normalized grand partition is
$$Z_{Q,L}^c=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[e^{\alpha N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta cN_{\Lambda_L}}\right] =E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}e^{(\alpha-\beta c)N_{\Lambda_L}} =\exp\!\left(L^3(e^{\alpha-\beta c}-1)\right)$$
by [F4] and the exponential addition law [F5].

By [F3], the $N$-point sector of $Q_{\Lambda_L}$ contributes $e^{-L^3}/N!$ times the positional integral in [A3]. Summing sectors therefore gives $Z_{Q,L}^c=e^{-L^3}\Xi_L^c$, so [A3] yields $\Xi_L^c=\exp(L^3e^{\alpha-\beta c})$. Its reduced pressure is $p(c)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-3}\log\Xi_L^c=e^{\alpha-\beta c}$ by [F6]. The SI conversion in [A3] is $P_{\rm SI}(c)=E_0p(c)/(\beta\ell_0^3)$ pascals.

Repeating steps 1.1–2.1 in the $c_{\rm SI}=0$ member of [A3]'s model family gives $p(0)=e^\alpha$. For the selected $c_{\rm SI}>0$, $\beta c=\beta_{\rm SI}c_{\rm SI}>0$, so strict monotonicity [F5] yields $p(c)=e^{\alpha-\beta c}<e^\alpha=p(0)$. The fixed-activity SI pressures differ by the same positive factor $E_0/(\beta\ell_0^3)$, while the volume term is not covered by the restricted exterior-boundary theorem in [F1]. Thus the stated universal claim is false.

Assume AC. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space and use $D(P\Vert Q)$ as defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(P(\phi)-\log Q(e^\phi)\right),$$
where $B_b$ is the set of bounded real measurable functions. In particular $D\geq0$. If $T$ is measurable, then $D(P\circ T^{-1}\Vert Q\circ T^{-1})\leq D(P\Vert Q)$.

For standard-Borel spaces $X,Y$, probability reference measures $Q_X,Q_Y$, and a joint probability $P_{XY}\ll Q_X\otimes Q_Y$ with finite $D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)$, let $P_{Y|X=x}$ be the conditional law supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for random variables $R,S,Y$ taking values in standard-Borel spaces $\mathcal R,\mathcal S,\mathcal Y$, with $R=r(S)$ for a measurable $r:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$, and a probability reference $Q_Y$ on $\mathcal Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever $D(P_{S,Y}\Vert P_S\otimes Q_Y)<\infty$.

Assume AC. If $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures on the same measurable space, define
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int h\log h\,dQ,&P\ll Q\text{ and }h=dP/dQ,\\+\infty,&P\not\ll Q.\end{cases}$$
Use $0\log0=0$. The Radon–Nikodym derivative $h$ is unique up to $Q$-almost-everywhere equality, so the integral is independent of its representative. Its negative part is finite because $-u\log u\leq1/e$ for $0\leq u\leq1$ and $Q$ is a probability; hence $D(P\Vert Q)$ is a well-defined extended real number.

derivations.claim: If $D(P\Vert\bigotimes_iQ_i)=+\infty$, then the inequality holds because its left side is $+\infty$ and each summand on the right is nonnegative by [F1]. Suppose instead the joint entropy is finite. Repeatedly apply the conditional chain rule [F1] to the coordinate split $(X_1)$ and $(X_2,\ldots,X_m)$ and then to each remaining split. This gives the stated equality; finiteness ensures no subtraction of infinite terms.

For $i\ge2$, apply the conditioning monotonicity in [F1] with $Y=X_i$, $S=(X_1,\ldots,X_{i-1})$, and $R$ the constant observation. The expected conditional divergence given $R$ is exactly $D(P_i\Vert Q_i)$; the expected divergence given $S$ is the $i$th chain increment in step 1.1. Hence that increment is at least $D(P_i\Vert Q_i)$. The first chain term is $D(P_1\Vert Q_1)$, so summing proves the inequality. For $m=1$, the assertion is equality.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

$$\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-bp^2/(2mE_0)}dp=\sqrt{2\pi mE_0/b}.$$
Tonelli [F2] factors the nonnegative d-dimensional integral into d such terms. Dividing by p_*^d gives κ_b, so ν_b has mass one.

$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

Use $e^t:=\exp(t)$ for real $t$, with $\exp$ defined by [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]; for a real measurable function $f$, $e^f$ means the pointwise composition $\exp\circ f$. For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $\exp(-\lambda)\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to $\exp(-\lambda)\exp(\lambda)=\exp(0)=1$ by the exponential power series and [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. This item is a mathematical reference construction and makes no physical claim.

Let $\Omega$ be the positional configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. The **marked configuration space** $\Omega^{\rm mark}$ consists of marked point sets $\xi\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ with spatial projection $q=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\exists p\in\mathbb R^d,\ (x,p)\in\xi\}$ that is simple and locally finite, and with exactly one mark $p_x$ paired to each $x\in q$. Its sigma-algebra is generated by the marked counts $N_{A\times C}(\xi)=\#\{(x,p)\in\xi:x\in A,\ p\in C\}$ for bounded Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. The positional projection is $\pi(\xi)=q\in\Omega$. For a bounded Borel set $\Delta$, the **marked local restriction** is $\xi_\Delta=\{(x,p)\in\xi:x\in\Delta\}$ with the induced count sigma-algebra; write $N_\Delta(\xi)=\#\xi_\Delta$. A **marked-local observable on $\Delta$** is a real measurable function of $\xi_\Delta$; it is bounded when its supremum norm is finite.

Let $d\geq1$, $L>0$, and $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$. A finite marked configuration consists of a finite simple set of positions $q\subseteq\Lambda_L$ and a mark map $p:q\to\mathbb R^d$, as in [[def-csm-full-marked-model]]. Its **marked periodic continuation** is
$$\omega^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,q,p}:=\{(x+Lk,p_x):x\in q,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}.$$
The spatial positions in this set are distinct: if $x+Lk=y+Lj$ for $x,y\in[0,L)^d$, then coordinatewise $x-y=L(j-k)$ forces $j=k$ and $x=y$. Every bounded spatial region meets finitely many lattice translates of the finite set $q$, so the continuation has a locally finite spatial projection.

For a bounded Borel set $\Delta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, define its **marked local restriction** by
$$\omega^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,q,p}|_\Delta:=\{(y,p_x)\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,q,p}:y\in\Delta\}.$$
This is an element of $\Omega^{\rm mark}$, with the induced sigma-algebra of marked counts above. If $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda_L$, the restriction is exactly the original marked points with positions in $\Delta$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Let I=Z^d×N index one potential mark slot for each cell and each within-cell rank. For finite J⊂I prescribe the mark law ν^{⊗J}. These laws are consistent under coordinate restriction and are probabilities because ν is a probability by the Given hypothesis, so [F4] gives a probability ν^I under [A1]. The product probability P⊗ν^I exists by [F5].

For each cell i, write its finite positional list as x_{i,1},...,x_{i,N_i}, in the measurable lexicographic code of [F1]. Define Ψ(q,p) by pairing x_{i,k} with p_{i,k} for every i and 1≤k≤N_i(q). Every bounded spatial region meets finitely many unit cells, and each list is finite, so Ψ(q,p) is locally finite and simple in its positions. By [F2], it belongs to Ω^mark. For bounded Borel spatial A and Borel momentum set C, its marked count is the finite sum
$$N_{A\times C}(\Psi(q,p))=\sum_{i:C_i\cap A\ne\varnothing}\sum_{k=1}^{N_i(q)}1_{\{x_{i,k}\in A\}}1_{\{p_{i,k}\in C\}}.$$
Each summand is measurable in the cell code and mark coordinate by [F1, F4], so Ψ is measurable for the sigma-algebra generated by these counts from [F2]. Its pushforward of P⊗ν^I is the required law P^mark.

Given q, each occupied point uses a distinct coordinate of the product ν^I, so its finite mark families have product law ν^{⊗J}, independent of q. This proves the conditional independence property and fixes every finite marked-count cylinder probability. Those cylinders generate the marked configuration sigma-algebra by [F2], so any law with the same position marginal and conditional product kernel agrees with the pushforward in step 2.1 on a generating class and is identical. Thus the lift exists and is unique. By [F3], the Gaussian kernel ν_b of the model is an admissible probability choice for ν. For each y, the map T_y^mark is measurable because it sends the count N_{A×C} to N_{(A-y)×C}. If P is translation invariant, translating the constructed law by y leaves its positional marginal P and its conditional independent mark kernel ν unchanged; uniqueness therefore gives (T_y^mark)_#P^mark=P^mark.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB, and the superstable regular interaction of [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]], $\beta>0$, and an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. For integers $N_L$ with $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)$ be the $1/N_L!$-normalized positional partition on the periodized cube, with the image convention of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Then
$$L^{-d}\log Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho),$$
the same rate as the free cube. Let $C^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,N_L}$ be the periodic exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $R_{L,\omega}$ its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. For any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, these empirical fields concentrate in every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of the minimizer set of $I+\beta\Phi-\rho\log z$. Writing $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ for this minimizer set, the concentration means $(C^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,N_L})^*\{\omega:R_{L,\omega}\notin U\}\to0$ for every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of it. Here outer probability is as defined in [[lem-tdmath-canonical-empirical-field-conditioning]], and equals ordinary probability for measurable events. A singleton minimizer gives convergence in probability in this outer-probability sense in $\tau_L$.

Assume AC. Fix $d\geq1$ and let $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be the numerical even Borel pair potential. Assume the stability, cell-superstability, lower-regularity, and decreasing-integrable-tail conditions of [[def-csm-stable-superstable-continuum-interaction]], with its fixed cell side $\ell$, and the superstable regular interaction, unit-coordinate, and periodic-image conventions of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. These are model hypotheses; the definitions do not prove that a particular material satisfies them. Use the finite-region phase-space and statistical-state conventions of [[def-csm-statistical-state-observable]].

Let $E_0>0$ joules be the energy unit, $\ell_0>0$ metres the length unit, $m>0$ kilograms the particle mass, and $p_*>0$ kg m s$^{-1}$ the momentum reference. Positions $x=q/\ell_0$ are dimensionless numerical coordinates; write $V_L=L^d$ for numerical volume. The dimensionless positional energy $U_{L,bc}$ is the physical pair energy divided by $E_0$, with $bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}$ and the exact image convention above. If $T>0$ kelvin, put $\beta_{\rm phys}=1/(k_BT)$ in J$^{-1}$ and $b=\beta_{\rm phys}E_0=E_0/(k_BT)>0$.

Let $Q_L$ be the unit-intensity Poisson probability on positional configurations in $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, defined by [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Its $N$-particle conditional law $Q_{L,N}$ is uniform on the unordered simple $N$-point configurations; in labelled coordinates it is $L^{-dN}dx_1\cdots dx_N$ on the no-collision set. On an $N$-point configuration, attach one momentum $p_x\in\mathbb R^d$ to each point and use the symmetric product reference $r^{\otimes q}$ with $r(dp)=dp/p_*^d$. The finite phase reference is
$$R_{L,N}(dq,dp):=Q_L(dq)\,r^{\otimes q}(dp)\,1_{\{N(q)=N\}}.$$
It is sigma-finite; the factor $e^{-V_L}/N!$ from the Poisson sector is retained. In physical coordinates the corresponding one-particle product scale is $h_{\rm ref}^d=\ell_0^dp_*^d$, an action to the power $d$; it is a reference convention, not a derived quantum constant.

For a marked configuration define the total dimensionless energy
$$\mathcal H_{L,bc}(q,p)=U_{L,bc}(q)+\sum_{x\in q}K(p_x),\qquad K(p)=\frac{|p|^2}{2mE_0}.$$
For $b>0$, [[lem-csm-gaussian-mark-moments]] gives $\kappa_b=\int e^{-bK}r(dp)=(2\pi mE_0/(bp_*^2))^{d/2}$ and the probability kernel $\nu_b(dp)=\kappa_b^{-1}e^{-bK(p)}r(dp)$. Whenever the positional canonical partition is finite and positive, nonnegative product integration [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] gives exact identities
$$Z^{\rm ph}_{Q,L,N,bc}(b)=\int e^{-b\mathcal H_{L,bc}}dR_{L,N}=\kappa_b^N Z^{\rm pos}_{Q,L,N,bc}(b),\qquad C^{\rm ph}_{L,N,bc}=C^{\rm pos}_{L,N,bc}\,\nu_b^{\otimes q}.$$
Here $Z^{\rm pos}_{Q,L,N,bc}=E_{Q_L}[1_{\{N(q)=N\}}e^{-bU_{L,bc}}]$ and the canonical probabilities are the normalized respective integrands. Under a full grand preparation of activity $z_{\rm ph}$, integrating each momentum changes the positional activity to $z=z_{\rm ph}\kappa_b$; thus a positional activity $z=e^\alpha$ corresponds to $z_{\rm ph}=e^\alpha/\kappa_b$. These are exact definitions and normalizations; they do not assert dynamical equilibration or finite-volume grand convergence. For periodic boundary conditions, simultaneous translation of all positions modulo the period preserves $R_{L,N}$ and $\mathcal H_{L,\mathrm{per}}$: the conditional position law is uniform on the torus, the mark reference is invariant under relabelling points, and the image energy depends only on pair displacements. Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

Assume AC. Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$, use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define $|x|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$, and use the numerical coordinate conventions in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For a regular potential and sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. Under this regularity hypothesis, the far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where the tuple notation means $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=H_\phi(\{q_1,\ldots,q_N\})$ when the coordinates are distinct, and $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=+\infty$ on collision diagonals. The integrand is therefore zero on collisions; these diagonals have product Lebesgue measure zero by the no-collision construction in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], so this convention leaves all partition integrals unchanged. For $N=0$ the empty tuple has energy zero. Here $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. For a probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], stationarity means $P\circ T_x^{-1}=P$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. When $P$ is stationary and $E_PN_{[0,1)^d}<\infty$ (finite intensity), write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. Use the finite-region relative entropy $D$ defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. If $\phi$ is stable with constant $B$, then $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}\geq-BN_{\Lambda_L}$, so the negative part of $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ is $P$-integrable for every such $P$. Whenever the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
In the variational results below, $\Phi(P)$ denotes this same positional energy density: $\Phi(P):=\mathcal E(P)$. The cited results establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume either limit exists for every stationary finite-intensity law.

derivations.claim:
Integrating the marks in [[def-csm-full-marked-model]] gives the canonical marked partition as $\kappa_{b'}^{N_n}Z^{\rm pos}_{L_n,N_n,\mathrm{per}}(b')$. The exact-$N_n$ positional sector of the unit-intensity Poisson reference contributes the common factor $e^{-V_n}$ relative to the Lebesgue $1/N_n!$ partition; it cancels in the ratio of marked partition functions. By [F1], for each fixed $t$ with $b-t>0$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}V_n^{-1}\log E_{C_n^{\rm ph}}e^{t\mathcal H}=\Lambda(t):=F_{b-t}(\rho)-F_b(\rho)+\rho\log(\kappa_{b-t}/\kappa_b),$$
by [F1, F2]. Differentiability and the explicit Gaussian factor give $\Lambda(0)=0$ and $\Lambda'(0)=-F_b'(\rho)+d\rho/(2b)=e_b(\rho)$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the derivative at zero, choose a sufficiently small fixed $t>0$ so $\Lambda(t)-t(e_b+\varepsilon)<0$. On the upper event, $1\le e^{t(\mathcal H-V_n(e_b+\varepsilon))}$, so integrating this pointwise inequality gives
$$C_n^{\rm ph}(\mathcal H/V_n\ge e_b+\varepsilon)\le e^{-tV_n(e_b+\varepsilon)}E_{C_n^{\rm ph}}e^{t\mathcal H};$$
its logarithm divided by $V_n$ tends to that strictly negative number, so it is at most $-c_+V_n$ in the exponent for some $c_+>0$ and all large $n$. For each integer $j\ge1$, the fixed-width conclusion of step 2.1 supplies an integer $n_j$ increasing strictly such that for all $n\ge n_j$ the probability outside width $1/j$ is at most $1/j$. Let $j(n)=\max\{j:n_j\le n\}$ for $n\ge n_1$, and put $\delta_n=1/j(n)$; assign any positive nonincreasing values before $n_1$. Then $j(n)\to\infty$, so $\delta_n\downarrow0$, and the probability outside $A_n$ tends to zero. The sigma-finite product reference in [[def-csm-full-marked-model]] assigns finite measure to that bounded sector, so the band has finite reference measure.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB. Use the model and dimensionless energy $\mathcal H_{L,\mathrm{per}}$ of [[def-csm-full-marked-model]]. Let $L_n\to\infty$, $V_n=L_n^d$, and integers $N_n$ satisfy $N_n/V_n\to\rho>0$, where $\rho$ is an interior attainable density for the positional canonical rate. Fix $b>0$. Assume $F_b(\rho)$ is the periodic exact-particle log-partition rate supplied by [[thm-tdmath-periodic-fixed-n-limit]] for every $b'$ in a neighborhood of $b$, and is differentiable at $b$. Write $C_n^{\rm ph}$ for the full fixed-$N_n$ canonical law, and define
$$e_b(\rho)=-\partial_bF_b(\rho)+\frac{d\rho}{2b}.$$
Then, for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, there exist $c_\varepsilon>0$ and $n_0$ such that
$$C_n^{\rm ph}\!\left(\left|\mathcal H_{L_n,\mathrm{per}}/V_n-e_b(\rho)\right|>\varepsilon\right)\le 2e^{-c_\varepsilon V_n}\quad(n\ge n_0).$$
Consequently there is a nonincreasing sequence $\delta_n\downarrow0$ for which the full phase band
$$A_n=\{N=N_n,\ |\mathcal H_{L_n,\mathrm{per}}/V_n-e_b(\rho)|\le\delta_n\}$$
has $C_n^{\rm ph}(A_n)\to1$. It has positive finite phase-reference measure for all sufficiently large $n$. This constructs a controlled shrinking window; it makes no claim about every prescribed shell width or an exact energy surface.

Assume AC. Fix $d\geq1$ and let $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be the numerical even Borel pair potential. These are model hypotheses; the definitions do not prove that a particular material satisfies them. Use the finite-region phase-space and statistical-state conventions of [[def-csm-statistical-state-observable]].

Let $E_0>0$ joules be the energy unit, $\ell_0>0$ metres the length unit, $m>0$ kilograms the particle mass, and $p_*>0$ kg m s$^{-1}$ the momentum reference. Positions $x=q/\ell_0$ are dimensionless numerical coordinates; write $V_L=L^d$ for numerical volume. The dimensionless positional energy $U_{L,bc}$ is the physical pair energy divided by $E_0$, with $bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}$ and the exact image convention above. If $T>0$ kelvin, put $\beta_{\rm phys}=1/(k_BT)$ in J$^{-1}$ and $b=\beta_{\rm phys}E_0=E_0/(k_BT)>0$.

Let $Q_L$ be the unit-intensity Poisson probability on positional configurations in $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, defined by [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Its $N$-particle conditional law $Q_{L,N}$ is uniform on the unordered simple $N$-point configurations; in labelled coordinates it is $L^{-dN}dx_1\cdots dx_N$ on the no-collision set. On an $N$-point configuration, attach one momentum $p_x\in\mathbb R^d$ to each point and use the symmetric product reference $r^{\otimes q}$ with $r(dp)=dp/p_*^d$. The finite phase reference is
$$R_{L,N}(dq,dp):=Q_L(dq)\,r^{\otimes q}(dp)\,1_{\{N(q)=N\}}.$$
It is sigma-finite; the factor $e^{-V_L}/N!$ from the Poisson sector is retained. In physical coordinates the corresponding one-particle product scale is $h_{\rm ref}^d=\ell_0^dp_*^d$, an action to the power $d$; it is a reference convention, not a derived quantum constant.

$$\mathcal H_{L,bc}(q,p)=U_{L,bc}(q)+\sum_{x\in q}K(p_x),\qquad K(p)=\frac{|p|^2}{2mE_0}.$$
For $b>0$, [[lem-csm-gaussian-mark-moments]] gives $\kappa_b=\int e^{-bK}r(dp)=(2\pi mE_0/(bp_*^2))^{d/2}$ and the probability kernel $\nu_b(dp)=\kappa_b^{-1}e^{-bK(p)}r(dp)$. Whenever the positional canonical partition is finite and positive, nonnegative product integration [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] gives exact identities
$$Z^{\rm ph}_{Q,L,N,bc}(b)=\int e^{-b\mathcal H_{L,bc}}dR_{L,N}=\kappa_b^N Z^{\rm pos}_{Q,L,N,bc}(b),\qquad C^{\rm ph}_{L,N,bc}=C^{\rm pos}_{L,N,bc}\,\nu_b^{\otimes q}.$$
Here $Z^{\rm pos}_{Q,L,N,bc}=E_{Q_L}[1_{\{N(q)=N\}}e^{-bU_{L,bc}}]$ and the canonical probabilities are the normalized respective integrands. Hence normalized canonical and finite band restrictions are torus-translation invariant.

Assume AC. If $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures on the same measurable space, define
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int h\log h\,dQ,&P\ll Q\text{ and }h=dP/dQ,\\+\infty,&P\not\ll Q.\end{cases}$$
Use $0\log0=0$. The Radon–Nikodym derivative $h$ is unique up to $Q$-almost-everywhere equality, so the integral is independent of its representative. Its negative part is finite because $-u\log u\leq1/e$ for $0\leq u\leq1$ and $Q$ is a probability; hence $D(P\Vert Q)$ is a well-defined extended real number.

Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $Q_i$ be probability measures on $X_i$, and let $P$ be a probability on $\prod_{i=1}^mX_i$. Write $P_i$ for its $i$th marginal and use the directional extended relative entropy $D(\cdot\Vert\cdot)$ of [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_m)\geq\sum_{i=1}^mD(P_i\Vert Q_i).$$
If the left side is finite, the conditional chain rule gives the stronger equality
$$D(P\Vert\textstyle\bigotimes_iQ_i)=D(P_1\Vert Q_1)+\sum_{i=2}^m E_P\,D(P_{X_i\mid X_1,\ldots,X_{i-1}}\Vert Q_i),$$
and each conditional increment is at least $D(P_i\Vert Q_i)$. If the left side is infinite, the displayed inequality is understood in the extended order and is automatic. This applies to finitely many disjoint spatial blocks after their particle counts and positions have been fixed; zero-occupancy blocks contribute zero.

derivations.claim:
On A_n, the density of M_n^ph relative to C_n^ph is Z_n e^{bH}/R_n(A_n). Therefore
$$D_n=-\log R_n(A_n)+\log Z_n+bE_{M_n^{ph}}\mathcal H.$$
The lower band edge gives
$$R_n(A_n)=Z_nE_{C_n^{ph}}[1_{A_n}e^{b\mathcal H}]\ge Z_nC_n^{ph}(A_n)e^{bV_n(e_b-\delta_n)}.$$

The upper band edge gives $E_{M_n^{\rm ph}}\mathcal H\leq V_n(e_b+\delta_n)$. Substituting the step 1.1 lower bound for $R_n(A_n)$ yields
$$D_n\le-\log C_n^{ph}(A_n)+2bV_n\delta_n.$$
Relative entropy is nonnegative by [F3]; since $C_n^{\rm ph}(A_n)\to1$ and $\delta_n\to0$ by [F1], this proves $0\leq D_n/V_n\to0$.
