The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Under this assumption Lebesgue measure is the completion of Borel measure ([[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]), and every Lebesgue-measurable integrable class has a Borel representative ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]]). Write $\lambda_3$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). Fix a positive reference speed $v_0>0$, and put $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$. Let $X$ be the real vector space of equivalence classes modulo $\lambda_3$-almost-everywhere equality of measurable functions $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ with

$$\|f\|_{1,w_0}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}w_0(v)|f(v)|\,d\lambda_3(v)<\infty.$$

Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$. For a Borel set $E\subseteq S^2$, define the normalized finite angular measure

$$\sigma(E):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf 1_E(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\phi\,d\theta.$$

For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$ and $n\in S^2$, define the postcollision velocities

$$v'=v-((v-w)\cdot n)n,\qquad w'=w+((v-w)\cdot n)n.$$

The collision-parameter measure is $d\mu=d\lambda_3(v)\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Its angular factor is finite and normalized; there is no singular angular weight. For $f,g\in X$, choose Borel representatives and define the gain $\mathcal G(f,g)$ by the almost-everywhere integral

$$\mathcal G(f,g)(v):=\int_{\mathbb R^3\times S^2} f(v')g(w')\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n).$$

The value on any exceptional null set is immaterial because the output is an equivalence class. The next item proves that this definition is independent of the representatives, maps $X\times X$ to $X$, and has the stated collision and moment identities.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Write $\beta_n$ for the restriction of $\lambda_n$ to
the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is exactly the
completion domain of $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n), \beta_n)$
([[def-completion-of-a-measure-space]]), and $\lambda_n$ is the completed measure
there. Explicitly,

$$E \in \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) \iff E = A\cup N \text{ for some } A, Z \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \text{ with } N \subseteq Z \text{ and } \beta_n(Z) = 0,$$

The map $r\mapsto r-2(r\cdot n)n$ is reflection across the plane perpendicular to $n$: applying it twice returns $r$, and its squared norm is $|r|^2$. The center $c$ is fixed. Hence the pair map is an orthogonal involution on $\mathbb R^6$, its determinant has absolute value one, $v'+w'=v+w$, and $|v'|^2+|w'|^2=|v|^2+|w|^2$.

The defining integral of $\sigma$ has total mass $(4\pi)^{-1}(2)(2\pi)=1$. Every nonempty relative-open subset of $S^2$ contains a patch away from a coordinate pole and seam; its preimage contains an open rectangle on which $\sin\theta>0$, so it has positive $\sigma$-measure. Every nonempty open subset of the full parameter space contains a product of two Euclidean balls and such a sphere patch; each factor has positive measure, so $\mu$ has full support. For an elastic pair, set $c=(v+w)/2$, $r=(v-w)/2$, and $\tilde r=(\tilde v-\tilde w)/2$. Momentum and squared-speed conservation give the same center and $|\tilde r|=|r|$. If $\tilde r\ne r$, choose $n=(r-\tilde r)/|r-\tilde r|$; the equal-norm identity gives $2(r\cdot n)n=r-\tilde r$, hence the reflection sends $r$ to $\tilde r$. If $\tilde r=r$, choose any unit $n$ perpendicular to $r$ when $r\ne0$, and any unit $n$ when $r=0$. Thus every elastic pair is attained.

For each fixed $n$, let $T_n(v,w)=(v',w')$. If $h\in L^1(\mathbb R^6)$ is real-valued, write $h=h^+-h^-$, where $h^+=\max(h,0)$ and $h^-=\max(-h,0)$. Applying [F4] to $|h|$ shows that $h\circ T_n$ is absolutely integrable because $T_n$ has unit absolute Jacobian. Applying [F4] separately to $h^+$ and $h^-$, whose integrals are finite, and subtracting gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^6}h(T_n(v,w))\,dv\,dw=\int_{\mathbb R^6}h(v,w)\,dv\,dw.$$
For an absolutely integrable parameter-dependent signed integrand on $\mathbb R^6\times S^2$, [F3] permits integration of this equality in $n$. Thus the cited nonnegative change-of-variables result has the signed $L^1$ consequence used below.

Replace the representatives of $f$ and $g$ by Borel representatives using [F2]. Tonelli [F3] makes the sections measurable and permits integration in any order. For each fixed $n$, the pair reflection in step 1.1 is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with unit absolute Jacobian, so [F4] gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^6} h(v',w')\,dv\,dw=\int_{\mathbb R^6}h(v,w)\,dv\,dw.$$ It follows that $\int |\mathcal G(f,g)|\,dv\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_1$. The same change of variables shows that altering either representative on a Lebesgue-null set changes the integrand only on a $\mu$-null set; therefore the output class is independent of representatives. For the first moment, the same change of variables gives $\int v\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=\int v'f(v)f(w)\,d\mu$. The simultaneous exchange $(v,w,n)\mapsto(w,v,n)$ preserves $\mu$ and swaps $v'$ with $w'$, while $f(v)f(w)$ is unchanged. Averaging the two expressions replaces $v'$ by $(v'+w')/2=(v+w)/2$, yielding $M\int vf\,dv$. Applying the same averaging to the second moment uses $(|v'|^2+|w'|^2)/2=(|v|^2+|w|^2)/2$ and gives $M\int|v|^2f\,dv$. The first-moment change of variables is applied coordinatewise to signed integrable functions; finiteness follows from the finite mass and second moment.

Let $M=1$ and let $\varphi$ satisfy the four absolute-integrability conditions in the Statement. By step 2.1, $\int\varphi(v)\mathcal G(f,f)(v)\,dv=\int\varphi(v')A\,d\mu$. The incoming/outgoing involution sends $A$ to $B$ and $\Delta\varphi$ to $-\Delta\varphi$, so $\int(B-A)\Delta\varphi\,d\mu=-2\int A\Delta\varphi\,d\mu$. Combining these equalities gives the claimed factor $1/4$ identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Under this assumption Lebesgue measure is the completion of Borel measure ([[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]), and every Lebesgue-measurable integrable class has a Borel representative ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]]). Write $\lambda_3$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). Fix a positive reference speed $v_0>0$, and put $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$. Let $X$ be the real vector space of equivalence classes modulo $\lambda_3$-almost-everywhere equality of measurable functions $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ with

$$\|f\|_{1,w_0}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}w_0(v)|f(v)|\,d\lambda_3(v)<\infty.$$

Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$. For a Borel set $E\subseteq S^2$, define the normalized finite angular measure

$$\sigma(E):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf 1_E(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\phi\,d\theta.$$

For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$ and $n\in S^2$, define the postcollision velocities

$$v'=v-((v-w)\cdot n)n,\qquad w'=w+((v-w)\cdot n)n.$$

The collision-parameter measure is $d\mu=d\lambda_3(v)\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Its angular factor is finite and normalized; there is no singular angular weight. For $f,g\in X$, choose Borel representatives and define the gain $\mathcal G(f,g)$ by the almost-everywhere integral

$$\mathcal G(f,g)(v):=\int_{\mathbb R^3\times S^2} f(v')g(w')\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n).$$

The value on any exceptional null set is immaterial because the output is an equivalence class. The next item proves that this definition is independent of the representatives, maps $X\times X$ to $X$, and has the stated collision and moment identities.

Let $\mathcal G$, $v'$, $w'$, $X$, $w_0$, and $\mu$ be as in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. For $f,g\in X$, the gain is independent of the chosen Borel representatives, is bilinear, and satisfies

$$\|\mathcal G(f,g)\|_{1,w_0}\le 2\|f\|_{1,w_0}\|g\|_{1,w_0}.$$

For $f\ge0$ with finite mass $M=\int f\,dv$ and finite second moment, it also satisfies

$$\int\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M^2,\qquad \int v\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M\int vf\,dv,\qquad \int |v|^2\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M\int |v|^2f\,dv.$$

If $M=1$, set $A=f(v)f(w)$, $B=f(v')f(w')$, and $\Delta\varphi=\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w')$. For every real-valued measurable test $\varphi$ such that

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\varphi(v)|\mathcal G(f,f)(v)\,dv<\infty,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}|\varphi(v)|f(v)\,dv<\infty,\qquad \int |A\Delta\varphi|\,d\mu<\infty,\qquad \int |B\Delta\varphi|\,d\mu<\infty,$$

the following identity holds:

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\varphi(v)\bigl(\mathcal G(f,f)(v)-f(v)\bigr)\,dv=\frac14\int (B-A)\Delta\varphi\,d\mu.$$

For each fixed $n$, the map $(v,w)\mapsto(v',w')$ is a linear orthogonal involution, preserves $v+w$ and $|v|^2+|w|^2$, and has Jacobian determinant of absolute value one. The angular measure has full support, hence the product parameter measure $\mu$ has full support on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Every pair $(v,w)$ and $(\widetilde v,\widetilde w)$ with the same momentum and squared-speed sum is related by one such reflection.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F3], diagonalize $\Sigma$ in an orthonormal basis with eigenvalues $s_1^2,s_2^2,s_3^2\in[a,b]$. The linear substitution $y_i=(v-u)_i/s_i$ has Jacobian $\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2}$; [F4] in each coordinate gives $\int\gamma_{\Sigma,u}(v)\,dv=1$. The same eigenvalue bounds give $(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\in[b^{-3/2},a^{-3/2}]$ and $|v-u|^2/b\le(v-u)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(v-u)\le|v-u|^2/a$, proving the two Gaussian envelopes for each component and hence for every finite mixture.

Let $O_n:\mathbb R^6\to\mathbb R^6$ be the orthogonal pair map from [F2], and let $P:\mathbb R^6\to\mathbb R^3$ project onto the first component. For component densities $\gamma_{\Sigma,u}$ and $\gamma_{\Tau,u}$, the joint centered covariance is $S=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma,\Tau)$. Using [F6] under $O_n$, the density of the pair after reflection is the centered Gaussian with covariance $S_n=O_nSO_n^{\mathsf T}$ and mean $(u,u)$. Write $S_n$ in blocks as $\begin{pmatrix}C&D\\D^{\mathsf T}&E\end{pmatrix}$. Its first marginal is Gaussian with covariance $C$: indeed $C$ is positive definite, the Schur complement $H=E-D^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}D$ is positive definite, and block elimination gives $\det S_n=\det C\det H$ and $$(x,y)^{\mathsf T}S_n^{-1}(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}x+(y-D^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}x)^{\mathsf T}H^{-1}(y-D^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}x).$$ Integrating in $y$ using [F3], [F4], and [F7] gives the normalized marginal $\gamma_{C,u}$. Also $C=PS_nP^{\mathsf T}$ satisfies $aI\le C\le bI$: for every $z$, $z^{\mathsf T}Cz=(z,0)^{\mathsf T}O_nSO_n^{\mathsf T}(z,0)$ lies between $a|z|^2$ and $b|z|^2$.

Differentiating a component $\gamma_{\Sigma,u}$ in $v$ multiplies it by a polynomial in $\Sigma^{-1}(v-u)$; each coefficient is uniformly bounded because $\|\Sigma^{-1}\|\le a^{-1}$. The exponent has the upper bound from step 1.1, so every derivative of a finite mixture has the stated polynomial-Gaussian envelope, uniformly over all finite mixtures in this class.

Therefore $\mathcal G(\gamma_{\Sigma,u},\gamma_{\Tau,u})$ is the pointwise angular average $\int_{S^2}\gamma_{C_n,u}\,d\sigma(n)$ with $C_n\in K_{a,b}$. The map $n\mapsto C_n$ is continuous, and $C\mapsto\gamma_{C,u}$ is continuous in $X$: pointwise convergence follows from the formula, while the weighted upper Gaussian envelope from step 1.1 is an integrable dominator and [F5] gives weighted-$L^1$ convergence. For each $n$, continuity supplies a relative-open neighborhood on which the $X$-distance from $\gamma_{C_n,u}$ is less than $\varepsilon$; compactness of $S^2$ gives a finite subcover. Successively subtracting earlier open sets makes this a finite Borel partition $E_j$, and choosing one $n_j$ in each nonempty piece gives variation at most $2\varepsilon$ on that piece. Tonelli [F7] and the triangle inequality bound the weighted-$L^1$ distance from the angular average to $\sum_j\sigma(E_j)\gamma_{C_{n_j},u}$ by $2\varepsilon\sum_j\sigma(E_j)=2\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, the angular average belongs to $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$. Bilinear expansion proves the same for finite convex mixtures in both inputs.

For general $f,g\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$, choose finite-mixture sequences $f_k\to f$ and $g_k\to g$ in $X$. The bound [F2] gives $$\|\mathcal G(f_k,g_k)-\mathcal G(f,g)\|_{1,w_0}\le2\|f_k-f\|_{1,w_0}\|g_k\|_{1,w_0}+2\|f\|_{1,w_0}\|g_k-g\|_{1,w_0}\longrightarrow0.$$ Each $\mathcal G(f_k,g_k)$ is in $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ by step 2.2, so closedness proves $\mathcal G(f,g)\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$.

Let $f_k$ be finite mixtures converging in $X$ to $f\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$. By step 2.1, every derivative sequence $(\partial^\alpha f_k)_k$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on every closed ball, since the next derivatives have a common bound there. On the countable dense rational grid in each ball, bounded real sequences admit convergent subsequences: repeatedly bisect a bounded interval, retain a half containing infinitely many terms, and use the nested intervals of lengths tending to zero to select a convergent subsequence. A countable diagonal selection over grid points, integer-radius balls, and multi-indices makes every derivative converge on every grid. Equicontinuity and a finite rational $\delta$-net of each ball then make these subsequences uniformly Cauchy there, hence locally uniformly convergent. The fundamental theorem of calculus along coordinate segments identifies the limits as derivatives of a smooth function $\widetilde f$. Weighted-$L^1$ convergence identifies $\widetilde f=f$ almost everywhere on every ball, so $\widetilde f$ represents $f$. The pointwise envelopes and derivative bounds pass to the local uniform limit. This proves part 1 for every class element.

boundaries.evidence: K_{a,b} is nonempty: Sigma=aI satisfies aI<=Sigma<=bI. Each mixture has nonnegative weights summing to1, so the empty mixture has mass0 and cannot enter the normalized class. Step1.1 supplies a unit-mass Gaussian witness and step4.1 preserves mass in the weighted-space closure; no probability is normalized from an empty sum.

A one-term mixture with coefficient one is included, and step 1.1 proves its Gaussian normalization and envelopes.
Step 1.1 permits repeated eigenvalues and eigenvalues at either allowed spectral bound.
Step 1.1 covers covariance eigenvalues equal to a or b; the parameter constraint a<b is explicit.

No converse characterization of the mixture class is asserted.

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\varphi(v)\bigl(\mathcal G(f,f)(v)-f(v)\bigr)\,dv=\frac14\int (B-A)\Delta\varphi\,d\mu.$$

For each fixed $n$, the map $(v,w)\mapsto(v',w')$ is a linear orthogonal involution, preserves $v+w$ and $|v|^2+|w|^2$, and has Jacobian determinant of absolute value one. The angular measure has full support, hence the product parameter measure $\mu$ has full support on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Every pair $(v,w)$ and $(\widetilde v,\widetilde w)$ with the same momentum and squared-speed sum is related by one such reflection.

Fix $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and positive velocity-squared parameters $0<a<b$ (in a physical interpretation, both have units $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^2$). Let

$$K_{a,b}:=\{\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:\Sigma=\Sigma^{\mathsf T},\ aI\le\Sigma\le bI\},$$

where the matrix inequalities mean $a|z|^2\le z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z\le b|z|^2$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\Sigma\in K_{a,b}$, define the normalized Gaussian density

$$\gamma_{\Sigma,u}(v):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(v-u)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(v-u)\right).$$

Let $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ be the closure in the weighted space $X$ of all finite convex mixtures $\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\gamma_{\Sigma_j,u}$ with $\Sigma_j\in K_{a,b}$, $\alpha_j\ge0$, and $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$. Then:

1. Every $f\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ has a $C^\infty$ representative satisfying

$$ (2\pi b)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2a)}\le f(v)\le(2\pi a)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}.$$

For every multi-index $\alpha$, there is a finite constant $C_{\alpha,a,b}$, depending only on $\alpha,a,b$ and not on $f$, such that

$$|\partial^\alpha f(v)|\le C_{\alpha,a,b}(1+|v-u|^{|\alpha|})e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}.$$

The common derivative bounds imply that every sequence in $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ has a subsequence converging locally uniformly together with all velocity derivatives.

2. The gain in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]] maps this class into itself: $\mathcal G(f,g)\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: The weighted measure $w_0\,dv$ is sigma-finite because $w_0$ is bounded on every bounded ball. To prove $X$ complete, let $(g_n)$ be Cauchy in its norm and choose a subsequence $(g_{n_j})$ with $\|g_{n_{j+1}}-g_{n_j}\|_{1,w_0}\le2^{-j}$. By [F5], the nonnegative series $\sum_j w_0|g_{n_{j+1}}-g_{n_j}|$ is finite almost everywhere and has finite integral. Hence $g_{n_j}$ converges pointwise almost everywhere to a measurable $g$, and the integral of each tail is bounded by $\sum_{j\ge J}2^{-j}$, so $g_{n_j}\to g$ in $X$. The same estimates give $\|g\|_{1,w_0}<\infty$. Since the original sequence was Cauchy, it converges to the same $g$. Thus $X$ is complete.

Put $m_1=\int vf_0\,dv$ and $E_2=\int|v|^2f_0\,dv$, and let $K$ be the subset of $X$ of nonnegative functions with mass $1$, first moment $m_1$, and second moment $E_2$. It is nonempty because $f_0\in K$. It is closed: if $g_n\to g$ in $X$, then $\int|g_n-g|\le\|g_n-g\|_{1,w_0}$, $\int|v||g_n-g|\le(v_0/2)\|g_n-g\|_{1,w_0}$, and $\int|v|^2|g_n-g|\le v_0^2\|g_n-g\|_{1,w_0}$; also the negative part of $g$ is bounded by $|g-g_n|$ whenever $g_n\ge0$. Thus all constraints pass to the limit, and $K$ is complete. The continuous path space $C([0,T],K)$ with the supremum metric is complete: a uniformly Cauchy sequence has pointwise limits in $K$, converges uniformly, and the triangle inequality with one continuous approximant proves continuity of the limit.

Let $M_0=1+E_2/v_0^2$; every $g\in K$ has $\|g\|_{1,w_0}=M_0$. On $C([0,T],K)$ define $$\Phi(g)_t=e^{-\lambda t}f_0+\lambda\int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}\mathcal G(g_s,g_s)\,ds.$$ The integrand is norm-continuous because $s\mapsto g_s$ is continuous and [F2] bounds the bilinear map. Its Riemann sums are Cauchy in $X$ by uniform continuity on $[0,T]$ and completeness from step 1.1. The gain identities in [F2] show that $\Phi(g)_t$ has mass $1$, first moment $m_1$, and second moment $E_2$, since $e^{-\lambda t}+\lambda\int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}ds=1$; nonnegativity is preserved as well. Therefore $\Phi$ maps this path space into itself.

Bilinearity and [F2] give $$\|\mathcal G(g_s,g_s)-\mathcal G(h_s,h_s)\|_{1,w_0}\le2\|g_s-h_s\|_{1,w_0}(\|g_s\|_{1,w_0}+\|h_s\|_{1,w_0})=4M_0\|g_s-h_s\|_{1,w_0}.$$ Hence $\|\Phi(g)-\Phi(h)\|_{C([0,T],X)}\le4\lambda M_0T\|g-h\|_{C([0,T],X)}$. Choose $T=(8\lambda M_0)^{-1}$, so this constant is $1/2$. The nonempty complete path space from step 2.1 and [F4] yield a unique fixed point on $[0,T]$. Differentiating its norm-continuous mild integral gives $f'_t=\lambda(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t)$ in $X$.

Suppose $f_0\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$. The class is closed and convex by definition. If a path takes values in this class, [F3] puts every gain value in the class. For a partition $0=s_0<\cdots<s_N=t$, assign each subinterval $I_j=[s_{j-1},s_j]$ the exact nonnegative weight $\lambda\int_{I_j}e^{-\lambda(t-s)}\,ds$ and evaluate the gain at one point of that interval; these weights sum to $1-e^{-\lambda t}$. Adding the weight $e^{-\lambda t}$ on $f_0$ gives convex combinations in the class. As the mesh tends to zero, the Riemann sums converge in $X$ to $\Phi(g)_t$, so closedness puts $\Phi(g)_t$ in the class. Thus Picard iteration of $\Phi$ starting at the constant path $f_0$ remains in $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$, and [F4] makes its uniform limit the fixed point. Therefore every $f_t$ lies in this class and has the smooth positive representative and Gaussian envelopes from [F3].

At $t=T$ the solution is again in $K$. Restart the same construction with initial value $f_T$; the same $M_0$ gives the same positive interval length. Iterating constructs a solution on every $[0,kT]$, and uniqueness on overlaps makes the concatenation a unique global mild solution. Substituting the restarted mild formula into the preceding interval gives the displayed global formula. Since the gain is nonnegative, the formula also gives $f_t\ge e^{-\lambda t}f_0$ almost everywhere.

On any compact time interval, the uniform spatial derivative bounds from [F3] make the family of representatives locally relatively compact in $C^\infty$. If $t_j\to t$, continuity in $X$ gives $f_{t_j}\to f_t$ in weighted $L^1$. Every subsequence has a further locally uniformly convergent subsequence by [F3]; its limit equals almost everywhere the continuous representative of $f_t$, hence equals it everywhere. A subsequence on which local uniform convergence failed would contradict this property, so $t\mapsto f_t$ is locally uniformly continuous in velocity. For $v$ in a compact velocity set, the gain integrand $f_s(v')f_s(w')$ is continuous in $(s,v)$, and pair-energy preservation gives the integrable majorant $C e^{-|w-u|^2/(2b)}$, uniform on that compact set and compact time intervals. Dominated convergence [F6] therefore makes the pointwise gain integral finite and jointly continuous in $(s,v)$; it is a continuous representative of the $X$-class gain. In particular, for fixed $v$ this supplies the integrable majorant $$C(v)e^{-|w-u|^2/(2b)}$$ uniformly on compact time intervals.

For each fixed $t$, the Riemann sums defining the mild integral converge in $X$; their pointwise limits are the ordinary time integral because the gain is continuous in time by step 5.1. Choose a subsequence whose successive $X$-norm differences are summable; the Tonelli argument in step 1.1, using [F5], shows it converges almost everywhere to the $X$-class limit. Hence the pointwise time integral represents the mild right-hand side. It is continuous in velocity by the same compact-velocity Gaussian majorant in step 5.1. The left side has the smooth representative from step 3.2. Since these continuous representatives agree as $X$ classes, they agree everywhere; a continuous function vanishing almost everywhere vanishes everywhere. The ordinary fundamental theorem of calculus applied to the pointwise mild integral gives $\partial_t f_t(v)=\lambda(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)(v)-f_t(v))$. This proves the stated pointwise $C^1$ time regularity.

Use the velocity space $\mathbb R^3$ and Lebesgue measure $dv$ fixed by [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$ be a flat periodic spatial domain with periods $L_j>0$ (in metres in the physical interpretation), and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Let $F:\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\times I\to[0,\infty)$ be a measurable number density in position and velocity. At each $(r,t)$ where the integrals below are finite, assume $0<n(r,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F(r,v,t)\,dv<\infty$ and $\int |v|^3F(r,v,t)\,dv<\infty$. Fix a particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms, with number count dimensionless. In SI, $F$ has units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$.

Define $(x\otimes y)_{ij}=x_i y_j$, $\nabla_r\cdot T$ by $(\nabla_r\cdot T)_i=\sum_j\partial_{r_j}T_{ij}$, and $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. Define the number density $n$, mass density $\rho=mn$, mean velocity $u=n^{-1}\int vF\,dv$, kinetic covariance momentum flux

$$\Pi=m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)F\,dv,$$

internal kinetic-energy density $e=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\Pi$, and heat-flux vector

$$q=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)F\,dv.$$

Their SI units are respectively $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, pascals, $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. The tensor $\Pi$ is symmetric because each integrand $(v-u)\otimes(v-u)$ is symmetric, and it is positive semidefinite because for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, $\xi^{\mathsf T}\Pi\xi=m\int[\xi\cdot(v-u)]^2F\,dv\ge0$. It is the kinetic momentum-flux covariance; in the balance law below it enters with a plus sign, while a continuum tensile-stress variable defined from it would be $-\Pi$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Under this assumption Lebesgue measure is the completion of Borel measure ([[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]), and every Lebesgue-measurable integrable class has a Borel representative ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]]). Write $\lambda_3$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). Fix a positive reference speed $v_0>0$, and put $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$. Let $X$ be the real vector space of equivalence classes modulo $\lambda_3$-almost-everywhere equality of measurable functions $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ with

$$\|f\|_{1,w_0}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}w_0(v)|f(v)|\,d\lambda_3(v)<\infty.$$

Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$. For a Borel set $E\subseteq S^2$, define the normalized finite angular measure

$$\sigma(E):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf 1_E(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\phi\,d\theta.$$

For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$ and $n\in S^2$, define the postcollision velocities

$$v'=v-((v-w)\cdot n)n,\qquad w'=w+((v-w)\cdot n)n.$$

The collision-parameter measure is $d\mu=d\lambda_3(v)\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Its angular factor is finite and normalized; there is no singular angular weight. For $f,g\in X$, choose Borel representatives and define the gain $\mathcal G(f,g)$ by the almost-everywhere integral

$$\mathcal G(f,g)(v):=\int_{\mathbb R^3\times S^2} f(v')g(w')\,d\lambda_3(w)\,d\sigma(n).$$

The value on any exceptional null set is immaterial because the output is an equivalence class. The next item proves that this definition is independent of the representatives, maps $X\times X$ to $X$, and has the stated collision and moment identities.

Let $\mathcal G$, $v'$, $w'$, $X$, $w_0$, and $\mu$ be as in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. For $f,g\in X$, the gain is independent of the chosen Borel representatives, is bilinear, and satisfies

$$\|\mathcal G(f,g)\|_{1,w_0}\le 2\|f\|_{1,w_0}\|g\|_{1,w_0}.$$

For $f\ge0$ with finite mass $M=\int f\,dv$ and finite second moment, it also satisfies

$$\int\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M^2,\qquad \int v\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M\int vf\,dv,\qquad \int |v|^2\mathcal G(f,f)\,dv=M\int |v|^2f\,dv.$$

If $M=1$, set $A=f(v)f(w)$, $B=f(v')f(w')$, and $\Delta\varphi=\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w')$. For every real-valued measurable test $\varphi$ such that

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\varphi(v)|\mathcal G(f,f)(v)\,dv<\infty,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}|\varphi(v)|f(v)\,dv<\infty,\qquad \int |A\Delta\varphi|\,d\mu<\infty,\qquad \int |B\Delta\varphi|\,d\mu<\infty,$$

the following identity holds:

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\varphi(v)\bigl(\mathcal G(f,f)(v)-f(v)\bigr)\,dv=\frac14\int (B-A)\Delta\varphi\,d\mu.$$

For each fixed $n$, the map $(v,w)\mapsto(v',w')$ is a linear orthogonal involution, preserves $v+w$ and $|v|^2+|w|^2$, and has Jacobian determinant of absolute value one. The angular measure has full support, hence the product parameter measure $\mu$ has full support on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2$. Every pair $(v,w)$ and $(\widetilde v,\widetilde w)$ with the same momentum and squared-speed sum is related by one such reflection.

Fix $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and positive velocity-squared parameters $0<a<b$ (in a physical interpretation, both have units $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^2$). Let

$$K_{a,b}:=\{\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:\Sigma=\Sigma^{\mathsf T},\ aI\le\Sigma\le bI\},$$

where the matrix inequalities mean $a|z|^2\le z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z\le b|z|^2$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\Sigma\in K_{a,b}$, define the normalized Gaussian density

$$\gamma_{\Sigma,u}(v):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(v-u)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(v-u)\right).$$

Let $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ be the closure in the weighted space $X$ of all finite convex mixtures $\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\gamma_{\Sigma_j,u}$ with $\Sigma_j\in K_{a,b}$, $\alpha_j\ge0$, and $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$. Then:

1. Every $f\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ has a $C^\infty$ representative satisfying

$$ (2\pi b)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2a)}\le f(v)\le(2\pi a)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}.$$

For every multi-index $\alpha$, there is a finite constant $C_{\alpha,a,b}$, depending only on $\alpha,a,b$ and not on $f$, such that

$$|\partial^\alpha f(v)|\le C_{\alpha,a,b}(1+|v-u|^{|\alpha|})e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}.$$

The common derivative bounds imply that every sequence in $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ has a subsequence converging locally uniformly together with all velocity derivatives.

2. The gain in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]] maps this class into itself: $\mathcal G(f,g)\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Fix a reference speed $v_0>0$, a rate $\lambda>0$, and the weighted space $X=L^1(\mathbb R^3,w_0\,dv)$ with $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$, as in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. Let $f_0\in X$ be nonnegative with $\int f_0\,dv=1$, first moment $m_1=\int vf_0(v)\,dv$, and finite second moment $E_2=\int |v|^2f_0(v)\,dv$. Put

$$K:=\{g\in X:g\ge0\text{ a.e.},\ \int g\,dv=1,\ \int vg\,dv=m_1,\ \int|v|^2g\,dv=E_2\}.$$

Then there is a unique $f\in C([0,\infty),K)$, with continuity in the $X$ norm, satisfying

$$f_t=e^{-\lambda t}f_0+\lambda\int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}\mathcal G(f_s,f_s)\,ds,$$

where the time integral is the norm limit of Riemann sums in $X$. For all $t\ge0$, $f_t\ge0$, $\int f_t\,dv=1$, $\int vf_t\,dv=\int vf_0\,dv$, and $\int |v|^2f_t\,dv=E_2$. If $f_0>0$ almost everywhere, then $f_t\ge e^{-\lambda t}f_0$ almost everywhere.

If in addition $f_0\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ for some $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $0<a<b$, with $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ as in [[lem-csm-dk-gaussian-mixture-regularity]], then each $f_t$ has a positive $C^\infty$ velocity representative with the Gaussian bounds in that lemma; these representatives depend continuously on $t$ locally uniformly in velocity, are $C^1$ in $t$, and satisfy $\partial_t f_t=\lambda(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t)$ pointwise.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The bounds in [F3] give constants $c,C>0$ such that $c e^{-|v-u|^2/(2a)}\le f_t(v)\le C e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}$ for all $t,v$. The same upper Gaussian envelope holds for $\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)$ because [F3] preserves the mixture class; [F4] therefore bounds $|\partial_t f_t|$ by a constant times that envelope. The lower and upper bounds imply $|\log(v_0^3f_t(v))|\le C_1(1+|v-u|^2)$, after changing the finite constant $C_1$. Thus $f_t|\log(v_0^3f_t)|$ is integrable and the entropy derivative integrand has an integrable polynomial-Gaussian majorant on every compact time interval.

For each fixed $v$, the ordinary chain rule gives $\partial_t[f_t\log(v_0^3f_t)]=(1+\log(v_0^3f_t))\partial_t f_t$. The uniform majorant from step 1.1 also bounds the difference quotients by the scalar mean-value theorem. Dominated convergence [F5] therefore gives $H'(t)=\int(1+\log(v_0^3f_t))\partial_t f_t\,dv$. The mass of $f_t$ is constant by [F4], so $\int\partial_t f_t\,dv=0$ and the constant term drops. The integrand in the resulting formula is pointwise continuous in time by [F4] and has the same local integrable majorant from step 1.1; a second application of [F5] shows that $H'(t)$ is continuous.

Fix $t$ and write $\varphi(v)=\log(v_0^3f_t(v))$. The lower Gaussian bound makes $\varphi$ finite. The mean of $f_t$ is still $u$ by the moment conservation in [F4]. Also $A,B$ are bounded above by a constant times $e^{-(|v-u|^2+|w-u|^2)/(2b)}$, because the pair reflection fixes the common mean $(u,u)$ and preserves the sum of the two centered squared speeds. The Gaussian lower bound gives $|\log(A/B)|\le C_2(1+|v-u|^2+|w-u|^2)$. The same Gaussian upper bound holds for $\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)$ by [F3], so $\int|\varphi|f_t\,dv$ and $\int|\varphi|\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)\,dv$ are finite; the pair bound and polynomial bound on $\Delta\varphi$ give $\int|A\Delta\varphi|\,d\mu$ and $\int|B\Delta\varphi|\,d\mu$ finite. Thus the four conditions in [F2] hold. By [F2] and [F4],
$$H'(t)=\frac{\lambda}{4}\int(B-A)\Delta\varphi\,d\mu.$$
The reference factors cancel in the logarithm: $\Delta\varphi=\log(A/B)$. Hence $H'(t)=-\frac{\lambda}{4}\int(B-A)\log(B/A)\,d\mu$. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing, $(B-A)\log(B/A)\ge0$, proving the inequality.

If $H'(t)=0$, the continuous nonnegative integrand in step 3.1 vanishes $\mu$-almost everywhere. The product measure has full support by [F2]; a continuous function nonzero at one point is bounded away from zero on a nonempty open neighborhood of positive measure. Thus $A=B$ for every $(v,w,n)$. Conversely, this pointwise identity makes the production integral zero.

Put $g(v)=\log(v_0^3f_t(v))$, a $C^2$ function by [F3]. By the reflection coverage in [F2], for every center $c\in\mathbb R^3$ and every pair $r,r'\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|r|=|r'|$, the equality in step 4.1 gives $g(c+r)+g(c-r)=g(c+r')+g(c-r')$. For unit vectors $\theta,\eta$, take $r=s\theta$ and $r'=s\eta$. Taylor expansion at $c$ yields $g(c+s\theta)+g(c-s\theta)=2g(c)+s^2\theta^{\mathsf T}D^2g(c)\theta+o(s^2)$, with the same expression for $\eta$. Dividing by $s^2$ and taking $s\to0$ shows that the quadratic form of $D^2g(c)$ is constant on the unit sphere. Testing $e_i$ and $(e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2$ shows $D^2g(c)=\alpha(c)I$.

The off-diagonal Hessian entries vanish, so for each $i$, $\partial_i g$ depends only on its $i$th coordinate: changing any other coordinate leaves it fixed by the fundamental theorem of calculus along that coordinate segment. Write $\partial_i g(v)=G_i(v_i)$. The equal diagonal entries give $G_i'(v_i)=G_j'(v_j)$ for independently variable coordinates $v_i,v_j$; hence every such derivative is one constant $\alpha$. Integrating gives $g(v)=c_0+\beta\cdot v+\frac{\alpha}{2}|v|^2$.

Integrability of $f_t=e^{g}/v_0^3$ forces $\alpha<0$: if $\alpha>0$ the density grows in every sufficiently large direction, and if $\alpha=0$ an exponential of an affine function is nonintegrable on $\mathbb R^3$. Completing the square writes $f_t=C e^{-|v-\bar u|^2/(2s^2)}$ with $s^2=-1/\alpha>0$; Tonelli [F7] and the one-dimensional Gaussian integral [F6] give $\int e^{-|v-\bar u|^2/(2s^2)}dv=(2\pi s^2)^{3/2}$, so unit mass fixes the prefactor in the Statement. Conversely, for that Gaussian $\log f_t$ is a constant plus a linear function of $v$ and a scalar multiple of $|v|^2$; pair momentum and squared-speed conservation in [F2] give $A=B$ at every collision. Define $\operatorname{sgn}(x)=1,0,-1$ according as $x>0,x=0,x<0$, and set $\varphi=\operatorname{sgn}(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t)$. This test is bounded and measurable; since $\int A\,d\mu=\int B\,d\mu=1$, both sides of the weak identity are absolutely integrable. Applying [F2] gives $\|\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t\|_1=0$. The constant curve satisfies the mild equation because $e^{-\lambda t}+\lambda\int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}ds=1$, and uniqueness in [F4] makes this Gaussian stationary.

The density formula in [F3] factors for $aI$ and $bI$ into products of one-dimensional Gaussians; Tonelli [F7] and normalization [F6] give the first-coordinate marginal as their equal mixture. For a centered one-dimensional Gaussian of variance $s^2$, integration of the derivative of $x^{2k-1}e^{-x^2/(2s^2)}$ over $\mathbb R$ gives $\int x^{2k}e^{-x^2/(2s^2)}dx=(2k-1)s^2\int x^{2k-2}e^{-x^2/(2s^2)}dx$ for $k=1,2$; the boundary terms vanish by Gaussian decay. Thus the mixture's centered second moment is $(a+b)/2$ and its fourth moment is $3(a^2+b^2)/2$. A single Gaussian with the same second moment has fourth moment $3((a+b)/2)^2$, smaller by $3(a-b)^2/4>0$. Thus $f_0$ is not a single Gaussian. By the equality characterization in steps 4.1–7.1, the production at $t=0$ is strictly positive and $H'(0)<0$.

For this selected model, an identical classical particle is nonrelativistic in the explicit sense that its velocity is a vector $v\in\mathbb R^3$ and its kinetic energy is the Newtonian scalar $m|v|^2/2$. The mass $m>0$ is a primitive model parameter in kilograms. At time $t\ge0$, $f_t(v)$ is the probability density of velocity for a randomly selected particle with respect to Lebesgue measure $dv$; it is nonnegative, normalized by $\int f_t\,dv=1$, and therefore has SI units $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the completed Lebesgue measure used by the mathematical gain definition ([[def-countable-choice]]). A positive speed $v_0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is a reference scale used only to make the logarithm in the one-particle information functional dimensionless. The Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ is a primitive conversion factor when that functional is assigned entropy units.

Let $X$ and $w_0(v)=1+|v|^2/v_0^2$ be as defined in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. On the interior of a time interval $J\subseteq[0,\infty)$, an admissible classical trajectory is a map $t\mapsto f_t\in X$ continuously differentiable in the $X$ norm, with its derivative extending continuously to included endpoints by one-sided derivatives, and with $f_t\ge0$ almost everywhere and $\int f_t\,dv=1$ for every $t\in J$. Thus each admissible density has finite second velocity moment. The differential equation below is an equality in the normed space $X$, hence an equality of equivalence classes of functions of velocity. When a trajectory has a chosen representative $\widetilde f:J\times\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ that is continuously differentiable in $t$ and for which the gain integral is finite and continuous in $(t,v)$, the pointwise form $\partial_t\widetilde f(t,v)=\lambda(\mathcal G(\widetilde f_t,\widetilde f_t)(v)-\widetilde f(t,v))$ is required for every $(t,v)$ on that representative; this pointwise conclusion is not asserted for arbitrary representatives of an $X$ class.

Adopt the spatially homogeneous kinetic equation

$$\frac{d}{dt}f_t=\lambda\bigl(\mathcal G(f_t,f_t)-f_t\bigr)\quad\text{in }X,\qquad \lambda>0,$$

where $\mathcal G$ and the elastic reflection $(v,w)\mapsto(v',w')$ are exactly those of [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]] and [[lem-csm-dk-reflection-measure-and-gain-identities]]. The angular measure is the finite normalized area law specified there, and $\lambda$ is a prescribed rate in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, independent of relative speed; it is not a measured cross-section or a derived microscopic frequency. The selected incoming pair law is $f(v)f(w)\,dv\,dw$, and the gain uses the corresponding product $f(v')f(w')$ after reflection. This factorized independent-pair closure is adopted here; it is not deduced from reversible many-particle mechanics or from a molecular-chaos theorem. The mathematical existence and regularity claims are separate from this physical adoption.

The model's global mild evolution and its finite-energy hypotheses are mathematical claims treated separately from this physical adoption. This postulate makes no claim of a hard-sphere Boltzmann–Grad limit, generic gas applicability, spatially inhomogeneous PDE well-posedness, a hydrodynamic limit, or observed entropy increase.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $v_0>0$, $\lambda>0$, $u\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive velocity-squared parameters $0<a<b$. Let

$$f_0(v)=\tfrac12\gamma_{aI,u}(v)+\tfrac12\gamma_{bI,u}(v),$$

and let $f_t$ be its global solution from [[thm-csm-dk-global-cutoff-collision-evolution]]. Define the dimensionless one-particle functional

$$H(t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f_t(v)\log(v_0^3f_t(v))\,dv.$$

For every $t\ge0$, $H$ is finite and continuously differentiable, and with $A=f_t(v)f_t(w)$ and $B=f_t(v')f_t(w')$,

$$H'(t)=-\frac{\lambda}{4}\int_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times S^2}(B-A)\log(B/A)\,d\mu\le0.$$

The integrand is nonnegative. Equality holds at a time $t$ exactly when $f_t$ is a normalized isotropic Gaussian

$$f_t(v)=(2\pi s^2)^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{|v-\bar u|^2}{2s^2}\right)$$

for some $\bar u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $s>0$; every such Gaussian is stationary. The specified initial mixture is not a single Gaussian, so $H'(0)<0$.

The strict-production and equality clauses in [F1] transfer with the same positive factor $k_B$: the initial mixture has $S_B'(0)>0$, and at any later time $S_B'=0$ exactly when the velocity density has the normalized isotropic Gaussian form in the Statement. This is a deduction inside the adopted model and supplies no empirical premise.

Use the velocity space $\mathbb R^3$ and Lebesgue measure $dv$ fixed by [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]]. Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$ be a flat periodic spatial domain with periods $L_j>0$ (in metres in the physical interpretation), and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Let $F:\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\times I\to[0,\infty)$ be a measurable number density in position and velocity. At each $(r,t)$ where the integrals below are finite, assume $0<n(r,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F(r,v,t)\,dv<\infty$ and $\int |v|^3F(r,v,t)\,dv<\infty$. Fix a particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms, with number count dimensionless. In SI, $F$ has units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$.

Define $(x\otimes y)_{ij}=x_i y_j$, $\nabla_r\cdot T$ by $(\nabla_r\cdot T)_i=\sum_j\partial_{r_j}T_{ij}$, and $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. Define the number density $n$, mass density $\rho=mn$, mean velocity $u=n^{-1}\int vF\,dv$, kinetic covariance momentum flux

$$\Pi=m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)F\,dv,$$

internal kinetic-energy density $e=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\Pi$, and heat-flux vector

$$q=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)F\,dv.$$

Their SI units are respectively $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, pascals, $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. The tensor $\Pi$ is symmetric because each integrand $(v-u)\otimes(v-u)$ is symmetric, and it is positive semidefinite because for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, $\xi^{\mathsf T}\Pi\xi=m\int[\xi\cdot(v-u)]^2F\,dv\ge0$. It is the kinetic momentum-flux covariance; in the balance law below it enters with a plus sign, while a continuum tensile-stress variable defined from it would be $-\Pi$.

Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$ with $L_j>0$, let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be open, and fix $m>0$. Let $F:\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\times I\to[0,\infty)$ be $C^1$, with $n(r,t)=\int F(r,v,t)\,dv>0$. For every compact $J\subset I$, assume some $C_J<\infty$ and $N>6$ satisfy

$$|F|+|\partial_tF|+|\nabla_rF|+|\nabla_vF|\le C_J(1+|v|)^{-N}\qquad(t\in J).$$

Let $a:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ and independent of $v$. Let $Q(r,\cdot,t)$ be measurable with $\int(1+|v|^2)|Q|\,dv<\infty$ and

$$\int Q\,dv=0,\qquad \int vQ\,dv=0,\qquad \int |v|^2Q\,dv=0$$

at every $(r,t)$. Suppose pointwise that

$$\partial_tF+v\cdot\nabla_rF+a\cdot\nabla_vF=Q.$$

Define $\rho,u,\Pi,e,q$ as in [[def-csm-dk-kinetic-macroscopic-fields]]. Then the exact balances are

$$\partial_t\rho+\nabla_r\cdot(\rho u)=0,$$

$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\nabla_r\cdot(\rho u\otimes u+\Pi)=\rho a,$$

$$\partial_t\!\left(\frac12\rho|u|^2+e\right)+\nabla_r\cdot\!\left[\left(\frac12\rho|u|^2+e\right)u+\Pi u+q\right]=\rho a\cdot u,$$

and

$$\partial_te+\nabla_r\cdot(eu+q)+\Pi:\nabla_ru=0.$$

These identities are exact moment equations under the stated generic conservation assumptions on $Q$. They do not supply a constitutive relation for $\Pi$ or $q$, a closure, or a hydrodynamic limit.

In the SI physical interpretation, $t$ is measured in seconds, $a$ is acceleration in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and $Q$ has the units of $F$ per second.

Fix $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and positive velocity-squared parameters $0<a<b$ (in a physical interpretation, both have units $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^2$). Let

$$K_{a,b}:=\{\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:\Sigma=\Sigma^{\mathsf T},\ aI\le\Sigma\le bI\},$$

where the matrix inequalities mean $a|z|^2\le z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z\le b|z|^2$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\Sigma\in K_{a,b}$, define the normalized Gaussian density

$$\gamma_{\Sigma,u}(v):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(v-u)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(v-u)\right).$$

Let $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ be the closure in the weighted space $X$ of all finite convex mixtures $\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\gamma_{\Sigma_j,u}$ with $\Sigma_j\in K_{a,b}$, $\alpha_j\ge0$, and $\sum_j\alpha_j=1$. Then:

1. Every $f\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ has a $C^\infty$ representative satisfying

$$ (2\pi b)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2a)}\le f(v)\le(2\pi a)^{-3/2}e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}.$$

For every multi-index $\alpha$, there is a finite constant $C_{\alpha,a,b}$, depending only on $\alpha,a,b$ and not on $f$, such that

$$|\partial^\alpha f(v)|\le C_{\alpha,a,b}(1+|v-u|^{|\alpha|})e^{-|v-u|^2/(2b)}.$$

The common derivative bounds imply that every sequence in $\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ has a subsequence converging locally uniformly together with all velocity derivatives.

2. The gain in [[def-csm-dk-reflection-collision-gain]] maps this class into itself: $\mathcal G(f,g)\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal M_{u,a,b}$.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For $\Sigma_1=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and $\Sigma_2=\operatorname{diag}(\beta,\alpha,\gamma)$, define $F_j(r,v,t)=n_0\gamma_{\Sigma_j,0}(v)$ using [F3]. Each $F_j$ is smooth and rapidly decreasing in velocity, is constant in $r,t$, and solves the kinetic equation with zero acceleration and zero source. Gaussian normalization follows from [F4] by scaling each coordinate, and [F5] permits the product integration.

Each density has number density $n_0$ and mean $u=0$ by normalization and oddness. In one coordinate with variance $s^2$, differentiating $x\exp(-x^2/(2s^2))$ and integrating over $\mathbb R$ gives $\int x^2e^{-x^2/(2s^2)}dx=s^2\int e^{-x^2/(2s^2)}dx$; the boundary term vanishes because the Gaussian decays to zero. Thus both have $e=mn_0(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)/2$, while $\Pi_1=mn_0\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and $\Pi_2=mn_0\operatorname{diag}(\beta,\alpha,\gamma)$. Since $\alpha\ne\beta$, $\Pi_1\ne\Pi_2$, contradicting determination of $\Pi$ by $(n,u,e)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A **finite reversible stochastic rate model** consists of an integer $r\ge2$, the finite state set $E=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, real energy parameters $e_a\in\mathbb R$, an inverse-energy parameter $\beta>0$, and finite transition rates $w_{ab}\ge0$ for distinct $a,b\in E$. When physical units are assigned, $e_a$ is measured in joules, $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, and $w_{ab}$ in seconds$^{-1}$; this mathematical definition does not assert a physical realization. Define

$$Z:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta e_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta e_a}.$$

Then $Z$ is finite and positive, and $\pi$ is a strictly positive probability vector. Require $w_{ab}>0$ exactly when $w_{ba}>0$, require the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ to be connected, and impose detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$. Define the row generator $Q$ by $Q_{ab}=w_{ab}$ for $a\ne b$ and $Q_{aa}=-q_a$, where $q_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}$. Since $r\ge2$ and the graph is connected, every $q_a>0$. Thus $(Qf)_a=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$ for a column observable $f$, and a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pQ$.

For any observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$, write $\pi(f):=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_a$. For $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_ag_a$. Since $E$ is finite and every $\pi_a>0$, all real functions on $E$ belong to this finite-dimensional real inner-product space, denoted $L^2(E,\pi)$; equality in it is pointwise equality.

The associated jump-chain construction waits an exponential time of rate $q_a$ in state $a$ and then selects state $b\ne a$ with probability $w_{ab}/q_a$, using fresh independent random choices at successive jumps. Here an exponential time of rate $q>0$ has survival probability $\Pr(\tau>t)=e^{-qt}$ for $t\ge0$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ carry a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with future increments independent of the present sigma-algebra. Fix constants $\gamma>0$ and $\sigma>0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real random variable $X_0$ with finite second moment. A **continuous adapted solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation** on $[0,T]$ is a continuous adapted process $X$ satisfying, almost surely for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_s\,ds+\sigma B_t,$$
where the time integral is the ordinary Lebesgue integral along the continuous path. In differential notation this is $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, with the stochastic differential interpreted through the displayed integral equation.

The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. The Itô integral in the explicit representation is the square-integrable predictable-process integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Assume the filtered probability space, Brownian increment hypothesis, and initial data of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], including $\mathbb E X_0^2<\infty$ and future increments independent of $\mathcal F_0$. For $\gamma,\sigma>0$, on every finite time interval the process
$$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}\,dB_s$$
has a continuous adapted version, solves the stated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck integral equation, and is the unique continuous solution driven by the same $(X_0,B)$. Put $V=\sigma^2/(2\gamma)$. For $0\le s<t$, its transition law conditional on $\mathcal F_s$ is normal with mean $e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s$ and variance $V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. Consequently
$$\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+V(1-e^{-2\gamma t}).$$
From any such initial law, $X_t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,V)$. If $X_0\sim N(0,V)$ and is independent of future Brownian increments, the process is stationary Gaussian with covariance $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\gamma|\tau|}$, and its transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with the $N(0,V)$ density. Its transition density solves the Fokker–Planck equation for positive time. Under the convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$, the stationary spectrum and time-average bound are
$$S(\omega)=\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)},\qquad\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T X_t\,dt\right)\le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$
All these statements concern the specified linear stochastic model. An Einstein relation between $\sigma$ and a physical bath temperature would be an additional physical postulate.

Differentiation under this finite integral gives $g(0)=0$ and $g'(t)=-\gamma g(t)+u(t)/m$. Hence $V_t:=V^0_t+g(t)$ is continuous and satisfies [F1] with the added input term. If two forced solutions have the same initial state and Brownian path, their difference $z$ satisfies $z(t)=-\gamma\int_0^tz(s)\,ds$; with $H(t)=\int_0^t|z(s)|\,ds$, one has $H'(t)\le\gamma H(t)$ and $H(0)=0$, whence $H=0$ and $z=0$.

Since $V^0$ is centered and $g$ is deterministic, $\mathbb E V_t=g(t)$, giving the claimed mean. The parameter relation gives $\sigma^2/(2\gamma)=k_B\Theta/m=v_\Theta$, so [F2] gives stationarity, Gaussianity and the displayed covariance for the unforced solution.

For a uniform partition of $[0,t]$, the Riemann sums $S_n=(t/n)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}V_{jt/n}$ converge almost surely to $Y_t$ because $V$ has continuous paths. Each $S_n$ is centered Gaussian under $u=0$. By the covariance in step 2.1, its variance is a Riemann sum converging to $\int_0^t\int_0^t v_\Theta e^{-\gamma|s-r|}\,ds\,dr=2v_\Theta\int_0^t(t-a)e^{-\gamma a}\,da=2v_\Theta\left(\frac{t}{\gamma}-\frac{1-e^{-\gamma t}}{\gamma^2}\right)$. For each real $\xi$, almost-sure convergence and $|e^{i\xi S_n}|=1$ let bounded convergence give $\mathbb E e^{i\xi S_n}\to\mathbb E e^{i\xi Y_t}$. Therefore $Y_t$ has the stated Gaussian law and variance. Adding the deterministic $g$ to velocity changes only the mean of its integral, not this variance.

Dividing the variance formula in step 3.1 by $2t$ and letting $t\to\infty$ gives $D=v_\Theta/\gamma$. The centered displacement has Gaussian variance $2Dt-2v_\Theta(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma^2$; after division by $t$ this tends to $2D$, proving the distributional limit. For constant $u_0$, step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E V_t=u_0(1-e^{-\gamma t})/(m\gamma)$, so $\chi=1/(m\gamma)$ and $D=(k_B\Theta/m)/\gamma=\chi k_B\Theta$.

$$Z:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta e_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta e_a}.$$

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose $\Lambda>\max_aq_a$ and set $K=I+Q/\Lambda$. By [F1], $K$ is stochastic with positive diagonal, and for any distinct $a,b$ a positive-rate path of length $k$ gives $K^k_{ab}>0$; for $a=b$ take $k=0$. Connectedness forces all $r_a$ equal when the sum vanishes; normalization then gives $r_a=1$ and $p_t=\pi$.

Exponential convergence in [F2] gives $p_t\to\pi$ entrywise. The function $x\mapsto x\log(x/\pi_a)$ extends continuously to $x=0$ by value zero, so the finite sum $\mathcal D(p_t\Vert\pi)$ tends to zero. Combined with step 2.1 this proves all the relative-information claims.

For $f(a)=\bar f_i$ when $a\in C_i$, $(Qf)(a)=\sum_{j\ne i}q(a,C_j)(\bar f_j-\bar f_i)$ for $a\in C_i$. Every power $Q^n$ preserves $\mathcal H$, so the matrix series $P_t=e^{tQ}$ does too; for any block $C_j$, $P_t1_{C_j}$ is constant on each block and defines $\bar P_t=e^{t\bar Q}$.

The right side depends only on the current block. Use the finite state set, energies $e_a$, rates $w_{ab}$, Gibbs weights $\pi_a$, and row generator $Q$ defined in [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]]. Assign the state energies the physical meaning of coarse-state energies in joules. Use the primitive SI Boltzmann constant $k_B$ in joules per kelvin from [[post-csm-dk-selected-thermal-langevin-bath]], and set $\beta=(k_BT_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$ for the positive bath-temperature parameter $T_b$ in kelvins. Adopt the baseline transition rates $w_{ab}$ in seconds$^{-1}$ and the initial law $p_0=\pi$ for the equilibrium-response branch. These choices define a finite phenomenological thermal rate model; they do not say that a real material has these rates.

For a fixed state observable $B:E\to\mathbb R$ with units denoted $[B]$, a dimensionless control amplitude $\epsilon$, and a continuous field $h:[0,t_f]\to\mathbb R$ with units joules per $[B]$, adopt the controlled rates

$$w_{ab}^{\epsilon}(t)=w_{ab}\exp\!\left(\frac{\beta\epsilon h(t)}2(B_b-B_a)\right),\qquad a\ne b.$$

Their units remain seconds$^{-1}$ because the exponent is dimensionless. This is one explicit symmetric allocation of the field-dependent rate factor. For constant $h$, the rate ratio obeys

$$\frac{w_{ab}^{\epsilon}}{w_{ba}^{\epsilon}}=\exp\!\left(-\beta\left[(e_b-\epsilon hB_b)-(e_a-\epsilon hB_a)\right]\right),$$

so the Gibbs weights of the shifted energies $e_a-\epsilon hB_a$ satisfy detailed balance by direct multiplication. A rate ratio alone leaves state-pair prefactors undetermined; the symmetric splitting above is an additional modeling choice and is the specific perturbation analyzed in the consuming theorem. No experiment or empirical rate estimate is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A **finite reversible stochastic rate model** consists of an integer $r\ge2$, the finite state set $E=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, real energy parameters $e_a\in\mathbb R$, an inverse-energy parameter $\beta>0$, and finite transition rates $w_{ab}\ge0$ for distinct $a,b\in E$. When physical units are assigned, $e_a$ is measured in joules, $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, and $w_{ab}$ in seconds$^{-1}$; this mathematical definition does not assert a physical realization. Define

$$Z:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta e_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta e_a}.$$

Then $Z$ is finite and positive, and $\pi$ is a strictly positive probability vector. Require $w_{ab}>0$ exactly when $w_{ba}>0$, require the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ to be connected, and impose detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$. Define the row generator $Q$ by $Q_{ab}=w_{ab}$ for $a\ne b$ and $Q_{aa}=-q_a$, where $q_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}$. Since $r\ge2$ and the graph is connected, every $q_a>0$. Thus $(Qf)_a=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$ for a column observable $f$, and a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pQ$.

For any observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$, write $\pi(f):=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_a$. For $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_ag_a$. Since $E$ is finite and every $\pi_a>0$, all real functions on $E$ belong to this finite-dimensional real inner-product space, denoted $L^2(E,\pi)$; equality in it is pointwise equality.

The associated jump-chain construction waits an exponential time of rate $q_a$ in state $a$ and then selects state $b\ne a$ with probability $w_{ab}/q_a$, using fresh independent random choices at successive jumps. Here an exponential time of rate $q>0$ has survival probability $\Pr(\tau>t)=e^{-qt}$ for $t\ge0$. The Ionescu–Tulcea construction [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]] supplies the countable random sequence under the stated Choice assumption. The theorem on this page proves nonexplosion, identifies the transition semigroup, and establishes the positive reversible spectral gap. This is a finite mathematical rate model, not a derivation of rates from Hamiltonian mechanics.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], countable choice [[def-countable-choice]], and the model $E,\pi,w,Q$ of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]]. For any initial probability vector $p_0$, let $p_t=p_0P_t$, where $P_t=e^{tQ}$ is supplied by [[thm-csm-dk-nonexplosive-ctmc-and-gap]], and define the dimensionless relative information
$$\mathcal D(p_t\Vert\pi):=\sum_{a\in E}p_a(t)\log\frac{p_a(t)}{\pi_a},\qquad 0\log0:=0.$$
For every $t>0$, $p_a(t)>0$ for all states and
$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal D(p_t\Vert\pi)=-\frac12\sum_{a\in E}\sum_{b\ne a}\pi_aw_{ab}(r_b(t)-r_a(t))(\log r_b(t)-\log r_a(t))\le0,\qquad r_a(t):=\frac{p_a(t)}{\pi_a}.$$
At a positive time the derivative vanishes exactly when $p_t=\pi$, and $\mathcal D(p_t\Vert\pi)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

For every bounded observable $A:E\to\mathbb R$ and every initial law, the actual continuous-time average satisfies
$$\frac1T\int_0^T A(X_s)\,ds\longrightarrow\pi(A)\quad\text{almost surely as }T\to\infty.$$
Under stationary preparation, with $A_c=A-\pi(A)$ and spectral gap $\lambda_*$ from [[thm-csm-dk-nonexplosive-ctmc-and-gap]],
$$\operatorname{Var}_\pi\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T A(X_s)\,ds\right)\le\frac{2\|A_c\|_{L^2(\pi)}^2}{\lambda_*T}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], countable choice [[def-countable-choice]], and the rate model $E,\pi,w,Q$ of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]]. Let $X_t$ be the stationary two-sided chain of [[thm-csm-dk-nonexplosive-ctmc-and-gap]], with transition semigroup $P_t=e^{tQ}$. For any real observables $A,B:E\to\mathbb R$, write $A_c=A-\pi(A)$ and $B_c=B-\pi(B)$, and define
$$C_{BA}(t):=\langle B_c,P_tA_c\rangle_\pi,\qquad t\ge0.$$
Define $\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(A,B):=\pi(AB)-\pi(A)\pi(B)$, where $AB$ is pointwise multiplication.
For a continuous field $h:[0,t_f]\to\mathbb R$ and dimensionless $\epsilon$, prescribe rates
$$w^\epsilon_{ab}(t)=w_{ab}\exp\! \left(\frac{\beta\epsilon h(t)}2(B_b-B_a)\right),\quad a\ne b,$$
with negative row sums on the diagonal, and let $p^\epsilon(0)=\pi$ evolve by the resulting finite forward equation. The derivative of the observable mean at $\epsilon=0$ is
$$\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon}\sum_a p^\epsilon_a(t)A_a\right|_{\epsilon=0}=\int_0^t h(s)R_{AB}(t-s)\,ds,\qquad R_{AB}(u)=-\beta\,\frac{d}{du}C_{BA}(u).$$
For a constant field $h$, the perturbed Gibbs vector $\pi^\epsilon_a\propto\pi_a e^{\beta\epsilon hB_a}$ is stationary and its static susceptibility is $\beta h\,\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(A,B)$.

For any bounded vector observable $G:E\to\mathbb R^d$, set $G_c=G-\pi(G)$ and
$$C_{ij}(s):=\langle (G_c)_i,P_s(G_c)_j\rangle_\pi.$$
These correlations are absolutely integrable. The Green–Kubo covariance limit is
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(\int_0^T G(X_s)\,ds)}{2T}=D,\qquad D_{ij}=\int_0^\infty C_{ij}(s)\,ds=\langle (G_c)_i,(-Q)^{-1}(G_c)_j\rangle_\pi,$$
where $(-Q)^{-1}$ is the inverse on the mean-zero subspace and $D$ is positive semidefinite.

Since $E$ is finite and every $\pi_a>0$, all real functions on $E$ belong to this finite-dimensional real inner-product space, denoted $L^2(E,\pi)$; equality in it is pointwise equality.

The associated jump-chain construction waits an exponential time of rate $q_a$ in state $a$ and then selects state $b\ne a$ with probability $w_{ab}/q_a$, using fresh independent random choices at successive jumps. Here an exponential time of rate $q>0$ has survival probability $\Pr(\tau>t)=e^{-qt}$ for $t\ge0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and let $E,\pi,w,Q$ be the finite model data of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]], with $|E|=r\ge2$. For every initial probability row vector $p_0$, there exists a time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain $X_t$ on $E$, $t\ge0$, with no finite accumulation of jumps, transition matrix $P_t=e^{tQ}$, and law $p_t=p_0P_t$. The detailed-balance law $\pi$ is stationary. On the real inner-product space $L^2(E,\pi)$, $Q$ is self-adjoint and has an orthonormal eigenbasis $\phi_0=1,\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{r-1}$ with eigenvalues $0,-\lambda_1,\ldots,-\lambda_{r-1}$, where every $\lambda_j>0$. Thus the spectral gap $\lambda_*:=\min_j\lambda_j$ is positive and $P_t$ converges exponentially to projection onto constants.

Here a finite-state continuous-time Markov chain means a process with piecewise-constant paths whose conditional transition matrix over an interval of length $t$ is $P_t$, independent of the starting time. For initial law $\pi$, the chain has a two-sided stationary extension $X_t$, $t\in\mathbb R$, whose finite-dimensional laws at $t_1<\cdots<t_n$ are $\pi_{a_1}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}P_{t_{i+1}-t_i}(a_i,a_{i+1})$. Its sample paths are locally piecewise constant with finitely many jumps on every bounded time interval.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and the finite rate chain of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]] with transition semigroup supplied by [[thm-csm-dk-nonexplosive-ctmc-and-gap]]. Let $\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_k\}$ be a partition of $E$, meaning $k\ge1$, each $C_i$ is nonempty, the blocks are pairwise disjoint, and their union is $E$. For $a\in C_i$ and $j
e i$, set
$$q(a,C_j):=\sum_{b\in C_j}w_{ab}.$$
The projected process $ ar X_t=i$ when $X_t\in C_i$ has one time-homogeneous Markov generator valid for every initial microscopic probability law if and only if $q(a,C_j)$ is independent of $a\in C_i$ for every $i$ and $j
e i$. Under this condition, the coarse generator has off-diagonal entries $ ar q_{ij}=q(a,C_j)$ for any $a\in C_i$ and diagonal entries $ ar q_{ii}=-\sum_{j
e i} ar q_{ij}$. Its stationary weights $ ar\pi_i=\sum_{a\in C_i}\pi_a$ satisfy detailed balance.

derivations.claim: The positive-rate graph is the connected path $1\leftrightarrow2\leftrightarrow3$. Equal state energies give $\pi=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$, and every positive edge has equal forward and reverse rates, so $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$. Thus [F1] holds.

The exit rate from state $1$ to $C_2$ is $q(1,C_2)=w_{13}=0$, while from state $2$ it is $q(2,C_2)=w_{23}=1$. Starting with observed block $C_1$, [F2] gives $\Pr_1(\bar X_h=C_2)=O(h^2)$ and $\Pr_2(\bar X_h=C_2)=h+O(h^2)$, because a transition from $1$ to $3$ needs at least two jumps, while the direct $2\to3$ rate is $1$. The two preparations have the same initial block but different first-order block-transition probabilities.

Therefore no single transition law on $\{C_1,C_2\}$ can govern the projection for both microscopic preparations. Equivalently, the required block-rate constancy in [F3] fails. This refutes the universal all-preparations claim; it makes no assertion about special initial preparations.
