Here $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm defined in [[def-natural-logarithm]].

For each named finite classical model in this page, adopt the preparation explicitly stated in its theorem. In a canonical branch, take a measurable phase space with a specified reference measure $\nu$, a measurable Hamiltonian $H$, an inverse energy parameter $\beta>0$, and a finite positive partition function $Z=\int e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu$; the adopted probability measure is $dP=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu$. In a grand-canonical branch, take disjoint particle-number sectors with sector partition functions $Z_N$ and a dimensionless activity $z>0$ for which $\Xi=\sum_{N\ge0}z^N Z_N$ is finite; sector $N$ has probability weight $z^N Z_N/\Xi$. The spherical-shell and product preparations are separate explicitly specified probability laws in their consuming theorem statements. These are alternative model assumptions, not consequences of a Hamiltonian flow and not assertions that a laboratory system realizes them.

For a canonical model whose reference measure and Hamiltonian are fixed, adopt the statistical thermodynamic definitions $U=\mathbb E_P[H]$, $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, and $S=k_B(\log Z+\beta U)$ when the displayed integrals are finite. For a volume-dependent model, define the model pressure as $-\partial_V F$ only along the declared fixed-shape volume family. Here $k_B>0$ has SI units J K$^{-1}$, temperature $T>0$ has units K, and $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ has units J$^{-1}$. The fixed reference measure is part of the preparation; changing it changes the numerical partition function and entropy convention.

For the continuous particle examples, adopt the operational species and
counting convention of [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. Use
one fixed primitive action reference $a_0>0$ in J s, and write $h_0:=a_0$
where the consuming model uses the notation $h_0$. In a Cartesian physical
phase chart $dq\,dp$ has action dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$, so the
reference $dq\,dp/(\prod_sN_s!\,a_0^{dN})$ is dimensionless. Each model
retains its declared operational labels: an omitted factorial for resolved
harmonic coordinates is not replaced by a particle-exchange quotient. The
finite spin examples use their stated discrete counting measure, without a
continuous phase-cell factor. Choosing a numerical reference action, or
identifying it with Planck's constant, is an additional convention; no such
value or identification is imposed here. The Gaussian and gamma identities
in [[lem-csm-examples-gamma-gaussian-tools]] establish the mathematical
normalizations, not the physical preparation or empirical equilibration.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

A **real random variable** on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Its range $X(\Omega)$ is finite. The **distribution** or **law** of $X$ is the finite probability space on $X(\Omega)$ with
$$\mathbb P_X(x):=\mathbb P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}).$$
The weights $\mathbb P_X(x)$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because the fibres of $X$ form a finite partition of $\Omega$ ([[thm-finite-additivity-of-probability]]).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For a finite real random variable $X$, its **moment generating function** is the everywhere-defined function
$$M_X(t):=\mathbb E[\exp(tX)],\qquad t\in\mathbb R.$$
Finiteness of the outcome space makes this a finite sum, so no convergence hypothesis is needed.
This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

derivations.claim: The total weight is $\prod_{i=1}^n(p+(1-p))=1$, so the stipulated weights form a finite probability law. Summing over all coordinates except $i$ gives $P(X_i=1)=p$ and $P(X_i=0)=1-p$; the product factorization also gives independence. For $0\le k\le n$ put $c_{n,k}:=\#\{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:|S|=k\}$. The set of coordinates with value $1$ gives a bijection between outcomes with $K=k$ and such subsets, so $P(K=k)=c_{n,k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. By [F4] and [F12], $\mathbb E X_i=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\mathbb E[(X_i-p)^2]=p(1-p)$. For $i\ne j$, the product weights factor the finite sum, giving $\mathbb E[(X_i-p)(X_j-p)]=\mathbb E(X_i-p)\mathbb E(X_j-p)=0$. Expanding $K$ and $(K-np)^2$ therefore yields $\mathbb E K=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(K)=np(1-p)$.

The finite-sum definition [F5] and product weights give $$M_K(s)=\sum_{x\in\Omega_n}P_p(x)e^{s\sum_i x_i}=\prod_{i=1}^n\bigl((1-p)+pe^s\bigr)=(1-p+pe^s)^n.$$ This is a finite factorization, so no limiting interchange is involved.

On $0<a<1$, differentiating the displayed expression for $D$ with [F9] gives $D(p\Vert p)=0$, $\partial_aD(a\Vert p)|_{a=p}=0$, and $\partial_a^2D(a\Vert p)=1/[a(1-a)]\ge4$, since $a(1-a)\le1/4$. Let $G(a)=D(a\Vert p)-2(a-p)^2$. Then $G(p)=G'(p)=0$ and $G''\ge0$. For $a>p$, the mean value theorem applied first to $G'$ and then to $G$ gives $G'(a)\ge0$ and $G(a)\ge0$; for $a<p$, the same two applications give $G'(a)\le0$ and again $G(a)\ge0$. Thus $D(a\Vert p)\ge2(a-p)^2$ for interior $a$. At $a\downarrow0$, the only noncontinuous-looking term is $a\log a=-\log(1/a)/(1/a)$, which tends to zero by [F11]; at $a\uparrow1$ the analogous term is $(1-a)\log(1-a)$. The remaining factors are continuous, so the endpoint extensions preserve the inequality.

Fix $1\le k\le n-1$ and let $a=k/n$. For $0\le j\le n$ put $q_j=c_{n,j}a^j(1-a)^{n-j}$. These are the count probabilities under the finite product weights with parameter $a$; their sum is $1$ by factoring the total weight as $(a+(1-a))^n$. For each $0\le j<n$, count pairs $(S,T)$ with $S\subset T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $|S|=j$, and $|T|=j+1$. Choosing $S$ first gives $c_{n,j}(n-j)$ pairs, while choosing $T$ first gives $c_{n,j+1}(j+1)$; hence $c_{n,j+1}/c_{n,j}=(n-j)/(j+1)$. Therefore $$\frac{q_{j+1}}{q_j}=\frac{n-j}{j+1}\frac{a}{1-a}.$$ The factor $(n-j)/(j+1)$ decreases strictly with $j$, since $(n-j-1)(j+1)<(n-j)(j+2)$ for $j<n-1$. At $j=k-1$ the ratio is $(n-k+1)/(n-k)>1$, and at $j=k$ it is $k/(k+1)<1$. Thus the sequence increases through $q_k$ and decreases after it, so $q_k$ is the largest of its $n+1$ masses. Their sum is $1$, whence $1/(n+1)\le q_k\le1$.

Pointwise on $\Omega_n$, $\mathbf 1_{\{|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\}}\le (\overline X-p)^2/\varepsilon^2$. Summing this inequality with the finite weights and using step 1.1 gives the first probability bound.

Suppose first $p<a<1$ and put $s=\log\!\bigl(a(1-p)/(p(1-a))\bigr)>0$. For each named finite classical model in this page, adopt the preparation explicitly stated in its theorem. In a canonical branch, take a measurable phase space with a specified reference measure $\nu$, a measurable Hamiltonian $H$, an inverse energy parameter $\beta>0$, and a finite positive partition function $Z=\int e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu$; the adopted probability measure is $dP=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu$. In a grand-canonical branch, take disjoint particle-number sectors with sector partition functions $Z_N$ and a dimensionless activity $z>0$ for which $\Xi=\sum_{N\ge0}z^N Z_N$ is finite; sector $N$ has probability weight $z^N Z_N/\Xi$. The spherical-shell and product preparations are separate explicitly specified probability laws in their consuming theorem statements. These are alternative model assumptions, not consequences of a Hamiltonian flow and not assertions that a laboratory system realizes them.

For a canonical model whose reference measure and Hamiltonian are fixed, adopt the statistical thermodynamic definitions $U=\mathbb E_P[H]$, $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, and $S=k_B(\log Z+\beta U)$ when the displayed integrals are finite. For a volume-dependent model, define the model pressure as $-\partial_V F$ only along the declared fixed-shape volume family. Here $k_B>0$ has SI units J K$^{-1}$, temperature $T>0$ has units K, and $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ has units J$^{-1}$. The fixed reference measure is part of the preparation; changing it changes the numerical partition function and entropy convention.

For the continuous particle examples, adopt the operational species and
counting convention of [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. Use
one fixed primitive action reference $a_0>0$ in J s, and write $h_0:=a_0$
where the consuming model uses the notation $h_0$. In a Cartesian physical
phase chart $dq\,dp$ has action dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$, so the
reference $dq\,dp/(\prod_sN_s!\,a_0^{dN})$ is dimensionless. Each model

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The representing series must converge throughout this neighbourhood ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]], [[def-neighbourhood-r]]). The radius and coefficients may initially depend on $c$.
If a real power series centred at $c$ has radius $R>0$, then its sum is real analytic on $(c-R,c+R)$, interpreted as all of $\mathbb R$ when $R=+\infty$.

On open real domains, sums and products of real-analytic functions are real analytic. If $g$ is nonzero throughout the domain, then $f/g$ is real analytic. If $g:U\to V$ and $f:V\to\mathbb R$ are real analytic, then $f\circ g$ is real analytic on $U$.

Let $f$ be a real analytic map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, $f$ has a real analytic local inverse near $f(a)$. Let $P(x,y)$ be real analytic near $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^k$, $k\ge1$, with $P(a,b)=0$ and $D_yP(a,b)$ invertible. On sufficiently small neighborhoods its zero set is exactly the graph of a unique real analytic $y=g(x)$ with $g(a)=b$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A **real random variable** on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Its range $X(\Omega)$ is finite. The **distribution** or **law** of $X$ is the finite probability space on $X(\Omega)$ with
$$\mathbb P_X(x):=\mathbb P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}).$$
The weights $\mathbb P_X(x)$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because the fibres of $X$ form a finite partition of $\Omega$ ([[thm-finite-additivity-of-probability]]).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

derivations.claim: If this family were product-additive under the definition in the Statement, its fixed alphabet would have $|\Gamma|=|\Omega_1|=6$, forcing $|\Omega_2|=|\Gamma|^2=36$. But $|\Omega_2|=1+1+4^2=18$. Thus no such product decomposition exists. The three sector weights in the finite exponential tilt are $1$, $x$, and $4^Nx^2$, where $x=e^{-\beta N\epsilon}>0$; they sum to the displayed positive finite $Z_N(\beta)$, so division by $Z_N$ gives a finite probability law as in [F10]. For $\beta>0$, [A1] and [F1] identify this normalized counting weight with the adopted canonical branch; for $\beta\le0$ it remains only the stated algebraic expression.

The energies of $A_N$ and $C_N$ differ from $N\epsilon$ by exactly $N\epsilon$. The condition $\Delta<N\epsilon$ excludes both sectors from $\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$, while $B_N\subseteq\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$. Thus the shell is exactly the one-state set $B_N$ and its uniform counting probability assigns $B_N$ probability one.

Put $M_N=\max\{1,4^Nx^2\}$. If $x\le1$, then $x\le M_N$; if $x>1$, then $4^Nx^2\ge x$ since $N\ge1$. Hence $M_N\le Z_N\le3M_N$. By [F2]–[F3], $$\frac1N\log M_N=\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\}=\psi(\beta),$$ so taking logarithms in $M_N\le Z_N\le3M_N$ gives $0\le\psi_N-\psi\le(\log3)/N$, and consequently $\psi_N\to\psi$.

By [F4], $\exp$ is a power series converging for every real argument, so [F6] makes $\exp$ real analytic on $\mathbb R$. The affine polynomial $\beta\mapsto-\beta N\epsilon$ is real analytic, hence [F7] makes $\beta\mapsto e^{-\beta N\epsilon}$ real analytic as well.
Since $(1-2^Nx)^2\ge0$, $1+4^Nx^2\ge2^{N+1}x$. Therefore $Z_N=1+x+4^Nx^2\ge(2^{N+1}+1)x$, and division by $Z_N>0$ gives $P_{\beta,N}(B_N)\le(2^{N+1}+1)^{-1}$.

The equality $\log4=2\log2$ from [F3] gives the unique corner $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon>0$. On $0<\beta<\beta_c$, the larger branch is $\log4-2\beta\epsilon$ and has slope $-2\epsilon$; on $\beta>\beta_c$ the larger branch is $0$ and has slope $0$. The one-sided slopes differ.

The exponential is positive, so $Z_N=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}>0$ for every real $\beta$. Its expression as a sum and product of the analytic function in step 1.4 is real analytic by [F7].

By [F12], with [F11] identifying $H_N$ as a finite real random variable, the mean energy per member is $u_N(\beta)=\epsilon\bigl(x+2\cdot4^Nx^2\bigr)/Z_N$ for $\beta>0$. If $0<\beta<\beta_c$, divide numerator and denominator by the high-sector weight $4^Nx^2$: the low-to-high ratio is $e^{-N(\log4-2\beta\epsilon)}\to0$ and the middle-to-high ratio is $e^{N(\beta\epsilon-\log4)}\le2^{-N}\to0$, so $u_N(\beta)\to2\epsilon$. If $\beta>\beta_c$, both non-low weights $x=e^{-\beta N\epsilon}$ and $4^Nx^2=e^{N(\log4-2\beta\epsilon)}$ tend to zero, so $u_N(\beta)\to0$. At $\beta=\beta_c$, the three sector weights are $1$, $2^{-N}$, and $1$, so $u_N(\beta_c)=\epsilon(2^{-N}+2)/(2+2^{-N})\to\epsilon$. These limits give the stated piecewise $u$ and its unequal one-sided limits.

Fix $\beta_0\in\mathbb R$ and put $z_0=Z_N(\beta_0)>0$. By step 1.4, $\exp$ is real analytic; [F9] gives $\exp'(\log z_0)=z_0\ne0$, so [F8] gives a real-analytic local inverse near $z_0$. By the inverse definition [F2], that local inverse is $\log$ on this neighborhood, hence $\log$ is real analytic near $z_0$.

By [F5] the target property is real analyticity, and [F7] makes the composition $N^{-1}\log Z_N$ real analytic using steps 2.3 and 3.2. Hence every finite-$N$ function $\psi_N$ is real analytic. The derivative jump in step 2.2 belongs to the limiting function, not to a finite-$N$ singularity.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space: $\Omega$ is a finite set, each weight $w(\omega)$ is nonnegative, and $\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1$. Let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a real random variable and let $\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega)$. Its **variance** is

All sums are finite, so the definition requires no additional integrability or moment hypothesis.

By independence and [F5], the characteristic function is $$\varphi_{S_j}(k)=\prod_{i=1}^{n_j}\mathbb E(e^{ik\ell_j\Xi_i})=\cos(\ell_j k)^{n_j}.$$ Fix $k$. Continuity of cosine and $\cos0=1$ make $\cos u>0$ for all sufficiently small $|u|$. For such $u$, put $f(u)=\log\cos u$. By the chain rule, $f'(u)=-\sin u/\cos u$ and $f'(0)=0$. The same derivative rules make $f$ twice differentiable on a neighbourhood of zero, so [F15] gives $\log\cos u=-u^2/2+o(u^2)$. For $t>0$, $n_j\delta t_j\to t$ because $0\le t-n_j\delta t_j<\delta t_j$, and therefore $$n_j\log\cos(\ell_jk)=-\frac{n_j\ell_j^2k^2}{2}+n_j\,o(\ell_j^2)\longrightarrow-Dtk^2.$$ Indeed $n_j\ell_j^2=2D n_j\delta t_j\to2Dt$, so $n_j\ell_j^2$ is bounded, while $o(\ell_j^2)/\ell_j^2\to0$; their product proves the remainder tends to zero. Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, and give $\Omega_n=\{0,1\}^n$ the explicitly stipulated product probability whose singleton weights are
$$P_p(\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\})=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i};$$
for an event $A\subseteq\Omega_n$, $P_p(A)$ is the sum of these weights over $x\in A$.
Write $X_i(x)=x_i$, $K=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$, and $\overline X=K/n$. These variables and all probabilities are dimensionless. The product law is an adopted sampling model; independence is an assumption of that law, not an inference about any apparatus or equilibrium system.

For $a\in(0,1)$ define the Bernoulli relative-entropy rate
$$D(a\Vert p)=a\log\frac ap+(1-a)\log\frac{1-a}{1-p},$$
and set $D(0\Vert p)=-\log(1-p)$ and $D(1\Vert p)=-\log p$. Then
$$\mathbb E K=np,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=np(1-p),$$
and for every dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_p\bigl(|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le\frac{p(1-p)}{n\varepsilon^2},\qquad P_p\bigl(|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.$$
For $p<a<1$ and $0<a<p$, respectively,
$$P_p(K\ge na)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)},\qquad P_p(K\le na)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}.$$
For each integer $0\le k\le n$, putting $a=k/n$ gives the point-mass bounds
$$\frac1{n+1}e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}\le P_p(K=k)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}.$$
Consequently, for every sequence of integers $k_n\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with $k_n/n\to a\in(0,1)$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log P_p(K=k_n)=-D(a\Vert p).$$
All conclusions are conditional calculations for this finite product model and make no claim that physical outcomes are independent or that a small model probability is a logical contradiction.

citations.quote: **Finite coarse-entropy model.** Let $\Omega=\{0,1,2,3\}$ with uniform reference probability and permutation $\mathcal T(0)=1,\mathcal T(1)=2,\mathcal T(2)=3,\mathcal T(3)=0$. Start from $\pi_0=(1/2,1/2,0,0)$, and evolve by pushforward under $\mathcal T$. For the coarse partition $\{\{0,1\},\{2,3\}\}$, let $(r_1,r_2)$ be any probability vector with $r_i\ge0$ and $r_1+r_2=1$, and define its coarse Shannon entropy by $H_c(r_1,r_2)=-\sum_{i:r_i>0}r_i\log r_i$ in nats. Define fine entropy analogously for a probability vector on the four states, using $0\log0=0$. The coarse entropies at times $0,1,2$ are $0,\log2,0$, while the fine entropy is $\log2$ at all three times. Thus deterministic invertibility and preservation of the uniform reference measure do not imply monotone coarse entropy.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$
be a trace-class operator on $H$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $E$ be a
Hilbert basis of $H$, **supplied as data**
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]];
existence of such a basis is not asserted here). The **trace of $T$ relative to
$E$** is
$$\operatorname{tr}_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle,$$
the sum of the scalar family $(\langle Te,e\rangle)_{e\in E}$ in the
finite-subset-net sense of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

**The family is absolutely summable, uniformly in $E$.** Let
$T=\sum_js_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ be the singular-value series
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]],
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]) with
$(e_j)_{j\in J}$, $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ orthonormal and $\sum_js_j=\|T\|_1<+\infty$
([[def-trace-class-operator]]). For every $e\in H$ the series
$\langle Te,e\rangle=\sum_{j}s_j\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle$
converges absolutely, because the moduli are bounded by
$s_1\sum_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le s_1\|e\|^2$ by
Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[lem-finite-bessel-inequality]]). Consequently, for every finite
$F\subseteq E$, using the interchange of finite sums with the nonnegative
finite-subset supremum over $j$ and then finite Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel twice,
$$\sum_{e\in F}|\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{j}s_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|=\sum_{j}s_j\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le\sum_{j}s_j\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle f_j,e\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sum_{j}s_j=\|T\|_1 ,$$
because for each $j$ the two finite coefficient sums are bounded by
$\|e_j\|=1$ and $\|f_j\|=1$ (finite Bessel). Hence the finite subsums of
$|(\langle Te,e\rangle)|_{e\in E}$ are bounded by $\|T\|_1$, the family is
absolutely summable, and an absolutely summable family of scalars is summable in
ZF with $|\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\|T\|_1$
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]). This justifies the
notation $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ before any basis-independence statement.

**Choice accounting and status.** Only a supplied basis $E$ and the singular
values of $T$ are used; no Hilbert basis of $H$ is assumed to exist, and the
next theorem proves that $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ does not depend on the
supplied basis and equals the basis-free trace of $T$
([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], write $\rho=\sum_{j\in J}p_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$, where $J$ is finite or countable, $p_j>0$, the $u_j$ are orthonormal, and the sum converges in trace norm. The diagonal trace formula [F3] on this eigenfamily and the trace-norm continuity in [F4] give $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=\sum_jp_j=1$.

By [F5], $\rho A$ is trace class. The trace pairing theorem [F4], applied first to finite partial sums and then to their trace-norm limit, gives
$
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_{j\in J}p_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle.
$
The series is absolutely convergent because $\sum_jp_j|\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle|\leq\|A\|\sum_jp_j=\|A\|$. Thus $\omega_\rho$ is a well-defined bounded linear functional with $|\omega_\rho(A)|\leq\|A\|$.

For $A=I$, step 2.1 gives $\omega_\rho(I)=\sum_jp_j=1$. If $A\geq0$, every $\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle\geq0$, so step 2.1 gives $\omega_\rho(A)\geq0$. Therefore the trace pairing is a positive normalized bounded functional, as asserted.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).
If $C$ is at most countable and $m\in\mathbb N$, then the finite product $C^m=\prod_{i<m}C$ is at most countable.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

derivations.claim: Choose the ordered orthonormal basis of [F3]. In its coordinates $q(u)=\langle Mu,u\rangle$ is a real continuous quadratic polynomial, bounded on the unit sphere by the finite sum of the absolute matrix entries. By [F4], enumerate all rational-coordinate vectors $y_k\in(\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q)^D$, and put $v_k=y_k/\|y_k\|$ when $y_k\ne0$ and $v_k=e_1$ otherwise. For any unit $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$, coordinatewise rational approximation gives $\|y-x\|<\min(\varepsilon/2,1/2)$ for such a $y$. Then $y\ne0$ and the reverse triangle inequality gives $\|y/\|y\|-x\|\le|1-\|y\||+\|y-x\|\le2\|y-x\|<\varepsilon$. Thus the $v_k$ are dense on the sphere; they are normalizations of rational-coordinate vectors, not necessarily rational-coordinate vectors themselves. Let $m=\sup_{\|u\|=1}q(u)$. For each $n\ge1$ take the least index $k(n)$ with $q(v_{k(n)})>m-1/n$, which exists by continuity and density. This deterministic rule uses no countable choice. By [F1] the bounded sequence $v_{k(n)}$ has a convergent subsequence; its limit has norm one and attains $m$.

Let $u$ be a maximizing unit vector and $w\perp u$. Differentiating $q((u+tw)/\|u+tw\|)$ at $t=0$ for real $t$ gives $2\operatorname{Re}\langle Mw,u\rangle=0$. Replacing $w$ by $iw$ shows that the imaginary part also vanishes. Hermiticity gives $\langle Mu,w\rangle=0$ for every $w\perp u$, so $Mu=q(u)u$ with real eigenvalue. Moreover $u^\perp$ is invariant, since $\langle Mw,u\rangle=\langle w,Mu\rangle=0$. Induction on $D$, including the one-dimensional case, gives an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues.

For $M=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda$, define $f(M)=\sum_\lambda f(\lambda)P_\lambda$. The full eigenspaces and their orthogonal projections are intrinsic, so this definition is independent of the basis within each eigenspace. It supplies positive square roots, exponentials and logarithms on positive supports. Finite coordinate sums give $\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)$, hence invariance under unitary changes of orthonormal basis. Diagonalizing $\rho$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for every complex matrix $A$, and in particular $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho B^*B)=\sum_jp_j\|Bu_j\|^2\ge0$.

Put $a=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$, $b=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho Y^*Y)$ and $c=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*X)$. Step 3.1 gives $c+za+\overline z\,\overline a+|z|^2b\ge0$ for all complex $z$. If $b>0$, take $z=-\overline a/b$ to get $|a|^2\le bc$. If $b=0$, varying $z$ with arbitrarily large magnitude forces $a=0$, giving the same inequality. This proves the stated weighted Cauchy–Schwarz formula (whose form is conjugate-linear in $X$).

The density eigenvalues satisfy $p_j\ge0$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)=\sum_jp_j^2\le1$, with equality exactly when one eigenvalue is one and all others vanish. If a rank-one density $\rho=|u\rangle\langle u|$ is $t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $0<t<1$, then every $v\perp u$ has $0=t\langle\sigma v,v\rangle+(1-t)\langle\tau v,v\rangle$. Positivity and the square roots from step 3.1 give $\sigma v=\tau v=0$. Self-adjointness puts their ranges in $\mathbb C u$, and trace one gives $\sigma=\tau=\rho$. Conversely, two positive eigenvalues allow a sufficiently small opposite transfer of weight, yielding distinct densities $\rho_+,\rho_-$ with midpoint $\rho$. Thus precisely the rank-one densities are extreme.

Steps 1.1–4.1 include scalar dimension, zero matrix observables and nonfaithful densities; weighted Cauchy–Schwarz handles its zero quadratic-form branch. Thus the empty-input case is determined by the stated normalization or nonempty-domain restriction.
The eigenvalue and purity calculation in step 5.1 records zero eigenvalues with zero weight; trace one excludes the all-zero operator.
Step 5.1 proves trace-one rank-one states attain purity one and are extreme.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

For indices $a,b$ in the same finite index set, the **Kronecker delta** is

$$\delta_{ab}:=\begin{cases}1,&a=b,\\0,&a\ne b.\end{cases}$$

Let $i<m$ and $j<n$. The **matrix unit** $E_{ij}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is the
matrix whose $(r,s)$-entry is

$$(E_{ij})_{rs}:=\delta_{ri}\delta_{sj}.$$

Thus $E_{ij}$ has entry $1$ in position $(i,j)$ and entry $0$ everywhere else.
When a dimension is zero, no index of that dimension exists and there are no
matrix units of the corresponding shape.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

A **possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra** is a complex vector space $A$
equipped with an associative complex-bilinear multiplication
$A \times A \to A$ ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]] for the bilinearity convention)
and a norm under which $A$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]],
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]), such that the norm is
**submultiplicative**:

$$\|ab\| \le \|a\|\,\|b\| \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

No multiplicative identity is assumed, and no real-algebra or unital
convention is imported from elsewhere.

A **complex C\*-algebra** is a possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra $A$
equipped with an **involution** $A \to A$, $a \mapsto a^*$, which is
conjugate-linear ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) and
satisfies

$$(a^*)^* = a, \qquad (ab)^* = b^*a^*, \qquad \|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2 \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

The last identity is the **C\*-identity**. Two immediate consequences are worth
recording, and both are proved from the displayed axioms alone:

- **the involution is isometric**: $\|a^*\| = \|a\|$. Indeed $\|a\|^2 = \|a^*a\| \le \|a^*\|\,\|a\|$ gives $\|a\| \le \|a^*\|$ when $a \ne 0$, and applying this inequality to $a^*$ and using $(a^*)^* = a$ gives $\|a^*\| \le \|a\|$; the case $a = 0$ is trivial;
- **no norm-uniqueness assertion is part of this definition**: such a theorem
  needs additional hypotheses and proof, and does not follow merely by naming
  the displayed C\*-identity.

Let $A$ and $B$ be complex C\*-algebras. A **bounded star-homomorphism**, or
bounded $*$-homomorphism, is a bounded complex-linear map
$\varphi : A \to B$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) satisfying

$$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b), \qquad \varphi(a^*) = \varphi(a)^* \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

A star-homomorphism is **not** required to be unital, and it is not required
that a unit be present or preserved; when $A$ and $B$ both happen to be unital,
$\varphi$ is called **unital** if $\varphi(1_A) = 1_B$. The bounded nonunital
star-homomorphisms are the arrows of the locally compact duality theorem on this
page ([[thm-locally-compact-gelfand-duality]]), with properness imposed there
through [[def-approximate-unit-and-proper-c-star-morphism]].

Let $A$ be a complex C\*-algebra ([[def-c-star-algebra]]) and recall that
positivity in $A$ is the algebraic condition $a=b^*b$, without spectral
hypotheses ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-elements-of-a-c-star-algebra]]).
A linear functional $\omega:A\to\mathbb C$ is **positive** if
$$\omega(a^*a)\ge0\qquad\text{for every }a\in A,$$
and a **state** if in addition $\|\omega\|=1$, the norm being the operator
norm of the bounded linear functional on $A$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

derivations.claim: Choose an ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_D$. Its matrix units form an ordered basis of the complex endomorphism space, since $A=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}E_{ij}$ uniquely. The operator norm is a norm: its triangle inequality and homogeneity follow by applying the vector norm to $Av$ for unit $v$, and norm zero implies $Ae_j=0$ for all $j$. Matrix composition is associative and complex bilinear, and conjugate transpose is conjugate-linear, involutive and reverses products. By [F2] the norm is submultiplicative, complete, and satisfies $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$. Thus all axioms of [F4] hold. The identity is nonzero and has norm one because $D\ge1$. The C*-identity and submultiplicativity give $\|A\|^2\le\|A^*\|\|A\|$, and applying this also to $A^*$ gives $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$, including $A=0$.

For every vector $v$, $\langle(\|A\|^2I-A^*A)v,v\rangle=\|A\|^2\|v\|^2-\|Av\|^2\ge0$. This Hermitian matrix is positive semidefinite, so [F1] gives its positive square root. The same spectral calculus shows that matrix positivity is equivalent to being $B^*B$, agreeing with the algebraic positivity used in [F4].

Let $\omega$ be complex linear and positive, and define $\rho_{ij}:=\omega(E_{ji})$. Finite expansion gives $\omega(A)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\omega(E_{ij})=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$. For a column vector $z$, take $B=e_1z^*$; then $B^*B=zz^*$, so $z^*\rho z=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho zz^*)=\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ is real. Substitution of $z=e_i$, $e_i+e_j$, and $e_i+i e_j$ shows that the diagonal is real and $\rho_{ji}=\overline{\rho_{ij}}$; hence $\rho$ is Hermitian and its nonnegative quadratic forms make it positive semidefinite. Taking $A=I$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=\omega(I)$. The formula on the matrix units forces every entry of any representing matrix, proving uniqueness.

Conversely let $\rho\ge0$ and diagonalize it by [F1] as $\rho=\sum_j p_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$, $p_j\ge0$. Then $\omega_\rho(A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ is complex linear and $\omega_\rho(B^*B)=\sum_jp_j\|Bu_j\|^2\ge0$. For every complex $A$, vector Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\omega_\rho(A)|\le\sum_jp_j\|Au_j\|\le(\sum_jp_j)\|A\|$. Thus its functional norm is at most $\operatorname{Tr}\rho$, and evaluating at the norm-one identity gives the reverse inequality. This proves the norm formula, including $\rho=0$. The preceding reconstruction and this converse give the full bijection; imposing norm one is exactly imposing trace one by [F4], with no faithfulness requirement.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $K$ with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$. Then $Z_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta\lambda_j}$ is a finite sum of strictly positive real numbers, so $Z_\beta>0$. The operator $\rho_\beta$ is diagonal in this basis with positive entries $e^{-\beta\lambda_j}/Z_\beta$, whose sum is one; [F2] therefore makes it a density operator.

Keep the arbitrary ordered orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ and its given reference copy $(e'_j)$ from the Statement. Put $T=e^{-\beta K/2}$, so the defining vector is $\Psi_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1/2}\sum_j Te_j\otimes e'_j$. Orthogonality of the reference vectors gives $\|\Psi_\beta\|^2=Z_\beta^{-1}\sum_j\|Te_j\|^2=Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(T^*T)=1$, because [F1] gives $T^*=T$ and $T^*T=e^{-\beta K}$, and step 1.1 gives its trace $Z_\beta$. This uses the given basis, without requiring it to diagonalize $K$.

In those same given bases, $\Psi_\beta$ has coefficient $T_{j\ell}/\sqrt{Z_\beta}$ at $e_j\otimes e'_\ell$. Thus [F3] gives the reduced matrix entry $Z_\beta^{-1}\sum_\ell T_{j\ell}\overline{T_{k\ell}}=(TT^*)_{jk}/Z_\beta=(\rho_\beta)_{jk}$, since $TT^*=e^{-\beta K}$ by [F1]. Equivalently, the reduction is $Z_\beta^{-1}\sum_\ell|Te_\ell\rangle\langle Te_\ell|=TT^*/Z_\beta$. The intrinsic characterization [F4] identifies this coordinate result with the finite partial trace, so the system marginal equals $\rho_\beta$ for every allowed original basis and reference copy. No basis independence of the purification vector itself is asserted.

derivations.claim: On a compact interval of $s$, the matrix norms of $M(s)$ and $M'(s)$ are bounded. The exponential power series and its differentiated series converge uniformly there, since the derivative of $M^n$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}M^jM'M^{n-1-j}$, whose norm is at most $n\|M\|^{n-1}\|M'\|$. Expanding both exponentials in the integral, integrating term by term, and using $\int_0^1(1-u)^ju^k\,du=j!k!/(j+k+1)!$ (obtained by integration by parts) gives the same differentiated series. This proves the Duhamel formula.

Take the trace in step 1.1. Cyclicity from [F1] makes every integrand trace equal to $\operatorname{Tr}(e^M M')$. Since $Z=\operatorname{Tr}e^M>0$, the scalar chain rule gives $(\log Z)'=\operatorname{Tr}(e^MM')/Z=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho M')$. Setting $M'=X_a$ proves the first control derivative.

Differentiate $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X_b)$ in the $X_a$ direction using step 1.1 and the quotient rule. The result is $ \int_0^1\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{1-u}X_a\rho^uX_b)\,du -\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X_a)\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X_b). $ Because $\rho^{1-u}\rho^u=\rho$, cyclicity shows that replacing each $X$ by its centered version $\delta X$ changes the integral by exactly the subtracted product, giving the stated Hessian.

Diagonalize the positive definite $\rho$ with eigenvalues $p_i>0$. For Hermitian $X$, the quadratic form equals $\sum_{i,j}|\delta X_{ij}|^2L(p_i,p_j)$, where $L(a,b)=\int_0^1a^{1-u}b^u\,du>0$. Thus it is real and nonnegative. For $a\ne b$, direct integration gives $L(a,b)=(a-b)/(\log a-\log b)$, and $L(a,a)=a$. Substituting the matrix entries yields the upper bound by $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(\delta X)^2)$, the variance. If $X$ commutes with $\rho$, its entries between distinct eigenspaces vanish, so $L(p_i,p_i)=p_i$ on every remaining term and equality holds.

For $H(h)=H_0-hB$, put $M=-\beta H(h)$. Then $M'=\beta B$, so step 3.1 gives $\partial_h\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_hB)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}_{KM,\rho_h}(B,B)\geq0$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first argument. An operator $\rho\in\mathcal B(H)$ is a **density operator** when it is positive, trace class, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Here trace class means compact with summable singular values, and $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the basis-independent trace of a trace-class operator.

The **normal density state represented by $\rho$** is the functional on bounded operators
$
\omega_\rho(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(H).
$
In this page, “normal density state” means this specified trace-pairing representation; no equivalence with other definitions of normal functionals is assumed. The trace pairing is used only for bounded $A$. Unbounded observables are treated through their spectral probability measures in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Since $0<p_j\leq1$, every term $-p_j\log p_j$ is nonnegative, so the entropy sum is well defined in $[0,\infty]$; multiplying by the given $k_B>0$ preserves that range. It can diverge: let $c^{-1}=\sum_{n\geq2}(n(\log n)^2)^{-1}$ and $p_n=c/(n(\log n)^2)$. The normalizing series converges because the block $2^k\leq n<2^{k+1}$ contributes at most $1/(k\log2)^2$, and $\sum_k k^{-2}$ converges by grouping dyadic blocks. For sufficiently large $n$, $-p_n\log p_n\geq c/(2n\log n)$. Each dyadic block contributes at least $1/(4(k+1)\log2)$ to $\sum_n1/(n\log n)$, so that entropy series diverges.

For pairwise disjoint $C_k$, the PVM property gives $\|E_A(\bigcup_k C_k)u_j\|^2=\sum_k\|E_A(C_k)u_j\|^2$, since the projected vectors are orthogonal. The nonnegative double series may be summed in either order; therefore $\mu_\rho(\bigcup_kC_k)=\sum_k\mu_\rho(C_k)$. Completeness in [F3] gives a trace-class limit. Its trace is one by [F2] and trace continuity; its quadratic forms are nonnegative as limits of nonnegative quadratic forms. Thus the countable mixture is again a normal density state and the convergence is in trace norm.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first argument. An operator $\rho\in\mathcal B(H)$ is a **density operator** when it is positive, trace class, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Here trace class means compact with summable singular values, and $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the basis-independent trace of a trace-class operator.

The **normal density state represented by $\rho$** is the functional on bounded operators
$
\omega_\rho(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(H).
$
In this page, “normal density state” means this specified trace-pairing representation; no equivalence with other definitions of normal functionals is assumed. The trace pairing is used only for bounded $A$. Unbounded observables are treated through their spectral probability measures in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]].

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $\rho$ a trace-class normal density state. Its positive eigenvalues $p_j$ and orthonormal eigenvectors $u_j$ satisfy $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$ in trace norm and $\sum_jp_j=1$. For bounded $A$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$, with absolute value at most $\|A\|$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho)$. For a self-adjoint observable $A$ with spectral PVM $E_A$, the scalar law
$
\mu_\rho(B)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_A(B))=\sum_jp_j\|E_A(B)u_j\|^2
$
is a probability measure. Its first absolute moment defines a scalar mean, and its second moment defines a variance; these are not defined as arbitrary unbounded products $\rho A$. For a fixed positive Boltzmann scale $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), the von Neumann entropy is $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_jp_j\log p_j\in[0,\infty]$, and need not be finite. Countable convex mixtures of normal density states converge in trace norm.

derivations.claim: In finite dimension, support inclusion means every positive eigenvector of $\rho$ lies in the span of positive eigenvectors of $\sigma$. Each positive eigenvalue in either support is a positive real number, so its logarithm is finite; the zero eigenspaces contribute no $\rho$-weight under the stated support inclusion. Therefore both trace terms in the finite formula are finite real sums, and the formula has no undefined product $0\log0$. The Axiom of Choice is present only through the explicitly retained spectral-calculus supplier closure.

In the trace-class case, every summand in $C(\rho,\sigma)$ is nonnegative because $0<s_j\leq1$. The sum is therefore defined unambiguously as the supremum of its finite partial sums in $[0,\infty]$. Grouping equal eigenvalues replaces the basis coefficients by traces of products of the corresponding spectral projections, so the resulting value is independent of basis choices within eigenspaces. The definition distinguishes finite subtraction from the undefined case of two infinite terms.
