derivations.claim: On a zero-dimensional Hilbert space the unique endomorphism is $I=0$, and its exponential is $I$, so the unitary and group identities hold directly. There is no trace-one density there; the remaining density and normalized-Gibbs clauses have no instance. On a nonzero space, diagonalize $H$ by [F1], with eigenvalues $E_j$. Then $U(t)$ has eigenvalues $e^{-itE_j/\hbar}$ of modulus one, so it is unitary. In the same eigenbasis, multiplying scalar exponentials gives $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$. The finite exponential series differentiates termwise and yields $i\hbar U'(t)=HU(t)$.

In the eigenbasis of $H$, every matrix entry of $e^{izH/\hbar}Be^{-izH/\hbar}$ is a constant times $e^{iz(E_j-E_k)/\hbar}$, an entire scalar function. Thus $F_{A,B}$ is entire. For $z=t+iy$, $0\leq y\leq\beta\hbar$, the real-time factors are unitary and the imaginary-time factors have norm at most $e^{\beta\|H\|}$ each. The trace against a density is bounded by operator norm, so $|F_{A,B}(z)|\leq\|A\|\|B\|e^{2\beta\|H\|}$ throughout the closed strip.

Cyclicity [F1] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(U\rho U^*A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho U^*AU)$. Unitary conjugation preserves positivity, trace, and eigenvalues; therefore it preserves the finite entropy $-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$. Since $\sigma_\beta$ is a function of $H$, it commutes with $U(t)$, hence is stationary.

At $z=t+i\beta\hbar$, $\alpha_z(B)=e^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)e^{\beta H}$. Hence $ F_{A,B}(t+i\beta\hbar)=Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}A e^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)e^{\beta H}) =Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(A e^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)) =\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta\alpha_t(B)A), $ where the first equality uses the definition, the second uses finite trace cyclicity, and the third uses it again. The strip boundary identity follows.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathfrak H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension
$d\ge1$ with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $H:\mathfrak H\to\mathfrak H$ be a self-adjoint
linear operator with real eigenvalues $E_1,\dots,E_d$ (repeated according to
multiplicity) and orthonormal eigenbasis $(v_1,\dots,v_d)$, and let $\beta>0$.
Write
$$Z:=\sum_{j=1}^d e^{-\beta E_j}\in(0,\infty),\qquad \rho_\beta:=\frac1Z\sum_{j=1}^d e^{-\beta E_j}T_{v_j,v_j},$$
where $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). Let
$\mathcal D$ be the set of density operators on $\mathfrak H$, i.e. positive
self-adjoint trace-class operators $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]), and
for $\rho\in\mathcal D$ with eigenvalues $w_1,\dots,w_d\ge0$ (counted with
multiplicity and in any order) define the entropy
$$s(\rho):=-\sum_{i:\,w_i>0}w_i\log w_i\in[0,\log d]$$
([[def-natural-logarithm]]). Then:

(a) $\rho_\beta\in\mathcal D$, $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)=\frac1Z\sum_je^{-\beta E_j}E_j$,
and
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho_\beta)=-\beta^{-1}\log Z ;$$

(b) for every $\rho\in\mathcal D$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho)\ \ge\ -\beta^{-1}\log Z ;$$

(c) for every $\rho\in\mathcal D$, $s(\rho)\le\log d$, with $s(\rho)=\log d$ if
and only if $\rho=d^{-1}\,\mathrm{id}$; when $H=0$ one has $Z=d$,
$\rho_\beta=d^{-1}\mathrm{id}$ and the bound in (b) is attained there.

The combination $\operatorname{tr}(\rho H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho)$ is a purely
mathematical functional of $(\rho,H,\beta)$; identifying $\beta$ with an
inverse physical temperature and $\rho_\beta$ with a thermal equilibrium state
are additional physical assumptions not asserted here.

derivations.claim: By [F1], write $H=\sum_jE_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ with real $E_j$. Then $e^{-\beta H}$ has strictly positive eigenvalues $e^{-\beta E_j}$, so $Z=\sum_je^{-\beta E_j}>0$, $\sigma$ is faithful, and $\log\sigma=-\beta H-(\log Z)I$.

By [F2] and step 1.1, $ D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)+\beta\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H)+\log Z =\beta\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H)-TS(\rho)-F_\beta\bigr). $ All terms are finite because the dimension is finite and $\sigma$ is faithful.
Apply [L1] with $s(\rho)=S(\rho)/k_B$ and $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$. It gives the displayed free-energy inequality for every density, and step 2.1 identifies its gap with $\beta^{-1}D(\rho\|\sigma)$.

For the equality case, diagonalize $\rho=\sum_iw_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ on its support and let $q_j=e^{-\beta E_j}/Z>0$ be the eigenvalues of $\sigma$ in the $v_j$ basis. Set $r_i=\sum_j|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2q_j>0$. The overlap weights in each row sum to one, so concavity of $\log$ gives $\sum_j|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\log q_j\leq\log r_i$, with equality only when all $q_j$ having positive overlap in that row are equal. Also $-\log(r_i/w_i)\geq1-r_i/w_i$, with equality only at $r_i=w_i$. Consequently $ D(\rho\|\sigma)\geq\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i\log(w_i/r_i) \geq\sum_{i:w_i>0}(w_i-r_i)\geq0, $ because $\sum_iw_i=1$ and $\sum_{i:w_i>0}r_i=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma P_{\operatorname{supp}\rho})\leq1$. If $D=0$, all inequalities are equalities. Strictness of the scalar inequality gives $r_i=w_i$; equality in strict concavity of $\log$ means $u_i$ lies in one eigenspace of $\sigma$, so $\sigma u_i=w_i u_i$. The sum of the $r_i$ is then one, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma(I-P_{\operatorname{supp}\rho}))=0$. In an orthonormal basis of that finite complement every diagonal quadratic form of $\sigma$ is nonnegative and their sum is zero, so each vanishes. Its positive square root therefore annihilates that basis and the entire complement. For every $v$ in that orthogonal complement, this gives $\|\sigma^{1/2}v\|^2=\langle\sigma v,v\rangle=0$, hence $\sigma v=0$; therefore $\sigma$ has no support outside $\operatorname{supp}\rho$. Together with $\sigma u_i=w_i u_i$, this proves $\rho=\sigma$. Conversely $\rho=\sigma$ gives $D=0$.

For $\rho=\sigma$, step 1.1 gives $S(\sigma)=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\log\sigma)=k_B(\log Z+\beta\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H))$. Substitution of $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$ and $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ gives $F_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H)-TS(\sigma)$, as stated.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement requires nonzero finite H and finite beta>0, so its positive finite partition function cannot be an empty trace. The equality proof permits a rank-deficient competitor but forces equality to the faithful Gibbs state. Thus the empty-input case is determined by the stated normalization or nonempty-domain restriction.
For H=0, step 1.1 gives sigma=I/d and step 3.2 proves equality only at sigma.
When d=1 there is only one density matrix; steps 3.2 and 4.1 give the equality case and energy-entropy identity.
Step 1.1 uses the full spectral basis and step 3.2 uses overlap weights, so degeneracy is retained.
The Statement assumes beta>0 and finite d; zero-temperature and infinite-dimensional limits are not included.
The Statement is finite-dimensional and the proof uses only finite spectral bases; no choice axiom is needed for this calculation.
Step 3.2 proves D=0 forces rho=sigma, hence equality in the variational inequality.
For rho=sigma, step 4.1 gives equality in the energy-entropy formula.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathcal H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\geq1$, $K=K^*$ an endomorphism, and $\beta>0$. Define $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta K})$ and $\rho_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta K}$. Given an ordered orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j=1}^d$ and its identified copy in a reference space $\mathcal H_R$, define
$
|\Phi_d\rangle=d^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^d e_j\otimes e_j,\qquad
|\Psi_\beta\rangle=\sqrt{d/Z_\beta}(e^{-\beta K/2}\otimes I_R)|\Phi_d\rangle.
$
Then $Z_\beta>0$, $\rho_\beta$ is a density operator, $|\Psi_\beta\rangle$ is a unit vector, and $\operatorname{Tr}_R(|\Psi_\beta\rangle\langle\Psi_\beta|)=\rho_\beta$. If $K$ is interpreted as energy, the product $\beta K$ is dimensionless.

**Input:** a nonzero finite-dimensional Hilbert space of dimension $d$, a Hermitian Hamiltonian matrix $K$, an inverse-energy parameter $\beta>0$ such that $H=\beta K$ is dimensionless, the ordered reference preparation $|\Phi_d\rangle$ from [[def-qsm-finite-gibbs-purification]], an output vector-error tolerance $\varepsilon_{\rm out}>0$, and a rational failure target $0<\rho<1$. The input contract must additionally supply every sparse-oracle, block-encoding, controlled-evolution, inverse, norm-bound, energy-shift, coefficient-generation, precision, reference-preparation, and cost object required by the published procedure [[alg-qa-30-sdp-gibbs-purification]]. No matrix exponential, trace, exact spectral minimum, or gate is free input.

**Procedure:** invoke the normalized-output branch of [[alg-qa-30-sdp-gibbs-purification]] on $K$ with coefficient $\eta=\beta$, the stated error, failure target, and complete access/cost certificates. Retain its frozen energy shift and all declared finite subroutines. Measure only its specified good/bad flag. On a good branch return the normalized system-reference vector; on a cap failure return the explicit output FAIL. If the certified shift event fails, do not assert the Gibbs approximation guarantee; any overall failure probability includes the supplied shift-confidence budget.

**Output:** either FAIL, or a normalized vector-register state in the successful branch, with the error and success guarantees supplied by [[thm-qa-30-sdp-gibbs-state-error-cost]]. An identity energy shift changes neither the normalized Gibbs density nor its canonical purification, since $e^{-(\beta K+cI)}=e^{-c}e^{-\beta K}$ and the trace is multiplied by the same scalar. This is a mathematical state-preparation procedure under the stated finite access model; it is not a physical bath or thermalization process.

Let the ideal unnormalized Gibbs amplitude on the reference state be $|v\rangle=((e^{-G/2}/B)\otimes I)|\Phi_d\rangle$ with ideal flag probability $p_G=\|v\|^2>0$, where $B>0$ is the declared block-encoding normalization. Suppose the implemented flagged preparation has good-branch vector $|\widetilde v\rangle$ with $\|\widetilde v-v\|\le\zeta$, and assume $0\le\zeta\le\sqrt{p_G}/2$. Then its normalized conditional state is within $2\zeta/\sqrt{p_G}$ in vector norm of the ideal Gibbs purification. Its actual success probability is at least $p_G/4$. There exists a positive rational $q$ with $p_G/8<q<p_G/4$. CapAmplify supplied any certified such $q$ returns that implemented good ray with probability at least $2/3$ using $O(p_G^{-1/2})$ preparation, inverse, and reflection calls. The floor certificate is a supplied input to this call; obtaining and verifying it are separately charged and are not an exact trace oracle. The total cost also includes QSVT/block access, phase compilation, reference preparation, and all gate/precision costs.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **trace distance** is
$$D(\rho,\sigma):=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The factor $1/2$ is part of this state-distance convention. The diamond norm below is an unhalved norm on maps.

For every linear map $A:H\to K$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces,

$$\|A\|_1=\operatorname{tr}_H\!\left(\sqrt{A^*A}\right).$$

Here $A^*A$ and its non-negative square root are endomorphisms of the domain
$H$; the trace is taken on $H$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a
non-negative operator $R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$,
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)$ is non-negative and

$$\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R))=\operatorname{tr}(R).$$

Here $\operatorname{End}(H)$ is the set of linear maps $H\to H$ as in
[[def-qc-partial-trace]], $I_H$ denotes the identity map $x\mapsto x$, and both
conclusions include zero-dimensional factors.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: Multiply $|\widetilde\Psi_\beta\rangle$ by a phase so $s=\langle\Psi_\beta,\widetilde\Psi_\beta\rangle$ is real and $0\leq s\leq1$. If $s=1$, their rank-one projections agree. Otherwise write $\widetilde\Psi_\beta=s\Psi_\beta+\sqrt{1-s^2}\,w$, with $w\perp\Psi_\beta$ and $\|w\|=1$. On the span of $\Psi_\beta,w$, the difference of their rank-one projections has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1-s^2&-s\sqrt{1-s^2}\\-s\sqrt{1-s^2}&-(1-s^2)\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues are $\pm\sqrt{1-s^2}$; it vanishes on the orthogonal complement. By [F4] and [F5], the pure-state trace distance is $\sqrt{1-s^2}$. Since $\|\Psi_\beta-\widetilde\Psi_\beta\|^2=2(1-s)$ and $1-s^2\leq2(1-s)$, this distance is at most the vector distance.

Let $X$ be any finite Hermitian trace-zero matrix and write its positive and negative parts $X=X_+-X_-$. Their traces agree and equal $\|X\|_1/2$. For every effect $0\leq E\leq I$, cyclicity and square roots from [F8] give $0\leq\operatorname{Tr}(EX_\pm)=\operatorname{Tr}(X_\pm^{1/2}EX_\pm^{1/2})\leq\operatorname{Tr}X_\pm$, hence $|\operatorname{Tr}(EX)|\leq\|X\|_1/2$. Put $Y=\operatorname{Tr}_R X$. By setting $A=I$ in [F6], $\operatorname{Tr}Y=\operatorname{Tr}X=0$. Its positive spectral projection $E_Y$ is an effect and satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}(E_Y Y)=\|Y\|_1/2$ by [F5]. Again by [F6], $\operatorname{Tr}(E_Y Y)=\operatorname{Tr}((E_Y\otimes I_R)X)$; diagonalizing $E_Y$ shows $E_Y\otimes I_R$ is an effect. Applying the preceding bound to this effect yields $\|Y\|_1\leq\|X\|_1$.

Apply step 1.1 to the normalized output on the successful branch [F2] and ideal vector from [F3]. Their pure-state trace distance is at most $\varepsilon_{\rm out}$. Set $X=|\widetilde\Psi_\beta\rangle\langle\widetilde\Psi_\beta|-|\Psi_\beta\rangle\langle\Psi_\beta|$, which is Hermitian with trace zero. Step 1.2 contracts its trace norm under $\operatorname{Tr}_R$. By [F1], the ideal system marginal is $\rho_\beta$; [F7] ensures both marginals are density operators, so [F4] applies and gives the claimed bound. The conclusion remains conditional on the successful branch and shift event.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement requires a nonzero finite input register and normalized preparation; the partial trace and circuit error estimates include zero error and one-dimensional factors without asserting converse bounds. Thus the empty-input case is determined by the stated normalization or nonempty-domain restriction.
If the vector error is zero, step 1.1 gives identical pure projections and step 2.1 leaves zero marginal error.
The trace-distance bound in step 1.1 remains valid at maximal overlap s=1.
The Statement covers arbitrary finite matrices, and step 1.2 uses spectral positive and negative parts without a nondegeneracy assumption.
The guarantee is conditional on the successful branch and shift event; failure branches are excluded by the Statement.
The Statement uses finite registers and finite-dimensional matrix spectral calculus, so no choice axiom is needed.

The public assertion supplies the stated forward conclusion; it does not infer its hypotheses from the conclusion.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $\rho$ a trace-class normal density state. Its positive eigenvalues $p_j$ and orthonormal eigenvectors $u_j$ satisfy $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$ in trace norm and $\sum_jp_j=1$. For bounded $A$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$, with absolute value at most $\|A\|$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho)$. For a self-adjoint observable $A$ with spectral PVM $E_A$, the scalar law
$
\mu_\rho(B)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_A(B))=\sum_jp_j\|E_A(B)u_j\|^2
$
is a probability measure. Its first absolute moment defines a scalar mean, and its second moment defines a variance; these are not defined as arbitrary unbounded products $\rho A$. For a fixed positive Boltzmann scale $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), the von Neumann entropy is $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_jp_j\log p_j\in[0,\infty]$, and need not be finite. Countable convex mixtures of normal density states converge in trace norm.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

derivations.claim: Write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Put $w_{ij}=|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2$, so $\sum_jw_{ij}=1$ because $u_i\in\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, and $\sum_iw_{ij}\leq1$. Define $q_i=\langle\sigma u_i,u_i\rangle=\sum_jw_{ij}s_j>0$; then $Q=\sum_iq_i=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma P_{\operatorname{supp}\rho})\leq1$.

For $q>0$ and $x>0$, $\log x\leq\log q+(x-q)/q$, because $t-1-\log t\geq0$ for $t=x/q$, as its derivative $1-1/t$ has its unique minimum at $t=1$. Applying this tangent inequality to $s_j$ with weights $w_{ij}$ gives $\sum_jw_{ij}(-\log s_j)\geq-\log q_i$. Since $C<\infty$, $T:=\sum_i p_i(-\log q_i)\leq C<\infty$.

For a finite initial set $1\leq i\leq N$, let $a_N=\sum_{i\leq N}p_i$ and $b_N=\sum_{i\leq N}q_i$. Applying the finite-density case of [L1] to $(p_i/a_N)$ and $(q_i/b_N)$ gives $ \sum_{i\leq N}-p_i\log p_i\leq\sum_{i\leq N}p_i(-\log q_i)-a_N\log a_N+a_N\log b_N \leq T-a_N\log a_N, $ because $0<b_N\leq1$. As $N\to\infty$, $a_N\to1$ and $-a_N\log a_N\to0$. The nonnegative partial entropy sums are therefore bounded, so $S(\rho)/k_B=\sum_i-p_i\log p_i<\infty$. This also makes both scalar logarithm series below absolutely defined.

Normalize $q_i$ by $Q$, so $q_i'=q_i/Q$ is a probability distribution with $q_i'>0$. Apply [L1] to $p_i$ and $q_i'$: $\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/q_i')\geq0$, hence $\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/q_i)\geq-\log Q\geq0$. Combining this with the nonnegative Jensen gaps from step 2.1 gives $C-S(\rho)/k_B\geq0$.

Since steps 3.1–4.1 prove that $S(\rho)$ and $T$ are finite, and $q_i'=q_i/Q$, direct logarithm algebra gives $ D(\rho\|\sigma)=C-\frac{S(\rho)}{k_B} =(C-T)+\sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{q_i'}-\log Q. $ The first term is the sum of the nonnegative Jensen gaps from step 2.1, the middle term is the countable relative entropy from [L1], and the last term is nonnegative because $Q\leq1$. If $D(\rho\|\sigma)=0$, all three vanish. Thus $Q=1$; equality in [L1] gives $p_i=q_i'=q_i$ for every $i$. The Jensen gap is $\sum_i p_i\bigl[\sum_jw_{ij}(-\log s_j)+\log q_i\bigr]$; each bracket is nonnegative by step 2.1 and each $p_i>0$, so a zero sum forces equality in every bracket. Strictness of $\log x\leq\log q_i+(x-q_i)/q_i$ then forces $s_j=q_i$ whenever $w_{ij}>0$, and the spectral expansion gives $\sigma u_i=q_i u_i=p_i u_i$. The equality $Q=1$ says $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma(I-P_{\operatorname{supp}\rho}))=0$. Put $P=P_{\operatorname{supp}\rho}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\rho,\sigma$ be trace-class normal densities on a separable complex Hilbert space, with $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$. Define $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $D(\rho\|\sigma)$ as in [[def-qsm-relative-entropy-domain]]. If $C(\rho,\sigma)<\infty$, then $S(\rho)<\infty$, $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B\geq0$, and equality holds exactly when $\rho=\sigma$. This restricted cross-log domain makes no assertion about an undefined $\infty-\infty$ difference.

Let $V,W$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner product spaces with orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_m)$ of $V$ and $(f_1,\dots,f_n)$ of $W$, let $V\otimes W$ be their tensor product with the inner product of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], and let $\operatorname{tr}$ denote the basis-independent trace of an endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

(a) For every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$ there is a unique endomorphism $\operatorname{Tr}_W R$ of $V$ with

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes I_W)\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\operatorname{End}(V),$$

namely $\operatorname{Tr}_WR=\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi_j\circ R\circ\iota_j$, where $\iota_j(v)=v\otimes f_j$ and $\varphi_j(x\otimes w)=\langle w,f_j\rangle x$; it does not depend on the orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of $W$, and the analogous definition gives $\operatorname{Tr}_V R$ with $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_VR)B)=\operatorname{tr}(R(I_V\otimes B))$.

(b) $\operatorname{Tr}_W$ is linear, positive (it maps positive endomorphisms to positive endomorphisms) and trace preserving on density matrices: if $R\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}R=1$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_WR=1$; and $\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ for every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$, where $C:W\to V$ is the coefficient map determined by $\Psi=\sum_jCf_j\otimes f_j$.

(c) *Schmidt decomposition.* Every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$ admits an expansion

$$\Psi=\sum_{r=1}^{k}s_r\,v_r\otimes u_r,$$

with $k\le\min(m,n)$, orthonormal families $(v_r)\subseteq V$, $(u_r)\subseteq W$ and $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_k>0$ uniquely determined by $\Psi$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient map; moreover $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_rs_r^2$. For $\|\Psi\|=1$ the reduced density $\rho=\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=\sum_rs_r^4$, and $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=1$ holds exactly when $k=1$, i.e. exactly when $\Psi$ is a product vector; mixed-state separability is not decided by this criterion.

(d) *Finite nonselective no-signalling.* If $(M_a)_{a=1}^p$ are endomorphisms of $W$ with $\sum_aM_a^*M_a=I_W$ then for every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$

$$\operatorname{Tr}_W\Bigl(\sum_a(I_V\otimes M_a)R(I_V\otimes M_a^*)\Bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_WR .$$

This is an identity for the specified finite local instrument; selective conditioning (dividing one summand by its nonzero trace) is not covered.

derivations.claim: Let $\rho=\sum_at_a\rho_a$, $t_a\geq0$, $\sum_at_a=1$. If $v\in\ker\rho$, then $0=\langle\rho v,v\rangle=\sum_at_a\langle\rho_av,v\rangle$; positivity forces $\rho_av=0$ whenever $t_a>0$. Hence $\operatorname{supp}\rho_a\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\rho$ for every positive-weight term.

If $\rho,\sigma$ have eigenvalues $p_i,q_j$, then $\rho\otimes\sigma$ has eigenbasis $u_i\otimes v_j$ and eigenvalues $p_iq_j$. Summing $-k_Bp_iq_j\log(p_iq_j)$ and using $\sum_ip_i=\sum_jq_j=1$ yields $S(\rho\otimes\sigma)=S(\rho)+S(\sigma)$.

Put $P_A=\operatorname{supp}\rho_A$. For $v\in\ker\rho_A$, the partial-trace formula in [L1] gives $0=\langle\rho_Av,v\rangle=\sum_j\langle R(v\otimes f_j),v\otimes f_j\rangle$. Each summand is nonnegative, so each is zero; positivity gives $R^{1/2}(v\otimes f_j)=0$, hence $R(v\otimes f_j)=0$. By linearity, $R$ vanishes on $\ker\rho_A\otimes H_B$, so its range is orthogonal to that subspace and lies in $P_A\otimes H_B$. Applying the same argument to the other marginal gives range $R\subseteq H_A\otimes P_B$. The intersection of these two subspaces is $P_A\otimes P_B$, as follows by using orthonormal bases adapted to the two support/kernel decompositions. Therefore $\operatorname{supp}R\subseteq P_A\otimes P_B$.
On those supports, expanding the finite traces gives $ S(\rho)-\sum_at_aS(\rho_a)=k_B\sum_at_aD(\rho_a\|\rho)\geq0 $ by [F1]. Thus entropy is concave under finite mixing.

Diagonalize $\rho_A,\rho_B$ on their supports. Their positive eigenvalues show $ \log(\rho_A\otimes\rho_B)=\log\rho_A\otimes I+I\otimes\log\rho_B $ on $P_A\otimes P_B$. The trace-pairing identities in [L1] then give $D(R\|\rho_A\otimes\rho_B)=[S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)-S(R)]/k_B\geq0$ by [F1]. Its equality condition in [F1] is exactly $R=\rho_A\otimes\rho_B$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be self-adjoint with regular Borel projection-valued measure $E$ from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], with $E((-\infty,a))=0$ for finite $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $\gamma>0$, define the bounded Gibbs operator $K_\gamma:=\Phi_E(f_\gamma)$ using the bounded Borel PVM integral of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], where $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma\lambda}$ for $\lambda\ge a$ and $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma a}$ for $\lambda<a$. Fix $\beta>0$ and suppose $K_\beta$ is trace class in the sense of [[def-trace-class-operator]]. Then $K_\beta$ is injective and has a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $\mathcal H$ with $Au_j=E_ju_j$, $E_j\ge a$, and $K_\beta u_j=e^{-\beta E_j}u_j$. Its partition function $Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta E_j}$ is positive and finite, and $\rho_\beta:=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=1$. For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\sum_j(e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta)\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$ absolutely. Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\gamma\log Z_\gamma=\bar E_\gamma$, $\partial_\gamma^2\log Z_\gamma=\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E)$, and $S_\gamma=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\bar E_\gamma$ as in [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]. Countable nonnegative sums use the finite-subsum supremum convention of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]].

Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Then $Z$ is positive, finite, and $C^2$ on $J$, with $Z'(\beta)=-\sum_i g_iE_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ and $Z''(\beta)=\sum_i g_iE_i^2\exp(-\beta E_i)$. The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized. Define $\bar E:=\langle E\rangle_\beta$ and $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E):=\sum_i p_i(E_i-\bar E)^2$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.

Let $\rho,\sigma$ be trace-class normal densities on a separable complex Hilbert space, with $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$. Define $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $D(\rho\|\sigma)$ as in [[def-qsm-relative-entropy-domain]]. If $C(\rho,\sigma)<\infty$, then $S(\rho)<\infty$, $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B\geq0$, and equality holds exactly when $\rho=\sigma$. This restricted cross-log domain makes no assertion about an undefined $\infty-\infty$ difference.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $Z_\beta$ is finite and positive and $\rho_\beta$ is a faithful trace-class density with a complete eigenbasis $u_j$ of $A$, $Au_j=E_ju_j$, and eigenvalues $q_j=e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta>0$. The spectral logarithm is $-\log\rho_\beta=\beta A+(\log Z_\beta)I$ on the corresponding spectral form domain.

Let $\rho=\sum_i p_i|v_i\rangle\langle v_i|$ be a normal density with the stated finite absolute form energy. Its cross-log moment against $\rho_\beta$ is $ C(\rho,\rho_\beta)=\sum_i p_i\sum_j|\langle v_i,u_j\rangle|^2(-\log q_j) =\beta\mathcal E_A(\rho)+\log Z_\beta, $ because $-\log q_j=\beta E_j+\log Z_\beta$, and the absolute first-moment hypothesis permits the signed sum. This value is finite.

Let $K=[b,B]\subset I$ be compact and choose $\beta_0\in I$ with $\beta_0<b$. For $E\geq0$, the function $(1+E^2)e^{-(b-\beta_0)E}$ is bounded; for $a\leq E\leq0$, $(1+|E|^2)e^{-(\beta-\beta_0)E}$ is uniformly bounded over $\beta\in K$ by compactness. Thus for a finite $C_K$, $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\beta E_j}\leq C_K e^{-\beta_0E_j}$ for every $j$ and $\beta\in K$. The right side is summable because $Z_{\beta_0}<\infty$ by [F2]. This is the exact uniform moment envelope required by [F3]; applying that supplier yields finite energy, finite entropy, and $S(\rho_\beta)=k_B(\log Z_\beta+\beta U_\beta)$, with $U_\beta=\mathcal E_A(\rho_\beta)$.

Since $\rho_\beta$ is faithful by [F2], $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\rho_\beta$. Apply [F4] to step 1.2: $S(\rho)<\infty$ and $ \beta\mathcal E_A(\rho)+\log Z_\beta-\frac{S(\rho)}{k_B} =D(\rho\|\rho_\beta)\geq0, $ with equality exactly when $\rho=\rho_\beta$. Rearranging and using $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$, $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$ gives the claimed inequality and equality case.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

Fix the positive Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in J/K and adopt two preparation rules within the normal-state model of [[post-qsm-normal-measurement-state]].

**Energy-band preparation.** Let $H=H^*$ have spectral PVM $E_H$, and let $P=E_H(B)$ be a nonzero finite-rank projection for a specified Borel energy band $B\subseteq\mathbb R$. When the model declares preparation in this band without additional constraints, adopt the density $\rho=P/\operatorname{Tr}P$. This is a uniform preparation over the finite-dimensional range of $P$; it is not asserted for infinite-rank projections.

**Grand preparation.** Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be the Hilbert space of a finite or countable model with a specified nonempty finite or countably infinite common orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_j)_{j\in J}$ for the self-adjoint energy operator $H$ and the dimensionless particle-number operator $N$: $Hu_j=E_ju_j$, $Nu_j=n_ju_j$, where each particle count $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$. Let $K_{\beta,\mu}=H-\mu N$ be self-adjoint on its declared domain, bounded below, and assume
$
0<\Xi(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{j\in J} e^{-\beta(E_j-\mu n_j)}<\infty.
$
Adopt the normal density $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}e^{-\beta(H-\mu N)}$. For response claims, also require the uniform joint-moment envelopes in [[thm-tdmath-grand-response-covariance]]. Here $E_j,\mu$ are in J, $n_j$ is dimensionless, $\beta=1/(k_BT)$ is in J$^{-1}$, and $\Xi$ is dimensionless.

These are adopted preparation assumptions, not consequences that a physical system is actually prepared in these states. They do not assert dynamical thermalization, an infinite-rank microcanonical state, or a grand ensemble for noncommuting $H,N$. The mathematical variational results to which they refer do not prove the physical postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $A=A^*$ a densely defined Hamiltonian bounded below by $a\in\mathbb R$. Assume $e^{-\beta A}$ is trace class for every $\beta$ in an open interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$. For each $\beta\in I$, put $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})$ and $\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta A}/Z_\beta$. Then $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$ and $\rho_\beta$ is a faithful normal density. For the entropy and optimization clause, fix $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), put $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$ and $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$, and let $\rho$ be any normal density with finite spectral form energy
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda)<\infty.
$
Then $\rho$ has finite entropy and satisfies
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality exactly at $\rho=\rho_\beta$. The prepared Gibbs state also has
$
S(\rho_\beta)=k_B\bigl(\log Z_\beta+\beta\mathcal E_A(\rho_\beta)\bigr).
$
The trace-class and open-interval hypotheses are essential; a lower bound on $A$ alone does not imply finite $Z_\beta$.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $w:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $X_a:X\to\mathbb R$ ($1\le a\le r$) be measurable, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)$, define $\theta\cdot X(x):=\sum_{a=1}^r\theta_aX_a(x)$. Set $Z(\theta):=\int w\exp(\theta\cdot X)\,d\mu$ and assume $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$ on $U$. Suppose for every compact $K\subset U$ there is an integrable $G_K\ge0$ such that $w e^{\theta\cdot X}(1+\sum_a|X_a|^2)\le G_K$ pointwise for all $\theta\in K$. For the normalized density $p_\theta=w e^{\theta\cdot X}/Z(\theta)$, define $\mathbb E_\theta Y:=\int Yp_\theta\,d\mu$ when integrable and $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b):=\mathbb E_\theta[(X_a-\mathbb E_\theta X_a)(X_b-\mathbb E_\theta X_b)]$. Then $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$ and $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b)$. Thus the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite. This is a mathematical model identity; it assumes no independence or absence of correlations.

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Adopt the following measurement interpretation for this nonrelativistic quantum-statistical model. A prepared normal state is a trace-class density operator $\rho$ on a specified separable complex Hilbert space $H$. A sharp measurement of a self-adjoint observable $A$, with spectral PVM $E_A$, assigns probability
$
\mathbb P_\rho\{A\in C\}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_A(C))
$
to each Borel outcome set $C\subseteq\mathbb R$. Finite projective measurements use the same rule with their orthogonal projections. This adopts a physical probability interpretation for the mathematical state law proved in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]]; it does not derive the Born rule, assert that an apparatus realizes a specified PVM, or report experimental outcomes. Infinite algebraic states not represented by trace-class density operators are not included.

The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the unbounded spectral theorem and its spectral-calculus supplier closure. Its strength is retained in the mathematical dependencies. The scalar probability and bounded cyclicity clauses now use the exact canonical suppliers cited by [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]]; this source adoption supplies no native readiness or empirical validation, and implies no weaker foundation.

Adopt canonical preparation as follows. Fix the positive Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in J/K. Let $H=H^*$ act on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\geq1$, or be self-adjoint on a nonzero separable Hilbert space, bounded below and satisfying $e^{-\beta H}\in\mathcal S_1$ for $\beta$ in an open interval about the chosen value. For temperature $T>0$, put $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ and adopt
$
\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z_\beta},\qquad Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).
$
In the infinite-dimensional case all scalar energy moments used in a conclusion must also be finite on the actual spectral domain, as required by [[thm-qsm-trace-gibbs-variational]]. With $H$ in joules, $k_B$ in J/K, $T$ in K, and $\beta$ in J$^{-1}$, the exponent is dimensionless and $Z_\beta$ is a dimensionless trace.

This is an adopted preparation rule in the normal-state framework. It is not a theorem that unitary dynamics equilibrates, does not specify a bath or equilibration time, and makes no empirical claim. The finite and trace-Gibbs variational results describe the mathematical optimization associated with this state but do not establish that a physical system is prepared in it.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $\rho$ a trace-class normal density state. Its positive eigenvalues $p_j$ and orthonormal eigenvectors $u_j$ satisfy $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$ in trace norm and $\sum_jp_j=1$. For bounded $A$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$, with absolute value at most $\|A\|$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho)$. For a self-adjoint observable $A$ with spectral PVM $E_A$, the scalar law
$
\mu_\rho(B)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_A(B))=\sum_jp_j\|E_A(B)u_j\|^2
$
is a probability measure. Its first absolute moment defines a scalar mean, and its second moment defines a variance; these are not defined as arbitrary unbounded products $\rho A$. For a fixed positive Boltzmann scale $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), the von Neumann entropy is $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_jp_j\log p_j\in[0,\infty]$, and need not be finite. Countable convex mixtures of normal density states converge in trace norm.

Let $\mathcal H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $H=H^*$ be a Hamiltonian on $\mathcal H$ with energy unit J; let $\hbar>0$ have unit J s. For real $t$ measured in seconds, $U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ is unitary and $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$. For a trace-one density $\rho$ on $\mathcal H$, the Schrödinger state $U(t)\rho U(t)^*$ and the Heisenberg observable $\alpha_t(A)=U(t)^*AU(t)$ have the same trace expectation. Fix $k_B>0$ in J/K for the entropy convention; then the von Neumann entropy is unchanged. If $d=\dim\mathcal H\geq1$, $\beta>0$ has unit J$^{-1}$, and $\sigma_\beta=e^{-\beta H}/Z_\beta$ with $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}$, then it is stationary and satisfies the finite Gibbs KMS strip identity
$
F_{A,B}(t+i\beta\hbar)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta\alpha_t(B)A),\qquad
F_{A,B}(z)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta A\alpha_z(B)),
$
where $\alpha_z(B)=e^{izH/\hbar}Be^{-izH/\hbar}$, with complexified time $z$ measured in seconds. The function is entire and bounded on $0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\hbar$ seconds. No infinite-volume KMS existence or approach to equilibrium follows.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and for a bounded measurable $f$ write $\Phi_E(f)=\int f\,dE$ for
the operator of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]. Then:

1. $\Phi_E$ is linear and unital: $\Phi_E(\mathbf 1_X)=I$ and
   $\Phi_E(af+bg)=a\Phi_E(f)+b\Phi_E(g)$ for bounded measurable $f,g$ and
   $a,b\in\mathbb C$;
2. $\Phi_E$ is multiplicative: $\Phi_E(fg)=\Phi_E(f)\Phi_E(g)$;
3. $\Phi_E$ preserves conjugation: $\Phi_E(\overline f)=\Phi_E(f)^*$;
4. if $(f_n)$ are bounded measurable with $\sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty$, $f$
   is bounded measurable, and $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere,
   meaning $E_x$-almost everywhere for every $x\in H$, then
   $\Phi_E(f_n)\to\Phi_E(f)$ in the strong operator topology.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F6], the bounded Borel function $f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}$ defines a unitary $U(t)=f_t(E_H)$ for each real $t$. By [F3], write $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$ in trace norm, with $p_j>0$, orthonormal $u_j$, and $\sum_jp_j=1$. Since $U(t)$ is bounded, [F5] preserves trace class under $U(t)\rho U(t)^*$. Its quadratic forms are nonnegative because $\langle U\rho U^*v,v\rangle=\langle \rho U^*v,U^*v\rangle\geq0$. The bounded cyclic trace identity [L1] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(U\rho U^*)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho U^*U)=1$. The vectors $Uu_j$ are orthonormal eigenvectors with the same eigenvalues $p_j$; the orthogonal complement of their span is the conjugated kernel. Therefore the entropy sum is termwise identical to that of $\rho$. Since all summands are nonnegative, the equality also holds when the sum is $+\infty$. This mathematical statement is interpreted under [F1].

In finite dimension, apply [F4] to the canonical state from [F2]; it gives stationarity and the analytic strip identity under the exact bounded-matrix hypotheses. The entropy invariance in step 1.1 also applies to this finite Gibbs state. The conclusions are conditional predictions of this unitary model, with no claim that a system reaches the canonical state dynamically.

Let $H=H^*$ act on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\geq1$, $\beta>0$, $k_B>0$, $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$, and $Z=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$. Put $\sigma=e^{-\beta H}/Z$, $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, and $S(\rho)=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$, with $0\log0=0$. Then every density matrix $\rho$, including rank-deficient matrices, satisfies
$
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality if and only if $\rho=\sigma$. Moreover $S(\sigma)=k_B(\log Z+\beta\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H))$, so $F_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H)-TS(\sigma)$. This is finite-dimensional mathematical optimization; actual preparation is a separate postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $A=A^*$ a densely defined Hamiltonian bounded below by $a\in\mathbb R$. Assume $e^{-\beta A}$ is trace class for every $\beta$ in an open interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$. For each $\beta\in I$, put $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})$ and $\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta A}/Z_\beta$. Then $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$ and $\rho_\beta$ is a faithful normal density. For the entropy and optimization clause, fix $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), put $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$ and $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$, and let $\rho$ be any normal density with finite spectral form energy
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda)<\infty.
$
Then $\rho$ has finite entropy and satisfies
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality exactly at $\rho=\rho_\beta$. The prepared Gibbs state also has
$
S(\rho_\beta)=k_B\bigl(\log Z_\beta+\beta\mathcal E_A(\rho_\beta)\bigr).
$
The trace-class and open-interval hypotheses are essential; a lower bound on $A$ alone does not imply finite $Z_\beta$.

derivations.claim: In finite dimension, [F2] gives $S(\sigma)=k_B(\log Z_\beta+\beta U)$. Multiplying by $T$ and using $k_BT=\beta^{-1}$ gives $TS=\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta+U$; since $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$, rearrangement yields $F_\beta=U-TS$. The units match: both $U$ and $TS$ are joules.

In the self-adjoint trace-class case, [F3] supplies the entropy identity with $U=\mathcal E_H(\rho_\beta)$, the scalar spectral first moment. The same multiplication by $T$ and rearrangement prove the displayed free-energy identity on this stated form-energy domain. No trace of an undefined unbounded product is used.

Let $M(s)$ be a continuously differentiable path of Hermitian $D\times D$ matrices, $D\geq1$. Then
$
\frac{d}{ds}e^{M(s)}=\int_0^1 e^{(1-u)M(s)}M'(s)e^{uM(s)}\,du,\qquad
\frac{d}{ds}\log\operatorname{Tr}e^{M(s)}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_sM'(s)),
$
where $\rho_s=e^{M(s)}/\operatorname{Tr}e^{M(s)}$. For real controls $M(\theta)=M_0+\sum_a\theta_aX_a$ with Hermitian $X_a$,
$
\partial_a\log Z=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X_a),\qquad
\partial_a\partial_b\log Z=\int_0^1\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{1-u}\delta X_a\rho^u\delta X_b)\,du,
$
where $Z=\operatorname{Tr}e^M$, $\delta X_a=X_a-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X_a)I$. The diagonal quadratic form of this Hessian is nonnegative. It equals the ordinary variance when $X_a$ commutes with $\rho$, and in general is bounded above by that variance. For $H(h)=H_0-hB$, $\beta>0$, and Hermitian $B$, the static susceptibility satisfies $\partial_h\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_hB)=\beta\,\operatorname{Cov}_{KM,\rho_h}(B,B)\geq0$. No infinite-dimensional or dynamical response is asserted.

derivations.claim: The parameter matrix is $M(h)=-\beta H(h)=-\beta H_0+\beta hB$, so $M'(h)=\beta B$. The finite Duhamel/quotient calculation in [F2] therefore gives $d\langle B\rangle_h/dh=\beta\operatorname{Cov}_{KM,\rho_h}(B,B)$, with $\rho_h$ given by [F1].

The eigenbasis expression in [F2] writes the Kubo–Mori quadratic form as a sum of $|(\delta B)_{ij}|^2L(p_i,p_j)$, where $L(p_i,p_j)>0$. Every summand is nonnegative, so the susceptibility is nonnegative. If $[H(h),B]=0$, then $B$ commutes with $\rho_h$, and [F2] gives the ordinary variance formula; no ordinary-variance identity is inferred without this commutation condition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be
nonzero complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$H\widehat\otimes K$ be their completed tensor product with inclusion $\kappa$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). Density operators are
the self-adjoint positive trace-class operators of trace one
([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a),
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), and for $u,u'\in H$, $v,v'\in K$ the rank-one
operator $T_{u\otimes v,\,u'\otimes v'}$ is the one of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]].

**(a) Product vectors and pure product states.** A vector $\Psi\in
H\widehat\otimes K$ is a **product vector** when $\Psi=\kappa(u\otimes v)$ for
some $u\in H$, $v\in K$. A **pure product state** of the composite is a
density operator of the form
$$T_{\Psi,\Psi},\qquad \Psi=\kappa(u\otimes v),\quad \|u\|=\|v\|=1 .$$
A vector is **non-product** when it is not a product vector.

**(b) Separable states.** Write $\mathcal P$ for the set of all pure product
states, a subset of the set $D(H\widehat\otimes K)$ of density operators. The
**separable states** are the elements of the trace-norm closed convex hull
$$\mathcal S(H,K):=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\,\mathcal P \ \subseteq\ D(H\widehat\otimes K),$$
where $\operatorname{conv}$ denotes the set of finite convex combinations and
the closure is taken in the trace norm $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ of
[[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]. A state
$\rho\in D(H\widehat\otimes K)$ is **entangled** (with respect to the
declared splitting $H,K$) when $\rho\notin\mathcal S(H,K)$.

**(c) Conventions and elementary consequences of the form of the definition.**
The set $\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P$ consists exactly of the finite sums
$\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}T_{\Psi_{j},\Psi_{j}}$ with $n\ge1$, weights $w_{j}\ge0$,
$\sum_{j}w_{j}=1$ and unit product vectors $\Psi_{j}$: such sums are convex
combinations of density operators and hence density operators
([[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-density-set-convex-and-complete]] clause (a)),
without any orthogonality requirement on the product vectors.
Every element of $\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P$ is a density operator, and
$\mathcal S(H,K)$ is a convex subset of $D(H\widehat\otimes K)$: if $\rho,\sigma$
are limits of convex combinations $\rho_{n}\to\rho$, $\sigma_{n}\to\sigma$ and
$t\in[0,1]$, then $t\rho+(1-t)\sigma$ is the trace-norm limit of the convex
combinations $t\rho_{n}+(1-t)\sigma_{n}$. Separability of a state is a
property of the declared splitting $(H,K)$; no assertion is made here about
its behaviour under a different factorization of a larger space.

**(d) Finite dimension.** When $H$ and $K$ are finite dimensional,
$\mathcal P$ is compact and $\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P$ is already closed
in the trace norm (it is a compact, hence closed, convex set in the
finite-dimensional space of endomorphisms of $H\widehat\otimes K$), so
$\mathcal S(H,K)=\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P$ and no closure convention is
needed. In the general case the closure in clause (b) is declared explicitly
and is part of the definition.

**(e) Pure-state specialization and status.** A pure state $T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ with $\|\Psi\|=1$ is separable in the precise trace-norm closed-convex-hull sense of clause (b) exactly when $\Psi$ is a product vector of clause (a); otherwise it is entangled. This is the proved mathematical specialization of [[lem-nrqm-composites-pure-state-separability-criterion]], whose locally defined $\mathcal P,\mathcal S$ are exactly those above. Clauses (a)-(e) fix mathematical vocabulary and adopt no physical assumption, dynamics, measurement or probability law. Whether a laboratory preparation realizes a separable or entangled state for the declared splitting remains a tested identification with uncertainty, not a consequence about nature of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be arbitrary nonzero complex Hilbert spaces, with inner products linear in the first argument, and put $L=H\widehat\otimes K$ with the isometric inclusion $\kappa$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Write $T_{x,y}z=\langle z,y\rangle x$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Set
$$\mathcal P=\{T_{\kappa(a\otimes b),\kappa(a\otimes b)}:\|a\|=\|b\|=1\},\qquad \mathcal S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P}^{\|\cdot\|_1},$$
with trace class as in [[def-trace-class-operator]], where the convex hull consists of finite convex combinations, and the closure is taken in the trace-class operators on $L$. For each unit $\Psi\in L$, let $P_\Psi=T_{\Psi,\Psi}$. Then
$$P_\Psi\in\mathcal S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Psi=\kappa(a\otimes b)\text{ for some unit }a\in H,\ b\in K.$$

More precisely, let $\Psi=\sum_{r\in J}s_r\kappa(v_r\otimes u_r)$ be any finite or countably infinite positive Schmidt expansion from [[thm-nrqm-composites-infinite-schmidt-decomposition]], and put $\lambda_r=s_r^2$. The number $m=\max_{r\in J}\lambda_r$ exists. Every pair of unit vectors $a,b$ satisfies $|\langle\Psi,\kappa(a\otimes b)\rangle|^2\le m$, with equality at a Schmidt pair whose weight is $m$. Every $\sigma\in\mathcal S$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma P_\Psi)\le m$, whereas $\operatorname{tr}(P_\Psi^2)=1$. If $\Psi$ is non-product then $m<1$ and, for every $\sigma\in\mathcal S$,
$$\|P_\Psi-\sigma\|_1\ge 1-m>0.$$
The factors need not be separable; only the support of the single tensor vector has a countable Schmidt expansion. These are mathematical trace pairings, with no measurement or Born-rule assumption.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a
non-negative operator $R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$,
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)$ is non-negative and

$$\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R))=\operatorname{tr}(R).$$

Here $\operatorname{End}(H)$ is the set of linear maps $H\to H$ as in
[[def-qc-partial-trace]], $I_H$ denotes the identity map $x\mapsto x$, and both
conclusions include zero-dimensional factors.

For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

For the positive entropy scale $k_B>0$ fixed in [[def-qsm-relative-entropy-domain]] (in SI units J/K), entropy is concave under finite mixing and additive on product states for finite-dimensional density matrices. If $R$ is a density matrix on $H_A\otimes H_B$, with marginals $\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_B R$, $\rho_B=\operatorname{Tr}_A R$, then
$
S(R)\leq S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B),
$
with equality exactly when $R=\rho_A\otimes\rho_B$. These finite statements include rank-deficient densities and assert neither strong subadditivity nor general infinite-dimensional data processing.

Adopt the following measurement interpretation for this nonrelativistic quantum-statistical model. A prepared normal state is a trace-class density operator $\rho$ on a specified separable complex Hilbert space $H$. A sharp measurement of a self-adjoint observable $A$, with spectral PVM $E_A$, assigns probability
$
\mathbb P_\rho\{A\in C\}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_A(C))
$
to each Borel outcome set $C\subseteq\mathbb R$. Finite projective measurements use the same rule with their orthogonal projections. This adopts a physical probability interpretation for the mathematical state law proved in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]]; it does not derive the Born rule, assert that an apparatus realizes a specified PVM, or report experimental outcomes. Infinite algebraic states not represented by trace-class density operators are not included.

The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the unbounded spectral theorem and its spectral-calculus supplier closure. Its strength is retained in the mathematical dependencies. The scalar probability and bounded cyclicity clauses now use the exact canonical suppliers cited by [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]]; this source adoption supplies no native readiness or empirical validation, and implies no weaker foundation.

derivations.claim: Under the retained choice hypotheses [A1], the imported pure-state criterion applies. Suppose $|\Phi\rangle=a\otimes b$, where $a=a_0|0\rangle+a_1|1\rangle$ and $b=b_0|0\rangle+b_1|1\rangle$. Comparing coefficients with $(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ gives $a_0b_0=a_1b_1=1/\sqrt2$ but $a_0b_1=a_1b_0=0$. The first pair makes all four factors nonzero, contradicting the second pair. Thus $|\Phi\rangle$ is not a product vector, so [F2] makes $\rho_\Phi$ entangled under the exact definition [F1].

In the product basis, the partial-trace rule [F3] removes $|00\rangle\langle11|$ and $|11\rangle\langle00|$, since the traced factor basis indices differ, and retains the two diagonal terms. Therefore both reductions of $\rho_\Phi$ are $I_2/2$; positivity and trace preservation in [F3] make them density matrices. The mixture already has only diagonal terms, and tracing either factor likewise gives $I_2/2$. The spectrum of $\rho_\Phi$ is $(1,0,0,0)$, whereas that of $\rho_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is $(1/2,1/2,0,0)$; each marginal has spectrum $(1/2,1/2)$. Substituting these eigenvalues into the entropy definition [F4] gives the displayed three entropy values. In particular both pairs obey the finite subadditivity inequality in [F4].

The mixture is the convex combination with weights $1/2,1/2$ of the two pure product densities $|00\rangle\langle00|$ and $|11\rangle\langle11|$; hence it lies in the finite convex hull in [F1] and is separable. Put $|\Phi_\pm\rangle=(|00\rangle\pm|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$; then $W|\Phi_\pm\rangle=\pm|\Phi_\pm\rangle$, and $W$ vanishes on the orthogonal span of $|01\rangle,|10\rangle$. The Bell state is $|\Phi_+\rangle$, so [F5] assigns probability one to $+1$. Each of $|00\rangle,|11\rangle$ has squared overlap $1/2$ with each of $|\Phi_+\rangle,|\Phi_-\rangle$, so the equal mixture gives probability $1/2$ to each of $+1,-1$ and zero to $0$.
