citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first argument. An operator $\rho\in\mathcal B(H)$ is a **density operator** when it is positive, trace class, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Here trace class means compact with summable singular values, and $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the basis-independent trace of a trace-class operator.

The **normal density state represented by $\rho$** is the functional on bounded operators
$
\omega_\rho(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(H).
$
In this page, “normal density state” means this specified trace-pairing representation; no equivalence with other definitions of normal functionals is assumed. The trace pairing is used only for bounded $A$. Unbounded observables are treated through their spectral probability measures in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]].

For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

Adopt canonical preparation as follows. Fix the positive Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in J/K. Let $H=H^*$ act on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\geq1$, or be self-adjoint on a nonzero separable Hilbert space, bounded below and satisfying $e^{-\beta H}\in\mathcal S_1$ for $\beta$ in an open interval about the chosen value. For temperature $T>0$, put $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ and adopt
$
\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z_\beta},\qquad Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).
$
In the infinite-dimensional case all scalar energy moments used in a conclusion must also be finite on the actual spectral domain, as required by [[thm-qsm-trace-gibbs-variational]]. With $H$ in joules, $k_B$ in J/K, $T$ in K, and $\beta$ in J$^{-1}$, the exponent is dimensionless and $Z_\beta$ is a dimensionless trace.

This is an adopted preparation rule in the normal-state framework. It is not a theorem that unitary dynamics equilibrates, does not specify a bath or equilibration time, and makes no empirical claim. The finite and trace-Gibbs variational results describe the mathematical optimization associated with this state but do not establish that a physical system is prepared in it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $A=A^*$ a densely defined Hamiltonian bounded below by $a\in\mathbb R$. Assume $e^{-\beta A}$ is trace class for every $\beta$ in an open interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$. For each $\beta\in I$, put $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})$ and $\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta A}/Z_\beta$. Then $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$ and $\rho_\beta$ is a faithful normal density. For the entropy and optimization clause, fix $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), put $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$ and $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$, and let $\rho$ be any normal density with finite spectral form energy
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda)<\infty.
$
Then $\rho$ has finite entropy and satisfies
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality exactly at $\rho=\rho_\beta$. The prepared Gibbs state also has
$
S(\rho_\beta)=k_B\bigl(\log Z_\beta+\beta\mathcal E_A(\rho_\beta)\bigr).
$
The trace-class and open-interval hypotheses are essential; a lower bound on $A$ alone does not imply finite $Z_\beta$.

derivations.claim: Let $\lambda_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)$. Finite-support vectors lie in $D(H)$, so the domain is dense. Since each $\lambda_n$ is real, the diagonal operator is symmetric. If $y\in D(H^*)$, there is $z\in\ell^2$ such that $\langle Hc,y\rangle=\langle c,z\rangle$ for every $c\in D(H)$. Testing $c=e_n$ gives $z_n=\lambda_ny_n$, so $(\lambda_ny_n)\in\ell^2$, which is exactly $y\in D(H)$. Conversely, if this sequence is square summable, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\langle Hc,y\rangle=\langle c,(\lambda_ny_n)\rangle$ for every $c\in D(H)$. Thus $D(H^*)=D(H)$ and $H^*=H$.

The diagonal exponential has eigenvalues $e^{-x(n+1/2)}$. The finite geometric sum identity and $r^n\to0$ give $\sum_{n\geq0}r^n=(1-r)^{-1}$, so $Z_\beta=e^{-x/2}/(1-r)<\infty$. For any compact interval $[b,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, the moment terms $(1+\lambda_n^2)e^{-\beta\lambda_n}$ are bounded by $(1+\lambda_n^2)e^{-b\lambda_n}$; this series converges by the ratio test, so the trace and first-moment hypotheses hold locally. Hence [F1] and [F2] make $\rho_\beta$ a normal density, and [F4] identifies it with the adopted canonical preparation.

The normalized weights are $p_n=(1-r)r^n$. Absolute convergence permits subtracting the two convergent series to get $(1-r)\sum_{n\geq0}nr^n=\sum_{n\geq1}r^n=r/(1-r)$; therefore $\sum n p_n=r/(1-r)$. This gives $U_\beta=\sum_np_n\lambda_n=\hbar\omega(\tfrac12+r/(1-r))$. Also $\log p_n=\log(1-r)+n\log r$, so summing $-k_Bp_n\log p_n$ using [F3] yields $S=k_B[-\log(1-r)-(\log r)r/(1-r)]=k_B[-\log(1-r)+xr/(1-r)]$. Replacing $r/(1-r)$ by $1/(e^x-1)$ gives the displayed formulas. The direct sums verify the moment hypotheses of [F5], whose energy-entropy identity agrees with this calculation.

For $H=0$ on an infinite-dimensional $\ell^2$, every basis vector is an eigenvector of $e^{-\beta H}=I$ with eigenvalue one. Their eigenvalue sum diverges, so [F1] says $I$ is not trace class. Its trace cannot be normalized to a finite partition function, establishing the contrasting failure without assuming a lower-bound-only Hamiltonian is normalizable.

Adopt the finite canonical state rule of [[post-qsm-thermal-gibbs-preparation]]. Let $H(h)=H_0-hB$ on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\geq1$, where $H_0,B$ are Hermitian, $h$ is a real static control, $hB$ has units J, and $\beta>0$ is fixed in J$^{-1}$. Put $\rho_h=e^{-\beta H(h)}/Z(h)$. With $\delta B=B-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_hB)I$, define
$
\operatorname{Cov}_{KM,\rho_h}(B,B)=\int_0^1\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_h^{1-u}\delta B\rho_h^u\delta B)\,du.
$
Then the static susceptibility is
$
\frac{d}{dh}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_hB)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}_{KM,\rho_h}(B,B)\geq0.
$
It equals $\beta$ times the ordinary variance only when $[H(h),B]=0$; for noncommuting matrices the Kubo–Mori expression is the applicable covariance. This is a static model deduction, not a dynamical response or observation.

derivations.claim: Write $r(h)=\sqrt{(\epsilon/2)^2+h^2}$. Direct matrix multiplication gives $H(h)^2=r(h)^2I$ and $\operatorname{Tr}H(h)=0$. Splitting the exponential power series into even and odd powers therefore gives $e^{-\beta H(h)}=\cosh(\beta r(h))I-(\sinh(\beta r(h))/r(h))H(h)$, hence $Z(h)=2\cosh(\beta r(h))$. Also $\operatorname{Tr}(H(h)\sigma_x)=-2h$, so $\langle\sigma_x\rangle_h=h\tanh(\beta r(h))/r(h)$. Dividing by $h$ and taking $h\to0$ yields $\chi=\tanh(\beta\epsilon/2)/(\epsilon/2)=\beta\tanh(x)/x$.

At $h=0$, the Gibbs density is diagonal in the displayed basis, so $\langle\sigma_x\rangle_0=0$. Since $\sigma_x^2=I$, its variance is $1$. The commutator of $\operatorname{diag}(-\epsilon/2,\epsilon/2)$ with $\sigma_x$ has nonzero off-diagonal entries for $\epsilon>0$, so the commuting equality case in [F1] does not apply. Finally, for $x>0$,
$
x-\tanh x=\int_0^x(1-\operatorname{sech}^2t)\,dt>0,
$
because the integrand is strictly positive for $t>0$. Thus $0<\chi<\beta$. At the zero-gap boundary, $\lim_{x\downarrow0}\tanh(x)/x=1$, so the response tends to the commuting value $\beta$.

boundaries.evidence: The Example fixes a two-dimensional nonzero register. $$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces

$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to

citations.quote:
Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.
If $C$ is at most countable and $m\in\mathbb N$, then the finite product $C^m=\prod_{i<m}C$ is at most countable.

derivations.claim: Define $e:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$ by $e(2n)=n$ and $e(2n+1)=-(n+1)$. Every natural number is uniquely even or odd, and every integer is either a natural number or the negative of a positive natural number; these two descriptions show that every integer is a value of $e$. Thus $e$ is a surjection.
Since $\mathbb{Z}$ is nonempty, [F2] applied to $e$ shows that $\mathbb{Z}$ is at most countable in the sense of [F1].
Since $d$ is finite and positive, [F3] with $C=\mathbb{Z}$ and $m=d$ gives that $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ is at most countable.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows from $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$.

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

derivations.claim: Under [F1], $T\mapsto T\otimes I$ preserves products and adjoints because $(T\otimes I)(S\otimes I)=TS\otimes I$ and $(T\otimes I)^*=T^*\otimes I$; it sends $I_\Lambda$ to $I_{\Lambda'}$. The configuration-basis factorization is associative, so for nested regions the two successive inclusions and the direct inclusion act identically on every configuration basis vector and hence are equal operators.

Let $K=\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, and choose its finite orthonormal configuration basis $e_1,\ldots,e_s$. Every $\xi\in\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes K$ has a unique expansion $\xi=\sum_{j=1}^s \xi_j\otimes e_j$, with $\|\xi\|^2=\sum_j\|\xi_j\|^2$. Therefore $\|(T\otimes I)\xi\|^2=\sum_j\|T\xi_j\|^2\le\|T\|^2\|\xi\|^2$, so $\|T\otimes I\|\le\|T\|$.

If $T=0$, both norms are zero. Otherwise, for every $\varepsilon>0$ the supremum definition in [F2] gives a unit vector $u\in\mathcal H_\Lambda$ with $\|Tu\|>\|T\|-\varepsilon$. Since $q\ge1$, $K$ is nonzero; choose a unit configuration vector $v\in K$. Then $\|(T\otimes I)(u\otimes v)\|=\|Tu\|\|v\|>\|T\|-\varepsilon$, so $\|T\otimes I\|\ge\|T\|-\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in step 1.3 and combining with step 1.2 gives $\|\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}(T)\|=\|T\|$. Step 1.1 supplies the unital $*$-homomorphism and composition identities, completing the claim.

Fix $d\ge1$, $q\ge1$, and finite regions $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ as in [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. Then the factor inclusion $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}(T)=T\otimes I$ is an isometric unital $*$-homomorphism:

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a normed space. A **completion of $X$** is a pair
$\bigl(\widehat X,\iota\bigr)$ such that

- $\widehat X$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]);
- $\iota:X\to \widehat X$ is a linear isometry
  ([[def-linear-isometry-and-isometric-isomorphism]]);
- $\iota[X]$ is dense in $\widehat X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

Equivalently, a completion of a normed space is a completion of its norm metric
([[def-metric-completion]]) together with compatible linear structure on the
complete space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space. The published metric completion of the norm metric on $X$ admits
a unique vector-space structure and norm whose induced metric is the
published completion metric and such that the constant sequence embedding
$i:X\to \widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry. With this structure,
$\widehat X$ is a Banach space.

In the published Cauchy-sequence model of the metric completion of a normed
space, if $[x_n]$ and $[y_n]$ denote equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences,
then

$$[x_n]+[y_n]:=[x_n+y_n],\qquad \lambda[x_n]:=[\lambda x_n],\qquad \|[x_n]\|:=\lim_n \|x_n\|$$

are well defined.

A **possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra** is a complex vector space $A$
equipped with an associative complex-bilinear multiplication
$A \times A \to A$ ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]] for the bilinearity convention)
and a norm under which $A$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]],
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]), such that the norm is
**submultiplicative**:

$$\|ab\| \le \|a\|\,\|b\| \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

No multiplicative identity is assumed, and no real-algebra or unital
convention is imported from elsewhere.

A **complex C\*-algebra** is a possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra $A$
equipped with an **involution** $A \to A$, $a \mapsto a^*$, which is
conjugate-linear ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) and
satisfies

$$(a^*)^* = a, \qquad (ab)^* = b^*a^*, \qquad \|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2 \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

The last identity is the **C\*-identity**. Two immediate consequences are worth
recording, and both are proved from the displayed axioms alone:

- **the involution is isometric**: $\|a^*\| = \|a\|$. Indeed $\|a\|^2 = \|a^*a\| \le \|a^*\|\,\|a\|$ gives $\|a\| \le \|a^*\|$ when $a \ne 0$, and applying this inequality to $a^*$ and using $(a^*)^* = a$ gives $\|a^*\| \le \|a\|$; the case $a = 0$ is trivial;
- **no norm-uniqueness assertion is part of this definition**: such a theorem
  needs additional hypotheses and proof, and does not follow merely by naming
  the displayed C\*-identity.

Let $A$ and $B$ be complex C\*-algebras. A **bounded star-homomorphism**, or
bounded $*$-homomorphism, is a bounded complex-linear map
$\varphi : A \to B$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) satisfying

$$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b), \qquad \varphi(a^*) = \varphi(a)^* \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

A star-homomorphism is **not** required to be unital, and it is not required
that a unit be present or preserved; when $A$ and $B$ both happen to be unital,
$\varphi$ is called **unital** if $\varphi(1_A) = 1_B$. The bounded nonunital
star-homomorphisms are the arrows of the locally compact duality theorem on this
page ([[thm-locally-compact-gelfand-duality]]), with properness imposed there
through [[def-approximate-unit-and-proper-c-star-morphism]].

derivations.claim: For $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$, both embed into $\mathcal A_{\Lambda\cup\Delta}$ by [F1]. Thus their sum, product and adjoint are defined in a common finite matrix algebra, so $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is a unital $*$-algebra. If $A$ has two localization regions, embedding into their union and isometry [F1] show that both assigned norms equal its norm in that common algebra; hence the local norm is well defined.

By [F3] and [F4], the norm completion is a Banach space and sums, scalar multiples and the limit norm are well defined on Cauchy-sequence classes; the constant sequence at the local unit is its candidate unit, and the local algebra is dense by the definition of completion.

In any common finite matrix algebra, the operator norm is submultiplicative, the adjoint preserves norm, and [F2] supplies the C*-identity $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$. Isometric inclusions [F1] transfer these identities to $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$, so it is a normed $*$-algebra with the C*-identity.

Let $(A_n)$ and $(B_n)$ be Cauchy sequences in $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Each is bounded: after some index its terms lie within one unit of a fixed term, and the finitely many earlier terms have a finite maximum norm. Then
$$\|A_nB_n-A_mB_m\|\le\|A_n\|\,\|B_n-B_m\|+\|A_n-A_m\|\,\|B_m\|$$
shows that $(A_nB_n)$ is Cauchy. If either sequence is replaced by an equivalent one, the same estimate makes the product sequences equivalent. Thus multiplication $[A_n][B_n]:=[A_nB_n]$ is well defined on the completion and obeys $\|xy\|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$.

Since $\|A_n^*-A_m^*\|=\|A_n-A_m\|$ in the local algebra by step 2.1, $[A_n]^*:=[A_n^*]$ is a well-defined involution on the completion. The Cauchy-sequence identities for product and adjoint show $(xy)^*=y^*x^*$ and associativity; continuity of multiplication and the limit norm pass $\|x^*x\|=\|x\|^2$ from [F2] to every $x$ in the completion. The unit class $[I_{\mathrm{loc}}]$ acts as an identity by termwise multiplication and has norm one by isometry, so $\mathcal A$ satisfies the C*-algebra definition in [F5].

If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ with $\Lambda\cap\Delta=\varnothing$, in $\mathcal A_{\Lambda\cup\Delta}$ they have forms $A_\Lambda\otimes I_\Delta$ and $I_\Lambda\otimes B_\Delta$. Both products equal $A_\Lambda\otimes B_\Delta$, so $AB=BA$. This proves locality for disjoint finite local factors.

In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

Consequently the canonical states of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] are exactly the trace pairings of density operators of [[def-qc-density-operator]]; for a positive functional, normalization $\omega(I)=1$ is equivalent to norm one. The result includes zero positive functionals, nonfaithful densities and $D=1$; it makes no infinite-dimensional density representation assertion.

Let $\mathcal A$ be the unital quasi-local spin C*-algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]], whose C*-structure uses Countable Choice as in [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. An **infinite algebraic state** is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ satisfying $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$.

For each finite region $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, the restriction $\omega|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ is a finite-matrix state. By [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], every positive normalized functional on a finite matrix algebra is represented by a unique density matrix. Define its **local density matrix** $\rho_\Lambda$ by

$$\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}(\rho_\Lambda A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda),$$

where $\rho_\Lambda=\rho_\Lambda^*\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}\rho_\Lambda=1$. For $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, the local densities are **consistent** when $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$, with partial trace characterized by its pairing against every $A\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. No density operator on a globally chosen Hilbert space is part of this definition.

This agrees with the canonical state convention of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]]: the finite restrictions have norm one by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], giving $|\omega(A)|\le\|A\|$ on the dense local algebra and hence on its completion; evaluation at the norm-one identity gives $\|\omega\|=1$. No global density representation is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows from $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$.

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.
For every positive integer $d$, the integer lattice $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ is at most countable. Countability here means finite or in bijection with $\mathbb{N}$, as in [[def-countable]].
If $C$ is at most countable and $m\in\mathbb N$, then the finite product $C^m=\prod_{i<m}C$ is at most countable.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of at most countable sets
([[def-countable]]) indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Then

$$U = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$$

is at most countable.

**The role of $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.** It is spent at exactly one step, step 3.1 below, where a surjection $\mathbb N\to A_n$ is selected simultaneously for each nonempty $A_n$. The individual countability hypotheses assert that these sets of surjections are nonempty; they specify no simultaneous selection.

and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.
If $C$ is at most countable and $m\in\mathbb N$, then the finite product $C^m=\prod_{i<m}C$ is at most countable.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

$a$ and $s$ alone.

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ be a closed bounded interval
with $a_k \le b_k$ ([[def-interval]]), and suppose the family is **nested**:

$$I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \ge 0$ for the length of $I_k$. Then:

1. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is **nonempty**. More precisely,
   with $a = \sup\{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and
   $b = \inf\{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both of which exist, one has $a \le b$
   and $$\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k = [a, b].$$
2. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is a **single point** if and only
   if $\ell_k \to 0$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

Every hypothesis is load bearing. Dropping closedness makes the intersection
empty; dropping boundedness does the same; and dropping nonemptiness of the
individual intervals is vacuously fatal.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.

Assume Countable Choice for the norm completion in [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]]. Let $\{\rho_\Lambda\}$ be positive trace-one matrices, one on each finite-region algebra $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], such that for every $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$ their partial traces agree: $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$. There is a unique infinite algebraic state $\omega$ on $\mathcal A$ whose restriction to each $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ is $A\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}(\rho_\Lambda A)$.

derivations.claim: For each $m\in\mathbb N$, let $R_m$ be the set of ranges of all $m$-tuples in $\Gamma^m$, including tuples with repeated entries. Since $\Gamma^m$ is at most countable by [F1], a surjection $\mathbb N\to\Gamma^m$ composed with the range map shows $R_m$ is at most countable by [F2]. Every finite region is the range of a tuple of its cardinality, with the empty region the range of the unique $0$-tuple. Thus all finite regions form the countable union $\bigcup_m R_m$, which is at most countable by [F1] and [A1]. For each region $\Lambda$, rational real and imaginary matrix entries give a countable subset of $\mathcal A_\Lambda$: it is a finite Cartesian power of $\mathbb Q$, so [F1]–[F2] apply. These matrices are norm dense: for a $D_\Lambda\times D_\Lambda$ error matrix $E$ whose entries have modulus at most $\delta$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|Ev\|_2^2\le\sum_{i,j}|E_{ij}|^2\|v\|_2^2\le D_\Lambda^2\delta^2\|v\|_2^2$, so $\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le D_\Lambda\delta$. A second countable union, using [A1], therefore gives a countable norm-dense set $D$ in $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$, hence in its completion $\mathcal A$.

By [F2], choose a surjection $s:\mathbb N\to D$ and enumerate its values as $D_1,D_2,\ldots$. For each fixed $j\ge1$, the scalar sequence $z_n^{(j)}:=\omega_n(D_j)$ is bounded: $D_j$ is local, and the finite-dimensional state/density interface [F3] gives $|\omega_n(D_j)|\le\|D_j\|$. The same estimate extends each $\omega_n$ from the dense local algebra to all of $\mathcal A$, so $\|\omega_n\|=1$ by normalization.

We specify a deterministic convergent-subsequence rule for any bounded complex sequence $z_n$. Choose $M>0$ with $z_n\in[-M,M]^2$ under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$. Subdivide the current closed square into its four closed equal subsquares in fixed lexicographic order; at least one contains infinitely many terms, and the rule takes the first such square. At the first stage choose the least index whose term lies in that square; at every later stage choose the least index exceeding the previous one whose term lies in the selected square. Writing the nested squares as $I_j\times J_j$, their closed coordinate intervals are nested and have lengths tending to zero. [F5] gives unique $x\in\bigcap_j I_j$ and $y\in\bigcap_j J_j$, so $(x,y)$ is the unique common point of the squares. The subsequence terms after stage $j$ lie in the $j$th square, whose diameter tends to zero, hence converge to $(x,y)$. Every choice in this rule is determined by a finite ordering or a least natural index; it uses no additional choice axiom.

Apply the deterministic rule of step 1.3 recursively to the coordinate sequences $z_n^{(j)}$ along nested subsequences for $j\ge1$. More precisely, start with $i_0(n)=n$; at stage $j$, write the resulting subsequence as $i_j(n)=i_{j-1}(s_j(n))$ with $s_j$ strictly increasing, so $s_j(j)\ge j$. By [F5] and recursion, these maps are defined for every positive $j$. Put $r_j=i_j(j)$ for $j\ge1$. For $j\ge2$, $r_j=i_{j-1}(s_j(j))\ge i_{j-1}(j)>i_{j-1}(j-1)=r_{j-1}$, so $(r_j)_{j\ge1}$ is increasing. For fixed $m\ge1$ and $j\ge m$, nestedness gives $r_j=i_m(t_{m,j})$ where $t_{m,j}\ge j$; hence these are tails of the convergent coordinate subsequence selected at stage $m$, and $\omega_{r_j}(D_m)$ converges.

For any $A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $D_m$ with $\|A-D_m\|<\varepsilon/4$ by density. Since each $\omega_{r_j}$ has norm one,
$$|\omega_{r_j}(A)-\omega_{r_k}(A)|\le2\|A-D_m\|+|\omega_{r_j}(D_m)-\omega_{r_k}(D_m)|.$$
The last term tends to zero as $j,k\to\infty$ by step 2.1. Thus $\omega_{r_j}(A)$ is Cauchy and converges for every local $A$. Define $\omega_0(A):=\lim_j\omega_{r_j}(A)$ on $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$. For local $A,B$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, the equalities $\omega_{r_j}(A+\lambda B)=\omega_{r_j}(A)+\lambda\omega_{r_j}(B)$ pass to the limit, and $\omega_0(I)=1$. For every local $X$, $\omega_0(X^*X)=\lim_j\omega_{r_j}(X^*X)\ge0$. Finally $|\omega_0(A)|=\lim_j|\omega_{r_j}(A)|\le\|A\|$. Thus $\omega_0$ is a bounded normalized positive functional on $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

On each finite region $\Lambda$, write $\rho_\Lambda^{(j)}$ for the density of $\omega_{r_j}|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$. For each matrix unit $E_{ab}$, its entries are rational, so $E_{ba}\in D$; the trace-pairing formula gives $(\rho_\Lambda^{(j)})_{ab}=\omega_{r_j}(E_{ba})$. Thus every matrix coefficient converges by step 2.1. The entrywise limit $\rho_\Lambda$ is Hermitian and trace one because these are finite linear equalities; for every vector $v$, $\langle\rho_\Lambda v,v\rangle=\lim_j\langle\rho_\Lambda^{(j)}v,v\rangle\ge0$, so it is positive. Every partial-trace consistency equation is a finite linear equation in these entries and therefore passes to the limit. Hence $\{\rho_\Lambda\}$ is a consistent family.

By [F6], the consistent family of step 4.1 extends to a unique state $\omega$ on $\mathcal A$, and $\omega|_{\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}}=\omega_0$. For any $A\in\mathcal A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose local $B$ with $\|A-B\|<\varepsilon/4$. Then
$$|\omega_{r_j}(A)-\omega(A)|\le2\|A-B\|+|\omega_{r_j}(B)-\omega(B)|,$$
whose right side is eventually less than $\varepsilon$ by step 3.1. Therefore $\omega_{r_j}(A)\to\omega(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$, proving sequential compactness in the pointwise topology.

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

derivations.claim: For $a,b\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$, positivity makes $Q(z):=\omega((a+zb)^*(a+zb))\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$. Expanding gives $Q(z)=\omega(a^*a)+z u+\overline z\,v+|z|^2c$, where $u=\omega(a^*b)$, $v=\omega(b^*a)$, and $c=\omega(b^*b)\ge0$. Taking real $z=t$ and purely imaginary $z=it$ shows respectively that $u+v$ is real and $i(u-v)$ is real, so $v=\overline u$. If $c>0$, take $z=-v/c$ to obtain $Q(z)=\omega(a^*a)-|v|^2/c\ge0$. If $c=0$ and $v\ne0$, taking $z=-t v$ for sufficiently large real $t>0$ gives $Q(z)=\omega(a^*a)-2t|v|^2<0$, a contradiction; hence $v=0$. Therefore $|\omega(b^*a)|^2\le\omega(a^*a)\omega(b^*b)$.

Define $N:=\{a\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}:\omega(a^*a)=0\}$. If $a,b\in N$, step 1.1 makes both mixed terms $\omega(a^*b)$ and $\omega(b^*a)$ zero, so $\omega((a+b)^*(a+b))=0$; scalar multiples stay in $N$ by homogeneity. Thus $N$ is a vector subspace. The same inequality makes $\langle[a],[b]\rangle:=\omega(b^*a)$ independent of representatives in $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}/N$. This form is linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric, and positive definite on the quotient: $\langle[a],[a]\rangle=0$ implies $a\in N$ and hence $[a]=0$.

Let $a,b\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and choose one finite region containing both. In its matrix representation, $c:=\|a\|^2I-a^*a$ is Hermitian and positive, since $\langle c\xi,\xi\rangle=\|a\|^2\|\xi\|^2-\|a\xi\|^2\ge0$ for every vector $\xi$. By [F2], $c^{1/2}$ exists in that same finite matrix algebra. Therefore $b^*cb=(c^{1/2}b)^*(c^{1/2}b)$ and positivity of $\omega$ gives $\omega(b^*a^*ab)\le\|a\|^2\omega(b^*b)$. In particular, the null space $N$ of step 2.1 is a left ideal under multiplication by local $a$: if $b\in N$, the inequality gives $\omega((ab)^*(ab))=0$.

Define $\pi_0(a)[b]:=[ab]$ for $a,b\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Step 3.1 shows this is well defined on the quotient. The bound there gives $\|\pi_0(a)[b]\|^2\le\|a\|^2\|[b]\|^2$, so $\pi_0(a)$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator on the Hilbert completion $\mathcal H_\omega$, with $\|\pi_0(a)\|\le\|a\|$. On quotient vectors, multiplication gives $\pi_0(a)\pi_0(d)[b]=\pi_0(ad)[b]$, and $\langle\pi_0(a)[b],[c]\rangle=\omega(c^*ab)=\langle[b],\pi_0(a^*)[c]\rangle$; continuity extends these identities to $\mathcal H_\omega$.

For $A\in\mathcal A$, represent it by a Cauchy sequence $(a_n)$ in $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$, as in the norm-completion construction. The estimate $\|\pi_0(a_n)-\pi_0(a_m)\|\le\|a_n-a_m\|$ makes the operators operator-norm Cauchy. For each $\xi\in\mathcal H_\omega$, completeness gives $T\xi:=\lim_n\pi_0(a_n)\xi$; this is linear and bounded because $(a_n)$ is norm bounded and $\|\pi_0(a_n)\xi\|\le\|a_n\|\|\xi\|$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, for all sufficiently large $n,m$ the operator difference has norm at most $\varepsilon$; fixing such $n$ and passing $m\to\infty$ gives $\|(\pi_0(a_n)-T)\xi\|\le\varepsilon\|\xi\|$, hence $\|\pi_0(a_n)-T\|\le\varepsilon$. Thus $T\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\omega)$ is the operator-norm limit. Equivalent representatives give the same limit by the same estimate, defining $\pi_\omega(A):=T$. Linearity follows because local approximants to $A,B$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ give approximants $a_n+\lambda b_n$ to $A+\lambda B$, and each $\pi_0$ is linear. Passing $\|\pi_0(a_n)\|\le\|a_n\|$ to the limit also gives $\|\pi_\omega(A)\|\le\|A\|$, so $\pi_\omega$ is bounded and contractive. If $(b_n)$ represents $B$, then $(a_nb_n)$ represents $AB$ by continuity of multiplication in $\mathcal A$, and $\pi_0(a_nb_n)=\pi_0(a_n)\pi_0(b_n)$; taking operator-norm limits gives multiplicativity. For any $x$ in a C*-algebra, $\|x^*\|^2=\|xx^*\|\le\|x\|\|x^*\|$ by the C*-identity and submultiplicativity; this gives $\|x^*\|\le\|x\|$, and applying it to $x^*$ yields equality. Hence $(a_n^*)$ represents $A^*$; the adjoint identity from step 4.1 and norm continuity of Hilbert adjoints [F6] give $\pi_\omega(A^*)=\pi_\omega(A)^*$. The constant sequence at $I$ gives $\pi_\omega(I)=I$.

Put $\Omega_\omega:=[I]$. Its squared norm is $\omega(I)=1$. For every local $a$, $\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega=[a]$; these classes are dense by the definition of $\mathcal H_\omega$, so $\Omega_\omega$ is cyclic. For local $a$, $\langle\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega,\Omega_\omega\rangle=\omega(a)$ by the quotient inner product. Both sides are continuous in $a$ and $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is dense in $\mathcal A$, so the identity holds for every $A\in\mathcal A$.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows from $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$.

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

Fix $d\ge1$, $q\ge1$, and finite regions $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ as in [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. Then the factor inclusion $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}(T)=T\otimes I$ is an isometric unital $*$-homomorphism:

$$\|\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}(T)\|=\|T\|\qquad(T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda).$$

For nested finite regions $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'\subseteq\Lambda''$, the inclusions compose: $\iota_{\Lambda',\Lambda''}\circ\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}=\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda''}$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Cauchy-sequence completion. For the local spin system of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], the normed $*$-algebra $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and its completion $\mathcal A$ of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] are well defined; $\mathcal A$ is a unital complex C*-algebra and $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is norm dense in it. If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ for disjoint finite regions $\Lambda,\Delta$, then $AB=BA$.

derivations.claim: Direct matrix multiplication gives $X^*=X$, $Z^*=Z$, $X^2=Z^2=I$, and $\|X\|=\|Z\|=1$ because each preserves the Euclidean norm and is nonzero. By [F2], the embedded $X_x$ and $Z_y$ have the same adjoint, square and norm properties.

If $x<y$, lexicographic factor order gives $X_x=X\otimes I$ and $Z_y=I\otimes Z$, so $(X\otimes I)(I\otimes Z)=X\otimes Z=(I\otimes Z)(X\otimes I)$. If $y<x$, the factors are interchanged and both products are $Z\otimes X$. Thus in either ordering $X_xZ_y=Z_yX_x$.
The supports $\{x\}$ and $\{y\}$ are disjoint; the computed commutation is therefore the stated instance of the general disjoint-locality clause.

derivations.claim: Fix any finite region $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z$. Enumerate the finite set $F:=\Lambda\cap\{n\in\mathbb Z:0<n\}$ as $n_1,\ldots,n_r$, and put $S:=\sum_{j=1}^{r}n_j$, taking $S=0$ when $r=0$. By induction on the number of terms, every finite sum of positive integers is nonnegative: the empty sum is $0$, and if a partial sum $R\ge0$ then adding a positive integer $n$ gives $R+n>R\ge0$, since $0<n$ translates to $R+0\le R+n$ by [F1], and equality would cancel $R$ in the additive group $\mathbb Z$ to give $0=n$. If $k\in F$, write $S=k+R$, where $R$ is the sum of the remaining positive terms; the same induction gives $R\ge0$, and order-compatibility yields $S\ge k$. Set $m:=S+1$. Since $1>0$ by [F2] and $S\ge0$, order-compatibility gives $m>S\ge0$, so $m>0$. If $m\in\Lambda$, then $m\in F$ and the preceding bound gives $S\ge m$, contradicting $m>S$. Thus every finite region omits a positive integer site.

If $M>N$, the triangle inequality and isometric inclusions give $\|H_M-H_N\|\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}2^{-n}<2^{-N}$. Thus $(H_N)$ is Cauchy in $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and converges to some $H\in\mathcal A$ by completion. Since each $H_N$ is self-adjoint and the adjoint extends continuously, $H^*=H$.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows from $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$.

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

Let $\mathcal A$ be the unital quasi-local spin C*-algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]], whose C*-structure uses Countable Choice as in [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. An **infinite algebraic state** is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ satisfying $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$.

For each finite region $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, the restriction $\omega|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ is a finite-matrix state. By [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], every positive normalized functional on a finite matrix algebra is represented by a unique density matrix. Define its **local density matrix** $\rho_\Lambda$ by

$$\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}(\rho_\Lambda A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda),$$

where $\rho_\Lambda=\rho_\Lambda^*\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}\rho_\Lambda=1$. For $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, the local densities are **consistent** when $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$, with partial trace characterized by its pairing against every $A\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. No density operator on a globally chosen Hilbert space is part of this definition.

This agrees with the canonical state convention of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]]: the finite restrictions have norm one by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], giving $|\omega(A)|\le\|A\|$ on the dense local algebra and hence on its completion; evaluation at the norm-one identity gives $\|\omega\|=1$. Conversely a canonical state has local restrictions with density matrices of trace one, since the finite norm formula and continuity on the dense local algebra imply $\|\omega\|=\omega(I)$. No global density representation is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice for the norm completion in [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]]. Let $\{\rho_\Lambda\}$ be positive trace-one matrices, one on each finite-region algebra $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], such that for every $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$ their partial traces agree: $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$. There is a unique infinite algebraic state $\omega$ on $\mathcal A$ whose restriction to each $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ is $A\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}(\rho_\Lambda A)$.

derivations.claim: Each $\rho_\Lambda$ is positive because it is a positive scalar multiple of the identity. Its trace is $q^{-|\Lambda|}\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(I_\Lambda)=1$ by [F1], including $\Lambda=\varnothing$ where $q^0=1$.

Put $\Delta=\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda$ and $r=|\Delta|$. For every $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$, the defining partial-trace pairing gives
$$\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda\!\left(A\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(I_\Lambda\otimes I_\Delta)\right)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'}((A\otimes I_\Delta)(I_\Lambda\otimes I_\Delta))=q^r\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(A),$$
where the last equality follows by summing the diagonal matrix coefficients over a configuration basis of $\mathcal H_\Delta$, which has $q^r$ elements. The trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}(AT)=0$ for every matrix $A$, taking $A=E_{ji}$ makes each entry $T_{ij}$ zero. Hence $\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(I_\Lambda\otimes I_\Delta)=q^rI_\Lambda$. Since $|\Lambda'|=|\Lambda|+r$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(\rho_{\Lambda'})=q^{-|\Lambda'|}q^rI_\Lambda=q^{-|\Lambda|}I_\Lambda=\rho_\Lambda.$$
Thus the family is consistent for every inclusion, including equality of regions ($r=0$).

By [F3], this family extends to a unique algebraic state $\omega$ on $\mathcal A$, and its local restriction is $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(\rho_\Lambda A)=q^{-|\Lambda|}\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$.

If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ for disjoint finite regions, choose orthonormal configuration bases $(e_i)$ and $(f_j)$ for their local Hilbert spaces. The tensor basis gives
$$\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda\cup\Delta}(A\otimes B)=\sum_{i,j}\langle Ae_i,e_i\rangle\langle Bf_j,f_j\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(A)\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(B).$$
Substitution into step 2.1 gives $\omega(AB)=\omega(A)\omega(B)$ on these disjoint local factors; this product formula follows from the displayed density family and is not an assumption about arbitrary states.

For $t=0$, both sides of the stated estimate vanish. For $t\ne0$, put $\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(t)\in\{-1,1\}$, and for $s$ between $0$ and $t$, set $G(s)=\alpha_s^{\Lambda'}(\alpha_{t-s}^{\Lambda}(A))$. Differentiating the finite matrix exponentials gives
$$G'(s)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\alpha_s^{\Lambda'}\!\left([H_{\Lambda'}-H_\Lambda,\alpha_{t-s}^{\Lambda}(A)]\right).$$
Indeed, the derivative of $\alpha_s^{\Lambda'}$ contributes $(i/\hbar)[H_{\Lambda'},\cdot]$, while differentiating $\alpha_{t-s}^{\Lambda}$ contributes $-(i/\hbar)[H_\Lambda,\cdot]$; the outer map $\alpha_s^{\Lambda'}$ is unitary conjugation and hence isometric. Integrating from $0$ to $t$, reversing the orientation for $t<0$, and using $u=|t-s|$ gives intermediate evolution time $t-s=\sigma u$. Expanding $H_{\Lambda'}-H_\Lambda$ therefore yields
$$\|\alpha_t^{\Lambda'}(A)-\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)\|\le\frac1{\hbar}\int_0^{|t|}\sum_{\substack{Z\subseteq\Lambda'\\Z\not\subseteq\Lambda}}\|[\Phi(Z),\alpha_{\sigma u}^\Lambda(A)]\|\,du.$$
Terms with $Z\cap\Lambda=\varnothing$ commute with $\alpha_{\sigma u}^\Lambda(A)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and contribute zero; only interaction sets crossing the boundary of $\Lambda$ remain.

For each crossing $Z$, apply [F2] to $A$ and $\Phi(Z)$ at the signed time $\sigma u$. Its bound depends on $|\sigma u|=u$, so the same positive integrand estimate holds for either sign of $t$. For any $y\in Z\setminus\Lambda$, choose $z\in Z$ minimizing the distance from $X$ to $Z$. Since $\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z\le R$, the triangle inequality gives $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})\le\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Z)+R$, so
$$e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Z)}\le e^{\mu R}e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})}.$$
Summing over every exterior $y$ overcounts each crossing interaction and therefore gives an upper bound. By the definition of $\kappa$,
$$\sum_{\substack{Z\subseteq\Lambda'\\Z\not\subseteq\Lambda\\Z\cap\Lambda\ne\varnothing}}\|\Phi(Z)\|e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Z)}\le\kappa e^{\mu R}\sum_{y\notin\Lambda}e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})}.$$
The displayed inequality is independent of $\Lambda'$; integrating the time factor in [F2] over an interval of length $|t|$ proves the claimed estimate.

For each $r\ge1$, the max-metric shell around one lattice site has $(2r+1)^d-(2r-1)^d$ sites. A finite union bound over $x\in X$ shows that $\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})}<\infty$, since a polynomial shell count is summable against $e^{-\mu r}$. Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $D=\dim H\ge1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. With composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity and the induced operator norm, $\mathcal B(H)$ is a nonzero unital complex C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

derivations.claim: Fix local $A\in\mathcal A_X$; if its displayed localization is empty, embed the scalar $A\in\mathbb C I$ into any one-site algebra, so take $X\ne\varnothing$. Thus the limit is independent of the exhaustion. The finite-matrix premise [A1] is supplied by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]; this proof uses that earlier result rather than reproving it.

Every finite-volume map is an isometric unital $*$-automorphism by conjugation with the unitary matrix exponential in [F4]. Norm limits of these complex-linear maps preserve addition and scalar multiplication, so the limit on local observables is complex-linear. The limits also preserve the unit, adjoints, products on local observables, and norm. For products, if local sequences $A_n\to A$ and $B_n\to B$ are used, submultiplicativity gives $\|A_nB_n-AB\|\le\|A_n\|\|B_n-B\|+\|A_n-A\|\|B\|$, so multiplication passes continuously to the completion; the adjoint is norm-continuous as well. By density of $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and the isometry bound, each $\alpha_t$ extends uniquely to an isometric complex-linear unital $*$-homomorphism of $\mathcal A$.

For local $A$, $\alpha_0(A)=\lim_\Lambda\alpha_0^\Lambda(A)=A$, and density extends $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$ to all $A\in\mathcal A$. For local $A$ and fixed $s,t$, choose local $C$ with $\|C-\alpha_t(A)\|<\varepsilon$. For large $\Lambda$, both $\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $\alpha_t(A)$ and $\alpha_s^\Lambda(C)$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $\alpha_s(C)$. By isometry, replacing $\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)$ with $C$ in $\alpha_s^\Lambda\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)$ costs at most $2\varepsilon$, and replacing $\alpha_s^\Lambda(C)$ by $\alpha_s(C)$ costs at most $\varepsilon$. $$\|\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)-A\|\le\frac{|t|}{\hbar}\|[H_\Lambda,A]\|\le\frac{2\kappa |X|\|A\|}{\hbar}|t|,$$

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1: a scalar observable in the empty local algebra embeds into any one-site algebra, so the nonempty-localization proof covers it.
Steps 1.1 and 3.1: if kappa=0 the finite-volume dynamics are identity maps and the limiting group is the identity.
Steps 1.2 and 3.1: q=1 gives scalar local algebras and the identity group, consistent with the norm-continuity estimate.
Steps 1.1 and 3.1: for R=0 the interactions are onsite and the boundary tail estimate still gives convergence; no cross-site propagation is used.
Steps 2.1 and 3.1: the group law includes t=0 and the increment estimate tends to zero from both signs of t.
Step 1.1 carries Countable Choice explicitly as A2 for the completion; the finite-volume exhaustion argument itself uses only finite unions.

boundaries.reason: This theorem constructs an exhaustion-independent automorphism group from bounded finite-range data; it does not characterize which groups arise from such interactions.

derivations.claim:
Every nonzero term $\Phi(Z)$ meeting $X$ has $Z\subseteq X^{+R}:=\{y\in\mathbb Z^d:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})\le R\}$, a finite set. There are finitely many subsets of $X^{+R}$, so
$$D_0(A):=\frac{i}{\hbar}\sum_{Z:\,Z\cap X\ne\varnothing}[\Phi(Z),A]$$
is a finite local sum. If $X\subseteq X'$, each term present in the sum for $X'$ but not for $X$ has support disjoint from $X$ and therefore commutes with $A\in\mathcal A_X$; hence both sums agree. For any two localization regions, compare each with their union to obtain the same conclusion. Thus $D_0(A)$ is independent of the chosen region. For every finite $\Lambda$ containing $X^{+R}$, finite-volume differentiation gives $\delta_\Lambda(A)=\frac{i}{\hbar}[H_\Lambda,A]=D_0(A)$ and
$$\alpha_t^\Lambda(A)-A=\int_0^t\alpha_s^\Lambda(D_0(A))\,ds.$$
Here the finite-dimensional integral is the coordinatewise Riemann integral; differentiating the finite exponential gives the integrand.

By [F2], $\alpha_s^\Lambda(A)$ and $\alpha_s^\Lambda(D_0(A))$ converge in norm uniformly on compact time intervals as $\Lambda$ exhausts the lattice. A continuous Banach-valued function has a Riemann integral because uniform continuity makes its Riemann sums Cauchy in the complete algebra; uniform convergence of the finite-volume integrands lets their integrals pass to the limit. This gives
$$\alpha_t(A)-A=\int_0^t\alpha_s(D_0(A))\,ds.$$
By [F1], $s\mapsto\alpha_s(D_0(A))$ is norm-continuous at $0$; the difference between its average over $[0,t]$ and its value at $0$ is at most $\sup_{|s|\le|t|}\|\alpha_s(D_0(A))-D_0(A)\|$, which tends to zero. Therefore $A\in D(\delta)$ and $\delta(A)=D_0(A)$.

Let $A_n\in D(\delta)$ with $A_n\to A$ and $\delta(A_n)\to B$ in norm. For $h=t/N$, the group law gives the exact telescope
$$\alpha_t(A_n)-A_n=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_{kh}(\alpha_h(A_n)-A_n)=h\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_{kh}(\delta(A_n))+h\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_{kh}\!\left(\frac{\alpha_h(A_n)-A_n}{h}-\delta(A_n)\right).$$
As $N\to\infty$, the second sum has norm at most $|t|\|(\alpha_h(A_n)-A_n)/h-\delta(A_n)\|$, which tends to zero by the definition of $\delta(A_n)$. The first sum is a Riemann sum for the continuous function $s\mapsto\alpha_s(\delta(A_n))$; its integral exists because the algebra is complete and the function is uniformly continuous on compact intervals. Hence $\alpha_t(A_n)-A_n=\int_0^t\alpha_s(\delta(A_n))\,ds$. Then $S(\rho)=-\sum_{\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\log\lambda_j\ge0$. For each positive $\lambda_j$, the scalar inequality $-\log x\ge1-x$ at $x=(D\lambda_j)^{-1}$ gives $\lambda_j\log(D\lambda_j)\ge\lambda_j-D^{-1}$. Summing over the positive eigenvalues yields $\log D-S(\rho)\ge1-r/D\ge0$, where $r$ is the rank. Thus $0\le S(\rho)\le m\log q$.

Translation invariance gives $\omega(\Phi(S+x))=\omega(\Phi(S))$. Therefore $\omega(H_{Q_L})/L^d=\sum_{S\in\mathscr S_\Phi}(N_S(L)/L^d)\omega(\Phi(S))\to\sum_{S\in\mathscr S_\Phi}\omega(\Phi(S))=u_\Phi(\omega)$.

By step 1.1 the last term is at most $|E_L|\log q$; if $E_L=\varnothing$, its scalar local density has entropy zero. Dividing by $L^d$ and taking the upper limit gives $\limsup_L S_{Q_L}(\omega)/L^d\le S_{Q_\ell}(\omega)/\ell^d$. Every ratio is at least their infimum over $\ell$, so the limit exists and equals that infimum.

On a fixed finite region, pointwise convergence of algebraic states gives convergence of all matrix coefficients of their density matrices by [F2] and [F4], hence convergence in operator norm. Ordered eigenvalues are continuous in that norm: the finite-dimensional min-max formula follows from an ordered orthonormal eigenbasis, since any $k$-dimensional subspace meets the span of the last $D-k+1$ eigenvectors, while the span of the first $k$ realizes the reverse bound; each Rayleigh quotient changes by at most the operator norm of the matrix difference. The function $-x\log x$, extended by $0$ at $x=0$, is continuous on $[0,1]$, so each $S_{Q_\ell}(\omega)$ is continuous under pointwise convergence. By [L2] every sequence in the full state space has a pointwise-convergent subsequence; the closed invariant subset is therefore sequentially compact.

A block meeting $\Lambda'$ but not $\Lambda$ is traced over completely and contributes $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\ell^{(k)})=1$. The partial trace of a tensor product factors by the same finite sums, so $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$. The state $\eta_\ell$ is invariant under shifts in $\ell\mathbb Z^d$ because these shifts permute identical block factors, using the covariance and action law [F6]–[F7]. Average its $\ell^d$ translates over residues $r\in\{0,\ldots,\ell-1\}^d$ to obtain $\omega_\ell=\ell^{-d}\sum_r\eta_\ell\circ\tau_r$. The group law in [F6] makes each lattice translation permute the residue classes modulo $\ell$, so $\omega_\ell\in\mathcal S_{\mathrm{inv}}$.

At each finite $L$, concavity in [L2] gives $S_{Q_L}(\omega_\ell)\ge\ell^{-d}\sum_r S_{Q_L}(\eta_\ell\circ\tau_r)$. derivations.claim: The finite spectral calculus [F6] defines $Z_n=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda_n}(e^{-\beta H_{\Lambda_n}})>0$ and the positive trace-one matrix $\rho_n=e^{-\beta H_{\Lambda_n}}/Z_n$. For any finite $X\subseteq\Gamma$, use the tensor factorization of [F1] on $X\cup\Lambda_n$ and set $\widehat\rho_X^{(n)}:=\operatorname{Tr}_{(X\cup\Lambda_n)\setminus X}\!\left(\rho_n\otimes q^{-|X\setminus\Lambda_n|}I_{X\setminus\Lambda_n}\right)$, where $\rho_n$ is placed on $\Lambda_n$ and each added site has density $q^{-1}I$. Tensor trace factorization shows that if $X\subseteq Y$, then tracing $\widehat\rho_Y^{(n)}$ over $Y\setminus X$ gives $\widehat\rho_X^{(n)}$: each removed added site contributes $\operatorname{Tr}(q^{-1}I)=1$, while any removed site in $\Lambda_n$ is traced from the same $\rho_n$ before or after adjoining the identity densities. By [F3], these local algebras sit in the norm-completed $\mathcal A$; thus the consistent family [F8] gives an algebraic state $\omega_n$ whose restriction to $\mathcal A_{\Lambda_n}$ is the finite Gibbs state.

Applying [F9] to $(\omega_n)$ gives at least one pointwise-convergent subsequence. Now fix any pointwise-convergent subsequence, write it as $(\omega_{n_k})$, and denote its state limit by $\omega$. The rest of the proof applies to this arbitrary convergent subsequence. This extraction is conditional on the exact interface [A2], not on the draft supplier's status label.

Fix local $A\in\mathcal A_X$ and $B\in\mathcal A_Y$. If $X=\varnothing$ or $Y=\varnothing$, the corresponding local algebra is $\mathbb C I$ by [F1], so embed that scalar observable in any one-site local algebra; the identity-preserving inclusion leaves both correlation functions unchanged. We may therefore take $X,Y\ne\varnothing$. Since $R<\infty$, the set $X^{+R}=\{y:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,\{y\})\le R\}$ is finite, so for all sufficiently large $k$, $X\cup Y\cup X^{+R}\subseteq\Lambda_{n_k}$. For those $k$, define the finite-volume entire function $F_k(z):=\omega_{n_k}\!\left(A\alpha_z^{\Lambda_{n_k}}(B)\right)$, where $\alpha_z^{\Lambda}(C):=e^{izH_\Lambda/\hbar}Ce^{-izH_\Lambda/\hbar}$. Because the restrictions of $\omega_{n_k}$ to $\mathcal A_{\Lambda_{n_k}}$ are the Gibbs states, [F7] gives both KMS boundary identities. On either boundary the finite trace state has norm one by [A2], so $|F_k|\le\|A\|\|B\|$ there. For any finite $\Lambda$, put $H=H_\Lambda=H^*$; diagonalizing this finite matrix shows that for $C\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $z=t+is\in S_b$, $0\le s\le b$, $\|\alpha_z^\Lambda(C)\|\le\|e^{izH/\hbar}\|\,\|C\|\,\|e^{-izH/\hbar}\|\le e^{2s\|H\|/\hbar}\|C\|\le e^{2\beta\|H\|}\|C\|$. Consequently each $F_k$ is bounded on $S_b$, with the crude bound $e^{2\beta\|H_{\Lambda_{n_k}}\|}\|A\|\|B\|$, which need not be uniform in $k$. This establishes the bounded-strip hypothesis for [F10]; its three-lines estimate uses the uniform boundary bounds and gives $|F_k(z)|\le\|A\|\|B\|$ throughout $S_b$.

On every compact real-time interval, [F4] gives $\alpha_t^{\Lambda_{n_k}}(B)\to\alpha_t(B)$ uniformly in norm. The orbit $K_T=\{A\alpha_t(B):|t|\le T\}$ is compact because $t\mapsto\alpha_t(B)$ is norm-continuous. For any $\varepsilon>0$, cover $K_T$ by finitely many norm-balls of radius $\varepsilon/4$, with centers $C_1,\dots,C_m\in K_T$. Pointwise convergence in [F9] makes $\max_j|\omega_{n_k}(C_j)-\omega(C_j)|<\varepsilon/2$ for large $k$; the norm-one bounds in [A2] make the difference at any point of $K_T$ at most this maximum plus $2(\varepsilon/4)$. Combining this with uniform convergence of the dynamics proves $F_k(t)\to\omega(A\alpha_t(B))$ uniformly for $|t|\le T$. The same finite-net estimate applied to $\{\alpha_t(B)A:|t|\le T\}$ proves uniform convergence of the upper edges to $\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)$.

For $B\in\mathcal A_Y$, [F5] gives the local generator value $\delta(B)$. Every interaction term meeting $Y$ is supported in the finite neighborhood $Y^{+R}$, so when $\Lambda_{n_k}$ contains $Y^{+R}$ the finite-volume generator satisfies $\delta_{n_k}(B)=\frac{i}{\hbar}[H_{\Lambda_{n_k}},B]=\delta(B)$. Differentiating the finite matrix exponential then gives $F_k'(z)=\omega_{n_k}\!\left(A\alpha_z^{\Lambda_{n_k}}(\delta(B))\right)$. Taking $C=\delta(B)$ in the finite-volume estimate of step 2.2 shows that for each $k$, $F_k'$ is bounded on $S_b$ by $e^{2\beta\|H_{\Lambda_{n_k}}\|}\|A\|\|\delta(B)\|$; this crude bound is finite but need not be uniform in $k$. The same finite Gibbs boundary identity [F7] applies to the pair $A,\delta(B)$. Its two real-time boundaries have modulus at most $\|A\|\|\delta(B)\|$ by the finite state norm bound [A2]. Since the required boundedness is now established, [F10] gives the uniform estimate $|F_k'(z)|\le L:=\|A\|\|\delta(B)\|$ on $S_b$. Integrating along the straight segment from $z$ to $w$ (which stays in the convex strip) yields $|F_k(w)-F_k(z)|\le L|w-z|$. Thus the functions are uniformly Lipschitz on the whole strip; if $L=0$, they are constant there.

For $m\ge1$ and $r\ge1$, let $G_{m,r}:=\left\{-m+\frac{2mj}{2^r}+i\frac{b\ell}{2^r}:0\le j,\ell\le2^r\right\}\subset[-m,m]+i[0,b]$. The union of these grids over $m,r$ is countable and dense in the closed strip: for any point in a fixed rectangle, choosing $r$ large makes each coordinate mesh $2m/2^r$ and $b/2^r$ arbitrarily small. Enumerate the grid points by increasing $m+r+j+\ell$, breaking ties lexicographically. For a bounded complex sequence, enclose its values in a fixed square $[-M,M]^2$ with $M>0$; subdivide the current square into four closed subsquares in a fixed lexicographic order and take the first containing infinitely many terms. Choose at each stage the least natural index larger than the previous one whose value lies in that square. At least one subsquare contains infinitely many terms because there are only four. The two coordinate intervals of the nested squares are closed, nested, and have lengths tending to zero; [F11] gives their unique common coordinates, and the selected values converge to that complex point. This defines a deterministic subsequence rule $E$ for each bounded complex sequence. Starting with $i_0(n)=n$, at grid point $g_j$ apply $E$ to $F_{i_{j-1}(n)}(g_j)$, obtaining a strictly increasing index map $s_j$, and set $i_j=i_{j-1}\circ s_j$. The deterministic recursion [F12] defines all $i_j$. The diagonal indices $k_j:=i_j(j)$ are strictly increasing; for each fixed $r$, the tail $(k_j)_{j\ge r}$ is a subsequence of $i_r$, so $F_{k_j}(g_r)$ converges. Thus one subsequence converges at every grid point without an additional choice principle.

Fix $m$ and $\varepsilon>0$. If $L=0$, convergence at a single grid point and constancy give uniform convergence on the rectangle $K_m=[-m,m]+i[0,b]$. If $L>0$, choose $r$ so that every point of $K_m$ is within $\varepsilon/(8L)$ of some point of $G_{m,r}$. The grid is finite, so the diagonal subsequence is uniformly Cauchy on that grid: for sufficiently large $p,q$, the values $F_{k_p},F_{k_q}$ differ by less than $\varepsilon/2$ at every grid point. At an arbitrary $z\in K_m$, choose a grid point $g$ within $\varepsilon/(8L)$; the two Lipschitz estimates from step 3.2 and the grid difference give $|F_{k_p}(z)-F_{k_q}(z)|\le L|z-g|+|F_{k_p}(g)-F_{k_q}(g)|+L|g-z|<\varepsilon$. Thus the subsequence is uniformly Cauchy on each $K_m$. Completeness of $\mathbb C$ gives a limit $F_{A,B}$ locally uniformly on the closed strip; step 2.2 gives $|F_{A,B}(z)|\le\|A\|\|B\|$.

Each $F_k$ is entire, and step 4.1 gives locally uniform convergence on every compact subset of $S_b^\circ$. By [F13], $F_{A,B}$ is holomorphic there; uniform convergence on compact rectangles including their horizontal edges makes it continuous on $S_b$. Step 3.1 gives uniform convergence of the two boundary sequences on every compact real interval, so the lower and upper boundaries of $F_{A,B}$ are respectively $\omega(A\alpha_t(B))$ and $\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)$ for every real $t$. Hence the stated local-pair strip conclusion holds.

For each integer $k$, define $\widetilde F(t+iy):=F(t+i(y-kb))$ when $kb\le y\le(k+1)b$. At a shared seam the lower and upper definitions agree by step 1.1, so the definition is single-valued. It is holomorphic away from the horizontal seams because there it is a translate of $F$ on its open strip.

Fix a point on a seam and choose a disk about it that meets no other seam. Let $T$ be any filled triangle in this disk. If $T$ crosses the seam, cut it along that horizontal line; the resulting at most two polygons can each be triangulated by joining one vertex to the other vertices. Every resulting small triangle lies in one of the two closed half-disks. If a small triangle touches the seam, translate it a distance $\epsilon>0$ into that half's open strip; for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$, its translate remains inside that strip and the translated contour integral is zero by [F2]. Uniform continuity of $\widetilde F$ on a compact neighborhood of the original contour implies the translated integrals converge to the original integral as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Hence each small triangle has zero integral. Summing their boundary integrals cancels shared edges with opposite orientations and yields $\int_{\partial T}\widetilde F(z)\,dz=0$. Triangles wholly on one side also have zero integral by [F2].

Step 3.1 applies to every triangle in the disk. The function $\widetilde F$ is continuous there by step 2.1, so [F3] makes it holomorphic across the seam in that disk. Away from seams it was already holomorphic by step 2.1; since the point on the seam was arbitrary, $\widetilde F$ is entire on $\mathbb C$.

Step 2.1 gives a global bound on $\widetilde F$, so [F4] makes it constant. Its restriction to the real axis is $g(t)=\omega(\alpha_t(B))$ by step 1.1, and at $t=0$ this is $\omega(B)$. Therefore $\omega(\alpha_t(B))=\omega(B)$ for every real $t$. Since $B$ was arbitrary, $\omega$ is invariant.

Direct multiplication gives $E_{ab}E_{cd}=\delta_{bc}E_{ad}$, and the exponential action gives $\alpha_z^H(E_{ij})=e^{iz(E_i-E_j)/\hbar}E_{ij}$ for $z\in\mathbb C$. This formula is used only for finite matrices, where the exponentials and scalar entries are entire.

Fix $i\ne j$ and apply [F1] to $A=E_{jj}$, $B=E_{ij}$. Since $E_{jj}E_{ij}=0$, the lower boundary of its KMS function is identically zero. By [F2] this KMS function vanishes on the whole strip. Its upper edge at $t=0$ is $\omega(E_{ij}E_{jj})=\omega(E_{ij})$, so $\omega(E_{ij})=0$ for every off-diagonal matrix unit.

For arbitrary $i,j$, set $\Delta=E_i-E_j$ and use [F1] with $A=E_{ji}$, $B=E_{ij}$. The lower edge is $e^{it\Delta/\hbar}\omega(E_{jj})$. The candidate $g(z)=e^{iz\Delta/\hbar}\omega(E_{jj})$ is entire and bounded on $0\le\operatorname{Im}z\le\beta\hbar$, since $|e^{i(t+iy)\Delta/\hbar}|=e^{-y\Delta/\hbar}$ and $y$ ranges over a compact interval. It has the same lower boundary as the KMS function, so [F2] identifies them. At the upper edge and $t=0$, the KMS identity is therefore $\omega(E_{ii})=e^{-\beta(E_i-E_j)}\omega(E_{jj})$.

The ratios in step 2.2 show that $e^{\beta E_i}\omega(E_{ii})$ is a constant $c$ independent of $i$.
