Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

derivations.claim: Applying the three tensor products in [F1] to the ordered basis $(00,01,10,11)$ gives the matrix with outer diagonal entries $1,1$, middle block $\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and all other entries zero.

The outer basis vectors are eigenvectors with eigenvalue $1$. The middle block sends $(01-10)/\sqrt2$ to $-3(01-10)/\sqrt2$ and $(01+10)/\sqrt2$ to $(01+10)/\sqrt2$. They are also orthogonal to $00,11$, so together the four nonzero eigenvectors form an orthonormal basis and give the full spectrum.

derivations.claim: Write $\rho=\begin{pmatrix}u&z\\\overline z&1-u\end{pmatrix}$, where $u\in\mathbb R$ because $\rho$ is Hermitian and the lower diagonal entry is fixed by $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Direct multiplication gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\sigma_j)=a_j$ for each $j$, so the entries of $\rho$ force uniqueness and each coefficient is real.

The constructed matrix is $\rho_a=\begin{pmatrix}p&w\\\overline w&q\end{pmatrix}$ with $p=(1+a_z)/2$, $q=(1-a_z)/2$, and $w=(a_x-ia_y)/2$. Its quadratic form at $(x,y)$ is $p|x|^2+w y\overline x+\overline w x\overline y+q|y|^2$. If $p>0$, completing the square gives $p|x+(w/p)y|^2+(q-|w|^2/p)|y|^2$, so positivity is equivalent to $q-|w|^2/p\ge0$. If $p=0$, positivity forces $w=0$ (otherwise choosing $y=1$ and $x=-tw$ for sufficiently large $t>0$ makes the quadratic form negative), and then is equivalent to $q\ge0$. Every Hermitian trace-one $2\times2$ matrix $\rho$ has a unique vector $a=(a_x,a_y,a_z)\in\mathbb R^3$ such that

For every separable two-qubit density matrix $\rho$ and exchange operator $C$ from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]],
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho C)\ge-1.$$

For $n\in\{\pm\mathbf e_x,\pm\mathbf e_y,\pm\mathbf e_z\}$, with the standard vectors from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], put $\rho_n=(I+n_x\sigma_x+n_y\sigma_y+n_z\sigma_z)/2$. The matrix
$$\rho_*:=\frac16\sum_{n\in\{\pm e_x,\pm e_y,\pm e_z\}}\rho_n\otimes\rho_{-n} =\frac14\left(I_4-\frac13C\right)$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: The projections $P_s,P_t$ are orthogonal and have ranks one and three by [F1]. Their weighted sum in the definition of $\rho_x$ is therefore positive, and its trace is $e^{3x}+3e^{-x}>0$; division normalizes its trace to one. By [F2] this is a two-qubit density matrix. Its singlet probability is $p_s=e^{3x}/(e^{3x}+3e^{-x})=e^{4x}/(e^{4x}+3)$.

Using the two eigenvalues in [F1], $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_xC)=-3p_s+(1-p_s)=1-4p_s=3(1-e^{4x})/(e^{4x}+3)=:c$. For $x\ge0$, $e^{4x}\ge1$, hence $-3\le c\le0$, and $c<-1$ exactly when $e^{4x}>3$, equivalently $x>(\log3)/4$ by [F7].
If $x>(\log3)/4$, step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_xC)=c<-1$. This contradicts the lower bound [F5] satisfied by every separable state, so $\rho_x$ is entangled.

If $0\le x\le(\log3)/4$, step 2.1 gives $-1\le c\le0$. The spectral projections in [F1] give $\rho_x=\tfrac14(I_4+(c/3)C)$; substituting [F6] yields $\rho_x=(-c)\rho_*+(1+c)I_4/4$. Both coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one; [F3] makes $I_2/2$ a qubit density matrix, so $I_4/4=(I_2/2)\otimes(I_2/2)$ is a product density matrix. Thus [F4] and [F6] make $\rho_x$ separable, including at equality $c=-1$.

citations.quote:
For a declared QSM model, let $I$ be a specified finite or countably infinite mode set with a fixed enumeration and let $\mathfrak h=\ell^2(I)$. The model assigns a nonzero separable complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ and declares whether it is a fixed-particle-number sector or the Fock space $\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$ of [[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. By that definition, $\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$ is the Hilbert direct sum of the symmetric or antisymmetric $n$-particle tensor sectors for $n\ge0$, including the vacuum sector $\mathbb C$. The assignment is a physical model assumption. The symmetric or antisymmetric sector is selected independently for bosons or fermions; this selection is not derived from the Fock construction or from a nonrelativistic spin-statistics theorem.

The words **pure preparation** and **state** have the exact meanings in clauses (i)–(iii) of [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]]: a pure preparation is a unit ray in $\mathcal H$, and a general state is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. These mathematical state definitions are used for the QSM Hilbert spaces declared above; the reference does not extend that NRQM postulate's fixed-particle-number physical scope to a variable-number grand-canonical system. The countable-choice hypothesis is [[def-countable-choice]].

A **sharp measurement** is specified by a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subseteq\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$, its declared physical unit, and its spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$, as in clauses (i)–(iii) of [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]. Here a projection-valued measure is a map from Borel sets to orthogonal projections with $E_A(\varnothing)=0$, $E_A(\mathbb R)=I$, $E_A(B\cap C)=E_A(B)E_A(C)$, and strong countable additivity. The adopted Born law is $\mu^A_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_A(B))$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R$; clauses (a)–(b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] give a probability measure under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For a finite unsharp measurement, a specified finite family of bounded effects $0\le F_a\le I$ with $\sum_aF_a=I$ has outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$, as in clause (iv) of [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]. The arbitrary self-adjoint spectral construction in that postulate also assumes the Axiom of Choice; any use inherits that exact mathematical premise.

An Axiom of Choice hypothesis [[def-axiom-of-choice]] accompanies the general self-adjoint spectral construction in P2. A model Hamiltonian is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H:D(H)\subseteq\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ representing energy, with its domain and energy unit declared. For a canonical preparation, write $H_N$ for the Hamiltonian on the declared fixed-number sector and adopt $\rho=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N}$ only when the spectral-calculus exponential has $0<Z=\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta H_N})<\infty$. For a grand-canonical preparation on the declared Fock space, let $|n|:=\sum_jn_j$ for a finite-support occupation configuration $n$ of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]] and define the particle-number operator by $N|n\rangle=|n||n\rangle$ on $D(N)=\{c\in\ell^2(\Omega_\pm):\sum_n|n|^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$, as in [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]]. Require $K_\mu$ to be a specified self-adjoint realization of $H-\mu N$ on a stated domain; self-adjointness of $H$ and $N$ separately does not by itself specify a self-adjoint domain for their difference. For $T>0$ in K, $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in J$^{-1}$, and chemical potential $\mu$ in J, adopt $\rho=\Xi^{-1}e^{-\beta K_\mu}$ only when $0<\Xi=\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta K_\mu})<\infty$.

For the additive diagonal Fock model, the trace and occupation statements of [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]] hold only under that lemma's mode-summability hypotheses and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Under those hypotheses its finite collections of grand-canonical mode occupations are independent. This independence is not asserted for interacting Hamiltonians; conditioning a product grand law on a fixed total number generally couples the modes.

If the spectral law $\mu^H_\rho$ has finite first absolute moment, define the model mean energy by $U(\rho;H):=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu^H_\rho(\lambda)$. If the nonzero eigenvalues $r_j$ of $\rho$, repeated with multiplicity, satisfy $\sum_j-r_j\log r_j<\infty$, define its von Neumann entropy by $S(\rho):=-k_B\sum_jr_j\log r_j$, with $0\log0:=0$; where finite, this is $-k_B\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)$. This postulate does not define Helmholtz free energy, grand potential, or other thermodynamic potentials; model-specific items define them with their own hypotheses. Identifying these quantities with measured macroscopic thermodynamic variables requires a separate physical bridge. No thermalization mechanism, empirical value, or law for a particular material is postulated here.

For two $2\times2$ matrices $A,B$, their tensor product acts by $(A\otimes B)(u\otimes v)=Au\otimes Bv$ and is extended linearly.

On elementary tensors this definition gives $(A_1\otimes B_1)(A_2\otimes B_2)=(A_1A_2)\otimes(B_1B_2)$. The product inner product also gives $(A\otimes B)^*=A^*\otimes B^*$: both sides have the adjoint pairing on elementary tensors, and those tensors span the product space.

Write $I_2:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ for the identity on $\mathbb C^2$, use $I:=I_2$ when its domain is clear, and set $I_4:=I_2\otimes I_2$. Define the everywhere-defined matrices

$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Define the dimensionless exchange matrix

$$C:=\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_x+\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_y+\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z.$$

Direct conjugate-transpose and multiplication of the displayed matrices give $\sigma_x^*=\sigma_x$, $\sigma_y^*=\sigma_y$, $\sigma_z^*=\sigma_z$, and $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I_2$. In the ordered tensor-product basis,

$$C=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\0&-1&2&0\\0&2&-1&0\\0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$

so $C^*=C$ as well. These matrices have their full finite-dimensional domains. For a finite matrix $A$, $\operatorname{tr}(A)$ denotes the sum of its diagonal entries in the displayed basis.

For $C$ from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], “$v$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$” has the exact meaning from [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]: $v\ne0$ and $Cv=\lambda v$. The singlet vector $s=(e_0\otimes e_1-e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$ has eigenvalue $-3$, and the three orthonormal triplet vectors $e_0\otimes e_0$, $(e_0\otimes e_1+e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$, and $e_1\otimes e_1$ have eigenvalue $1$. Here $\sqrt2$ is the unique positive square root supplied by [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. These four vectors are an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$.

Use $C$ from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], with singlet projection $P_s=|s\rangle\langle s|$ and triplet projection $P_t=I_4-P_s$, where $s=(e_0\otimes e_1-e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$. For each dimensionless $x\ge0$, define the finite two-qubit density matrix
$$\rho_x:=\frac{e^{3x}P_s+e^{-x}P_t}{e^{3x}+3e^{-x}}.$$
Then $\rho_x$ is separable exactly when $x\le(\log 3)/4$, and it is entangled exactly when $x>(\log 3)/4$. In particular, the equality state at $x=(\log 3)/4$ is separable.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open ([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]). A function $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is **real analytic on $U$** if, for every $c\in U$, there are a real $r>0$ and real coefficients $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that $N_r(c)\subseteq U$ and

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n\qquad(x\in N_r(c)).$$

The representing series must converge throughout this neighbourhood ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]], [[def-neighbourhood-r]]). The radius and coefficients may initially depend on $c$.
If a real power series centred at $c$ has radius $R>0$, then its sum is real analytic on $(c-R,c+R)$, interpreted as all of $\mathbb R$ when $R=+\infty$.

On open real domains, sums and products of real-analytic functions are real analytic. If $g$ is nonzero throughout the domain, then $f/g$ is real analytic. If $g:U\to V$ and $f:V\to\mathbb R$ are real analytic, then $f\circ g$ is real analytic on $U$.

Let $f$ be a real analytic map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, $f$ has a real analytic local inverse near $f(a)$. Let $P(x,y)$ be real analytic near $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^k$, $k\ge1$, with $P(a,b)=0$ and $D_yP(a,b)$ invertible. On sufficiently small neighborhoods its zero set is exactly the graph of a unique real analytic $y=g(x)$ with $g(a)=b$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: In the ordered basis $e_0e_0,e_0e_1,e_1e_0,e_1e_1$, the field operator $\sigma_z\otimes I+I\otimes\sigma_z$ has eigenvalues $2,0,0,-2$. The middle two basis vectors combine into the singlet and the $m=0$ triplet of [F2]; both have field eigenvalue $0$. The outer vectors are the $m=+1$ and $m=-1$ triplets, with field eigenvalues $2$ and $-2$. Thus the singlet and triplet basis from [F2] is a common orthonormal eigenbasis for $C$ and the field operator. The displayed real eigenvalues make $H_{J,h}$ self-adjoint on its full domain $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$; the singlet energy is $-3J$ and the triplet energies are $J-2h,J,J+2h$.

The canonical trace is the sum of the four positive weights associated with step 1.1. It is therefore finite and positive, and the adopted preparation [A1] gives the displayed partition function. At $h=0$ and $J>0$, setting $x=\beta J$ identifies its normalized state with $\rho_x$ in [F3], so that theorem gives the exact separability and entanglement alternatives, including the equality case.

Fix $J,h$ and let $E_{\min}$ be the least of the four energies from step 1.1, with multiplicity $g$. Write the other energies as $E_{\min}+\Delta_i$ with $\Delta_i>0$. After factoring out $e^{-\beta E_{\min}}$, the denominator is $D_\beta=g+\sum_i e^{-\beta\Delta_i}\to g$ and $1\le D_\beta\le4$. The Gibbs probability of each ground vector is $1/D_\beta$, so the total ground entropy tends to $-k_Bg(1/g)\log(1/g)=k_B\log g$. For an excited vector, $p_i=e^{-\beta\Delta_i}/D_\beta$ and $-p_i\log p_i=p_i(\beta\Delta_i+\log D_\beta)\le e^{-\beta\Delta_i}(\beta\Delta_i+\log4)$; this tends to zero by [F9], so the finite sum of excited entropy terms vanishes. At $h=0$, the triplet is the three-dimensional ground space for $J<0$, all four levels coincide for $J=0$, and the singlet is the unique ground state for $J>0$, giving the stated limits.

Fix $J,h$ and any $\beta_0>0$. For each of the four energies $E$ from step 1.1, the addition formula [F4] gives $e^{-\beta E}=e^{-\beta_0E}\sum_{n\ge0}[-E(\beta-\beta_0)]^n/n!$, a convergent power series about $\beta_0$. The four-term sum $Z(\beta)$ is therefore real analytic near $\beta_0$ by [F5]–[F6], and $Z(\beta_0)>0$ by step 2.1. Put $y_0=\log Z(\beta_0)$. By [F8], $\exp(y_0)=Z(\beta_0)$; by [F7], $\exp'(y_0)=\exp(y_0)=Z(\beta_0)\ne0$. The real analytic inverse theorem gives a local analytic inverse to $\exp$ near $Z(\beta_0)$, and [F8] identifies that inverse with $\log$. The composition clause of [F6] now makes $\log Z$ real analytic near $\beta_0$. Since $\beta_0$ was arbitrary, $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ is real analytic for every $\beta>0$: the identity and constant functions have local polynomial series, so the quotient clause of [F6] makes $\beta\mapsto\beta^{-1}$ analytic on this domain. Thus the finite-volume free energy has no singularity at the entanglement threshold.

For $J>0$, the lowest triplet energy is $J-2|h|$. It equals the singlet energy $-3J$ exactly at $|h|=2J$. The two energy levels can cross as parameters vary, but step 2.1 is a strictly positive finite sum of exponentials at every $\beta>0$, so this zero-temperature ground-space crossing creates no finite-temperature singularity.

boundaries.evidence: Proof 2.1 sums exactly four positive Boltzmann weights. In 2.2 the excited list can be empty at J=h=0; then D_beta=g=4 and the entropy is k_B log4.
step 2.2 covers J=0 at zero field, where all four levels are degenerate.
steps 1.1–2.1 include h=0 and its three triplet weights in the finite partition.
step 2.2 treats the ground-space multiplicities for J<0 and J=0.
steps 2.2–4.1 cover the zero-temperature limit and the finite-β field crossing.
Proof 1.1 gives all four energy vectors explicitly;2.2 chooses a minimum of that finite list and sums its multiplicities, requiring no infinite selection.
At h=0,J>0, Proof 2.1 invokes the exact dimer criterion: an entangled Gibbs state must have beta J>log(3)/4, since at or below equality [F3] supplies separability.
At h=0,J>0, beta J>log(3)/4 gives the entangled branch of [F3] in Proof 2.1; equality is explicitly separable.

At h=0, J>0 has one singlet ground state, J<0 has three triplet ground states, and J=0 has all four states degenerate; the entropy limits are k_B log 1, k_B log 3, and k_B log 4.

citations.quote:
For a declared QSM model, let $I$ be a specified finite or countably infinite mode set with a fixed enumeration and let $\mathfrak h=\ell^2(I)$. The model assigns a nonzero separable complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ and declares whether it is a fixed-particle-number sector or the Fock space $\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$ of [[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. By that definition, $\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$ is the Hilbert direct sum of the symmetric or antisymmetric $n$-particle tensor sectors for $n\ge0$, including the vacuum sector $\mathbb C$. The assignment is a physical model assumption. The symmetric or antisymmetric sector is selected independently for bosons or fermions; this selection is not derived from the Fock construction or from a nonrelativistic spin-statistics theorem.

The words **pure preparation** and **state** have the exact meanings in clauses (i)–(iii) of [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]]: a pure preparation is a unit ray in $\mathcal H$, and a general state is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. These mathematical state definitions are used for the QSM Hilbert spaces declared above; the reference does not extend that NRQM postulate's fixed-particle-number physical scope to a variable-number grand-canonical system. The countable-choice hypothesis is [[def-countable-choice]].

A **sharp measurement** is specified by a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subseteq\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$, its declared physical unit, and its spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$, as in clauses (i)–(iii) of [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]. Here a projection-valued measure is a map from Borel sets to orthogonal projections with $E_A(\varnothing)=0$, $E_A(\mathbb R)=I$, $E_A(B\cap C)=E_A(B)E_A(C)$, and strong countable additivity. The adopted Born law is $\mu^A_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_A(B))$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R$; clauses (a)–(b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] give a probability measure under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For a finite unsharp measurement, a specified finite family of bounded effects $0\le F_a\le I$ with $\sum_aF_a=I$ has outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$, as in clause (iv) of [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]. The arbitrary self-adjoint spectral construction in that postulate also assumes the Axiom of Choice; any use inherits that exact mathematical premise.

An Axiom of Choice hypothesis [[def-axiom-of-choice]] accompanies the general self-adjoint spectral construction in P2. A model Hamiltonian is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H:D(H)\subseteq\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ representing energy, with its domain and energy unit declared. For a canonical preparation, write $H_N$ for the Hamiltonian on the declared fixed-number sector and adopt $\rho=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N}$ only when the spectral-calculus exponential has $0<Z=\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta H_N})<\infty$. For a grand-canonical preparation on the declared Fock space, let $|n|:=\sum_jn_j$ for a finite-support occupation configuration $n$ of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]] and define the particle-number operator by $N|n\rangle=|n||n\rangle$ on $D(N)=\{c\in\ell^2(\Omega_\pm):\sum_n|n|^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$, as in [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]]. Require $K_\mu$ to be a specified self-adjoint realization of $H-\mu N$ on a stated domain; self-adjointness of $H$ and $N$ separately does not by itself specify a self-adjoint domain for their difference. For $T>0$ in K, $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in J$^{-1}$, and chemical potential $\mu$ in J, adopt $\rho=\Xi^{-1}e^{-\beta K_\mu}$ only when $0<\Xi=\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta K_\mu})<\infty$.

For the additive diagonal Fock model, the trace and occupation statements of [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]] hold only under that lemma's mode-summability hypotheses and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Under those hypotheses its finite collections of grand-canonical mode occupations are independent. This independence is not asserted for interacting Hamiltonians; conditioning a product grand law on a fixed total number generally couples the modes.

If the spectral law $\mu^H_\rho$ has finite first absolute moment, define the model mean energy by $U(\rho;H):=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu^H_\rho(\lambda)$. If the nonzero eigenvalues $r_j$ of $\rho$, repeated with multiplicity, satisfy $\sum_j-r_j\log r_j<\infty$, define its von Neumann entropy by $S(\rho):=-k_B\sum_jr_j\log r_j$, with $0\log0:=0$; where finite, this is $-k_B\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)$. This postulate does not define Helmholtz free energy, grand potential, or other thermodynamic potentials; model-specific items define them with their own hypotheses. Identifying these quantities with measured macroscopic thermodynamic variables requires a separate physical bridge. No thermalization mechanism, empirical value, or law for a particular material is postulated here.

Use the usual complex field $\mathbb C$; its scalar metric is $d_{\mathbb C}(z,w)=|z-w|$ from [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. On $\mathbb C^2$, use the standard basis $e_0=(1,0)$, $e_1=(0,1)$ and inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=x_0\overline{y_0}+x_1\overline{y_1}$, linear in its first variable. On $\mathbb R^3$, define $a\cdot b:=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z$, $|a|:=\sqrt{a\cdot a}$ using the unique nonnegative square root from [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and the standard unit vectors $\mathbf e_x=(1,0,0)$, $\mathbf e_y=(0,1,0)$, and $\mathbf e_z=(0,0,1)$.

For a finite complex matrix $A=(a_{jk})$, define its adjoint by $A^*:=(\overline{a_{kj}})_{j,k}=\overline A^{\,T}$, where the bar is entrywise complex conjugation from [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and $T$ is transpose. The matrix is **Hermitian** exactly when $A=A^*$. For vectors $u,v$ in a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$ with the stated linear-first convention, define the rank-one operator $|u\rangle\langle v|:V\to V$ by

$$|u\rangle\langle v|(x):=\langle x,v\rangle u.$$

This action is linear in $x$ under the linear-first convention.

Use the ordered tensor-product basis $(e_0\otimes e_0,e_0\otimes e_1,e_1\otimes e_0,e_1\otimes e_1)$ of $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$. Its inner product is the linear-first product inner product, specified on elementary tensors by $\langle u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'\rangle=\langle u,u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly. For two $2\times2$ matrices $A,B$, their tensor product acts by $(A\otimes B)(u\otimes v)=Au\otimes Bv$ and is extended linearly.

On elementary tensors this definition gives $(A_1\otimes B_1)(A_2\otimes B_2)=(A_1A_2)\otimes(B_1B_2)$. The product inner product also gives $(A\otimes B)^*=A^*\otimes B^*$: both sides have the adjoint pairing on elementary tensors, and those tensors span the product space.

Write $I_2:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ for the identity on $\mathbb C^2$, use $I:=I_2$ when its domain is clear, and set $I_4:=I_2\otimes I_2$. Define the everywhere-defined matrices

$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Define the dimensionless exchange matrix

$$C:=\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_x+\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_y+\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z.$$

Direct conjugate-transpose and multiplication of the displayed matrices give $\sigma_x^*=\sigma_x$, $\sigma_y^*=\sigma_y$, $\sigma_z^*=\sigma_z$, and $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I_2$. In the ordered tensor-product basis,

$$C=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\0&-1&2&0\\0&2&-1&0\\0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$

so $C^*=C$ as well. These matrices have their full finite-dimensional domains. For a finite matrix $A$, $\operatorname{tr}(A)$ denotes the sum of its diagonal entries in the displayed basis.

Fix $\beta>0$ and $J,h\in\mathbb R$. For $N\ge2$, let $s_i\in\{-1,1\}$, $s_{N+1}=s_1$, $H_N(s)=-J\sum_{i=1}^Ns_is_{i+1}-h\sum_{i=1}^Ns_i$, and $Z_N=\sum_se^{-\beta H_N(s)}$. Define $\cosh x:=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$, $\sinh x:=(e^x-e^{-x})/2$, and $T_{s,t}:=e^{\beta Jst+\beta h(s+t)/2}$. Then $Z_N=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N$, where $\lambda_\pm=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)\pm\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}$ and $\lambda_+>|\lambda_-|$. Therefore $N^{-1}\log Z_N\to\log\lambda_+$. On every compact subset of $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$ in $(\beta,J,h)$, the limit and its derivatives of every fixed finite order converge uniformly. This is a result for the specified one-dimensional periodic two-state model only.

Use the real exponential $\exp(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!$ of [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and the hyperbolic functions $\cosh x=(\exp x+\exp(-x))/2$, $\sinh x=(\exp x-\exp(-x))/2$. Define $\tanh x:=\sinh x/\cosh x$; the denominator is positive for every real $x$. Let $N\ge2$, let $\Omega_N=\{-1,1\}^N$ with cyclic indexing $s_{N+1}=s_1$, and count exactly the $N$ indexed periodic bonds (so $N=2$ has two bonds). For coupling $J\ge0$ in joules, zero field, and $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, adopt the finite canonical law
$$\mathbb P_N(s)=Z_N^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta J\sum_{i=1}^Ns_is_{i+1}\right).$$
Set $t=\tanh(\beta J)\in[0,1)$. For $1\le r\le N-1$,
$$\mathbb E_N[s_i]=0,\qquad \mathbb E_N[s_i s_{i+r}]=\frac{t^r+t^{N-r}}{1+t^N}.$$
For each fixed positive integer separation $r$ and $N\to\infty$, the correlation tends to $t^r$, with absolute error at most $t^{N-r}+t^{N+r}$. When $J>0$, define the limiting correlation length $\xi>0$ in lattice spacings as the unique number satisfying $t^r=e^{-r/\xi}$ for every positive integer separation $r$; equivalently, $\xi=-1/\log t$. The zero-field susceptibility per spin, defined by $\chi_N:=N^{-1}\partial_h\mathbb E_{N,h}[\sum_i s_i]|_{h=0}$ for the field-coupled law with energy $-\!J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}-h\sum_i s_i$, where the field parameter $h\in\mathbb R$ is in joules, has limit
$$\chi_\infty=\beta\frac{1+t}{1-t}.$$
Both $\chi_N$ and $\chi_\infty$ have units J$^{-1}$ per spin (the spin variables are dimensionless).
Define the finite-ring model free energy by $F_N:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N$ and its limiting free energy per spin, when the limit exists, by $f_\infty:=\lim_{N\to\infty}F_N/N$. Then $f_\infty=-\beta^{-1}\log(2\cosh(\beta J))$, analytic at every finite positive temperature. No statement is made for arbitrary one-dimensional interactions.

Fix $N\ge1$ and $\epsilon>0$ joules. Let $\Omega_N=A_N\sqcup B_N\sqcup C_N$ be disjoint finite sectors with $|A_N|=1$, $|B_N|=1$, and $|C_N|=4^N$, and define the energy $H_N$ to be $0$, $N\epsilon$, and $2N\epsilon$ on those sectors, respectively. The model is global and size-dependent. Here *product-additive* means that one fixed finite one-site alphabet $\Gamma$ supplies $\Omega_N=\Gamma^N$ for every $N$, and one fixed one-site energy function $h:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ (with values measured in joules) satisfies $H_N(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_N)=\sum_{i=1}^Nh(\gamma_i)$. The present family is non-product-additive; no local, short-range, or fluid interpretation is assumed.

Use counting measure on each $\Omega_N$ as the reference measure, so every individual state has weight one. For a real inverse-energy parameter $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, define the finite exponential-tilt probability by
$$Z_N(\beta)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_N}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon},\qquad P_{\beta,N}(\omega)=\frac{e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}}{Z_N(\beta)}.$$
For $\beta>0$ this is the adopted canonical preparation. For $\beta\le0$ it is only the same finite counting formula used algebraically; no negative-temperature reservoir is asserted. Also, for a shell half-width $\Delta$ in joules with $0\le\Delta<N\epsilon$, define $\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}=\{\omega:|H_N(\omega)-N\epsilon|\le\Delta\}$ and give it the uniform counting probability $Q_{N,\Delta}(\omega)=|\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}|^{-1}$ for $\omega\in\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$.

For every real $\beta$, the finite exponential-tilt probability of $B_N$ obeys
$$P_{\beta,N}(B_N)\le\frac{1}{2^{N+1}+1},$$
whereas the shell probability of $B_N$ is $1$. Define the dimensionless normalized log partition function $\psi_N(\beta)=N^{-1}\log Z_N(\beta)$. Then
$$\psi_N(\beta)\longrightarrow\psi(\beta):=\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\},\qquad 0\le\psi_N(\beta)-\psi(\beta)\le\frac{\log3}{N}.$$
For $\beta>0$, define the canonical mean energy per member by $u_N(\beta):=N^{-1}\mathbb E_{P_{\beta,N}}[H_N]$ and, when the limit exists, set $u(\beta):=\lim_{N\to\infty}u_N(\beta)$. The corner occurs at the positive inverse temperature $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon$. The limit $u(\beta)$ exists for every $\beta>0$ and equals $2\epsilon$ for $0<\beta<\beta_c$, $\epsilon$ at $\beta=\beta_c$, and $0$ for $\beta>\beta_c$. In this item, a **first-order transition point** means a positive-$\beta$ point where $u$ has finite but unequal one-sided limits; thus the jump at $\beta_c$ is first order under this explicit convention. Every finite-$N$ function $\psi_N$ is real analytic. This is one explicit global finite-state countermodel, not a universal criterion for phase transitions or ensemble equivalence in short-range matter.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open ([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]). A function $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is **real analytic on $U$** if, for every $c\in U$, there are a real $r>0$ and real coefficients $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that $N_r(c)\subseteq U$ and

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n\qquad(x\in N_r(c)).$$

The representing series must converge throughout this neighbourhood ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]], [[def-neighbourhood-r]]). The radius and coefficients may initially depend on $c$.
If a real power series centred at $c$ has radius $R>0$, then its sum is real analytic on $(c-R,c+R)$, interpreted as all of $\mathbb R$ when $R=+\infty$.

On open real domains, sums and products of real-analytic functions are real analytic. If $g$ is nonzero throughout the domain, then $f/g$ is real analytic. If $g:U\to V$ and $f:V\to\mathbb R$ are real analytic, then $f\circ g$ is real analytic on $U$.

derivations.claim: Each $Z_i$ is diagonal in the orthonormal product basis $|s_1,\ldots,s_N\rangle$, with eigenvalue $s_i$. Therefore $H_N^{\mathrm q}|s\rangle=H_N^{\mathrm{cl}}(s)|s\rangle$ with real eigenvalues. This diagonal representation proves self-adjointness on the full domain $D(H_N^{\mathrm q})=\mathcal H_N$. The finite canonical trace is the sum of these positive weights by [F6], so $Z_N^{\mathrm q}=\sum_s e^{-\beta H_N^{\mathrm{cl}}(s)}$ and the diagonal Gibbs probability of each $|s\rangle$ equals the classical probability of $s$. This proves the claimed finite correspondence without interpreting off-diagonal quantum observables classically.

The direct sum in the second model has multiplicities $1,1,4^N$, so summing its three energy weights gives $Z_N^{\mathrm g}=1+x+4^Nx^2$ where $x=e^{-\beta N\epsilon}>0$. Its real diagonal entries show that $H_N^{\mathrm g}$ is self-adjoint on the stated full domain. Since $(1-2^Nx)^2\ge0$, $1+4^Nx^2\ge2^{N+1}x$, whence the middle-sector probability $x/Z_N^{\mathrm g}\le(2^{N+1}+1)^{-1}$. For $0\le\Delta<N\epsilon$, the sectors at energies $0$ and $2N\epsilon$ lie exactly $N\epsilon$ from the middle energy; the only basis vector in the shell is $|B\rangle$, so $\rho_{N,\Delta}^{\mathrm{shell}}=|B\rangle\langle B|$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{N,\Delta}^{\mathrm{shell}}|B\rangle\langle B|)=1$. Identifying the three CSM sectors with $|A\rangle$, $|B\rangle$, and the final product-basis vectors preserves each energy and multiplicity; for every $\beta>0$ it therefore preserves the canonical sector weights and mean energy per member. [F4] These are the same finite-model values, now realized on the displayed quantum Hilbert space.

The definitions in [F5] agree with the exponential definitions of $\sinh$ and $\cosh$ in [F2] and of $\tanh$ in [F3]; in particular $\cosh(\beta J)>0$, so the zero-field correlation parameter $\tanh(\beta J)$ is defined. Applying [F2] to this identical finite energy function gives the displayed transfer eigenvalues, limiting normalized log partition, and compact-uniform derivative convergence. In the restricted case $J\ge0,h=0$, the equality of diagonal probabilities from step 1.1 transports each $\sigma_z$ correlation to the classical spin correlation in [F3], under exactly that supplier's hypotheses.

Put $M_N=\max\{1,4^Nx^2\}$. If $x\le1$, then $x\le M_N$; if $x>1$, then $4^Nx^2\ge x$ for $N\ge1$. Hence $M_N\le Z_N^{\mathrm g}\le3M_N$. By the logarithm product law in [F6], $N^{-1}\log M_N=\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\}$, so taking logarithms gives the stated error bound and limit. Since $\log4=2\log2$, the two branches meet at $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon$. By [F4] and the exact finite-weight identification in step 1.2, the limits of the quantum mean energy per member are $2\epsilon$ for $0<\beta<\beta_c$, $\epsilon$ at $\beta_c$, and $0$ for $\beta>\beta_c$. Fix $N$ and the other model parameters. The Ising partition function is the finite sum $\sum_{s\in\{-1,1\}^N}\exp(-\beta H_N^{\mathrm{cl}}(s))$, and the global partition function is the finite sum of its three sector weights. Each energy in these sums is fixed as a function of $\beta$, so the map $\beta\mapsto-\beta E$ is affine and real analytic. The exponential is a power-series sum and therefore real analytic by [F6]–[F7]; composing with the affine maps and taking finite sums preserves real analyticity by [F7]. Thus each fixed-parameter finite-$N$ partition function is real analytic on $\mathbb R$, in particular at every positive canonical parameter. For a declared QSM model, let $I$ be a specified finite or countably infinite mode set with a fixed enumeration and let $\mathfrak h=\ell^2(I)$. The model assigns a nonzero separable complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ and declares whether it is a fixed-particle-number sector or the Fock space $\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$ of [[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. By that definition, $\mathcal F_\pm(\mathfrak h)$ is the Hilbert direct sum of the symmetric or antisymmetric $n$-particle tensor sectors for $n\ge0$, including the vacuum sector $\mathbb C$. The assignment is a physical model assumption. The symmetric or antisymmetric sector is selected independently for bosons or fermions; this selection is not derived from the Fock construction or from a nonrelativistic spin-statistics theorem.

The words **pure preparation** and **state** have the exact meanings in clauses (i)–(iii) of [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]]: a pure preparation is a unit ray in $\mathcal H$, and a general state is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. These mathematical state definitions are used for the QSM Hilbert spaces declared above; the reference does not extend that NRQM postulate's fixed-particle-number physical scope to a variable-number grand-canonical system. The countable-choice hypothesis is [[def-countable-choice]].

A **sharp measurement** is specified by a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subseteq\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$, its declared physical unit, and its spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$, as in clauses (i)–(iii) of [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]. Here a projection-valued measure is a map from Borel sets to orthogonal projections with $E_A(\varnothing)=0$, $E_A(\mathbb R)=I$, $E_A(B\cap C)=E_A(B)E_A(C)$, and strong countable additivity. The adopted Born law is $\mu^A_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_A(B))$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R$; clauses (a)–(b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] give a probability measure under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For a finite unsharp measurement, a specified finite family of bounded effects $0\le F_a\le I$ with $\sum_aF_a=I$ has outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$, as in clause (iv) of [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]. The arbitrary self-adjoint spectral construction in that postulate also assumes the Axiom of Choice; any use inherits that exact mathematical premise.

An Axiom of Choice hypothesis [[def-axiom-of-choice]] accompanies the general self-adjoint spectral construction in P2. A model Hamiltonian is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H:D(H)\subseteq\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ representing energy, with its domain and energy unit declared. For a canonical preparation, write $H_N$ for the Hamiltonian on the declared fixed-number sector and adopt $\rho=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N}$ only when the spectral-calculus exponential has $0<Z=\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta H_N})<\infty$. For a grand-canonical preparation on the declared Fock space, let $|n|:=\sum_jn_j$ for a finite-support occupation configuration $n$ of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]] and define the particle-number operator by $N|n\rangle=|n||n\rangle$ on $D(N)=\{c\in\ell^2(\Omega_\pm):\sum_n|n|^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$, as in [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]]. Require $K_\mu$ to be a specified self-adjoint realization of $H-\mu N$ on a stated domain; self-adjointness of $H$ and $N$ separately does not by itself specify a self-adjoint domain for their difference. For $T>0$ in K, $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in J$^{-1}$, and chemical potential $\mu$ in J, adopt $\rho=\Xi^{-1}e^{-\beta K_\mu}$ only when $0<\Xi=\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta K_\mu})<\infty$.

For the additive diagonal Fock model, the trace and occupation statements of [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]] hold only under that lemma's mode-summability hypotheses and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Under those hypotheses its finite collections of grand-canonical mode occupations are independent. This independence is not asserted for interacting Hamiltonians; conditioning a product grand law on a fixed total number generally couples the modes.

If the spectral law $\mu^H_\rho$ has finite first absolute moment, define the model mean energy by $U(\rho;H):=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu^H_\rho(\lambda)$. If the nonzero eigenvalues $r_j$ of $\rho$, repeated with multiplicity, satisfy $\sum_j-r_j\log r_j<\infty$, define its von Neumann entropy by $S(\rho):=-k_B\sum_jr_j\log r_j$, with $0\log0:=0$; where finite, this is $-k_B\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)$. This postulate does not define Helmholtz free energy, grand potential, or other thermodynamic potentials; model-specific items define them with their own hypotheses. Identifying these quantities with measured macroscopic thermodynamic variables requires a separate physical bridge. No thermalization mechanism, empirical value, or law for a particular material is postulated here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$

In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. $$

$$

Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. Fix $n\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb R^n$. A real analytic germ at $a$ is an equivalence class of real functions agreeing on a neighborhood of $a$, represented on some polydisc $|x_i-a_i|<r_i$, $r_i>0$, by an absolutely convergent series $f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^n}c_\alpha(x-a)^\alpha$ with real coefficients. Here $0\in\mathbb N$, $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, and $c_\alpha=D^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$. A vector germ has a finite positive number of such components, with a common polydisc obtained by taking coordinatewise minima of their radii.

The multi-index convention and absolute convergence are those of [[def-multivariable-power-series]]; for $n=1$ this agrees with [[def-real-analytic-function]]. The same coefficients define the complexification. Indeed choose a positive real polyradius $s<r$; absolute convergence at $a+s$ bounds $|c_\alpha|s^\alpha$ uniformly. [[thm-power-series-define-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables]] therefore gives a holomorphic sum on the complex $s$-polydisc and the displayed derivative formula. Restriction to the real slice recovers $f$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ be sequences of reals and suppose there is
$K \in \mathbb{N}$ with

$$0 \;\le\; a_k \;\le\; b_k \qquad \text{for all } k \ge K .$$

Then:

1. if $\sum b_k$ converges then $\sum a_k$ converges ([[def-series]]);
2. if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sum b_k$ diverges.

The same statement holds verbatim for series with a general starting index $m$,
applied to the shifted sequences of [[def-series]].

The hypothesis is on the terms from some index on, not on all of them: finitely
many terms of either sequence may violate it, or be negative, without affecting
the conclusion. What may not be dropped is nonnegativity of $(a_k)$ from that
index on.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$, a polyradius $r$, a real $M\ge0$ and
coefficients $c:\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ with

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}\qquad\text{for every multi-index }\alpha.$$

Then:

1. for every $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
   $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
   $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$, so its sum $g$ is defined on
   $\Delta_r(a)$;
2. $g$ is holomorphic on $\Delta_r(a)$, with
   $$Dg(z)h=\sum_{k<m}b_k(z)h_k,\qquad b_k(z)=\sum_{\alpha}\alpha_k\,c_\alpha(z-a)^{\alpha-e_k},$$
   the $k$th series running over the multi-indices with $\alpha_k\ge1$ and
   converging absolutely on $\Delta_r(a)$; equivalently
   $\partial_{z_k}g=b_k$;
3. for every $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the derived coefficients
   $\alpha_kc_\alpha$, re-indexed as a power series, obey a bound of the same
   shape on the polyradius $\theta r$, so the differentiation may be iterated;
   and every iterated complex partial derivative
   $\partial^\beta_zg:=\partial_{z_0}^{\beta_0}\cdots\partial_{z_{m-1}}^{\beta_{m-1}}g$
   exists on $\Delta_r(a)$ with
   $$\partial^\beta_zg(a)=\beta!\,c_\beta .$$

Every absolutely convergent complex series converges, and every rearrangement has the same sum. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]], [[thm-absolute-convergence-in-rn]].

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $w:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $X_a:X\to\mathbb R$ ($1\le a\le r$) be measurable, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)$, define $\theta\cdot X(x):=\sum_{a=1}^r\theta_aX_a(x)$. Set $Z(\theta):=\int w\exp(\theta\cdot X)\,d\mu$ and assume $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$ on $U$. Suppose for every compact $K\subset U$ there is an integrable $G_K\ge0$ such that $w e^{\theta\cdot X}(1+\sum_a|X_a|^2)\le G_K$ pointwise for all $\theta\in K$. For the normalized density $p_\theta=w e^{\theta\cdot X}/Z(\theta)$, define $\mathbb E_\theta Y:=\int Yp_\theta\,d\mu$ when integrable and $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b):=\mathbb E_\theta[(X_a-\mathbb E_\theta X_a)(X_b-\mathbb E_\theta X_b)]$. Then $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$ and $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b)$. Thus the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite. This is a mathematical model identity; it assumes no independence or absence of correlations.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim: The one-mode case of [F1] identifies the number basis with the standard basis of $\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)$, whose finite-support span is dense. For any real diagonal multiplier with entries $\lambda_n$, testing the adjoint identity on each basis vector forces the adjoint image to have coordinates $\lambda_nc_n$, so its adjoint domain is contained in $\{c:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$. Conversely, on that weighted domain [F11] makes the pairing bounded and identifies the adjoint action with the same multiplier. Thus its maximal diagonal domain is self-adjoint. Applying this calculation to $E_B(n)$, $n$, and $K_B(n)$ establishes the three domains in the Statement.

Consecutive Bose grand energies on the number basis [F1] satisfy $K_B(n+1)-K_B(n)=\epsilon-\mu+Un$, a strictly increasing affine sequence in $n$. It is positive at every $n\ge0$ when $\mu<\epsilon$, so $0$ uniquely minimizes. For $r\ge1$, it is negative through $n=r-1$ and positive from $n=r$ exactly when $\epsilon+U(r-1)<\mu<\epsilon+Ur$, so $r$ uniquely minimizes. At $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$, the increment at $n=r$ is zero while all earlier increments are negative and all later increments positive; exactly $r,r+1$ minimize.

The four Fermi basis states have grand energies $0$, $\epsilon-\mu-h$, $\epsilon-\mu+h$, and $2(\epsilon-\mu)+U$, respectively. Summing their four positive weights gives the displayed $\Xi_F$, and summing $n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow$ or $n_\uparrow n_\downarrow$ against those weights gives the stated mean and double-occupation probability. The state is well-defined because this is a finite positive sum, as required by [A1] and [F3].

For fixed real $a$ and $n\ge0$, completing the square gives $|a|n\le Un^2/4+a^2/U$. Hence, for $P_a(n)=Un^2/2+an$, $Un^2/4\le|P_a(n)|+a^2/U$, so $n^2\le(4/U)|P_a(n)|+4a^2/U^2$. Since $|P_a(n)|\le1+P_a(n)^2$, this bound shows that the maximal diagonal domain associated with either quadratic sequence $E_B(n)$ or $K_B(n)$ is contained in $D(N_B)$. On $D(H_B)$, $K_Bc=H_Bc-\mu N_Bc$ is square-summable, so $D(H_B)\subseteq D(K_B)$; on $D(K_B)$, $H_Bc=K_Bc+\mu N_Bc$ is square-summable, so $D(K_B)\subseteq D(H_B)$. Thus $D(H_B)=D(K_B)\subseteq D(N_B)$, and the operator sum $H_B-\mu N_B$, whose domain is $D(H_B)\cap D(N_B)$, equals $K_B$ on its maximal domain.

In a strict interval with unique minimizer $r$, let $\delta$ be the smaller positive adjacent energy gap from $r$ (use only the upward gap when $r=0$). For $n>r$, the gap is a sum of increments from step 1.2, each at least the upward gap at $r$; for $n<r$, it is a sum of reversed increments, each at least the downward gap from $r-1$. Hence $K_B(n)-K_B(r)\ge\delta|n-r|$. The total relative excited weight is therefore at most $2\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta\delta\ell}=2e^{-\beta\delta}/(1-e^{-\beta\delta})$, which tends to zero. At a boundary $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$, the increments are $K_B(n+1)-K_B(n)=U(n-r)$, so exactly $r,r+1$ minimize. To the right, $K_B(r+1+\ell)-K_B(r+1)=U(1+\cdots+\ell)\ge U\ell$; to the left, $K_B(r-\ell)-K_B(r)=U(1+\cdots+\ell)\ge U\ell$ whenever $r\ge\ell$. Thus the total relative excited weight is at most $2\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta U\ell}=2e^{-\beta U}/(1-e^{-\beta U})$. The normalized Gibbs probabilities from [F3] therefore concentrate on the unique number state in a strict interval, or tend to $1/2,1/2$ on the adjacent pair at a boundary.

Put $a=\epsilon-\mu-U/2$. Completing the square gives $K_B(n)=\frac U4n^2+\frac U4(n+2a/U)^2-a^2/U\ge\frac U4n^2-a^2/U$. For $n\ge1$, $n^2\ge n$, so $e^{-\beta K_B(n)}\le e^{\beta a^2/U}q^n$ with $q=e^{-\beta U/4}$. Since $\beta U/4>0$, [F5] gives $0<q<1$, and [F6] makes the geometric upper bound summable. The $n=0$ term is $1$, so $0<\Xi_B<\infty$ and [A1], [F3] give a well-defined normalized grand state for the exact operator $H_B-\mu N_B=K_B$ from step 2.1. The free-mode product trace formula in [F2] is not used.

Let $g=1$ in a strict interval and $g=2$ at a boundary, and shift all energies by their minimum so the ground energy is zero. The diagonal entropy from [F3] is $S_B/k_B=\log D_\beta+\beta\sum_{n\ge0}p_nK_B(n)$, where $D_\beta=g+R_\beta$ and $R_\beta$ is the total relative excited weight from step 2.2. Thus $D_\beta\to g$ by step 2.2 and $\log D_\beta\to\log g$ by continuity [F10]. In either case, for each distance $\ell\ge1$ there are at most two excited states; their lower gaps are $\delta\ell$ by step 2.2 and their upper gaps are $C(1+\ell^2)$ because $K_B(n)$ is quadratic in $n$. Here $C$ is fixed and $\delta=U$ at a boundary. For $\beta\ge1$, [F9] makes $(1+\ell^2)e^{-\delta\ell/2}$ bounded; splitting $e^{-\beta\delta\ell}=e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}$ therefore bounds $\beta\sum_{\ell\ge1}(1+\ell^2)e^{-\beta\delta\ell}$ by a constant times $\beta\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}=\beta q_\beta/(1-q_\beta)$, where $q_\beta=e^{-\beta\delta/2}$. This tends to zero by [F5], [F6], and [F9]. Consequently the excited contribution to the entropy vanishes, while the normalized ground weights contribute $0$ for $g=1$ and $\log2$ for $g=2$.

Fix $(\beta_0,\mu_0)$ with $\beta_0>0$, put $u=\beta-\beta_0$, $v=\mu-\mu_0$, $a_0=\epsilon-\mu_0-U/2$, and $K_n^0=Un^2/2+a_0n$. Then $-\beta K_B(n;\mu)=-\beta_0K_n^0-uK_n^0+\beta_0vn+uvn$, so [F5] expands each summand as $e^{-\beta_0K_n^0}e^{-uK_n^0}e^{\beta_0vn}e^{uvn}$. On radii $r_\beta=\beta_0/2$ and any fixed $r_\mu>0$, the sum of the absolute values of all terms of these three exponential power series, over all $n$, is bounded by $\sum_{n\ge0}\exp(-\beta_0K_n^0+r_\beta|K_n^0|+\beta_0r_\mu n+r_\beta r_\mu n)$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $K_n^0\ge0$ and $|K_n^0|\le Un^2/2+|a_0|n$, so the exponent is at most $-\beta_0Un^2/4+Cn$ for a finite constant $C$. Increasing the cutoff so $Cn\le\beta_0Un^2/8$ leaves a tail bounded by $e^{-\beta_0Un/8}$, whose series converges by [F5]–[F6]; the finitely many initial terms are finite. Thus the total absolute coefficient sum is finite. Grouping $r+t=p$ and $s+t=q$ gives $c_{pq}=\sum_{n\ge0}e^{-\beta_0K_n^0}\sum_{t=0}^{\min(p,q)}\frac{(-K_n^0)^{p-t}(\beta_0n)^{q-t}n^t}{(p-t)!(q-t)!t!}$. The absolute bound and [F7] justify these coefficient sums and rearrangement, and give $\sum_{p,q}|c_{pq}|r_\beta^p r_\mu^q<\infty$, hence $|c_{pq}|\le M r_\beta^{-p}r_\mu^{-q}$ for some finite $M$. Applying the multivariable power-series theorem [F7] gives a holomorphic sum on the complex polydisc; its real restriction is the absolutely convergent germ in [F4]. Since $(\beta_0,\mu_0)$ was arbitrary, $\Xi_B$ is jointly real analytic on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$.

Fix $\beta>0$ and let $\mu$ range over a compact interval. The quantity $a=\epsilon-\mu-U/2$ is then bounded, so the square bound in step 3.1 gives $e^{-\beta K_B(n;\mu)}\le C e^{-\beta U n^2/4}$ for a constant $C$ uniform on that interval. Put $q=e^{-\beta U/8}\in(0,1)$. Since $n^2\ge n$, $(1+n^2)e^{-\beta K_B(n;\mu)}\le C(1+n^2)q^{2n}$. By [F9], $(1+n^2)q^n$ is bounded, so the right side is at most $C'q^n$, a summable geometric envelope. Apply [F8] on $\mathbb N_0$ with the counting measure [A2], weight $w(n)=e^{-\beta E_B(n)}$, observable $X(n)=n$, and natural parameter $\theta=\beta\mu$. Its hypotheses hold by this compact envelope and step 3.1; it gives $\partial_\theta\mathbb E(N_B)=\operatorname{Var}(N_B)$. The chain rule [F12] yields the displayed response, while the normalized weights give the expectation formula.

The normalized means are $\langle n_\uparrow\rangle=(w_\uparrow+w_2)/\Xi_F$ and $\langle n_\downarrow\rangle=(w_\downarrow+w_2)/\Xi_F$, while $\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle=w_2/\Xi_F$. Subtracting the product of the means yields $\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow)=(w_2-w_\uparrow w_\downarrow)/\Xi_F^2$. Since $w_\uparrow w_\downarrow=e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}$ and $w_2=e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}e^{-\beta U}$, this is the displayed formula; $U\ge0$ makes it nonpositive, with equality exactly at $U=0$.

The covariance numerator is e^{−2β(ε−μ)}(1−1)=0, confirming factorization at zero interaction.

**Periodic commuting Ising model.** For $N\ge2$, let $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ with its product inner product, and let $Z_i$ act as $\sigma_z$ on tensor factor $i$ and as identity on the others; each $Z_i$ acts on all of $\mathcal H_N$. With periodic indexing $Z_{N+1}=Z_1$, count exactly the $N$ indexed bonds, so $N=2$ has two bonds. For real energies $J,h$ and $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, adopt the finite matrix
$$H_N^{\mathrm q}=-J\sum_{i=1}^N Z_iZ_{i+1}-h\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i,\qquad D(H_N^{\mathrm q})=\mathcal H_N.$$
For each site set $|+1\rangle:=e_0$ and $|-1\rangle:=e_1$, so $\sigma_z|s_i\rangle=s_i|s_i\rangle$; define $|s_1,\ldots,s_N\rangle:=|s_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|s_N\rangle$. Its energy equals $H_N^{\mathrm{cl}}(s)=-J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}-h\sum_i s_i$. Thus the quantum Gibbs density is diagonal in this basis, and its partition function and diagonal probabilities agree exactly with the specified classical finite ring. In particular, when $J\ge0$ and $h=0$, its $\sigma_z$ correlations are those of [[pthm-csm-ising-ring-correlation]]. Use $\sinh x=(e^x-e^{-x})/2$, $\cosh x=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$, and $\tanh x=\sinh x/\cosh x$ from [[def-hyperbolic-functions]], where $\cosh x>0$ for every real $x$, and put
$$\lambda_\pm=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)\pm\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}.$$
Then $N^{-1}\log Z_N^{\mathrm q}\to\log\lambda_+$, with every fixed finite order of derivatives converging locally uniformly on compact subsets of $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$. This is the exact commuting one-dimensional model, not a theorem for noncommuting interactions.

**Global three-sector countermodel.** For $N\ge1$ and $\epsilon>0$ joules, let $\mathcal K_N=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C\oplus(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes 2N}$ with its orthogonal direct-sum inner product, and write $I_{4^N}$ for the identity on the final $4^N$-dimensional summand. Let $|A\rangle,|B\rangle$ be the standard unit vectors in the first and second summands, and let $|s\rangle$ range over the standard product basis in the final summand. Define the finite matrix $H_N^{\mathrm g}=0\oplus N\epsilon\oplus2N\epsilon I_{4^N}$ on the full domain $\mathcal K_N$, so the basis energies are $E(A)=0$, $E(B)=N\epsilon$, and $E(s)=2N\epsilon$. For $0\le\Delta<N\epsilon$, define the spectral-shell basis subset $S_{N,\Delta}:=\{v:|E(v)-N\epsilon|\le\Delta\}$ and its uniform state $\rho_{N,\Delta}^{\mathrm{shell}}:=|S_{N,\Delta}|^{-1}\sum_{v\in S_{N,\Delta}}|v\rangle\langle v|$. For $\beta>0$ this finite quantum model has
$$Z_N^{\mathrm g}=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}.$$
For every real $\beta$ as an algebraic finite-weight extension, the normalized exponential-tilt weight of the one-dimensional middle sector is at most $(2^{N+1}+1)^{-1}$; the shell state above assigns that sector probability $1$. The term “probability” here is the trace of the state against the middle-sector projection $|B\rangle\langle B|$. Also
$$\frac1N\log Z_N^{\mathrm g}\longrightarrow\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\},\qquad 0\le\frac1N\log Z_N^{\mathrm g}-\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\}\le\frac{\log3}{N}.$$
The limiting function has a corner at $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon>0$ J$^{-1}$. For $\beta>0$, define the canonical mean energy per member of the global model by

$$\bar E_N(\beta):=\frac{N\epsilon e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+2N\epsilon\,4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}}{NZ_N^{\mathrm g}(\beta)}.$$

The limit $u(\beta):=\lim_{N\to\infty}\bar E_N(\beta)$ exists for all $\beta>0$ and equals $2\epsilon$ for $0<\beta<\beta_c$, $\epsilon$ at $\beta=\beta_c$, and $0$ for $\beta>\beta_c$. Thus the one-sided limits of the thermodynamic-limit mean energy are $2\epsilon$ as $\beta\uparrow\beta_c$ through positive values and $0$ as $\beta\downarrow\beta_c$ from above. The finite partition expressions are real analytic as functions of $\beta\in\mathbb R$ for fixed remaining model parameters; this is a regularity statement about the finite formulas, while the canonical preparation and mean-energy claims use only $\beta>0$. This global, size-dependent family is not a product of one fixed finite one-site alphabet and makes no claim about local or short-range matter.

reviewed.reason: The source Statement has two separately named models. Its N>=2 bound belongs to the periodic commuting Ising ring; the Global three-sector countermodel explicitly starts at N>=1 and gives exactly the partition and shell formulas restated in [F1]. The Example and Verification1.1–2.1 fix N=2 in that global branch, obtain Z_2=9/4 and middle probability1/9, and use the shell interval0<=Delta<2epsilon. Neither the F1 restatement nor either use widens the ring model.

derivations.claim: At $N=2$ and $\beta=\beta_c$, $e^{-\beta N\epsilon}=e^{-2\log2}=1/4$ and $4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}=16e^{-4\log2}=1$. Hence $Z_2=9/4$ and the middle-sector Gibbs probability is $(1/4)/(9/4)=1/9$. The finite partition is a sum of positive exponentials, so it is analytic at this parameter.

Since $2\epsilon$ is the distance from the middle energy to either outer energy at $N=2$, every shell with $0\le\Delta<2\epsilon$ selects exactly the one-dimensional middle sector and gives it uniform probability $1$. Thus the two specified finite preparations disagree on this observable, while the analytic finite sum and limiting cusp remain distinct claims.

Let $e_0,e_1$ and $\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z,C$ be as in [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], with $\sigma_z e_0=e_0$ and $\sigma_z e_1=-e_1$. By [[lem-qsm-pauli-dimer-spectrum]], the normalized singlet $s=(e_0\otimes e_1-e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$ has $C$-eigenvalue $-3$, and the three orthonormal triplets have eigenvalue $1$. Adopt the two-spin Hamiltonian as a finite matrix on $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$, with full domain $D(H_{J,h})=\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$:
$$H_{J,h}:=JC-h(\sigma_z\otimes I+I\otimes\sigma_z),$$
where $J,h\in\mathbb R$ are energies in joules. For inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, use the canonical Gibbs preparation only after normalizing its finite trace. Its singlet energy is $-3J$; its triplet energies are $J-2h$, $J$, and $J+2h$. Here $\cosh y:=(e^y+e^{-y})/2$.
$$Z(\beta,J,h)=e^{3\beta J}+e^{-\beta J}\bigl(1+2\cosh(2\beta h)\bigr)>0.$$
At $h=0$ and $J>0$, the Gibbs density matrix is entangled exactly when $\beta J>(\log3)/4$, and is separable at and below equality. This exact threshold is a finite-state quantum-model conclusion. For every fixed $J,h$, $Z$ and the free energy $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ are real analytic for $\beta>0$; the entanglement threshold is not a finite-temperature thermodynamic singularity. At zero field the entropy tends to $0$ as $\beta\to\infty$ for $J>0$, to $k_B\log3$ for $J<0$, and to $k_B\log4$ for $J=0$. For $J>0$, a nonzero field makes the singlet and the field-aligned triplet cross at $|h|=2J$ at zero temperature; this ground-space crossing does not make $Z$ singular at finite positive temperature.

derivations.claim: Substituting $\beta J=(\log3)/4$ into [F1] gives the separable equality state; taking any $\beta J>(\log3)/4$ gives the entangled branch. These are conclusions about the defined two-qubit density matrix.

At $h=0$, $Z=e^{3\beta J}+3e^{-\beta J}$ is a finite positive sum of exponentials, so $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ is analytic for $\beta>0$, including at the separability threshold. Therefore this state-property boundary is not a thermodynamic singularity of the finite dimer.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

**Repulsive single-mode Bose site.** Let $\mathcal H_B=\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)$ with orthonormal occupation basis $|n\rangle$, supplied by the one-mode specialization of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]]. Put $E_B(n):=\epsilon n+\frac U2n(n-1)$, where $\epsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $U>0$ are in joules. Define $H_B$ and $N_B$ as real diagonal multipliers $H_B|n\rangle=E_B(n)|n\rangle$ and $N_B|n\rangle=n|n\rangle$ on their maximal domains
$$D(H_B)=\left\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}E_B(n)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(N_B)=\left\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, define $K_B$ directly as the real diagonal multiplier with eigenvalues
$$K_B(n):=E_B(n)-\mu n=\frac U2n^2+\left(\epsilon-\mu-\frac U2\right)n$$
on the exact maximal domain $D(K_B)=\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}K_B(n)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$. These diagonal multipliers are self-adjoint on their displayed domains. The grand partition sum
$$\Xi_B(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta K_B(n)}$$
is finite and positive for every such $(\beta,\mu)$. It is jointly real analytic locally on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, meaning it has an absolutely convergent power-series representation in the two real parameters near every point. Its normalized diagonal Gibbs state has weights $p_n=\Xi_B^{-1}e^{-\beta K_B(n)}$ and
$$\langle N_B\rangle=\Xi_B^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}n e^{-\beta K_B(n)},\qquad \partial_\mu\langle N_B\rangle=\beta\,\operatorname{Var}(N_B).$$
In the zero-temperature limit $\beta\to\infty$, the unique minimizing occupation is $0$ when $\mu<\epsilon$, and is $r\ge1$ when $\epsilon+U(r-1)<\mu<\epsilon+Ur$. At each boundary $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$ for $r\in\mathbb N_0$, exactly the adjacent occupations $r,r+1$ minimize $K_B$; their probabilities tend to $1/2$ each and the model entropy $S=-k_B\operatorname{tr}(\rho_B\log\rho_B)$ from [[post-qsm-models-statistics-and-preparation]] tends to $k_B\log2$. In a strict interval, the unique minimizing number state has probability tending to one and entropy tending to zero.

**Two-mode Fermi Hubbard atom.** On $\mathcal H_F=\mathbb C^4$ with orthonormal occupation basis $|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$, $n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\in\{0,1\}$, define $n_\uparrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle=n_\uparrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$ and $n_\downarrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle=n_\downarrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$, and adopt
$$H_F=\epsilon(n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow)+U n_\uparrow n_\downarrow-h(n_\uparrow-n_\downarrow),$$
where $\epsilon,\mu,U,h$ are in joules, $U\ge0$, and $\beta>0$. With $K_F=H_F-\mu(n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow)$, its grand partition function and weights are
$$\Xi_F=1+w_\uparrow+w_\downarrow+w_2,\quad w_\uparrow=e^{-\beta(\epsilon-\mu-h)},\quad w_\downarrow=e^{-\beta(\epsilon-\mu+h)},\quad w_2=e^{-\beta(2(\epsilon-\mu)+U)}.$$
Thus $\langle n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow\rangle=(w_\uparrow+w_\downarrow+2w_2)/\Xi_F$, the double-occupation probability $\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle$ is $w_2/\Xi_F$, and, with $\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow):=\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle-\langle n_\uparrow\rangle\langle n_\downarrow\rangle$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow)=\frac{e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}(e^{-\beta U}-1)}{\Xi_F^2}\le0.$$
The covariance is zero at $U=0$ and strictly negative at $U>0$. These are exact conditional model calculations, not claims about measured atoms.
