citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be separable, $K=K^*$ densely defined and bounded below with energy unit J, and let $e^{-sK}$ be trace class for every $s$ in an open interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$ measured in J$^{-1}$. Fix $\beta\in I$, $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta K})$, $\sigma_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta K}$, and $U(t)=e^{-itK/\hbar}$ for $\hbar>0$ in J s and $t$ in s. For bounded $A,B$, let $C_{AB}$ and $S_{AB}$ be the correlation function and finite spectral measure defined in [[lem-qsm-dt-trace-gibbs-correlation-series]]. Write $S_{BA}(-\cdot)$ for the pushforward under $\omega\mapsto-\omega$. Then for every bounded Borel test function $f$ with compact support,
$$\int f(\omega)\,S_{BA}(-d\omega)=\int f(\omega)e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}\,S_{AB}(d\omega).$$
The weighted measure on the right extends to a finite complex measure: the reindexed coefficient family is absolutely summable and has the same total-variation bound as $S_{BA}$. For Hermitian $A=B$, $S_{AA}$ is a positive finite measure. This is a discrete-spectrum equilibrium correlation identity; it asserts no temporal decay, continuum limit, or ordinary zero-frequency transport coefficient.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Statement, centered nonzero observable: On a one-dimensional space centered self-adjoint A must be0, contradicting A≠0; hence there is no admissible one-level instance of this obstruction.
Repeated gaps are explicitly grouped into w_omega in 1.1; the mean-square limit in 2.1 uses distinct grouped frequencies, preserving zero-gap degeneracy instead of assuming phase cancellation.
Proof 2.1 takes T to infinity after integrating the finite-time average, with a summable majorant on the countable pair set; no ordinary absolutely convergent endpoint dc integral is inferred.
[A1] retains full Choice for the energy basis; grouping positive coefficients by equality of their numeric frequencies in 1.1 needs no chosen representative vector.

boundaries.reason: Nonintegrability is a consequence of this faithful pure-point Gibbs setting and A≠0, not a characterization of all systems lacking dc coefficients.
The theorem rules out an absolutely integrable isolated correlation here; failure of that integral does not imply discrete spectrum or exclude other transport limits.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $D=\dim H\ge1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. With composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity and the induced operator norm, $\mathcal B(H)$ is a nonzero unital complex C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

Consequently the canonical states of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] are exactly the trace pairings of density operators of [[def-qc-density-operator]]; for a positive functional, normalization $\omega(I)=1$ is equivalent to norm one. The result includes zero positive functionals, nonfaithful densities and $D=1$; it makes no infinite-dimensional density representation assertion.

Use $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge1$, finite on-site dimension $q\ge1$, and a uniformly bounded finite-range interaction $\Phi$ with parameters $M\ge1$, $R<\infty$, $\kappa<\infty$, and $\hbar>0$ as in [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]]. Assume Countable Choice and the exact finite-matrix C$^*$-identity condition supplied in [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. Let $\mathcal A$ be the norm-completed quasi-local spin algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]], and let $\alpha_t$ be the strongly continuous automorphism group of [[thm-qsm-finite-range-spin-dynamics]]. Let $\{\rho_\Lambda\}$ be consistent positive trace-one local density matrices; write $\phi$ for their unique state extension supplied by [[lem-qsm-consistent-local-states]], and additionally assume $\phi\circ\alpha_t=\phi$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$. This is an algebraic state on $\mathcal A$, not a trace-class density on an infinite tensor-product Hilbert space.

For $A\in\mathcal A$, $B=B^*\in\mathcal A$, continuous real $h:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$, finite $T>0$, and dimensionless $\epsilon\in\mathbb R$, put $B_t=\alpha_t(B)$ and let $W_\epsilon$ solve
$$W_\epsilon'(t)=\frac{i\epsilon h(t)}{\hbar}B_tW_\epsilon(t),\qquad W_\epsilon(0)=I.$$
The C$^*$-algebra Dyson solution is unitary. Define $\alpha_t^\epsilon(A)=W_\epsilon(t)^*\alpha_t(A)W_\epsilon(t)$,
$$R_{AB}(u)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\phi([\alpha_u(A),B]),\qquad C_T=\frac2\hbar\int_0^T|h(s)|\,\|B\|\,ds.$$
Then
$$\phi(\alpha_t^\epsilon(A))=\phi(\alpha_t(A))+\epsilon\int_0^t h(s)R_{AB}(t-s)\,ds+r_\epsilon(t),\qquad |r_\epsilon(t)|\le\|A\|\frac{(|\epsilon|C_T)^2e^{|\epsilon|C_T}}2.$$
When energy is the interpretation of $H_\Lambda$ and $hB$, their units are J, $t$ is s, $\hbar$ is J s, and $C_T$ is dimensionless. No global trace Hamiltonian, spatial-to-temporal decay implication, or dc coefficient follows.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a unital complex C$^*$-algebra, and let $(\alpha_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ be a group of $*$-automorphisms of $\mathcal A$, so $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$ and $\alpha_{s+t}=\alpha_s\circ\alpha_t$. Assume point-norm continuity: for each $X\in\mathcal A$, the orbit map $t\mapsto\alpha_t(X)$ is norm-continuous. Let $\phi:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ be a bounded linear functional with $\phi(I)=1$, $\phi(X^*X)\ge0$ for every $X\in\mathcal A$, and $\phi\circ\alpha_t=\phi$ for every $t$. For $m\ge1$, take self-adjoint $V_1,\ldots,V_m\in\mathcal A$ with $\phi(V_a)=0$. For $T>0$, define the norm-Riemann integrals
$$X_{a,T}=\int_0^T\alpha_t(V_a)\,dt,$$
and for $s\ge0$ define
$$G_{ab}(s)=\frac12\left(\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_a\alpha_s(V_b))+\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_b\alpha_s(V_a))\right).$$
Then each $X_{a,T}$ is self-adjoint and
$$\frac{1}{2T}\operatorname{Re}\phi(X_{a,T}X_{b,T})=\int_0^T\left(1-\frac{s}{T}\right)G_{ab}(s)\,ds.$$
The real symmetric matrix with entries on the left is positive semidefinite.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: The algebraic group/state hypotheses follow from [A1], [F1], and the exact interaction and state assumptions carried by [F2]; applying the stationary covariance identity [F3] to the scalar observable gives $$\frac{\phi(X_T^2)}{2T}=\int_0^T\left(1-\frac{t}{T}\right)G(t)\,dt.$$ Extend the integrand by zero for $t>T$. For each fixed $t\ge0$ it converges to $G(t)$ as $T\to\infty$, and its absolute value is at most $|G(t)|$, which is integrable by hypothesis. Applying [F4] on $[0,\infty)$ yields the limit $\int_0^\infty G(t)dt$.
For finite $T$, $X_T=X_T^*$ by [F3], so $\phi(X_T^2)=\phi(X_T^*X_T)\ge0$. The limit in step 1.1 is therefore nonnegative.

For $m$ observables, [F3] gives the finite-time real symmetric covariance matrix with entries $D_{ab}(T)=\int_0^T(1-t/T)G_{ab}(t)dt$; for every real vector $c$, $c^TD(T)c=\phi((\sum_a c_aX_{a,T})^2)/(2T)\ge0$. Each entry converges to $D_{ab}=\int_0^\infty G_{ab}(t)dt$ by the same dominated-convergence argument as step 1.1. For any $c$, $c^TDc=\lim_Tc^TD(T)c\ge0$, so $D$ is positive semidefinite.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $A=A^*$ a densely defined Hamiltonian bounded below by $a\in\mathbb R$. Assume $e^{-\beta A}$ is trace class for every $\beta$ in an open interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$. For each $\beta\in I$, put $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})$ and $\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta A}/Z_\beta$. Then $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$ and $\rho_\beta$ is a faithful normal density. For the entropy and optimization clause, fix $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), put $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$ and $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$, and let $\rho$ be any normal density with finite spectral form energy
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda)<\infty.
$
Then $\rho$ has finite entropy and satisfies
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality exactly at $\rho=\rho_\beta$. The prepared Gibbs state also has
$
S(\rho_\beta)=k_B\bigl(\log Z_\beta+\beta\mathcal E_A(\rho_\beta)\bigr).
$
The trace-class and open-interval hypotheses are essential; a lower bound on $A$ alone does not imply finite $Z_\beta$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, $H=H^*$ a densely defined Hamiltonian on $D(H)$ with unit J, $\hbar>0$ with unit J s, $\rho$ a positive trace-class density with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$ and $\rho U_0(t)=U_0(t)\rho$, and $A=A^*\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. Fix a reference energy $E_0>0$ in joules and equip $D(H)$ with the graph norm $\|\psi\|_G:=\|\psi\|+\|H\psi\|/E_0$. Let $B=B^*\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ with unit $[B]$. Assume $B(D(H))\subseteq D(H)$ and that $[H,B]\psi=HB\psi-BH\psi$ on $D(H)$ extends to a bounded operator $C$ on $\mathcal H$. Let $h:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous for finite $T>0$ with $h(t)B$ in J, and let $\epsilon\in\mathbb R$ be dimensionless. Then the bounded-observable response and remainder from [[thm-qsm-dt-normal-state-kubo]] hold. In addition, with $U_0(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$, $B_t=U_0(t)^*BU_0(t)$, and $W_\epsilon'(t)=i\epsilon h(t)B_tW_\epsilon(t)/\hbar$, $W_\epsilon(0)=I$, the interaction-picture propagator maps $D(H)$ onto itself, and
$$\Psi(t)=U_0(t)W_\epsilon(t)\psi$$
is a strong solution on $[0,T]$ for each $\psi\in D(H)$, meaning that $\Psi:[0,T]\to\mathcal H$ belongs to $C([0,T];D(H))$ for the graph norm and to $C^1([0,T];\mathcal H)$, satisfies $\Psi(0)=\psi$, and satisfies $i\hbar\Psi'(t)=(H-\epsilon h(t)B)\Psi(t)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$ (with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints). No domain-preservation claim is made for a general bounded $B$ without the stated commutator hypothesis.

derivations.claim: Finite-support sequences are dense in $\ell^2$, so $D(H)$ is dense. The diagonal real operator is symmetric. If $y\in D(H^*)$, testing the adjoint relation against each $e_n$ forces $(H^*y)_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)y_n$; this vector belongs to $\ell^2$ exactly when $\sum_n(n+\tfrac12)^2|y_n|^2<\infty$. Thus $D(H^*)=D(H)$ and $H^*=H$.

The Gibbs eigenvalues are $(1-q)q^n$, since $\sum_{n\ge0}e^{-\beta\hbar\omega(n+1/2)}=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega/2}/(1-q)$; hence $Z_\beta=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega/2}/(1-q)$ is finite for every $\beta>0$ and [F1] applies. The Gibbs matrix is positive trace one and commutes with $U(t)$ because both are functions of $H$. The operator $B$ has norm $|b_0|$; its image lies in $\operatorname{span}\{e_0,e_1\}\subset D(H)$, so it maps $D(H)$ into itself. Its commutator $C=[H,B]$ is the finite-rank bounded operator $Ce_0=\Delta b_0e_1$, $Ce_1=-\Delta b_0e_0$, $Ce_n=0$ for $n\ge2$.

Since $B$ only connects $e_0$ and $e_1$, the unperturbed expectation $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta\alpha_t(B))$ is zero. Direct multiplication of the two nonzero matrix blocks gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta[\alpha_t(B),B])=-2i b_0^2(1-q)^2\sin(\omega t)$, so $R_{BB}(t)=2b_0^2(1-q)^2\sin(\omega t)/\hbar$. The constant-field convolution in [F2] is therefore $$\epsilon h_0\int_0^tR_{BB}(u)\,du=\frac{2\epsilon h_0b_0^2(1-q)^2}{\Delta}(1-\cos(\omega t)).$$ Here $C_T=2|h_0||b_0|T/\hbar$; the response theorem also bounds the omitted term by $|b_0|(|\epsilon|C_T)^2e^{|\epsilon|C_T}/2$.

The two-dimensional space $V=\operatorname{span}\{e_0,e_1\}$ and its orthogonal complement are invariant under the constant controlled Hamiltonian. Put $d=\Delta/2>0$, $g=\epsilon h_0b_0$, and $R=(d^2+g^2)^{1/2}>0$. On $V$, let $X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Then $H-\epsilon h_0B=\Delta I-dZ-gX$ and $(dZ+gX)^2=R^2I$. Its exact propagator on this block is therefore $e^{-it\Delta/\hbar}[\cos(Rt/\hbar)I+i\sin(Rt/\hbar)(dZ+gX)/R]$. The initial diagonal block has entries $p_0=1-q$ and $p_1=(1-q)q$, with $p_0-p_1=(1-q)^2$; the complementary levels contribute zero to the expectation of $B$. Multiplying these two-by-two matrices gives the exact expectation $$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\epsilon(t)B)=\frac{b_0gd(1-q)^2}{R^2}\bigl(1-\cos(2Rt/\hbar)\bigr).$$ For $\epsilon=0$ this is zero, and its first derivative at $\epsilon=0$ is the coefficient computed in step 3.1. The formula holds on every stated finite control interval. For the consistent extension using the same constant control for all $t\ge0$, it is nonconstant and periodic whenever $\epsilon h_0b_0\ne0$, so the exact expectation has no infinite-time limit; this conclusion follows from the exact block formula, not from extrapolating the finite-time remainder. This concerns the bounded projected transition observable, not oscillator position or an empirical measurement.

Let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$, $H=H^*$ with energy unit J, $\hbar>0$ with unit J s, $\beta>0$ with unit J$^{-1}$, and let $\sigma=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ be the stationary Gibbs density from [[thm-qsm-dt-finite-unitary]]. Let $A=A^*$ and $B=B^*$ be matrices, let $T>0$ be finite in s, let $h:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $\epsilon\in\mathbb R$ be dimensionless; $h(t)B$ has unit J. Put $U_0(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ for time $t$ in s, $\alpha_t(A)=U_0(t)^*AU_0(t)$, and $B_t=\alpha_t(B)$. Let $W_\epsilon$ solve
$$W_\epsilon'(t)=\frac{i\epsilon h(t)}{\hbar}B_tW_\epsilon(t),\qquad W_\epsilon(0)=I,$$
and set $U_\epsilon(t)=U_0(t)W_\epsilon(t)$ and $\rho_I(t)=W_\epsilon(t)\sigma W_\epsilon(t)^*$. Then $U_\epsilon$ solves $i\hbar U_\epsilon'(t)=(H-\epsilon h(t)B)U_\epsilon(t)$, $U_\epsilon(0)=I$, and $\rho_\epsilon(t):=U_\epsilon(t)\sigma U_\epsilon(t)^*$ satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\epsilon(t)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_I(t)\alpha_t(A))$. Define
$$R_{AB}(u)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma[\alpha_u(A),B]\right),\qquad C_T=\frac{2}{\hbar}\int_0^T|h(s)|\,\|B\|\,ds.$$
Then $W_\epsilon(t)$ is unitary and, for $0\le t\le T$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_I(t)\alpha_t(A))=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\alpha_t(A))+\epsilon\int_0^t h(s)R_{AB}(t-s)\,ds+r_\epsilon(t),\qquad |r_\epsilon(t)|\le\|A\|\frac{(|\epsilon|C_T)^2e^{|\epsilon|C_T}}2.$$
The initial Gibbs matrix is fixed as $\epsilon$ varies. The result is an exact finite-time first variation with a controlled remainder, not a static derivative of a re-prepared Gibbs family. $C_T$ and $\epsilon$ are dimensionless, and $R_{AB}$ has units $[A][B]/(\mathrm J\,\mathrm s)$.

Let $\mathcal H$ be finite-dimensional, $H=H^*$ with unit J, $\hbar>0$ with unit J s, $\beta>0$ with unit J$^{-1}$, and $\sigma=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ as in [[thm-qsm-dt-finite-unitary]]. Let $A=A^*$ be a matrix observable, write $Hu_i=E_i u_i$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis, $r_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z_\beta$, $A_{ij}=\langle Au_j,u_i\rangle$, and $\omega_{ji}=(E_j-E_i)/\hbar$. Define the finite positive spectral measure
$$S_{AA}=2\pi\sum_{i,j}r_i|A_{ij}|^2\,\delta_{\omega_{ji}},$$
where $\delta_\nu$ is unit point mass at frequency $\nu$ and $S_{AA}(-\cdot)$ denotes pushforward under $\omega\mapsto-\omega$; $\omega_{ji}$ has unit s$^{-1}$. With observable unit $[A]$, the atomic masses of the finite measure $S_{AA}$ have units $[A]^2$. For every smooth compactly supported complex-valued function $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$, the distribution represented by the measure $S_{AA}$ acts as $\langle S_{AA},\varphi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(\omega)\,dS_{AA}(\omega)$. In the Fourier convention below, the generalized density $S_{AA}(\omega)$ relative to $d\omega$ has units $[A]^2$ multiplied by seconds; it is a finite sum of Dirac distributions, not an ordinary function density. The equilibrium correlation is $C_{AA}(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\alpha_t(A)A)$, and its Fourier convention is $S_{AA}(\omega)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{i\omega t}C_{AA}(t)\,dt$ in the distributional sense.

For $t\ge0$, set $R_{AA}(t)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma[\alpha_t(A),A])$ and, for $\eta>0$, define the retarded transform $\chi_\eta(\omega)=\int_0^\infty e^{(i\omega-\eta)t}R_{AA}(t)\,dt$. Then
$$\chi_\eta(\omega)=\sum_{i,j}\frac{(r_i-r_j)|A_{ij}|^2}{\hbar(\omega_{ji}-\omega-i\eta)}.$$
As $\eta\downarrow0$, its boundary value is the corresponding sum of principal-value real parts and Lorentzian imaginary terms weighted by $r_i-r_j$, and distributionally
$$\operatorname{Im}\chi=\frac{1}{2\hbar}(1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega})S_{AA}(\omega).$$
Detailed balance is $S_{AA}(-d\omega)=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}S_{AA}(d\omega)$. Thus, on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$,
$$S_{\mathrm{sym}}(d\omega)=\hbar\coth\!\left(\frac{\beta\hbar\omega}{2}\right)\operatorname{Im}\chi(d\omega),\qquad S_{\mathrm{sym}}=\tfrac12(S_{AA}+S_{AA}(-\cdot)).$$
Any zero-frequency mass of $S_{AA}$ is retained separately: the commutator factor vanishes there, so the formula does not determine that atom or define a value for the singular product with $\coth$ at $\omega=0$.

Let $M(s)$ be a continuously differentiable path of Hermitian $D\times D$ matrices, $D\geq1$. Then
$
\frac{d}{ds}e^{M(s)}=\int_0^1 e^{(1-u)M(s)}M'(s)e^{uM(s)}\,du,\qquad
\frac{d}{ds}\log\operatorname{Tr}e^{M(s)}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_sM'(s)),
$
where $\rho_s=e^{M(s)}/\operatorname{Tr}e^{M(s)}$. For real controls $M(\theta)=M_0+\sum_a\theta_aX_a$ with Hermitian $X_a$,
$
\partial_a\log Z=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X_a),\qquad
\partial_a\partial_b\log Z=\int_0^1\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{1-u}\delta X_a\rho^u\delta X_b)\,du,
$
where $Z=\operatorname{Tr}e^M$, $\delta X_a=X_a-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X_a)I$. The diagonal quadratic form of this Hessian is nonnegative. It equals the ordinary variance when $X_a$ commutes with $\rho$, and in general is bounded above by that variance. For $H(h)=H_0-hB$, $\beta>0$, and Hermitian $B$, the static susceptibility satisfies $\partial_h\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_hB)=\beta\,\operatorname{Cov}_{KM,\rho_h}(B,B)\geq0$. No infinite-dimensional or dynamical response is asserted.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $X^2=Y^2=Z^2=I$, $YX=-iZ$, and $[Z,X]=2iY$. The Gibbs matrix is $\sigma=(I-\tanh(x)Z)/2$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma Z)=-\tanh(x)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma X)=0$.

Conjugation by $e^{-itH/\hbar}$ yields $\alpha_t(X)=X\cos(\omega t)-Y\sin(\omega t)$. Hence $C_{XX}(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\alpha_t(X)X)=\cos(\omega t)-i\tanh(x)\sin(\omega t)$ and $R_{XX}(t)=2\tanh(x)\sin(\omega t)/\hbar$. The spectral measure has its two transition atoms at $\pm\omega$ and satisfies $S_{XX}(-\omega)=e^{-\beta\Delta}S_{XX}(\omega)$, in agreement with [F2].

For comparison, the static Gibbs family for $H(h)=H-hX$ has $Z(h)=2\cosh(\beta\sqrt{(\Delta/2)^2+h^2})$. By [F3], $\partial_h\log Z(h)=\beta\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_hX)$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_hX)=\frac{h}{\sqrt{(\Delta/2)^2+h^2}}\tanh\!\left(\beta\sqrt{(\Delta/2)^2+h^2}\right)$ and $\left.\partial_h\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_hX)\right|_{h=0}=\frac{2}{\Delta}\tanh(x)$. Since $\operatorname{Var}_\sigma(X)=1$ and $\tanh(x)<x$ for $x>0$ (the derivative of $x-\tanh x$ is $\tanh^2x>0$), this static susceptibility is strictly below $\beta\operatorname{Var}_\sigma(X)=\beta$. Thus the noncommuting Gibbs derivative is not replaced by $\beta$ times ordinary variance.

Integrating the kernel for constant $h_0$ gives $\delta\langle X(t)\rangle=\frac{2\epsilon h_0}{\Delta}\tanh(x)(1-\cos(\omega t))+r_\epsilon(t)$, with $|r_\epsilon(t)|\le(|\epsilon|C_T)^2e^{|\epsilon|C_T}/2$ and $C_T=2|h_0|T/\hbar$, because $\|X\|=1$.

When $\epsilon h_0\ne0$, the leading response oscillates without a long-time limit; the finite-time theorem does not imply relaxation to the static Gibbs derivative. This is an exact model calculation, not an observation.

derivations.claim: By matrix multiplication and the diagonal-sum trace, $\operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\sum_{i=1}^e\sum_{j=1}^dA_{ij}B_{ji}$. These are finite scalar sums, so reordering them gives $\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_{i=1}^eB_{ji}A_{ij}=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA)$. Taking $e=d$ gives square trace cyclicity.

If $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for all $X$, choose $X=E_{ij}$. Direct multiplication gives $\operatorname{Tr}_d(E_{ij}C)=C_{ji}$, so $C_{ji}=0$ for every $i,j$. Thus every matrix entry of $C$ vanishes and $C=0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. Let $d,e\geq1$. For $A\in M_{e\times d}(\mathbb C)$ and $B\in M_{d\times e}(\mathbb C)$,
$$ \operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA), $$
where $\operatorname{Tr}_r$ is the diagonal-sum trace on $M_r(\mathbb C)$. This includes cyclicity for square matrices. For $C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the bilinear trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, then $C=0$. No adjoint is inserted in this pairing.

derivations.claim: Let $\Omega=\sum_{i=1}^{d}|i\rangle\otimes|i\rangle$ in the input-reference and input tensor factors. Then $\Omega\Omega^*=\sum_{i,j}E_{ij}\otimes E_{ij}\geq0$, and $(\operatorname{id}_d\otimes\Phi)(\Omega\Omega^*)=J(\Phi)$. If $\Phi$ is completely positive, [F1] applied with ancilla dimension $d$ gives $J(\Phi)\geq0$.

Suppose $J(\Phi)\geq0$. By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $J(\Phi)$, absorb each positive eigenvalue's square root into its eigenvector, and write $J(\Phi)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}|w_a\rangle\langle w_a|$, where $q=\operatorname{rank}J(\Phi)\leq de$; if $J(\Phi)=0$, take $q=0$. For each $a$, uniquely define $K_a:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ by $w_a=\sum_i|i\rangle\otimes K_a|i\rangle$.

Expanding each rank-one term gives $|w_a\rangle\langle w_a|=\sum_{i,j}E_{ij}\otimes K_aE_{ij}K_a^*$. Comparing the coefficients of the linearly independent first-factor matrix units in $J(\Phi)$ yields $\Phi(E_{ij})=\sum_aK_aE_{ij}K_a^*$. Since $(E_{ij})$ is a basis and both sides are linear in the input, $\Phi(X)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^*$ for every $X$.

For any $r\geq1$ and any $P\geq0$ on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$, the Kraus formula gives $(\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi)(P)=\sum_a(I_r\otimes K_a)P(I_r\otimes K_a)^*\geq0$; hence $\Phi$ is completely positive. For a Kraus representation, cyclicity [F3] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\Phi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\sum_aK_a^*K_a)$. Thus $\sum_aK_a^*K_a=I_d$ implies trace preservation, and if trace preservation holds then testing $\operatorname{Tr}(X(\sum_aK_a^*K_a-I_d))=0$ on every matrix unit $X=E_{ij}$ forces every entry of the difference to vanish.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Let $d,e\geq1$. For $A\in M_{e\times d}(\mathbb C)$ and $B\in M_{d\times e}(\mathbb C)$,
$$ \operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA), $$
where $\operatorname{Tr}_r$ is the diagonal-sum trace on $M_r(\mathbb C)$. This includes cyclicity for square matrices. For $C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the bilinear trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, then $C=0$. No adjoint is inserted in this pairing.

derivations.claim: Using the Kraus form in [F2] and finite trace cyclicity [F3], $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X)A)=\sum_a\operatorname{Tr}(K_aXK_a^*A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\sum_aK_a^*AK_a)$. Thus $\Phi^\dagger(A)=\sum_aK_a^*AK_a$ satisfies the trace-pairing identity.

If $\Psi(Y)=\sum_bL_bYL_b^*$ is another channel, then $(\Psi\circ\Phi)(X)=\sum_{a,b}(L_bK_a)X(L_bK_a)^*$, and $$ \sum_{a,b}(L_bK_a)^*(L_bK_a)=\sum_aK_a^*\left(\sum_bL_b^*L_b\right)K_a=\sum_aK_a^*K_a=I_d. $$ If $\Phi_r(X)=\sum_aK_{r,a}XK_{r,a}^*$ and $p_r\geq0$, $\sum_rp_r=1$, then $\sum_rp_r\Phi_r$ has Kraus matrices $\sqrt{p_r}K_{r,a}$, whose adjoint-square sum is $\sum_rp_r I_d=I_d$. In both cases [F2] gives a channel.

If $B,C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ both satisfy the pairing identity for a fixed $A$, then $\operatorname{Tr}(X(B-C))=0$ for every $X$. By [F3], taking $X=E_{ij}$ gives every entry of $B-C$ equal to zero, so uniqueness follows. The Kraus form in step 1.1 is completely positive by [F2], and $\Phi^\dagger(I_e)=\sum_aK_a^*K_a=I_d$ by [F1] and [F2].

Let $\Phi_n\to\Phi$ in the stated induced norm, with each $\Phi_n$ completely positive. Since $\|E_{ij}\|_\infty=1$, each block $\Phi_n(E_{ij})$ converges to $\Phi(E_{ij})$; the finite Choi sums therefore converge in matrix norm. Every $J(\Phi_n)\geq0$ by [F2], and for every vector $v$, $\langle J(\Phi)v,v\rangle=\lim_n\langle J(\Phi_n)v,v\rangle\geq0$, so $J(\Phi)\geq0$. The equivalence in [F2] gives complete positivity. If each $\Phi_n$ is trace-preserving, then for every $X$, continuity of finite matrix trace gives $\operatorname{Tr}\Phi(X)=\lim_n\operatorname{Tr}\Phi_n(X)=\operatorname{Tr}X$; thus $\Phi$ is trace-preserving as well.

step 3.1 separately shows CP limits remain CP, including a zero limit; channel limits also retain trace preservation.

Step 1.2 permits zero convex weights through sqrt(p_r)K_r,a; step 3.1 proves closure with nonstrict quadratic-form inequalities, so a singular Choi limit remains admissible.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be a finite channel as defined in [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]]. There is a unique linear map $\Phi^\dagger:M_e(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ satisfying the trace-pairing identity

$$\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\Phi^\dagger(A))\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C),\ A\in M_e(\mathbb C)).$$

If $\Phi(X)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^*$, then $\Phi^\dagger(A)=\sum_aK_a^*AK_a$; in particular, $\Phi^\dagger$ is completely positive and unital. Composition and finite convex combinations of channels are channels. A limit in the induced operator norm $\|\Psi\|_{\infty\to\infty}:=\sup_{\|X\|_\infty\leq1}\|\Psi(X)\|_\infty$, where $\|X\|_\infty:=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Xv\|$, of channels $M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ is also a channel. Moreover, a norm limit of completely positive maps of these fixed finite dimensions is completely positive.

Let $d,e\geq1$. For $A\in M_{e\times d}(\mathbb C)$ and $B\in M_{d\times e}(\mathbb C)$,
$$ \operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA), $$
where $\operatorname{Tr}_r$ is the diagonal-sum trace on $M_r(\mathbb C)$. This includes cyclicity for square matrices. For $C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the bilinear trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, then $C=0$. No adjoint is inserted in this pairing.

derivations.claim: Put $D=\sum_aL_a^*L_a$, $K=-iH/\hbar-D/2$, $\mathcal N(X)=KX+XK^*$, and $\mathcal J(X)=\sum_aL_aXL_a^*$. Then $\mathcal L=\mathcal N+\mathcal J$. Left multiplication by $K$ and right multiplication by $K^*$ commute; expanding their absolutely norm-convergent exponential series and using the binomial formula gives $e^{t\mathcal N}(X)=e^{tK}Xe^{tK^*}$. For every ancilla dimension $r$, the amplification is conjugation by $I_r\otimes e^{tK}$, hence preserves positivity. Thus $e^{t\mathcal N}$ is completely positive.

The map $\mathcal J$ is completely positive by [F3], and every iterate $\mathcal J^n$ is completely positive by composition. For $t\geq0$, the series $e^{t\mathcal J}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^n\mathcal J^n/n!$ converges in finite-dimensional map norm; its partial sums are completely positive, so [F4] implies that $e^{t\mathcal J}$ is completely positive.

For $h\geq0$, the exponential series gives $\|e^{hA}-I-hA\|\leq\frac12 h^2\|A\|^2e^{h\|A\|}$ for each finite linear map $A$. Applying this to $\mathcal N,\mathcal J,\mathcal N+\mathcal J$ shows that for fixed $t$, $\|e^{h\mathcal N}e^{h\mathcal J}-e^{h(\mathcal N+\mathcal J)}\|\leq C_t h^2$ for $0\leq h\leq t$, with finite $C_t$. Set $h=t/n$. The telescoping identity for the difference of the $n$th powers and the bound $\|e^{sA}\|\leq e^{s\|A\|}$ show
$$ \left\|\left(e^{t\mathcal N/n}e^{t\mathcal J/n}\right)^n-e^{t(\mathcal N+\mathcal J)}\right\| \leq n C_t(t/n)^2e^{t(\|\mathcal N\|+\|\mathcal J\|)}\longrightarrow0. $$
Each product on the left before taking the limit is completely positive by step 1.1 and step 2.1; [F4] therefore proves that $e^{t\mathcal L}$ is completely positive.

Cyclicity of finite trace [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal L(X))=0$ for every $X$: the commutator trace vanishes, and each $\operatorname{Tr}(L_aXL_a^*)$ cancels $\frac12\operatorname{Tr}(L_a^*L_aX+XL_a^*L_a)$. The norm-convergent exponential series differentiates term-by-term on bounded time intervals, so $\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Tr}(e^{t\mathcal L}X)=\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal L(e^{t\mathcal L}X))=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{t\mathcal L}X)=\operatorname{Tr}X$. The exponential law gives $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and the series gives norm continuity. Together with complete positivity from step 3.1, [F2] makes every $T_t$ a channel.

boundaries.evidence: The GKSL data allow m=0. Then step 1.1 has D=0 and J=0, the completely positive jump exponential in step 2.1 is the identity, and the product-limit proof still applies.
Statement: The zero generator yields T_t=id; the proof includes the exponential series at t=0.
Statement: The scalar d=1 case gives the identity semigroup.
Steps 1.1–4.1 work when all jumps vanish or H has repeated eigenvalues: matrix exponentials and trace cancellation use no inverse generator or positive spectral gap.
step 4.1 explicitly gives T_0=id and the statement covers all t≥0.
Step 3.1 uses the explicit sequence of products with h=t/n, and step 4.1 the exponential power series; the limiting channels are not obtained by selecting arbitrary witnesses.

boundaries.reason: The theorem proves that a supplied GKSL generator yields channels for t≥0; it does not claim that this implication alone characterizes all channel families.
Recovering GKSL form from a norm-continuous channel semigroup belongs to the separate necessity theorem; this statement assumes the generator formula at the outset.

finite_checks.evidence: For d=1 every commutator and scalar dissipator vanishes, so T_t=id for all t≥0; step 4.1 includes T_0=id.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$, let $H=H^*$ be a Hamiltonian with energy unit J, and let $\hbar>0$ have unit J s. A **finite density matrix** is a positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. For time $t\in\mathbb R$ measured in s, set $U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ and $\alpha_t(A)=U(t)^*AU(t)$. Then $U(t)$ is a unitary group, $\alpha_t$ is a group of matrix $*$-automorphisms, and for every finite density matrix $\rho$ and matrix $A$,

$$\operatorname{Tr}(U(t)\rho U(t)^*A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\alpha_t(A)).$$

The von Neumann entropy $S(\rho)=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$ is finite and unchanged by $U(t)\rho U(t)^*$. For $\beta>0$ with unit J$^{-1}$, let $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$ and $\sigma_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$. Then $Z_\beta>0$, $\sigma_\beta$ is stationary, and the finite Gibbs correlation has the KMS strip identity

$$F_{A,B}(t+i\beta\hbar)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta\alpha_t(B)A),\qquad F_{A,B}(z)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta A\alpha_z(B)),$$

where $\alpha_z(B)=e^{izH/\hbar}Be^{-izH/\hbar}$. The function $F_{A,B}$ is entire and bounded on $0\le\operatorname{Im}z\le\beta\hbar$. This finite-dimensional result asserts no approach to equilibrium.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(|k\rangle)_{k=1}^m$ of $\sigma_E$, with $\sigma_E=\sum_kp_k|k\rangle\langle k|$, $p_k\geq0$, and $\sum_kp_k=1$. The unitary assertion in [F3] applies to $H_{\mathrm{tot}}$ on the finite tensor space, so $U_t^*U_t=I$ for each real $t$.

For system basis indices $a,b$, environment indices $j,k$, and the matrix entries of $U_t$, define $(K_{jk})_{ab}:=\sqrt{p_k}\,(U_t)_{(a,j),(b,k)}$. Applying the coordinate formula [F4] to $R=U_t(\rho\otimes\sigma_E)U_t^*$ gives $$ (\Phi_t(\rho))_{ab}=\sum_{j,k,c,d}(K_{jk})_{ac}\rho_{cd}\overline{(K_{jk})_{bd}} =\left(\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}\rho K_{jk}^*\right)_{ab}. $$ Thus $\Phi_t(\rho)=\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}\rho K_{jk}^*$ for every matrix $\rho$. The basis independence in [F5] ensures that this is the same partial-trace map if a different environment basis is used.

For any system indices $b,d$, unitarity in step 1.1 gives $$ \left(\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}^*K_{jk}\right)_{bd} =\sum_kp_k\sum_{a,j}\overline{(U_t)_{(a,j),(b,k)}}(U_t)_{(a,j),(d,k)} =\sum_kp_k\delta_{bd} =\delta_{bd}. $$ Hence $\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}^*K_{jk}=I_d$; by [F6], the Kraus formula in step 2.1 is completely positive and trace-preserving, which is the channel property in [F1].

boundaries.evidence: Statement imposes d,m≥1 and Tr(sigma_E)=1; step 1.1 has a finite environment eigenbasis with weights summing to one, so neither the environment nor all its weights can be empty.
Statement: The map sends the zero matrix to zero by its linear partial-trace formula; the normalization in step 3.1 establishes trace preservation.
Statement: The proof permits d=1 or m=1; both reductions are calculated in the finite check.
step 1.1 permits repeated or zero eigenvalues p_k of σ_E; no nondegeneracy is assumed.
Statement: The parameter includes t=0, where U_0=I and Φ_0 is the identity channel.
step 1.1 uses a finite orthonormal eigenbasis of σ_E, available for m≥1.

boundaries.reason: The assertion sends a fixed product preparation through a fixed unitary and proves that its reduced map is a channel; it is not an equivalence characterizing all channels.
No dilation converse is stated. In particular the explicit scope sentence declines a marginal-only assertion for correlated joint preparations.

trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to

of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$, let $H=H^*$ be a Hamiltonian with energy unit J, and let $\hbar>0$ have unit J s. A **finite density matrix** is a positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. For time $t\in\mathbb R$ measured in s, set $U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ and $\alpha_t(A)=U(t)^*AU(t)$. Then $U(t)$ is a unitary group, $\alpha_t$ is a group of matrix $*$-automorphisms, and for every finite density matrix $\rho$ and matrix $A$,

$$\operatorname{Tr}(U(t)\rho U(t)^*A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\alpha_t(A)).$$

The von Neumann entropy $S(\rho)=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$ is finite and unchanged by $U(t)\rho U(t)^*$. For $\beta>0$ with unit J$^{-1}$, let $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$ and $\sigma_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$. Then $Z_\beta>0$, $\sigma_\beta$ is stationary, and the finite Gibbs correlation has the KMS strip identity

$$F_{A,B}(t+i\beta\hbar)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta\alpha_t(B)A),\qquad F_{A,B}(z)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\beta A\alpha_z(B)),$$

where $\alpha_z(B)=e^{izH/\hbar}Be^{-izH/\hbar}$. The function $F_{A,B}$ is entire and bounded on $0\le\operatorname{Im}z\le\beta\hbar$. This finite-dimensional result asserts no approach to equilibrium.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\Phi^\dagger$ is positive. For any Hermitian $H\in M_e(\mathbb C)$, its finite spectral decomposition [F3] is $H=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda$, where each $\lambda$ is real and each spectral projection $P_\lambda$ is positive semidefinite. Hence every $\Phi^\dagger(P_\lambda)$ is Hermitian, so $\Phi^\dagger(H)$ is Hermitian. Write an arbitrary $A$ as $A=H+iK$, where $H=(A+A^*)/2$ and $K=(A-A^*)/(2i)$ are Hermitian. By complex linearity, $\Phi^\dagger(A^*)=\Phi^\dagger(H)-i\Phi^\dagger(K)=\Phi^\dagger(A)^*$.

For any $n\geq1$ and $Z\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, use the standard inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_k u_k\overline{v_k}$, linear in its first argument, and define $|u\rangle\langle v|$ as the map $x\mapsto\langle x,v\rangle u$. Since $Z^*Z$ is positive, with $\langle Z^*Zv,v\rangle=\|Zv\|^2$, [F3] diagonalizes it in an orthonormal basis $(v_j)$ with eigenvalues $s_j^2\geq0$. For each $s_j>0$, put $u_j=Zv_j/s_j$. Then $\langle u_j,u_k\rangle=\delta_{jk}$, and $Z=\sum_{s_j>0}s_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|$. The positive square root of $Z^*Z$ has eigenvalues $s_j$, so $\|Z\|_1=\sum_j s_j$.

For $A\in M_e(\mathbb C)$, the block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}A^*A&A^*\\A&I_e\end{pmatrix}$ is positive semidefinite because its quadratic form at $(x,y)$ is $\|Ax+y\|^2$. Apply $\operatorname{id}_2\otimes\Phi^\dagger$: by [F2] the trace dual is completely positive, and the definition in [F1] makes its extension by the two-dimensional ancilla positive. By unitality in [F2] and adjoint preservation from step 1.1, the resulting block is $\begin{pmatrix}\Phi^\dagger(A^*A)&\Phi^\dagger(A)^*\\\Phi^\dagger(A)&I_d\end{pmatrix}\geq0$.

For any $n\geq1$, $Z\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, and $B\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ with $\|B\|_\infty\leq1$, write $Z_{ab}=\sum_{s_j>0}s_j(u_j)_a\overline{(v_j)_b}$ using step 1.2. Expanding both diagonal-sum traces gives $\operatorname{Tr}(BZ)=\sum_{a,b}B_{ab}Z_{ba}=\sum_{s_j>0}s_j\sum_{a,b}B_{ab}(u_j)_b\overline{(v_j)_a}$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(ZB)=\sum_{a,b}Z_{ab}B_{ba}=\sum_{s_j>0}s_j\sum_{a,b}B_{ab}(u_j)_b\overline{(v_j)_a}$. The inner sum is $\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle$ for the inner product fixed in step 1.2. For each unit $v_j$, $0\leq\|Bu_j-\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle v_j\|^2=\|Bu_j\|^2-|\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle|^2$, so both trace magnitudes are at most $\sum_js_j=\|Z\|_1$. Extend the two finite orthonormal lists $(u_j)$, $(v_j)$ to orthonormal bases and choose a unitary $B$ carrying each $u_j$ to $v_j$; then both trace magnitudes equal $\sum_js_j$. Thus $\|Z\|_1=\sup_{\|B\|_\infty\leq1}|\operatorname{Tr}(BZ)|=\sup_{\|B\|_\infty\leq1}|\operatorname{Tr}(ZB)|$, including $Z=0$.

In the positive block from step 2.1, evaluate the quadratic form at $(x,-\Phi^\dagger(A)x)$. This gives $\langle(\Phi^\dagger(A^*A)-\Phi^\dagger(A)^*\Phi^\dagger(A))x,x\rangle\geq0$ for every $x$, so $\Phi^\dagger(A)^*\Phi^\dagger(A)\leq\Phi^\dagger(A^*A)$. Also $A^*A\leq\|A\|_\infty^2I_e$; positivity and unitality in [F2] then give $\Phi^\dagger(A)^*\Phi^\dagger(A)\leq\|A\|_\infty^2I_d$, proving $\|\Phi^\dagger(A)\|_\infty\leq\|A\|_\infty$.

Apply the second dual norm formula from step 2.2 in output dimension $e$ to $\Phi(X)$. For each $A\in M_e(\mathbb C)$ with $\|A\|_\infty\leq1$, step 3.1 gives $\|\Phi^\dagger(A)\|_\infty\leq1$, so the same formula in input dimension $d$ bounds $|\operatorname{Tr}(X\Phi^\dagger(A))|\leq\|X\|_1$. The trace-pairing identity [F2] therefore gives $\|\Phi(X)\|_1=\sup_{\|A\|_\infty\leq1}|\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X)A)|=\sup_{\|A\|_\infty\leq1}|\operatorname{Tr}(X\Phi^\dagger(A))|\leq\|X\|_1$.

boundaries.evidence: Given requires d,e≥1. In step 1.2 an empty list of positive singular values means X=0, and step 2.2 explicitly includes that case in the trace-dual norm formula.
Statement: The inequality for X=0 is equality; the proof is for arbitrary complex matrices.
Statement: The scalar channel case gives equality in both inequalities.
Step 1.2 divides only by s_j>0; zero singular values are omitted. Step 2.2 extends the resulting finite orthonormal lists, so rank-deficient X is covered.

boundaries.reason: The operator-norm and trace-norm inequalities quantify arbitrary finite matrices without a time variable or limiting endpoint; the unit ball in step 2.2 includes its boundary by ≤1.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.2 completes two finite orthonormal lists and chooses one unitary between finite bases; this finite basis construction requires no arbitrary-index choice axiom.

boundaries.reason: Channelhood is a premise for the two contraction inequalities; the statement supplies no equivalence between contraction and complete positivity.
The proof concludes norm contraction by trace duality in step 4.1, without claiming that a trace-norm contraction must be a channel.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite GKSL generator on $M_d(\mathbb C)$, $d\geq1$, with the units and conventions of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. Then $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ is a finite channel for every $t\geq0$. The family satisfies $T_0=\operatorname{id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and is norm-continuous. Time is measured in seconds; no negative-time channel or physical bath limit is asserted.

Let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be a finite channel as defined in [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]]. There is a unique linear map $\Phi^\dagger:M_e(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ satisfying the trace-pairing identity

$$\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\Phi^\dagger(A))\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C),\ A\in M_e(\mathbb C)).$$

If $\Phi(X)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^*$, then $\Phi^\dagger(A)=\sum_aK_a^*AK_a$; in particular, $\Phi^\dagger$ is completely positive and unital. Composition and finite convex combinations of channels are channels. A limit in the induced operator norm $\|\Psi\|_{\infty\to\infty}:=\sup_{\|X\|_\infty\leq1}\|\Psi(X)\|_\infty$, where $\|X\|_\infty:=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Xv\|$, of channels $M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ is also a channel. Moreover, a norm limit of completely positive maps of these fixed finite dimensions is completely positive.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real vector space ([[def-vector-space]]) with a norm $\|\cdot\|$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) whose metric $d(x,y):=\|x-y\|$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). Let $a<b$ be reals ([[def-interval]]) and let $g:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). For endpoints $c,d\in[a,b]$, set $\int_c^c g:=0_X$ and, when $c>d$, set $\int_c^d g:=-\int_d^c g$; for $c<d$ use the Riemann-sum construction below on the restriction to $[c,d]$. Then:

1. **Integral.** For every sequence of tagged partitions of $[a,b]$ whose mesh tends to $0$, the Riemann sums $\sum_i(t_{i+1}-t_i)\,g(s_i)$ converge in $X$; the limit, written $\int_a^b g$, is independent of the sequence, and
$$\Bigl\|\int_a^b g\Bigr\|\;\le\;(b-a)\sup_{t\in[a,b]}\|g(t)\| .$$
2. **Fundamental theorem.** The curve $G:[a,b]\to X$, $G(t):=\int_a^t g$, is well defined, satisfies $\|G(t)-G(s)\|\le(t-s)\sup_{[s,t]}\|g\|$ for $a\le s\le t\le b$, and is differentiable with $G'=g$ on $[a,b]$ in the one-sided sense at the endpoints.
3. **Linearity.** For continuous $g,h:[a,b]\to X$ and reals $\alpha,\beta$: $\int_a^b(\alpha g+\beta h)=\alpha\int_a^b g+\beta\int_a^b h$; and for $a\le c\le b$, $\int_a^b g=\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$.
4. **Bounded linear images.** If $Y$ is a normed real vector space and $T:X\to Y$ is linear with $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some $C<+\infty$ and all $x$, then $T\circ g$ is continuous and $T\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b (T\circ g)$; in particular, for every real-linear functional $\Lambda:X\to\mathbb R$ with $|\Lambda x|\le C\|x\|$, $\Lambda\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b\Lambda\circ g$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal E=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(M_d(\mathbb C))$ with the induced map norm. It has finite complex dimension $d^4$, so it is complete as a real normed space by [F5]. Set $M:=\sup_{u\in I}\|\mathcal L_u\|<\infty$. For fixed $s$, define $D_0(t)=I$ and recursively $D_n(t)=\int_s^t\mathcal L_uD_{n-1}(u)\,du$ for $n\geq1$, using [F6]. Induction with the integral norm bound gives $\|D_n(t)\|\leq M^n(t-s)^n/n!$; hence $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}D_n(t)$ converges uniformly on $[s,s_1]$. Calling its sum $\Lambda(t,s)$, uniform convergence and boundedness of $\mathcal L_u$ allow passage through the integral, giving $\Lambda(t,s)=I+\int_s^t\mathcal L_u\Lambda(u,s)\,du$. Also $\|\Lambda(u,s)\|\leq e^{M(u-s)}$.

Let $t_j=s+j(t-s)/n$ be a uniform partition of $[s,t]$ and freeze $\mathcal L_u$ to $\mathcal L_{t_j}$ on each interval $[t_j,t_{j+1})$. The resulting propagator is the time-ordered composition $e^{(t-t_{n-1})\mathcal L_{t_{n-1}}}\circ\cdots\circ e^{(t_1-t_0)\mathcal L_{t_0}}$. Each factor is a channel by [F2], and the composition is a channel by [F3].

By the fundamental theorem [F6], the integral equation in step 1.1 is differentiable and satisfies $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$, with $\Lambda(s,s)=I$. If another solution differs by $D$, then $D(t)=\int_s^t\mathcal L_uD(u)\,du$. With $C=\sup_{u\in[s,s_1]}\|D(u)\|<\infty$, repeated application of the integral norm bound gives $\|D(t)\|\leq C M^n(t-s)^n/n!$ for every $n\geq0$. This tends to zero, proving uniqueness.

Let $\delta_n=\sup_{u\in[s,t]}\|\mathcal L^{(n)}_u-\mathcal L_u\|$; uniform continuity gives $\delta_n\to0$. Subtract the integral equations for the frozen propagator $\Lambda_n$ and $\Lambda$. For $s\leq u\leq t$, the norm difference is bounded by $M\int_s^u\|\Lambda_n(v,s)-\Lambda(v,s)\|\,dv+\delta_n(t-s)e^{M(t-s)}$, using the bound in step 1.1. Iterating this scalar integral inequality yields $\|\Lambda_n(t,s)-\Lambda(t,s)\|\leq\delta_n(t-s)e^{2M(t-s)}\to0$. The channel set is closed under this norm limit by [F3], so $\Lambda(t,s)$ is a channel. For $s=t$ it is $I$, also a channel.

Step 1.1 permits M=sup||L_u||=0: all D_n with n≥1 vanish and Lambda=I. Step 2.1 proves uniqueness without dividing by M or t−s.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a real vector space ([[def-vector-space]]) with a norm $\|\cdot\|$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) whose metric $d(x,y):=\|x-y\|$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). Let $a<b$ be reals ([[def-interval]]) and let $g:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). For endpoints $c,d\in[a,b]$, set $\int_c^c g:=0_X$ and, when $c>d$, set $\int_c^d g:=-\int_d^c g$; for $c<d$ use the Riemann-sum construction below on the restriction to $[c,d]$. Then:

1. **Integral.** For every sequence of tagged partitions of $[a,b]$ whose mesh tends to $0$, the Riemann sums $\sum_i(t_{i+1}-t_i)\,g(s_i)$ converge in $X$; the limit, written $\int_a^b g$, is independent of the sequence, and
$$\Bigl\|\int_a^b g\Bigr\|\;\le\;(b-a)\sup_{t\in[a,b]}\|g(t)\| .$$
2. **Fundamental theorem.** The curve $G:[a,b]\to X$, $G(t):=\int_a^t g$, is well defined, satisfies $\|G(t)-G(s)\|\le(t-s)\sup_{[s,t]}\|g\|$ for $a\le s\le t\le b$, and is differentiable with $G'=g$ on $[a,b]$ in the one-sided sense at the endpoints.
3. **Linearity.** For continuous $g,h:[a,b]\to X$ and reals $\alpha,\beta$: $\int_a^b(\alpha g+\beta h)=\alpha\int_a^b g+\beta\int_a^b h$; and for $a\le c\le b$, $\int_a^b g=\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$.
4. **Bounded linear images.** If $Y$ is a normed real vector space and $T:X\to Y$ is linear with $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some $C<+\infty$ and all $x$, then $T\circ g$ is continuous and $T\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b (T\circ g)$; in particular, for every real-linear functional $\Lambda:X\to\mathbb R$ with $|\Lambda x|\le C\|x\|$, $\Lambda\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b\Lambda\circ g$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be a finite channel as defined in [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]]. There is a unique linear map $\Phi^\dagger:M_e(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ satisfying the trace-pairing identity

$$\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\Phi^\dagger(A))\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C),\ A\in M_e(\mathbb C)).$$

If $\Phi(X)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^*$, then $\Phi^\dagger(A)=\sum_aK_a^*AK_a$; in particular, $\Phi^\dagger$ is completely positive and unital. Composition and finite convex combinations of channels are channels. A limit in the induced operator norm $\|\Psi\|_{\infty\to\infty}:=\sup_{\|X\|_\infty\leq1}\|\Psi(X)\|_\infty$, where $\|X\|_\infty:=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Xv\|$, of channels $M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ is also a channel. Moreover, a norm limit of completely positive maps of these fixed finite dimensions is completely positive.
