The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: Fix $\gamma>0$ in ${\rm s}^{-1}$ and $t>0$ in seconds, so $0<e^{-\gamma t}<1$ by [F6]–[F8]. On $\mathbb C^2$, define $K_0=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-\gamma t/2},1)$, $K_1=\sqrt{1-e^{-\gamma t}}\,|1\rangle\langle0|$, and $\Phi_t(X)=K_0XK_0^*+K_1XK_1^*$. Since $K_0^*K_0+K_1^*K_1=I_2$, [F2] and [F1] show that $\Phi_t$ is a finite channel.

The matrix $\rho_0=I_2/2$ is positive semidefinite with trace one. Direct multiplication gives $\Phi_t(\rho_0)=\operatorname{diag}(p,1-p)$, where $p=e^{-\gamma t}/2\in(0,1/2)$ by [F6]–[F8]. The entropy difference is $S(\rho_0)-S(\Phi_t(\rho_0))=k_B(\ln2-h(p))$, where $h(p)=-p\ln p-(1-p)\ln(1-p)$. For the binary laws $P=(p,1-p)$ and $Q=(1/2,1/2)$, [F4] gives $D(P\|Q)=\ln2-h(p)$; since $P\ne Q$, [F5] gives $D(P\|Q)>0$. With $k_B>0$, this yields $S(\Phi_t(\rho_0))<S(\rho_0)$ and refutes the universal claim.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 exhibits two specified 2×2 Kraus matrices with adjoint-square sum I_2, and step 2.1 uses rho_0=I_2/2; this witness has neither an empty matrix space nor an empty Kraus family.
Statement: The zero matrix is outside the positive trace-one input hypothesis; the witness ρ₀=I₂/2 is full rank.
The counterexample uses dimension two in step 1.1. In dimension one a trace-one density is the scalar 1 and its entropy is zero, so strict entropy decrease cannot supply this witness.
Step 1.1 requires gamma,t>0, yielding 0<e^(−gamma t)<1; step 2.1 then has p in (0,1/2) and P≠Q. At zero damping or zero elapsed time that strict KL comparison would vanish.
The witness in step 1.1 is at finite t>0, excluding the identity endpoint t=0. Step 2.1 never needs the t→infinity limit or a logarithm of a zero output eigenvalue.
Given and A1 explicitly retain full AC for the KL nonnegativity/equality supplier F5 used in step 2.1; the two Kraus matrices themselves are explicitly constructed.

boundaries.reason: Statement refuted is universal entropy monotonicity for channels, rather than a biconditional; step 2.1 disproves it with one strict reverse entropy inequality.
The exhibited amplitude-damping channel refutes the universal assertion; it does not classify channels from their entropy behavior in a converse direction.

finite_checks.evidence: Choose γ=log(2) s⁻¹ and t=1 s in the displayed Kraus family, with ρ₀=I₂/2. Then p=1/4 and S(ρ₀)−S(Φ_tρ₀)=k_B D((1/4,3/4)||(1/2,1/2))>0 by the cited strict KL result.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

derivations.claim: The transpose is complex-linear and preserves trace because it fixes the diagonal entries. For any $X\geq0$, [F2] gives $X=YY^*$ for some matrix $Y$; hence $T(X)=X^{\mathsf T}=\overline Y Y^{\mathsf T}=\overline Y(\overline Y)^*\geq0$. Thus $T$ is positive and trace-preserving.

Its Choi matrix is $J(T)=\sum_{i,j=0}^1E_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}$, the swap operator $F(|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle)=|b\rangle\otimes|a\rangle$. For $\eta=(|0\rangle\otimes|1\rangle-|1\rangle\otimes|0\rangle)/\sqrt2$, one has $F\eta=-\eta$; therefore $J(T)\not\geq0$. By [F3], $T$ is not completely positive.

boundaries.evidence: Given fixes C² and step 2.1 uses its four matrix units to form the Choi swap; no empty space or missing tensor factor is used.
Statement: The zero matrix is mapped to zero; the counterexample witness is instead the nonzero antisymmetric Choi vector in step 2.1.
Step 2.1 needs the nonzero antisymmetric vector (|01>−|10>)/sqrt(2) in two qubits. Scalar transpose is the identity, so dimension one is not this counterexample.
Step 1.1 factors every positive semidefinite X as YY*, including singular X; step 2.1 finds the explicit negative Choi eigenvalue −1, rather than relying on strict input positivity.

boundaries.reason: Transpose and its swap Choi matrix are fixed linear operators; the negative eigenvector test in step 2.1 involves no evolving or limiting parameter.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 supplies eta explicitly and step 1.1 uses a finite positive square root; neither construction invokes an arbitrary family of nonempty sets.

boundaries.reason: The refuted assertion is the implication positive and trace-preserving implies completely positive; positivity is verified and its purported consequence fails.
No converse to that implication is challenged: complete positivity implies ordinary positivity by r=1, while the constructed transpose fails the forward implication.

citations.quote:
For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

Let $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, with $d,m\geq1$, in fixed ordered orthonormal bases. Let $H_{\mathrm{tot}}=H_{\mathrm{tot}}^*$ be a matrix on $H_S\otimes H_E$ with energy units joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and set $U_t=e^{-itH_{\mathrm{tot}}/\hbar}$ for $t\in\mathbb R$ measured in seconds. Let $\sigma_E\geq0$ with $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma_E=1$, and define

$$\Phi_t(\rho):=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(\rho\otimes\sigma_E)U_t^*\right)\qquad(\rho\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

For each $t$, $\Phi_t:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ is a finite quantum channel. The theorem concerns the product preparation $\rho\otimes\sigma_E$; it makes no claim that a correlated initial joint state defines a map of the system marginal alone.

derivations.claim: Let $|\psi_\pm\rangle=(|00\rangle\pm|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and $\omega_\pm=|\psi_\pm\rangle\langle\psi_\pm|$; each $\omega_\pm$ is positive semidefinite with trace one. Using [F1], the cross terms $|00\rangle\langle11|$ and $|11\rangle\langle00|$ vanish under $\operatorname{Tr}_E$ because their environment indices differ, while the diagonal terms give $\operatorname{Tr}_E\omega_+=\operatorname{Tr}_E\omega_-=I_2/2$.

Define $U|a,b\rangle=|a,a\oplus b\rangle$ for $a,b\in\{0,1\}$, where $\oplus$ is addition modulo two. This CNOT map permutes the orthonormal product basis and is therefore unitary. It sends $|\psi_\pm\rangle$ to $|\pm\rangle\otimes|0\rangle$, where $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}_E(U\omega_\pm U^*)=|\pm\rangle\langle\pm|$, and the outputs are distinct because their $(0,1)$ matrix entries are $1/2$ and $-1/2$. Equal system marginals therefore do not determine the final system state for these correlated preparations, refuting the claim. The product-preparation theorem [F2] is unaffected.

boundaries.evidence: Given supplies two qubit factors; step 1.1 explicitly normalizes two Bell vectors and obtains the trace-one marginal I_2/2, ruling out an empty or unnormalized witness.
Statement: Zero joint matrices are outside the trace-one witness class; the counterexample uses two rank-one trace-one states.
The distinct outputs in step 2.1 require the two system basis labels and a two-level environment. A one-dimensional system has only one density, so these two output coherences would not exist.
Step 1.1 uses rank-one joint densities with the same full-rank marginal; their singularity is allowed. Step 2.1 gives unequal output entries +1/2 and −1/2 under the same basis permutation.

boundaries.reason: The example fixes a single CNOT unitary and two joint preparations; no duration, endpoint, or limiting bath parameter enters the witness.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1–2.1 explicitly specify both Bell vectors, the CNOT basis permutation, and both output coherences; the witness requires no selection principle.

boundaries.reason: The universal assertion concerns determination of the final marginal from the initial marginal; two explicit inputs disprove determination, without an equivalence to test.
No reconstruction of a joint preparation from its output marginal is asserted; step 2.1 distinguishes outputs for equal initial marginals only.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $d,e\geq1$. For $A\in M_{e\times d}(\mathbb C)$ and $B\in M_{d\times e}(\mathbb C)$,
$$ \operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA), $$
where $\operatorname{Tr}_r$ is the diagonal-sum trace on $M_r(\mathbb C)$. This includes cyclicity for square matrices. For $C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the bilinear trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, then $C=0$. No adjoint is inserted in this pairing.

derivations.claim: The square root $\sigma^{1/2}$ exists by [F2] and is invertible because $\sigma>0$. Thus $\langle A,A\rangle_\sigma=\operatorname{Tr}((A\sigma^{1/2})^*(A\sigma^{1/2}))>0$ for every nonzero $A$. Linearity in the first variable is immediate, and cyclicity [F3] gives Hermitian symmetry; hence the displayed form is a positive-definite inner product.

For the Hamiltonian term, cyclicity in [F3] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(-i[H_{\rm s},X]A/\hbar)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\,i[H_{\rm s},A]/\hbar)$. Indeed, $\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\rm s}XA)=\operatorname{Tr}(XA H_{\rm s})$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(XH_{\rm s}A)$ is already in the desired input-first order.

For each jump matrix, $\operatorname{Tr}(L_jXL_j^*A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X L_j^* A L_j)$. The first anticommutator term satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}(L_j^*L_jXA)=\operatorname{Tr}(X A L_j^*L_j)$ by cyclicity, and the second is already $\operatorname{Tr}(X L_j^*L_j A)$. Thus the trace-dual dissipator is exactly the displayed $D$. Substituting $A=I$ cancels $L_j^*L_j-\frac12(L_j^*L_j+L_j^*L_j)=0$ term by term, so $D(I)=0$.

Let $d\geq1$ be finite, let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ with its standard inner product, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ for its matrices. Let $H_{\rm s}=H_{\rm s}^*\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be a Hamiltonian in joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $m\geq0$ be an integer with $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ a finite family of jump matrices in seconds$^{-1/2}$. Matrices on which the generators act are dimensionless. The Schrödinger generator $\mathcal L$ is the finite GKSL generator of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]].

Its trace-dual observable generator is

$$G(A)=\frac{i}{\hbar}[H_{\rm s},A]+D(A),\qquad D(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(L_j^*AL_j-\frac12\{L_j^*L_j,A\}\right).$$

Here $[U,V]=UV-VU$, $\{U,V\}=UV+VU$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. The units of $G$, $D$, and $\mathcal L$ are seconds$^{-1}$. The generator preserves the identity, $D(I)=0$, so $e^{tD}(I)=I$.

Let $\sigma=\sigma^*>0$ be a dimensionless density matrix on $\mathcal H$, so $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1$. Define

$$\langle A,B\rangle_\sigma:=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma B^*A),\qquad \|A\|_\sigma:=\langle A,A\rangle_\sigma^{1/2}.$$

This inner product is linear in its first variable. It is positive definite because $\sigma>0$. The data satisfy **the specified finite GNS detailed-balance convention** when $[H_{\rm s},\sigma]=0$ and $D$ is self-adjoint for this inner product, meaning $\langle D(A),B\rangle_\sigma=\langle A,D(B)\rangle_\sigma$ for all $A,B\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. The Hamiltonian part of $G$ is kept separate and is anti-self-adjoint. Quantum detailed-balance conventions vary; in particular, this definition does not identify GNS symmetry with KMS or Kubo–Mori symmetry.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite GKSL generator on $M_d(\mathbb C)$, $d\geq1$, with the units and conventions of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. Then $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ is a finite channel for every $t\geq0$. The family satisfies $T_0=\operatorname{id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and is norm-continuous. Time is measured in seconds; no negative-time channel or physical bath limit is asserted.

Let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be a finite channel as defined in [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]]. There is a unique linear map $\Phi^\dagger:M_e(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ satisfying the trace-pairing identity

$$\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\Phi^\dagger(A))\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C),\ A\in M_e(\mathbb C)).$$

If $\Phi(X)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^*$, then $\Phi^\dagger(A)=\sum_aK_a^*AK_a$; in particular, $\Phi^\dagger$ is completely positive and unital. Composition and finite convex combinations of channels are channels. A limit in the induced operator norm $\|\Psi\|_{\infty\to\infty}:=\sup_{\|X\|_\infty\leq1}\|\Psi(X)\|_\infty$, where $\|X\|_\infty:=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Xv\|$, of channels $M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ is also a channel. Moreover, a norm limit of completely positive maps of these fixed finite dimensions is completely positive.

Let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be a finite channel, and define $\|X\|_\infty=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Xv\|$ and $\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^*X}$. Its trace dual $\Phi^\dagger:M_e(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ from [[thm-qsm-dt-channel-duality]] satisfies

$$\|\Phi^\dagger(A)\|_\infty\leq\|A\|_\infty\qquad(A\in M_e(\mathbb C)).$$ For every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the Schrödinger map contracts the trace norm: $$\|\Phi(X)\|_1\leq\|X\|_1.$$

The second inequality applies to arbitrary complex matrices, not only density matrices.

Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $d,e\geq1$. For $A\in M_{e\times d}(\mathbb C)$ and $B\in M_{d\times e}(\mathbb C)$,
$$ \operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA), $$
where $\operatorname{Tr}_r$ is the diagonal-sum trace on $M_r(\mathbb C)$. This includes cyclicity for square matrices. For $C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the bilinear trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, then $C=0$. No adjoint is inserted in this pairing.

derivations.claim: If $d=1$, then $\mathcal M_0=\{0\}$ and the only density matrix is $\sigma$, so all assertions are immediate. For the remainder assume $d>1$. By [F1], self-adjointness and $D(I)=0$ give $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma D(A))=\langle D(A),I\rangle_\sigma=\langle A,D(I)\rangle_\sigma=0$. For the Hamiltonian part, cyclicity [F6] and $[H_{\rm s},\sigma]=0$ give $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma K(A))=0$. Since $G$ is the trace dual of $\mathcal L$, differentiating $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma e^{tG}A)$ now shows it is constant. Applying the same calculation with $K=0$ shows $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma e^{tD}A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma A)$. Thus $\sigma$ is stationary for both dual semigroups.

Let $\mathcal L_D(X)=\sum_j(L_jXL_j^*-\frac12\{L_j^*L_j,X\})$, the Schrödinger GKSL generator with zero Hamiltonian and the same jump matrices. The finite trace calculation in [F1], [F6] shows its trace dual is $D$. Applying [F2] to $\mathcal L_D$ and [F3] to its channel semigroup makes $e^{tD}$ unital and completely positive. The Schwarz inequality [F4] and stationarity from step 1.1 give
$$
\|e^{tD}A\|_\sigma^2=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma(e^{tD}A)^*e^{tD}A)\leq\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma e^{tD}(A^*A))=\|A\|_\sigma^2.
$$
Differentiating at $t=0$ yields $\operatorname{Re}\langle D(A),A\rangle_\sigma\leq0$; self-adjointness in [F1] makes this quantity real.

The subspace $\mathcal M_0$ is the orthogonal complement of $\mathbb C I$, and [F1] gives $D(\mathcal M_0)\subseteq\mathcal M_0$. The finite-dimensional spectral theorem [F5] applies to the self-adjoint endomorphism $D$ on $(M_d,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\sigma)$. Step 2.1 makes all eigenvalues nonpositive; $\ker D=\mathbb C I$ excludes zero on $\mathcal M_0$. Because $d>1$, $\mathcal M_0\ne\{0\}$, so its finite nonempty list of eigenvalues has maximum $-\gamma<0$, and $\langle D(A),A\rangle_\sigma\leq-\gamma\|A\|_\sigma^2$.

By [F6] and $[H_{\rm s},\sigma]=0$, $K$ is anti-self-adjoint for $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\sigma$. Both $K$ and $D$ preserve $\mathcal M_0$: for $D$ this follows from step 1.1, and for $K$ from the same trace-cyclicity calculation. For $A_t=e^{tG}A$ with centered $A$, differentiating gives
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\|A_t\|_\sigma^2=2\operatorname{Re}\langle G(A_t),A_t\rangle_\sigma=2\langle D(A_t),A_t\rangle_\sigma\leq-2\gamma\|A_t\|_\sigma^2.
$$
Thus $e^{2\gamma t}\|A_t\|_\sigma^2$ is nonincreasing, proving the asserted decay. Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] then bounds each centered correlation by $e^{-\gamma t}\|A\|_\sigma\|B\|_\sigma$, an integrable function.

The decay in step 4.1 makes $Y:=\int_0^\infty e^{tG}A\,dt$ converge in the finite-dimensional space $\mathcal M_0$. Differentiating $e^{tG}A$ and integrating gives $-GY=A$. If $GZ=0$ for centered $Z$, then step 4.1 gives $\|Z\|_\sigma=\|e^{tG}Z\|_\sigma\leq e^{-\gamma t}\|Z\|_\sigma$, so $Z=0$; hence $-G|_{\mathcal M_0}$ is invertible and $Y=(-G|_{\mathcal M_0})^{-1}A$.

Let $Y$ be as in step 5.1. Then $\Gamma(A)=\operatorname{Re}\langle Y,-G(Y)\rangle_\sigma$. The anti-self-adjoint $K$ contributes zero real part, while step 3.1 gives $\langle Y,-D(Y)\rangle_\sigma\geq\gamma\|Y\|_\sigma^2\geq0$. Therefore $\Gamma(A)\geq0$.

Let $X=\rho-\sigma=X^*$, and take any $A$ with $\|A\|_\infty\leq1$. Set $A_0=A-\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma A)I$. Stationarity and trace duality give $\operatorname{Tr}((\rho_t-\sigma)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X e^{tG}A_0)$. By cyclicity [F6], the trace-norm dual formula [F4] applies to this product order. Put $C=e^{tG}A_0$. Since $\operatorname{Tr}(XC)=\operatorname{Tr}(CX)=\operatorname{Tr}((C\sigma^{1/2})(\sigma^{-1/2}X))$, the Hilbert–Schmidt trace inequality $|\operatorname{Tr}(UV)|\leq\|U\|_2\|V\|_2$ yields
$$
|\operatorname{Tr}(X e^{tG}A_0)|\leq\|\sigma^{-1/2}X\|_2\,\|e^{tG}A_0\|_\sigma\leq\|\sigma^{-1/2}X\|_2e^{-\gamma t}\|A_0\|_\sigma.
$$
The identity $\|A_0\|_\sigma^2=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma A^*A)-|\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma A)|^2\leq\|A\|_\infty^2\leq1$ gives a bound independent of $A$. Taking the supremum in [F4] proves the stated trace-norm relaxation estimate.

Let $d\geq1$ be finite, let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ with its standard inner product, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ for its matrices. Let $H_{\rm s}=H_{\rm s}^*\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be a Hamiltonian in joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $m\geq0$ be an integer with $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ a finite family of jump matrices in seconds$^{-1/2}$. Matrices on which the generators act are dimensionless. The Schrödinger generator $\mathcal L$ is the finite GKSL generator of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]].

Its trace-dual observable generator is

$$G(A)=\frac{i}{\hbar}[H_{\rm s},A]+D(A),\qquad D(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(L_j^*AL_j-\frac12\{L_j^*L_j,A\}\right).$$

Here $[U,V]=UV-VU$, $\{U,V\}=UV+VU$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. The units of $G$, $D$, and $\mathcal L$ are seconds$^{-1}$. The generator preserves the identity, $D(I)=0$, so $e^{tD}(I)=I$.

Let $\sigma=\sigma^*>0$ be a dimensionless density matrix on $\mathcal H$, so $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1$. Define

$$\langle A,B\rangle_\sigma:=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma B^*A),\qquad \|A\|_\sigma:=\langle A,A\rangle_\sigma^{1/2}.$$

This inner product is linear in its first variable. It is positive definite because $\sigma>0$. The data satisfy **the specified finite GNS detailed-balance convention** when $[H_{\rm s},\sigma]=0$ and $D$ is self-adjoint for this inner product, meaning $\langle D(A),B\rangle_\sigma=\langle A,D(B)\rangle_\sigma$ for all $A,B\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. The Hamiltonian part of $G$ is kept separate and is anti-self-adjoint. Quantum detailed-balance conventions vary; in particular, this definition does not identify GNS symmetry with KMS or Kubo–Mori symmetry.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite GKSL generator on $M_d(\mathbb C)$, $d\geq1$, with the units and conventions of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. Then $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ is a finite channel for every $t\geq0$. The family satisfies $T_0=\operatorname{id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and is norm-continuous. Time is measured in seconds; no negative-time channel or physical bath limit is asserted.

Let $d\geq1$, and let $G=K+D$ and the faithful density matrix $\sigma$ satisfy [[def-qsm-dt-gns-detailed-balance]], with $\ker D=\mathbb C I$. Write $\mathcal M_0=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma A)=0\}$. If $d>1$, the restriction $D|_{\mathcal M_0}$ has only strictly negative eigenvalues. Define

$$\gamma:=\min\{-\lambda:\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(D|_{\mathcal M_0})\}>0.$$

Then for every $A\in\mathcal M_0$ and $t\geq0$,

$$\|e^{tG}A\|_\sigma\leq e^{-\gamma t}\|A\|_\sigma.$$

For every density matrix $\rho$, let $\rho_t=e^{t\mathcal L}\rho$, where $\mathcal L$ is the Schrödinger trace-dual generator. Then

$$\|\rho_t-\sigma\|_1\leq\|\sigma^{-1/2}(\rho-\sigma)\|_2e^{-\gamma t}.$$

Here $\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^*X}$ and $\|X\|_2=(\operatorname{Tr}X^*X)^{1/2}$. For centered $A,B\in\mathcal M_0$, the correlation $t\mapsto\langle e^{tG}A,B\rangle_\sigma$ is absolutely integrable. Also

$$\Gamma(A):=\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty\langle e^{tG}A,A\rangle_\sigma\,dt=\operatorname{Re}\langle(-G|_{\mathcal M_0})^{-1}A,A\rangle_\sigma\geq0.$$

For $d=1$, $\mathcal M_0=\{0\}$, $\rho=\sigma$, and all centered and relaxation claims are trivial; no $\gamma$ is defined. The units of $\gamma$ are seconds$^{-1}$. These are finite-dimensional conditional model results; they assert no infinite-dimensional bath limit.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $d,e\geq1$. For $A\in M_{e\times d}(\mathbb C)$ and $B\in M_{d\times e}(\mathbb C)$,
$$ \operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA), $$
where $\operatorname{Tr}_r$ is the diagonal-sum trace on $M_r(\mathbb C)$. This includes cyclicity for square matrices. For $C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the bilinear trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, then $C=0$. No adjoint is inserted in this pairing.

derivations.claim: The finite sum $Z_\beta$ is strictly positive, so each $\pi_a>0$ and $\sum_a\pi_a=1$. Hence $\sigma>0$, $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1$, and $[H_{\rm s},\sigma]=0$. The finite GKSL semigroup exists by [F2].

Put $R=\sum_{x\ne y}L_{xy}^*L_{xy}=\sum_a r_a|a\rangle\langle a|$. For a diagonal density $\rho=\sum_a p_a|a\rangle\langle a|$, $L_{xy}\rho L_{xy}^*=w_{xy}p_x|y\rangle\langle y|$, while the anticommutator contributes $-r_ap_a|a\rangle\langle a|$. Summing entries gives the Schrödinger population equation
$$
\dot p_a=\sum_{b\ne a}(p_bw_{ba}-p_aw_{ab}),
$$
For a diagonal observable $f=\sum_a f_a|a\rangle\langle a|$, direct multiplication gives
$$
D(f)=\sum_a\left(\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)\right)|a\rangle\langle a|,
$$
so its diagonal action is exactly $W$.
For $a\ne b$, every gain term $L_{xy}|a\rangle\langle b|L_{xy}^*$ vanishes; the $R$ anticommutator contributes $-(r_a+r_b)|a\rangle\langle b|/2$, and the Hamiltonian commutator contributes $-i(E_a-E_b)|a\rangle\langle b|/\hbar$. Thus the coherence equation is
$$
\dot\rho_{ab}=\left(-\frac{i(E_a-E_b)}{\hbar}-\frac{r_a+r_b}{2}\right)\rho_{ab}.
$$
For $c_{ab}:=\pi_aw_{ab}=c_{ba}$ and sums over $a\ne b$, the cross terms satisfy $\sum_{a\ne b}c_{ab}f_bg_a=\sum_{a\ne b}c_{ab}f_ag_b$ after swapping $a,b$, so $\langle Wf,g\rangle_\pi=\langle f,Wg\rangle_\pi$. Symmetrizing the quadratic form gives
$$
-\langle Wf,f\rangle_\pi=\frac12\sum_a\sum_{b\ne a}\pi_aw_{ab}|f_b-f_a|^2,
$$
so $W$ is self-adjoint on the diagonal subspace.

For $a\ne b$, direct multiplication with diagonal $\sigma$ gives $\langle |a\rangle\langle b|,|c\rangle\langle d|\rangle_\sigma=0$ unless $(a,b)=(c,d)$, and $\||a\rangle\langle b|\|_\sigma^2=\pi_b$. Also each jump gain $L_{xy}^*|a\rangle\langle b|L_{xy}$ is zero when $a\ne b$, and the anticommutator with $R$ gives $D(|a\rangle\langle b|)=-(r_a+r_b)|a\rangle\langle b|/2$. Diagonal and off-diagonal subspaces are orthogonal. Together with the diagonal self-adjointness from step 1.2, these real eigenvalues prove that $D$ is self-adjoint on all of $M_d(\mathbb C)$.

Connectivity and $d\geq2$ imply $r_a>0$ for each $a$, so every off-diagonal matrix unit has a strictly negative $D$-eigenvalue. The Dirichlet identity in step 1.2 vanishes only when $f_a=f_b$ along every positive-rate edge; connectedness then forces $f$ to be constant. Therefore the diagonal kernel is $\mathbb C I$, the off-diagonal kernel is zero, and $\ker D=\mathbb C I$. Applying the finite spectral theorem [F4] to the self-adjoint $W|_{\pi^\perp}$ shows its finite list of eigenvalues is strictly negative; their minimum absolute value is $\gamma_{\rm cl}>0$.

Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, and 3.1 verify every hypothesis of [[def-qsm-dt-gns-detailed-balance]] and [F3]. Applying [F3] yields the positive gap, exponential relaxation, trace-norm bound, and absolutely integrable centered correlations for this Gibbs jump generator.

Statement assumes finite energies and beta>0, with no zero-temperature beta→infinity limit. Step 1.1 obtains strictly positive finite Gibbs weights; its finite semigroup includes time zero through F2.

Step 4.1 applies the generic gap theorem after checking its premises; it asserts no converse that an arbitrary gapped generator has this particular energy-resolved form.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $d\geq2$, let $E=\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let $E_a\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies in joules, and let $\beta>0$ have units joule$^{-1}$. Define

$$Z_\beta:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta E_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta E_a}.$$

For each $a\ne b$, let $w_{ab}\geq0$ be a rate in seconds$^{-1}$ satisfying Gibbs detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$, and assume the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ is connected. On $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$, fix an orthonormal energy basis $(|a\rangle)$, set $H_{\rm s}=\sum_aE_a|a\rangle\langle a|$, and define $L_{ab}=\sqrt{w_{ab}}|b\rangle\langle a|$ for $a\ne b$. Fix $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. For real functions $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_a\pi_af_ag_a$, and define the row-generator action on column observables by $(Wf)_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$. Let

$$\sigma:=\sum_a\pi_a|a\rangle\langle a|,\qquad r_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}.$$

Use the finite GKSL generator with Hamiltonian $H_{\rm s}$ and the jump matrices $L_{ab}$. Its observable dissipator $D$ is self-adjoint for the $\sigma$-GNS inner product of [[def-qsm-dt-gns-detailed-balance]], $H_{\rm s}$ commutes with $\sigma$, and $\ker D=\mathbb C I$. On diagonal observables, $W$ is self-adjoint on $L^2(E,\pi)$ with constants as its kernel; for $d\geq2$ its restriction to $\pi^\perp:=\{f:E\to\mathbb R:\sum_a\pi_af_a=0\}$ has a positive spectral gap $\gamma_{\rm cl}$. Thus the generator satisfies the specified finite GNS detailed-balance convention and the generic gap conclusion of [[thm-qsm-dt-detailed-balance-gap]] applies. This claim does not assert a microscopic bath limit.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and let $E,\pi,w,Q$ be the finite model data of [[def-csm-dk-finite-reversible-rate-model]], with $|E|=r\ge2$. For every initial probability row vector $p_0$, there exists a time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain $X_t$ on $E$, $t\ge0$, with no finite accumulation of jumps, transition matrix $P_t=e^{tQ}$, and law $p_t=p_0P_t$. The detailed-balance law $\pi$ is stationary. On the real inner-product space $L^2(E,\pi)$, $Q$ is self-adjoint and has an orthonormal eigenbasis $\phi_0=1,\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{r-1}$ with eigenvalues $0,-\lambda_1,\ldots,-\lambda_{r-1}$, where every $\lambda_j>0$. Thus the spectral gap $\lambda_*:=\min_j\lambda_j$ is positive and $P_t$ converges exponentially to projection onto constants.

Here a finite-state continuous-time Markov chain means a process with piecewise-constant paths whose conditional transition matrix over an interval of length $t$ is $P_t$, independent of the starting time. For initial law $\pi$, the chain has a two-sided stationary extension $X_t$, $t\in\mathbb R$, whose finite-dimensional laws at $t_1<\cdots<t_n$ are $\pi_{a_1}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}P_{t_{i+1}-t_i}(a_i,a_{i+1})$. Its sample paths are locally piecewise constant with finitely many jumps on every bounded time interval.

derivations.claim: The jump matrices give $L_{ab}^*L_{ab}=w_{ab}|a\rangle\langle a|$, so $R=\sum_a r_a|a\rangle\langle a|$ and $K^*+K=-R$. Hence $M_0(dt)^*M_0(dt)=I-Rdt+o(dt)$, while the sum of jump effects is $Rdt$; the total effect is $I+o(dt)$ as required for a normalized infinitesimal instrument. Also $K|a\rangle=(-iE_a/\hbar-r_a/2)|a\rangle$, so $\|e^{tK}|a\rangle\|^2=e^{-r_at}$. The no-click survival probability is exactly the exponential holding-time law of rate $r_a$.

For a short interval $dt$, the instrument outcome $a\to b$ has probability $dt\,\langle a|L_{ab}^*L_{ab}|a\rangle+o(dt)=w_{ab}dt+o(dt)$. Summing over $b\ne a$ gives total jump rate $r_a$, and conditioning on a jump gives destination probability $w_{ab}/r_a$. The post-jump normalized state is $|b\rangle$.

For an arbitrary matrix $X$, the no-click branch contributes $M_0(dt)XM_0(dt)^*=X+dt(KX+XK^*)+o(dt)$, and the jump branches contribute $dt\sum_{a\ne b}L_{ab}XL_{ab}^*+o(dt)$. Since $K=-iH_{\rm s}/\hbar-R/2$ and $R=\sum_{a\ne b}L_{ab}^*L_{ab}$, their sum is $X+dt\mathcal L(X)+o(dt)$ with exactly the generator in [F2]. Thus the selected infinitesimal outcomes have the specified GKSL generator.

The holding-time and destination laws in steps 1.1–1.2 are exactly those of the chain in [F3]. Full AC [A1] and [F3] supply its joint path law and nonexplosion; hence the specified instrument's recorded path is the finite continuous-time chain with generator $W$, not a law inferred from noncommuting one-time correlations.

derivations.claim:
The population equation in [F1] is $p'_t=p_tW$ for row probability vectors, so $p_t=p_0e^{tW}$. Let $\lambda>\max_a r_a$ and $P:=I+W/\lambda$. Then $P$ is a finite stochastic matrix with $P_{aa}>0$, and the matrix exponential satisfies
$$
e^{tW}=e^{-\lambda t}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}P^n.
$$
For any initial probability vector, choose $a$ with $p_a(0)>0$. For every $b$, graph connectivity gives a finite positive-rate path from $a$ to $b$; the corresponding power $P^n$ has $(P^n)_{ab}>0$. Its coefficient in the series is positive for $t>0$, so $p_b(t)>0$.

For $t>0$, put $u_a=p_a(t)/\pi_a>0$ and, for $a\ne b$, put $c_{ab}:=\pi_aw_{ab}=c_{ba}$. Differentiating $K$ and using $\sum_a p'_a=0$ gives
$$
\frac{d}{dt}K(p_t\mid\pi)=\sum_a p'_a\log u_a=\sum_{a\ne b}c_{ab}(u_b-u_a)\log u_a.
$$
Pairing the $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ terms yields the displayed symmetric formula. Since $\log$ is increasing, each $(u_a-u_b)(\log u_a-\log u_b)\geq0$.

Equality in step 2.1 forces $u_a=u_b$ on every positive-rate edge. Connectedness makes all $u_a$ equal, and $\sum_a p_a=\sum_a\pi_a=1$ then gives $u_a=1$, so $p_t=\pi$. Conversely $p_t=\pi$ makes every term zero. Finally $x\log(x/\pi_a)\to0$ as $x\downarrow0$, so $K(p_t\mid\pi)$ is continuous at $t=0$; applying the derivative inequality on $[\varepsilon,t]$ and taking $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves nonincrease from any initial probability vector.

derivations.claim: Cauchy–Schwarz in the finite weighted inner product and [F1] give $|C_{A,B}(t)|\leq e^{-\gamma t}\|A\|_\sigma\|B\|_\sigma$. The right side is integrable on $[0,\infty)$, so the correlation integral converges absolutely.

The integral $Y:=\int_0^\infty e^{tG}A\,dt$ converges in the finite-dimensional invariant space $\mathcal M_0$. Let $d\geq1$ be finite, let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ with its standard inner product, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ for its matrices. Let $H_{\rm s}=H_{\rm s}^*\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be a Hamiltonian in joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $m\geq0$ be an integer with $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ a finite family of jump matrices in seconds$^{-1/2}$. Matrices on which the generators act are dimensionless. The Schrödinger generator $\mathcal L$ is the finite GKSL generator of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]].

Its trace-dual observable generator is

$$G(A)=\frac{i}{\hbar}[H_{\rm s},A]+D(A),\qquad D(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(L_j^*AL_j-\frac12\{L_j^*L_j,A\}\right).$$

Here $[U,V]=UV-VU$, $\{U,V\}=UV+VU$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. The units of $G$, $D$, and $\mathcal L$ are seconds$^{-1}$. The generator preserves the identity, $D(I)=0$, so $e^{tD}(I)=I$.

Let $\sigma=\sigma^*>0$ be a dimensionless density matrix on $\mathcal H$, so $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1$. Define

$$\langle A,B\rangle_\sigma:=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma B^*A),\qquad \|A\|_\sigma:=\langle A,A\rangle_\sigma^{1/2}.$$

This inner product is linear in its first variable. It is positive definite because $\sigma>0$. The data satisfy **the specified finite GNS detailed-balance convention** when $[H_{\rm s},\sigma]=0$ and $D$ is self-adjoint for this inner product, meaning $\langle D(A),B\rangle_\sigma=\langle A,D(B)\rangle_\sigma$ for all $A,B\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. The Hamiltonian part of $G$ is kept separate and is anti-self-adjoint. Quantum detailed-balance conventions vary; in particular, this definition does not identify GNS symmetry with KMS or Kubo–Mori symmetry.

Let $I=[s_0,s_1]\subset\mathbb R$ be a compact time interval in seconds, $d\geq1$, $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ continuous with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ in joules, and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ continuous with finite $a=1,\ldots,m$ in ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$. At each $t\in I$, form $\mathcal L_t$ by [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. For every $s\leq t$ in $I$, the propagator $\Lambda(t,s)$ solving

$$\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s),\qquad \Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id},$$

exists uniquely and is a finite channel. No semigroup law is asserted when $t\mapsto\mathcal L_t$ varies.

Let $d\geq1$, and let $G=K+D$ and the faithful density matrix $\sigma$ satisfy [[def-qsm-dt-gns-detailed-balance]], with $\ker D=\mathbb C I$. Write $\mathcal M_0=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma A)=0\}$. If $d>1$, the restriction $D|_{\mathcal M_0}$ has only strictly negative eigenvalues. Define

$$\gamma:=\min\{-\lambda:\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(D|_{\mathcal M_0})\}>0.$$

Then for every $A\in\mathcal M_0$ and $t\geq0$,

$$\|e^{tG}A\|_\sigma\leq e^{-\gamma t}\|A\|_\sigma.$$

For every density matrix $\rho$, let $\rho_t=e^{t\mathcal L}\rho$, where $\mathcal L$ is the Schrödinger trace-dual generator. Then

$$\|\rho_t-\sigma\|_1\leq\|\sigma^{-1/2}(\rho-\sigma)\|_2e^{-\gamma t}.$$

Here $\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^*X}$ and $\|X\|_2=(\operatorname{Tr}X^*X)^{1/2}$. For centered $A,B\in\mathcal M_0$, the correlation $t\mapsto\langle e^{tG}A,B\rangle_\sigma$ is absolutely integrable. Also

$$\Gamma(A):=\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty\langle e^{tG}A,A\rangle_\sigma\,dt=\operatorname{Re}\langle(-G|_{\mathcal M_0})^{-1}A,A\rangle_\sigma\geq0.$$

For $d=1$, $\mathcal M_0=\{0\}$, $\rho=\sigma$, and all centered and relaxation claims are trivial; no $\gamma$ is defined. The units of $\gamma$ are seconds$^{-1}$. These are finite-dimensional conditional model results; they assert no infinite-dimensional bath limit.

Let $d,e\geq1$. For $A\in M_{e\times d}(\mathbb C)$ and $B\in M_{d\times e}(\mathbb C)$,
$$ \operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA), $$
where $\operatorname{Tr}_r$ is the diagonal-sum trace on $M_r(\mathbb C)$. This includes cyclicity for square matrices. For $C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the bilinear trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, then $C=0$. No adjoint is inserted in this pairing.

Put $V(X):=i[B,X]/\hbar$. The perturbed Schrödinger generator is $\mathcal L_\epsilon(t)=\mathcal L_0+\epsilon h(t)V$. Since $\mathcal L_0$ leaves $\sigma$ stationary by [F3], variation of constants gives
$$
\rho^\epsilon_t=\sigma+\epsilon\int_0^t h(s)e^{(t-s)\mathcal L_0}V(\sigma)\,ds+\epsilon^2\int_{0\leq u\leq s\leq t}h(s)h(u)e^{(t-s)\mathcal L_0}V e^{(s-u)\mathcal L_0}V(\rho^\epsilon_u)\,du\,ds.
$$
The second integral is $O(\epsilon^2)$ uniformly on $[0,T]$: $h$ is bounded, $V$ is a bounded linear map on the finite matrix space, $\sup_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T}\|e^{(t-s)\mathcal L_0}\|_1<\infty$, and $\|\rho^\epsilon_u\|_1=1$ because [F2] gives a channel propagator. $$
\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(Ae^{\tau\mathcal L_0}V(\sigma)\right)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma[e^{\tau G}A,B]\right).

Let $C=e^{\tau G}A_0$. The gap theorem gives $\|C\|_\sigma\leq e^{-\gamma\tau}\|A_0\|_\sigma$. If $\mu>0$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $\sigma$, then
$$
\|C\|_\infty\leq\frac{\|C\sigma^{1/2}\|_2}{\sqrt\mu}=\frac{\|C\|_\sigma}{\sqrt\mu}.
$$
The finite density trace satisfies $|\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma M)|\leq\|M\|_\infty$: diagonalize $\sigma$, write its nonnegative eigenvalues summing to one, and bound each diagonal matrix element of $M$ by $\|M\|_\infty$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the finite energy basis, energies $E_a$, rates $w_{ab}$, Hamiltonian $H_{\rm s}$, and jump matrices $L_{ab}=\sqrt{w_{ab}}|b\rangle\langle a|$ of [[thm-qsm-dt-gibbs-jump]]. Define $R:=\sum_{a\ne b}L_{ab}^*L_{ab}=\sum_a r_a|a\rangle\langle a|$ and the no-click matrix $K:=-iH_{\rm s}/\hbar-R/2$. The **specified energy-resolved instrument** has the following outcomes:

1. If the current state is the energy eigenstate $|a\rangle$, then during a no-click interval of length $t$ the unnormalized state is $e^{tK}|a\rangle$.
2. In an infinitesimal interval $dt$, the outcome labelled $a\to b$ has jump operation $\sqrt{dt}\,L_{ab}$ and probability $dt\,\langle a|L_{ab}^*L_{ab}|a\rangle+o(dt)$. Its normalized post-click state is $L_{ab}|a\rangle/\|L_{ab}|a\rangle\|=|b\rangle$.
3. The no-click operation over $dt$ is $M_0(dt)=I+Kdt+o(dt)$. Since $K^*+K=-R$ and $\sum_{a\ne b}L_{ab}^*L_{ab}=R$, the no-click and jump effects sum to $I+o(dt)$.
4. After each recorded jump, repeat the same rule from the new energy label.

The output path records the current label $a(t)\in E$. This is one selected instrument model; the one-time GKSL semigroup alone does not specify a unique record process.

Let $d\geq2$, let $E=\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let $E_a\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies in joules, and let $\beta>0$ have units joule$^{-1}$. Define

$$Z_\beta:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta E_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta E_a}.$$

For each $a\ne b$, let $w_{ab}\geq0$ be a rate in seconds$^{-1}$ satisfying Gibbs detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$, and assume the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ is connected. On $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$, fix an orthonormal energy basis $(|a\rangle)$, set $H_{\rm s}=\sum_aE_a|a\rangle\langle a|$, and define $L_{ab}=\sqrt{w_{ab}}|b\rangle\langle a|$ for $a\ne b$. Fix $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. For real functions $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_a\pi_af_ag_a$, and define the row-generator action on column observables by $(Wf)_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$. Let

$$\sigma:=\sum_a\pi_a|a\rangle\langle a|,\qquad r_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}.$$

Use the finite GKSL generator with Hamiltonian $H_{\rm s}$ and the jump matrices $L_{ab}$. Its observable dissipator $D$ is self-adjoint for the $\sigma$-GNS inner product of [[def-qsm-dt-gns-detailed-balance]], $H_{\rm s}$ commutes with $\sigma$, and $\ker D=\mathbb C I$. On diagonal observables, $W$ is self-adjoint on $L^2(E,\pi)$ with constants as its kernel; for $d\geq2$ its restriction to $\pi^\perp:=\{f:E\to\mathbb R:\sum_a\pi_af_a=0\}$ has a positive spectral gap $\gamma_{\rm cl}$. Thus the generator satisfies the specified finite GNS detailed-balance convention and the generic gap conclusion of [[thm-qsm-dt-detailed-balance-gap]] applies. This claim does not assert a microscopic bath limit.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The path in [F1] has locally piecewise-constant sample paths with finitely many jumps on bounded intervals. Each coordinate $a(s)$ is measurable under the supplied path law; since $E$ is finite, $(s,\omega)\mapsto v_{a(s,\omega)}$ is jointly measurable and bounded, so its time integral $Y_T$ is a measurable bounded random variable. It is stationary when initialized with $\pi$, since [F2] gives $\pi W=0$. For $s,t\geq0$, stationarity and the transition semigroup give
$$
\mathbb E_\pi[v_{a(s)}v_{a(t)}]=\langle v,e^{|t-s|W}v\rangle_\pi=C_v(|t-s|).
$$
For $t\geq s$, this is the Markov property; for $s>t$, the same scalar follows by self-adjointness of $e^{(s-t)W}$. Since $v$ is centered, $\mathbb E_\pi[Y_T]=0$.

The function $v_{a(s)}$ is bounded because $E$ is finite, so the product covariance is bounded on the finite square $[0,T]^2$ and Fubini's theorem applies. Therefore
$$
\operatorname{Var}_\pi(Y_T)=\int_0^T\int_0^T\mathbb E_\pi[v_{a(s)}v_{a(t)}]\,ds\,dt =2\int_0^T(T-s)C_v(s)\,ds,
$$
using the covariance identity from step 1.1 and splitting the square into its two triangles.

Expand $v$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis of the self-adjoint $W|_{\pi^\perp}$. Its eigenvalues are at most $-\gamma_{\rm cl}<0$, so the expansion gives $|C_v(s)|\leq e^{-\gamma_{\rm cl}s}\|v\|_\pi^2$. The finite matrix exponential makes $C_v$ continuous. On $[0,\infty)$, set $f_T(s)=\mathbf1_{[0,T]}(s)(1-s/T)C_v(s)$. For every sequence $T_n\to\infty$, $f_{T_n}(s)\to C_v(s)$ pointwise and $|f_{T_n}(s)|\leq\|v\|_\pi^2e^{-\gamma_{\rm cl}s}$, an integrable majorant.

Applying [F3] to step 2.2 gives $\int_0^{T_n}(1-s/T_n)C_v(s)\,ds\to\int_0^\infty C_v(s)\,ds$ for every $T_n\to\infty$, hence the real-$T$ limit exists and equals that integral. The same finite spectral expansion gives $\int_0^\infty e^{sW}v\,ds=(-W|_{\pi^\perp})^{-1}v$, so the integral is $\langle(-W|_{\pi^\perp})^{-1}v,v\rangle_\pi$. Each eigencomponent contributes its squared coefficient divided by a positive gap eigenvalue, proving nonnegativity.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$Y_T:=\int_0^T v_{a(s)}\,ds,\qquad C_v(s):=\langle v,e^{sW}v\rangle_\pi,$$

$$D_{\rm rec}:=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}_\pi(Y_T)}{2T}=\int_0^\infty C_v(s)\,ds=\langle(-W|_{\pi^\perp})^{-1}v,v\rangle_\pi\geq0.$$

$$|C_{A,B}(t)|\leq e^{-\gamma t}\|A\|_\sigma\|B\|_\sigma,\qquad t\geq0,$$

$$\Gamma(A):=\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty\langle e^{tG}A,A\rangle_\sigma\,dt$$

is nonnegative. Its real polarization on any finite list of Hermitian centered observables is a positive-semidefinite real symmetric correlation-integral matrix. No mixing, central-limit theorem, or infinite-volume transport claim follows.

Let $\mathcal L_0$ be the finite Schrödinger generator trace-dual to $G$ in [[def-qsm-dt-gns-detailed-balance]], and assume the gap hypotheses of [[thm-qsm-dt-detailed-balance-gap]] with $d>1$. $$R_{AB}(\tau):=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma[e^{\tau G}A_0,B]\right).$$

$$\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^\epsilon_tA)\right|_{\epsilon=0}=\int_0^t h(s)R_{AB}(t-s)\,ds.$$

$

$$\langle A,B\rangle_\sigma:=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma B^*A),\qquad \|A\|_\sigma:=\langle A,A\rangle_\sigma^{1/2}.$$

The data satisfy **the specified finite GNS detailed-balance convention** when $[H_{\rm s},\sigma]=0$ and $D$ is self-adjoint for this inner product, meaning $\langle D(A),B\rangle_\sigma=\langle A,D(B)\rangle_\sigma$ for all $A,B\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice and the connected finite Gibbs jump data of [[thm-qsm-dt-gibbs-jump]]. Use the energy-resolved record path supplied by [[def-qsm-dt-monitored-chain]], initialized with law $\pi$. Let $v:E\to\mathbb R$ be a real velocity observable with units metres per second and $\pi(v):=\sum_a\pi_av_a=0$. Define the record displacement

$$Y_T:=\int_0^T v_{a(s)}\,ds,\qquad C_v(s):=\langle v,e^{sW}v\rangle_\pi,$$

where $Wf(a)=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$, $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi=\sum_a\pi_a f_ag_a$, and $\pi^\perp:=\{f:E\to\mathbb R:\sum_a\pi_af_a=0\}$. Then for every $T\geq0$,

$$\mathbb E_\pi[Y_T]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_\pi(Y_T)=2\int_0^T(T-s)C_v(s)\,ds.$$

If $\gamma_{\rm cl}>0$ is the reversible spectral gap of $W$ on $\pi$-centered functions, then $|C_v(s)|\leq e^{-\gamma_{\rm cl}s}\sum_a\pi_av_a^2$, and

$$D_{\rm rec}:=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}_\pi(Y_T)}{2T}=\int_0^\infty C_v(s)\,ds=\langle(-W|_{\pi^\perp})^{-1}v,v\rangle_\pi\geq0.$$

The units of $D_{\rm rec}$ are square metres per second. This proves a variance coefficient for the selected finite record model; it does not prove a central-limit theorem or a generic quantum transport law.

Let $d\geq2$, let $E=\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let $E_a\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies in joules, and let $\beta>0$ have units joule$^{-1}$. Define

$$Z_\beta:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta E_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta E_a}.$$

For each $a\ne b$, let $w_{ab}\geq0$ be a rate in seconds$^{-1}$ satisfying Gibbs detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$, and assume the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ is connected. On $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$, fix an orthonormal energy basis $(|a\rangle)$, set $H_{\rm s}=\sum_aE_a|a\rangle\langle a|$, and define $L_{ab}=\sqrt{w_{ab}}|b\rangle\langle a|$ for $a\ne b$. Fix $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. For real functions $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_a\pi_af_ag_a$, and define the row-generator action on column observables by $(Wf)_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$. Let

$$\sigma:=\sum_a\pi_a|a\rangle\langle a|,\qquad r_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}.$$

Use the finite GKSL generator with Hamiltonian $H_{\rm s}$ and the jump matrices $L_{ab}$. Its observable dissipator $D$ is self-adjoint for the $\sigma$-GNS inner product of [[def-qsm-dt-gns-detailed-balance]], $H_{\rm s}$ commutes with $\sigma$, and $\ker D=\mathbb C I$. On diagonal observables, $W$ is self-adjoint on $L^2(E,\pi)$ with constants as its kernel; for $d\geq2$ its restriction to $\pi^\perp:=\{f:E\to\mathbb R:\sum_a\pi_af_a=0\}$ has a positive spectral gap $\gamma_{\rm cl}$. Thus the generator satisfies the specified finite GNS detailed-balance convention and the generic gap conclusion of [[thm-qsm-dt-detailed-balance-gap]] applies. This claim does not assert a microscopic bath limit.

derivations.claim: The Gibbs weights are $\pi_0=b/(a+b)$ and $\pi_1=a/(a+b)$: their ratio is $b/a=e^{-\beta\Delta}=e^{-\beta(E_0-E_1)}$, and they sum to one. Thus $\pi_0a=\pi_1b$ and $\pi(v)=0$. The two-state generator has centered eigenvector $Z-z_{\rm eq}I$ with eigenvalue $-(a+b)$; therefore $e^{sW}v=e^{-(a+b)s}v$ and $\langle v,v\rangle_\pi=v_0^2(1-z_{\rm eq}^2)$.

Substituting this covariance into [F1] gives
$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_T)=2v_0^2(1-z_{\rm eq}^2)\int_0^T(T-s)e^{-(a+b)s}\,ds.
$$
Evaluating the integral gives the displayed finite-time formula. Dividing by $2T$ and letting $T\to\infty$ gives $v_0^2(1-z_{\rm eq}^2)/(a+b)$.
