Use the connected stationary thermal carrier of [[post-tgr-stationary-equilibrium]] on $O$. Let $N_\xi=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$, $u=\xi/N_\xi$, and $\beta=u/(k_BT)$ as there, and assume the postulated Killing condition on $\beta$. Then a positive constant $T_K$ exists such that

$N_\xi(x)T(x)=T_K\quad\text{and}\quad \beta=\frac{\xi}{k_BT_K}\qquad(x\in O).$

In the same convention, $\xi(N_\xi)=0$, the observer acceleration satisfies $a=\nabla\log N_\xi$, the expansion and shear vanish, and

$\nabla\log T=-a.$

For any chosen reference event $x_{\rm ref}\in O$, $T_K=N_\xi(x_{\rm ref})T(x_{\rm ref})$. If the reference normalization has $N_\xi(x_{\rm ref})=1$, then $T_K$ is the local temperature at that event. Rescaling $\xi$ by a constant $b>0$ rescales $N_\xi$ and $T_K$ by $b$ while leaving the local scalar $T$ unchanged. The result is a conditional deduction from the selected physical postulate and the stated mathematical supplier; it is not a thermometer law for arbitrary observers or a KMS-existence theorem.

Let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and let $\mathcal H:=\ell^2(\mathbb N_0,\mathbb C)$ be the complex square-summable sequences with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{n\ge0}x_n\overline{y_n}$, linear in its first argument. Let $e_n$ be the sequence with value $1$ at $n$ and $0$ elsewhere. Write $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ for the bounded complex-linear operators on $\mathcal H$, with operator norm $\|B\|:=\sup_{\|x\|_2\le1}\|Bx\|_2$; for $C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $C^*$ is its bounded Hilbert-space adjoint, characterized by $\langle Cx,y\rangle=\langle x,C^*y\rangle$. A state on this operator algebra means a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega$ with $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(C^*C)\ge0$ for every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. Define the occupation-number operator
$$D(\mathcal N):=\left\{x\in\mathcal H:\sum_{n\ge0}n^2|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (\mathcal Nx)_n:=nx_n.$$
For a densely defined operator $T$ on this space, use the adjoint relation
$$D(T^\dagger):=\left\{y\in\mathcal H:\exists z\in\mathcal H\ \forall x\in D(T),\ \langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle\right\},\qquad T^\dagger y:=z.$$
The representing $z$ is unique when $D(T)$ is dense; here “self-adjoint” means $D(T^\dagger)=D(T)$ and $T^\dagger x=Tx$ on that domain.

Let $\epsilon>0$ be in joules, $m\in\mathbb Z$ a dimensionless azimuthal mode number, $\Omega\in\mathbb R$ an angular velocity in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and $\beta_K>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. Set
$$H:=\epsilon\mathcal N,\qquad J:=\hbar m\mathcal N,\qquad a:=\epsilon-\hbar m\Omega.$$ 
For $m\ne0$, $J$ has domain $D(\mathcal N)$; for $m=0$, $J$ is the zero operator on all of $\mathcal H$. The operator $H$ has energy units J, $J$ has angular-momentum units J s, and $a$ has energy units J, so $\Omega J$ also has units J. Define $K_0:=H-\Omega J$ on the common domain $D(\mathcal N)$ and let $K:=\overline{K_0}$ be its operator closure. For $a\ne0$, $K=a\mathcal N$ has domain $D(\mathcal N)$; for $a=0$, $K$ is the zero operator on all of $\mathcal H$. Thus $K$ is the self-adjoint closure of the rotating generator $H-\Omega J$, including at the zero threshold. Then $\mathcal N$, $H$, $J$ and $K$ are self-adjoint on the stated domains.

Define the one-mode occupation partition sum by
$$Z_{\beta_K}(a):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty e^{-\beta_Kan}\in[0,+\infty].$$
It is the diagonal trace of the positive Gibbs weights in the occupation basis whenever the sum is finite. This sum is finite exactly when $a=\epsilon-\hbar m\Omega>0$, in which case
$$Z_{\beta_K}(a)=\frac{1}{1-e^{-\beta_Ka}}.$$
For $a>0$, the weights $p_n=Z_{\beta_K}(a)^{-1}e^{-\beta_Kan}$ sum to one and define the diagonal Gibbs functional
$$\omega_a(B):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}p_n\langle Be_n,e_n\rangle,\qquad B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H).$$
The proof shows that this is a state in the stated sense. For $a\le0$, the occupation partition sum diverges, so no normalized Gibbs state of this trace form exists. This is a single bosonic mode calculation; it constructs no continuum field state or rotating-spacetime equilibrium.

derivations.claim: The Rindler metric is independent of $x^0$, so $\xi_R$ is Killing. Its norm is $g(\xi_R,\xi_R)=-(a_0x/c^2)^2<0$ on $x>0$, hence $N_R=a_0x/c^2$. Differentiating $\log N_R$ gives $a_x=1/x$, whose metric norm is $1/x$.

In the rotating Minkowski metric, $\partial_{x^0}$ and $\partial_\phi$ are Killing fields and $\Omega$ is constant, so their displayed linear combination $\xi_\Omega$ is Killing. Its squared norm is $-1+\Omega^2r^2/c^2$, which is negative exactly for $r<c/|\Omega|$ when $\Omega\ne0$; therefore $N_\Omega=\sqrt{1-\Omega^2r^2/c^2}$.

For a nonconstant angular velocity, the coordinate formula for the Lie derivative gives $(\mathcal L_\xi g)_{r\phi}=g_{\phi\phi}\partial_r(\Omega/c)=r^2\Omega'(r)/c$. Thus if $\Omega'(r)\ne0$, this field is not Killing and the selected stationary theorem does not apply.

By [F1] and [A2], the selected Rindler bath has $T_R=T_K/N_R=T_Kc^2/(a_0x)$ and physical proper acceleration $c^2|a|=c^2/x$. The point $x_{\rm ref}=c^2/a_0$ has $N_R=1$, so it provides the stated reference normalization.

Applying [F1] on that selected timelike domain yields $T_\Omega=T_K/N_\Omega$. Differentiating $\log N_\Omega$ gives $a_r=-\Omega^2r/[c^2(1-\Omega^2r^2/c^2)]$. Since $g_{rr}=1$, its physical magnitude is $c^2|a_r|=\gamma^2\Omega^2r$. At the light cylinder the norm tends to zero and the timelike-field hypothesis of [F1] fails.

Under [A3], the mode generator has coefficient $a=\epsilon-\hbar j\Omega$ in the exact occupation model of [F2]. Applying [F2] gives a finite trace exactly for $a>0$. This condition is logically separate from the geometric timelike-domain condition in step 1.2 and supplies no continuum-field conclusion.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: For physical unit assignments use length coordinates $x^0=ct_{\rm phys}$ and spatial coordinates in metres, where $c>0$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. In this convention the metric components, a unit observer $u$, and a length-normalized Killing field $\xi$ are dimensionless. Other coordinate choices transform component units by their coordinate Jacobians. State maps and geometric currents have the types and units in [[def-tgr-local-fluid-state]]: a formal marker density $n$ is $\mathrm{marker\,m^{-3}}$; entropy density $s$ is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$; a $C^1$ entropy current $S^a$ has components $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$; and its physical flux is $cS^a$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. Its geometric divergence $\nabla_aS^a$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-4}}$, so $c\nabla_aS^a$ is entropy production per physical volume per second. The symmetric stress tensor $\mathsf T^{ab}$ has components in pascals in length coordinates; it is a tensor, not an observer-independent array of energy densities. The state-function energy density $\varepsilon$ and the observer projection $\mathsf T^{ab}u_a u_b$ remain distinct unless a material model identifies them.

For each cell $i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$, let $\mathcal H_i$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d_i\ge1$, let $H_i=H_i^*$ be a Hermitian proper Hamiltonian in joules, and let $Q_i=Q_i^*$ be a dimensionless number observable whose eigenvalues lie in $\mathbb N_0$. Assume $[H_i,Q_i]=0$. Operators $H_i,Q_i$ on the total space $\mathcal H:=\bigotimes_{i=1}^r\mathcal H_i$ mean their lifts acting on the $i$th tensor factor and as the identity on the other factors; no intercell interaction is included.

Adopt the selected stationary bath of [[post-tgr-stationary-equilibrium]] on its connected smooth Lorentzian domain. A finite-cell preparation in this item means exactly the setup of [[thm-tgr-finite-cell-gibbs-factorization]]: finitely many $r\ge1$ noninteracting cells with finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_i$, Hermitian proper Hamiltonians $H_i$ in joules, and dimensionless Hermitian number matrices $Q_i$ with nonnegative integer eigenvalues and $[H_i,Q_i]=0$. Their tensor product is $\mathcal H=\bigotimes_{i=1}^r\mathcal H_i$; each cell operator acts as the identity on the other factors.

A state $\omega$ is a **$\beta$-KMS state for $\alpha$ in physical time** when for every $A,B\in\mathcal A$ there is a bounded function $F_{A,B}:S_b\to\mathbb C$ (that is, $\sup_{z\in S_b}|F_{A,B}(z)|<\infty$) that is continuous on $S_b$, complex-differentiable at every point of $S_b^\circ$, and satisfies

Let $\mathcal A$ be a unital complex $C^*$-algebra and let $t\mapsto\alpha_t$ be a strongly continuous one-parameter group of $*$-automorphisms of $\mathcal A$. Let $\omega$ be a $\beta_K$-KMS state for $\alpha$ in the physical-time convention of [[def-qsm-kms-state]], where $\beta_K>0$ has units $\mathrm{J}^{-1}$ and $\hbar>0$ has units $\mathrm{J\,s}$. For a constant dimensionless $\lambda>0$, define
$$\alpha^\lambda_\tau:=\alpha_{\tau/\lambda},$$
where $t$ and $\tau$ are real time parameters in seconds. Then $\omega$ is a $\lambda\beta_K$-KMS state for $\alpha^\lambda$, with strip width $\lambda\beta_K\hbar$ seconds. Conversely, if $\omega$ is a $\widehat\beta$-KMS state for $\alpha^\lambda$, then it is a $(\widehat\beta/\lambda)$-KMS state for $\alpha$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the full product state is $\beta_K$-KMS for the grand-generator dynamics. The embedded cell algebra $\mathcal A_i$ is invariant under that dynamics: all lifted cell generators commute, and conjugation by the other tensor factors cancels, leaving $\alpha^{K,i}_{t_K}$. Restricting the full-state strip functions to observables in this invariant subalgebra gives the KMS boundary values for $\omega_i$, since the product density restricts to $\rho_i$. Thus $\omega_i$ is $\beta_K$-KMS for $\alpha^{K,i}$.

Since $G_{K,i}=N_iG_i$ and $N_i$ is constant along the selected orbit, $\alpha^{\mathrm{loc},i}_{\tau}=\alpha^{K,i}_{\tau/N_i}$. Apply [F3] with $\lambda=N_i$ to obtain the $N_i\beta_K$-KMS strip and width $\hbar N_i\beta_K$. The stationary normalization in [F3] gives $T_i=T_K/N_i$, so $N_i\beta_K=N_i/(k_BT_K)=1/(k_BT_i)$. If $X\in\mathcal A_i^0$, then conjugation by $e^{i\tau\mu_iQ_i/\hbar}$ fixes $X$, so the local grand and physical $H_i$ automorphisms agree there.

citations.quote: Adopt the selected stationary bath of [[post-tgr-stationary-equilibrium]] on its connected smooth Lorentzian domain. A finite-cell preparation in this item means exactly the setup of [[thm-tgr-finite-cell-gibbs-factorization]]: finitely many $r\ge1$ noninteracting cells with finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_i$, Hermitian proper Hamiltonians $H_i$ in joules, and dimensionless Hermitian number matrices $Q_i$ with nonnegative integer eigenvalues and $[H_i,Q_i]=0$. Their tensor product is $\mathcal H=\bigotimes_{i=1}^r\mathcal H_i$; each cell operator acts as the identity on the other factors.

Fix a cell label $i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$ in [[thm-tgr-finite-cell-gibbs-factorization]], let $x_i=\chi(i)$ be its assigned point, and write $N:=N_i=N(x_i)>0$, $H_{\mathrm{loc}}:=H_i$, $Q:=Q_i$, and $\mu_{\mathrm{loc}}:=\mu_i$. Let $\beta_K>0$ in joules$^{-1}$ and $\mu_K$ in joules be the global parameters supplied there. Put $G_{\mathrm{loc}}:=H_{\mathrm{loc}}-\mu_{\mathrm{loc}}Q$ and $G_K:=NG_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Let $\sigma$ be the cell Gibbs density supplied by that theorem, so $\sigma=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}G_{\mathrm{loc}}}=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta_KG_K}$ with $\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}=N\beta_K$. For neutral Hermitian matrices, define
$$\alpha^{\mathrm{loc}}_\tau(C):=e^{iG_{\mathrm{loc}}\tau/\hbar}Ce^{-iG_{\mathrm{loc}}\tau/\hbar},\qquad \alpha^K_t(C):=e^{iG_Kt/\hbar}Ce^{-iG_Kt/\hbar}.$$
For this selected cell, let $q$ be the common charge in coulombs and $\Phi_i:=\Phi_\xi(x_i)$ its compensated potential in volts from the supplier. Define $H_{K,i}:=NH_{\mathrm{loc}}+q\Phi_iQ$ in joules, and write $H_K:=H_{K,i}$ in the physical control below. The supplier normalization gives $N\mu_{\mathrm{loc}}+q\Phi_i=\mu_K$, hence $H_K=G_K+\mu_KQ$.

Let $A=A^*$ and $B=B^*$ satisfy $[A,Q]=[B,Q]=0$. Then their local proper-time and Killing-time dynamics agree after $\tau=Nt$.

Let $h:[0,S]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $S>0$ seconds, and let $h(\tau)B$ have units joules. For dimensionless $\epsilon\in\mathbb R$, the proper-time grand-generator control $G_{\mathrm{loc}}-\epsilon h(\tau)B$ corresponds in Killing time to $G_K-\epsilon N h(Nt)B$. Define $E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau)$ and $E_K(t)$ as the finite-time expectations of $A$ from the same initial density $\sigma$ under these controls. Because $A$ and $B$ commute with $Q$, replacing each grand generator by its physical Hamiltonian changes the propagator only by a unitary generated by a constant multiple of $Q$ and leaves the expectation of $A$ unchanged. Thus these expectations also equal those obtained from the respective physical controls $H_{\mathrm{loc}}-\epsilon h(\tau)B$ and $H_K-\epsilon Nh(Nt)B$. In particular,
$$E_K(t)=E_{\mathrm{loc}}(Nt)\qquad(0\le t\le S/N).$$
The finite-time Kubo expansions have identical first-order terms under this rescaling and the same quadratic remainder bound. With
$$R_{\mathrm{loc}}(u):=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma[\alpha^{\mathrm{loc}}_u(A),B]\right),\qquad C_S:=\frac{2}{\hbar}\int_0^S|h(s)|\,\|B\|\,ds,$$
the local expansion is
$$E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau)=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\alpha^{\mathrm{loc}}_\tau(A))+\epsilon\int_0^\tau h(s)R_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau-s)\,ds+r_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau),\qquad |r_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau)|\le\|A\|\frac{(|\epsilon|C_S)^2e^{|\epsilon|C_S}}2.$$
Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, so $C_S$ is dimensionless and $R_{\mathrm{loc}}$ has units $[A][B]/(\mathrm{J\,s})$. The Killing-time response kernel is $R_K(t)=R_{\mathrm{loc}}(Nt)$ and its control amplitude is $Nh(Nt)$.

For the equilibrium correlation spectral measures, use the Fourier convention of [[thm-qsm-dt-spectral-fdt]]. If $D_N(\omega):=N\omega$, then
$$S_K=(D_N)_*S_{\mathrm{loc}},\qquad S_K(\omega)=N^{-1}S_{\mathrm{loc}}(\omega/N)$$
in distribution notation; the measure form preserves the weights of delta-function spectral lines. Since $\beta_K\hbar(N\omega)=\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\hbar\omega$, detailed balance is unchanged. Any zero-frequency atom remains an atom at zero and is not assigned a value by the coth formula, which remains restricted to nonzero frequencies.

For a static local perturbation $G_{\mathrm{loc}}-\lambda B$, where $\lambda B$ has units joules, the re-prepared Gibbs family satisfies
$$\left.\frac{d}{d\lambda}\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\lambda B)\right|_{\lambda=0}=\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathrm{KM},\sigma}(B,B)=N\beta_K\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathrm{KM},\sigma}(B,B)\ge0.$$
Here $\delta B:=B-\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma B)I$ and
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathrm{KM},\sigma}(B,B):=\int_0^1\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma^{1-u}\delta B\,\sigma^u\delta B\right)\,du.$$
It reduces to the ordinary variance when $B$ commutes with $G_{\mathrm{loc}}$; no such reduction is asserted otherwise. These are exact finite-dimensional deductions for the constructed neutral cell. They imply no infinite-time relaxation, dc transport coefficient, or response law for arbitrary interacting reduced states.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

derivations.claim: The postulated preparation [F1] supplies a finite-dimensional cell density $\sigma$ and $[H_i,Q_i]=0$. The Hamiltonian matrices in the two displayed control equations are continuous and Hermitian on their compact time intervals. For either equation write it as $U'(s)=K(s)U(s)$ with continuous matrix $K$ and $M:=\sup_s\|K(s)\|<\infty$. The ordered-integral series $I+\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{0\le s_n\le\cdots\le s_1\le s}K(s_1)\cdots K(s_n)\,ds_n\cdots ds_1$ converges uniformly, since its $n$th term has norm at most $(Ms)^n/n!$, and solves the integral equation by termwise integration. If $U,V$ were two solutions, their difference $D:=U-V$ would satisfy the homogeneous integral equation; iterating it bounds $\|D(s)\|$ by $\sup_s\|D(s)\|(Ms)^n/n!$ for every $n$, so $D=0$. Differentiating $U^*U$ and using Hermiticity of each controlled Hamiltonian gives $(U^*U)'=0$; the identity initial value therefore makes each solution unitary.

Define $V(t):=e^{-iq\Phi_iQ_it/\hbar}U_{\mathrm{loc}}(N_it)$. Since $[Q_i,H_i]=[Q_i,B]=0$, differentiating and using the chain rule gives $i\hbar V'(t)=[H_{K,i}-\epsilon N_i h(N_it)B]V(t)$, with $V(0)=I_{\mathcal H_i}$. By uniqueness from step 1.1, $V=U_K$. The factor $e^{-iq\Phi_iQ_it/\hbar}$ commutes with $A$, so the trace definition gives $E_K(t)=E_{\mathrm{loc}}(N_it)$.

Retain the inherited smooth-geometry premise [F3] when using the charged-stationarity relation $N_i\mu_i+q\Phi_i=\mu_K$ supplied by the prepared-cell data [F1]. Put $\widehat U_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $\widehat U_K$ for the propagators of the grand-generator controls stated in [F2]. The identities $H_i=G_i+\mu_iQ_i$ and $H_{K,i}=N_iG_i+\mu_KQ_i$, where $N_i\mu_i+q\Phi_i=\mu_K$, imply $U_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau)=e^{-i\mu_iQ_i\tau/\hbar}\widehat U_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau)$ and $U_K(t)=e^{-i\mu_KQ_it/\hbar}\widehat U_K(t)$. These relations follow by differentiating each right-hand side and using $[G_i,Q_i]=[B,Q_i]=0$. Since $[A,Q_i]=0$, the trace expectations under the physical and grand-generator propagators agree. Therefore [F2] applies to the explicitly defined expectations.

Apply [F2] to the same fixed initial density for the finite-time response, to its spectral statement for the equilibrium correlations, and to its separately re-prepared Gibbs family for the static derivative. The first preparation remains $\sigma$ throughout the finite-time controls; $\sigma_\lambda$ is a distinct re-preparation, and none of these deductions is an observed measurement or an infinite-time limit.

In this convention the metric components, a unit observer $u$, and a length-normalized Killing field $\xi$ are dimensionless. Other coordinate choices transform component units by their coordinate Jacobians. State maps and geometric currents have the types and units in [[def-tgr-local-fluid-state]]: a formal marker density $n$ is $\mathrm{marker\,m^{-3}}$; entropy density $s$ is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$; a $C^1$ entropy current $S^a$ has components $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$; and its physical flux is $cS^a$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. Let $O$ be a connected domain with the stationary Lorentzian data, potential
$A$, field $F=dA$, Killing field $\xi$, lapse $N=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}$, future
unit stationary observer $u=\xi/N$, and charged transport on the future mass
shell from [[def-tgr-charged-liouville-data]]. Let $m>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$,
$\beta:=u/(k_BT)$ for a smooth proper-temperature scalar $T:O\to(0,\infty)$,
and $\zeta:=\mu/(k_BT)$ for a smooth chemical-potential scalar
$\mu:O\to\mathbb R$. Define $f(x,P)=\exp(\zeta+g(\beta,P))$. Without any global
potential-symmetry assumption,
$$\mathcal L_{F,q}f=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \beta\text{ is Killing and }d\zeta=-cq\,\iota_\beta F.$$

Let $r\ge1$ be finite. For each cell $i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$, let $\mathcal H_i$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d_i\ge1$, let $H_i=H_i^*$ be a Hermitian proper Hamiltonian in joules, and let $Q_i=Q_i^*$ be a dimensionless number observable whose eigenvalues lie in $\mathbb N_0$. Assume $[H_i,Q_i]=0$. Operators $H_i,Q_i$ on the total space $\mathcal H:=\bigotimes_{i=1}^r\mathcal H_i$ mean their lifts acting on the $i$th tensor factor and as the identity on the other factors; no intercell interaction is included.

Fix one cell $i$ of the finite preparation in [[post-tgr-selected-gibbs-kms-preparation]], at its assigned event $p_i\in O$, with $N_i=N_\xi(p_i)$, $T_i=T(p_i)$, and $\mu_i=\mu(p_i)$. Set $\beta_K:=(k_BT_K)^{-1}>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. Let $\mathcal A_i=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_i)$, let $G_i:=H_i-\mu_iQ_i$ be its proper grand generator in joules, let $G_{K,i}:=N_iG_i$ be its Killing-time grand generator, and let $\omega_i(X):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_iX)$. Use length coordinates $x^0=ct$, with $c>0$ the speed of light in metres per second and the reference-normalized $\xi$ dimensionless in these coordinates. Choose an open interval $I_{K,i}\subseteq\mathbb R$ containing $0$ on which the integral curve through $p_i$ remains in $O$. Define the unique smooth curve $\gamma_i:I_{K,i}\to O$ by
$$\gamma_i(0)=p_i,\qquad \frac{d\gamma_i}{dt_K}(t_K)=c\,\xi_{\gamma_i(t_K)},$$
where $t_K$ is physical Killing time in seconds; the equation states its parameterization by the reference-normalized Killing field. This curve is future-directed timelike. The stationary normalization used in [[thm-tgr-kms-orbit-time-rescaling]] gives $\xi(N_\xi)=0$, so $N_\xi(\gamma_i(t_K))=N_i$ throughout this interval. Its proper-time parametrization is
$$\Gamma_i:N_iI_{K,i}\to O,\qquad \Gamma_i(\tau):=\gamma_i(\tau/N_i),$$
which satisfies $g(d\Gamma_i/d\tau,d\Gamma_i/d\tau)=-c^2$. Thus $\tau$ is proper time in seconds and $\tau=N_it_K$ on the geometric orbit. No completeness of $\xi$ is assumed: the geometric curve is defined on its flow interval, while the finite-matrix dynamics below are defined for all real parameters by their generators and use the same constant rescaling.

Define

$$\alpha^{K,i}_{t_K}(X):=e^{it_KG_{K,i}/\hbar}Xe^{-it_KG_{K,i}/\hbar},\qquad \alpha^{\mathrm{loc},i}_{\tau}(X):=e^{i\tau G_i/\hbar}Xe^{-i\tau G_i/\hbar},$$

where both $t_K$ and $\tau$ are measured in seconds, and $N_i>0$ is dimensionless. Write $\mathcal A_i^0:=\{X\in\mathcal A_i:[X,Q_i]=0\}$ for the neutral observable algebra. Then $\omega_i$ is $\beta_K$-KMS for $\alpha^{K,i}$ and is $\beta_{\mathrm{loc},i}$-KMS for $\alpha^{\mathrm{loc},i}$, where

$$\beta_{\mathrm{loc},i}=N_i\beta_K=\frac{1}{k_BT_i},\qquad \hbar\beta_{\mathrm{loc},i}\text{ is the strip width in seconds}.$$

On $\mathcal A_i^0$, the same proper-time automorphism is generated by the physical Hamiltonian $H_i$, because its chemical-potential term commutes with every observable in that subalgebra. Thus the local temperature is $T_i=T_K/N_i$ for this constructed state and selected orbit. The conclusion is only orbitwise; it does not make a position-dependent lapse into one global time-rescaled dynamics.

derivations.claim: The metric is smooth and has signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $x>0$. The coordinate transformation $X=x\cosh(x^0/L)$, $X^0=x\sinh(x^0/L)$ gives $-(dX^0)^2+dX^2=-(x/L)^2(dx^0)^2+dx^2$, so this is the Rindler wedge. The metric coefficients are independent of $x^0$, hence $\xi$ is Killing, and $g(\xi,\xi)=-(x/L)^2<0$ gives $N=x/L$. Moreover $\partial_{x^0}X^0=(x/L)\cosh(x^0/L)>0$, so $\xi$ is future directed.

With $T=T_KL/x$, $u=\xi/N$ gives $\beta=u/(k_BT)=\xi/(k_BT_K)$, a Killing field. By [A3]–[A4], the auxiliary inputs have $F=dA=0$, $\zeta=\mu/(k_BT)=0$, and $q=0$, so $d\zeta=-cq\,\iota_\beta F=0$ in the exact transport formulation. The forward direction of [F2] therefore gives whole-future-shell stationarity and the global compensator condition required by [F3].

At $x_1=L$ and $x_2=2L$, step 1.1 gives $N_1=1$ and $N_2=2$. The adopted field has $T_i=T_K/N_i$, and the two cells satisfy $[H_i,Q_i]=0$, $Q_i=0$, and $\mu_i=q=0$. Thus the finite-cell hypotheses of [F3] hold with $G_K=N_1H_1+N_2H_2=H_1+2H_2$ and $\beta_i=N_i\beta_K$. Applying [F3] gives the positive finite partition sums and the product state in the Example. The construction is conditional on [F5], inherited through [F2].

The eigenvalues of $H_i$ in the displayed basis are $0$ and $\Delta_i$, so their traces are $Z_i=1+e^{-\beta_i\Delta_i}$ and the normalized diagonal densities are exactly the displayed $\rho_i$. Since $\beta_i=N_i\beta_K$, their tensor product equals $e^{-\beta_K(H_1+2H_2)}/(Z_1Z_2)$.

Apply [F4] separately to the two cells. Their Killing-time KMS parameter is $\beta_K$; the constant lapse rescalings give local parameters $N_1\beta_K$ and $N_2\beta_K$, equal to $(k_BT_1)^{-1}$ and $(k_BT_2)^{-1}$. This establishes the stated model prediction only and reports no experiment.

citations.quote:
Choose positive lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3$, the rectangular box $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$, and an open neighborhood $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ of $\overline\Omega$. Let $N\in C^\infty(U,(0,\infty))$ satisfy $0<N_{\min}\leq N(x)\leq N_{\max}<\infty$ on $\overline\Omega$. On $M=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times U$, use $x^0=ct_K$, where $c>0$ is in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and the fixed metric

$$g=-N(x)^2(dx^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(dx^i)^2.$$

The coordinates $x^i$ and lengths $L_i$ are measured in metres, $t_K$ in seconds, and the lapse $N$ is dimensionless. The metric is independent of $x^0$ and has no time-space cross terms; this is the static background in this model. Give $M$ time orientation $\xi=\partial_{x^0}$. Then $\xi$ is a future timelike Killing field, $N=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}$, and $u=N^{-1}\xi$ is the smooth future unit timelike observer congruence in the conventions of [[def-tgr-framework-units]]. Here a frame means this vector field and its pointwise rest spaces, not a coordinate chart or tetrad. The material is held at rest in this congruence; no flow evolution is included. The scalar $T>0$ is proper temperature in kelvins, and $\vartheta:=NT$ is the Killing-normalized (redshifted) temperature of [[def-tgr-framework-units]]; this definition alone does not assert that $\vartheta$ is constant.

Adopt the fixed-composition material branch of [[post-tgr-local-material-thermodynamics]] with constants $C_V,n_0,T_{\rm ref}>0$, $\sigma_{\rm ref}\in\mathbb R$, and $e_0\in\mathbb R$. The units are $C_V$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}K^{-1}}$, $n_0$ in $\mathrm{marker\,m^{-3}}$, $T_{\rm ref}$ in kelvins, $\sigma_{\rm ref}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}marker^{-1}}$, and $e_0$ in $\mathrm{J\,marker^{-1}}$. Put $c_v=C_V/n_0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}marker^{-1}}$ and choose the state function on $X=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ to be

$$e(v,\sigma_p)=c_vT_{\rm ref}\exp\!\left(\frac{\sigma_p-\sigma_{\rm ref}}{c_v}\right)+e_0,$$

independent of the rest volume per marker $v$. For a given positive $T$, set $v=1/n_0$ and $\sigma_p=\sigma_{\rm ref}+c_v\log(T/T_{\rm ref})$. For this branch define $n=v^{-1}$, $s=n\sigma_p$, $\epsilon=ne$, $T=\partial_{\sigma_p}e$, and $p=-\partial_ve$, using the units of [[def-tgr-framework-units]] and the adopted material convention of [[post-tgr-local-material-thermodynamics]]. These maps give $n=n_0$, $p=0$, $\epsilon=C_VT+n_0e_0$, and $s=n_0\sigma_{\rm ref}+C_V\log(T/T_{\rm ref})$. These assignments describe the selected model only; they do not assert a measured equation of state.

Take an admissible initial redshifted-temperature profile $\vartheta_0\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ with constants $0<m_0\leq M_0<\infty$ such that $m_0\leq\vartheta_0\leq M_0$, and require a $C^2$ extension $\widetilde\vartheta_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ with the same bounds, period $2L_i$ in each coordinate $x^i$, and evenness under each reflection $x^i\mapsto-x^i$. Its even periodic extension makes the normal derivative vanish at both faces in each coordinate once evolved smoothly. The initial proper temperature is $T(0,x)=\vartheta_0(x)/N(x)$.

On $O=(0,\infty)\times\Omega$, identified with the subset of $M$ by $x^0=ct_K$, the admissible temperature field is a positive map $T:[0,\infty)\times\overline\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ continuous with initial trace $T(0,x)=\vartheta_0(x)/N(x)$ and $C^\infty$ on $O$. For every $0<a<b<\infty$, it extends smoothly in all space-time variables to a neighborhood of $[a,b]\times\overline\Omega$; no smoothness across $t_K=0$ is required. The state map on $O$ is

$$v=1/n_0,\qquad \sigma_p=\sigma_{\rm ref}+c_v\log(T/T_{\rm ref}).$$

Define the derived per-marker heat capacity $c_v=C_V/n_0$, with units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}marker^{-1}}$, and the local mathematical material state function on $X=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ by
$$
e(v,\sigma_p)=c_vT_{\rm ref}\exp\!\left(\frac{\sigma_p-\sigma_{\rm ref}}{c_v}\right)+e_0,
$$
independent of $v$. For a positive proper temperature $T$, set $\sigma_p=\sigma_{\rm ref}+c_v\log(T/T_{\rm ref})$ and $v=1/n_0$. The state definitions of [[def-tgr-local-fluid-state]] give $n=n_0$, $p=0$, $\epsilon=C_VT+n_0e_0$, and $s=n_0\sigma_{\rm ref}+C_V\log(T/T_{\rm ref})$.

Let $\vartheta_0\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ satisfy $0<m_0\le\vartheta_0\le M_0$ and admit a $C^2$ extension $\widetilde\vartheta_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ with the same bounds, period $2L_i$ in coordinate $x^i$, and evenness under $x^i\mapsto-x^i$ for each $i$. These conditions make the extension even about every face $x^i=0,L_i$. Set $T_0=\vartheta_0/N$. Define the physical heat flux, conductivity, static heat balance, and insulated-face condition by
$$
q=-\kappa_{\rm th}(\nabla_xT+T\nabla_x\log N),\qquad \kappa_{\rm th}=A_0/N,\qquad NC_V\partial_{t_K}T+\operatorname{div}_x(N^2q)=0,\qquad N^2q\cdot\nu=0\ \text{on each face},
$$
where $q$ has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $\kappa_{\rm th}$ has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\nu$ is the outward Euclidean unit normal to a face. In the entropy identity use zero particle diffusion and zero shear and bulk viscosity, $V=0$ and $\eta=\zeta_{\rm b}=0$, so $\Pi=0$ and $\pi^{ab}=0$. The thermal diffusivity $A_0/C_V$ has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. There is a unique solution $T\in C([0,\infty)\times\overline\Omega)\cap C^{2,1}((0,\infty)\times\overline\Omega)$, where $C^{2,1}$ means two continuous spatial derivatives and one continuous time derivative up to the box faces, satisfying the heat balance, the face condition, and the initial condition $T(0,x)=T_0(x)=\vartheta_0(x)/N(x)$. It is given by
$$\vartheta(t_K,x):=N(x)T(t_K,x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma\!\left(x-y,\frac{A_0}{C_V}t_K\right)\widetilde\vartheta_0(y)\,dy\quad(t_K>0),\qquad \vartheta(0,x)=\vartheta_0(x),\qquad \Gamma(z,t)=(4\pi t)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4t)},\quad z\in\mathbb R^3,\ t>0.$$
Thus $T=\vartheta/N$. It satisfies $C_V\partial_{t_K}\vartheta=A_0\Delta_x\vartheta$, $\partial_\nu\vartheta=0$ on each face, and $m_0\le\vartheta\le M_0$.

For this solution set $Q^0=0$, $Q^i=q^i/c$, $J=n_0u$, and
$$
\mathsf T^{ab}=\epsilon u^au^b+u^aQ^b+Q^au^b,\qquad f^b:=\nabla_a\mathsf T^{ab}.
$$
Here $Q=q/c$ has units $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\mathsf T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $f$ has units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. Then $\nabla_aJ^a=0$ and $u_bf^b=0$: $f$ is an explicitly defined external support that supplies no local power. The entropy current $S^a=su^a+Q^a/T$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}m^{-3}}$ and total entropy $\mathcal S(t_K)=\int_\Omega s(t_K,x)\,dx$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, with
$$
\frac{d\mathcal S}{dt_K}=A_0\int_\Omega\frac{|\nabla_x\vartheta|^2}{\vartheta^2}\,dx\ge0.
$$
The lapse-weighted energy $\mathcal E_K(t_K)=\int_\Omega N\epsilon\,dx$ is constant in $\mathrm{J}$. If $\overline\vartheta=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega\vartheta_0\,dx$ and $C_\Omega=\frac32(\max_iL_i)^2$, then
$$

This is a mathematical solution of the specified fixed-background, supported first-order heat model; it asserts no Einstein equation, general dissipative-fluid initial-value theorem, or finite propagation speed.

Use the fixed static box, positive bounded lapse $N$, constants, material state function, observer field, heat flux, support, initial-data class, and SI conventions of [[post-tgr-supported-static-heat-model]]. Let $\widetilde\vartheta_0$ be its positive $C^2$ even periodic extension, and define $|\Omega|=L_1L_2L_3$, $\overline\vartheta=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega\vartheta_0\,dx$, and $C_\Omega=\frac32(\max_iL_i)^2$. Use Euclidean Lebesgue volume $dx$ and the associated $L^2(\Omega)$ norm. Then the model has a unique solution

$$T\in C([0,\infty)\times\overline\Omega)\cap C^{2,1}((0,\infty)\times\overline\Omega),$$

where $C^{2,1}$ means two continuous spatial derivatives and one continuous time derivative up to the box faces at positive times. With $\vartheta=NT$ and $\Gamma(z,\tau)=(4\pi\tau)^{-3/2}\exp(-|z|^2/(4\tau))$ for $z\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\tau>0$, the solution is

$$\vartheta(t_K,x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma\!\left(x-y,\frac{A_0}{C_V}t_K\right)\widetilde\vartheta_0(y)\,dy\quad(t_K>0),\qquad \vartheta(0,x)=\vartheta_0(x),\qquad T=\frac{\vartheta}{N}.$$

It satisfies $C_V\partial_{t_K}\vartheta=A_0\Delta_x\vartheta$, the six insulated-face conditions $\partial_\nu\vartheta=0$, and $m_0\leq\vartheta\leq M_0$. The lapse-weighted material energy

$$\mathcal E_K(t_K)=\int_\Omega N(x)\epsilon(t_K,x)\,dx$$

is constant. For the entropy current $S^a=su^a+Q^a/T$ and total entropy $\mathcal S(t_K)=\int_\Omega s(t_K,x)\,dx$, the exact model rate is

$$\frac{d\mathcal S}{dt_K}=A_0\int_\Omega\frac{|\nabla_x\vartheta|^2}{\vartheta^2}\,dx\geq0.$$

Moreover,

$$\left\|\vartheta(t_K,\cdot)-\overline\vartheta\right\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{A_0t_K}{C_VC_\Omega}\right)\left\|\vartheta_0-\overline\vartheta\right\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$

Thus $T$ converges in $L^2(\Omega)$ to the positive proper-temperature profile $T_{\rm eq}(x)=\overline\vartheta/N(x)$, while the redshifted temperature $NT$ converges to the constant $\overline\vartheta$. These are conditional predictions of the adopted model. They do not establish that a real material obeys the postulates, and they do not assert a full Einstein-fluid solution, causal or stable relativistic-fluid evolution, or finite propagation speed. No empirical data are used.

derivations.claim: Extend the displayed initial profile to all $\mathbb R^3$ by the same cosine formula. It is $C^\infty$, even and $2L_i$-periodic in every coordinate. Its values lie between $\overline\vartheta-|\delta|$ and $\overline\vartheta+|\delta|$, so the strict inequality on $\delta$ gives positive lower and finite upper bounds. Its average on $\Omega$ is $\overline\vartheta$, because the integral of $\cos(\pi x^1/L_1)$ from $0$ to $L_1$ is $0$.

Put $r=A_0\pi^2/(C_VL_1^2)>0$. Differentiating the proposed solution gives $\partial_{t_K}\vartheta=-r\delta e^{-rt_K}\cos(\pi x^1/L_1)$ and $\Delta_x\vartheta=-(\pi^2/L_1^2)\delta e^{-rt_K}\cos(\pi x^1/L_1)$, hence $C_V\partial_{t_K}\vartheta=A_0\Delta_x\vartheta$. Its initial trace is $\vartheta_0$. Also $\partial_{x^1}\vartheta=-(\pi\delta/L_1)e^{-rt_K}\sin(\pi x^1/L_1)$ vanishes at $x^1=0,L_1$, and $\partial_{x^2}\vartheta=\partial_{x^3}\vartheta=0$, so every face has zero normal derivative. Uniqueness in [F1] identifies this function with the model solution.

The exponential factor tends to zero, so $\vartheta(t_K,x)\to\overline\vartheta$. Because $N$ is time independent and positive, $T=\vartheta/N\to\overline\vartheta/N$ pointwise. The latter is nonconstant by the stipulated nonconstancy of $N$. Direct integration using $\int_0^{L_1}\cos^2(\pi x^1/L_1)\,dx^1=L_1/2$ gives the exact norm $\left\|\vartheta(t_K,\cdot)-\overline\vartheta\right\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=|\delta|\sqrt{|\Omega|/2}\,e^{-rt_K}$. Thus this example realizes a decaying redshifted mode with a spatially varying proper-temperature equilibrium in the selected model.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: In one dimension set $y=\sqrt{\beta/(2m)}\,x$; the substitution and [F1] give $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\beta x^2/(2m)}dx=\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$. Taking the product of $d$ such factors and applying [F2] repeatedly gives the displayed exact $d$-dimensional integral.

Put $\alpha=\beta_0/(2m)>0$. For any integer $s\ge1$, the function $x\mapsto |x|^{2s}e^{-\alpha x^2/2}$ is bounded: it is continuous on $[-1,1]$ and tends to zero at both infinite ends. Hence $|x|^{2s}e^{-\alpha x^2}\le C_{s,\alpha}e^{-\alpha x^2/2}$; on $[-1,1]$ the same bound holds after increasing $C_{s,\alpha}$. By the scaled one-dimensional Gaussian integral, both $\int e^{-\alpha x^2}dx$ and $\int |x|^{2s}e^{-\alpha x^2}dx$ are finite.

For $\beta\ge\beta_0$, $e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\le e^{-\alpha|p|^2}$. If $s\ge1$, $(\sum_{i=1}^d p_i^2)^s\le d^{s-1}\sum_{i=1}^d|p_i|^{2s}$; for $s=0$ the weight is one. Factor the remaining coordinate Gaussians and apply [F2] and the one-dimensional bounds from step 1.2. The resulting finite upper bound depends only on $d,s,m,\beta_0$, not on $\beta$ in the stated interval.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, and suppose $Dg(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in U$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact and Jordan measurable. For a bounded function $f:g(K)\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is Riemann integrable on $g(K)$;
2. $x\mapsto f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|$ is Riemann integrable on $K$.

When either condition holds,
$$\int_{g(K)}f(y)\,dy=\int_K f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|\,dx.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, and suppose $Dg(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in U$. If $K\subseteq U$ is compact and Jordan measurable, then $g(K)$ is compact and Jordan measurable.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: Fix a sphere of radius $r>0$. At least one coordinate of every point on it has absolute value at least $r/\sqrt3$. On each of the six patches where a specified coordinate is largest in absolute value and has a specified sign, write that coordinate as $\pm\sqrt{r^2-u^2-v^2}$ over a bounded disk with $r^2-u^2-v^2\ge r^2/3$. The graph gradient is uniformly bounded. A grid of squares of side $\delta$ covers the disk with $O(\delta^{-2})$ squares; the graph over each square fits in a rectangular box of base area $\delta^2$ and height $O(\delta)$, so the total covering volume is $O(\delta)$. Thus the sphere has content zero. The sphere at radius zero is a point and is covered by one cube of arbitrarily small volume. Since $\partial A_{a,b}$ is contained in the union of the spheres of radii $a$ and $b$, [F1] makes the bounded shell Jordan measurable.

If $a=b$, then $A_{a,b}$ is a sphere of Jordan content zero by step 1.1, so both integrals are zero. Now assume $0<a<b$. For $0<\varepsilon<\min\{\pi/4,(b-a)/2\}$ put $K_\varepsilon=[a,b]\times[\varepsilon,\pi-\varepsilon]\times[\varepsilon,2\pi-\varepsilon]$ and $\Psi(r,\theta,\phi)=(r\sin\theta\cos\phi,r\sin\theta\sin\phi,r\cos\theta)$. On the open domain with $r>0$, $0<\theta<\pi$ and $0<\phi<2\pi$, $\Psi$ is injective and $C^1$ with determinant $r^2\sin\theta>0$; its inverse is given by radius, polar angle and the unique azimuth in $(0,2\pi)$. The compact set $K_\varepsilon$ is Jordan, and [F2] makes $x\mapsto F(|x|)$ integrable on $\Psi(K_\varepsilon)$. Applying [F3] gives
$$\int_{\Psi(K_\varepsilon)}F(|x|)\,dx=\left(\int_a^bF(r)r^2\,dr\right)\left(\int_\varepsilon^{\pi-\varepsilon}\sin\theta\,d\theta\right)(2\pi-2\varepsilon).$$

The missing part of $A_{a,b}$ outside $\Psi(K_\varepsilon)$ is contained in the union of the polar-cap box $[-b\sin\varepsilon,b\sin\varepsilon]^2\times[-b,b]$ and the azimuth-seam box $[-b,b]\times[-b\sin\varepsilon,b\sin\varepsilon]\times[-b,b]$. Their total volumes are at most $8b^3(\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon)$, which tends to zero. Since $F$ is bounded, the difference between its integral on the whole shell and on $\Psi(K_\varepsilon)$ tends to zero. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in step 2.1 gives the formula and the angular factor $2\cdot2\pi=4\pi$. If $a=0$, first apply the result to $[\eta,b]$ and then let $\eta\downarrow0$; the omitted ball lies in $[-\eta,\eta]^3$ and contributes at most $8\eta^3\sup_{[0,b]}|F|$, while the absolute value of the omitted radial integral is at most $\sup_{[0,b]}|F|\eta^3/3$. Both tend to zero.

finite_checks.calculation: For a=b the shell is a sphere of content zero and the radial interval has integral zero; for a=0<b the omitted ball and radial integral vanish at rates O(η³).
The limiting angular factors are ∫₀^π sinθ dθ=2 and ∫₀^{2π}dφ=2π, giving 4π.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use SI dimensions for the numerical model parameters: Newton constant $G$ has units $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, each mass $m_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg}$, each position $q_i$ has units $\mathrm{m}$, each momentum $p_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, energy $H$ has units $\mathrm{J}$, Boltzmann constant $k_B$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, and inverse energy $\beta$ has units $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. Fix an action reference $h_*>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$; it is a normalization convention and is not identified with Planck's constant.

For an integer $N\ge1$, any Lebesgue measurable position region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and equal particle mass $m>0$, define the ordered phase space $\Gamma_N=B^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)$. This phase space and measure are allowed even when $B$ is unbounded or has infinite volume; finite canonical preparations separately require a positive finite partition integral. The dimensionless reference measure for identical classical particles is
$$d\nu_N=\frac{d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p}{N!h_*^{3N}}.$$
For a measurable real Hamiltonian $H$ and $\beta>0$ with $0<Z_N(\beta):=\int_{\Gamma_N}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define the canonical density $p_\beta=Z_N(\beta)^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ relative to $\nu_N$. For a probability density $\rho$ with $\int|\rho\log\rho|\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define its reference-relative entropy $S(\rho)=-k_B\int\rho\log\rho\,d\nu_N$.

When $H$ is fixed and a Gibbs-volume function $\Omega(E)=\nu_N\{H\le E\}$ satisfies $0<\Omega(E)<\infty$, the Gibbs-volume entropy convention is $S_G(E)=k_B\log\Omega(E)$ and its temperature is defined by $1/T_G=dS_G/dE$ where that derivative exists and is positive. If $\omega(E)=\Omega'(E)>0$, a distinct surface-entropy convention with fixed energy width $\Delta E>0$ is $S_B(E)=k_B\log(\omega(E)\Delta E)$. These conventions are definitions; they need not assign the same finite-system temperature.

The measure is dimensionless because $d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p$ and $h_*^{3N}$ have the same units. The definition supplies no physical assertion that the chosen Hamiltonian describes nature and no mechanism of dynamical equilibration.

citations.quote:
Use the phase space and dimensionless reference measure of [[def-tgr-gravitating-phase-reference]]. Fix an integer $N\ge1$, a bounded Lebesgue measurable $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with positive finite volume, a common mass $m>0$, a gravitational coupling $G>0$, and a softening length $a>0$. On $\Gamma_N=B^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ define
$$H_{N,a}(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}+U_a(q),\qquad U_a(q)=-\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\frac{Gm^2}{\sqrt{|q_i-q_j|^2+a^2}}.$$
The positions and momenta are mathematical phase variables; the softening is a fixed regulator parameter. The Hamiltonian is measurable and its potential is bounded because each pair denominator is at least $a$. A point-particle model is a different Hamiltonian and is not included at $a=0$.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, $m>0$, and $0<\beta_0\le\beta_1<\infty$. For every $\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\,dp=\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{d/2}.$$
For every integer $s\ge0$, the polynomially weighted Gaussian has a uniform finite bound
$$\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]}\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|p|^{2s})e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\,dp<\infty.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Each pair denominator is at least $a$, so $-C_N\le U_a\le0$ and $K_N\ge0$. Consequently $e^{-\beta K_N}\le e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}\le e^{\beta C_N}e^{-\beta K_N}$. Tonelli [F4] and [F2] evaluate the momentum integral as $(2\pi m/\beta)^{3N/2}$; the position integral is $|B|^N$, so the stated positive lower and finite upper bounds follow after division by $N!h_*^{3N}$.

Fix a compact interval $[\beta_0,\beta_1]\subset(0,\infty)$. Since $|U_a|\le C_N$ and $K_N=|p|^2/(2m)$ in $d=3N$ momentum coordinates, for every fixed $j$ there is a finite $A_j$ such that
$$|H_{N,a}|^j e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}\le A_j(1+|p|^{2j})e^{-\beta_0|p|^2/(2m)}$$
for every $\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]$ and every phase point. The right side is integrable by [F2] times the finite position volume $|B|^N$. This proves all absolute energy moments and supplies an integrable compact-parameter envelope.

For each $j$, the parameter derivative of $(-H_{N,a})^j e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}$ is $(-H_{N,a})^{j+1}e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}$; its measurability and an integrable uniform bound are provided by step 2.1 at order $j+1$. Apply [F3] successively on compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$, starting with $j=0$, to differentiate under the integral any finite number of times. The formula for $Z_N^{(j)}$ follows by induction, and the moment of order zero gives the positive normalized density.

finite_checks.calculation: C_N=0 because N(N−1)=0; both partition bounds coincide with |B|/(h_*³)(2πm/β)^{3/2}.

citations.quote:
Use the box, mass $m$, integer $N\ge1$, regulator $a>0$, and Hamiltonian $H_{N,a}=K_N+U_a$ of [[def-tgr-softened-gravity-finite-phase]], with $K_N=\sum_i|p_i|^2/(2m)$. Put $C_N=Gm^2N(N-1)/(2a)$ and use the reference measure of [[def-tgr-gravitating-phase-reference]]. For every $\beta>0$,
$$0<\frac{|B|^N}{N!h_*^{3N}}\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{3N/2} \le Z_N(\beta) \le e^{\beta C_N}\frac{|B|^N}{N!h_*^{3N}}\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{3N/2}<\infty.$$
The density $p_\beta=Z_N^{-1}e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}$ is a positive probability density. For each integer $j\ge0$, $\int_{\Gamma_N}|H_{N,a}|^j e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}d\nu_N$ is finite, and $Z_N$ is $C^\infty$ on $(0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_N^{(j)}(\beta)=\int_{\Gamma_N}(-H_{N,a})^j e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}\,d\nu_N.$$
On every compact positive $\beta$ interval, one integrable majorant works for each fixed derivative order.

derivations.claim: Differentiating $\log Z_N$ and using $Z_N'=-\int H_{N,a}e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}d\nu_N$ gives $-\partial_\beta\log Z_N=Z_N^{-1}\int H_{N,a}e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}d\nu_N=\langle H_{N,a}\rangle_\beta$.

The quotient rule and $Z_N''=\int H_{N,a}^2e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}d\nu_N$ give
$$\partial_\beta\langle H_{N,a}\rangle_\beta=-\frac{Z_N''}{Z_N}+\left(\frac{Z_N'}{Z_N}\right)^2 =-\left(\langle H_{N,a}^2\rangle_\beta-\langle H_{N,a}\rangle_\beta^2\right) =-\operatorname{Var}_\beta(H_{N,a}).$$
All terms are finite by [F1].

Since $dT_K/d\beta=-1/(k_B\beta^2)$, the chain rule yields $C_K=(d\langle H\rangle/d\beta)/(dT_K/d\beta)=k_B\beta^2\operatorname{Var}_\beta(H_{N,a})$. The variance is the expectation of the nonnegative square $(H_{N,a}-\langle H_{N,a}\rangle)^2$, so $C_K\ge0$.

u_N+R_t$$

Fix an integer $N\ge1$, a bounded Lebesgue measurable $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with positive finite volume, a common mass $m>0$, a gravitational coupling $G>0$, and a softening length $a>0$. On $\Gamma_N=B^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ define
$$H_{N,a}(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}+U_a(q),\qquad U_a(q)=-\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\frac{Gm^2}{\sqrt{|q_i-q_j|^2+a^2}}.$$
The positions and momenta are mathematical phase variables; the softening is a fixed regulator parameter. The Hamiltonian is measurable and its potential is bounded because each pair denominator is at least $a$. A point-particle model is a different Hamiltonian and is not included at $a=0$.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, $m>0$, and $0<\beta_0\le\beta_1<\infty$. For every $\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\,dp=\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{d/2}.$$
For every integer $s\ge0$, the polynomially weighted Gaussian has a uniform finite bound
$$\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]}\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|p|^{2s})e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\,dp<\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure

derivations.claim: Choose an interior point $q_0$ of the box and a length $\ell>0$ small enough that the cubes below lie in the box for all sufficiently large integers $n$. Let $Q_{1,n}=q_0+(0,\ell/n)^3$ and $Q_{2,n}=q_0+(2\ell/n,0,0)+(0,\ell/n)^3$. They are disjoint, have volumes $(\ell/n)^3$, and every pair satisfies $0<|q_2-q_1|\le\sqrt{11}\ell/n$. On their product the point-potential Boltzmann weight is at least $\exp(\beta Gm^2 n/(\sqrt{11}\ell))$, so its positional integral is at least $(\ell/n)^6\exp(\beta Gm^2 n/(\sqrt{11}\ell))$. This lower bound tends to infinity, proving divergence of the positional integral. The independent momentum Gaussian integral is positive and finite by [F3]; Tonelli [F4] therefore makes the full partition integral infinite.

In the softened model, when every $q_i\in C$, all pair distances are at most $D$ and hence $U_a(q)\le-Gm^2N(N-1)/(2\sqrt{D^2+a^2})=-cN(N-1)$. Restricting the nonnegative partition integral to $C^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ and integrating momenta gives
$$Z_N(\beta)\ge \frac{v^N}{N!h_*^{3N}}e^{\beta cN(N-1)}\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{3N/2}.$$
Use $N!\le N^N$, divide logarithms by $N$, and gather all $N$-independent terms into $K_\beta$ to obtain the claimed bound. Since $\beta cN-\log N\to+\infty$, the free-energy conclusion follows.

For each fixed $N=n^3$, the hard-core condition bounds each pair attraction below by $-Gm^2/a$; the finite box and Gaussian momentum integral therefore make its partition function finite. Fix $d>a+2\delta$ with $0<\delta<d$. In $B_n=(0,nd)^3$, place centers at $d(k_1+\frac12,k_2+\frac12,k_3+\frac12)$ for $k_i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and choose the open cube of side $\delta$ centered at each center. These cubes lie in $B_n$ and have positive volume. Distinct grid centers are at least $d$ apart, and two points in their cubes differ from their centers by at most $\sqrt3\delta$; hence every particle separation exceeds $d-\sqrt3\delta>a$, since $2>\sqrt3$. The product cubes are admissible. Each pair distance is at most $\sqrt3(n-1)d+\sqrt3\delta\le c_rnd$ with $c_r=\sqrt3$. Since $|B_n|=n^3d^3=Nd^3$, this sequence has fixed number density $d^{-3}$. There are $N(N-1)/2$ pairs; for $N\ge2$,
$$U_N\le-\frac{Gm^2}{c_rnd}\frac{N(N-1)}2\le-c_0N^{5/3},\qquad c_0=\frac{Gm^2}{4c_rd}>0,$$
because $n=N^{1/3}$. Restricting the finite partition integral to these product cubes, integrating momenta, and using $N!\le N^N$ gives $\log Z_N/N\ge\beta c_0N^{2/3}-\log N+K_\beta\to+\infty$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use SI dimensions for the numerical model parameters: Newton constant $G$ has units $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, each mass $m_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg}$, each position $q_i$ has units $\mathrm{m}$, each momentum $p_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, energy $H$ has units $\mathrm{J}$, Boltzmann constant $k_B$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, and inverse energy $\beta$ has units $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. Fix an action reference $h_*>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$; it is a normalization convention and is not identified with Planck's constant.

For an integer $N\ge1$, any Lebesgue measurable position region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and equal particle mass $m>0$, define the ordered phase space $\Gamma_N=B^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)$. This phase space and measure are allowed even when $B$ is unbounded or has infinite volume; finite canonical preparations separately require a positive finite partition integral. The dimensionless reference measure for identical classical particles is
$$d\nu_N=\frac{d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p}{N!h_*^{3N}}.$$
For a measurable real Hamiltonian $H$ and $\beta>0$ with $0<Z_N(\beta):=\int_{\Gamma_N}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define the canonical density $p_\beta=Z_N(\beta)^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ relative to $\nu_N$. For a probability density $\rho$ with $\int|\rho\log\rho|\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define its reference-relative entropy $S(\rho)=-k_B\int\rho\log\rho\,d\nu_N$.

When $H$ is fixed and a Gibbs-volume function $\Omega(E)=\nu_N\{H\le E\}$ satisfies $0<\Omega(E)<\infty$, the Gibbs-volume entropy convention is $S_G(E)=k_B\log\Omega(E)$ and its temperature is defined by $1/T_G=dS_G/dE$ where that derivative exists and is positive. If $\omega(E)=\Omega'(E)>0$, a distinct surface-entropy convention with fixed energy width $\Delta E>0$ is $S_B(E)=k_B\log(\omega(E)\Delta E)$. These conventions are definitions; they need not assign the same finite-system temperature.

The measure is dimensionless because $d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p$ and $h_*^{3N}$ have the same units. The definition supplies no physical assertion that the chosen Hamiltonian describes nature and no mechanism of dynamical equilibration.

Use SI units, positive masses $m_1,m_2$ in $\mathrm{kg}$, reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$, gravitational parameter $A=Gm_1m_2$ in $\mathrm{J\,m}$, relative position $q\in\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm m$, relative momentum $p\in\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, and a fixed action reference $h_*>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Assume $r_0>0$ and $R>16r_0$. The relative phase domain is
$$\Gamma_{\mathrm{rel}}=\{(q,p):r_0\le |q|\le R,\ p\in\mathbb R^3\},\qquad d\nu_{\mathrm{rel}}=\frac{d^3q\,d^3p}{h_*^3},$$
with no center-of-mass variables or factor $1/2!$. The relative Hamiltonian is
$$h(q,p)=\frac{|p|^2}{2\mu}-\frac{A}{|q|}.$$

For $E=-e<0$ with $A/R<e\le A/(16r_0)$, put $\delta=e r_0/A\in(0,1/16]$ and
$$J(\delta)=\int_\delta^1s^{1/2}(1-s)^{3/2}\,ds,\qquad \Omega(E)=\nu_{\mathrm{rel}}\{(q,p)\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{rel}}:h(q,p)\le E\}.$$
The radial integration formula of [[lem-tgr-annular-radial-integration]] gives the explicit phase volume
$$\Omega(-e)=\frac{(4\pi)(4\pi/3)(2\mu)^{3/2}A^3}{h_*^3}\,e^{-3/2}J(\delta).$$
This is finite and positive on the stated branch.

Define $S^2=\{u\in\mathbb R^3:|u|=1\}$ and $p_*(r,E)=\sqrt{2\mu(E+A/r)}$ for $r_0\le r\le A/e$. Let $d\sigma$ be the angular area measure of total mass $4\pi$ from [[lem-tgr-annular-radial-integration]]. Push the finite measure $(\mu p_*/h_*^3)d^3q\,d\sigma(u)$ on $\{r_0\le|q|\le A/e\}\times S^2$ forward by $(q,u)\mapsto(q,p_*(|q|,E)u)$; call the resulting measure $\Sigma_E$. Its candidate normalized shell law is $P_E=\Sigma_E/\Omega'(E)$. The separate result [[lem-tgr-regulated-kepler-shell-law-normalization]] proves $\Omega'(E)>0$, finite total mass, and $P_E(\{h=E\})=1$. Thus the energy-shell preparation is explicitly defined; it is not inferred from phase-volume counting alone.

The entropy convention attached to this model is Gibbs volume, $S_G(E)=k_B\log\Omega(E)$, with $1/T_G=dS_G/dE$ and $C_G=dE/dT_G$ where defined. Other finite-system entropy conventions are distinct.

Let $0\le a<b<\infty$ and let $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The closed radial shell $A_{a,b}=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:a\le|x|\le b\}$ is Jordan measurable, and
$$\int_{A_{a,b}}F(|x|)\,dx=4\pi\int_a^b F(r)r^2\,dr.$$
The angular area measure used below is the pushforward of $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$ on $[0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]$ under $(\theta,\phi)\mapsto(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)$; its total mass is $4\pi$.

derivations.claim:
The inequalities $A/R<e$ and $e\le A/(16r_0)$ imply $r_0<A/e<R$. At fixed $q$ with $r=|q|$, the momentum sublevel $h(q,p)\le-e$ is the ball $|p|\le\sqrt{2\mu(A/r-e)}$, which is nonempty exactly for $r_0\le r\le A/e$. By [F2] its momentum volume is $\frac{4\pi}{3}[2\mu(A/r-e)]^{3/2}$. Integrating the resulting radial function over $q$ by [F2], then substituting $s=er/A$, gives
$$\Omega(-e)=\frac{(4\pi)(4\pi/3)(2\mu)^{3/2}A^3}{h_*^3}e^{-3/2}J(\delta), \qquad \delta=\frac{er_0}{A}.$$
The integration interval is compact and has positive length, while the integrand is continuous and positive in its interior, so $\Omega$ is finite and strictly positive.

Put $f(s)=s^{1/2}(1-s)^{3/2}$ for $0<s<1$. For $h\ne0$ small enough that $\delta+h\in(0,1)$, the oriented-integral identity gives $(J(\delta+h)-J(\delta))/h=-(1/h)\int_\delta^{\delta+h}f(s)\,ds$. Its difference from $-f(\delta)$ has absolute value at most $\sup_{s\text{ between }\delta\text{ and }\delta+h}|f(s)-f(\delta)|$, which tends to zero by continuity. Thus $J'(\delta)=-\delta^{1/2}(1-\delta)^{3/2}$. Differentiating the explicit phase-volume formula with $E=-e$ now yields
$$\Omega'(E)=\frac{(4\pi)(4\pi/3)(2\mu)^{3/2}A^3}{h_*^3}e^{-5/2} \left[\frac32J(\delta)+\delta^{3/2}(1-\delta)^{3/2}\right]>0.$$
The bracket is finite and positive, so the derivative is finite and strictly positive.

Integrating the defining pushforward density over its entire source gives
$$\Sigma_E(\{h=E\})=\frac{16\pi^2\mu}{h_*^3}\int_{r_0}^{A/e}r^2\sqrt{2\mu(A/r-e)}\,dr =\frac{16\pi^2\mu\sqrt{2\mu}}{h_*^3}A^3e^{-5/2} \int_\delta^1s^{3/2}(1-s)^{1/2}\,ds,$$
where [F2] supplies the spatial radial measure and $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ supplies the momentum-direction factor. Put $g(s)=s^{3/2}(1-s)^{3/2}$. Direct differentiation and integration on $[\delta,1]$ give
$$\frac32J(\delta)+\delta^{3/2}(1-\delta)^{3/2} =\frac32\int_\delta^1s^{3/2}(1-s)^{1/2}\,ds.$$
Since $\mu\sqrt{2\mu}=\frac12(2\mu)^{3/2}$, this identity makes the preceding shell mass exactly the $\Omega'(E)$ in step 2.1.

Every image point has $|p|=p_*(r,E)$, hence $h=|p|^2/(2\mu)-A/r=E$. The measure is finite by step 3.1 and has total mass $\Omega'(E)>0$; division by this total therefore defines a probability supported on the energy surface.

finite_checks.calculation: At r=A/e the momentum radius vanishes; p* is continuous there and the radial shell integral remains finite.
Integration by parts gives I=∫δ¹s^{3/2}(1−s)^{1/2}ds=J(δ)+(2/3)δ^{3/2}(1−δ)^{3/2}, matching Ω′ exactly.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, $m>0$, and $0<\beta_0\le\beta_1<\infty$. For every $\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\,dp=\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{d/2}.$$
For every integer $s\ge0$, the polynomially weighted Gaussian has a uniform finite bound
$$\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]}\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|p|^{2s})e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\,dp<\infty.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
On $Q$, $-A/r_0\le-A/|q|\le-A/R$. Therefore
$$e^{\beta A/R}e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2\mu)} \le e^{-\beta h(q,p)} \le e^{\beta A/r_0}e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2\mu)}.$$
The position volume is positive and finite by [F2]. Tonelli [F5] and the Gaussian formula [F3] integrate the momentum factor as $(2\pi\mu/\beta)^{3/2}$, proving both strict positivity and the stated finite bounds.

Fix $[\beta_0,\beta_1]\subset(0,\infty)$. Since $|{-A/|q|}|\le A/r_0$, for every integer $j\ge0$ a finite constant $B_j$ gives
$$|h(q,p)|^je^{-\beta h(q,p)} \le B_j(1+|p|^{2j})e^{-\beta_0|p|^2/(2\mu)}.$$
This is integrable on $Q\times\mathbb R^3$ by [F2] and [F3], independently of $\beta$ in the compact interval. The integrand derivatives are $(-h)^j e^{-\beta h}$, so [F4] applied successively proves all moment and derivative formulas.

The first two derivatives are $Z'_{\mathrm{rel}}=-\int h e^{-\beta h}d\nu$ and $Z''_{\mathrm{rel}}=\int h^2e^{-\beta h}d\nu$. Dividing by $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}>0$ and differentiating the quotient gives $d\langle h\rangle_\beta/d\beta=-\langle h^2\rangle_\beta+\langle h\rangle_\beta^2=-\operatorname{Var}_\beta(h)$. Since $dT_K/d\beta=-1/(k_B\beta^2)$, the chain rule yields the displayed $C_K\ge0$.

finite_checks.calculation: r₀>0 and R<∞ bound the potential between −A/r₀ and −A/R, so both partition bounds are finite and strictly positive.
The identity permits Varβ(h)=0 and then C_K=0; only nonnegativity is asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

derivations.claim: Write $e=-E$ and $\delta=er_0/A$. For $f(s)=s^{1/2}(1-s)^{3/2}$ and $h\ne0$ with $\delta+h\in(0,1)$, $(J(\delta+h)-J(\delta))/h=-(1/h)\int_\delta^{\delta+h}f(s)\,ds$; continuity of $f$ makes this quotient tend to $-f(\delta)$. Hence $J'(\delta)=-\delta^{1/2}(1-\delta)^{3/2}$. Differentiating $\log\Omega=C_1-\frac32\log e+\log J(\delta)$ with respect to $E=-e$ gives $dS_G/dE=k_B(\frac32+z)/e=k_B\mathcal B/e$. Its reciprocal is the stated positive $T_G$.

Differentiating $T_G=e/[k_B\mathcal B(\delta)]$ with respect to $e$, using $d\delta/de=\delta/e$, yields
$$\frac{dT_G}{de}=\frac{\mathcal B-\delta\mathcal B'}{k_B\mathcal B^2}.$$
Since $E=-e$, inversion gives the displayed formula for $C_G$, provided $\mathcal B-\delta\mathcal B'>0$.

Logarithmic differentiation of $z$ gives
$$\delta z'=\frac32z\frac{1-2\delta}{1-\delta}+z^2\le\frac32z+z^2,$$
because $0<\delta\le1/16$ makes $(1-2\delta)/(1-\delta)\le1$. Therefore
$$\mathcal B-\delta\mathcal B'=\frac32+z-\delta z' \ge\frac32-\frac z2-z^2\ge1$$
when $0<z\le1/2$. Step 2.1 now gives $C_G<0$ throughout the branch.

For an integer $N\ge1$, any Lebesgue measurable position region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and equal particle mass $m>0$, define the ordered phase space $\Gamma_N=B^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)$. This phase space and measure are allowed even when $B$ is unbounded or has infinite volume; finite canonical preparations separately require a positive finite partition integral. The dimensionless reference measure for identical classical particles is
$$d\nu_N=\frac{d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p}{N!h_*^{3N}}.$$
For a measurable real Hamiltonian $H$ and $\beta>0$ with $0<Z_N(\beta):=\int_{\Gamma_N}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define the canonical density $p_\beta=Z_N(\beta)^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ relative to $\nu_N$. For a probability density $\rho$ with $\int|\rho\log\rho|\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define its reference-relative entropy $S(\rho)=-k_B\int\rho\log\rho\,d\nu_N$.

derivations.claim: In a local orthonormal coframe, $p_i=e_i{}^a\hat p_a$ and $h_{ij}=\sum_a e_i{}^ae_j{}^a$, so $|\det(e_i{}^a)|=\sqrt{\det h}$. Hence $d^3p_i=\sqrt{\det h}\,d^3\hat p$ and $d^3x\,d^3p_i=dV_h\,d^3\hat p$. The transition matrix between orthonormal coframes is orthogonal and has absolute determinant one, so this fibre measure is independent of the chosen local coframe.

In the orthonormal momentum variables, $E(\hat p)\ge c|\hat p|$, so $e^{-\beta_K\mathcal N E}\le e^{-\beta_K\mathcal N_0c|\hat p|}$. The right side is integrable on $\mathbb R^3$: $|\hat p|\ge(|\hat p_1|+|\hat p_2|+|\hat p_3|)/\sqrt3$ reduces its integral to a product of three finite one-dimensional exponential integrals. The same comparison with polynomial factors gives every energy moment and a common majorant for $\beta_K$ in compact positive intervals. Each $\beta_K$ derivative of the integrand is $(-H_K)^j e^{-\beta_KH_K}$; [F2] therefore gives $Z_1^{(j)}=\int(-H_K)^j e^{-\beta_KH_K}dV_h\,d^3\hat p/h_*^3$ for every finite order. The proper volume of $\overline B$ is finite by compactness and the metric eigenvalue bounds, and positive because $B$ has positive volume and $\det h>0$. Thus $Z_1$ is finite and strictly positive. For $M$ independent labelled particles, Tonelli [F3] factors the product integral; the fixed classical indistinguishable-particle counting convention divides by $M!$, giving $Z_M=Z_1^M/M!$. Summing grand weights yields $\sum_{M\ge0}(zZ_1)^M/M!=e^{zZ_1}$.

At a fixed $x$, put $ eta_{\mathrm{loc}}= eta_K\mathcal N(x)$. On a momentum cube $[-R,R]^3$, integrate
$$\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{\hat p_i}\left(\hat p_i e^{- eta_{\mathrm{loc}}E}ight) =3e^{- eta_{\mathrm{loc}}E}- eta_{\mathrm{loc}}(\hat p\cdot
abla_{\hat p}E)e^{- eta_{\mathrm{loc}}E}.$$
The constant factor $z h_*^{-3}$ in $f$ cancels from the moments. Here $
abla_{\hat p}E=c^2\hat p/E$ and $\hat p\cdot
abla_{\hat p}E\le c|\hat p|$, so the divergence terms are integrable under the exponential bound of step 1.2. On a face with $|\hat p_i|=R$, $|\hat p|\ge R$ and $|\hat p|\ge(|\hat p_j|+|\hat p_k|)/\sqrt2$, hence $|\hat p|\ge R/2+(|\hat p_j|+|\hat p_k|)/(2\sqrt2)$. Each face integral is therefore bounded by a constant times $R e^{- eta_{\mathrm{loc}}cR/2}\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{- eta_{\mathrm{loc}}c(|y|+|z|)/(2\sqrt2)}dy\,dz$, which tends to zero. The integral of the divergence over $\mathbb R^3$ is zero, and division by $3 eta_{\mathrm{loc}}$ gives $P=n/ eta_{\mathrm{loc}}=nk_BT_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

For each spatial coordinate $x^i$, $\partial_i f=-\beta_K(\partial_i\mathcal N)E f$. The derivatives of the lapse are bounded on the compact closure, $\mathcal N\ge\mathcal N_0$, and $Ef$ has the integrable majorant from step 1.2. Hence [F2] gives $\partial_i n=-\beta_K(\partial_i\mathcal N)\varepsilon$. Differentiating $P=n/(\beta_K\mathcal N)$ and substituting this identity yields
$$\partial_iP=-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mathcal N}\partial_i\mathcal N -\frac{n}{\beta_K\mathcal N^2}\partial_i\mathcal N =-(\varepsilon+P)\partial_i\log\mathcal N.$$
Finally, rewriting $\beta_K(\mathcal N E-\mu_K)$ as $\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(E-\mu_{\mathrm{loc}})$ gives $\mu_{\mathrm{loc}}=\mu_K/\mathcal N$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
Here $q_*=0$ by convention when $I$ is empty; for nonempty $I$ the displayed supremum is unchanged. In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, if for every compact $B\subset J\subset(0,\infty)$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each finite mode, $E_j-\mu_K$ is real and finite, so $q_j=e^{-\beta_K(E_j-\mu_K)}>0$. A finite family of positive numbers has finite sum, and it has only finitely many negative energy gaps. Therefore the finite-mode hypotheses of [A1] hold under [A2]; conditional on the supplier's stated result, which is not independently approved here, it gives the exact trace product and normalized diagonal state.

The supplier's finite fermion marginal is $\mathbb E[n_j]=q_j/(1+q_j)=1/(e^{\beta_K(E_j-\mu_K)}+1)$ by substituting $q_j$. Since $E_j=\mathcal N_j\epsilon_j$, this exponent is $\beta_K(\mathcal N_j\epsilon_j-\mu_K)$.

The definitions $\beta_j=\beta_K\mathcal N_j$ and $\mu_j=\mu_K/\mathcal N_j$ give $\beta_j(\epsilon_j-\mu_j)=\beta_K(\mathcal N_j\epsilon_j-\mu_K)$. Substitution proves the displayed local-parameter form exactly for each supplied mode. The statement uses only this finite regulator and makes no claim about an unprovided continuum mode spectrum.

Under [[def-tgr-regulated-kepler-shell-law]], let $E=-e$, $\delta=er_0/A\in(0,1/16]$, and
$$z(\delta)=\frac{\delta^{3/2}(1-\delta)^{3/2}}{J(\delta)},\qquad \mathcal B(\delta)=\frac32+z(\delta).$$
For the Gibbs-volume entropy $S_G(E)=k_B\log\Omega(E)$ and temperature convention $1/T_G=dS_G/dE$,
$$T_G(E)=\frac{e}{k_B\mathcal B(\delta)},\qquad C_G(E):=\frac{dE}{dT_G} =-\frac{k_B\mathcal B(\delta)^2}{\mathcal B(\delta)-\delta\mathcal B'(\delta)}<0.$$
The denominator is at least $1$. This is a finite regulated mathematical branch with the stated entropy convention; it does not identify a universal operational temperature or dynamical stability.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $x:(\alpha,\beta)\to\mathbb R^n$ solve a Picard-Lindelof ODE and suppose $\beta<\infty$. If there are $t_j\uparrow\beta$ for which $(t_j,x(t_j))$ lies in one compact subset $K$ of the open ODE domain, then $x$ extends to a solution beyond $\beta$. A solution whose graph has a sequence approaching a compact interior endpoint state extends past that endpoint. The reflected statement holds at a finite left endpoint.

derivations.claim: Since $S_i'=1/T_i$, differentiation with respect to energy gives $S_i''=-T_i^{-2}(dT_i/dE_i)=-1/(T_i^2C_i)$.

The first derivative of $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is $S_1'(x)-S_2'(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-x)$, so it vanishes exactly at common temperature. The second derivative is the sum $S_1''(x)+S_2''(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-x)$, which by step 1.1 is the stated expression. If $C_1<0<C_2$, then $S_{\mathrm{tot}}''<0$ exactly when $1/C_2>1/|C_1|$, equivalently $C_2<|C_1|$; continuity and the second-derivative test give a strict local maximum.

For the displayed bath entropy, $S_b'=C_b/(E_b-E_0)$, hence $T_b=(S_b')^{-1}=(E_b-E_0)/C_b$ and $dE_b/dT_b=C_b$. Setting $E_b=E_0+C_bT_*$ makes $T_b=T_*$; with $C_b<|C_G(E_*)|$, step 2.1 gives strictly negative total entropy curvature. Thus the finite bath realizes the claimed stabilizing parameter range in the specified exchange direction.

At a strict local maximum $x_*$, continuity of $S_{\mathrm{tot}}''$ gives a compact interval $I_0$ about $x_*$ in its open domain and $a>0$ with $S_{\mathrm{tot}}''\le-a$ there. Integrating from $x_*$, where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}'=0$, gives $(x-x_*)S_{\mathrm{tot}}'(x)\le-a(x-x_*)^2$. The vector field $L S_{\mathrm{tot}}'$ is $C^1$ and hence locally Lipschitz, so [F2] gives a unique local solution; the chain rule gives $dS_{\mathrm{tot}}/dt=L(S_{\mathrm{tot}}')^2\ge0$ and
$$\frac{d}{dt}|x-x_*|^2\le-2La|x-x_*|^2.$$
Multiplying by $e^{2Lat}$ and differentiating yields $|x(t)-x_*|\le e^{-La t}|x(0)-x_*|$. Thus the solution stays in a compact interior interval. If its maximal forward endpoint were finite, points on a sequence approaching that endpoint would lie in one compact subset of the open ODE domain, so [F3] would extend the solution, a contradiction. The local basin therefore exists for all forward times and converges exponentially.

finite_checks.calculation: At C₂=|C₁| the reciprocal-capacity sum is zero and the second derivative test gives no strict maximum; the stated sufficient condition is strict C₂<|C₁|.
On an interval with S_tot″≤−a, d|x−x*|²/dt≤−2La|x−x*|² and therefore |x(t)−x*|≤e^(−Lat)|x(0)−x*|.
