citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Fix an integer $n\geq1$.  A **tempered distribution** on $\mathbb R^n$ is a
continuous complex-linear functional

$$u:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow\mathbb C,$$

where Schwartz space and its locally convex topology are those of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]].  The space of all such functionals
is denoted $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

We write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$.  This pairing is bilinear:
the test variable is not conjugated.  Thus $u(a\varphi+b\psi)=
a\langle u,\varphi\rangle+b\langle u,\psi\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$.
The zero functional is tempered.  Continuity is topological continuity, and,
because the Schwartz topology is generated by a countable cofinal family of
seminorms, it is equivalently continuity on every convergent sequence.  No
choice principle is used in this definition.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.
No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and let $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ be its bosonic Fock space and finite-particle domain.
For $h\in H$ define on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the Segal field
$$\phi_0(h):=2^{-1/2}\bigl(a^\dagger(h)+a(h)\bigr).$$
For $h\ne0$, this symmetric operator is essentially self-adjoint; write
$\Phi(h)=\overline{\phi_0(h)}$. If $r=\|h\|$, $e=h/r$, $K=e^\perp$,
$G=\mathcal F_s(K)$, choose a countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $G$
whose vectors are finite-particle, and use the one-mode splitting of
[[lem-qft-fock-one-mode-splitting]] followed by the Hermite unitary
$|n\rangle\mapsto g_n$ into $L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$ with pairing
$\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int\overline f g$ to write a vector as
$(f_j)_{j\in J}\in\ell^2(J;L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C))$. Then the exact domain and
action are
$$D(\Phi(h))=\left\{(f_j):\sum_{j\in J}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+r^2x^2)|f_j(x)|^2\,dx<\infty\right\},\qquad (\Phi(h)f)_j(x)=rx f_j(x).$$
For $h=0$, $\phi_0(0)$ closes to the zero operator on all of $\mathcal F_s(H)$.

Define $\epsilon(z)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}z^{\otimes n}/\sqrt{n!}$ for $z\in H$.
There are unitaries $W(h)$ determined on these total exponential vectors by
$$W(h)\epsilon(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|h\|^2}{4} +\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\langle h,z\rangle_2\right) \epsilon\!\left(z+\frac{i h}{\sqrt2}\right).$$
They obey
$$W(h)W(k)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i}{2}\operatorname{Im}\langle h,k\rangle_2\right)W(h+k),\qquad \langle\Omega,W(h)\Omega\rangle_2=e^{-\|h\|^2/4},$$
and $h\mapsto W(h)$ is strongly continuous. For every $h$, the one-parameter
group $t\mapsto W(th)$ has norm derivative at zero exactly on
$D(\Phi(h))$, with derivative $i\Phi(h)$ (for $h=0$ this is the zero
generator). Thus the displayed bounded Weyl operators have precisely the
closed Segal fields as their generators; no point-field or measurement claim
is included.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. For every $\mu\ge0$, the
space $H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu)$ of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] is separable (has a countable norm-dense subset), and
$$\{K_\mu f:f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)\}$$
is dense in $H_\mu$. If $\mu>0$, the range contains every function in
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$; if $\mu=0$, it contains every function in
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]], exactly as required by the
published Schwartz Fourier theorem.  For $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$
put

$$\widehat\varphi(\xi)=\mathcal F\varphi(\xi) =\int_{\mathbb R^n}\varphi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$

For $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ define its **Fourier transform** by

$$\langle\mathcal Fu,\varphi\rangle =\langle u,\mathcal F\varphi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)).$$

The published automorphism
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]
sends Schwartz tests continuously to Schwartz tests, so composition with the
continuous functional of [[def-tempered-distribution]] is again a continuous
complex-linear functional.  Hence $\mathcal Fu\in\mathcal S'$.  The pairing
is bilinear: there is no conjugation and no inverse transform on the
right-hand side.  Countable Choice is used only through the cited published
Fourier construction; transposition itself uses no additional choice.

Assume Countable Choice.  The Fourier transform
$\mathcal F:\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ is
well-defined and complex-linear.  It is continuous for both the weak topology
$\sigma(\mathcal S',\mathcal S)$ and the strong topology
$\beta(\mathcal S',\mathcal S)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

The test-function topology exists as a Hausdorff locally convex vector topology, induces the prescribed topology on each $\mathcal D_K$, and is the finest locally convex topology making all inclusions $\mathcal D_K\to\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous. A linear map $L:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to E$ to a locally convex space is continuous if and only if each restriction $L|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous. An increasing compact exhaustion whose interiors cover $\Omega$ gives the same topology, independently of the exhaustion. Thus this is an LF topology of the complete metrizable fixed-support spaces. All these claims hold in ZF.

In particular, for $\kappa>0$ in inverse length, take $A=\kappa^2/(16\pi)$ and $b=\kappa/2$. Then $L=1/(4\pi)$, $\beta=2\pi/\kappa$, and $C_{A,b}$ is precisely the tested chiral covariance $C_\kappa$ of [[lem-tgr-exponential-current]]. Its spectrum and detailed balance are
$$S_\kappa(\omega)=\frac{\omega}{2(e^{2\pi\omega/\kappa}-1)},\qquad S_\kappa(0)=\frac{\kappa}{4\pi},\qquad S_\kappa(-\omega)=e^{2\pi\omega/\kappa}S_\kappa(\omega)\quad(\omega>0).$$
Here $C_\kappa$ has units of inverse length squared and $S_\kappa$ inverse length. This is a two-point strip and detailed-balance statement, including the specified chiral current as a specialization. It does not assert a norm-continuous $C^*$-algebra KMS dynamics or an exact detector transition probability.

Assume Countable Choice. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2((0,\infty),dk;\mathbb C),\qquad
\langle h,q\rangle_2=\int_0^\infty\overline{h(k)}q(k)\,dk,$$
using the second-variable-linear convention. For
$f\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ define
$$h_f(k)=\sqrt{\frac{k}{4\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}f(U)e^{ikU}\,dU\quad(k>0).$$
Then $h_f,h_{\bar f}\in\mathcal H$, and $f\mapsto h_f$ is continuous on each fixed-compact-support test space. With the bosonic Fock conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], define on its finite-particle domain
$$J(f)=a(h_{\bar f})+a^\dagger(h_f).$$
This is a complex-linear operator-valued distribution on that invariant domain. For real $f$, its closure is $\overline{J(f)}=\sqrt2\,\Phi(h_f)$, where $\Phi(h_f)$ is the closed Segal field of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]; the corresponding Weyl one-parameter group has generator $i\Phi(h_f)$. The vacuum two-point form is positive type and has boundary kernel
$$C(s)=-\frac{1}{4\pi(s-i0)^2},$$
where $s-i0$ means the distributional limit from $s-i\epsilon$, $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

For $\kappa>0$ with units of inverse length, let $u,U$ have units of length and set
$$U_\kappa(u)=-\kappa^{-1}e^{-\kappa u},\qquad
u_\kappa(U)=-\kappa^{-1}\log(-\kappa U)\quad(U<0).$$
For $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ put $f_g(U)=g(u_\kappa(U))$ for $U<0$ and $f_g(U)=0$ for $U\ge0$, and define $j_\kappa(g)=J(f_g)$. The zero extension is smooth and compactly supported. Its vacuum covariance is the positive-type distribution
$$C_\kappa(s)=-\frac{\kappa^2}{16\pi}\,\operatorname{csch}^2\!\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}(s-i0)\right).$$
Here the notation is fixed as follows: for $b=\kappa/2$, set $Y_b(s)=\sinh(bs)/b$. Since $Y_b'(s)=\cosh(bs)>0$ and $Y_b(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$, it is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism. Define $\operatorname{csch}^2(b(s-i0)):=b^{-2}Y_b^*((y-i0)^{-2})$, where
$$\langle Y_b^*T,\varphi\rangle:=\left\langle T,\varphi(Y_b^{-1}(y))(Y_b^{-1})'(y)\right\rangle.$$
This is a one-dimensional chiral test-coordinate model. It asserts no restriction of a four-dimensional field to a null curve.

derivations.claim: Fix a compact set $K\Subset I$ containing $\operatorname{supp}f$ and let $d=\min_{\tau\in K}(\dot\gamma^0-|\dot{\boldsymbol\gamma}|)>0$. For $\mathbf k=r\mathbf n$, $r>0$, $|\mathbf n|=1$, the phase is $r\phi_{\mathbf n}(\tau)$ with $\phi'_{\mathbf n}=\dot\gamma^0-\mathbf n\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\gamma}\ge d$. All derivatives of $1/\phi'_{\mathbf n}$ are uniformly bounded on $K\times S^2$. Since $e^{ir\phi}=(ir\phi')^{-1}\partial_\tau e^{ir\phi}$, repeated integration by parts gives $|K_\gamma f(r\mathbf n)|\le C_N r^{-N}$ for every $N$ and $r\ge1$, with $C_N$ bounded by finitely many test-function seminorms on $K$. Boundary terms vanish because $f$ is compactly supported. For $0<r\le1$, $|K_\gamma f(r\mathbf n)|\le\|f\|_{L^1(K)}$.

Put $\kappa=a/c$ and $\ell=c^2/a$. Direct differentiation gives $\dot\gamma_a=(c\cosh(\kappa\tau),c\sinh(\kappa\tau),0,0)$, $\eta(\dot\gamma_a,\dot\gamma_a)=-c^2$, and $\ddot\gamma_a=(a\sinh(\kappa\tau),a\cosh(\kappa\tau),0,0)$, $\eta(\ddot\gamma_a,\ddot\gamma_a)=a^2$. Hence the curve is future unit timelike and its proper acceleration magnitude is $a$. With $s=\tau-\tau'$ and $v=(\tau+\tau')/2$, the differences satisfy $$X+Y=2\ell e^{\kappa v}\sinh(\kappa s/2),\qquad X-Y=2\ell e^{-\kappa v}\sinh(\kappa s/2),$$ where $Y=\Delta x^1$. Therefore $Y^2-X^2=-4\ell^2\sinh^2(\kappa s/2)$, and the regulated denominator factors exactly as $$Y^2+(\epsilon+iX)^2=(Y-X+i\epsilon)(Y+X-i\epsilon).$$

In polar coordinates $d\nu_0=r\,dr\,d\Omega/(2(2\pi)^3)$. The low-frequency bound makes $\int_0^1r|K_\gamma f|^2dr$ finite; the estimate of 1.1 with, for example, $N=2$ makes $\int_1^\infty r|K_\gamma f|^2dr$ finite, uniformly in $\mathbf n$. The same estimates bound the norm by finitely many seminorms of $f$ on $K$, so $K_\gamma|_{\mathcal D_K(I)}$ is continuous for each compact $K\Subset I$ and $K_\gamma f\in\mathcal H_0$. Since $K_\gamma$ is complex-linear, [F13] gives its continuity from the LF test-function topology on $\mathcal D(I)$ to the norm topology of $\mathcal H_0$. The Hilbert-space vector is therefore defined before it is used in a field expression.

The creation and annihilation formulas in [F2] define $\Phi_\gamma(f)$ on the finite-particle domain because $K_\gamma f\in\mathcal H_0$. For real $f$, it equals $\sqrt2$ times the Segal field with vector $K_\gamma f$ on that domain. Separability [F6] meets the hypothesis of [F5], which gives its self-adjoint closure. Mutual adjointness [F10] makes the finite-domain field symmetric. The vacuum is annihilated by $a(K_\gamma f)$ by [F10]. Therefore $\Phi_\gamma(g)\Omega=a^\dagger(K_\gamma g)\Omega$ and symmetry of $\Phi_\gamma(f)$ gives $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\gamma(f)\Phi_\gamma(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\gamma f,K_\gamma g\rangle_2$. This defines only the tested field and makes no point-field assumption.

For $\epsilon>0$ insert $e^{-\epsilon r}$ in the shell integral. With $X=\Delta x^0$ and $R=|\Delta\mathbf x|$, absolute convergence permits angular integration and Fubini [F9]: $$W_\epsilon(X,R)=\frac{1}{4\pi^2R}\int_0^\infty e^{-(\epsilon+iX)r}\sin(rR)\,dr =\frac{1}{4\pi^2\bigl(R^2+(\epsilon+iX)^2\bigr)}.$$ The value at $R=0$ is the continuous limit. The integral identity follows by writing the sine as two exponentials and integrating each, since $\operatorname{Re}(\epsilon+iX)>0$. For compact real tests $f,g$, the shell-paired expression converges to $\langle K_\gamma f,K_\gamma g\rangle_2$: $e^{-\epsilon r/2}K_\gamma f\to K_\gamma f$ in $\mathcal H_0$ by [F7], and Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] passes the inner products to the limit. Thus the damped kernel is an actual regulator for the constructed covariance, not a formal substitution of a worldline into a point field.

For compact real tests $f,g$, the linear change $v=(\tau+\tau')/2$, $s=\tau-\tau'$ has Jacobian of absolute value one and takes $f(\tau)g(\tau')$ to a compact smooth test $\varphi(v,s)$. On the compact average-time projection of its support, write $A(v)=2\ell e^{-\kappa v}>0$ and $B(v)=2\ell e^{\kappa v}>0$. The factors $Y-X+i\epsilon$ and $Y+X-i\epsilon$ are respectively $-A(v)(x-i\epsilon/A(v))$ and $B(v)(x-i\epsilon/B(v))$, where $x=\sinh(\kappa s/2)$. For positive $\alpha,\beta$ the identity $$\frac{1}{(x-i\alpha\epsilon)(x-i\beta\epsilon)} =\int_0^1\frac{dt}{(x-i((1-t)\alpha+t\beta)\epsilon)^2}$$ follows by integrating the derivative of $[x-i((1-t)\alpha+t\beta)\epsilon]^{-1}$ in $t$ and dividing by $i(\beta-\alpha)\epsilon$ when $\alpha\ne\beta$; for $\alpha=\beta$ both sides agree directly. It shows that both dampings have the same boundary. To justify that boundary, for a compact smooth test $\psi$ choose an even compact smooth $\chi$ equal to one near zero and write $\psi(x)=\psi(0)\chi(x)+x\rho(x)$, where $\rho$ is smooth and compactly supported. The constant term satisfies $$\int\frac{\chi(x)}{x-i\lambda\epsilon}\,dx =i\lambda\epsilon\int\frac{\chi(x)}{x^2+(\lambda\epsilon)^2}\,dx\longrightarrow i\pi$$ for each $\lambda>0$, since its odd real part integrates to zero. The other term is $x\rho(x)/(x-i\lambda\epsilon)=\rho(x)+ i\lambda\epsilon\rho(x)/(x-i\lambda\epsilon)$; the last integral is $O(\epsilon|\log\epsilon|)$ uniformly for $\lambda$ in a compact positive interval. Thus $(x-i0)^{-1}=\operatorname{PV}(1/x)+i\pi\delta_0$, where $\operatorname{PV}(1/x)$ acts by $\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\int_{|x|>\delta}\psi(x)/x\,dx$. Differentiating this distributional identity gives $(x-i0)^{-2}=\operatorname{Pf}(1/x^2)-i\pi\delta_0'$, where $\langle\delta_0',\psi\rangle=-\psi'(0)$ and $$\left\langle\operatorname{Pf}(1/x^2),\psi\right\rangle =\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\left(\int_{|x|>\delta}\frac{\psi(x)}{x^2}\,dx-\frac{2\psi(0)}{\delta}\right).$$ Integration by parts on $|x|>\delta$ identifies this finite part with $-(\operatorname{PV}(1/x))'$. The bounds are uniform when the positive damping coefficient ranges in a compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$, as it does for $v$ in a compact set. To identify the pullback with the usual $s-i0$ boundary, note that $\sinh(bs-i\epsilon b)=\sinh(bs)-i\epsilon b\cosh(bs)+O(\epsilon^2)$. More generally, for a positive smooth regulator $\lambda(v,x)$, Taylor expand $\lambda=\lambda_0(v)+\lambda_1(v)x+x^2r(v,x)$. The linear part factors as $$x-i\epsilon(\lambda_0+\lambda_1x) =(1-i\epsilon\lambda_1)\left(x-\frac{i\epsilon\lambda_0}{1-i\epsilon\lambda_1}\right).$$ Its pole has positive imaginary part comparable to $\epsilon$ and real displacement $O(\epsilon^2)$, so the preceding test-subtraction calculation gives the same boundary. The quadratic remainder changes the inverse square by at most $C\epsilon x^2/(x^2+\epsilon^2)^{3/2}$ on a small interval; its integral is $O(\epsilon|\log\epsilon|)$. Thus the smooth positive regulator, including the one induced by $\sinh(b(s-i\epsilon))$, has the same boundary as the constant positive regulator. The change $x=\sinh(\kappa s/2)$ is orientation-preserving with positive derivative. Consequently the test-paired limit of step 3.2 is $$C_a(s)=-\frac{1}{16\pi^2\ell^2}\operatorname{csch}^2\!\left(\frac{\kappa(s-i0)}{2}\right) =-\frac{a^2}{16\pi^2c^4}\operatorname{csch}^2\!\left(\frac{a(s-i0)}{2c}\right).$$ Thus $\langle K_{\gamma_a}f,K_{\gamma_a}g\rangle_2$ equals $\left\langle C_a(s),\int f(t)g(t-s)\,dt\right\rangle$. This proves stationarity and the stated covariance boundary from ordinary regulated shell pairings. To verify temperedness explicitly, set $q=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\coth(\kappa(s-i\epsilon)/2)$ in the distribution sense and $r(s)=\coth(\kappa s/2)-2/(\kappa s)$ for $s\ne0$. The Taylor expansion of $\coth$ at zero extends $r$ smoothly there, and $r'(s)=-(\kappa/2)\operatorname{csch}^2(\kappa s/2)+2/(\kappa s^2)$ is bounded: its apparent singularity cancels at zero, and both terms are bounded at infinity. Since $1/(s-i0)=\operatorname{PV}(1/s)+i\pi\delta_0$, the decomposition is $q=(2/\kappa)\operatorname{PV}(1/s)+r+(2\pi i/\kappa)\delta_0$. Distributional differentiation of $q_\epsilon(s)=\coth(\kappa(s-i\epsilon)/2)$ gives $C_a=(a^2/(8\pi^2c^4\kappa))q'$. For $m,n\ge0$ set $p_{m,n}(\varphi)=\sup_s(1+s^2)^{m/2}|\varphi^{(n)}(s)|$, a Schwartz seminorm. For $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$, the symmetric principal-value formula gives $\left|\left\langle\operatorname{PV}(1/s),\varphi'\right\rangle\right|\le 2p_{0,2}(\varphi)+C p_{2,1}(\varphi),$ because subtracting $\varphi'(0)$ on $|s|<1$ bounds the local integral by $2\sup|\varphi''|$, while the $|s|\ge1$ integral is bounded by $p_{2,1}\int_{|s|\ge1}[|s|(1+s^2)]^{-1}ds$. Also $|\int r'(s)\varphi(s)ds|\le C p_{2,0}(\varphi)$ and $|\langle\delta_0',\varphi\rangle|\le p_{0,1}(\varphi)$. Hence $|\langle C_a,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{a,c}\bigl(p_{0,2}(\varphi)+p_{2,1}(\varphi)+p_{2,0}(\varphi)+p_{0,1}(\varphi)\bigr),$ a finite Schwartz-seminorm bound. By [F2], $C_a\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R)$, as required for its subsequent Fourier transform.

On the inertial curve, direct radial integration gives $$W_{0,\epsilon}(s)= rac{1}{4\pi^2}\int_0^\infty r e^{-(\epsilon+ics)r}\,dr = rac{1}{4\pi^2(\epsilon+ics)^2}.$$ Its boundary is $C_0(s)=-1/(4\pi^2c^2(s-i0)^2)$. Reparameterizing the massless shell by $\omega=cr$ gives $C_0(s)=(4\pi^2c^2)^{-1}\int_0^\infty\omega e^{-i\omega s}d\omega$ as a tempered boundary distribution. Fourier transformation with $e^{-i
u s}$ then yields $S_0(
u)=\max(-
u,0)/(2\pi c^2)$, including continuous value zero at $
u=0$. Specifically, the inverse-Fourier identity from [F11], after $
u=2\pi\xi$, gives $\mathcal F_-(e^{-i\omega s})(
u)=2\pi\delta_0(

Let $\alpha=a/c^2>0$, which has units of inverse length, and use the supplier's length coordinate $u=cs$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the affine Minkowski
space, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, shell pairing
$p\circ x=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x$, and massless one-particle space
of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. Thus $x^0,\mathbf x$ have length units,
$\mathbf k$ has inverse-length units, the omitted shell apex $\mathbf k=0$
has measure zero, and
$$d\nu_0(\mathbf k)=\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3 2|\mathbf k|},\qquad \mathcal H_0=L^2(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\},d\nu_0;\mathbb C).$$
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open proper-time interval, with $\tau$ in
seconds, and let $\gamma=(\gamma^0,\boldsymbol\gamma)\in
C^\infty(I,\mathbb R^4)$ satisfy
$$\eta(\dot\gamma(\tau),\dot\gamma(\tau))=-c^2,\qquad \dot\gamma^0(\tau)>|\dot{\boldsymbol\gamma}(\tau)|$$
for all $\tau\in I$, where $c>0$ is in metres per second. This defines a
future-directed timelike curve parametrized by proper seconds. For
$f\in C_c^\infty(I;\mathbb C)$ define its curve-smearing amplitude by
$$K_\gamma f(\mathbf k)=\int_I f(\tau) e^{i(|\mathbf k|\gamma^0(\tau)-\mathbf k\cdot\boldsymbol\gamma(\tau))}\,d\tau.$$
Then $K_\gamma f\in\mathcal H_0$, and on every fixed compact support set the
map $f\mapsto K_\gamma f$ is continuous in the test-function topology. If
$f$ has units metres per second, then $K_\gamma f$ has units metres and its
$\mathcal H_0$ norm is dimensionless. For real $f$, define the actual
finite-particle-domain field
$$\Phi_\gamma(f)=a(K_\gamma f)+a^\dagger(K_\gamma f)$$
using the bosonic Fock space and creation/annihilation conventions of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. It is symmetric on the finite-particle
domain and has the self-adjoint Segal closure supplied by
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]. Its vacuum covariance on real compact tests is
the well-defined pairing $\langle K_\gamma f,K_\gamma g\rangle_2$. This
construction is an additional temporal smearing of the massless shell; it
does not define a point field or an interaction.

For $a>0$ in metres per second squared, put $\ell=c^2/a$ and define the
uniformly accelerated curve on $I=\mathbb R$ by
$$\gamma_a(\tau)=\bigl(\ell\sinh(a\tau/c),\ell\cosh(a\tau/c),0,0\bigr).$$
It has proper acceleration magnitude $a$. The restriction of the massless
Minkowski-vacuum covariance constructed above is stationary and, in the
distributional boundary-value sense on the real line, is
$$C_a(s)=-\frac{a^2}{16\pi^2c^4}\,\operatorname{csch}^2\!\left(\frac{a(s-i0)}{2c}\right).$$
Here $\operatorname{csch}z=1/\sinh z$, and the displayed expression means
the limit of the smooth damped shell pairings against compact smooth tests;
no product or pullback of point-field distributions is assumed. With the
angular-frequency convention
$$S_a(\nu)=\mathcal F_{-}C_a(\nu),\qquad \mathcal F_{-}C(\nu)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\nu s}C(s)\,ds$$
interpreted distributionally, the local conclusion about the spectrum is conditional on the current
batch-74 draft suppliers [[lem-tgr-thermal-contour-spectrum]] and its
prerequisite [[lem-tgr-exponential-current]]. Their carriers exist in the
batch-74 manifest, and both items have status `draft`. The current run's
Step-1 records report `ready` for both items; this is authoring-readiness
evidence, not proof acceptance. The contour item's actual statement uses a length
coordinate and an inverse-length parameter (renamed from its $\kappa$ to
$\alpha$ here); the proof below uses
$\alpha=a/c^2$ and $u=cs$, for which the covariance obeys
$C_a(s)=\pi^{-1}C_\alpha(cs)$. Under the contour item's exact conditional
Fourier formula and this rescaling,
$$S_a(\nu)=\frac{\nu}{2\pi c^2\bigl(e^{2\pi c\nu/a}-1\bigr)},\qquad S_a(0)=\frac{a}{4\pi^2c^3},\qquad S_a(-\nu)=e^{2\pi c\nu/a}S_a(\nu)\quad(\nu>0).$$
The continuous value at zero is the removable limit. $\nu$ has units
seconds$^{-1}$ and $S_a$ has units seconds per square metre; the spectral
claim remains conditional until both draft suppliers are accepted.

For comparison, on the inertial curve $\gamma_0(\tau)=(c\tau,0,0,0)$ the
same construction gives
$$C_0(s)=-\frac{1}{4\pi^2c^2(s-i0)^2},\qquad S_0(\nu)=\frac{\max(-\nu,0)}{2\pi c^2}.$$
These are mathematical covariance and Fourier-transform statements in the
specified representation. They do not assert a measured spectrum or a
detector transition probability.

In particular, for $\kappa>0$ in inverse length, take $A=\kappa^2/(16\pi)$ and $b=\kappa/2$. Then $L=1/(4\pi)$, $\beta=2\pi/\kappa$, and $C_{A,b}$ is precisely the tested chiral covariance $C_\kappa$ of [[lem-tgr-exponential-current]]. Its spectrum and detailed balance are
$$S_\kappa(\omega)=\frac{\omega}{2(e^{2\pi\omega/\kappa}-1)},\qquad S_\kappa(0)=\frac{\kappa}{4\pi},\qquad S_\kappa(-\omega)=e^{2\pi\omega/\kappa}S_\kappa(\omega)\quad(\omega>0).$$
Here $C_\kappa$ has units of inverse length squared and $S_\kappa$ inverse length. This is a two-point strip and detailed-balance statement, including the specified chiral current as a specialization. It does not assert a norm-continuous $C^*$-algebra KMS dynamics or an exact detector transition probability.

Assume Countable Choice. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2((0,\infty),dk;\mathbb C),\qquad
\langle h,q\rangle_2=\int_0^\infty\overline{h(k)}q(k)\,dk,$$
using the second-variable-linear convention. For
$f\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ define
$$h_f(k)=\sqrt{\frac{k}{4\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}f(U)e^{ikU}\,dU\quad(k>0).$$
Then $h_f,h_{\bar f}\in\mathcal H$, and $f\mapsto h_f$ is continuous on each fixed-compact-support test space. With the bosonic Fock conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], define on its finite-particle domain
$$J(f)=a(h_{\bar f})+a^\dagger(h_f).$$
This is a complex-linear operator-valued distribution on that invariant domain. For real $f$, its closure is $\overline{J(f)}=\sqrt2\,\Phi(h_f)$, where $\Phi(h_f)$ is the closed Segal field of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]; the corresponding Weyl one-parameter group has generator $i\Phi(h_f)$. The vacuum two-point form is positive type and has boundary kernel
$$C(s)=-\frac{1}{4\pi(s-i0)^2},$$
where $s-i0$ means the distributional limit from $s-i\epsilon$, $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

For $\kappa>0$ with units of inverse length, let $u,U$ have units of length and set
$$U_\kappa(u)=-\kappa^{-1}e^{-\kappa u},\qquad
u_\kappa(U)=-\kappa^{-1}\log(-\kappa U)\quad(U<0).$$
For $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ put $f_g(U)=g(u_\kappa(U))$ for $U<0$ and $f_g(U)=0$ for $U\ge0$, and define $j_\kappa(g)=J(f_g)$. The zero extension is smooth and compactly supported. Its vacuum covariance is the positive-type distribution
$$C_\kappa(s)=-\frac{\kappa^2}{16\pi}\,\operatorname{csch}^2\!\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}(s-i0)\right).$$
Here the notation is fixed as follows: for $b=\kappa/2$, set $Y_b(s)=\sinh(bs)/b$. Since $Y_b'(s)=\cosh(bs)>0$ and $Y_b(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$, it is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism. Define $\operatorname{csch}^2(b(s-i0)):=b^{-2}Y_b^*((y-i0)^{-2})$, where
$$\langle Y_b^*T,\varphi\rangle:=\left\langle T,\varphi(Y_b^{-1}(y))(Y_b^{-1})'(y)\right\rangle.$$
This is a one-dimensional chiral test-coordinate model. It asserts no restriction of a four-dimensional field to a null curve.

Fix an integer $n\geq1$.  A **tempered distribution** on $\mathbb R^n$ is a
continuous complex-linear functional

$$u:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow\mathbb C,$$

where Schwartz space and its locally convex topology are those of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]].  The space of all such functionals
is denoted $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

We write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$.  This pairing is bilinear:
the test variable is not conjugated.  Thus $u(a\varphi+b\psi)=
a\langle u,\varphi\rangle+b\langle u,\psi\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$.
The zero functional is tempered.  Continuity is topological continuity, and,
because the Schwartz topology is generated by a countable cofinal family of
seminorms, it is equivalently continuity on every convergent sequence.  No
choice principle is used in this definition.

Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]], exactly as required by the
published Schwartz Fourier theorem.  For $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$
put

$$\widehat\varphi(\xi)=\mathcal F\varphi(\xi) =\int_{\mathbb R^n}\varphi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$

For $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ define its **Fourier transform** by

$$\langle\mathcal Fu,\varphi\rangle =\langle u,\mathcal F\varphi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)).$$

The published automorphism
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]
sends Schwartz tests continuously to Schwartz tests, so composition with the
continuous functional of [[def-tempered-distribution]] is again a continuous
complex-linear functional.  Hence $\mathcal Fu\in\mathcal S'$.  The pairing
is bilinear: there is no conjugation and no inverse transform on the
right-hand side.  Countable Choice is used only through the cited published
Fourier construction; transposition itself uses no additional choice.

Assume Countable Choice.  The Fourier transform
$\mathcal F:\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ is
well-defined and complex-linear.  It is continuous for both the weak topology
$\sigma(\mathcal S',\mathcal S)$ and the strong topology
$\beta(\mathcal S',\mathcal S)$.

Assume Countable Choice.  Fourier transformation is a topological
automorphism of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ for both the weak and strong dual
topologies.  If

$$\langle Ru,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi(-\,\cdot)\rangle,$$

then $\mathcal F^2u=Ru$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F=\mathcal FR$.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the massless accelerated
covariance $C_a$ and its conditional spectrum $S_a$ from
[[lem-tgr-timelike-scalar-acceleration]], with $a>0$ in metres per second
squared, $c>0$ in metres per second, and angular frequency in seconds$^{-1}$.
The conditional detailed-balance input is the actual Statement of the
current batch-74 draft [[lem-tgr-thermal-contour-spectrum]], reproduced in
[L1] below. Its declared prerequisite [[lem-tgr-exponential-current]] is also
a draft. The current run's Step-1 records report `ready` for both items;
these are authoring-readiness records, not proof acceptance. The inertial
pair $(C_0,S_0)$ is the unconditioned comparison from
[[lem-tgr-timelike-scalar-acceleration]]. Both spectra are continuous and
globally Lipschitz. The conventions are $S=\mathcal F_-C$ with kernel
$e^{-i\nu s}$ and $C$ paired bilinearly with Schwartz tests.

Let $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$ be nonzero, let the switching
duration $\mathsf T>0$ be measured in seconds, and put
$$\widehat h(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}h(u)e^{-izu}\,du,\qquad K_h=\frac{1}{2\pi\|h\|_2^2}\int_{\mathbb R}|z|\,|\widehat h(z)|^2\,dz.$$
For either stationary pair $(C,S)=(C_a,S_a)$ or $(C_0,S_0)$ define the
switched coefficient
$$R_{\mathsf T}^{(C)}(\nu)=\left\langle C(s),e^{-i\nu s} \int_{\mathbb R}h(t/\mathsf T)h((t-s)/\mathsf T)\,dt\right\rangle.$$
Then $K_h<\infty$ and, for every $\nu\in\mathbb R$,
$$R_{\mathsf T}^{(C)}(\nu)=\frac{\mathsf T^2}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb R}S(\omega)|\widehat h(\mathsf T(\nu-\omega))|^2\,d\omega,$$
so $R_{\mathsf T}^{(C)}(\nu)\ge0$, and
$$\left|\frac{R_{\mathsf T}^{(C)}(\nu)}{\mathsf T\|h\|_2^2}-S(\nu)\right| \le\frac{\operatorname{Lip}(S)K_h}{\mathsf T},\qquad \operatorname{Lip}(S)=\sup_{x\ne y}\frac{|S(x)-S(y)|}{|x-y|}<\infty.$$
This proves the leading switched coefficient limit and its explicit error;
it is not a convergence theorem for an all-order detector transition
probability or an exact infinite-time probability.

There is also the following separately defined two-state continuous-time
Markov model. Choose an energy $E>0$ in joules, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds,
$k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin, and a coupling $\gamma_d>0$ in square metres
per square second. For the accelerated spectrum set
$$r_+=\gamma_d S_a(E/\hbar),\qquad r_-=\gamma_d S_a(-E/\hbar).$$
These are positive rates in seconds$^{-1}$. Let $p(t)$ be the probability
of the excited state in the two-state chain with ground-to-excited rate
$r_+$ and excited-to-ground rate $r_-$. For $t\ge0$ and any initial probability $p(0)\in[0,1]$, then
$$p(t)=p_*+(p(0)-p_*)e^{-(r_++r_-)t},\qquad p_* =\frac{1}{1+e^{2\pi cE/(a\hbar)}}.$$
If the effective thermometer temperature $T_{\rm eff}>0$ is defined by
$p_*/(1-p_*)=e^{-E/(k_BT_{\rm eff})}$, then
$$T_{\rm eff}=\frac{\hbar a}{2\pi c k_B}.$$
This is an exact result for the specified Markov chain. It is not a weak
coupling or point-detector thermalization theorem.

For $C_0$, [F1] gives the same bound with $S_0$. Since $\nu>0$, $S_0(\nu)=0$. On this shell $j\le |n|\le\sqrt3j$, so $q_n\le e^{-\beta a j}$ and $\epsilon_n^p q_n\le (a\sqrt3)^p j^p e^{-\beta a j}$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

derivations.claim: On $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$ define the continuous periodic representative $F(y)=(2\pi y)^2$. Its normalized Fourier coefficients are $c_n=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2e^{-inx}\,dx$ after the change $x=2\pi y$. Direct integration gives $c_0=\pi^2/3$; for $n\ne0$, two integrations by parts give $c_n=2(-1)^n/n^2$ because the first boundary term cancels at $x=\pm\pi$ and $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-inx}\,dx=0$.

The normalized squared norm is $(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^4\,dx=\pi^4/5$. Under the stated Countable Choice assumption [F1], Parseval [F2] therefore gives $\pi^4/5=|c_0|^2+\sum_{n\ne0}|c_n|^2=\pi^4/9+8\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-4}$, whence $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-4}=\pi^4/90$.

For $m\ge1$ and $p=0,1,2,3$, put $J_p(m)=\int_0^\infty x^pe^{-mx}\,dx$. Direct integration gives $J_0(m)=1/m$; integration by parts on $[0,R]$ and then $R\to\infty$ gives $J_p(m)=pJ_{p-1}(m)/m$, since $R^pe^{-mR}\to0$ (for example, $e^{mR}\ge(mR)^{p+1}/(p+1)!$). Hence $J_3(m)=6/m^4$ and $J_2(m)=2/m^3$. The finite geometric identity and its limit give $(e^x-1)^{-1}=\sum_{m\ge1}e^{-mx}$ for $x>0$. The partial sums $x^3\sum_{m\le N}e^{-mx}$ are nonnegative measurable and increase pointwise; the monotone-convergence theorem [F3] for the integral defined in [F4] gives the first integral as $\sum_{m\ge1}J_3(m)=6\sum_{m\ge1}m^{-4}=\pi^4/15$.

For $0<z<1$, the geometric series is uniformly convergent on $[0,z]$, so integrating its partial sums gives $-\log(1-z)=\sum_{m\ge1}z^m/m$. At $z=e^{-x}$ the nonnegative partial sums $x^2\sum_{m\le N}e^{-mx}/m$ increase pointwise to the second integrand. Applying [F3] to the integral defined in [F4] and using step 3.1 gives its integral as $\sum_{m\ge1}J_2(m)/m=2\sum_{m\ge1}m^{-4}=\pi^4/45$. The integral ratio is therefore $1/3$.

Let $L,\beta,\hbar,c>0$ be real parameters, set $a=2\pi\hbar c/L$, and for
$n\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$ define
$$\epsilon_n=a|n|,\qquad q_n=e^{-\beta\epsilon_n},$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. For $j\ge1$, the integer max-norm shell
$$\{n\in\mathbb Z^3:|n|_\infty=j\}$$
has $24j^2+2$ points. Consequently
$$\sup_{n\ne0}q_n=e^{-\beta a}<1,\qquad \sum_{n\ne0}q_n<\infty,\qquad \sum_{n\ne0}\epsilon_n^p q_n<\infty$$
for every integer $p\ge0$. In particular, the positive mode-energy sum
$$\sum_{n\ne0}\frac{\epsilon_n}{e^{\beta\epsilon_n}-1}$$
is finite. Repeating each mode twice for two polarization labels preserves all
these conclusions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For a continuous compactly supported $h:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, the cubes $Q_{n,d}=dn+[-d/2,d/2]^3$ tile $\mathbb R^3$ up to boundaries of volume zero. Uniform continuity of $h$ bounds $|d^3\sum_nh(dn)-\int h|$ by the volume of one fixed enlarged support box times the modulus of continuity at $\sqrt3d/2$, which tends to zero. Taking $h(x)=\psi(|x|)$ proves the compactly supported radial lattice limit. To rewrite its integral when $\psi$ is signed, apply [F2] separately to the nonnegative radial functions $h_+(x)=\max(h(x),0)$ and $h_-(x)=\max(-h(x),0)$; both are continuous and compactly supported, so their integrals are finite. Subtracting the resulting identities and using $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ from [F3] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}h(x)\,d^3x=4\pi\int_0^\infty r^2\psi(r)\,dr$. Omitting $n=0$ changes the sum by $d^3\psi(0)\to0$.

For $0<r\le1$, $f(r)\le1$ and $1-e^{-r}\ge r/2$, so $0\le g(r)\le C(1+|\log r|)$. Formulae [F2] and [F3] give the small-ball integral bound because, for $0<\delta\le1$, $\int_0^\delta r^2(1+|\log r|)\,dr=\delta^3(4/9+|\log\delta|/3)$. For the discrete sum with $0<d|n|\le\delta$, put $j=|n|_\infty$; then $dj\le\delta$ and $d|n|\ge dj$. Group the shells by $dj\in(\delta2^{-\ell-1},\delta2^{-\ell}]$. If such a group is nonempty, then $d\le\delta2^{-\ell}$ and its shell indices obey $j\le J_\ell:=\lfloor\delta2^{-\ell}/d\rfloor$. By [F1], the number of lattice points in shells up to $J_\ell$ is $\sum_{j\le J_\ell}(24j^2+2)\le C J_\ell^3\le C(\delta2^{-\ell}/d)^3$. Every point in the selected small-ball subset of this group has $d|n|\ge dj>\delta2^{-\ell-1}$ and $d|n|\le\delta\le1$, so its entropy value is at most $C(1+|\log\delta|+\ell)$. Multiplication by the cell volume $d^3$ bounds this group's contribution by $C\delta^3 2^{-3\ell}(1+|\log\delta|+\ell)$. Summing the convergent geometric series over $\ell\ge0$ gives $C'\delta^3(1+|\log\delta|)$ uniformly in $d$.

The function $f$ is continuous at zero since $\lim_{r\downarrow0}r/(e^r-1)=1$, and for $r\ge1$ it is bounded by $C(1+r)e^{-r}$. For $0<d\le1$ and $x\in Q_{n,d}$, $||dn|-|x||\le\sqrt3/2$. Thus, for $R\ge2$, each cube with $|dn|>R$ lies in $|x|>R-\sqrt3/2>1$, and the exponential bound yields $\sum_{|dn|>R}d^3f(d|n|)\le C'\int_{|x|>R-\sqrt3/2}(1+|x|)e^{-|x|}\,d^3x$. The integral tail tends to zero as $R\to\infty$, uniformly in $0<d\le1$. Apply step 1.1 on compact cutoffs and then this uniform tail bound to obtain the asserted $f$ limit and integrability.

For each fixed $d>0$, only finitely many lattice points have $d|n|<1$, and there are only finitely many shells with $dj<1$. On every remaining shell, $dj\ge1$, the Euclidean norm satisfies $j\le|n|\le\sqrt3j$, and the exponential bound gives $f(d|n|),g(d|n|)\le C(1+dj)e^{-dj}$. The shell count [F1] therefore bounds the shell contribution by $Cj^2(1+dj)e^{-dj}\le Cj^3(1+dj)e^{-dj}$. The comparison series converges by the ratio test, since the ratio of consecutive terms tends to $e^{-d}<1$. For $r\ge1$, $-\log(1-e^{-r})\le e^{-r}/(1-e^{-r})$, so $g(r)\le C(1+r)e^{-r}$; the cube estimate of step 2.1 then gives uniformly vanishing large-radius tails for the integral and the lattice sum. On each annulus $\delta\le|x|\le R$, $g(|x|)$ is continuous and the compact Riemann-sum argument of step 1.1 applies with a continuous radial cutoff equal to one on that annulus and zero near the origin and outside a larger ball. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ and $R\to\infty$ using the small-ball bound of step 1.2 and these tail bounds proves the $g$ limit and its finiteness.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
Here $q_*=0$ by convention when $I$ is empty; for nonempty $I$ the displayed supremum is unchanged. In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, if for every compact $B\subset J\subset(0,\infty)$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

derivations.claim: For $i=(n,s)$ with $n\ne0$, $|n|\ge1$, so $\epsilon_i\ge2\pi\hbar c/L>0$. Thus $q_i\le e^{-2\pi\beta\hbar c/L}<1$, and [F3] gives $\sum_{i\in I}q_i<\infty$ with the required strict supremum bound.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as defined in [[def-countable-choice]]. Fix $L,T,\hbar,c,k_B>0$ with SI units respectively metre, kelvin, joule-second, metre per second, and joule per kelvin. Let $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in inverse joules. The mathematical periodic-box mode set is $I=(\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\})\times\{1,2\}$, with two polarization labels and the enumeration by increasing max-norm shells and then lexicographic order; within each shell use lexicographic order on $(n,s)$. For $i=(n,s)$ set $\epsilon_i=\hbar c(2\pi/L)|n|$ in joules and $\omega_n=2\pi c|n|/L$ in inverse seconds. The zero wavevector is excluded and no zero-point energy is included.

Let $\Omega_B$ be the finite-support maps $m:I\to\mathbb N_0$, set $E(m)=\sum_{i\in I}\epsilon_i m_i$, and let $\mathcal H_B=\ell^2(\Omega_B,\mathbb C)$ with its occupation basis. Define the nonnegative diagonal multiplier $H$ by $(Ha)_m=E(m)a_m$ on $D(H)=\{a\in\ell^2(\Omega_B,\mathbb C):\sum_m E(m)^2|a_m|^2<\infty\}$, so $H|m\rangle=E(m)|m\rangle$. For each $\gamma>0$ in inverse joules define the bounded positive diagonal multiplier $e^{-\gamma H}$ by $e^{-\gamma H}|m\rangle=e^{-\gamma E(m)}|m\rangle$, and set $Z_L(\gamma)=\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}e^{-\gamma E(m)}$; the proof shows this sum is finite and equals the operator trace $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\gamma H})$. Set $q_n=e^{-\beta\epsilon_{(n,1)}}$, $Z_L=Z_L(\beta)$, $\rho_L=Z_L^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$, and $p_m=e^{-\beta E(m)}/Z_L$. Define the diagonal-state entropy by $S_L=-k_B\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}p_m\log p_m$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

The finite-box trace, energy and entropy are actual diagonal sums, not continuum mode integrals. The partition function $Z_L$ and occupations $q_n$ are dimensionless, $\rho_L$ has trace one, energy and $U_L$ have units joules, and $S_L$ has units joules per kelvin. The sums satisfy $Z_L=\prod_{n\ne0}(1-q_n)^{-2}<\infty$, $\rho_L$ is a positive trace-one trace-class operator, and every nonnegative integer energy moment under $\rho_L$ is finite. Moreover,
$$U_L=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_LH)=2\sum_{n\ne0}\frac{\epsilon_{(n,1)}}{e^{\beta\epsilon_{(n,1)}}-1}<\infty.$$
The entropy is
$$S_L=k_B(\log Z_L+\beta U_L)=2k_B\sum_{n\ne0}\left[-\log(1-q_n)+\frac{\beta\epsilon_{(n,1)}q_n}{1-q_n}\right]<\infty.$$

With $u_L=U_L/L^3$ and $s_L=S_L/L^3$ in joules per cubic metre and joules per kelvin per cubic metre, respectively, their thermodynamic-volume limits at fixed $T$ exist. For every continuous compactly supported $\psi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$, the limiting spectral energy measure is
$$\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{2}{L^3}\sum_{n\ne0}\frac{\hbar\omega_n}{e^{\beta\hbar\omega_n}-1}\psi(\omega_n)=\frac{\hbar}{\pi^2c^3}\int_0^\infty\frac{\omega^3\psi(\omega)}{e^{\beta\hbar\omega}-1}\,d\omega.$$
The integrated limits are
$$u=\lim_{L\to\infty}u_L=\frac{\pi^2k_B^4T^4}{15\hbar^3c^3},\qquad s=\lim_{L\to\infty}s_L=\frac{4u}{3T}.$$

In a separately specified isotropic freely streaming ray model, directions have uniform angular density $u/(4\pi)$ for energy and $s/(4\pi)$ for this coarse mode entropy on the unit sphere; each ray has velocity $c\hat n$. Define one-sided flux through a plane by integrating the outward normal velocity component over the outward hemisphere. Then $F=cu/4=\sigma T^4$ and $F_S=cs/4=(4/3)F/T$, where $F$ is in watts per square metre, $F_S$ in joules per kelvin per square metre per second, and $\sigma=\pi^2k_B^4/(60\hbar^3c^2)$ in watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth power. This is a mathematical model deduction; it does not assert an observed blackbody, an equilibration mechanism, or a horizon-emission law.

derivations.claim: Substitution of $r_H=2GM/c^2$ gives $A_H=16\pi G^2M^2/c^4$, $\kappa=c^2/(4GM)$, $T_\infty=\hbar c^3/(8\pi GMk_B)$, and $S_B(M)=4\pi k_BG M^2/(\hbar c)+S_0$. Differentiating the last expression yields $T_\infty\,dS_B/dM=c^2$.

By [F1] the effective-area power is $P=\eta A_H\sigma T_\infty^4=\eta\hbar c^6/(15360\pi G^2M^2)$. The adopted balance equation [A1] is therefore $M'=-\alpha M^{-2}$ with $\alpha=\eta\hbar c^4/(15360\pi G^2)>0$.

Along any positive solution, $(M^3)'=3M^2M'=-3\alpha$, hence the initial condition forces $M(t)^3=M_0^3-3\alpha t$. The positive cube root is differentiable and satisfies the ODE until it reaches the positive cutoff, giving the stated solution and time $\tau=(M_0^3-M_{\min}^3)/(3\alpha)$. This also proves uniqueness among positive solutions because every such solution has the same cube.
Integrating $P=-c^2M'$ from $0$ to $\tau$ gives $\int_0^\tau P\,dt=c^2(M_0-M_{\min})$. Differentiating $S_B(M(t))$ and using step 1.1 and $M'=-P/c^2$ yields $S_B'=-P/T_\infty$.

The entropy flux in [F1], multiplied by the stated area $A_{\rm eff}$, is $S_{\rm rad}'=(4/3)P/T_\infty$. Thus $(S_B+S_{\rm rad})'=P/(3T_\infty)\ge0$ and integration gives the two endpoint entropy formulas. Since $S_B(M)=4\pi k_BG M^2/(\hbar c)+S_0$ has positive quadratic coefficient and $M_0>M_{\min}>0$, its difference is positive and the offset cancels. No physical generalized-second-law conclusion follows beyond this stipulated model.
